THIS REVIEW WILL BE UPDATED AS I USE THE CARD MORE.  I purchased this device to use with a Nikon D300s in both ad-hoc and infrastructure environments. I am an advanced photographer and computer user, with significant experience in setting up wireless networks of various complexities.  I considered using the Nikon WT-4a wireless transmitter.  However, the $800.00 price tag turned me off as I am only a semi-pro.  That price seems cheap in comparison to a photo shoot experience I had last night using the Eye-Fi card.Initial PerceptionThe card arrived in decent packaging. Card installation process, only mildly confusing, was not bad and took about 15 minutes.  No instructions are provided with the device.  So do not look for any. However, only true novices will require written instructions up front as the software does a good job of guiding you in the process.  A card reader is supplied with the Eye-Fi card.  However, the design of the reader prevents the user from installing it easily in many USB ports, especially those surrounded by ports already in use (you need a lot of clearance). Following installation, the device worked in repeated tests within my existing wireless network at home.  Transferring basic jpeg files from the point of capture to the designated computer took about 3-5 seconds (on average), provided I was within good range (expected).  The card of course is also a class 6 SDHC card for local storage.  You can set Adobe Lightroom to "watch" certain folders in which the photos are transferred or you can simply use the provided software interface with the provided Internet account.  With a high speed connection, photos were showing up in my Eye-Fi account (jpeg basic) within minutes.  Raw files are handled adequately in the environment described. Write speed to the card seemed a little slow however (just my perception).  I also noted the card did not seem to "fit well" in my SD card slot in the D300s.  I am comparing the physical fit to that of a SanDisk Extreme SDHC card.  A close visual inspection did not show any physical differences however.First Real UseTwo days after receiving this card, I had a photo shoot.  Though I did not intend to wirelessly transmit at the shoot, I left the card in anyway. I set my D300s to write raw to the CF (primary card) and basic jpeg to the SDHC card (for proof purposes).  The D300s has a menu interface with the Eye-Fi card to enable or disable the card transmitter.  However, I did not set the camera to disable the card as most people report minimal battery usage with the eye-fi card inserted.  Well into the shoot, I notice my camera write speeds dropping drastically.  The Nikon D300s is a fast camera on all counts.  The only way I can describe what was happening is by describing the camera as operating very sluggishly.  In fact, I was concerned my camera woould cease functioning altogether at some point and almost panicked.  I then received an error message indicating the Eye-Fi card was corrupt.  I tried reformatting the card in camera but the camera reported the card was corrupt and locked up my shooting ability.  I then took notice of the rapid depletion of the batteries (I use two EN-EL3e's in the Nikon MB-D10 grip).  I ejected the SDHC card and reset the camera.  Camera functions immediately returned to normal.  I then re-inserted the eye-fi card and set the D300s to disable the card as a radio tramsitter.  The camera became sluggish again, with horrible write speeds to even the CF card.  I completed the rest of the shoot without the card.Ad-Hoc Attempts10 minutes into attempting to setup an ad-hoc connection (Windows 7 laptop computer with 802.11 b/g/n), I decided I would need more time than I had to try and set this up.  Keep in mind that to change any network settings (add, remove, adjust, etc..) YOU MUST connect the card to a computer with the Eye-Fi card/software interface.  You cannot simply use any laptop or existing network unless that network is first added to the card via the provided interface and a card reader (supplied).General CommentsI am going to perform more tests on this card in a controlled environment to reassess performance and reliability.  It is possible I was doing something wrong or I simply received a bad card (Internet reports indicate this is a possibility).  HOWEVER, at this time I cannot recommend this card for anything other than non-mission critical point and shoot use.Since I have about 27 days to return this card, I will update this review following some trouble shooting and more sustained use in different environments.  But, I must caution prosumers, semi-pro and even pro users (some pros are using this as an alternative to the Nikon transmitters)to NOT deploy this card in mission critical environments.  Typical POS end users may find the card usable (acceptable).  Either way, it appears anyone at the semi-pro level or greater will need to spend the $800 on a the Nikon transmitter (or equivalent) to obtain reliability.

BOTTOM LINE: Anyone who can adapt to new technology quickly and has a need for cursor control away from a desk will love this mouse.LENGTH OF USE: About 2 months.TECH LEVEL: Professional programmer and designer, consultant, trainerI always investigate my purchases extensively and I was a bit concerned about the re-centering problems after reading some negative reviews. A couple reviews hinted that the problem was a misunderstanding on the part of other reviewers, so I decided to give this mouse a shot.I'm glad I did! This mouse works flawlessly. While the movement is very smooth, it will likely take a bit of practice before you develop the muscle control to make the fine movements required to click what you want every time. It took me a couple of days.The re-centering problem other users have reported is entirely a result of their misunderstanding. The device is not supposed to be tethered to the direction of the screen, in fact, that's the greatest thing about this mouse. I can point the mouse at the floor, to the side, or behind me and it works just as well. As with a normal mouse, when the cursor is dragged off the screen, the cursor stays at the edge no matter how far the mouse actually tells it to go. This means that reorienting the mouse is instantaneous. Just as fast and easy as doing so with a regular mouse.I even tried gaming with the air mouse and, while I didn't have the coordination to do well on a first person shooter, with time, I might prefer this method of control even for gaming.Right now I use the air mouse for media control and presentations. My presentations include videos, websites, PowerPoints, and other applications like mind mapping software. This mouse performs flawlessly as a presentation remote that gives you the freedom to actually use a mouse anywhere in the room whenever needed. I've used this mouse to teach Photoshop classes on the screen while working with students in the back.Freezing the mouse is easy - just press the back button for a couple of seconds and the cursor freezes. The other controls allow you to step back and forth through slides, play and pause media, and change the volume, even while the cursor is frozen.BOTTOM LINE: Anyone who can adapt to new technology quickly and has a need for cursor control away from a desk will love this mouse.

I'm rating this a harsh 1 star because I'm forced to obsolete the router due to a glaring technical limitation.  Should new firmware be released, fixing the problem, I'll give it a 5-star.  Until then, I have nothing but buyer's remorse.I would consider this router - and certainly it's price bracket - to be upper-end/high-end.  And, in terms of speed and reliability, it hasn't let me down.  However, one glaring oversight is the relatively few number of port forwards and DHCP assigned static addresses.  In both cases, the router cannot handle more than 32 IPs.That means if you want to forward more than 32 distinct ports from the web to your LAN devices, you're screwed.  Even my 10 year old WRT54G was unlimited.  32 may seem like a lot, but as homes become more and more wired, each device takes up a slot.  TIVO?  VoIP service?  Security cameras? XBox?  Media servers?  And on and on.My home network has over 32 devices.  Mostly IP security cameras.  Yet, I'm now forced to abandon this otherwise brilliant piece of equipment (and forfeit the dollars paid to buy it) because of this limitation.  What sucks is, this is not the kind of information that is in their manual or literature.  So until you try, you won't know the problem exists.As for the DHCP, if you have a mobile Wifi device (think tablet) and want to use it at home and work - but need it to have the same IP address at home (i.e. remote access), you can set this router up to assign the same IP address to the device every time.  The feature works just as it should.  However, once again, if you need to apply this to more than 32 devices, you're screwed.  Fortunately, the work around is to hard-code each device's IP address.  That works good for devices that never leave your network, but if they do, you have to reconfigure the IP address from static to dynamic (and then back to static when you come home).  Hardly practical for such an expensive device.At this point, probably less than 10% of home users will run into either of these limitations.  But, as time goes by, and everything from your fridge to your TV gets its own IP address, this router will be forcefully obsoleted.Would I have bought had I known, ABSOLUTELY NOT.  If they can fix this, I'd say it's the best router I've ever owned.  Until then, buyer beware.

I found this cable while searching for a video output solution for my Galaxy Note II. Brand name cables are in the realm of $30 to $40.00, so the price and overall rating of this cable was attractive.This cable will transmit a video signal to any HD TV or monitor with an HDMI input via the phone's micro USB port. It is essential to plug the male USB connector on the cable to a charging source rated at least 5v/1A. Most, if not all TVs and monitors with USB ports will not be able to source enough power to charge the phone for allowing use of the HDMI connection, so a standard USB wall charger will suffice as long as it provides enough power.It was packaged appropriately, neatly coiled up in a plastic bag within a padded envelope. The cable itself seems to be of around average quality, and is on the flexible [more "rubbery" than "plasticky"] side... which may or may not be a good thing. The actual micro USB, Male USB and HDMI connectors feel a little cheap, but it isn't especially glaring.I unplugged my Blu-Ray player which functions on the HDMI port I used to test this cable. This cable's HDMI connection felt a little less than confident. I did at first attempt to plug the USB power connection into my Samsung HDTV's nearby USB port [right next to the HDMI input], but it did not source enough power to charge the phone while it was connected and therefore the TV did not recognize my Note II.The USB power cord of the cable isn't very long, which lead me to believe it was designed to plug into the monitor's USB port as a power source, but does in fact need the juice from a wall charger. I eagerly dug up a surge protector and rigged an extension with a quality USB wall charger. The phone was not recognized via HDMI even after several reboots of both it and the Samsung TV [in different orders, as suggested by some users] and accessing/refreshing the TV's sources.I tried again with a standalone LG monitor. It was at a different location and I packed the cable to bring with me and try it out, thinking my own TV could be the problem. I plugged everything in, again needing to figure out how I was going to plug the USB power cord into a wall outlet, and... nothing. Upon wiggling the connectors and cables a little bit, a picture finally came up and my phone recognized the monitor.I spent a few minutes flipping through applications and generally embellishing the big screen experience, but the display would intermittently turn black, sometimes showing static momentarily between the connections/disconnections.I believe the problem lies in where the cables and connectors are fused. Things are a little thin overall and I wouldn't be surprised if just a few light tugs/pulls from normal use and rolling up for storage could result in a poor connection. HDMI cables in general need to be pretty thick and generally provide a robust connection; USB cables are more prone to damage even from coiling up or tugging associated with typical use.I am unsure if I will be trying another one of these as an alternative to a brand name cable. Even if the next one of these worked perfectly right out of the box, I doubt it would last with regular use and storage. I believe many negative reviews for cables like these are the result of user error [getting the wrong cable for a device, not setting up correctly, overall lack of troubleshooting, etc.] and don't reflect the actual experience with the product. Therefore, I am more inclined to purchase a cable by Samsung or other in hopes it is slightly higher quality.

These days I see so many people with a gaggle of USB hard drives for media storage, backups, and simply data hoarding.  A solution like this is far more practical and potentially a bit better in terms of retention (RAID is not really a backup, but a backup that is RAID is better).  I own aSynology DiskStation 8-Bay (Diskless) Network Attached Storage - Black (DS1812+), which is uber high end compared to this and aWD My Book Live Duo 4TB Personal Cloud Storage NAS Share Files and Photoswhich is similar in scope, but complete with drives.  I must say that the BYO disk approach is great in the larger setups, as the flexibility it offers combined with the cost savings (that multiply as you add drives) makes it hard to match by OEMs.  With a two drive setup, honestly I prefer the OEM approach.  They beat what we have here in terms of simplicity, polish, and often cost.  You still get a bit more flexibility and features here, but it's a bit muted, as there's only so much you can do with a two drive setup.My experience here is somewhat as expected.  I needed to download and install software on my computer, which then updates the device, which then needed drives (the mediocre build quality of the unit came out then), and then wait forever. If I had to write this review when I first received this unit, I'd have given it 0 stars. But with the passage of time, I'm inclined to be a bit more generous.Update 04/21: I changed my router recently to a Belkin N600. Even though all my other wireless/wired devices reconnected without any problems, the iConnect refuses to acknowledge my router, even though it is hard wired to it. I haven't had the time to re-run the steps below - but it definitely is trying my patience to have a device that behaves like a 2-year old throwing a tantrum. Clipping 1-star as a result.The pros:#######1. Supports up to 4 USB devices (hard drives or printers).2. Supports secured access to attached storage3. Works as a Torrent client (see note below about a possible con here).4. Awesome technical support. May be the luck of the draw, but I dealt with an awesome specialist.5. Firmware based web application for its setup/administration. The software even displays the operating temperature of the NIC and its CPU(!).The cons:#######1. Needs technical support to get going. As you will see below, this process is not for the faint of heart. In my view, a consumer-oriented networking device should not require a PhD in networking. Add to this the fact that you *have* to go via the Chat option first, and that support is only available Mon-Fri from 9am to 10pm EST, and I struggled to find a time to get in touch with them.2. No support for WPA2 wireless security - it only supports WPA-PSK. Reducing network security just to use this device wirelessly was not acceptable to me. I chose to use it wired rather than compromise the security of my home network.In conclusion, I've tested out most of the features of this unit (except for the print server), and they seem to work as advertised. I am not a Torrent power user - but did note that while I could queue up Torrent downloads, these seemed to be sequential. I.e., the next in line didn't start up until the previous one finished. I don't recall encountering this restriction on other clients (such as uTorrent). (I didn't add this as a con as it could very well be user error on my part.)On paper, it seems like a no brainer that this device should be a 5-star product. However, each of its cons led me to deduct a star.Detailed troubleshooting steps:#####################Running on Windows 7 x64, the iConnect software did not detect this unit even though both were hardwired to my router using this configuration (as recommended by the very pitiful documentation): computer --cat5-> Router <-cat5-- iConnect <-usb-- DiskDriveGiving up, I contacted iomega's chat-based tech support. The agent very quickly threw up his hands, and asked me to call them instead.When I did get in touch with phone support, I was very impressed by the quality of their tech support (a shout out to Joshua).I'm not a networking neophyte, but the steps were still fairly laborious. I'm adding them in here in the hopes that they might help someone else avoid wasting precious hours of their life.1. Turn off the WiFi card/adapter on your computer2. Connect iConnect directly to the computer via ethernet cable (iConnect --Cat5-> computer)3. In a command prompt, execute "NET VIEW" ... you should now see the iConnect showing up as //STORAGE4. In a command prompt, ping //STORAGE - you will get an IP address on which to access the iConnect5. Start up Internet Explorer on the computer, and enter that IP address in the browser bar.You should see the iConnect's admin console. Choose Network Services >  Network Settings.Deselect "Automatically configure all network settings"For Network ID 1 (wired), uncheck the DHCP box.This forces the iConnect to take hold of a single IP address that will survive router restarts.6. Click save settings. This restarts the device. (This restart can take over 15 minutes!)7. Wait for the device to come back on.8. Connect a disk drive to the iConnect, the iConnect to the router, and the computer to the router - all hard wired.Disk drive --usb-> iConnect --cat5-> router <--cat5- Computer9. Get the IP address assigned by the router to the iConnect (see Attached Devices in the router's admin console)10. Use Internet Explorer to navigate to the iConnect's admin console using this IP address.11. To get this to work wirelessly (assuming you are okay with not using WPA2): choose Settings> Network Services > Network Settings in the admin page. Click the Wrench next to Network ID 2 (the wireless connection), choose "Enable Wireless Network", select your network's SSID, and enter the password. As before, uncheck the DHCP checkbox.Phew!I suspect you may not need all these steps, but this is what got the device on to my network. Good luck!Happy Networking!

My experience in the past with a fat separator was with an Oxo brand that had a long spout that started near the bottom of the pitcher through which you poured the liquids while the fat pooled at the top. This is the standard type which uses gravity and the natural action of fats rising to the top to pour from the bottom to get the separated juices. While I found that type of fat separator to be acceptable, it did have one serious weak point - the long spout was tough to clean by hand. As a marginal second weak point, it was sometimes hard to get out most of the liquid without tipping in some of the fat.This fat separator attempts to get around those issues by putting a hole in the bottom of the cup and using a plug to stop it up while the juices separate. Having no spout to clean is definitely a plus. Also, the juices drain straight out the bottom so you can very easily see when the fat reaches gets near the bottom and there is much less of a chance of fat coming out as you don't need to tip it to extract the juices.The design troubled me a little at first because I received it with the cap screwed on, but the plug, a plastic armature with a rubber stopper at the end, was not in the hole. I thought that it may not effectively plug the hole and juices might leak out while waiting for the fat to rise to the top. Fortunately, this was not the case. The plug blocked the hole 100% until I pressed the lever on the handle to release the liquid. It is definitely a more sophisticated design. It was also easy to exercise control on the rate of the liquid draining out using the control lever on the handle. Being able to stop it on a dime is important to get as much juice out as possible while leaving the fat behind.My main concern about this product is that, in the long run, the plug may not always work. Through time and wear, I'm not certain that it will block the hole completely, even if it does so perfectly now. That being said, this isn't the kind of kitchen gadget that sees heavy use anyway. It usually is used only for roasting bigger birds and making gravy. It would probably take many years before my concerns would have a chance to be realized. My only other concern is that, as someone who washes dishes by hand, I think that the grooves in the plastic armature that controls the level may slowly get gunk in them which would be hard to wash out. This is a very small concern (and a scrubbing with a toothbrush might allay such concerns), but I wouldn't want bacteria from embedded juice or fat that accumulate through time to get into my food.Given the common design for fat separators like the Oxo one that I used to have, I do believe this is a superior design. However, I also believe that it carries some risks that old-style ones do not. The fussier the mechanism, the greater the chance something might go wrong. If you're an infrequent gravy maker (say, a three or four times a year for special occasions), I'd say this is a good choice. If you're making it all of the time, I'd go for the old style one which has some problems, but still works and doesn't have a mechanism that may wear through time.

I’ve tried a lot of headphones and earbuds over the years, but these are my first pair from NuForce.  Since I love my other Nuforce products, (uDAC-2, uDAC-3, MMP, and Icon DAC), I thought I would give these earbuds a try.  I’ve used these buds with different sources, DACs, and amps, but my primary listening configuration has been playing 320kbps MP3’s via Google Play Music with my Toshiba Chromebook through my Nuforce uDAC-3.  This combination does not allow for any equalization, so I haven’t been coloring the sound beyond what may be present in the uDAC.  I listen/listened to everything from classical to heavy metal, and I also waited until I had approximately 120 hours on these buds before giving my opinions.  The first thing I’ve really come to like about these buds is the width of the soundstage.  With some of my buds, the sound seems stuck between my ears, but these buds give a much more spacious sound.  These buds also give excellent response in the middle to upper bass range.  Im talking about where you hear the pluck of a lower guitar string or a bass guitar, or that initial hit of a drum head.  Very hard to describe.  Where my other buds will reproduce low bass they just don’t seem to have that upper-bass,  lower-midrange “hit”.  The improved presence of sound in this frequency range really adds to the overall musical detail.  I do wish they were a little brighter on the high end (I use my Sony VR-6 phones a lot and they are incredibly bright) but this hasn’t hurt my enjoyment of these buds. and if you have an EQ in you setup you can always dial up the high end a little bit.  I do have to admit that I was surprised with the overall size of these buds as they are pretty big.  Still, with a wide variety of silicone tips included it was easy to find a comfortable fit with a good seal.  I have found myself tempted to pull these out of my ears at the point where the wire enters the housing, but I really try to remove them by the barrel.  Hopefully this will improve their lifespan.  Overall, a really nice sounding set, and another great product from Nuforce.  As of today, I wouldn’t hesitate buying these again.  Well done.

This review is hard for me to write.  This camera is a great camera, and everyone who has credentials says that it takes great pictures--almost as good as more expensive cameras.  This may be true for some, but it has proven to be problematic for me.My gripe is with the sharpness of the images I get.When I take a picture with this camera in anything but perfect conditions (e.g., outside on a sunny day with the sun at my back), I see blur in the image long before I see pixels.  My wife has an ancient Canon SD200 (3.2 MPixel) camera, and in all situations (except "perfect"), in an A-B comparison of the two images (one from her camera and one from the XSi), the SD200 images are usually sharper.  I can zoom in on the pixels in the two images, and at the zoom level at which I see pixels in the SD200 image, I see blur in the XSi image.I know, I know, "apples and oranges".  The SD200 lens is an f8 (or something) 8mm and this one is an f3.5 18mm.  But what do I know?  I know which image is sharper, and it is the SD200.The really frustrating thing for me is that the images on the SD200 in low light are better, too.  Of course, the image stabilization of the 18-55 lens helps a bit, and the XSi will "win" sometimes because of this (the SD200 does not have IS).  But, again, the A-B comparison is revealing: the SD200 wins most of the time.Forget about low-light close-ups with this camera.  Use a small-sensor camera for that!  You can get a LOT closer with those tiny, stopped-down lenses!They say, on the Internets, that there is a possibility of the focusing hardware being slightly off and in need of "calibration"--that would explain my troubles.  But I have tried f22 tests, tripod tests, and manual focus (intentionally putting the image slightly out of focus in each direction).  I have also tried RAW capture and playing with the sharpness in the Canon-supplied software.I just cannot get truly sharp images with this camera.I suspect that there may be something wrong with the specific instance of the Canon XSi that I own.  Maybe my camera was manufactured on a Friday afternoon before a 3-day weekend, and that my wife's SD200 is one of those incredible convergences of a happy day with happy workers making a perfect instance of a good camera.I just purchased a Canon 7D to replace this camera.  I'll let you know how this 18.1 MPixel "Image Monster" compares to the SD200. :-)  And look for my XSi on EBay soon.

I found this cable to be about what you'd expect for a Cat6 cable. It gets the job done, but it doesn't do anything extraordinary beyond what you'd expect from just about every other Cat6 cable out there. I do with they'd have at least done something with marking the cable so that it's more obvious what type it is, rather than just leaving us to hope that we remember.The short version is that if you already have older ethernet cables that you're using, it's probably not going to be worthwhile to switch them out unless there's something obviously wrong with them. Cat5 cables will do the job just fine for most home use because home Internet connections generally aren't so fast that the difference matters. In fact, if they hadn't offered me this as a review item I would still be using my Cat5 cable and leaving an upgrade to Cat6 on the 'someday' list. On the other hand if you're adding a new computer to your network or setting up a new network, the price difference is small enough that it's worth getting something like this so that you won't have to deal with the expense and hassle of going through an upgrade later if you find that you actually have a need for Cat6.

The tap water where I live tastes horrible, so I was excited about giving this water bottle a try.I am the first to admit that I am not mechanically inclined, and the use of this bottle, for me anyway, is not intuitive.  I was trying to release the filter from the little case it comes it for its requisite 15-second wash before using.  Genius that I am, I couldn't get it done and had to hand it over to my husband, who figured it out immediately.I compared this to fresh, unfiltered tap water, and the chlorine taste that is so very noticeable in the tap water was nonexistent in the Britta water.  Unfortunately, other than the chlorine, the water tasted the same, not pleasant at all.  I also compared to reverse osmosis water, and the RO water tastes much, much better.  The filter also takes out particulates, according to the instructions that came with the bottle, but I couldn't determine a difference.  To me that only means that my tap water doesn't have significant particulates or that they are so small I can't tell that they are there.  Anyway, it's nice that they are filtered out.Of course, this bottle doesn't sanitize water.  That is, don't take it camping and expect it to filter out the nasties from the half-submerged raccoon carcass upstream.  I think it is best if your tap water is tasty except for the chlorine because it seems to do a really good job with that.  For me though, I'll continue to drink RO water at home and use this for outings when I'd carry a water bottle anyway.The filter needs to be changed every two months and processes up to 40 gallons of water, according to Britta's information.  For my frugal ways, the filters are fairly pricy but compared to the expense and waste of buying numerous bottles of water, the filter is more economical.  Considering my tap water though, the expense isn't worth the amount of improvement in taste and I'll continue drinking RO water at home.

I purchased this unit about 3 months ago in preparation for an RV trip from home base (New Orleans) to Disney's Fort Wilderness in Florida.  I have used other GPS units before (TomTom and a built in unit in my Audi).  Yes, this 9145 is frickin' HUGE.  I imagine that it was design for the typical age group that rides in RVs because honestly I didn't see any beneficial use of all that screen real estate.  My review here is a bit critical mainly because at this price we should expect top shelf functions from this unit.  After using this unit on two separate RV trips (one trip was to Florida and back and lasted two weeks and included stops at 4 different RV parks) I was ready to put this thing up for sale on Ebay and use my 5 year old 3" screen TomTom.  Here's a few things that annoyed me during our trip:-The unit is painfully slow at reacting to your commands, sometimes it just gets stuck and you have to restart it, which also takes several minutes.-Forget trying plan a trip using routes that you would like to use.  This unit only allows you to use certain routes that it programs in when you give it the address.  If you want to change a route to bypass a certain road, the system lets you request another option to that road, then it recalculates your entire route over and changes other roads in your route, sometimes taking completely off track and adding hundreds of miles.  It does not let you go onto the map and re-route the road to a (for example to more scenic road off the interstate and then back in the interstate).  It only allows you to de-selected a road it has chosen for you, then it recalculates the route and gives you a different route which may or may not include your chosen route.  It's a bit frustrating, especially if you know the roads and you can't program this top shelf unit to choose a specific route. I can do that on my 5 year old Tomtom, I can do that in my car's GPS, I can do that on my cellphone GPS (Google Maps) and I can do it on the free internet Google Maps.  Why can't this top shelf unit do it?  My old Tomtom even allows me to use my laptop to plan a route based on available maps and send that route to the Tomtom to save for a future trip.  This Magellan computer connection ONLY allows me to update the Magellan software and/or maps.  Again, I expected MUCH more from a unit in this price range.-I know this is map database related but it is annoying when the Magellan will not let me input a street address that's not in it's system.  Even if the address is for example USA Street 101, and Magellan only knows about USA Street 100....it will not let you key in 101.  The only option is to pick the nearest number and go for it.-One thing that my other GPS untis do is tell me "miles to destination".  I always liked knowing how many miles I have left before I get to where I'm going.  Kind of gives my a timeframe to work because ALL GPS units always get time to destination wrong.  I really hate using time to destination from a GPS unit as my guide (The Magellan uses posted MPH to calculate it's time to destination which is not good for RV's).  This unit will only tell you miles until the next time it plans to say something like "ahead keep straight" meaning don't take that next exit.  That's fine and and dandy but for one thing I'm not gonna take an exit unless I need to, but the main issue that's frustrating is that the unit recalculates the miles till the next time it has to say "don't take this exit."  So, every 5, 10, 50 miles the unit gives you a readout of how many miles till it talks to you again, not how many miles remaining to your destination.  If you're traveling hundreds of miles in one day, at 55 MPH, this can be a bit frustrating.  I found myself checking my cellphone at fuel stops to see how many miles we had left to travel on that day.-I really didn't notice any features that would help have the RV keyed in.  It still routed me right through downtown Orlando, eventhough I knew a less busy route, it kept trying to get me to turn around on very very busy roads, with a 35 foot RV while pulling a toad.Yes, it has all the Goodsam's parks in it's database, and it has lots places to shop, eat etc., but honestly most all GPS units do this nowadays.The main good points about this unit are that my mom/dad loved it because it was very simple to use and has a big screen and it never got us lost.  The right lane feature works good.  It is now my parents' future X-mas present because I doubt I could get much money back for this unit, even on Ebay. I'm getting something more full featured for my RV.

I purchased a pair of C5 after lots of research and from my ownership of a Zeppelin and its amazing sound.  Unfortunately, I don't find them as comfortable as I had expected.  After trying all of the tips and various adjustments of the memory wire, I finally switched the tips out for a pair of comply tips (500s, I think) and bam!, what a difference.  I finally settled on bringing the loop to its smallest size so that it isn't actually attached to my ear and the comply tips hold the earbuds in perfectly.  If I use them during a lot of movement, I can always extend the loops back out for support.Also, before the comply tips, I had trouble with the sound changing when I would turn my head.  If the earphones we not pointed perfectly into my ear canal, I could hear attenuation (maybe because they don't go in as far as others I'm used to?). Again, the comply tips solved that issue, too.Previously, I had a pair of Ultimate Ears super.fi 5 and triple.fi 10. These B&W; definitely have a lot more punch and bass extension than either.  Overall, I think the UE have a little more high end and treble emphasis, but these C5s are no slouch, either.  For the price and sound quality, they are spectacular and hold up against the UEs well.  I would still prefer my triple.fi 10 in very noisy environments (like mowing the lawn), but the C5 are great for everyday use. Besides, the addition of the remote and mic are very convenient (without spending the extra $$$ in the triple.fi 10vi).For comparison sake, they have a lot more depth and midrange than my Bose QC15 (but not nearly as much noise reduction) and have a good soundstage (probably better than the UE TF10) but aren't as open as my Grado SR125i (but I would never expect them to be). I have a total of about 15 hours on them, so we'll see what happens as they burn in more.A great pair of headphones and a great price. I'm very happy with them!  If you do purchase them, or any other B&W; products, make sure to register them and get your 3 month membership to the Society of Sound.  There are some very good downloads there ands most of them are available in 16 bit Apple Lossless and 24 bit flac.

the Vado HD itself is surprisingly light, even with the battery inserted!(when inserting the battery, the side with information goes up)the controls are simple and easy to use.but it also lacks different options when taking a video, besides the three video qualities (HD+, HD, VGA).video quality is great, but I haven't owned any other ultra portable video camcorder.***AUDIO SYNC ISSUE (and my fix)the audio/video sync issue many people experience can be solved by watching the video on a higher spec computer.Or you can try getting a better codec for your own computer(which you should, as HD videos are becoming more and more common) as i did.my specs areAMD Athlon x2 Dual-Core QL-64 2.10Ghz2gb of DDR2 RAMRadeon 3100 with shared memory32-bit Win7used GOM player to view recorded videosi recorded a clip of my girlfriend brushing her teeth (~30 sec),connected the Vado to my laptop, and watched the video.I did not notice any audio sync problems, but it was a very short video.Then I proceeded to test the Vado Central software, which wanted me to install a codec.Then later when i watched the video again, (not with Vado Central, I used GOM player)I noticed significant audio sync issue!So i uninstalled the codec Vado Central gave me, then installed CoreAVC,changed GOM player setting to not use internal codec so that it will use CoreAVC,and my video was in perfect sync again.so if you encounter this sync issue, try finding a better codec (h.264) before you throw away your old computer.(I think the codec that Vado Central wants you to install isn't very efficient...)

It's ironic that I bought this Garmin unit just a few days before its new ultra thin line was announced. And I seriously considered returning it and waiting for the new ones. But I am not going to because the 5" screen makes all the difference. It makes the unit easier to manipulate.I have had three Garmin Nuvi's and to some degree have hated every one. The first two were very expensive and had limited use, were slow to acquire the satellites, would stop working for no reason usually from over heating. Don't ask me why. So I vowed never to buy another Garmin.I looked at Tomtom and Magellan units. I looked at the reviews. For the people who write neutral or slightly negative reviews in each line there were the same issues. I went to Best Buy to check out the Magellans and the TomToms but still preferred the Garmin product. Magellan produces a GPS with a 7" display that was very attractive and about the same price but it would take up a lot of interior driver space since I don't place the unit on my dash.What I liked about the Garmin 1490T was the larger screen. What I don't like about the larger screen is that Garmin did not increase the resolution. No big deal but I think they could have gone the extra mile and done it. But the fit and finish to the unit is fabulous and it acquires a fix very quickly which is a great improvement. The speaker in the unit is tinny which is a surprise. With the extra room I would have assumed a better speaker but the old familiar voices are there.Routing seems good and it has this Eco function that seems more gimmicky than functional but it gives some interesting information about fuel usage and driving. It needs a better fill up and mileage function. Hey Garmin if I can buy an app on iTunes that I put in the odometer reading at each fill and the litres of gas and it calculates the rest and keeps a running total of gas and mileage you should be able to too.Now why only three stars? Pure and simple it's content and functionality outside of navigation. Sure the 1490T has a 6,000,000 POI database but it is not presented in any different way then it always has been. For instance fuel is by station but not by fuel type for instance I would like to find all the diesel stations but it is not separated out. Garmin has the maps down and obviously with the next generation it has the physical footprints down but it really needs to work on the presentation of its content. It's old and it desperately needs updating and I don't mean a cosmetic fix I mean an operating system overhaul. I should be able to designate all the stations that sell diesel and have them pop up on the map. That can't be rocket science to program.So folks at Garmin it is time to stop thinking hardware and start thinking software and firmware and give us folks a meaningful and useful update.Update: I was optimistic that my 1490 would not experience the same problems as others have in their reviews i.e. random restarts and freezing. And it didn't. Until one day this week when the unit lost its sound and mysteriously went from calculating routes in seconds to minutes. All updates were installed and I have no idea what happened but I returned the unit as I was near the end of the return period. Every one of my Nuvi's (360, 660, and 1490) has failed within the period of two years - the worst was the 1490 which lasted only 3 months. We will see what happens with my new Garmin 3790. Four times lucky right?

This French press is a beautiful design.  The polished stainless steel is easy to keep clean and I think the press is just the right size for handling and pouring.  However, despite the manufacturer's claims about the press being double-walled with good insulation, it does a poor job of keeping hot liquids hot or cold liquids cold for more than about 10 minutes.Pros:- Hefty, stainless steel design.- The press mechanism on mine worked well.- Easy to handle and pour.- Makes a good cup of coffee.- Replacement parts are available.Cons:- The body becomes hot to the touch about 5 minutes after filling with a hot liquid.  In my case, filling it with near boiling water for a beverage made is almost too hot to handle after that 5 minutes.  Rather than being insulative, the press is actually rather conductive and performs poorly for a "double-walled insulated" pot.  If you expect to keep beverages hot or cold (such as tea or milk) longer than about 10 minutes, I think you'll be disappointed with its performance.Bottom line--If all you do is brew coffee for the recommended 4 minutes and then transfer your coffee to a different container, it'll work great.  If you expect to use it for other beverages, I think you may be disappointed with its insulative performance.  I returned mine and will search for another product that does a better job of living up to the manufacturer's claims of being a multi-purpose appliance.

I gave this product two stars to acknowledge my appreciation for a great idea.  After all, any product that eliminates a dangling cord at the gym has something going for it.  Unfortunately, the execution didn't live up to the promise.First, the sound is among the worst I've ever experienced from a set of headphones (even from the cheapest ones).  The highs are muted.  The mid-range is muddy.  The bass is flaccid -- that is, I can sometimes tell it's flaccid when the right speaker doesn't happen to be buzzing loudly due to distortion.  All in all, an abysmal listening experience.Second, the product is simply cheaply made and feels incredibly flimsy in your hand.  While my little orange Shuffle clicked into place with certainty, everything else about the phones feels like the company spared every expense.  Am I nitpicking?  I don't think so.  When you pay 50 bucks for a set of headphones, you expect a level of quality commensurate with that price.  But if you didn't know how much they cost, the iFreePlay phones feel and sound like headphones in the 12-dollar range.Finally, I again want to say how much I like the idea behind these headphones.  It was a pleasure to click my Shuffle into the little dock on the left earphone and go through a gym workout without a dangling cord catching on any of the equipment.  And if the sonic quality these headphones produce was even merely competent, I'd be satisfied.  But the sound is just unacceptable.I feel bad because I know how even one negative review on Amazon can have a profound effect on the future of a product.  And my review may severely retard sales of the iFreePlay.  But Monster should have spent far more time in focus groups and quality control before releasing this product.  They should also cut the price in half.The bottom line:  I'll wait for another company with higher standards to make a similar product.  Or I'll wait for Monster to get its act together.

This is a well-made case which would work well for a few folks. Here are the pros and cons:Pros:-Well made with real leather that feels and smells great. I wish I could get my car's leather seats back to smelling  this good.-Has several detents to hold the iPad solidly in several angles all in the landscape orientation.-Has business card holders and a loop for carrying a stylus which are both features important to business users.-Affords good protection for your iPad Air.Cons:-Is quite heavy adding a good deal of weight to the iPad Air thus removing one of the reasons (lightness) that people want an iPad Air for.-Is thick. The iPad Air in the Apple leather case is a total of about a half inch (1.1 cm) thick where when in this case it's almost double that. Again, the thinness of the iPad Air is a feature people buy it for.-The auto shutoff doesn't work. This is baffling since auto shutoff has been a feature since the iPad Gen 2.-The case closes using a magnetic tab which, when the case is open, is a nuisance and sometimes gets in the way of thescreen.-The cover is very stiff to fold back which is an issue for those who'd wish to use their iPad like a book. I had high hopes for this stylus.  I am an avid user of Paper by 53, and the new Pencil offers some features I've been wanting for awhile.  Unfortunately, the stylus isn't all its cracked up to be.  First off, be aware if purchasing that despite the rugged look of the tip, it is made of flimsy rubber like so many other styluses.The device pairs to bluetooth easily enough, simply by touching it to a dot on the screen when Paper 53 is on.  You can set a few different parameters in the app preferences.The literature boasts that the iPad knows the difference between the Pencil and your hand - supposedly you can use your hand for blending and the pencil for drawing.  I find that this is not always the case.  Frequently the iPad reads the Pencil tip as a finger and shifts spontaneously to blend mode, which is annoying when I'm working with sharp line tools.  The only way I've been able to work around that is to manually turn the blend option on and off in preferences, which requires backing out of the drawing I'm working on and a few moves in the menu to accomplish - hardly the most convenient feature.  Another workaround is to shut off the bluetooth connection when working with the line tools, but this shuts off the eraser function as well as the drawing function, which kind of defeats the purpose of having the thing in the first place.So I'm sticking with my Adonit Jot Pro for now.This thing is pretty and a great idea, but there are lots of adjustments necessary before it is really ready for the consumer.

I was a little concerned about my purchase as so many reviewers seemed to have difficulties getting this case on and off their iPod--even to the extent of trashing the case by cutting it off. Also, there were complaints about the green color being dark and dull, rather than a vibrant green as depicted on the Shades website and Amazon.Well, I worried for nothing. My case is exactly the color I expected from the pictures--a bright, vibrant green which reminds me of creme de menthe or old fashioned mint jelly. I do have the silver Classic 160 GB, so there's nothing to deepen the color to the forest green some reviewers have described. I'm assuming they have a black iPod. The case, though colored, is translucent and will not be the intense green pictured over a dark object. The truth is that all of the colors are going to be prettier over the light colored iPod.My other concern about getting the case on and off in one piece was also for naught. I put the case on and took it off three times to satisfy myself that it fit properly. The fit is super snug, and a little patience and "go slow" is required the first time, but the little piece of stiff white card included with the case allows the screen to slide easily over the polyurethane without sticking. A genius idea really. Frankly, I don't know how I would have managed without it, both to insert the iPod and remove it. If someone accidentally discarded the little slider card not realizing its purpose, I can see how they would not be happy with the case.I don't expect this case offers much protection from being smashed or other heavy "impact" accidents, but it is very well protected from the occasional "butterfingers" drop, dirt, dust, moisture, and being bumped around in a crowded purse. Scratches simply couldn't occur.My iPod sits in a small JBL speaker dock with no problem. The iPod is only marginally larger with the case on and fits in the adapter perfectly, with a little room to spare.I had no trouble at all with operating the click wheel through the case. It may be very slightly less sensitive, but all functions work just fine. I have no complaints and I'm very pleased to have the wheel protected from daily grunge and grime.I think this is a terrific product which performs exactly as advertised and is well worth the money. I may get a couple more colors just to change things up a bit.Next Day: I decided to add a little more to this review regarding the fit of the case and sliding the iPod into and out of the case. Every time I take the iPod out and put it back in the process is easier and easier, exactly as stated on the Shades website. There are also some helpful videos showing the best way to accomplish the task. I cannot emphasize enough the importance of the little piece of stiff card placed over the front side of the iPod to facilitate the process. By following the instructions as given I had no problems at all. The case has very sturdy fused sideseams and hasn't split or stretched in weird ways despite 7 or 8 on/offs in the last day. I really like this level of protection for an expensive gadget and the fact that the entire front is covered without the need for clear plastic stick on protectors that always have bubbles, no matter how careful my application. As long as you order the correct size case for your device, I see no reason that anyone would not make it past the learning curve for getting the case on and off. There's just a very specific way to do it successfully (like lying down to zip up a really, really tight pair of jeans).

I don't have this model, but I do have two other HP Desktops.  The point of this review is to warn you that most HP Desktops are significantly under-powered.  The 6200 unit has a 250w power supply and the 6230 has 300w(per their parts list on the web site)... Although there is a lot of room to add-on, you can't do much with only 250watts.  Most decent PCIe video boards require at least 350w.  I have a model a1450n (300w) and a a6009n (250w), both AMD 64x2 CPUs.  The a6009n has a mother board with a 24-pin input socket for power(as do most new motherboards), but the power supply only has the older 20-pin output (the extra 4-pins are supposed to be to get extra power to the mother board to accomodate various add-ons, including accessories/peripherals that use USB ports. It works, but just minimal power.The thing that burns me is HP makes it quite difficult to get power supply specs because they know they would be a liability (but they sure promote the extra slots and expandability).  The only way to find out is to actually look inside the case or check the parts list on their web site.The bottom line is you should plan to replace the power supply if you're going to add-on much to your system.  Besides the inconvenience, that's an extra $50-$150... and a wasted, useless replaced power supply.

How many pictures will it store?  It is the most commonly asked question from digital camera enthusiast but usually the question that is the most difficult to get a straight answer about.  Well, considering I worked in the memory industry for over 7 years I can help clarify this perplexing question and do so unbiased as I have since changed industries.The SanDisk SDSDB-512-A10 512MB Secure Digital Card, like most 512MB cards, will store on average 568 pictures when used with a 2 megapixel camera, 426 images when used with a 3 megapixel camera,  256 pictures when used with a 4 megapixel camera, 204 images when used with a 5 megapixel camera, and 160 pictures when used with a 6 megapixel camera.  These numbers are based off the assumption that you are going to shoot your images at the highest quality JPEG setting available for the camera and understand that they are estimates and may be off by as much as 10 percent due to numerous factors including the complexity of the scene being shot and the compression algorithm used by your specific camera.I truly hope this review was helpful to you in determining whether this 512MB card is the right capacity for your specific needs.

It took it 30 minutes (!) to uninstall the trial microsoft office version on it. Skype communication was exhausting the cpu resources. You cannot do more than one thing at a time thanks to the single core processor; having a voice chat and opening a browser at the same time? forget about it...- Cheap, terrible wireless card. THIS was THE deal-breaker. What is the point of having a lightweight, mobile computer if not to use wi-fi? the reception of the built-in card (Broadcom G) was very finicky and temperamental. In spots where I was able with my Thinkpad T400 to have skype video calls, the S12 wouldn't connect to the network at all, although it was detecting it and showing it among the networks detected. If the network didn't show full, near perfect reception (4-5 bars) it simply wouldn't connect to it. Download speeds were varying tremendously as well, and never reached the speeds of my Thinkpad in comparison.- Cheap, weak built in Microphone. The mic was at its max sensitivity plus boost, and still the voice sounded faint at best. After troubleshooting with the tech support, which included of course a lengthy (because of the slow processor) uninstallation and re-installation of the audio software and drivers, the results were identical. The enhancements of the audio software were turned on, and off, and some on some off, but nothing helped. In fact, as is usually the case, the enhancements only deteriorated the sound quality. In short, garbage hardware. Once again, comparing with the built in mic of the thinkpad, the difference was astounding. The sound on the Thinkpad was loud, and crystal clear.- Built in camera... Garbage. enough said.- Scrolling with the mouse: the surface was VERY particular about where my finger is placed for scrolling. If I didn't place it exactly on the thin scrolling arrow marked on the surface it wouldn't scroll.All in all, some bad, cheap hardware choices made by Lenovo really hold this computer back. For the money you pay, this computer would have been a terrific choice for a netbook if only it was paired with a faster, DUAL core cpu, such as the one in the ASUS 1201N. This is 2010, and single core chips are simply not up to the task of making daily computing a pleasant experience. The wireless card choice is simply inexcusable. The rest is not as important, unless you plan like me to use the computer when traveling as a communication tool via skype video calls, among other uses. What is the point of having a built in Mic and Camera that are so bad, you have to carry a separate USB ones as well?In one word, Save yourself the hassle. There are cheaper options out there that won't leave you pulling your hair out as you realize you wasted your money.

I've owned every Jawbone and many other BT headsets over the years; Plantronics, Blue ANT, Motorola... I was looking for an alternative to Plantronics Voyager Pro that wouldn't interfere with sunglasses, so I gave this FLIP a try.In short, the product design itself is good, but the noise reduction is non-existent. While using apps that show your "speaking volume" on-screen, the Voyager Pro shows very little level when not talking while in my car going freeway speeds, but this FLIP in the same environment shows very high level while not talking, and barely moves when talking loudly. Voice commands don't work at all unless I'm in a quiet environment. For the price of the FLIP, it simply does not perform as well as better headsets, and the same performance can be had for much less cost.Pros:Soft earpieces in different sizes, even a no-hearhook option.Simple operation; open = on, closed = off.Announces remaining battery level when powered on, press both Volume buttons any time to hear the remaining level.Fastest A2DP response I've ever seen; Bluetooth powers down when the connection is "idle" and re-establishing takes a moment. With other A2DP headsets, I notice the first part of sounds can be cut off, and short sounds can go entirely unheard. This FLIP got every sound, even short ones. Excellent.Cons:If you don't like the included earpieces, the size of the speaker is unique/large so no other brand such as Jabra EarGels will fit.I already addressed No Noise Reduction, this headset is only useful in quiet environments. For me this is a complete deal-breaker; if you don't need noise reduction I still maintain that at this price, this should perform as a Premium not Basic headset.You cannot wear this while it is closed/off; there is simply no room for your ear when the FLIP is closed. Since it doesn't come with a case you will have to figure out where to put it besides leaving it on your ear when it's off, or else disable Bluetooth on your phone if you want audio to come from the phone's speaker.

This is an awesome drive (I bought the 500 GB model), but it can be very slow. I notice that connecting to the drive causes my laptop to freeze for about 45 seconds, then it comes back up. Don't get me wrong, I really love my drive, but it is very slow.It was also a bit tricky to install, but I didn't have too many problems. BE ABSOLUTELY SURE TO READ THE SETUP PART OF THE MANUAL INCLUDED! IT WILL SAVE MUCH FRUSTRATION! (sorry for caps, but I think this part is extremely important)The drive has excellent security features. It will automatically find all the user accounts on your computer and put those accounts on the drive. You can also manually add accounts via the web-based setup, which is excellent if you have multiple computers using the drive. I would recommend locking this drive down as tight as you possibly can. This way, if a peeping neighbor comes across the drive, they can't get into your files (even by mistake). Post a comment if you need help securing your drive, I would be happy to help!As far as the noise goes, I don't notice any, but my drive is in my basement with the home theater and a dehumidifier which drown out any noise it may make.This part will sound very hypocritical: I know I said that it can be slow, but that's for connecting to it. Even with Wireless-G (54.0 Mbps all over in my house), transfer speeds are good.I have not tested the software that comes with the drive for automatic backups, I use SyncBack (Google it, 2BrightSparks makes it). This combined with the drive make for good transfer speeds.TIPS FOR SUCCESS WITH YOUR DRIVE:- As stated above, lock the drive down tight. This prevents neighbors from seeing files, or even dropping their own in the drive. It uses basic security, but it's very difficult to get around it.-Secure your wireless network. If you don't have remote access enabled, this makes it about 10 times more difficult to get into the drive.-"User Accounts" on the drive:~Be sure to create a folder for everyone in the web-based setup. (Login using the IP address of the drive and click 'Folders' on the left-hand menu panel.)~Make an account for everyone with each having a unique password. If you have a user account for each person on your computer, then attach each folder to the computer on the individual account to prevent users from seeing each others' files.-Be sure that you use a STATIC IP address for the drive. (Login -> Click "System" icon on the left -> Click "Network" at the top -> set it to MANUAL, not automatic -> give it an IP address that you will remember.) This makes it alot easier to have it connected to user accounts since it won't be hopping all over your network addresses.-Obviously, never tell anyone the drive's password. Write it down if you think you won't remember it, then hide the password somewhere safe.-Put the drive in a locked closet that only you have the key to. This prevents someone from pressing the RESET button and wiping the drive completely (no way to recover these lost files!)Best of luck to you and be sure to comment if you need help!UPDATE (11.15.09): I am getting extremely fed up with this drive. It is giving me more headaches than it is worth. I attempted to use the Print Server feature on the drive, and it knocked my drive offline. I couldn't figure out was wrong at first because my network said it was there, but my PCs wouldn't find it. Then when I went to reset it, I couldn't tell when it was resetting because the LED light wasn't changing at all. Furious at the time, I pulled the power cord out of it and plugging it back in and then it decided to work. The manual specifically said that it has a print server and that all you had to do was plug the printer into your drive; needless to say, that didn't work. Neither of my PCs would connect to the printer. And the "best" part of it: my printer didn't work correctly when I plugged it back into the computer! Then I had to spend more time figuring that out. Another "wonderful" part of this drive: if you don't connect to it very often, it disconnects itself, but it doesn't disappear from your computer so you can't re-mount it unless you restart your computer altogether. Now I need to go take an aspirin because I am very angry after having just edited this review! I know I originally said the drive was great, but spend the extra money to get a better one. The original rating of this drive was 4/5, but now it is down to 2/5.UPDATE (1.20.10): I regret to have to say that with less than 5 months, my drive failed. The network port on it died and iomega wanted to charge me to replace it. I am so very disappointed with this company. Their customer "service" is atrocious, the online representative decided to take an attitude with me. They have lost the very little respect I had for them and  they have also lost a customer. I hope you heed my warning--do not buy this product. It's much much more trouble than it's worth. I am so infuriated with iomega and their support. The rep I spoke to is lucky I did not contact his manager--I would have made sure he lost his job.Rating dropped from 2/5 to 1/5, but I wish I could give it 0/5. Update.Camera going back for the third time. Now I have the dreaded lens error issue where the lens won't retract and the camera won't shoot. This is subject of a repair notice which should make it free. Still the camera has been a nightmare for me. I require reliability. This has not been the case.I have had this camera for a year and a half. I wanted to have a pocket-size all-purpose camera for shooting kids and to use while skiing. I am a photographer and always like to have a camera with me. Cell phones are useful but in general won't do if you want good quality and to make larger prints. This camera takes great shots. It focuses fast and accurately and handles most scenes quite well.I use the program or scene modes frequently and find that I only use manual mode rarely. The images from this camera will not hold up to close inspection with larger sensor cameras but will give you good shots in most situations. Color saturation and dynamic range as well as detail will not be as good as C size or full frame sensors. That doesn't mean that you won't get acceptable pictures depending on your purpose.The problems that I've had with this camera have been significant to me. The first is that this battery cannot stand up to exposure to cold weather for even a brief period. You may get one or two Shots off when taking pictures on a mountain while skiing or even 15 seconds of video but no more. The red battery light comes on telling you that you need to change your battery and this even though the battery is fully charged. I returned my camera to Canon who told me nothing was wrong and that the camera was up to spec. This camera is not guaranteed to take pictures at temperatures below 32. All my previous PowerShot cameras have been fine under the circumstances in fact I have never had a problem before. I Returned my camera a second time when this continued to happen this year and they change the motherboard. The camera is a little better but it's clear that the problem relates to this particular battery. The battery has been changed For the S110 which is back to the battery used in the S95. Interestingly my wife has the S95 and that is the camera that we used this season for our ski pictures without a problem.The camera makes beautiful videos in high definition of indoor sporting events with the only problem being again the battery not lasting that long. It gives beautiful pictures, beautiful videos and has state-of-the-art functionality for a point-and-shoot camera.If you plan on just going out and shooting a couple of snapshots, the battery will do fine. If you're going to use this to shoot events make sure you buy an extra battery. If you plan on using this outdoors in cold weather buy something else.ps. Canon Service was actually quite good. Update 4/2013 - I had previously reviewed this as 5-star, but deducting 2 stars now.  I really WANT this thing to be awesome, but the build quality turns out to be poor - the selector switches get stuck, and the USB might not charge more modern smartphones.  There are some newer models that seem to have better tuning of weather and fix some of the switches, plus some other features.  Look at the FRX1 for similar price (without cellphone charging), or the FRX2 or WR-333 for more comparable features (The WR-333 also lets you pop in AAA batteries to top off your cellphone from them too)FRX2 here: [...]  (you can also select the FRX1 and FRX3 at that page - read reviews carefully, as they are all mixed together as for which model they are for)----The concept is great, and the unit is so tiny and cheap, it seems like a no brainer to keep one of these in an evacuation kit.Every few months, top-off the internal battery by USB (from computer, wall adapter, or car).  During use, charge by Solar or hand-crank.  Besides the super bright LED flashlight and AM/FM radio, the weather-band radio is very handy, and the ability to siphon some of the internal battery power into another USB device is critical.What sets this unit apart from other similar models is this "siphoning" -- with other similar models, you have to continuously crank to charge USB devices.  It comes with both micro- and mini- USB to charge your devices.  The internal battery isn't huge, might only charge your cell phone to 1/3 capacity, but given the compact size I'd say it's a good trade-off; you always have the hand-crank once the internal battery is dead.The only improvement I could think of would be to allow me to manually choose which weather channel it tunes to.  For some reason I don't totally trust the "auto-tuning" concept, since there is no indication of what's happening inside the radio.  But I guess this makes the operation simpler, and makes it cheaper to produce, so I'll live with it.I ordered 3 units, 2 as gifts, because they were so cheap and clever.  One of the units had a problem receiving weather signal - it was extremely weak and noisy compared to the others.  If your weather reception is spotty, especially compared to another weather radio, you should consider an exchange before writing the unit off.  It was hard to reach Ambient Weather by phone, but eventually I got them by email and they worked with me to replace the unit - even before I had returned the bad unit, and even through some shipping snafus.  I see now that orders are being fulfilled by Amazon, instead of directly from Ambient, so perhaps this will change the return process.

I had high hopes for this radio, hoping that I could replace my much-used and beat up Eton E5. Sadly, this will not be the case. While the G3 adds some features such as the Aircraft band, LSB/USB switch, RDS and Sync detector (which sorta works), several important traits/features of the E5 are not carried over to the new model.1. FM sensitivity is not as good. Several FM stations in Eugene Oregon (about 110 miles away) that are easy catches for the E5 can still be heard with the G3 but not as clearly, and with much more effort to get the antenna "just right".2. MW (AM) sensitivity is not as good...side by side comparison on several weak AM stations that yield decent reception with the E5 are heard with more noise and hiss on the G3.3. Ditto for LW... several aircraft beacons are heard, but with more hiss on the G3.4. The "wide/narrow" switch does not also function as "voice/music" tone control on FM, as it does on the E5.5. The push-buttons are NOT illuminated on the G3.6. Tuning steps increased from 25 kHz to 50Khz on FM... not what is needed to pull in a weak DX station that is first adjacent to a strong local!The good points:1. The RDS functions well.2. SSB stations are MUCH easier to tune with the G3 than the E5.3. The Aircraft band works well, this will be great for airshows.4. Under some conditions (stations that are not too weak) the sync detector does provide improvement. I find that I must tune 1 kHz LOW to get it to work, so there could be some alignment issues with my particular radio. The feature does not work as well as it does on my Sony ICF-SW7600GR and is not even close to the performance of my Sony ICF 2010!5. The G3 is less likely to "overload" in strong signal areas than the E5... perhaps the sensitivity was reduced on purpose to provide better reception for city dwellers, at the expense of reducing DX capabilities.So, I will keep my beat up old Eton E5, and use both... sad!Update: 5/19/10  I have read several reviews/comments that seem to indicate that the sensitivity and Sync detector problems on early production units have been fixed. This model might be worth a second chance.

June 14, 2011 UPDATE:  This year when the leaves starting to populate the trees the signals from the TV became weaker and now the signals are weak at best.  I've tried reprogramming them but that does not alleviate the weak signal.  Our home is in the valley between two mountains and even a Direct TV or Dish signal will not reach us.  The main signals go flying over the house and over the trees.  When the signal comes in the picture and sound are fantastic.I purchased another brand a few months ago and while its reviews were solidly in favor of its attributes I found that it was just an unidirectional amplified antenna with nothing much to praise other than the fact that it worked fundamentally well.  Having a sense of perfection in some things, I bought this RCA 1650 antenna becasue of the write up and recognizing fully that some reviewers compared it to rabbit ears or worse.  Upon opening the box I immediately saw that the dimensions were stated incorrectly.  The antenna is NOT 1.7X8.9X2.6.  It is about the size of a sheet of government paper (8X10) and about 1 inch thick.  NO big thing but a consideration I had since I had the perfect mounting spot for the dimensions reported.  I further expected an omnidirectional antenna and received another unidirectional antenna.  Perhaps a note of disclosure would be appropriate here.  We live in the valley between two mountains (hills to some until you try to climb one) next to the creek.  The terrain suggests, rightly so, that any antenna would not work well and sure enough this one does not work much better than the other one as far as signal strength.  Given the flat design compared to some modern art stature that looks ugly and the simple and most imporant fact that this antenna draws in most of the digital and high definition stations in this area I would have to give a significant number of kudos to the RCA compared to the other.  Another slight factor is the manner in which the hardwired coaxial cable exits the bottom of the flat piece.  At the bottom of the flat piece (I do not know the technical name of this but I hope you can see what I am attempting to describe) the cable exits on its way to the amplifier or the TV's connection point.  The manner in which the cable exits causes it to put pressure on the flat piece in such a manner that connecting the provided stand not to work properly.  An attempt to have the cable run below the stand did not work well nor did placing the cable over the stand work well either.  A design flaw that should be corrected with the next model.  The coaxial cable's gauge should be a bit larger in an effort to handle digital signals.  In the directions it suggests that the antenna not be placed near metal so that the signal would not be diminished but it would be well worth the slight extra cost to make the cable shielded to eliminate that condition if possible.  I know picky, picky.  Bottom line:  it works fairly well and it is better than the other one that I bought.

(Apparently Linksys thinks its consumers are willing to understand the difference between an IP address, subnet, gateway, DNS, DHCP routing and static routing.) This problem was so difficult it required the work of two graduates from the Rochester Institute of Technology (one of whom is solely responsible for a retail website whose biggest customer is Microsoft) and a Software Engineer. Individuals with only basic computer backgrounds will have a much more difficult time!My only other complaint is with the interface. If you have a car with a keyless entry system beware that the Garmin will/could at some time most likely interfere with your ability to gain entry, start and egress your vehicle.  My wife and I we're stuck in our 2008 Corvette for about 15 minutes.  At the time I was unaware of the Nuvi interference problem.  The vehicle was towed to the dealership and no problems could be found.  After later reading a GM bulletin I found that the Nuvi was the culprit.  I've tested the Nuvi 255w and the Nuvi 750 with my 2008 Corvette (1100 miles on the odometer).  The 255w is much worse than the 750.  At one point the 255w disabled the Onstar system, the starter and the door locks. (Note: Manual door releases are located on the floor by the doors) Inserting the FOB into the Glove box plug did not overcome the interference.  Interference can occur randomly.  If you are having a random "FOB NOT FOUND" message and have a Nuvi you can check to see if the Nuvi is at fault by placing the FOB in close proximity to the Nuvi.  If the Nuvi is at fault you'll see the FOB NOT FOUND message.  Once you see the message simply turn off the Nuvi and the vehicle should find the FOB within a few seconds.I've contacted Garmin about this problem and they insist that they are in total compliance with FCC Rule Part 15 which states that "Digital devices that comply with the FCC technical standards (Part 15) and have been certified and marketed in accordance with the FCC rules may not cause interference and must accept any interference that they receive."Based on the fact that I've had two Nuvi's interfere with the operation of my Corvette and have seen others talk about interference with their particular vehicles I've found that Garmin is NOT in compliance with the FCC rule 15.The last correspondence I had with Garmin's legal staff stated "The operator of a device bears a responsibility for operation in a manner that avoids interference to other devices."  Based on this response I guess Garmin thinks I should stick the Nuvi on the rear window.  This might help the interference problem but would make navigation via the rear mirror a bit tedious.

I am not an audiophile. However, I am quite a fan of heaphones/earphones and I own a good few of them. I stayed quite in love with Ultrasone products and I have now the 700-DVD, the HFI-15G and now the HFI-780S (since about 6 months now). I also own the ATH-900, the AKG Q-701 (the Quincy Jones signature), Grado SR-60i, Sony MDR-V6 and one Beyerdynamics.All of this to serve as means of comparison.The 780-S are in the price range of the ATH-900 and in competition with it because the AKG are open headphones and should not be compared.I had quite a hard time determining which one was my favorite Headphone between the two because, although they are in a similar price range and both closed, they sound different.The Ultrasone has a very pronounced bass feel, a strong "in your face" medium and highs that can get a bit sibilant. Where they fail in my opinion is in the comfort.The ATH-900 have less bass (but not lacking), more recessed mediums and fine highs. Where they shine in my opinion is in the soundstage. They are also very comfortable and can be kept for a long time without tiring.At the end, I use the ATH more often because of the comfort and the great soundstage.On a sidenote, I have tried replacing the pads on the Ultrasone but it changed the quality of the sound and make them feel even more sibilant. On top of it, the discomfort does not really comes from the earpads but on the heavy pressure the headband is exerting on my skull.Let's recapitulate:Pros:- Overall very good sound.- Very good bass.- Give a very energetic rendition of the recordings. Very good for rap/ Rock etc...- Easy to drive- Very good for games and movies.Cons:- Extremely uncomfortable. Hard to keep for more than 30mn at a time in a standing position. Laying down relieves some of the pressure exerted on the skull.- A bit sibilant.A final note:The Sony MDR-V6 may have been my revelation for this year. The cost is about one third of the Ultrasone but not the performance. These headphones may have been a bit forgotten since they came out last century but they are very solid performers all around.
