All our rental homes throughout Italy had this pot or similar espresso pots and I loved the strong, rich tasting coffee. When at Peet's Coffee a few weeks ago, I was awed at the quality of this solid aluminum Bialetti 6-cup Moka Express, and couldn't resist buying it.Aluminum holds heat, one of the secrets to good espresso. However, aluminum is highly reactive to acid from coffee. Paradox? Well, not if you clean WITHOUT soaps or detergents but only use hot water to rinse. However, as many reviews point out, to get a good cup without the aluminum taste (from the coffee acid leaching aluminum into the water) you have to make a few pots first.Why? Like properly seasoning any reactive metal (i.e. seasoning cast-iron skillets to avoid reaction to tomato sauce and other acidic foods) aluminum is also as reactive, and no exception! Many have misconceptions that aluminum is like stainless steel. Well, it is, provided it's seasoned with oil! You can waste coffee grounds to season the pot with coffee bean oils, drinking aluminum tasting coffee until the pot is seasoned, or can season your Moka Express the good old fashioned Italian way, with high quality Italian olive oil. (I used Bariani Extra-Virgin Olive Oil for all inside parts that come in contact with coffee, and Celtic Silicone (silicon) Spray containing pure food grade silicon for all outside parts, including the handles and lid joints. You can buy the pure silicone spray on Amazon, and it's great for other uses like semi-permanently lubricating shower suction cups for attaching soap dispensers to shower walls, conditioning leather and vinyl, and so on.)To properly season WITHOUT baking (which some chefs insist on doing in an oven at 500 degrees, which will MELT your handles and rubber filter seal internally!), I simply prepared the pot (a one-time operation that will last a few years, I would expect, then maybe I'll do it again) to "hit the ground running." (That is, to deliver an outstanding tasting espresso from the first use WITHOUT aluminum oxidation.) The steps I used are as follows:(1) Lay out paper towels on the counter.(2) Remove your Moka Express from its sealed bag in the box, unscrew, and place on towels.(3) Spray top and bottom outside parts with pure liquid silicone (silicon) including lid joint, and plastic handles on side and lid. (These are excellent quality by the way but will melt if abused as I'll later discuss.) Wipe towel covered with silicone around aluminum threads where top aluminum piece screws onto bottom aluminum piece. If you get a little inside don't worry. But I wouldn't recommend dousing inside with silicone even though it's food grade. This is for the olive oil to do in next step.(4) Pour small amount of extra-virgin olive oil, the highest quality Italian you can find (such as Bariani brand or other family grown oil) into both sections. Drench filters. Turn top upside-down and pour small amount into filter, making sure to cover rubber seal. After thoroughly washing hands, rub fingers into every nook and cranny. Pour oil back and forth inside all hidden areas of filters that will become exposed to coffee and grounds. (There are hidden areas you can see where coffee will enter through filters that should be covered with oil.)NOTE: Since you're never going to use soap to wash this pot, a thin film of oil, with additional coffee oil, will always remain on every inner and outer exposed aluminum surface, since it molecularly penetrates microscopic pores on the surface. That is how seasoning works. That is why soaps and detergents are the kiss of death for cast iron and aluminum cookware.Take a dry clean towel and wipe down the outside, buffing it to a sheen, removing as much silicone as possible. A microscopic thin film is all you need! Take a separate dry clean towel and do the same for all exposed parts inside. Turn over the bottom onto the paper towel on the counter, rest the open top part on the paper towel, and allow these to "cure" for 24 hours. Buff them again with a towel so there is no oil residue (only sheen from the shiny, beautiful aluminum), screw together, and store until use.HOW TO USE POT AFTER ONE-TIME ABOVE PREPARATION:Now for the first and subsequent uses; boil a pot of water. Unscrew top and bottom, then remove bottom filter. Lay out paper towel(s) on counter, set parts down. Pour boiling water into the bottom reservoir (with bottom filter removed), one half inch from the top. Grind your favorite coffee bean fine (or use finely ground fresh coffee). Hint to keep fresh: Freeze coffee beans or grind, remove from freezer and grind beans frozen or use frozen grinds.Scoop fine coffee grind into filter (holding filter with one hand, scoop with other) level with top; do not pack coffee but you can pat it down a little so it's not too loose.Lower filter very slowly and carefully into hot water in bottom aluminum part of coffee pot. If a little water comes out, that's why you have paper towels below it. If there's a little too much water, let the filter float on surface of water (where some water may overflow). Place top of coffee maker on screw threads, make sure it feels seated, and screw into place. DO NOT OVER-TIGHTEN. Just screw in firmly but if you force it to tighten, who knows it might get stuck (I didn't over-tighten to find out!).LOW HEAT is the operative here! Otherwise you will MELT the handles and rubber seal internally!Place on low heat, and let simmer. BABYSIT pot! Do not leave room! Open top occasionally to check, in a few minutes the coffee will rise to top part of pot. If not, turn up heat slightly until this happens, and quickly turn down heat if it rises too fast. This patented pot has been used since 1933 in Italy, so I get a sense you really have to be a klutz to mess this up. Once the top is full, you'll hear a slight gurgle to signify the water is gone from the bottom part on the burner, and heat-forced into the top part.You can now pour this into a mug. For one person, it makes 2/3 of a giant Starbucks porcelain mug. For two or more, use those tiny Italian coffee cups (the kind they serve you WITHOUT REFILLS in Italy for the equivalent of $5.00). Welcome to Italy. This is NOT Starbucks, so venti coffee drinkers might think this is a rip-off. As a venti coffee drinker, I thought so until I tasted it with pure organic whipping cream. WOW. This is the real deal, espresso that is so strong and rich; all the flavor of a large Starbucks or Peet's coffee is compressed into about half the volume... well worth it. However, like everything in Italy, it's a "big to do" for one of "life's little pleasures." However, it's a novelty for coffee lovers, that's worth it, if done patiently and properly.One last comment: Do NOT forget to rinse all parts of your coffee pot in hot water, WITHOUT using anything except cleaned hands and fingers. Wipe dry with paper towels. After my first use it looked brand new, with no coffee stains! I really expected coffee stains because the high pressure (even on low heat) as the coffee is forced from bottom to top, surely would stain the aluminum? No, probably because the pot is seasoned. Hot water causes everything to wash right off. Dry with clean paper towel. Place a folded towel in the bottom part before attaching top (to absorb excess moisture and completely dry the internal part of the bottom filter during storage), and place in cupboard until next use.

This pedometer measures only the number of steps. It will not measure how many miles have you walked. It will store your last 7 days of workout,.you just need to press the Memo button to go back to your history. There are 2 buttons at the back and you will need a sharp object to press them. The System Rest button, is a factory reset, this will delete all data and put the setting back to default. The other button is the Set button, used for setting up the time.While in use, the LCD will turn off after 5 minutes to save battery consumption (but the pedometer will still continue counting steps). Press Memo button to wake up the display again.There is only one button for the basic operation and it is labeled MEMO, located just at the top of the Omron name. It is too wake up the display or recall 7 days of activity history.ACCURACY:I actually counted 200 steps and it recorded 201. The error probably is my own or my position. But that is 0.5% error in accuracy.BATTERY:It was shipped with a 3 volts, Energizer Watch/Electronic Batteries, 3 Volts,Energizer Watch/Electronic Batteries, 3 Volts, 2032, 2 batteries (Lithium Button Cell), 2 batteries (Lithium Button Cell) Maxell battery. To open the battery compartment, you will need those small watch screw drivers. 2 screws at the back. There is a low battery indicator to prompt you when you need to replace the battery.Honestly, for a few bucks more get theOmron HJ-151 Hip Pedometer for Aerobic Activity. I have been playing with this hub for about a week and so far at least on my desktop computer I have not had any problems with it.Pros:* 7 ports* Comes with external power adapter* No noticeable slowdownCons:* Power adapter cord is way too short* Random blinking color changing LED looks gaudy* Likely a power hog* Port LEDs vary significantly in brightness (green, blue and cyan are bright, red and yellow are dim)* Would be nice if LEDs indicated port activityIn my testing with this hub I have connected multiple thumb drives and an IOmega 64GB USB 3.0 SSD drive. With the SSD drive I did some performance benchmarking comparing with vs without the hub and could not measure any difference when using Linux. The controller chip is made by Terminus Technology in China. The hub reports that it draws a maximum of 100ma, but I suspect that with all of the LEDs and even according to the datasheet it likely draws more. The USB standard requires that a computer supply 500ma of current and have overload protection. With the hub drawing so much it's not all that difficult to assume that a lot of people are seeing problems due to it overloading the power supplied to the USB port.The controller chip supports transaction translation, which basically translates transactions from slow devices (1.5 and 12Mbps) to high-speed (480mbps) transactions, allowing more efficient use of the USB bus when slow devices are connected.

First this is my second Transformer, I had the original a couple of years ago with the dock and sort of liked it, except of the issue that there was almost no apps for the tablet. I sold it since I had an iPad anyways, but I always really liked the keyboard and mouse option and wanted to see if Android for tablets ever improved.Second, I have 4 Google TV devices and this if my 3rd Android tablet (the original Transformer, the Nexus 7 and finally this, the TF300 tablet) so I'm not an anti-Android person. I also have an iPad (3rd generation currently) so I have something to compare it to -- and the comparison isn't even close. The iPad is a superior device in every single way, from the screen, to performance to apps to battery life.Here's my review.I had the retina iPad for a while before I picked up this tablet, I knew it wasn't a high resolution screen going in so it wasn't a shock but I was still surprised at how quickly I got use to the iPad screen, the Transformer screen doesn't compare at all. This is to be expected however so I'm not taking off any points, just giving a heads up for people making the jump.Since this is the latest and greatest from Nvidia I was expecting something that would match the iPad 3 performance, again this tablet doesn't even come close. It's flat out slow compared to the iPad 3. You can put it into 'performance' mode which helps a bit (but kills the battery faster) but it's still slow. Not sure if this is a hardware issue or an Android issue but I'm baffled at the sluggishness of the thing. I even did a factory reset to make sure there wasn't an issue, but it's exactly the same. This isn't to say it's as slow as the original Transformer or the original iPad, but surprisingly I'd say it's slower than the iPad 2, at least that's my feeling.Also speaking of the battery, this thing drains when the unit is off at an unbelievable rate if you have it plugged into the dock. It was so bad I returned the dock for a new one and it's exactly the same. Here's an example, if my iPad 3 is at 87% and I don't use it for 2 weeks when I pick it up again it will be at around 82% - after 2 weeks! For the Transformer, if it's in the dock, it dies within 2 days of not being used. Unbelievable. Without the dock it's better but still seems to drain at least 10-15% a day, meaning it will be dead within a week even if you don't use it at all. This is ridiculous - not sure if it's an Android issue or an Asus issue but someone needs to fix it.Let see, oh yes the Apps situation -- it's barely improved. Again and again applications just don't take advantage of the additional screen size of the tablets. The Android platform is still 95% based on phones and not tablets - it's a bad situation.Also the device feels cheap, yes it is cheaper than the iPad and if you touch both devices you'll know instantly which one is the cheaper one.Anything positive? The speakers are OK, but don't get very loud but they're acceptable. I like the idea of the keyboard dock with the mouse and I like that you can hook-up things like blue-tooth gaming pads - that is something the iPad really needs to allow, both the mouse if you have a keyboard attached and game pads.Summary - buy an iPad - it's better in every way. I own both platforms, I love my Google TVs but the Android tablets are just not very good, mainly due to the horrible software situation. I had an Nexus 7 for a while as well and had the same situation with the battery and apps (although the build quality was quite good). The iPad 3 or 4 is much faster, has a much much better screen, has a huge software library that actually takes advantage of the screen space and is always a much better to hold due to the 4:3 shape as opposed to the 16:9 or 16:10 shape of the Android tablets. In your hand something more squarish is easier to hold when you're talking about a 10" tablet, the longer the tablet the better for movies (in theory) but for everything else, and I mean everything, the 4:3 feels much more natural and is easier to hold.Again, I own this and I own an iPad -- I'm not an Apple fanboy and obviously I'm not an Android fanboy, I just want what is best I can get for my money and I can clearly state the iPad is a better device.

First the good:The laptop seems to be of reasonable build quality and seems fairly sturdy.  It doesn't flex when picked up by one side, the keyboard feels pretty solid, the lid has a nice, stiff hinge, and the display is decent. This will allow you to easily move files from your digital camera, digital video camera, or any other device that uses standard flash memory.  The reader does not support compact flash cards used in high-end digital cameras.Now for the bad:Maybe it is just a bad unit (and I certainly hope that this is the case), but there is a consistent issue where you are typing or looking at web pages and a new window will pop up over whatever you are doing, or the browser will change to a different page.  This happens without any intervention on the part of the user and is inexplicable.  You can get back to your previous window by pressing command-tab, but it is unusual to say the least.I am not fond of the keyboard layout at all, as I am accustomed to the keyboard on my 17" MacBook Pro, where the keyboard is located directly in the center of the computer.  The Acer has the keyboard offset to the side, due to the inclusion of the numeric pad on the right side.  The inclusion of a numeric pad is an excellent addition if you need to enter numbers frequently, as entry is considerably quicker with the 10-key pad, but I would argue that the majority of users would prefer a more comfortable main keyboard layout over the inclusion of a numeric pad.The offset keyboard causes me to mistype at times, as I am not used to the position.  This might not cause you any problems, so take this as my opinion only.I can not stand Windows 8.  There, I've said it.  I can't stand it and I cannot understand what Microsoft was thinking when they abandoned the standard desktop operating system in favor of a pseudo-tablet interface.  This is a giant misstep and it will not be accepted in a corporate environment at all, so I just don't get it.  There wouldn't be any problem at all if they offered an official shell that made it look and act like Windows 7.  The changes under the hood might be great, but the paint job is not good.The speakers on this laptop are on the bottom of the computer, so you will get extremely poor audio when using it on your lap, but not so bad when it is on a desk.  The speakers had to be placed on the bottom to accommodate the keypad, I suppose.  At any rate, don't expect good audio with this computer because you won't get it.Bottom Line: Worth a look, but not highly recommended3.5 out of 5 stars

I put this Kingston 128 gig SSD in my 5 year old laptop that had an old 5400 120 gig hard drive. It was kinda slow. My custom purple laptop has an AMD Turion 64x2 2000mhz processor and maxes out with 2 gigs of ram running Windows 7 64 Bit. I know that if I had a newer processor this drive would be even faster. I am pretty sure that my hard drive is faster than my ram.Everything that you know about what to do to configure Windows for a regular hard drive has changed. You do not want to use prefetch since the standard fetch is faster access than those pesky extra files created for a fast boot with a regular drive. With a regular mechanical spinning hard drive it took a few minutes to come out of sleep mode so I did not let it sleep. With the SSD it comes out of sleep state instantly. And you know how when your system has to move your currently accessed files to the swap file? Well now the swap file is FASTER than the regular ram. So I gave myself a very large swapfile so in reality I have added ram, reall random access memory, to my system.This bundle comes with a great external 2.5 inch hard drive case which I put my old hard drive in and now I have another little usb powered hard drive for free.For the past 14 years I have always spent more for Kingston ram in my computers because they never fail. So it was a natural choice to purchase my SSD from my favorite ram manufacturer. I was lucky because the week I bought my SSD there was a $55 mail in rebate which brought my price to a very reasonable $178. Be sure to do a Google search and find a reseller who is offering some kind of rebate. I usually always buy from Amazon but NewEgg had a $55 rebate so I pulled out my credit card and never looked back. Remember the cost of SSDs will only go down as time goes by and the sizes will become larger. This will happen fast. SSD is the future. Mechanical hard drives are a technology that has been around since IBM had room size hard drives in 1960.Of course it goes without saying that you do not want to store large amounts of data, movies and music on this drive. You should already have your priceless data on external hard drives and backed up.My 5 year old computer boots (after the bios loads) in 7 seconds and shuts down in 3 seconds. Everything happens instantly. You realize that your bottle neck is no longer your hard drive it is retrieving date from the Internet or your external hard drives.The future is here and now and the price is rapidly going down each month. You cannot do anything for any price that will speed up your laptop more than giving it a Solid State Drive.

I got a bottle of this free when I bought two regular OPI polishes.  I love the OPI polish.This top coat, however, is a real disappointment, and I would be furious had I paid the regular $12.00 retail for it.The biggest problem I have is that if you attempt to use a normal sized coat on top of your polish, the top coat's thickness, in conjunction with the brush, ruins the actual manicure!  I wind up having noticeable marks on my nails where application of the top coat actually removed my regular polish.  The first couple times it happened, I just assumed I didn't wait long enough for the regular polish to dry.  The next time I tried it, I waited a full five minutes and it still removed layers of polish (I had two coats applied - no base coat).  What this means is that in order to avoid removing, and ruining, your polish, you have to apply a really thick coat.Which leads us to our next problem.  Using a thick coat inevitably leads to air bubble formation underneath the top coat, again ruining my manicure.  Any attempt to apply a thin coat leads to the aforementioned polish removal, or streaks.Tonight, for example, I applied two coats of regular polish, and one of my regular top coat (more on that later).  After an hour or two, I decided to apply the OPI rapid dry top coat.  Now I have bubbles all over my nails, whereas before I applied the polish, the manicure was fairly perfect.  The bubbling is not an isolated problem.The last problem is that it honestly doesn't dry itself, or the under layers, as fast as it thinks it does.  My usual top coat dries faster and allows me to use and touch my nails within about a minute.Especially given the price tag on this one, I would skip it.  It really doesn't deserve to carry the OPI label, to be honest.  It doesn't hold a candle to the quality exhibited in their other products.Instead, try Sally Hansen Mega Shine.  It applies smooth, shines like crazy, and actually dries within the minute it claims to.  It leaves no streaks (and actually seems to self-correct streak mistakes I have made), it has never bubbled on me, and it even helps the undercoats dry quickly as well.

I ordered these to communicate with the rack of equipment in a closet. The transmission seems to work okay but it has a very small spread transmitting the IR signal to my equipment. It has to be directly facing the specific piece of gear I'm using rather than being able to broadly send out an IR burst like other repeaters do… The Logictech Harmony blaster, for example, can sit on a shelf in front of the receiver but also is able to control devices on the shelf below it and above it as well as a tv mounted higher up on the wall. This StarTech unit us basically useless to me… so if you just need to transmit to a single device or maybe two devices side by side then it may work for you but if you have a couple shelves of equipment then I'd say look elsewhere. The external IR port, to which I connected a second IR blaster, does work but the way this thing is built I'd need a port for every device -- not worth it.  Also the field of view for the transmitter device out where I am sitting is very narrow… I have to be angling my remote directly in front of it at "eye level" with the tiny window for it to even see the signal. Some remotes seem to not even be recognized by it… like the small wireless HDMI switcher remote I have.  Spend a little more and get something with more R&D behind it.

I find it difficult to get the cord in and out if the iPad is in the case, closed up against the keys.I see there is no camera hole, but since the iPad goes to sleep when you lay it glass side down against the keyboard, an internal magnet shuts it down, I suppose this is irrelevant.Really unhappy with the very short, 8.5 in (21 cm) charging cord the keyboard came with. I was at a big box store today checking out the Logitech Fold-Up Keyboard:Logitech Fold-Up Keyboard for iPad 2 (920-003544), as I was considering this instead of the case/keyboard I have now, and saw that their Logitech model 920-003402 has a longer charging cord than mine. I was told that the model I have (which has the same number on the box but not on the bottom of the keyboard itself) is a slightly older version and the cord is shorter in mine. So, despite the fact that the model number is the same, it's not really the same. It can be plugged into the iPad's charger too, but that cord is also too short for my liking. I'm going to return this one to where I bought it, or see if there's an extension cord that might work. I think Apple sells a longer charging cord for the iPad 2, which I find is also too short. Guess I'll have to get that.I don't know why Zagg or Logitech designed the charging cord to be like this. The small end looks like it's for a cell phone charger. I'm worried it might not last long, as others have reported. Also not happy there isn't a place for cord storage on or in the keyboard. I suppose if I get a neoprene case for it to fit into, the cord can slip in too. Otherwise, I'll have to design a better case myself.Presently, I'm using a Hempmania Hemp Travel Bag (PUR120-H) to carry my iPad 2 in. It's the perfect size for the iPad (or most any notebook computer or e-reader) with just about any case on it. These knives are very sharp and sturdy. In addition to all the other reviews, I wanted to point out a few things that may not be apparent prior to purchasing:1. The handles are all the same size and length for all four knives. If you're used to handles that are about the same length as the blade, this may come as a surprise. It's not a bad thing; it just takes some getting used to (especially with the smallest curved blue knife.)2. The blade is on the opposite side of what a novice might first think. (I don't know why, but many people think the curved side of the blade is the sharp side. It isn't. Don't cut your fingers.)3. There are two versions of this color four-piece paring knife set. One is made by J.A. Henckels (the higher quality brand made only in Germany) and the other by Henckels International (the value brand made in China.) They are not the same set of knives, but they look almost identical and come in similar packaging. I noticed that some of the reviewers had some negative comments, and I presume that they might have mistakenly been referring to the Henckels International version, widely available at Target, or possibly one of the many copycat versions not made by Henckels at all.Hope this note is helpful for those looking to purchase the right set of paring knives.Happy cooking!----------------Update 6/22/2011: After nearly three years of daily usage, the knives are still sharp without having sharpened them. We don't specially treat them, so they get tossed into the sink or washed in the dishwasher. As a result, or in spite of that, there's a tiny bit of rusting on the flat side of the blade where it meets the handle. Most of it can be scrubbed off. We tend to use the longer red and green knives for cutting sandwiches and fruit--small jobs. The yellow and blue ones are used when the others are not available. I'm thinking about getting the Kuhn Rikon Classic Serrated Utility Knives, Set of 3, as a replacement to the yellow and blue knives in this set, and to supplement the red and green.

The only way to get rid of that light is to tape over it (and if you're using tape to cover a supposedly stylish stand, then what's the point in shelling out for said stand?) or unplug it because the stand does not have a power switch.At first, I thought I made a good decision in purchasing this.  The N10 does not (as of this writing) have an OEM dock available, so this looked like a good substitute.  The pictures made it look like it would be able to handle my N10 and maybe a phone or something else like a champ.  It doesn't.  First, I like to have my tablets set in landscape mode when charging, and this stand is *just long enough* for that alone.  On top of that, and this isn't necessarily a ding on the Converge, but the POGO connectors are at the bottom of the tablet when docked in this position, so I had to turn it upside down and have the charger snaking out from the top.  To make things worse, and this is a direct ding on the Converge, it's frustratingly difficult to get the tablet to stay on the stand, in either landscape or portrait mode.  The plastic of this stand is unbelievably slick and the tiny strip of rubber at the bottom doesn't do nearly enough to hold gadgets in place.  You have to set your devices onto this stand very slowly and precariously because if it slips, it slips fast.  I found it's easier to balance my tablet on the stand in landscape mode and it was damn near impossible to get it to stay on in portrait mode.  The biggest problem I have with this stand is the fact that it puts out VERY little power to your device.  With nothing else but the N10 plugged into it, it still wasn't charging it at all.  I thought it might just be charging more slowly.  It wasn't.  It wasn't charging at all.  I had to unplug my charging cable from the USB port on the stand and directly into the wall.  So now I'm using the stand as just that--a simple stand.  And the thought of me having paid so much for a dumb simple stand is a little irritating.  I bought my product direct through the Quirky website and am just holding onto it rather than go through the hassle of trying to ship it back for a refund.This may work well with smaller gadgets/cameras/phones, but it didn't work for any of my devices.

I knew the moment I became a loyal Apple follower: the day I purchased this keyboard. I have a few Apple products that I use daily for work, including an Apple iMac and an Apple MacBook Pro. I didn't like just blogging on them for long periods of time, and I swear, they both just got heavier and heavier with every trip.I was going to get a clamshell keyboard for my iPad, and I found a few on Kickstarter that I really liked, but I needed a solution immediately, and not, you know, the mandatory 12 months it would take to build the clamshell keyboard of my dreams.The most logical thing was to pair my work Apple keyboard with my iPad and suck it up.Then one day, the idea struck for me to pair my iMac Apple keyboard with my iPhone. I can't believe that I never thought about it until that moment! Since I was holding out for the clamshell iPad keyboard of my dreams, I didn't want to buy an extra dock to connect the keyboard and iPad together, which made my set up extra bulky. And if you've ever ridden on the Caltrain, typing like this without a table is seriously not ideal. Anyway.Enter the magic ability to type on my iPhone! If you're a writer and you happen to love your iPhone, try out this set-up and see if it doesn't change your life. What I mean is, if I've connected the keyboard to my iPad, I can't connect it at the same time with the iPhone and just choose which machine I want to use it with. I have to select the "Forget this device" option, or "Disconnect" the keyboard from the iPad first, and only then, can I pair it with the iPhone. Secondly, I highly recommend getting Eneloop rechargeable batteries with it. They last a very long time without needing to go for a recharge.And then, the last note I'll make is that I've noticed that the reaction time between the Apple keyboard and the Apple iPhone is much better than my Logitech keyboard and the Apple iPhone. I could have just used my Logitech keyboard as my commuting device, but I decided that the connection lag and unresponsiveness of the Logitech keyboard with the iPhone in particular was enough for me to buy a second keyboard just for commuting. Plus, the JavoEdge keyboard cases were way too cute to pass up.

It is rather ironic that I am able to review the SOUL High Definition Noise Canceling Headphones by Ludacris at this time. The reason being is that I recently purchased another very high quality noise canceling headset, theBose QuietComfort 15 Acoustic Noise Cancelling Headphones NEWEST MODELa couple of weeks ago and have been using that every day. As a result, I've now had a chance to compare two different headphones, side-by-side. Overall, I have found the Ludacris to be well made and it looks rather cool, it's larger than the Bose but it's also very comfortable to wear. The ear cups fit comfortably over my ears and feel good.As expected, it's necessary to first install two AAA batteries prior to use. The battery compartment is located in the right ear cup (the left and right sides are clearly marked on the inside of the headset). In order to install the batteries, I had to read the instructions; otherwise, it would difficult to determine where they go as well as how to open the well-hidden compartment. Even then, it took a little bit of effort to get the compartment open. After installing the batteries, it's important to also set a switch inside the compartment to adjust for the sound levels of your output device. The default is set to "hi" and the manufacturer suggests that if you use very high output devices, you should set it to "lo" in order to "lower the overall output of [the] headphones". As I never play anything with very high output, I left it at the default setting. Replace the battery cover when finished and the SOUL is ready to go.In order to operate, there's a switch located on the left ear cup that needs to be turned on - it doesn't slide as easily as one might expect and this is disappointing. Once the headphones are turned on, a blue LED indicates it's ready for use. There is also a second button located on the inside of the headphone - the instructions indicated that this is the "headphone badge light button" - at first, I couldn't figure out what it does but after taking the headphones into a darker location, I noticed that the Soul Logo on each side of each of the ear cups lights up. I'm sure that the only reason for this is to make the headphones "look cool" during use. There is no indication as to how much this may tax battery life so I really don't use this "feature".While the headphones can be used alone for noise cancelling without listening to music, two "flat tangle free cables" are provided, along with a couple of adapters that may be used to connect to different devices, including use on an airplane. As a stand-alone noise cancelling headphone, the SOUL does a fairly good job. I can still hear a slight sound - similar to the "ocean" sound one might hear when placing a placing an ear to a seashell or the sound of air moving through the trees in a forest. Although it's very quiet, when compared to my Bose, it's certainly evident.I generally listen to music on my iPod so that's what I'll use to discuss my experience. Let me state upfront that I'm a classically trained musician so I usually listen to classical music. As these are new headphones, I tried to listen to really high quality recordings to write this review. One of those is a recording of theMozart: Violin Concerto No. 3; Symphony No. 41 "Jupiter"played by Itzhak Perlman. I'm afraid I was disappointed - the recording sounds rather muffled through the SOUL, it's almost as if the headphones are cutting out a lot of the higher overtones which takes away the brilliance in the music. Just to compare, I listened to exactly the same pieces with my Bose and the difference is very significant- the Bose simply sounds much better. I also tried different EQ settings on my iPod (just to make sure) and every time the Bose sounds better.  Listening to different music also produces the same results.Overall, this is a good headphone but as it is the same price as the Bose, I would consider that first. Had I not been able to compare the two side-by-side, my response might not have been as critical but there really is a significant difference between the two.Update: After I wrote this review, I had a couple of interesting questions and I wanted to respond to them in the review itself. The first question concerned whether or not these headphones were "properly burned-in". "Burning-in" is a process that appears to be nothing more than an urban myth and there is no research, none at all, on whether or not it makes a difference. It includes playing music or many other sounds (white noise, pink noise, "frequency sweeps", etc.) for an extended period of time in order to "break-in" the headphone by "loosening the diaphragm of a newly crafted headphone". Again, this is an urban myth and there has been no research to substantiate its effectiveness. Just the same, to appease those who suggest that this is important, I have "burned-in" the Soul headphones by playing many types of sounds (especially those that are freely available on the Internet that have been created specifically for this purpose) for many days. As I noted that the sound quality of my new Bose headphones are superior to the Soul (and I've only had those for a few weeks), I did not "burn-in" those - just to see if the Soul could "catch up" in sound quality. Considering this information, the Bose remains superior, in fact vastly superior, to the sound quality of the Soul. I've spent a considerable amount of time going back and forth between the two headsets and, in my opinion, the Bose is far better. Specifically, the Soul lacks clarity and is "muddy" when compared to the Bose. I've listened to many pieces of music - again, I'm a classically trained musician and have played professionally for many years. The Bose allows each nuance to be heard while the Soul covers up many of the subtleties in the music. I'm not saying that because I have any reason to like one over the other - in fact, I wished that the Soul was better as I received a review set and I paid full price for the Bose. If the Soul was better, I wouldn't think twice about returning the Bose. Unfortunately, I can't do that because the Bose is superior - and I'm now convinced of that.Another question concerned how the Soul compares to the Bose when noise canceling is shut off. Shutting off the Soul decreases the volume and the overall sound quality is less. The Bose must be used with noise canceling on - it's not possible to listen to music if it's not. This brings up another issue - batteries. The Soul requires two and the Bose only needs one. I've really grown to dislike the battery compartment on the Soul as it is frustratingly difficult to get off - I think this is a significant design flaw - especially for a $300 headphone. It is much easier to replace the single battery in the Bose.Overall, the Soul remains a good, comfortable headphone but when compared side-by-side with the Bose QuietComfort, the Bose is superior. I wish that weren't true as I could have saved $300.

I was attracted to this sheet set from the outset because of the color. This is a nice, rich color which could go well with a masculine bedroom palette.But that is where the attraction stops.It's odd that this product made it through U.S. customs, because according to several sources I found online, it's against the law to sell a finished consumer product without disclosing the fiber content (cotton, wool, poly, etc.) on that product by labeling or packaging. NOWHERE on this product does it say what these sheets are made from. Sorry, Lamma, but "micro fiber" does not cut it. I'm guessing it's a cotton-poly blend and the fact that they say to wash in cool water means either all stitching is done with cotton thread (which will pucker when washed in warm/hot water) or there is some cotton content which will shrink the fabric a bit. These are made in China and that's about all the info you get otherwise. The 1500 means virtually nothing, it's certainly not the thread count. I compared a pillow case with another 400-thread count pillow case I own under a magnifying glass and it isn't even a close match. I'd say at most this is 150 thread count.The embroidery on the pillow cases is at best uneven. On one pillow case, there is a big flaw right in the middle where the needle simply stopped for a moment. As well, the thickness of this effect varies greatly across the width of the pillow case.Upon removing them from the washer (washed to get the manufacturer-applied sizing out) there were quite a few threads I had to snip. Compared to a normal set of sheets where there may be one or two. I washed these in cold water and dried them on low yet there was quite a bit of puckering on the hems of all pieces.Yes, these sheets are soft and I'll use them on the queen bed at my summer cottage. But they are rather thin. Hopefully, if they are MOSTLY cotton and not all poly, I'll stay cool on them during the months when I'm residing there. I've tested out the pillow cases here and they seem rather comfortable to lay your face on.Unfortunately, I cannot give this product high marks because savvy consumers these days want to know what things are made from. This is a mystery product in that regard and nobody likes to sleep on mystery fabric, especially given the high number of allergy sufferers there are these days.Three stars, one for color, one for softness and one for price. Two stars taken away for mystery fabric and poor workmanship.UPDATE:  No more mystery!  I cut a tiny piece of the fabric from the inside of the pillowcase cuff (easy to repair) and did the burn test with a lighter. It melted instead of burned, and that usually means 100% man-made. I'm guessing brushed polyester or a blend with very little cotton. Even so, this stuff reminds me of stone-washed silk, it's very smooth and light. Expect them to last a long time, but I wouldn't use them on the bed in summer or in hot climates.

After 3 weeks of using this camera (and tons of research), I am very impressed.  The image quality is far superior than any other point & shoot camera, and IMO better than most DLSRs.  I've even seen the DP1 create better photos than a $4500 Canon setup and a $2500 Olympus set up.But even if other companies started putting larger sensors into small bodies, I would still buy another Sigma.  Why?  Because of the Foveon sensor!I was almost discouraged from buying this camera due to many of the negative comments about poor speed and lack of features.  Now I am very happy that I went ahead and bought the Sigma DP1.I understand some customer disastisfaction with the slower in-camera image processing speed, limit of rapid fire shots, and lack of face/smile recognition.  Yes, this camera is lacking some of the modern bells and whistles of the digital camera age.  Rather than a major con, however, I see it as something positive.This camera forces the photographer to slow his itchy trigger finger and be present with the subject.  Being forced to slow down returns the photographer to the simple beauty of photography.  The fine details of the subject and the camera settings become important again.  The removal of "auto-everything" features restore the magic of photography and imbue the photos with individual personality.The Foveon sensor is simply amazing.  When compared to every other Bayer-sensored DSLR (Canon, Nikon, etc), the over-saturated cartoonishly fake colors become very apparent.  Foveon sensors capture real color, while Bayer sensors guesstimate colors with mathematics.  In this age of simulated reality (TV shows, Hollywood blockbusters, XBox 360), the DP1 may seem a bit out of place.  But I prefer to capture the natural beauty of our lovely world and not some artificial reconstruction.If you want a simple and authentic camera, then the Sigma DP1 may very well be for you.  I've read a few stories of loyal film photographers finally taking the plunge to digital with the DP1, and being very pleased.However, if you want to shoot 1,000 photos of your son's soccer game and skip the post processing, then go with another brand.  You may get frustrated with the patience and peace of using such a simple camera.But you'll miss the amazing photos!

I've managed to keep my Windows 98 system stable for over five years now, mostly through a rigorous and sometimes annoying process of keeping my system files safe, my registry clean, and the startup files to a minimum.  I thought I might even set a world record for "longest use of a Microsoft product without a major system crash."  Unfortunately, this diminuitive little terror was too much for my poor system and it finally gave up the ghost.I bought the Netgear MR814 router and two of these MA101 adapters; one for my Win98 system and another for my WinXP system.  I will say the router installed without a hitch.  These things on the other hand are junk, to put it mildly, and the tech support staff were about as helpful as a blindfold.First off, the Win98 system just could not recognize the device upon startup.  It would show up in the device manager but as disabled.  The only way to get it working was to remove the device, reinstall it, and reconnect to the network every time I started the computer.  Even this process was slow and annoying, taking well over two minutes while the system hangs and tries to figure out what this foreign object is.  Based on the other reviews here, you will note that I'm not the only reviewer that has had this problem.Tech support?  Well, this can take anywhere from five to forty-five minutes and, assuming you're not hung up on, you might as well start dialing the instant you have problems.  Reason?  Even though I told the techs repeatedly that I've done all the "basic" troubleshooting like removing and reinstalling drivers, removing, unplugging, and reinstalling the device, etc... they make you go through the entire process anyway.  After three separate calls, totalling an hour and a half of hold time and another hour and a half of reinstalling things, the best the tech could say was "reinstall Windows."  This is techspeak for "I have no clue."  Against my better judgement, I did it anyway except Windows messed up the reinstall.  One computer dead, one to go.I'm "happy" to report the WinXP computer did install the device but there was just one slight problem.  It could recognize the network and even saw the router's SSID, but it would not connect to it.  Here we go again.  After two different phone calls, and a lot of inane disconnecting and reconnecting, the best the techs could tell me was it was due to interference.  Strange, considering my other computer could recognize the network fine before meeting its untimely death and it's the same distance from the router.  Again, techspeak for "I have no clue."  Ironically, I did manage to get it to work after I hung up on the tech.  Don't ask me how because I really don't know.So now, after the added expense of a Windows XP "upgrade" and the loss of an entire weekend, I have my network set up.  One final problem.  If I try any WEP encryption keys, I will lose the connections on both computers.  I was able to get the router to allow access to these two computers only. Assuming this actually works, that should be secure enough, but I'm still not too keen about all my data passing back and forth unencrypted.Hopefully this review will convince you to look elsewhere.

I have had the 3 TB unit for about 20 days now.  I have set up several users, and I have set up a backup schedule.  Overall it is a good unit, but backup is not 100% reliable.I can get to the unit remotely from my android phone and android tablet, and it is reasonably fast.Set up was easy and only took less than an hour including downloading and installing all the applications.  I had to reboot the router before the WD drive could be detected by other network devices.For a test, I set up several users.  I gave the users some of their own "share", and some directories were shared by all users.  I was able to log in as each user, and got to the directories (shares) which they were set up to use.  So, setting directories (shares) and security for users and shares all work fine.I tested the security of the unit as much as I could, and I did not see an obvious way one can get into areas they are not allowed to get to, but I am not a hacker either.  So, security seems to be without a problem based on my limited testing.The major issue is the backup application.  I set up a backup schedule.  The data to backup was about 41 GB.  It took about 4.5 hours for the backup to complete which is slow.  This backup job was set up as "Continues" back up.  Continues backup does not work for Microsoft files, such as Outlook and Word which I tested.  During the past 20 days, it has detected about 5% of the times when the Outlook file has changed.  So, about 95% of times it does not back up MS files when they are changed.  It is better with add and delete than it is with update.  My Outlook file (outlook.pst) has changed about 200 times (most of it intentionally for testing) during the past 20 days, and it has only backed it up 4 times so far.  This is not acceptable.I upgraded the WD SmartWare to the pro version.  After the upgrade and a reboot, I noticed that the backup application started running constantly.  The rolling horizontal bar under the Backup tab started rolling, and it showed "Copying files...".  I also noticed that the backup process was using about 25-35% of the CPU time.  This went on for hours and actually for the whole time PC was on that day.  This continued for about 2 days, and I finally disabled the backup job.  During the 2 days that this was going on no backup took place.  Nothing was being backed up.  A day after I disabled the backup, I decided to enable it again to see what happens.  It started up again, but the ad "Upgrade to WD SmartWare Pro" appeared again.  This means that somehow and by itself, it went back to the regular version.  However, this fixed the constantly running problem.  Application wasn't running constantly now, and everything went back to the way they were before the upgrade to the Pro version.  Backup of MS files still didn't work, but backing up of other files started working again.I called WD and talked to level 2 support about this, and he did not believe this was a problem.  He said that backup of Outlook.pst files should be every 24 hours even if you have selected Continues backup.  The problem is that it doesn't even back up every 24 hours either.  Last backup of my Outlook.pst file was 6 days ago.The workaround/trick in making your Word and Excel files to back up is to let Word or Excel do the save when you exit Word or Excel.  I have a habit of hitting the "save" button from inside of Word or Excel once every few minutes when I am editing a file, and when I exit the file, there may be nothing to save since I had done a manual save myself.  If you follow this habit, WD will not backup the file you changed.  To get WD to backup Word/Excel files, press exit and let Word/Excel ask you if you want to save your changes, select "Save", and then WD will most likely backup that file after you have exited Word/Excel.  Level 2 support saw this as the way backup should work.  I see this as a workaround for a software bug.  Especially since WD backup works if you manually update a text file, but not MS files.  Unfortunately, this trick does not work for Outlook.pst since you don't have any control over when and how Outlook updates its file.I also set up a backup job from another PC (Windows7-32bit), and results were the same.  MS files do not get backed up each time they are changed.The other issue I noticed is the speed.  I didn't run any benchmark programs, so what I am writing is only my observation, and what Windows displays during copy.  The values below are read and write speeds from a wired and a wireless connected PC to the network.  This was one single file and it was about 349mb in size.  Router is Netgear WNDR3400 - N600 Dual Band.Wireless PC (Windows7-32bit):Read = about 3 MB/secondWrite = about 2.6 MB/secondWired PC to Router (Windows7-64bit):Read = about 11.4 MB/secondWrite = about 11.4 MB/secondI will update if any of the above changes, or if I find out I have done something wrong to cause any of the above issues.

After reading customer service problems with Jambox, I bought my wife a Jabra Solemate for Christmas.  She wanted to use her iPhone 4s for music and as a speakerphone in her office at work.  The Solemate ($150) works perfectly.  After a couple days, she said to me, "You've got to get one of these for yourself."  Well, we can't really afford two $150 Bluetooth speakers, so I searched for something less expensive.  I found this one.First thing.  Unlike others, this does NOT use a USB-based adapter/charger, but rather it uses a conventional AC adapter and AA batteries.  That means you can't power it with a USB port on the computer, a USB AC Adapter, or a USB car adapter, and that's an inconvenience by modern standards.  Also, the AC adapter is just that.  It will power the device, but it is not a charger.  You could use rechargeable AA batteries in this, but you'll have to charge them separately.As a speakerphone, this device is only OK.  Speakerphone volume (with iPhone 4s) is so low, you have to turn the volume up all the way.  That means, when you get a call, you must quickly hit the volume up and hold it until it hits max.  Then when you hang up the call, just as quickly turn the volume back down, or music will be too loud.  I suppose if you had a phone with separate volume controls for phone and music, this could work better.  iPhone has one volume control, though.The sound is pretty good, albeit not the quality of the $150 Solemate.  Buttons on top of the device are handy.  Rewind-Pause/Play-FF, Volume down/up, Bass Boost, Stereo widening, PTT, and Power.  Bass Boost has fairly little, but noticeable effect.  Stereo widening, similarly, has little effect--mostly reduces volume and leaves a "hole" in the center of the sound.  PTT is for pairing and then to answer or ignore an incoming call.Pairing with the iPhone is easy enough, and the pairing survives the device being turned of and on again. It doesn't have voice prompts and confirmations like the Solemate, but at least the pairing instructions are on a label on the back of the device.  I also tried this briefly with an iPad, with which it also connected easily enough--given the usual Bluetooth constraints (disconnect from one before connecting to another).  iTunes music played fine.  Netflix movie sound comes through very well on the iPad.Bottom line:  If you're buying this mainly to listen to music or movies on a phone or tablet, it works well enough for about 37% of the price of the Solemate.  For music and movies, I'd give it 4 stars (one off for the old-style power).  As a speakerphone device for the iPhone, it's somewhat limited due to speaker volume issues.

I am new to the whole coffee/espresso scene; probably a carry-over from being raised Mormon as a kid. I therefore did some research on espresso makers, which brought me to this unit. I'm still trying to perfect my skill, but the machine is user-friendly.Unlike a lot of standard coffee makers, this unit is small (about the size of a toaster, turned on its side), so it doesn't take up a lot of room on the counter. The contents were packaged well, and once it was out of the box, there wasn't a lot of set-up required. It was necessary to wash/clean everything thoroughly, however, as it had a metallic/industrial smell. Once I had it cleaned and flushed, this went away.The volume of espresso produced is small, so you want to have an appropriate cup on hand. Otherwise, you'll have a standard teacup with what appears to be two tablespoons of liquid in it.Per the recommendation of others on this site, I bought a separate tamper. There is a tamper attached to the unit, but it's in an awkward position, and I like having an external one to use. The unit does not come with a frothing pitcher, so buy one at the same time you buy the unit if you intend to make steamed milk. The positioning of the frothing tube is also somewhat low, which requires good coordination in order to make steamed milk without having it spill out (I'm still working on this one).I also researched which coffee to buy, and I ended up buying Lavazza, as this is the product most reviewers on Amazon raved about. I bought Lavazza on Amazon, and though expensive (I think it was over $25 for 2.2 pounds), you have the option of joining a 'coffee club,' whereby they'll send you the coffee on an interval schedule at a discount. The Lavazza brand is very good, but being a novice to all of this, I can't really compare it to other products.Overall, this unit is easy to set-up, use, and clean. Again, make sure you have the appropriate cup size on hand, and if steaming milk, you'll need a tamper.

I've been in the market for a fast 50mm lens and heard that Sigma might be an excellent alternative to the expensive Canon 50mm L-series lens. And unfortunately, I'm still in the market for a professional 50mm as this model isn't reliable enough for what I mainly do: weddings and photojournalism.The biggest problem this lens is the unreliable focusing. I tested it on the 1D Mark IV and no matter which of the 45 points I used, it would have issues, especially at the edges. Front-focus, back-focus, "hunting", all kinds of issues that would happen somewhat randomly. Sometimes it would lock-on and be TACK SHARP, but then the next frame would be soft. While the image quality was very surprising and excellent, the AF was unreliable enough to make it unsuitable for professional use.Another issue was the image softness at the edges below f/2.8. Now, I'm not expecting the world and for it to sing and dance for me, but the softness is very apparent when you view the photos on your computer. Couple that with unreliable focus and any off-center photos will be unusable. All lenses are soft(er) at the wider apertures, but this one in-your-face.This lens isn't garbage, when it does focus, you get excellent results with incredible separation and smooth bokeh. The in-focus images were so nice, I almost overlooked the AF problems. They were that good.It is true what people say about this lens from Sigma: if you get a good copy, you'll love it. Otherwise, return it.I have to rate it 3-stars mainly because of its unreliable focusing. The edge softness I can deal with as a "quirk." But I cannot afford to upset a bride or an editor because I missed a moment due to focusing issues.

Intel/Apple created the problem with the Thunderbolt spec, and Seagate, rather than simply build a drive that has a Thunderbolt connector, has added to it by choosing to make a little box into which the drive slides, adding a little weight to the overall package. Before ordering this, I searched for any clue that there was or was not a Thunderbolt cable included in the box. The product number supplied by Amazon doesn't exist on the Seagate website, and the product description on the Seagate website said no cable was included. So I ordered one separately, to be prepared. I didn't need it: there's one in the box.The drive arrives mounted to the adapter, but it must be disconnected to remove all the shrinkwrap, so it's not clear why the shrinkwrap was needed. Indeed, one has to wonder whether the speed claims justify the creation of the adapter at all.There are no instructions to speak of other than a picture showing the drive plugged into the cable and a computer, but if you are buying this, you probably already know how it operates. The Mac recognized the drive instantly and it was ready for use. I did not install Seagate's software pending a decision on whether or not it will be useful.After twenty minutes, I decided to disconnect the drive and resume testing later. I was surprised at how hot the cable was on the Mac end when I touched the Thunderbolt connector. Given that I had done no real file transfers in either direction, the cable really hadn't any reason for becoming warm.I will update this review after a bit more testing. On balance, however, I'm not yet enthusiastic about using a drive that requires a double connection to work. Perhaps transfer speeds will justify this approach.

These are surprisingly good headphones at a great price. Considering the price, it doesn't get much better than these headphones.As a replacement for the cheap earbuds that come with most devices, these are an excellent upgrade. The sound is warm, with a good deep bass. Midrange is particularly nice, vocals are crisp and clear. Highs are slightly rolled off softening the detail just a bit. The soundstage is nice. Instruments are pretty well defined. If I had no idea how much these cost, I would put them in that medium level quality of headphones, similar to the $60 price point.The construction is solid. I like the black matte rubber insulation on the wires. The headphone has a good rubber coating where the wires enter the speaker. I really like the design of the speaker portion. They fit nicely and end up flush with the outside of my ear, perfect for sleeping. They stay put in my ear and seal up well to block out external noise. There are a set of pretty standard silicone rubber ear tips. It is important to use exactly the right size for your ear. Getting a good seal improves bass response dramatically.The jack is always a balancing act between easy to insert, protection of the wire, and compact size to fit cases. RHA chose a beefy rubber over the jack. The end of the jack is at about a 45 degree angle. I have a difficult iPhone case - the headphone jack is deeply recessed and there isn't a lot of clearance for the jack case. This jack just barely fits into my case. This would never be a problem with no case on an iPhone or iPad. There is no problem with my Otterbox case on my iPad.The packaging is one of those neat things. It is simple and light cardboard box, with a cardboard insert, and a minimum of plastic bags. The green footprint of these speakers must be small. RHA has worked hard to get the packaging exactly small enough and still protect the headphones. It won't look pretty on the shelf, but it is super nice arriving mail order.My frame of reference for these headphones is a wide range - from high end Shure and B&W;, through midrange Sennheiser and Dr. Dre Beats, to low end JLab, Skullcandy, and JBL. These are nowhere near the quality of those high end headphones, but at 1/10 the price, wow they give them a run for their money. They are significantly better than the similarly priced JLab, Skullcandy and JBL headphones.In some ways I like these better than the more expensive RHA MA350's. I like the rubber insulation on these wires; it feels good in my hand. No noise is transmitted into the headphones. Bass is deeper and these sound warmer.For the price, these are impressive headphones. They are a great upgrade from standard equipment from device manufacturers.The manufacturer provided me with a review sample.

I've used the Garmin Nuvi 1350 GPS for a month, including a road trip through the west coast US and Canada.Pros:- GPS works well most of the time - I found it easy to follow with clear voice annunciation of upcoming turns. The GPS did "get lost" when in downtown areas with high buildings.- A cool feature allows you to display the speed limit beside your actual speed. I found this very accurate throughout California, Oregon and Washington states, but doesn't work for Canadian roads.- Garmin phone support is good and they worked with me to solve several problems with their update softwareCons:- Updating the unit's maps is a hassle. First, you need to buy a USB-miniUSB cable specifically for data. To get the current maps and device software you must download a proprietary Garmin Communicator Plugin to your computer. The plugin is problematic on Apple Mac computers - I experienced this and Garmin's support rep admitted this fact. After at least an hour on the phone with Garmin support I finally had to revert to Windows XP and go through a cumbersome process to get the updates downloaded, which took another hour.- The unit works entirely by touch screen, but doesn't respond well to finger touches - often not responding, or responds as though I had touched something else near to where I touched. I found it worked best if I touched the screen only with a hard object like a pen.- Their search and points-of-interest references are woefully out of date. For example, when searching for fuel stations it listed numerous locations that have been CLOSED FOR OVER A DECADE. I also found their business search database to be very limited, usually showing the "spinning hourglass" for several minutes before I gave up.- The unit had several intermittent software bugs, like: toggling between full color maps and one color maps at random; mysteriously rebooting itself while driving; and occasionally telling me to take a meandering and time-consuming route when there were much more direct and safer routes available.- The in-vehicle power cord plug makes a high-pitched squeal. I tried exchanging it twice and they all made the same noise. My car is quiet inside so I found this bothersome.- Battery life is short (less than three hours) when not plugged into a power source if you want to use it on a bicycle or on foot.- The display is almost impossible to read in direct sunlight.
Not sure that it is a bad product, but the screen didn't look clear anymore, so I pulled it off and threw it out.

I no longer relish the hassle of carrying several lenses with my SLR camera. After deciding to purchase a bridge camera, I agonized over the wide variety of cameras available. Finally, I vacillated between the Fujifilm HS35EXR, the Fujifilm HS50EXR, Canon SX40, the Nikon P520 and this camera, the manual zoom Fujifilm XS-1.I have always used film manual focus SLR cameras, and my favorite camera was the Canon EF (the 70's model). That (all metal) camera epitomized ruggedness, versatility and ergonomics. Considering reviews of questionable image quality of the HS cameras, and being put off by the somewhat fragile feel of the Canon and Nikon, I decided to purchase the XS-1. I believe I made the correct decision.After reading stories on photography forums about XS-1s from Amazon, I had worried about receiving a camera which had been opened and returned for whatever reason. I ordered my camera from Amazon.com, so I cannot speak to units sold by their partners. My camera came in a sealed bag, as did the USB cable, the battery and strap. Upon startup, my camera prompted for the initial language, time and menu setups. There were no signs of previous usage. I was ELATED that I didn't have to return the camera.For a person coming from the older SLR cameras, the XS-1 feels nice and substantial. The machined metal knobs, the weight of the camera, and that large piece of glass in the front give the camera an air of quality and durability. The XS-1 doesn't have that "toy camera" feel of some of the other point and shoot models. I have read of issues with the XS-1 like the lens drooping at full zoom. I am happy to report that my camera - a 33 serial number- has very little play at full extension. I compared it to the wobble of my well-kept EF manual Canon telephoto at full zoom and the play was similar. There is no perceptible droop. The manual zoom is very smooth and a joy to use. For my own use, I find it much easier to find my desired framing with the manual zoom rather than pulling a button back and forth in order to find the sweet spot. The electronic viewfinder is bright and startlingly clear and offers adjustment for clarity. The back screen is large, clear and details are rendered very well. There are buttons scattered everywhere for quick access to the various functions . I have read complaints that these buttons tend to feel sticky, but on my camera I must honestly say I cannot find a single fault. Every function of the camera seems to work flawlessly. The build of this camera just gives the reassurance of quality.One area of which potential users of this camera ought to be aware is in the XS-1's complexity. While the EXR mode promises to allow the user a point and shoot experience, the myriad of options the camera offers is daunting. Each mode is seemingly customizable by the user. The XS-1 is wonderfully versatile! For the photographer who wants a tool that will grow with the user, you couldn't pick a better bridge camera. The lens will astound the user with its reach and it is faster than my Canon telephoto. I believe it will take me weeks just to get the gist of this camera.I must admit that I haven't yet taken images using all the modes, so I can't speak to the full abilities of the camera. I have used the EXR mode and plan to more thoroughly explore the Auto modes in the days to come. So far, the results I've achieved are stunning! I'm truly surprised at how good are the images made by this camera. I've mostly shot in reasonably bright light, and the camera has been a solid performer. The EXR mode seems to be a good all-round choice for point and shoot (even it can be tweaked to the user's satisfaction!), but for those with an artistic bent there are customizable presets, Auto, aperture and shutter- select modes, full manual and I'm sure some other modes I've yet to find! This camera is a keeper and seems built to serve me for years to come.I was pleased to find that Fuji provided an actual PAPER user's manual with the camera. It may sound like a small detail, but having book in hand provides quick reference when you're in the deep woods and you've forgotten how to delete a picture, what that button does, or how to compensate for exposure in low light. The manual reads like "War and Peace", so be prepared to curl up a bit with your new buddy's how-to guide.I've tried to think of areas in which the camera is lacking. Were someone wanting to take it hiking long distances, the XS-1's weight might be a detriment. To me it's heft is not only reassuring, but actually helps steady my aim. I've read that the lens produces soft images at full zoom. Perhaps so, but honestly, I'm just a middle-aged shade tree photographer. At a 624mm equivalent zoom, the image will suffer more from my shaky hands than any lens softness! I'm certain that whatever photos the camera produces will be better than I could achieve with my old Canon. To be truthful, I'm reaching for cons here, folks!The price from Amazon was EXCELLENT and the shipping was QUICK (although in full disclosure I must say the packing of the camera was poor- the XS-1 box was sliding back and forth with negligible padding inside an oversized shipping box).You will need an SD card (I chose a Class 10, but the manual says you can use Class 4 and above) and an extra battery is advisable. The camera comes with a reasonably good strap, the charger, battery, CD ROM with the Fuji software, lens cap, a metal lens hood, and USB cable.I am absolutely delighted with the Fujifilm XS-1! The only way it could make me happier is if it provided its own swimsuit model! ;)

The RAID management software for this unit on OS X has serious problems. As part of the install for their OS X "RAID Master" utility (current and most recent version rev358), they install copies of apache 2.2.22, php 5.3.16, openssl 1.0.1f. apache server is configured to listen on port 8848, and presents a RAID configuration interface.Problems:* The server listens to port 8848 on all interfaces.* The web service is unauthenticated. A network attacker or unprivileged local user can alter or destroy a RAID array using a regular web browser.* The web service does not sanitize browser input before concatenating it to a shell command and executing. At multiple points in ajax.php, a remote user can execute arbitrary shell commands as the 'daemon' user if he or she is willing to alter the RAID array as a side effect. Shell commands can be concatenated on each argument to the RAID setup.* The web service does not protect against CSRF. Third-party pages can manipulate the RAID if a user merely browses to any web page embedding RAID commands.* The bundled versions of apache2, php5 and openssl all contain multiple vulnerabilities, including further potential for remote users executing arbitrary code. There is no update mechanism in place, nor have they provided newer builds.* The RAID configuration utility does not advise the user that it is opening a service on all ports (or even disclose that it is installing a web server in the first place). Users may not realize that they are exposing a vulnerable service on the local network, or installing web services that need updates.* Security issues aside, the RAID configuration utility stops working 30 days after installation with a "License has expired" error. To avoid reinstalling the same version of the same software every 30 days, I had to alter the software. (Look at the IsExpired function in /usr/share/odm/home/*/ajax2.php if you want to fix your own copy - "default" is the choice if using English). The disabled state does NOT remove the security vulnerabilities above, it only prevents browsing the user interface.* No uninstaller is provided. Advanced knowledge is necessary to remove the software and the security problems it introduces.My recommendation is that you wait for other similar Thunderbolt RAID solutions until they get this under control.My original review:Title: Great performance, not quiet, some problems with SSDsStars: 3I would love for this enclosure to have worked out for me. Performance is wonderful, licking at just shy of 800 megabytes per second in both read and write with four SSDs in a RAID 0. But some noise and SSD recognition problems are deal breakers for my own desktop use.This unit is not quiet. If you put it behind an iMac, it still sounds several times louder than the iMac with the GPU and CPU fans running at full tilt. With the lid off, the fan is an acceptable low hum, but with the protective lid on it reverberates at a higher and inconsistent pitch. If you are looking for something as quiet as your Mac, this is not the RAID for you. It sounds like a commodity PC power supply.There is also a problem with SSDs (and possibly other hard drives with quick startup time) used in a JBOD configuration. When multiple drives come online quickly, they are not reported to the OS. It's necessary to pull and reinsert each unidentified drive one at a time in order to get them to be recognized by the OS. This behavior was consistent with Samsung 1TB 840 EVO, Crucial 960GB M500 and Intel 480GB 730 SSDs. I could not find a combination that consistently powered on properly. If you're using SSDs, you do not want to use this enclosure for JBOD.The Thunderbolt ports are recessed. This isn't a problem with the supplied cable, or with Apple's cables. It actually protects these plugs against shearing force. But be warned that many third-party Thunderbolt cables with wider shrouds will not fit. Given that the size of the shroud is part of the Thunderbolt spec, these third-party cables are technically non-compliant, however they are plentiful. Be careful about cable selection. The protective feature can cause a wasted cable order.Curiously, this enclosure includes a canvas-like carrying tote with a very tight fit. It was a clever and surprising extra that gave me a really positive impression initially. However the carrier isn't big enough to include the power supply and thunderbolt cable as well, or not without leaving the RAID itself squeezed part-way out of the tote.Also of note: One SSD/2.5" rail set is included. I didn't see this documented anywhere, and so I ordered four SSD kits directly from the manufacturer. I only needed to order three.

I've owned the 880 for more than a year. It is the first remote my wife and I have both found simple to use and simple to set up. I could quibble about the buttons being too small, but overall the remote is a good product.The failing grade is the result of a miserable piece of junk that is called the cradle/battery charger. It is a disaster. If you're lucky, you'll get one that actually charges the remote. Or you might get one that is fiddly and that takes shifting it around until you finally get a charge going.Or you might suffer through a frequently discharged battery because someone walked through the room with a heavy foot -- and then find yourself with a charger that is dead and not easy to replace if at all. Mine failed completely after making me miserable for a most of the time I;ve owned the 880.The design concept might or might not have been good, but the execution in any event is bad.  You can look on all sorts of forums and you'll find this is a common problem. Among myself and three friends who bought this remote, only one of us received a charger cradle that has worked with some consistency. And it's not great. That's only 25 percent. A local video store says it carries this remote but actively discourages its purchase because of this problem. They do recommend other Harmony remotes.I also have a Harmony 720, a Costco special. It does most of what the Harmony 880 does, i.e. it has less backlighting and small things. It costs a good bit less. And wonder of all, it has a cradle that at least consistently charges the battery. It works.In fact, were it not for the 720, I would have had to toss the 880. I use it to charge the 880 battery (the batteries can be swapped between the two). The design uses only two contact points and it does not require a lot of fiddling about.But I would not buy either of those remotes again despite their capability. The battery charger issue and Logitech's failure to stand behind its products is just too frustrating. This is a competitive field and there are other remotes with better support in terms of quality control.The only point here is that if you buy the remote, you'll like it. If you're lucky, you'll get a battery charger that works correctly. The 880 is a little like a Ferrari with an empty gas tank and no service station for a thousand miles.
