The selling points of this particular camera, for me, are the 720p@60 and 1080p@30 video modes.  The 720p@60 in particular (60 frames per second), is ideally suited for fast action.  It also has the widest field of view.  The 1080p@30 is an interesting alternative, for its higher resolution and less wide field of view.Also critical to my purchasing, was that the battery would last over 2 hours, as I want to record, without intervention -- as that's not practical -- for about that long (up to 2 hours).Unfortunately, I found out that the 720p@60 video mode crashes or stops recording after about 29 minutes!  After spending (wasting) hours of my time, I found out on different forums, that this is a common -- I suspect universal -- problem with this camera. I believe I read it may also be a problem with the other 60 frames per second, lower resolution, mode as well.There's some confusion because there are a _lot_ of complaints about problems with different SDHC cards.  For example, there is one forum thread that lists cards that work (finding one that does is an issue), and others then contradict the list and post that they _don't_ work!In my case, I'm using the SDHC card that is actually recommended and is used by GoPro.  I've systematically tested the 720p@60 and 1080p@30 modes.  The 1080p mode runs till the battery runs out.  The 720p@30 does the same.  But, the 720p@60 consistently crashes at 29 minutes +- a few seconds.  It does so after it begins the 2nd video file.  This is probably a problem with the camera design/firmware.Beyond the above, there is another feature (the ability to select up or upside-down recording) that is supposed to be available in a firmware upgrade.  There are no available firmware upgrades for this camera.  Other's have been waiting and waiting and waiting for GoPro to release an upgrade and it's one of those any-day-now things.  This is Spring and the camera has been out for a good while.  So, who knows when or if there will be such an upgrade.Bottom-line: I recommend to _not_ buy this camera until an actual firmware upgrade is released, and there are reports that it, at least, fixes the 720p@60 video mode recording problem.  This is a POV action camera.  It's a fundamental flaw that it can't record in its optimal video mode for more than 29 minutes without manual intervention.Another complaint... the camera can only be mounted when it is in its water proof housing.  This adds significantly to its weight and bulk (and awkward appearance).  For some uses, the waterproof housing makes sense.  For many other uses -- such as inside a car or cockpit or any non-wet or damaging environment -- it doesn't.  The camera itself, without the housing, is small.  But there's no way to mount it -- it doesn't even have the standard tripod screw opening that other cameras have.  So, I'm scratching my head trying to figure out a way to use the camera without its housing (and protect the lens w/out the housing-- it doesn't even have a lens cap)... yet another problem to be solved.

I've tried numerous times to get the video review upload to take, but it never works, so I'm just going to write a review...First of all, the problems with autofocus are real. It's quite unbelievable that Microsoft would release a product that literally has to re-focus every minute, or less.  When I say re-focus, it literally racks itself from one end of the focus spectrum to the other, blurring you severely when it does.  Horrible!  This seems to happen most when recording on 720p, and not so much on lower resolutions.  As mentioned, to remedy this, you have to turn the True Color function off, then go into the menus and check the box to make autofocus change to manual.Another thing is that this camera is not "really" HD.  It's the same resolution as a 640x480 camera, but with a wider width.  Higher resolutions above that are just dithered-in (interpolated?) using software.  The HD image is not really that impressive at all -- just an upscaled lower resolution.Audio is a disappointment.  It seems to record a slight hiss in the background, which is not a problem with other Microsoft models I've used. The signal-to-noise ratio is about that of an old cassette player using Dolby B.  Don't ask me why it's that way on a digital product, but it is -- there is some hiss there. Other webcams don't do this on my computer.I bought this camera to replace a Microsoft VX-5000 model that quit working after a year (I think the cleaning lady killed it).  I was satisfied with that model, and after owning the two, I feel the VX actually has a better overall image, and certainly better audio too.  The lower resolution VX does better in low-light, and has better overall contrast.  The HD-5000 has a lot of noise in the image.Do yourself a favor.  Avoid this camera.

This is a very dangerous product. I am a health care provider who works for the US government in the agency that inspects meat. The meat that you purchase that goes into ground beef is tested by the government for E. coli O157:H7 and six other strains of pathogenic E. coli starting June 2012. The reason that ground beef is tested is because it is considered a high risk product due to the increased surface area. If there were dangerous microbes present on the surface of the meat before grinding it will be throughout the product. That is why hamburgers need to be cooked thoroughly. The USDA only conducts  random sample testing on these meats that go into ground beef, thus it is a spot check on meat that is destined for ground meat and it is on the consumer to cook their ground meat thoroughly. Now, what does this have to do with intact meat? Nothing.Intact meat is visually inspected by the USDA, but not tested for these potentially deadly pathogens. The center of an intact steak is sterile. Thus, if one sears a steak on both sides and ingests it having been prepared rare, one is fairly safe, so long as the steak in its preparation was not pierced with a fork to bring the external microbes into the interior of the steak. However, if one takes a USDA visually inspected (but not tested for these pathogens) intact steak, and jaccards/mechanically tenderizes it the risk increases significantly. You might as well, cut your salad on the same cutting board as you trimmed your raw steak. (And it doesn't matter what grade the meat is, there is an inherent risk in beef due to the fact that these pathogens reside in the gut flora of the animal.) One of the problems of shopping online is getting a good idea of the size of something.While I have no problems with measuring cups and such, visualizing a "32 ounce" container isn't as easyas it sounds. To me, that's a quart, so I visualize a quart of milk or creamer.So, when I ordered these to store tea bags, I thought I was getting something a little different than I received.I ordered two of these. I already have one I keep green tea in that will hold three boxes of tea bags.  I had no idea aboit an ounce capacity, since I bought it off the shelf and could see the size.  Well, my containers arrived today.What a disappointment!  Have you seen those vacuum-sealed bricks of coffee?  A 28-ounce can of tomatoes?That's pretty much the size of these 32-ounce containers!  MUCH smaller than I expected!The 32-ounce Snapware container is actually a very small squarish container. Very small.I would say you could squeeze a box of Sweet-N-Low in one, or a 22-bag box of tea if you pack them down.One container was nice, clean and new, wrapped in plastic. The other was not in plastic and had a scratched up lid that looked like a return. There's a good chance it is going back again for another recycling too!Mfgs need to post photos of their containers with common foods or objects in them so we can better tell the size. This problem is not limited to Snapware... ALL the plastic containers need that. Amazon stopped allowing customers to upload their photos, so we can't rely on those anymore either.Overall, Snapware containers are great. But be aware of their sizing.The 32-oz is a short, tiny, square container, and while possibly useful for containing small items like sugar packets,it isn't large enough to be very useful. The 32-ounce package of flaxseed will not fit into this 32-oz container, so I'd saythey are using liquid measurements, which can vary a great deal from dry goods.

I bought this for my parent's new computer.  They are not nearby so I had it shipped to them and they had to set it up on their own.  Unfortunately, it should have been easier.  The monitor works fine, but here are a couple of cons:1) The base was difficult to snap into the monitor.  They were afraid to break it by pushing so hard, but eventually got it assembled.  It shouldn't be so tough that it makes you wonder if you are about to break it.2) Controls:  The controls for brightness, etc. are done via several buttons that are either not labeled or my parents could not easily find the button labels.  So we started guessing as to which button brought up the menu.  Eventually found it, but then the OSD (on screen display) would disappear before they could figure out which button navigated through the menu.  Then you need to figure out which button selects the item you are currently highlighting.  There is a timeout for the OSD but its in the menu too, and they simply couldn't work fast enough with the menu/navigation buttons to get into that menu option and change it to a longer timeout (catch 22).I wish Acer had provided some type of downloadable app that could change monitor settings via Windows as the monitor-based controls were very difficult for my parents to figure out.Overall they seem to like the picture, although it's a bit too bright.  At one point we could see in the menus that the brightness was at 100, but they couldn't work fast enough to figure out how to change it before the menu went away.  They're used to standard rotary dials for things like brightness and contrast, and needing to navigate menus with unmarked buttons just doesn't work for them.  My LG monitor works similarly, but the buttons are clearly labeled in white ink on the front bezel making it very clear how to bring up the menu and then navigate through it.It's a shame it was so frustrating for them since it was a gift.  I wouldn't recommend this monitor for people who are not tech-savvy or who prefer simpler controls.

I was very happy with this machine, which I bought about 3 years ago.  I've made maybe 80 loaves of bread and pizza dough in that time.  However, the last several loaves have had problems, and I can't recommend this machine any more.Further inspection has revealed the problem--the paddles that stir the bread are made of cheap metal and are deteriorating.  There are two paddles and they each fit over driver shafts that are square-shaped.  But the paddles are wearing away inside and becoming rounded, so that the square drive shafts spin but can't turn the now-rounded paddles.  Thus you watch your machine hum away and the drive shafts turn, but the paddles put on the drive shaft are so rounded out inside they often don't turn.  So your bread doesn't get mixed.  This is mitigated a bit because the machine momentarily stops, and then starts mixing in the opposite direction which gives you a few spins, but this still doesn't get you much time before the rounding of the paddles again defeats the mixing action. I can poke the paddles a bit, and gain a few minutes of spin action, but then the paddle stops spinning and the bread doesn't get mixed, except maybe the second paddle keeps going a bit longer or they reverse direction again.I haven't made any difficult stuff to stir that might have caused excessive wear on the paddles, so it just seems to be poor quality on the metals in the paddles.  Rest assured that I make sure the paddles are fully seated on the drive shafts (it is possible that the paddles could pop off the drive shafts when you put the bread pan in, but I always ensure the paddles are fully seated.)Finally, since the paddles have worn inside, and I've eaten the bread, I imagine I've eaten whatever the paddles were made of, that got rubbed off and thus fell into the bread, so call me metal-man.  I will order some new paddles to see if these are better.I have no financial or other interest in anything I review.

This a fantastic, kid-friendly and kid-pleasing idea that I seriously wanted to love, but just couldn't. We had two sets, these and theLunch Punch Animal Shape Sandwich Cutters (Set of 4)and found neither REALLY worked as designed, rarely cleaning cutting any sandwich we tried it on and, if you use anything other than Wonder Bread (i.e. anything natural, organic or whole wheat), the cutters will be incorrectly sized to your sandwich bread, thus missing a good bit of the design.In this set, the airplane was a dismal, useless failure and we discarded it pretty quickly, since it made nothing but a mess. The other three--car, train and truck--all *kind* of worked, but were also problematic. The main issue is that cutter isn't sharp or crisp enough to actually cleanly slice a sandwich, so you're mostly denting, then ripping and tearing the bread, rather than slicing through it. Also, the shapes, which look so cute on the cutter, don't come out ragged and smashed, and thus end up mostly unrecognizable. And the smaller bits--wheels, windshields, etc.--just end up looking like lumps of nothing. Unappetizing and useless, smashed bits of bread.They work best of simple things like PB&J; and are pretty much wasted on anything else (tuna salad or lunch meat), because even a tiny bit of filling trips these cutters up even more. I also tried just cutting the bread and then assembling the sandwich from the cut pieces, and the results were pretty similar, if slightly better. Still, even then, the small bits couldn't be successfully extracted. (And, even if they could, making a 1/2" sandwich so you'd have wheels after they were already cut, would be pretty difficult.)The idea of turning my son's school lunch into a puzzle shape, to help encourage him to eat, even when I'm not around, is a dynamite one--in theory. In reality, a sharp cookie cutter and a single shape is far more practical and likely to create a recognizable shape/character. Which is why these have been sitting in a drawer gathering dust for the better part of a year, and are now headed to Goodwill.

I'm leaving my original review below, so potential buyers can see how quickly my happiness turned to disappointment.  I've had my blender for five months, used it probably 6-7 times, when suddenly it died. None of the buttons worked, and changing outlets didn't help.  I contacted customer service on the Hamilton Beach website twice, asking them to repair or replace it (it's still within the three year warranty period), with no reply. I next plan to contact the Better Business Bureau and anyone else I can think of.  How dare they sell a mid-priced blender with a three year warranty and then ignore the consumer who contacts them!  Don't buy this blender, or you'll also be sorry.Edited again January 2010:  Hamilton Beach responded to the BBB complaint right away, and sent me a new blender free of charge.  I am required to cut the plug part off the power cord of the old one and mail it to them as proof (I guess) that I owned the old one or I'm not still using it.  I was pleased to get the new blender, and with how fast and courteous they were once I got their attention.  But overall I still would not buy this product again.  The hassle factor just isn't worth the price.----------------Original review:I had been looking at blenders for some time, when I found this one.  I was looking for a powerful one with a large glass pitcher and multiple buttons for different functions.  The ones I had seen in various stores had one or two buttons, which I don't think is enough. Also, most blenders have 300 to 500 watts of power - this one has 700 watts. I ordered this model from Amazon.com (free shipping, YAY!) and it arrived quickly.The first thing I did was grind coffee beans.  They all ground quickly, with a little "tornado" pulling the beans down to the blades.  The blender produced consistent sized grounds, and emptied easily.  The powerful motor never got hot despite 15 minutes of hard work.Next I made a smoothie, and it performed perfectly.  I did use the lid, to protect against splashing or surprises.  Then I used my blender to grind up peaches for peach butter.  It did a great job despite not adding any additional liquids.  Last night I made hummus with garbanzo beans, garlic, lemon juice and tahini (sesame oil), and the blender made a smooth paste in a short time.I have two complaints about this blender - the pitcher is oddly shaped inside, making scraping pasty contents out harder than a straight sided pitcher.  And the rubber gasket that seals the blades to the base is built into the blade assembly.  That means that when it needs to be replaced, the whole blade assembly will need to be replaced too.  So instead of a $2 gasket, it will be somewhat more expensive to replace.Other than these two points, I am very happy with my new blender.

After having had this tablet for the last two months, I wanted to post my thoughts of it.  I think this a great tablet and despite what other reviews have to say about it, its better to me than some of it's big named, higher priced competitors.  The pros and cons are:Pros:Weight-Too many people complain about it being on the heavy end as far as tablets go but I like the weight.  I don't feel like its going to break if I hold it or accidentally drop it.Ports-It comes with HDMI, USB and micro usb right out of the box...no adapters required.  I've even hooked up a 500 GB hard drive and watched videos from it, as well as a USB based mouse which worked.Sound-Its pretty loud when playing games but this is also a con (see below)Camera-While it's not a high end camera, it takes good pictures and records quality video.  It has a 2mp rear camera that also doubles as a video chat camera, and a 5mp front facing camera with flash.Cutomization-I like the fact that it is easily customizable to however you decide to set it up much like cell phones now with multiple screens.Battery life-On a single charge you can get a decent amount of use out of it.  If you charge it, and put it to sleep and come back later , or even the next day, you can expect to still have atleast 90% of your charge left.Price-Compared to more expensive tablets, you get more in functionality without having to spend more money on adapters.Cons:Power cord-This is absolutely ridiculous how short this cord is.  If you need to use it while its charging, be prepared to sit right next to the outlet.Screen freeze-I've occassionally had an issue with the screen freezing but I notice that it only happens when I haven't turned it off or left it in sleep mode with restarting for a couple of days.  When I resart it, it works fine.Sound- As I stated before, the sound when playing games is outstanding.  Whenever you watch movies, or videos, or play back any video you may have recorded, the sound drops off quite a bit.  Also the sound for recorded video sometimes sounds garbled even when in a small room and near the tablet.Resolution-The screen resolution washes almost completely out when outside.Overall, I think its a great tablet and I'd easily recommend it to anyone looking for a netbook, or even notebook replacement.UPDATE 03/14/14  While I still believe this is a great tablet, I can no longer say that I'd recommend it as a long term tablet built for everyday use.  The reason I say this is because about a year ago, the power/sleep button stopped working and whenever I plug it up, I can see the button light up orange to show it is charging, but the button can no longer power it on.  Additionally, I did research to try and see about getting it fixed, but came across multiple reviews of users being forced to pay for an item that should've been built a little better from the start, or the flat out refusal of Acer to either acknowledge or fix it.  As I said in my first review, I still think it's a great budget tablet for someone who is just getting into the tablet world (especially with all of the features it has), but the fact that the power button stopped functioning a little over a year into it, as well as the limited upgradeability of it caused me to replace it with a 4th generation iPad.

There are lots of styluses on the market but the Adonit is unique in that unlike the bulky, fat tips that are common on others it has a smaller precision disk in order to create thinner lines and more accurate strokes.  In essence, it tries to be closer to a true pen.  Immediately this appealed to me because I've resisted buying a stylus because they seem so bulky and unnatural to use.  Immediately when using this it was apparent that this handles and writes more like a true pen.  Though of course it's worthwhile to keep your expectations within reason.  Even though my penmanship with a standard pen and paper is pretty neat and tidy, it still registers on my screen as sloppy.  Still, it's an improvement from the styluses I've used with wider tips.I also like that this pen is well designed from an ergonomics perspective.  Again, no matter what stylus I'm using my hand tires more quickly than it does with a standard pen (I suspect because I am trying so hard to make my writing neat), but my hand does seem to tire less with this stylus over others.  I also like the design of it overall.  It looks sleek, polished and substantial like a nice pen.So with so many complements why only two stars?  As lovely as these features and benefits are to me they don't outweigh the fact that unless you use a screen protector (and a compatible one per the lists on their website as not every screen protector will do) you may find tiny scratches on your screen.  From spending a lot of time on their website they claim that it's not the stylus itself that is scratching your screen but dust that gets trapped under the disk.  But to me it's still an issue if the product makes it that easy for screen damaging dust to get stuck.  And from reading reviews of previous models of their styluses it sounds like it has been a problem that has been reported for awhile.  If you don't mind using this stylus with a screen protector I don't think this is a huge deal.  But I personally don't like how it affects the visual quality of my iPad.  To me I'd rather put up with a bulkier stylus (My father owns a Bamboo stylus and has had no problems with scratches) and put up with less accuracy and fatter script.  The latter is becoming less of an issue anyway as some of the apps I've been using seem to register any stroke as thin whether you're using this stylus, a stylus with a fatter tip, or your finger.  At the very least if scratching is a known issue and this stylus is not compatible with every screen protector I don't know why they just don't include one as a bundle with this product.  Or at the very least include a warning that dust can get trapped and create tiny scratches.Overall I think this stylus has a ton of great features but to me if it is going to create scratches on my iPad it pretty much negates their benefit.

Edit 2/3/14: I added several pictures in the customer image gallery.I bought this after shopping at Target. I went in to listen to the Bose soundlink mini and I was very disappointed with it (surprising with all the great reviews). That is when I stumbled on this unit and couldn't believe how good it sounded compared to all the other speakers on display. I decided to order it from Amazon. When it arrived I was surprised to see that what you hear with it plugged in with the AC adapter, and what you hear on battery are different. The wattage of the system is reduced when it is on battery so the sound is quite different. If you plan on leaving it plugged in, this may not be a big deal. But if you want to use this without the huge AC adapter, get ready for a lot less sound. If I had to guess, I would say the volume is reduced by 25-35% on battery. It doesn't sound bad, but it sucks Sony made this decision for you. If they wanted to reduce the power they should have offered a power save mode so you could decide between great sound or great battery life. They shouldn't decide that for you. Also, the NFC function is totally useless. (I use NFC tap-to-pay daily so I know how to use NFC) I have a Nexus 7, a Galaxy Nexus, and a LG G2. All of these have NFC and none of them work with it consistently. You have to install the Sony NFC app from the play store and then tap the phone to the NFC emblem 10-20 times for it to pair. Sometimes it would work after 5 or 6 tries, but typically it takes a couple dozen tries. In the amount of time it takes to get it to connect via NFC you could have connected via bluetooth and been halfway through your first song. I don't know if I got a lemon or what but the NFC is totally useless on my unit. The speaker isn't all bad. The sound quality is actually really good. Especially if you turn off the Sony sound gimmicks. Overall, I would buy this speaker again. For the price they are selling this for now, it is the best option out there. If you have to pay retail, then you have a tough decision to make and I would recommend going and listening for yourself. Definitely don't buy this for the NFC feature or you will most likely be disappointed. I expect this review to get pushed to the bottom. What a disappointment.  This product is extremely difficult to set up.  I am a very experienced and savvy computer user and setting the WRE54G up was a major headache.  If you Google "wre54g setup problems" you will see a laundry list of users complaining about the exact same setup problems.  If you can endure and get past the pain staking process of setting up the equipment, you will find that the performance is horrible.  It did expand my wireless signal... about 20 feet.  And the signal was extremely slow.  It was like being back on dial up.  Just utterly unacceptable!To put it into perspective: I live in a 2800 sq. ft. home and the expander didn't even cover my entire second floor where it is installed.  Granted the wireless range did widen, the increase was almost not noticeable and very slow.  I would recommend paying the extra money and just getting a higher end router with a wider range or look for another wireless expander.If you decide to give this piece of equipment a try, here is what I did to get it to connect to my network:1) Plug in the unit and hold down the reset button for about 20 seconds2) Connect the WRE54G directly to your router using the provided network cable3) Insert the setup CD and follow the directions4) During the last stage of the setup, the process will error out giving you some type message about not being able to complete the process.  Close out the setup program.5) Unhook the WRE54G from your router and move it to the location you want it to reside6) Unplug your router and wait 8 seconds before plugging it back in.7) Done.If this doesn't work, don't worry, it's not you.  It didn't work for a bunch of other people either.Good luck!

The implication of increased stability in the product description and related reviews may indicate to some that there is some sort of passive or active stabilization effect introduced by the X-Grip.  There is nothing that adds stability in this device except that it sometimes may reduce the shake of an awkward position.  The X-Grip is a hard plastic C-shaped grip with a padded handle to which you attach your camera in variable places that may allow you to hold your camera at a different angle or position than what is normally your comfortable vertical or horizintal position.  If you are a photographer of some experience, you have already figured out how to grip your camera and place your body in ways that best capture your subject, even if it is uncomfortable for a period of time.  The X-Grip is a device that requires one to learn how to use changes in grip.  But, when you experiment with different positions afforded by the X-Grip, the shutter button and other controls on your camera which were designed to be ergonomic and within the reach of certain fingers when the camera is held in a normal fashion, may not be positioned in a practical place when the X-Grip is used.  So while I think the X-Grip may bring improved camera holding positions with respect to the lens and its relationship with the subject, those positions may make adjustments to the camera very difficult.  I have found that there are some positions that give a better perspective of the subject, but such framing takes additional time to adjust your camera because the controls are in an relatively unfamiliar location.  Overall, I have to rate the X-Grip with 3 stars because it is not an improvement in the process of all the pictures you take, and the time it may take to change your camera to the X-Grip mount could cause you to lose a great image.  But, its grip is capable of holding the camera in a position that would be very difficult to do manually and could make some pictures better because of the unusual possibilities of placing the lens in relation to the subject at an angle or position that would be difficult manually.  I think that the grip and control access issue means that you have to make a decision as to whether to incorporate the X-Grip in all of your pictures, or none of your pictures.  Shifting back and forth is time consuming, from the mechanical change in mount and the required change in camera adjustment.  I have decided to use it on my various cameras for a few months and then make a decision which is best for me.  So I believe I owe an update because I have not taken a stronger position on the value of this product.

I read all the reviews on amazon.com and thought this NAV/GPS was the one I wanted.  The unit is good quality and feel. The interface is fast and the display is bright and clear.  The reason I give it three stars is the way the software calculates the route.  It has two modes, fastest distance and shortest route.  I have tried both and both get confused if you dont follow its route.  It always wants to go to the freeway and will think that it knows the only fastest way.  It has no understanding of "STOP LIGHTS".  Its fastest way takes you on the freeway then a route that includes 30 stop lights.  The faster way, slightly slower traveling (65 MPH instead of 75 MPH), but with far fewer stoplights, will be faster.  Once it took me to a road that didn't exist.  I had to go to the next turn and I ended up lost and miles from the checkered end flag.  When I got close to my destination, I told it to just get me there and it took me miles out of  my way because it thought it had a faster route on the freeway.  I was just 1.5 miles away and it went 6 miles on the freeway, through 10 stoplights, thinking it was the fastest way.  I was very late for my appointment because of this unit.  This was a test of the unit and I new the fastest way there (cost me 1/2 hour).  It just got confused and took me all over. I can't trust the unit to get me there fast.  Shortest route didnt work any better, just different.  I live in an area that is growing and has new roads built within the last 3 years.  It has no knowledge of these roads and takes you way out of your way because of not knowing about the new roads.  It would be better if it had a learning mode to instruct it about stop lights and new roads.  The data base can be updated, but it might takes years and dollars before it is updated.  The built in locations of shops and locations is already out of date and took me to many stores that no longer exist.  If the business is in a mall, it only takes you to the mall.  We have huge mall here with hundreds of stores, and then you have to look for yourself.  Then you find that the store is out of business!  Don't think you can go out and find a better NAV/GPS.  They all have this kind of problems.  Some are really slow and others don't have the graphics of this unit.  I still think it is the best one out there for the price.  I just wish it could be put in a learning mode.

I've had mine for about six months, and it's been working fine and sounds outstanding. Having read several reviews that led me to worry that turning it on and off a lot might cause it to fail, I leave it on all the time. The Tripath power amp IC is very efficient and very likely will benefit from the lack of power surges, so I recommend this approach (but you'll have to live with that bright blue volume control light on all the time).Aside from that, the amp's audio quality is excellent. There's virtually no hum, inaudible (and almost unmeasurable) distortion, and a surprisingly clean, full sound from such an inexpensive product. I'm sufficiently impressed that I'll probably build my own with the Tripath chip - at least it won't be a cheap piece of equipment (but it won't have any protective circuitry, either).If you get a power adapter with a decent amount of current, you can run it with very low distortion at levels approaching 10W/ch (which is deafeningly loud if run continuously, though that would surely cook this little amp). My first one came without a power adapter (at a time when the description said it had one), so I ordered a replacement, and meanwhile dug up one from my parts bin to use until the replacement amp arrived. The replacement came with the famous Vonage AC adapter, but I decided to stick with my own for the added margin (my supply is 12V @ 20A - more than adequate to operate the Tripath chip at its full rating with no supply voltage drop). The Vonage AC adapter (or whatever 1A or 2A adapter they're shipping now) will power the amp to adequate levels without distortion, but if you try to crank it up, or if you have very inefficient speakers (e.g., Magneplanars or some kind of sealed box design), you'll get unpleasant distortion.Is it worth the current price of around $25? That's a tough call. It certainly would be if (1) it reliably came with an AC adapter and (2) it didn't fail so often. But the poor build quality argues against a good rating at any price, so I think three stars may even be a little generous. Too bad, because when it works, it's an excellent value.

I picked up one of these years back when I got tired of running out of paper filers.  Seemed like a convenient idea, and an environmentally smart one.  The savings on the environment it is sorta of a no brainer.  Although paper filters aren't very big, you have to imagine them being tossed out by the millions.  Up front this one time purchase option seems like a good deal for the global warming adherent indeed.  However strictly on the basis of a functional coffee grounds holder, it's all downhill from there as far as I am concerned.  You have to dump the grounds and clean this thoroughly after each use.  And its not the easiest thing to clean for sure.  Its made of a very fine mesh that tends to hang on tenaciously to the wet grounds, and you have to flush it vigorously while holding it upside down to dislodge it all. You will end up digging at its insides manually to get them all out every time, which eventually bends the mesh out of shape. (The amount of water used in this process at least once daily I would say shouldn't set well with the environmentally conscious either). But the annoying cleaning process is not what bothers me most about this filter.  Over time the mesh greatly discolors and can never be cleaned thoroughly to a fresh look.  As someone that believes that the true key to a great cup of a coffee is spotlessly clean equipment, putting this grungy looking thing back in your basket holder day after day certainly isn't favorable to that theory.  If you buy one of these it certainly won't be your last one.  They have a life span like anything else, and chances are it will tend to get quite disgusting looking before you get around to replacing it.  I only recommend this filter if you truly distaste the waste of paper filters, and, don't really care all that much about the best cup of morning coffee you can brew...

Ok, I'm not the most knowledgable person out there on these things, but I like to think that I am. I can't vouch for high end Blu Ray players that cost the mortgage of my house but I could tell you one thing, if you haven't taken the step into the world of high def yet then it sure is the time.Stop being scared, this isn't a fad, it's not going to pass. You need to get into the now and this is a good way to start. Well, a HD T.V would be where to start but that's a totally different review. Let's talk Blu Ray..Since the PS3 was launched I've had a Blu Ray player and it is something else. But I couldn't trek the PS3 back and forth to the bedroom from the living room if we wanted to watch a Blu Ray movie in bed. So we went around and picked up this gem and I couldn't have been more happier. You hear people talking about how big of a deal it is to be able to see the individual strands of hair and beads of sweat on someone in a Blu Ray movie but you're probably like naaaaaaah who needs that...Ha, you do my friend, trust me.I have this player connected to the Samsung LN40A550 40" LCD in my bedroom and haven't had a good nights sleep since. Also added a mini fridge to the room and cut a hole in the wall for easier access to the bathroom... Ok, so I didn't cut a hole in the wall, but I bought a bedpan. Anyways, the combination of the two is amazing and works like a dream. Still floors me when I turn on the Blu Ray and the t.v knows it's on and switches to the input for it. Technology, lemme tell ya. The picture you get with an HDMI cable connected is so vivid and sharp you'll constantly find yourself wondering how in the world did you ever watch a movie without it looking anything like this. And don't think the magic is only with Blu Rays, because if you popped in a regular DVD let's say anything from Pixar, you'll notice a very, very impressive change from the upconversion that the player can do.Now, with it being in the bedroom I don't have it connected to any major sound system (had to have a reason to make me sit in the living room,) so I couldn't tell you anything about that. But, I can say that compared to my PS3 it is a bit slower starting up when turned on, maybe that pesky cell processor has something to do with it.Other than that I really have nothing bad to say about this player and like I mentioned before, unless you got your nose held high and need the most expensive thing out there to satisfy your ego, this player right here is the best investment that you could make to ensure that you see for yourself first hand what true HD is all about.And when you do get it I want you to honestly tell me that counting the beads of sweat on someone's head in a blu ray movie is not the greatest thing since sliced bread.UPDATE: November 2009About a year later it's amazing how things change. I had to send this player back to the retailer thanks to my warrenty because it just stopped reading disks. It froze up and refused to be recognized by my tv. With no problem at all I sent it back and received a check for the full amount. And with that check I purchased a newPlayStation 3 120 GBwhich by far is far superior to this player in terms of playing High Definition movies.I changed this original 5 star review to a 2 because it was a good player with excellent picture but it only gave me a little less than a year. You've been warned.

My recent history with headphones is that i used V-moda vibes for for about 3 years happily and decided i wanted something new so i gave them away to my mom. I tried out some mid-level cans including the v-moda Lp's and ultimately decided that earbuds were more to my liking than cans. More of a precise sound rather than a smothering sound is how i see it.The S4's are ok i am burning them in for one more day to be absolutely sure they are not gonna get better. Their strengths are that you will not hear alot of distortion or muddiness in them. Clarity is their strong suite. The clear unavoidable problem i have with these and many others like these, is that the high's and the treble are not prominent enough in the mix. This is critical for listening to rock and metal music. I want to feel my music, the crash and twang of symbols and guitars needs to be defined loud tight highs. If you go to your stereo and turn the EQ to bass at 60% the treble at 50% and the mids at 53% you will get a good sense of how the soundstage of these buds are mixed. I'm old school i like my treble set high on my stereo. High's/treble need to cut through the mix to bring out the best in rock music. These have that new laid back sound, neutered and sterile and dumbed down if you ask me. Furthermore the bass slightly spills over to the other frequencies in this headphone. The bass is not overwhelming or strong. It is just that it is not "tight" it does'nt stay in it's place where bass is supposed to in the mix of sound frequencies. If you have ever owned speakers by the brand Infinity you will have an example of "tight" bass in a mid-fi speaker.That said for the price they are still good headphones , i have A and B'd them back and forth with the V-moda's and allthought i prefer the rocking sound of the vibe's i conscend that the S4's have some clarity and additionally a little bit more of a colorful sound to them, they just leave me craving tighter bass and more prominent highs. Also note the high's that resonate out of these sound good, they just sound like they are not prominently arranged in the overall mix. They are not loud enough, not present enough. They fit pretty good, the curved earpiece is not better or worse then a straight one IMO.The other strong suite is that these can be gotten pretty cheap i paid 40$ for an open boxed returned pair. For me i think i am gonna go back to my old brand but get their current top end offering the V-moda Vibrato.Clarity 9/10Price and value 7/10Bass 7/10mid's 8/10Treble and high's 6/10P.S if you know of a earbud that you think is perfect for a metal loving treble head like myself write me a suggestion in the comments section.

First, the processor in this MacBook is definitely no slouch (and an expensive upgrade for most PC laptops).  The built-in camera is very handy, the 1GB of RAM is adequate for most things, and the built-in wireless and bluetooth are very nice for me.I was leary to go with the glossy screen because I feared the glare.  I admit that I bought this before I ever went to see one in a store.  However, it really hasn't been a problem for me.  Occasionally I'll see some reflection from bright objects, but not often.  I will say that the viewing angle on the screen is much more limited than I had expected (hence, the four-star rating).  Once I'm situated, it's fine.  However, moving up, down, or side to side dramatically reduces the quality of the picture.  The optimal viewing angle is not one in which the built-in iSight is pointed directly at me, so when I use iChat with my family (they all have Macs), I have to choose between a slightly washed out image of them or having them see only the top of my head.I like the design quite a bit.  Mine has a small imperfection in the trackpad that causes some irritation as I'm using it.  Also, the edges aren't rounded, so if you type with your arms resting against the bottom of the keypad then you'll feel some discomfort.  Other than that, it really is nice.  The screen is larger than I had expected. I have used Corsair Power GS supplies for 5 years and never had any issues with their lineup.  Since I've fully water cooled my rig (CPU and GPU), the GS800 PSU was the the one thing that kept my system from being very quiet.  I have a Lamptron FC5 fan controller dropping my Corsair AF and SP fans down to an almost inaudible 800rpms, so with that I figure I'd purchase a "silent" operating PSU.  Honestly, the only I love the semi modular design of the HX750 and the fact that is does run quiet...up to a certain point.  Everything went south when this PSU spun to 100% like a jet engine for 3-5 seconds at 5-10 minute intervals, even during idle!!  The ambient temps in my house are 26C here in Hawaii, not hot enough to build up heat every 5-10 minutes.  I built my system for quietness and this PSU just stands for everything against every reason why I build a quiet, water cooled rig.  Corsair advertises that the fan does not spin until it reaches a set temp or load, but what they don't advertise is what rpm's the fans spin up to when they do kick in.  And when the fan kicks in, it's so annoyingly loud that I can hear the fan spin up 20 feet away.  I can even hear it through my headset during gaming, 3 feet away from it, and it sounds like my GPU was put back on air!!.  The worst part is that when it spins down completely or stabilizes to run constantly, there is a chirping/ticking noise that drives me even more crazy, lol!!  It's so loud, I missed my GS800 so much (which runs much, much quieter even though it was still slightly audible), I ha to put it right back in.  Corsair really should have designed a better fan controller to cool this PSU.  They claim it generates less heat but my GS800 generates even lesser heat out the exhaust.  I RMA'd this unit and will be selling the new one because Corsair said, and I say "said", that the fan works like this by design and whatever new one you receive will do exactly the same.  I'd stay away from this PSU if you want "quiet".  "Quiet" for some can be deafening to others, and to me this is deafening...

Why did I purchase this bag?I had a shoulder carry laptop bag and that bag was unable to hold all the stuff I put in it. The old laptop bag was a Targus that worked quite well.Description of the bag:You can see the dimensions of the bag in the technical details but some of my critique discusses the compartmental layout.This bag has three zippered compartments.1 - Front compartment - holds letters, pens, cell phone, DVD or CD cases, and smaller misc items.2 - Center compartment - Has two smaller compartments in it.  One is fully padded where you can put your laptop.  The other compartment has no padding.  You could put folders, another laptop or tablet(or two, lots of room).  But no padding.3 - rear compartment - put paper documents, small manila folders or letter or legal sized pads in there.  Padding between 2&3 is NON-EXISTENT.  just a thin sheet of material to separate the two.  Note, this layer does NOT go all the way to the bottom so small items roll between the two compartments.Behind compartment 3, is another thin layer of material, no padding.  This is where the retracting handle resides.  If you place your hand in compartment 3, you feel every bit of that handle.  I'm going to place a small piece of dense foam there to help that a bit.PROS:Great PRICE.Fast shipping (received it within two days.enough room for all of my gear and then some.Laptop compartment is decently padded between the 1st and 2nd compartments. No 'flags' or loose threads out there yet.Bag looks goodSmall enough for under the seat or fit in the overhead bin of larger planes.Retractable handle goes all the way down and can be hidden in a zippered compartment.CONS:Overall insufficient padding between compartments 2 & 3.There is not a real divider between the retracting handle and compartment 3.  There is a piece of nylon liner material that fits over the back of the bag, covering the handle and fitting over the bottom of the bag, held down by Velco so it does not move.  That material does not provide any padding, just separation.No padding on floor outside of laptop padded area.No padding or stiff back where the retractable handle is.  There should be something besides that removable liner.Compartment 2 and 3 are not separate so small items roll in between them.  (I use ziplock bags to hold my cables and small stuff back there.Retractable handle is not separate from compartment 3 outside of a moveable liner.Summary:This is truly a case of you get what you pay for.  While the price of this bag is very good compared to other bags of it's type (50% cheaper than several I looked at), there are missing features that I would consider important in a travel bag.  This bag could use better padding, permanent separation between the two main compartments besides a removable liner.  It could us a somewhat stiff liner of some type between the retractable handle and the back compartment.Future actions on my part:I am keeping the bag.  The prices was right.  I like the looks of the bag.  It is large enough for my needs.  I can modify some of my actions to store items in the bag a bit more neatly (ziplock bags are great).  I will be seeing if I can add some stiff cushioning board or foam in a few spots.Your consideration:You get what you pay for.  If you do a lot of traveling in airplanes and such, get a better quality bag.  If you just use is occasionally, this bag may work for you.I hope to put an update by years end.  We'll see.Happy shopping.

This is an entry level book-style cover for your iPad Mini from Belkin. Obviously, if you are using an iPad Mini, it is likely that size and weight are a concern for you, and perhaps you bought the Mini so you could read it like a book.  For this purpose, the Belkin Classic Tab cover could be a good option.  However, I was disappointed when I found that the iPad is held into the cover by 4 flexible stitched cloth/leatherette tabs.  While my iPad felt more or less secure, it seemed to have some play and give.  Having just evaluated theBelkin Striped Cover / Case with Stand for Apple iPad mini (Gravel), I couldn't help but notice that this less expensive cover seemed to have a less durable retention mechanism.Other than retention, the case provides easy access to all ports and general protection to the whole device while leaving the screen open.  If you are concerned about scratches during use, you might pair this with a stick-on screen protector.The case closes like a book with a magnetic tab that latches it closed.  It is a strong magnet which holds tight, and also the latch folds backwards so it does not occlude the screen.  With the tab folded backwards, it also holds the cover behind so you can hold the device one handed while still in the case.  The cover also doubles as a stand, enabling you to prop up the iPad Mini for movie watching.While the cover is fairly thick with lots of stitching, the black overlay is stitched over a thinner lower layer, with the result being an uneven surface across the back.  It was doubtless a less expensive way to stitch the cover, but I don't like the effect.  I really detracted 1 star because for only a little bit more money, Belkin's Striped cover just seems to provide such a better value.I also detracted another star for the fact that Belkin should have embedded magnets to provide the smart cover on-off feature.  It perplexes me that they left off this critical feature.  Perhaps they want one design to work for all small tablets with minimal modification, but they really should have provided this customization for the iPad.  Hence, 3 stars for a decent cover that will work, but Belkin really makes better options for not a lot more money, such as the Striped cover mentioned above.

There are enough reviews out there on the internet about the Panasonic VIERA TC-P65GT30 65-Inch 1080p 3D Plasma HDTV and it's (TC-P65GT50) successor that I don't need to add much. Fantastic picture quality for the money and nothing really seems to come close. It is a Plasma so it has a fantastic viewing angle and great blacks but the screen is a bit reflective and not the brightest so you'll have to live with that. It's also one of the most power hungry TVs out there. Almost 600 watts!So why only 1-star? For many consumer products the warranty is important but not a key factor in a purchase decision. For a 65", 100+ pound behemoth that you get addicted to watching every day the warranty is important. So here's my story: I turn on the TV one morning and hear a pup followed by a loud buzzing sound. I take a closer look and find that a crack has developed underneath the front glass.So first thing I do is call panasonic but they're closed so I e-mail them. I get a response asking me to call. Great what was the point of the e-mail? So I call and the person tells me that they can't help and that I need to e-mail them a picture but he gives me a bad e-mail address. So I spend while finding customer services address on the web and all my mail gets bounced back since they seem to be bad addresses. I get on chat during business hours and again they can't help me but at least I get the right e-mail address.So I dutifully send the picture and wait, and wait another day then I start asking for updates every day or two. Still nothing. Finally I call again and I give them my case number and I'm told corporate has determined that this is not a manufacturing defect.Wait. What? Without physically looking at it or sending someone out to take a look? So I ask them if I can just get a service call so they can see that there is no damage to the set. Nope. It's on my dime. Finally I ask what would happen if the service person determines it's a manufacturing defect? They don't know. It's out of their hands.Stay away from Panasonic. At the very least I would expect a service call for something under warranty so they can actually determine what's going on with it.

Beware of this product! It really deserves negative stars. The unit I received was wired incorrectly. When turned on it formed a short circuit across the USB power. If your computer does not detect this condition and protect itself this could damage your computer's USB port.I think I am lucky. My laptop detected the excess power drain and protected itself. Amazon is handling the refund and return shipping. My main loss seems to be the time and hassle.The Amazon listing shows this as a product by DekCell and sold by "Super Deal". The box showed the product number DX-704. The package was shipped from DreamBargains.net, Inc. in Arizona. I include this information because sometimes Amazon reuses reviews when the product or supplier changes.If you have one of these, check the switch wiring. If only two terminals of the switch have wires connected then your unit has this problem. On mine, all the red wires from the fans were connected with one of the USB wires on one switch terminal and all the black wires from the fans were connected with the other USB wire on the other switch terminal. The fans run when the switch is in the off position. The USB supplied power is short-circuited when the unit is in the on position.

UPDATE: 11/2/2012Below is my original "5 Star" review, and everything I said below is still valid.  However, last night it broke, so I feel like it deserves a downgrade.  Here's the problem: The design of this unit is such that it adds length to your current HDMI cable.  With the cable hanging down, it torques the little adapter.  Unlike other adapters I have though, this is not a solid block of plastic.  It has two halves, which are not held together very well.  With only slight downward force, the plastic parts popped off and the HDMI plug bent.I did order a replacement, but I think an "HDMI Right Angle Adapter Male to Female" or a short male to female HDMI cable is required.  This will let the unit sit in a way that it does not apply torque to this weak point, and hopefully it'll last a long time.  This does add about $12 - $20 to the overall cost as you need one on both ends of the connection, but I still think this product is worth the money.ORIGINAL 5-Star REVIEW:The InjectIR does exactly what it says it'll do.  It uses the CEC channel on the HDMI cable, and sends whatever IR it "sees" through the HDMI cable.Pros:- Super clean installation.  No nest of wires in your AV closet as you run a new wire to each device.- No A/C plug needed.- 3 minute setup.  Just turn the switch on both devices to "IR", plug in the headphone cables to the receiver and transmitter, install one on each end of your HDMI cable, and that's it.- No need to run any other cables (which is a big deal if you have cables in your walls).  Your TV will already have an HDMI cable running to it, and that's all that's needed.Cons:- No instructions.  I didn't need them, but if you had to troubleshoot your set, you'd have no help.- The transmitter needs to be out in front of your AV components.  If you have your components on separate shelves and/or close to a cabinet door, there may not be room for the transmitter to "spray" and hit each component. This is the one advantage of repeaters that have separate wires that can be run to each device.- Single band only.  Check compatibility before ordering.Even with its faults, this is still a solid 5 star product.  It won't work for everyone or every device, but if it works with your devices and your setup, it's well worth the money.

This is a hard plastic case that is divided into two sections. One section fits inside the other and is then pushed forward to the point that the total length is just larger than the longest packed item. Then a metal insert is placed through a tab in both sections holding them in place. The lower section has two wheels and the upper section has a hole through which a handle can be attached. Imagine dragging your skis by the tips and having the bottom of the skis riding on wheels and you have an idea of what this is like.The case does what it is supposed to do - protect skis and poles from the craziness of airline baggage handling. However, there are some problems:1) After loading up one section with two pair of skis, two sets of poles, and a pair of boots, I tried to fit the two sections together. Easier said than done. I tried to stand up the loaded section. That doesn't work - it won't remain standing. I tried to fit the sections together on the floor. This worked, eventually, but only with an unreasonable amount of foul language.2) The sections are held together with a single metal rod inserted through holes in the two sections. This seems like a recipe for disaster. All it would take is one stray suitcase to knock the rod out, whereupon the entire assembly would disassemble and your skis, poles, and boots would dump all over the innards of an Airbus, or perhaps scatter themselves around the baggage carousel. I'd prefer a latch or buckle or something a bit more reliable.3) With two sets of skis, two sets of poles, and a pair of boots, I was at 40 lbs, so this was handled by United without any extra fee. I frankly wouldn't have wanted more, since even with the handle and wheels, this was already about at my limit to drag from baggage carousel to the rental car transport at DIA (along with other baggage simultaneously).All that said, my skis arrived without incident and that, of course, is why I bought this case. I'd buy it again, but a few upgrades would be welcome.

I imagine this kind of product basically has two use cases - a budget RAID case for video production, or aggregating a few drives for backup/media serving. I'll address the former, then the latter.Note: I tested the Probox using an early 2009 Mac Pro, with OSX Mountain Lion 10.8.3, via the Mac's built-in USB2.0 and an add-in PCI-E x1 Fresco Logic FL1009 USB3.0 card. Transfers were tested using an internal SSD, with a mix of 5900rpm and 7200rpm 1tb/1.5tb disks in the Probox. Also, Mediasonic states in their forums that Proboxes made on or before early 2012 have known issues with the built-in USB 3.0 on newer Macs. Mine was built in 2013, so I do not *think* this applies to this particular box.I wouldn't recommend the Probox for a professional workflow, at least not via USB3.0. Transfer rates are very erratic; 90-100mB/sec for smaller files (copying from the SSD), and similarly high for the first few hundred megabytes of larger (multi-gigabyte) files. However, after the first few hundred megabytes, the Probox would either inexplicably disconnect, or slow down to 10-20mB/sec. I could not reliably duplicate conditions causing the disconnect, leading me to think there's an issue with the SATA to USB bridge chip in this box. It may also be an incompatibility with the Fresco Logic chipset, but I have no way of verifying this. The box is rock-solid using USB2.0, but you're limited to ~30mB/sec (USB->internal SATA) or ~16mB/sec (USB->USB).For backup and media serving use, the Probox is pretty good, if you don't demand high transfer rates. USB3.0 is unusable (at least in my case), so multi-terabyte backups will be an overnight process (rsync and similar applications can alleviate this, by only copying changed files). However, note that the latest shipping firmware spins down/powers down all disks when not in use, and this can occur *independently* of your OS settings - this may cause issues if you're using a software RAID or media server software, as drive spinup can appear to be a failed drive if the application has too short a timeout. You'll need to go to mediasonic's forums to find an older firmware that does NOT have disk spin-down.I did not test this drive via eSATA - it's an outgoing standard and I really don't have the urge to buy a new eSATA card for a machine I might sell within the next year. However, from what I read it performs admirably via eSATA, so long as your interface supports Port Multiplication with FIS-based switching (not all cards do - search for Sil3132-based chipsets or the DATOptic eSATA->USB3.0 adapter).I uploaded screenshots showing the erratic transfer rates via USB3.0, when the Probox was not disconnecting from my machine. Again, this may be a chipset-specific issue, but I don't have the patience to buy several different USB3.0 cards to find out.[edit 2013 Sep]I bought a new/different USB 3.0 card to test in my mac pro (it's still based on a Fresco Logic chipset, but it's a FL1009 - based Orico card). I'm currently transferring data at about 100-150mB/sec to two drives. There seems to be none of the erratic speeds exhibited when I tried the other USB 3.0 card. However, it seems the drives still get randomly disconnected after sustained transfers. Unless you have more time than money I'd suggest looking to a higher-tier enclosure.

This version of Windows 8 is referred to as the "System Builder" in that it is a full installation of Windows 8 and not an upgrade.  Windows 8 is a multi-boot friendly OS and the intention behind this particular disc is that persons building new machines can have a full version of the Windows 8 OS and install it without having to own a prior version of Windows--but it can also be installed on any hardware that meets the system requirements.  It is uncertain at this time whether this brand replaces the "OEM" versions many of us are familiar with, but for now the "System Builder" editions of Windows 8 are the only versions of Windows 8 being sold that are not an upgrade.  If you're building a new Windows machine it might make sense to take the plunge and go with the newest Microsoft OS.  If you want to keep your options open and do a dual-boot install on an older machine, thus far I've seen Windows 8 to be fairly multi-boot friendly, and I've even heard that the "Windows Anywhere" concept would allow you to install the OS on a removable drive (NOTE:  I have not tried this and do not have experience with it).The different look and feel of Windows 8 boils down to one huge change:  the Start Menu that we have had since Windows 95 is no longer a menu.  It is a full-screen splash of tiles (formerly called "the Metro UI"), each of which represents something installed on your computer.  This makes sense in that some of today's programs are more like the Windows Desktop Gadgets we've seen in Vista and 7:  they sit idle, stream information to you, and need a bit more room to be easy to read than the older Start Menu could allow them to have--instead of icons they are square tiles, and some programs' tiles are two squares wide.  It may take some arranging by you to get the tiles presented in a layout that makes sense to you.  If you've used Windows Media Center, Office 2010, or an XBox 360, you've already been interacting with similar interfaces--this sort of UI has been slowly making its way into Microsoft's products for a while now, but it's been beefed up to be more touchscreen friendly.The rest of the Windows 8 OS spends its time balancing between the old and the new.  The desktop looks exactly like it did in Windows 7 and Vista, except there's no Start Button: you're expected to press the Windows key or move your mouse to the bottom corner of the screen to launch the tile dashboard.  Older programs run from within the Desktop view, but all programs can be launched directly off the tile screen:  programs unique to Windows 8 run one at a time in full screen, while older programs that run within the desktop can be resized. We have a version of Internet Explorer accessible from the desktop that looks just like IE 9 did in 7, then we have a version of Internet Explorer in the tile screen that looks entirely different.  Some parts of the Control Panel have the full-screen tile look and feel and often the options cascade left-to-right like the "File" menu in any MS Office 2010 product.  Other parts of the Control Panel look exactly like they did in Windows 7 and before.Windows 8 is not all about appearance however.  In earlier versions of Windows, the number of programs running in the background could get unwieldy and slow things down.  There was a shift to using more Services under the covers, which are listeners that sit idle waiting to launch programs so that the programs don't have to run all the time.  Windows 7 started to get bogged down with a lot of running Services though, and performance-tweaking power users got in the habit of going in and adjusting them all to get back lost performance.Microsoft have stripped several services out of Windows 8.  They have made the installation footprint (space taken and resources used) a bit smaller than Windows 7, and they've made Windows 8 run on any hardware that could run 7.  Programs that used to run, shut down, then have to be fully spooled up to run again are instead "exsanguinated" (Microsoft's term):  put on a virtual shelf and the resources they used handed back to the OS for other work.  Re-launch the program and it'll respond much faster due to having been left in this standby mode.  The Windows Vista and 7 "Aero effects" that gave your windows a glossy sheen and rounded corners used graphics and CPU to run, so they've been stripped out in favor of simple color schemes, blocky edges, and a bit of glassiness when looking at the Desktop.  Interaction with Windows in this new look and feel is easier if you have a touchscreen or you're using a tablet, and if you're a Windows Phone user the territory is already pretty familiar.  The downside is that those of us still relying on a mouse and keyboard find our time spent hunting along the edges of the screen for scrollbars and dragging our screens around to be able to interact most of the time.  As odd as the tile interface is, my chief complaint hasn't been with it so much as it's been that the scroll bars in most Windows 8 programs are too skinny.  This pixel-hunt can be very annoying when you see that 10 pixels more width would make this problem go away.Like all Windows OS releases, time will truly tell us the full story.  I've found the IE 10 browser to be less compatible and more cranky with websites, but I expect that to change given time.  I like the fact that antivirus and security are rolled into the OS without me having to take care of them or be interrupted with update notifications.  The OS runs updates on a schedule that's far less aggressive than previous versions and thus far hasn't forced me into a reboot.  I've been told that the performance for gaming is supposed to be greater simply by virtue of a cleaner codebase, but I haven't seen anything substantially different in my framerate despite higher benchmarks in 3DMark 11.  I have however seen faster boot-up and shut-down times on one machine.  And once my programs launch, I don't even think about that tile layout waiting for me underneath.The basic applications like Weather, Photos, Stocks, Mail, and more are very user-friendly, but solely within the context of the new look & feel:  expect little familar ground and a lot of new territory.  If you have a Windows Live account and/or SkyDrive, these can integrate fully into the OS:  so much so that you would sign in to the computer with your Windows Live/Hotmail account and everything you do would be synced to Microsoft's cloud.If you're considering Windows 8, there are many benefits under the covers.  The patchwork way in which the OS seems to meld old into new can be confusing, and it's clear the UI pays lip service to mice while eagerly awaiting your first touch-screen or touch-pad purchase.  But to give credit where credit is due, there are benefits under the surface to go with the drawbacks you see before your eyes.  Putting Windows 8 Pro on a new system is a good hedge against longevity, but will require experienced Windows 7 (and below) users to be patient with the newer parts of the UI.UPDATE:  Amazon customer Robert Haines says that there is a program called "Classic UI" that would restore the old look, so if you're dead-set on new code that skips the new UI, you might want to try that.  Other customers say that Stardock's program is worth the money.UPDATE: Amazon customer AJ points out that although Windows 8 Pro may in the future require you to purchase a license for Windows Media Center separately, right now you can get a serial key for free via the Windows 8 site: just go to the Windows 8 "Add Ons" section. You may request up to 5 serial keys using different e-mail addresses and Microsoft will e-mail them to you within 24-48 hours.UPDATE, 11/2013:  Microsoft has now released Windows 8.1, a minor update to the OS that mostly attempts to make the user experience better.  If you purhcase this copy of Windows 8, you will be offered the ability to update it to 8.1 at no additional cost.  The upgrade is pushed through the Windows Store that is part of Windows 8.  Personally, I've done clean installs of 8.1 from the MSDN media and done an in-place upgrade via the store, on both my desktop and laptop, and have not had good experiences.  I don't personally recommend the update at this time for that reason.  Peraps with time it will get better.This review was posted under the System Builder DVD product listing of Windows 8 Pro.  The three versions of Windows 8 are "just Windows 8" (which is like Windows Home in earlier versions), "Windows 8 Pro", and "Windows 8 Enterprise".  The generic Windows 8 that replaces "Home" in earlier versions has the basic feature set.  This "Pro" flavor adds the BitLocker drive encryption we previously had to buy Windows Ultimate to obtain.  It adds the ability to use Remote Desktop (that in my opinion should be in all versions of Windows), and it makes it easier to connect your computer to an Active Directory Domain.  Windows 8 Pro is best for the power user or the small business and most people hardware-savvy enough to build their own machines will most likely prefer the added control they gain from using Pro.  "Enterprise" takes things one step further by being designed for use in medium to large businesses with corporate networks.  There is also a "Windows 8 RT", but this version is solely intended for the ARM processors and other hardware built-in to tablet computers and is not intended for a desktop or laptop computer.

This product is truly a best vs worst scenario, hence the 3 rating. The good is the size. Convenient for traveling.  But then Garmin's stiff wire cigarette plug with large converter and oversize mounting bracket make the small size of the actual unit a not so great a feature.  Garmin seems like a very conservative design company with very old school ideas and for whatever reason just could not figure out that customers who buy  something as small as the Nuvi 350 don't want to carry another pound of necessary accessories.  Let's move on to the actual experience.  Turn the unit on and even if you default to accepting that you will die if you try to use the unit while in a moving vehicle, you are still presented with what amounts to a legal contract that if you press one button while the car is in motion, Garmin is eternally absolved from any blame.  Oh come on!  From there the user interface is ok.  Just ok.  For the most part it does most of what you would expect.  Entering a go-to address is time consuming and made somewhat ridiculous because you can't just enter a simple place with a zip code. Maybe 40% of the time it tried to insist that I wanted a similar address and would not take me where I wanted to go. I had to fake it by guessing why the Nuvi couldn't figure out the right address. It also would sometimes drive me insane with directions that I absolutely knew were wrong, like making me get off a freeway and then get right back on a few feet later. It probably made me do that based on some freeways having a slight jog that doesn't seem logical to Garmin.  I would like to see some sort of interface like Streets & Trips that lets you enter two or more points and it tells you what the total mileage will be, total driving time and will let you rubber band a slightly alternate route if you prefer.  For close to 5 big ones this unit could be a lot smarter. After 6 months my Nuvi started just going dumb with no reason. I tried to work with tech support and they were pretty resistent at first that one of their units could actually fail (reminders of HAL in the movie 2001?) After a lot of back and forth they agreed to let me send it back under warranty.  That's where I am today.  Ready to start a major driving trip and my Nuvi is on its way back to Garmin.  Stay tuned.  I'll let you know what happens.

My mother raves about Delonghis. I do not understand why. When I left my last apartment, I left my Delonghi (older model) out on the sidewalk for someone else to take home. (For those of you unfamiliar with this behavior, it's the underground economy in Seattle, everybody does it).I have used and owned many toaster ovens in my life, including in foreign countries where I can't always read the button labels or the instruction manuals. This appliance is worse than all of them when it comes to being intuitive or user-friendly. This model is even worse than the old one I gave away. It is awful. Really awful. I am currently baking an apple cake in it, and the experience of programming it was so frustrating (again) that I said this is it!  Today's the day I write a review and warn others.Here It is:See all those buttons in the photo? Yes, each one of them beeps (shrill!) individually. To set it for bake you have to go beep beep beep. Then set the temperature, from a default of 350 degrees. ... Let's just say it's rigidly programmed to not do what  you want, but force you to choose from a limited number of options.  And it beeps every time. 350 beep! 375 beep! .....you know the rest.Timer... every minute up or down sets off the ...beep!  six, seven, eight..... twenty-eight, twenty-nine, thirty minutes... equals thirty beeps. Sound fun?  And you are not done until you set the Start/stop, beep!!It took more than ten finger pushes to get it set to (approximately) what I really wanted.  Bake at 400 for 20 minutes. (I set it for ten minutes twice, yes, two sets of ten beeps)  Who designed this thing?The cake in the oven: It's puff pastry, so I had to watch it... and I can confirm that for sure, this toaster oven does n-o-t bake or brown evenly.This gadget is a nightmare. Unless perchance you consider a (required) series of shrill beeps music.There's more. It's not just the beep.  Anything sitting on top of the oven gets quite hot, and plastic clam shells melt. Fruit gets brown spots, etc.The temperature inside does not go high enough or low enough.  I have to go back to the older toaster oven on the counter to work at 450 and above. Ditto for lower at 'keep warm'.Does it do toast well? I don't know. Had I known, I would of steer clear. Now I am left with a batch of useless garbage!Update 04/21/2011:Luckily, Amazon e-mailed me a UPS label and took it back at no costs/no questions asked. Secondly, after use it should be sterilized again for your protection, even if we had the simpler form of sterilization in our homes (a autoclave) we wouldn't be able to use that with this since it's made of plastic.Next concern, if you don't have super clean hands, or skin you may have a problem. Think of common household pathogens that are found everywhere in the household, touch the faucet and your pass the pathogens to anything else you touch... set the Derma Roller down there your go again. And don't forget pathogens that pass on illnesses can be air born as well.Further concern is the slight puncture wounds to the skin and overly using this product (rolling it too much, or using it too often) can actually cause damage to perfectly healthy Elastin & Collagen, instead of helping your skin to develop more. And because of the puncture type wounds, although tiny, you will be causing some swelling and irritation... even if you don't notice it at first. As a result of these wounds to your skin you could suddenly become sensitive to your skin care regime, molecules from your hair spray or perfumes and even sensitive to your own makeup. Sunscreen could suddenly stop working the way it is supposed too and because it's penetrating deeper into your skin you may also run sensitivities to these as well.Now, I have Lupus SLE and I couldn't use the product because of that, to even test this out once... if you have any broken skin, sores, rashes or even ingrown hairs (and more) don't use this on your skin until you are healed. And if you are thinking about getting this to use at home, please talk to your doctor about it (describing the product, an appliance for what is commonly called "needling the skin" and the fact that it can't be boiled and has no instructions for cleaning the needles between use etc) and ask your doctor what they would recommend. Upon closer examination, however, the Seagate differs from other such powered drives in that it has a 4 stage capacity level guage and actually has an interchangable snap-on plastic base which appears to be designed so you can purchase another base with a different interface, e.g., Thunderbolt. Considering the cost of these proprietary Seagate adapters, however, this particular feature may not be all that useful.As for the drive's basic functions, it writes data about 25% faster than the USB powered USB 3.0 Seagate 500GB Expansion drive which makes it very fast indeed. Read speeds are on par with the USB 3.0 Seagate 500GB Expansion drive which is still about 4 times faster than when reading through a USB 2 interface. All in all, its a very fast and spacious drive if you have USB 3 available on your system.

I recently purchased this item to replace a dying mouse. I am used to using a 5-button mouse for tasks, so I thought this would be a suitable replacement.
