இ Fuzzy Wuzzy's Summary:ѾѾѾѾ Recommended with warm fuzzies.Antec makes a large variety of high-quality computer accessories, desktop tower cases, power supplies, and fans.  The Notebook Cooler's features are described and rated below:ѾѾѾѾѾ Excellent 5-fuzzies feature ratings:ѾѾѾѾѾ  This dual-fan design has good build quality, it circulates a pretty good volume of air, and provides effective cooling, especially when it is run at the high speed setting.ѾѾѾѾѾ The noise levels of 23 dBA at the low fan speed setting and 27 dBA at the high speed setting are pretty good relative to the size of the fans and the amount of air that is moved.  In fact, its high-speed noise level is still likely quieter than most internal laptop fans that operate at their highest speed setting.ѾѾѾѾѾ The Notebook Cooler S is powered by USB with a pass-through connector, so you do not lose a USB port when it is plugged in.ѾѾѾ Average not-good not-bad 3-fuzzies feature ratings:ѾѾѾ The two fan blowers pull air from the top of the cooler's honeycomb grill and blow that air through the front of the cooler.  However, the air that is circulated underneath your laptop (that rests on the two triangular rubber pads) is not uniformly distributed.  Both fans turn in a clockwise direction, and so most of the air flows from under the rear of the laptop and out through the left side of the laptop, leaving less air circulation to cool the right side of the laptop.  Perhaps Antec designed this to divert the warm air out through the left side so that right-handers do not feel the blown-out warm air while moving their mouse around on the right side of the laptop?  I think that the fan design could more uniformly circulate the air underneath the laptop if the right-side fan was configured to spin in a counterclockwise direction, thus directly an equal amount of air out through the right side of the laptop.ѾѾѾ This fan was designed specifically to be used on a desk or flat surface.  Since it lacks a platform for resting your laptop upon, it does not work well to place the blower on your lap and then prop your laptop on both your lap and the blower that is balanced on your knees.  You can set this up on your lap for a short period of time, but it quickly becomes unwieldy the moment that you move a leg or shift in your chair.  Because this cooler fan lacks a platform like other laptop cooling stands, it excels in portability and you can easily pack this in your laptop bag.  But it would be nice if the Notebook Cooler S was designed with a detachable stand base that could then allow it to be easily placed on your lap for extended use while sitting in a chair, sofa, or bench.௫ Fuzzy Wuzzy's Conclusion:This two-fan laptop cooler is an effective way to increase the ventilation of your laptop while you are working on a desk or flat surface.  Different laptops vary in the design of their venting mechanisms; some laptops have ventilation holes/slots/openings on their bottom while other laptops (e.g. Apple MacBook) mainly rely on openings along the top or sides to bring in or blow out air.  This underside cooling approach is best suited for laptops that have ventilation openings on the bottom of the laptop.

I got this for my daughter. I had very bad luck with Sony reliability a decade or so back; one Trinitron TV I bought died after 91 days - one day after the warranty ran out. Our Sony camcorder went in for repair every few months for years, until the extended warranty ran out. Even though we didn't pay to fix it, we missed a lot of memories while it was being repaired. After that, I swore no more Sony products.But my daughter really wanted this, and the reviews seemed OK, so I gave it a chance. It seemed OK until she lost the computer cable needed to download photographs. That's when I remembered the other reason I avoid Sony: The memory card is a weirdo format only made by Sony - it doesn't fit any of the standard card readers we have, either at home or at work. Same with the cable - Sony could have used an ordinary USB, but instead they put a non-standard Sony-only connector on the camera. Bottom line is that to get my daughters pictures I have to pay Sony a ridiculous price for a specialty item that is useless except for this camera. This time I swear: No more Sony for me.Too bad, because the camera is OK otherwise. It takes good pictures, is easy to use, and still works fine after 6 months.Update: I actually found a card reader at my local drugstore for $20 which read the Sony's goof-ball memory card. My daughter got her pictures, and I only wasted $20 and several hours of my time. I still wish Sony should use standard connectors and parts rather than trying to lock us in to their own non-standard designs, but except for that my daughter likes the camera; so I upped my rating to 3 stars. However for my next camera I'm going back to Canon - they make solid, standards-based cameras, even if they don't make a pink one; and every canon I ever bought still works - some (like my 35mm SLR film camera) over 20 years later. But if you never lose cables, don't want to swap or read memory cards, and really like Pink, then this Sony might be OK for you.

I find the positive click when a button is pressed much more satisfying than pressing a touch panel.  The time setting dial is a very nice solution, but it does start out with single seconds for a while which is rather useless (are you really going to microwave something for 3 seconds?)  It could probably start out going by 5 second increments and move up from there.  The power is very good, without being so high that you have to worry that you're going to vulcanize your food if you leave it in for a few seconds too long.Overall they did most everything right and the few drawbacks are very slight.

That is really good pre-seasoning.Lodge makes great cast iron...here in the USA which is a good thing too. So I recommend this product highly...but,after reading some of the other reviews, I do recommend that you know what the H you are doing before you cook in it ... otherwise, you might have results that have less to do with the cookware and more to do with the cook.

I'll start off with a disclaimer, that as a Vine member, this set was sent to me free to review. Now, I happen to be a bit of a knife snob. I've used a lot of knives and personally prefer Japanese made knives (Shun and Global are two brands here on Amazon that are quite good). However, I do use German knives from time to time as there are some types of knives that don't tend to be made by the Japanese makes.Wusthof is well known for making some very good quality knives, and the Classic is one of their better lines. I find the German knives rather heavy in general but I was pleasantly surprised to find that these are fairly well balanced and nice to hold. The sharpness out of the box was good and holds up well if properly cared for and used. This set includes the 6-inch chef's knife, 4-1/2 inch utility and a 3-1/2 inch paring. Also included are shears and a block with spaces for just these items. Clearly the chef knife is the star of the group and the one you would use the most. My biggest issue is with the short 6-inch length. If you have very small hands, this size may be okay, but really a larger knife is more ideal for most people. It's a bit short for larger items, but it may be okay if you don't do a whole lot of cooking. The paring knife is very nice and certainly will do that job well, no complaints there. The utility, well, that's a size I'm not sure is hugely useful, there's very little that couldn't be handled either by the smaller parer or the larger chef's knife, particularly since it's a fairly small chef. There are a lot of other kinds of knives most people would find more useful to round out a set. A decent bread or sandwich knife, a boning knife, or even a nice cheese knife. Maybe a good carving knife or even a cleaver. This is just one of those knives that no one particularly needs, but gets thrown into sets like this, because it fits in the smaller slots on the knife block.The shears are pretty good ones, I like that they come apart for easy washing, I like the Wustof shears compared to other brands. If you've never had good kitchen shears before, you'll love having these, I particularly like them for cutting up chickens or trimming fat off roasts. They're a welcome addition to any set.The other problem I have with this set though is simply that the knife block is so small. If you are really, really sure you aren't going to want any other knives than these, than this block may be okay. The name "studio" clearly means this is a set intended for really tiny kitchens that don't have much room, but in any case where you have room for a block at all, it only makes sense to invest in a large one that you can add more utensils to. You can't for instance, put a bread knife or honing blade into this block, it's simple too small and doesn't have the slots or length for these items. It's basically a choice between spending less and getting a set that might not have the best types of knives for your needs, like this one, whereas IMO it's often a better choice to buy your knife block separately and load it with the best knives for what you need and will use.So those are my caveats about this set and why I'm rating it fairly low. The quality of the knives is pretty good, even 4+ stars (although again, in my opinion, it doesn't match Japanese made knives like Shun). But the chef's is too small for most people to use comfortably and not good for larger items, the utility knife is really unnecessary, and the block too small and limited. Within these constraints, this still might be a great set for the right person. The price certainly makes it an attractive gift option as well. But I don't think it's the most ideal set for most, even just looking at the Wushtof Classic line. You might want to consider something like theCreate-A-Set Knife Storage Blockand then add a starter set like thisWusthof 9755 Classic 2-Piece Knife Starter Set. You get the much larger and more useful 8-inch cook's knife, and a block with room for other knives as you can add them.UPDATE: Currently this knife set is a fair bit lower in price than when I added my review, which does make this a much better buy than when it closer in price to the combination I listed above. I've left my original rating but I'd probably bump it up to 4 stars at the current price. Given that prices on this set and others can change regularly, consider the points raised in the review and your personal needs and budget when shopping. If this set stays at a good price point, it's definitely worth considering and is a great value. It's not my personal pick for a knife set but if you don't have a lot to spend, it would be at the top of the list to consider. It's definitely better to invest in a couple really nice sharp knives, than spend the same amount on a large set of poor quality ones!

I've had this camcorder for about a year now and love the HD video quality and ease of use.  When my Canon Elura100 died after a year of light use, I looked at taking the step up to a high definition camcorder.  There were several recording formats to choose from - flash memory, hard drives, and miniDV.  I ruled out the hard drive models since my brother-in-law's Sony hard drive camcorder crashed on him several times and he lost video footage each time.  The flash memory models were interesting but then I thought about the amount of hard drive space I would need to archive the videos and the high cost.  There was also the chance that the hard drive the videos were transferred to could also crash and would require a backup costing even more money.Since the only camcorders I've owned prior to this one used miniDV tapes, I still had a lot of blank tapes left over.  It's hard to believe that you can record high definition quality videos on regular miniDV tapes.  The price of these tapes are minimal and under the right conditions, the tapes should last a very long time.  To me, the cost and security of the archived video made this the best option.  The only downside is that the transfer to your computer must be done at real-time so a 1 hour tape will take 1 hour to transfer.  Also, if you are watching video directly from the tape, you will need to fast forward or rewind to find a particular scene.

I have previously owned 2 iPod nano, 1st and 2nd gen. I love them for their portability and accessibility, but the 4 and 8GB of memory was not enough for me, the price for iPods are too high, and the glitches of those two drove me crazy.  They both were gifts so I didn't have a say in the purchase.  This Zune HD was my decision after the 1st gen nano died and the 2nd gen didn't have enough memory for my music collection.Physical Product:I love the looks and feel of my 32GB ZuneHD.  Very nicely built, very sturdy.  I wanted the black color but it wasn't available. However, the two tone black/platinum color is actually really nice. I'd considered the iPod touch but it was just too big and the asking price for a 32GB is just outrageous.  I jog regular so the size is pretty important, especially when it is strapped to my arm.  The ZuneHD's size is perfect.  It is a little bigger than my nano but not too big.  The screen is beautiful, with really deep black.  The resolution isn't as great as the iPhone 4 but with what it has, it is really great.  Pictures are vibrant.  Movies are pretty clear for such a small screen.Music Player:As a music player, it is a wonderful piece of electronic.  It is a big step up from the nano.  The sound produced is very clear, vocals and instruments are excellent.  I just wished it has a custom equalizer because the presets doesn't give me quite enough bass for some of the music that I listen to.  The software takes a little bit of getting used to, but once you get the hang of it, it isn't too bad.  There are some things that it does better than itunes, and some things that it does worse. I have the hardest time trying to add and delete and edit songs.  Perhaps I have been using itunes for 4 years and only a week on the zuneHD that is why itunes seems easier.  As for the marketplace, I don't know much about its ease of usage and accessibility bc I prefer to buy my music from Amazon.  The one thing I hated the most is the lack of a physical button for volume and forward and backward.  I hate to have to push the volume button and look at the screen every time I want to change the volume or song.  It is so tedious and definitely a design flaw.  Besides that, I don't have anything else to complain about.  One thing I will say is that I love the screensaver and the albums picture and artist info scrolling on the screen while the music is playing. It may just be a novelty, but it is just so much fun to watch. I also love the wireless syncing.  It's very convenient.  The HD Radio is a really nice addition, esp if you like to listen to music from the radio.  Personally, I don't listen to it a lot.  However, I did try it out and the signal was strong with little interference. BTW, the battery life doesn't seem to last very long, i.e. less than the 33hrs stated by Microsoft.  I suspect that is because it is a product that has been in storage for 2 years and the battery is not as fresh as it was when it was first assemble. I estimate my zune to last between 20-25 hrs for music on minimum settings, with wireless off, and minimum usage of the screen. The battery meter was at 4/5 bar after about 5hrs of usage.Multimedia Player:As a movie player, it isn't too bad, for the screen of that size that is.  The pictures are clear and the color are pretty accurate.  However, watching a movie for an hour or two straight caused my eyes to become out of focus.  The one thing I noticed is that the screen is set on a certain rotation and will not rotate if you flip it to the other side.  I get about 5hrs of battery life for movie, which is less than the 8.5hrs suggested by Microsoft.  As an internet browser, it is functional but not great.  The speed is decent over wifi sitting in the same room.  The screen is quite good for browsing webpages, but for deleting and typing, it just doesn't work very well due to the screen and the interface.  Fortunately, I don't use it very often so I don't care too much for it.  If you are buying a music player that can also do internet browsing, then I recommend the fruit store. No matter how much I hate them, I can't deny that they have a better product for that.  The zuneHD has a couple of fun apps to play with but they are nothing to talk about.  Again, if you are into apps, then I recommend looking somewhere else or else you will be greatly disappointed.  Also, using the internet or playing with apps while listening to music drains the battery really fast, almost as fast, if not equal to watching a movie.I bought a MUSIC PLAYER with other functions and for that, I am very satisfied.  Is the zuneHD perfect???  No. Software could have been a bit easier to use, there should have been a physical button for volume and fwd/bkwd.  It takes too long to load up and to shut down. As a internet browser, it could have been better and battery could have lasted longer. Is it better than the iPod touch???  That depends on what you are looking for.  I wanted a great portable music player and that is exactly what I got.  It is definitely better than the ipod touch because of the low price for the amount of GB you get, the physical size, and the sound quality, assuming that the ipod touch uses the same EQ setting as the nano.  Personally, I like the styling of the zuneHD over the ipod touch.

I initially liked the sound quality, but after using them for awhile, discovered that the design is terrible. First, I have lost all but one of the silicon rubber adapters. Finding a lost one is almost as easy as finding a contact lens. I checked Philips customer support, but they don't stock replacement adapters. They referred me to a website, but the cost of the replacement plus s/h is as much as the price of a new set of earphones  in Amazon.Second, the earphones continually fall out if you are doing anything involving upper body movement, like yard work. Part of the problem is the conical shape which tends to put a lot of the weight/bulk and wire on the very end of the earphone. It is also due to the extremely long cord that seems to get hung up on everything, no matter how I wrap it around my body. The falling out is also due to the relatively large size of the cone end that goes in the ear canal. It does not fit my medium to small ear canal, even with the smallest silicone adapter.Finally, the design of the earphones makes them painful for my medium to small ear canal. It hurts when I insert the earphones and feels uncomfortable to wear. Wearing them for a long period of time makes the ear canal sore.The tight fit of the earphones does keep out a lot of external noise in situations like riding the bus or a plane. The sound quality is also better than regular OEM earphones that come with most mp3 players. However, I would not buy these earphones again if for no other reason than the unreplaceable silicon adapters.

I purchased this router for a few reasons; 1) price, 2) I had previously purchased a WD My Cloud and thought it would be more compatible, and 3) I liked the fact that it had bandwidth prioritization (QoS).Pros: 1) Price, was very affordable in comparison to others with similar features, a good bang for your buck (on paper). 2) I feel Western Digital to be a very reputable company, they've made solid products for many years and, despite them being relatively new to the networking world, I felt this to be no exception. 3) Advanced QoS (bandwidth prioritization), we do a lot of different things simultaneously and it's nice knowing that the bandwidth will be prioritized accordingly.Cons: 1) Range, the range of this router (2.4 or 5 GHz) is not as good as the 2Wire Gateway AT&T; provided me. This was the biggest letdown for me as the N900 unit is supposed to have the best range out of all their routers. 2) the QoS does not play nicely with torrents, if you are a torrent user you MUST turn QoS off as they are the absolute last priority and your transfer speeds will reflect this. 3) I have been forced to reset this router more frequently than my 2Wire, typically once a week or so whereas my 2Wire may have only been once a month. Not sure why, but it is frustrating.In the end, knowing what I do now, I would not likely purchase this router again, I would spend a little more and get something with better range. However, given the future of wireless connectivity, I simply needed something relatively inexpensive to hold me off until AC becomes more prevalent.

I have both the older 8gb Zen (2007) and a new 16gb Zen MX. They are basically the same except that the MX has integrated access to the removable SD card directly from the Creative Centrale software that comes with the it. With the old Zen you had to go into a removable card menu on the Zen and then access the card via the computer operating system to add or delete files. Zen MX also does not have the code for some video formats and the software has to convert them before transfer to the Zen MX; on the old Zen you could just transfer the video files directly to the Zen. Finally, the Creative Centrale software that comes with the new Zen MX does not seem as intuitive and user friendly as the older software that came with the Zen. If I had to do it again I would have bought the older Zen rather than the new Zen MX, but the older ones are becoming hard to find and are a lot more expensive. Strangely enough the 16gb version of the old Zen is more expensive than the 32gb version!To answer those who said the Zen MX will not play DRM protected files. Not true. It will play DRM9 protected files, but they have to be put on the Zen via the transfer function in the software, not through drag & drop, because the former also carries over the license info and the latter technique does not. Creative notes this on their web site.

While this product works as designed, it is being marketed in a deceptive manner.This is an eSATAp cable, NOT an eSATA cable.  The difference is crucial!This cable will only work if used with an eSATAp port.  It requires an eSATAp port so that it can power your drive from the eSATAp port.  If you have an eSATA port, your drive WILL NOT work using this cable.The cable has no support for using the power supply that came with your drive, and WILL NOT allow a Segate Goflex drive to work when plugged into a standard eSATA port as it's name implies.I have been using eSATA drives for years, and this cable will not work with any of my eSATA ports on any of my computers.  It plugs in fine, but it will not work.Do not buy this unless you have an eSATAp port.  Many newer eSATA ports may support eSATAp (or "Power over eSATA" as it may be called in some cases).

In addition to two 3TB drives, this product contains an APM82181 processor (a PowerPC 464 based system on a chip) and 256 MB of memory, running Linux.If you are a Linux administrator, and know how to turn on SSH access, you can make this box do additional things, like run rsync daemon.  In my case, this was necessary because synchronizing file systems over afpd protocol kept on losing connection (rsync daemon is much more reliable).While I was able to make this box do some good things, it's generally slow.  Logging in via web browser is very slow.  In operation, while copying large files can reach ~50 MB/s, more complex operations like file synchronization achieve only 2-3 MB/s.  This looks like a limitation of chatty protocols rather than a physical limitation of the hardware, but it means that performance is elusive.  WD provides a method to ask for support: my question about configuring this product for better performance went unanswered so far (over a week).Also, this box has no fan and runs hot.  Placing it over a PC exhaust fan helped.Built-in iTunes server doesn't seem to work with my equipment, but DLNA media server does work.  However, indexing media on a large drive takes forever (days!).  Much of this unit's idle time is spent on searching the drive and creating a tally of files it contains.I haven't tested access to MyBook Live from the Internet.A disappointment for Linux users: This unit doesn't allow NFS access to user shares.  Public share should be visible to NFS but I haven't tested that.  Perhaps WD chose this path to avoid complexities of Unix user ID mapping.As NAS, this product is much slower than my Linux file server, but MyBook is small and easy to transport, and can backup a ton of data.  I've decided to keep it for that reason, although its performance falls far short of my expectations.Update: This unit just died after only 8 months of almost adequate service (no network access, apparently drive A failed).  Returned to manufacturer under warranty and replaced with a working unit.

I was really exited to see the VooMote One as I have owned every model of iPhone that has been out and always thought it would be great to have IR emitter in one to use the phone as a remote. (modern smartphones really are virtual swiss army knives with all that they can do, so why not as a remote) I think the VooMote was one of those almost a great idea but not quite should have been carried thru with products. I think the manufacturer is just jumping  on the phone accessories bandwagon and trying to hit a home run with a novel, but flawed product as of this first edition.Pros:- Nice Graphical User Interface. I have owned several Harmony remotes since they first came out and even as of late since Logitech bought them out. They are in my opinion the best remotes that control the most number of devices reliably, that is out there. The VooMote has a wonderful looking screen (especially on the iPhone 4 retina display). I really like the way you can swipe across to different pages of buttons and change the layout. VooMote has really taken advantage of the iPhone's power and design to come out with a really great remote layout and feel. I like it much better than the arrow buttons I had to use on my old Harmony One remote to scroll thru different pages of buttons.- Organization by Rooms. This is a nice feature that many other universal remotes out there have not implemented as well as the VooMote. Harmony remotes can operate many different TV's but they are all in one menu location called devices. The idea to first pick your room and then only display those devices in that room is a great idea that really makes this kind of remote easy to really be a universal remote for your whole house.- Updating is easy. New updates and I hope they do come out with some... are really easy thanks to Apple. You don't have to download some 3rd party software to install and hookup a mini USB cable and go thru updates whenever you can remember to check to do so. The logictech programming software worked fine on my iMac but it was not nearly as seamless as an app.-Price. $69.99 as of the time of this review is a lot less than the $200 plus it takes to get a remote with this caliber of interface. If I already had an iPod touch around then this would make sense as a good purchase price in my opinion.Cons:- Buggy. For a remote you really have to release a polished product. Even if just one button doesn't work properly, people are going to get frustrated with the remote and not use it. This one is full of bugs. Can you imagine being able to turn up the volume but not down, or if the arrow keys worked but not the center select/OK button? Defeats the point if you have to grab one of your five original remotes to push the button you need. Universal remotes have to work flawless. When I finally got it to work a Dynex TV it moved the cursor two spaces every time I pushed an arrow direction button. I couldn't ever select what I was trying to select!  Not good...  I couldn't get it to work the UVerse at all.- Battery Life. I put the VooMote thru initial setup for about 20mins the very first time I used it and it drained my phones battery from 53% down to 37%. I was using it nonstop, but not that much more than it would get used watching a two hour movie. How about a 4 hour football game where channel changing and remote use would be a lot? If they want to continue with this product I would think that they must include a built-in battery that would supplement your phones and charge thru the dock connector.- Physical Design. You have to NOT have any cases on your iPhone/iPod. I have my iPhone in an otterbox and it is a real process to take it on and off the iPhone. If some of the other issues with the VooMote were resolved I might be inclined to purchase an iPod and leave it attached to the VooMote. Otherwise the necessity of removing my iPhones case is definitely a bothersome issue. I also do wonder about the pressure that the cradle exerts on my iPhone and if it could damage it with repeated use, or if it would loosen up over time.Closing thoughts.- I recently arrived at this thought. Apple did not design a built-in IR emitter into any of the iPhones for a reason. I am sure they have already thought of that. I think it eats too much battery life. My brother recently showed me how he took off the iPhone4's front and back covers and made his a red phone. He described the phone's internals as 70% space for the battery and a tiny little 30% left for actual phone electronics. That's amazing, but also a big statement to me that led me to think that IR may not be built-in for that reason.-So this led me to look for other Universal Remote phone apps that do not rely on a cradle or attachment to put on your phone, and I found some. I found one called Redeye that relies on your phones wireless abilities to communicate with Redeye's charger/base/IR emitter. You would have to purchase a Redeye base to put in line of sight of your equipment and in each room that you have gear that you would like to  control. So it or any of these other two would cost more money to control more than one room with. The plus side of it is that multiple iPhones and iPods could all act as remotes for the same equipment. You wouldn't have to pass your kid your iPhone if they had their own iPod to use as a remote. Another one is called peel by Griffin that uses zigbee to communicate to its base and the last is called Beacon that uses another 3rd party app called Digit and they use bluetooth. I am going to wait on all of these for the moment as all of them are fairly new to the market too, and wait for them to mature too.- Alas I still do not have a replacement for my old Harmony One remote that I and my family really liked. We suspect our 2 year old son thru it in the kitchen trash when he went thru that phase of throwing everything in the trash can at 10 months of age. It's nice to know that some affordable options are out there and in the works. I do like the idea of controlling my entertainment system with my iPhone..... even with the Harmony One things weren't perfect because I would often be saying "where's the remote? anyone know where the remote is?!!!"

I wanted to like this keyboard a lot more than I do. I think it will get some use on the go, but it just doesn't quite cut the mustard.PROS• Small form factor fits the iPad well.• Shortcut keys are included for certain iPad functions like volume and audio playback, but also to trigger Siri and use the clipboard• Works well as a case without adding too much extra bulk• Touch surface won't be marked up by the keys thanks to some foam rubber rests interspersed around the keyboard.CONS• The keys are FAR closer together than Belkin wants you to think. Uncomfortably close. It just may be that the iPad mini is not large enough to allow for a comfortable keyboard, but Belkin needs to not call this "true type".• Small oddities will throw your rhythm off. For example, the home row ends with L. The semicolon requires use of the FN key on the period. The apostrophe is down near the space bar. Many times I've gone to use a contraction and end up pressing "enter" and started a new line due to muscle memory, because that's where the apostrophe should be. "Delete" is located a bit differently as well, and you will definitely hit the "pair" key by accident due to the odd placement of delete.These are just two cons but they are BIG cons. I need something more intuitive, not something that requires me to retrain my typing abilities when it comes to certain keystrokes and uses. It's very off-putting to have to use FN+comma for a quotation mark, or to find the apostrophe by the space bar. I would rather use a larger keyboard even though it is less portable just because it would be more comfortable and more intuitive.

I had a pair of Shure E2c earbuds, and I thought that they delivered the best sound I'd ever experienced from anything smaller than my Bose noise-canceling headphones. When a piece broke off one of the buds and Shure wanted $50 to repair it (plus tax and shipping), I went looking; the Etymotic ER6 got good reviews, and Amazon offered it at a great price, so I went for it. And all I can say is "Wow!"First of all, the triple flange silicone tips fit perfectly; they are so comfortable I'm constantly in danger of forgetting that I have the phones in; and they do almost as good a job of isolating outside sounds as the Bose phones. And the sound is immaculate - not too much bass, crystal-clear highs, and midtones with no color at all. If you have a good equalizer (I use SRS iWOW on my Mac, and I love it), you'll hear every tiny nudge you give it.People who want a lot of bass might want to look elsewhere; the Etymotic phones won't deliver the thump that some folks seem to associate with "hi-fi" sound. But for those of us listening to acoustic music, classic rock, jazz, or classical, these phones deliver gladness and a joyful sound.My only quibble with the Etymotic phones is the cord, which seems a little skimpy; I'm not sure that it will be able to stand up to the relatively hard use I give it. I work all day long on my laptop, and I'll move, in the course of a typical day, to perhaps 5 different venues; each move involves wrapping the phones up and putting them away, then taking them out at the next place I settle down.But the sound! Ah, such sound! And for less than $75, delivered.Richard

These headphones are not very impressive. Based on the quality of the product, as well as the packaging, this is the type of item I would expect to find at stores that offer inexpensive off-brand, lower quality products. Overall, the fit is poor, the sound has issues, and the quality is lacking.Sound:I paired this with my smart phone and watched a couple of videos. I heard a high pitch hissing in the right side that was distracting. If it were not for the hissing, the sound might have been OK. Not GOOD, but not terrible.Physical Quality:The headphones are lightweight and are not very flimsy, but they don't feel like they are high quality. The band is is hefty enough and feels sturdy when I expand the length to fit my head. However, they look like they might break where the band attaches to the ear pieces.Comfort:These are the most uncomfortable headphones I've ever worn. The band feels tight and the headphones press against my ears and begin to hurt after just a few minutes. It's made worse by the poor fit of the ear cups. The padding on the ear pieces is not good quality. It's soft, but looks like it is made from cheap materials. More importantly, they do not cup my ears correctly and they feel awkward, especially since the foam padding is not good quality. They don't appear to be designed for adult size ears, as noted by other reviewers. The outer diameter is right, but the inner measurement and shape is wrong. No matter how many times I reposition them, they just feel awful. They also got hot after just a few minutes, which also indicated lower quality materials.Brand:I have never heard of the brand before, so I tried to find out more about it but came up empty. The manual that came inside the box is a tiny, poorly printed booklet that does not include a brand name or contact information, so it does not indicate who produces the product.On a hunch, I did an online search for the model number LD-9210 in case it was marketed under other brand names. I found out that it is a generic product manufactured by a company in China. It is then offered for sale with your own brand, so anyone can offer it as their own. The box is identical to the one I received, except for the addition of the customized brand name on the top. It appears possible that everything Francois et Mimi offers is like this, and they don't actually manufacture items themselves. Their website says they outsource products from international factories. I don't think there is anything French about this company, other than their name.Reliability:Since there is no contact information, you will not be able to get customer service if anything goes wrong. There isn't any type of warranty information in the package. The retailer that sells them through Amazon will offer the 30 day warranty that Amazon requires from their marketplace sellers, but that's the most you can expect from this purchase.I'll let my grandchildren use these headphones, if they don't hurt their ears. I think it will fit them better, and it won't matter if they break them. I guess that's the best use for them - when quality doesn't matter. I would not recommend these headphones to my friends.

TL;DR: Do not buy this. If you want a Crucial SSD, get the M4, not the V4. It's slightly more money but a world of difference.This SSD is significantly _slower_ than a spinning disk. Based upon the Windows 8 task manager "disk activity" section (and the AS SSD utility), it appears this drive does not have throughput for many operations per second. The data tab shows it peaking for minutes at a time. Minutes! Raw sequential data is very fast, but many threads asking for tiny bits of data and it fails very badly with latency approaching 10 seconds. Seconds! And that's the exact use-case where SSDs are supposed to shine. This drive has a very bad controller in it. Maybe they can fix it later with a firmware update, but right now, it's terrible. Do not buy. You will regret not spending $20 more for something better.I was running this Crucial V4 SSD 256 GB in an i7 laptop and attempted both Windows 8 Pro and Windows 7 Ultimate installs. Both installed fine and reported no issues, even with a chkdsk. But the drive is not fine. It's awful. This is my 4th SSD, all different brands, and I have never had an issue like this. My very first one was a relative slow performer back when SSDs were somewhat new, but nothing like this. I'm a long-time Crucial customer and frankly, they should take this product off the market until it's fixed.I was able to replace my 256 GB V4 with a 256 GB M4 and all my issues are completely gone. The M4 is very fast and responsive like an SSD should be. So I know it wasn't the OS or the hardware the drive was in. It was the drive. To Crucial's credit, they accepted the V4 via RMA and sent me an M4 for a very small fee (price difference).If you don't believe me, read the other reviews here and search the web for things like crucial v4 slow or crucial v4 freezes. The issue is all over Crucial's official forum and others.

Rightly or wrongly, I am comparing this with a CinemaTube box that I already own.  I needed another media streamer and decided to give the WD TV Live Plus box a try...As a prelude, my first frustrations began when I had to wait 20 minutes for 3 flashes to be applied. Yes, three updates and they are really slow.  I did the update from the box itself, and apparently the updates are not additive.  I had to apply all three of them.  Or, it could be that the upgrades are additive, but the box (or the upgrade service) isn't smart enough to say "he needs the latest firmware, I'll get the latest one and he'll be good to go." No, they were applied one at a time.  I wouldn't mind so much if it wasn't so slow.  When I turned on my CinemaTube after unboxing, it told me I needed an upgrade and applied it in a matter of minutes, possibly seconds.Start up time is also unusually slow, it probably takes a minute or so to come up after turning it on.  The CinemaTube takes seconds.I didn't have a good experience with this box at all.  I don't know why some people are praising it.  It took me three hours to get it to connect to my server and when it did the playback was choppy. I'm a technical user and one who works in IT; I can't imagine how frustrating this would be for a non-techie. The remote is tiny and better suited for travel, it's not media room friendly, at least it wasn't for me. By contrast the CinemaTube connects swiftly and playback has been flawless (Netflix through PlayOn can be iffy though, but that's PlayOn's issue not CinemaTube's) and the remote is larger and easier to hold.  It's not the best remote, mind you, but it more professional grade than the WD remote for the same amount of money.The navigation is counter-intuitive.  The cross-path design (one horizontal path and one vertical path), while clean and uncluttered, makes you click through a bunch of options that you don't care about.  It's pretty (I guess), but it's frustrating.  The CinemaTube menu is kind of cheesy, but it looks fine and incredibly simple(that's a good thing).  When it comes up your major options are super-easy to get to (Select Video, open a shortcut, and browse your media).VOB playback on this box is also pretty lame.  What is nice is that it's pretty quick to get the content started, the downside (the BIG downside) is navigation within the DVD structure is a mess.  The CinemaTube on the other hand has a handy, dedicated DVD menu button that always works, not matter where you are.  Press it during playback and your right back to the menu.  The WD box was iffy with the menu.  Sometimes it would bring up the menu, sometimes it wouldn't.I could go on.  I'm sure that this device is fine for some people (based on the reviews I've seen many are happy with it).  But it doesn't work for me.  Had this been my first media streamer, maybe I'd think all was fine.  The CinemaTube is not without its quirks. But they are minor by comparison.  Generally, I turn that box on and I'm watching a movie with a few clicks.  I don't need to be wowed by the interface, which actually looks pretty nice and clean.  It's rough around the edges, but who cares? I don't.I think that the WD box suffers from the "style over substance" syndrome.  They probably wanted to make the presentation look cool, and they've succeeded.  It does look nice, but using it as means to get to your content is another thing altogether.  It loses in that area of utility.  I think they may have gotten it right the the WD TV Hub's UI design, but I'd still be concerned about how well it functions during playback (which is what it's all about!).So, I'll be sending this back.  Too bad.  I wanted to like it and support WD.  I'll still buy my hard drives (or SSDs) from them, I've yet to have one of their drives fail over the 20 years I've been buying them.And yes, I did read the manual!I guess I'll just pick up another CinemaTube or a Zinwell (which is the same thing). Each to his own, I guess!Update:I tried out the WD TV Live Hub, please see my review on that.  It's much better than the Live but....

I had been wanting to try anodized cookware for about a year, specifically a 9" pan, because that is often the least expensive yet most useful piece to try out cookware with.  While more expensive than a traditional 9" anodized skillet, this set from Circulon has some advantages that make it worthwhile.Things I liked:- the silicone handles are cool to the touch, no hot pad or mitt needed as with some anodized brands with all-metal handles- I have a gas stove, so I appreciate that the bottoms are thick enough to evenly distribute heat without a hot spot circle in the center of the pans- the non-stick nature of the pans is excellent, although I still needed a little nonstick spray with eggs- oven safe to 400, nice for recipe versatility- the dual pans with interlocking handles made it possible to make a frittata without using an extra plate to flip, which was a lot less messy, not to mention much easier- the skillet with the wider bottom is my favorite for making omelettes, the narrower bottomed is nice for general small jobs- very easy to clean- I found I'll use this size pan a lot more than I used to use my old one of this size, just because I enjoy using themThings I disliked:- the interlocking feature is described as "tightly sealing", which I disagree with; if you hold the interlocking handles and the pan handles, there is still some shifting when you flip if you're not careful or not quick enough - this may take a little getting used to- the wider bottomed skillet is shallow, putting its handle very close to the cooktop surface- I have never been a fan of rivets inside pans - they are like magnets for food debris - my other pans have handles that screw to the outside, and I prefer it that way- the signature circles design of Circulon may be good for the nonstick coating, but I find it odd to see the design on the bottoms of my omelettes, which often happensThe drawbacks are not deal breakers for me.  I use this set a lot, and am very happy with its performance in general.

Well, I am not into swords, and never will be, but I know if you want a funcional sword, you DO NOT want stainless steel.However, since I really have no use for the sword ,I just bought it because is was cheap, and I didn't have one, and wanted to feel one in my hand for the first time ever.I wanted it for the blade alone, as I had always planned on putting a handle on it, as it is full tang, and even thought it is made of super hard/brittel stainless steel, it is cheap enough to experiment with the feel, and making a handle for it.The handle on this sword is super cheap!  It is made of two small peices of wood, wrapped onto each of the sides, with this really flimsy plastic type wrap.  On top of that, they wrap it in some type of thin shoe lace type nylon cord.The cord moves all around, and is slippery.If you want to buy this for the money, I would plan on making a custom handle for it, if you are a tinkerer, or hobbyist.The sword comes pretty sharp, so I think the original handle is dangerous.If I ever get the time, and am board, I was thinking of drilling some holes into the tang(although, I think the stainless might be too hard for that), and bolting two peices of symetrical wood onto each side, followed by wrapping it in a leather cord, or tong.However, I don't have the time, or need, or want, so I cut off the nylon cord, and the flimsy plastic tape wrap that was wrapped around the wood exposing the tang, and put a new quick handle on it.Quick working handle making:1. I used black electrical tape to wrap around those two pieces of cheap wood to bond them to the tang.2. Then I tightly wrapped the hole assembly in leather cord, to provide a no slip surface, to hold onto this sharp blade with.With the stock "handle", I think you would risk cutting yourself if you were to handle this very sharp item.From the little I know about metals, and what I have read, if you do want a functional sword, you want a high carbon steel that is not brittle like stainless.I would also say this is NOT a "wall hanger" either as it is very ugly, and cheap looking.The sheath, although functional is an ugly piece in line with the cheap price.For the 19 dollars I paid, I am not dissastisfied, however, I am not sure why I bought it in the first place...I have no use for it.It would be mostly worthless as a combat weapon(as said "zombies" ;)) and I could have used the money elsewhere...I am not sure for how brittle it is, it would make a good machete either.I don't plan on buying another, so I guess I have gotten my lifetime fill of sword ownership...I guess it works for the company that makes this as they got my money, and if they sell a million of these cheap swords, they can make some serious money...I wasn't going to bother writing this, but I thought it might help some others to save thier money.I would say, if you want a real sword, spend some money on one.  Cold Steel is supposed to make universally good products, and won't break the bank, if you want that kind of thing...If you want a sword to own just to hold in your hand and not really use, and you plan on putting a handle on it, maybe go for it. Otherwise save your money.

I've had a Plantronics Voyager Pro+ for years, and absolutely love it. (See my review at http://www.amazon.com/review/R3QREZHP0THQ7C). It's so comfortable that I can wear it all day and forget it's there. This headset has A2DP (Advanced Audio Distribution Profile), a Bluetooth feature that allows headsets to receive stereo media on my phone, so  it occured to me that I could also use it for listening to podcasts and webinars on my PC without having to switch headphones.Installing the BTD-400 adapter should have been trivial, but the instructions were brief to the point of being useless. On my PC running Windows 7 Professional 32-bit, the driver installation process took about 15 minutes. So, after I launched the installer without knowing what to expect next, I sat there for several minutes wondering if I'd hosed my HD before any prompts finally appeared. At the end of the installation I still didn't know what to do next, so I rebooted the PC. Then, when I looked in "Devices", I found a new icon for the Bluetooth app. When I clicked it, I was prompted to configure Bluetooth on my PC, then connect my Pro+, which went without a hitch. I'm a real "wirehead", so I can only guess what a non-technical user would have experienced in getting to this point!The Pro+ is capable of connecting to 2 sources simultaneously and, when everything works properly, the result is really sweet! I can listen to webinars and podcasts on my PC and any incoming calls simply override the media program. But when the Pro+ disconnects from either the phone or the PC, as when I walk away from either or put the PC on standby, the Pro+ doesn't automatically reconnect to either source. I can manually reconnect it to my phone at the Wireless/Bluetooth configuration page, or to my PC by clicking the icon in Devices, but it's really a hassle and I can't casually move around. Obviously, I need my Pro+ to stay seamlessly connected to my phone so, if I can't figure out how to address the problem, I'll probably just not use it often with my PC.If I discover a solution, or learn that the problem is other than with the BTD-400, I'll update this review to report my findings.

Pro: Will charge two LOW POWER USB devices, fairly compact, Input 100-240V is a plus for travel.Con: Misleading description. Does NOT charge iPad-2 - that being true, it is too large for only 2 USB ports.------------------------------A more accurate name for this product would be "iPad-1, 2-Port USB Adapter."Describing it as "IPAD-2USB: High Power," and claiming that it "will charge two high power electronics devices ... at the same time" leads one to believe that it will work with the current "high power" toy: the iPad-2. I guess that it depends upon one's interpretation of "high power."Still though, if the unit specs (at least as I read them) were actually met, then it *should* be able to charge an iPad-2 which requires a 10W 2A charger.This unit claims an output of 5V 2A, recalling that Watts = Amps x Volts then this should be enough power for the iPad-2. As my iPad-2 will NOT charge I can only conclude that 1) This unit is defective; 2) that the labeling is for the two USB ports summed together; or, 3) that my iPad is defective (but other chargers work fine).Given what I see as the deception in the naming and description of this product as "IPAD-2USB: High Power", I think "2" is the answer and that the output is split between the 2 USB ports - 2.5V 1A per port. I have not measured this.There are cables which will combine 2 USB ports into 1 in order to increase available power - but avoiding having to do things like that was the reason I sucked in on what I thought of as an "iPad-2 USB" charger. I do not think the manufacturer of this product left that space out by accident.I am keeping this to use at home to charge low-power devices, but it is not suitable for the purpose for which it was purchased: a backup USB travel charger for an iPad-2.

The only ultimate thing about this media player is its ability to suck at just about everything it does.  Don't let the sleek look and the touch screen fool you, this is a very basic device. The interface is very clunky, slow to use and not at all refined - there's no smoothness to it at all.  While the music section can play tunes in a number of different file formats, it is severely limited by the 4GB capacity, poor navigation and the lack of tone controls.  Same for the video section, 4GB is tiny!  And the screen's poor viewing angles does not lend itself to lengthy viewing.  Additionally, the screen does not have an aspect ratio of 16:9 or even 4:3 but is something in between that displays your videos with the wrong aspect ratio and there is no ability to compensate for it.  The only thing this player does offer is drag and drop, but many devices do that.  Unless you are looking for a very inexpensive first player for a young child, I cannot recommend this - and even then, this unit may prove to be an exercise in frustration.

Let me start this review by saying that I've been putting machines together since the days of CP/M and the S-100 bus, so I'm pretty sure that I know how to plug in a drive. The MOLEX power plug and the SATA connector are keyed so it would take a complete moron to connect them up incorrectly. I installed this power/data cable without shaving off any of the keys. The power and SATA connectors on this machine had been used previously so the wiring harness in the machine was not at fault. As soon as I powered on the machine I smelled the SMELL, the smell of an overheated circuit board and fried components.I powered down the machine and looked for the scorch marks, took out the drive cage and the circuit board on the just installed drive was hotter than what I would consider normal. Switched the drive back the old cable, dead as a doornail. Removed the drive from the cage and I could feel no  torgqu  as one would normally feel from a rotating drive..The only good thing about this is that the drive that was connected this cable was being wiped so that it coule be sent back to the manufacturer for reporting SMART (failed sector) errors. This drive had been working (booted and rebooted) and was working 15 minutes before being attached to this cable. Coincidence? I think not.

I'm so happy with these units from Pocketwizard. I've got cheap Yongnuo RF-602's (fairly reliable for something basic) for my speedlights (Nikon SB-600 and Yongnuo YN-560), but you lose the ability to adjust the flash at all from the camera position, one of the strengths of Nikon's CLS system. Sticking with optical CLS however (and using the popup flash on my D90 as a control), triggering is iffy: it usually works indoors, or outdoors with a limited range, *IF* the receiving flash is somewhere between you and the subject (forget it if it's behind you). No more worries with these newest pocketwizards. TTL and camera-adjustability is maintained (manual, if desired), as well as a potent radio signal with far more range than I'll ever need, without worrying about whether my flashes can see the optical signal from my camera. Now I can relax and just expect things to work, without limitation (I still need to adjust my Yongnuo flash manually, but will be getting another Nikon unit eventually).I don't yet have the AC3 control unit, which I think would be handy, and it's nice to know about the PowerMC2, should I end up purchasing an Einstein. But in the meantime, I've found the perfect control solution for triggering my off-camera lighting, and it's these.Note: this particular bundle includes one mini transmitter, and two larger flex transceivers. There's not much savings by buying this particular bundle, so search out the products individually if you don't need this exact combination.**EDIT: The bottom of the Flex transceiver (the shoe where it mounts onto a stand or camera) is plastic, not metal. Mine broke on the 2nd shoot I used it on.  We'll see how good Pocketwizard's service is when I call to get it returned. In the meantime, this drops my review from 5 stars to 4. Great units in terms of functionality, but even my $30 Yongnuo has a metal attachment shoe. The durability of this one sucks by comparison.**EDIT (again): So, apparently it's an advantage to have a [replaceable] plastic shoe rather than a metal one (still trying to accept this fact): With a plastic shoe, it'll be the weak spot, and will break before causing any damage to the flash or the pocketwizard itself. The shoe is intentionally and easily replaced. Basically, you remove four screws, detach a thin cable, pop the old one out, put a new one in (obtainable from the pocketwizard parts department for 20 bucks plus 3 shipping), and reattach everything. Takes about 5 minutes. Be prepared to do this once or twice if you buy these things... awesome product, but not indestructible. I'll stick with the four-star rating.

I am *really* lucky this didn't happen when I tried to download my images from my Sedona trip! I had one of these Transcend cards also fail last summer after a few uses but I thought it was a fluke. Transcend sent it back to me about six weeks later and said I had opened up the card up so the warranty was void! How preposterous. As an engineer, I am well aware of the kind of micro circuitry in a card like this and know there would be no reason to open it as I couldn't possibly service it. I also shipped it to them in the same box it came in so there shouldn't have been any shipping damage. I was ticked, so I called them. I talked with a lady with a heavy Asian accent. She pulled up my service number and said she would have one of their service people call within 48 hours. Never got a call. As inexpensive as this card was, I felt I had already wasted enough of my time with this company, so I gave up. If you are considering this card, think for a moment how you would feel if you lost all of your unreplaceable images unexpectedly due to a poor quality card. Then, remember how I was treated when I sent in their failed card for replacement.

I am a fairly experienced GPS receiver user. I am on my second handheld Garmin. I purchased this 765t because of its size. It is replacing a Garmin Streetpilot 2610.Other than size the 2610--with last years database--is superior in a lot of important respects.Here is a summary of + and minus of the 765 in comparison to the 2610:+ size/weight+ bluetooth+ built in database+ works on batteryI haven't tried/experienced the lane assist feature so I'll leave that in the neutral category.- - the Garmin registration process, more later- the poi database is lacking, more later- either voice or mute, no chime-only option- short battery lifeRe the Garmin registration process:Plan on a bunch of hours to register. Before Garmin lets you register you have to upgrade the unit's software. Then you have to use your one-time, 60 day long privilege to  free-upgrade your maps and load them onto your computer. This is a 2 GB file and even with high speed it is lengthy. In the case of my DSL it took nearly 4 hours. That gets the file into your computer. Then it takes another chunk of time to get the database into the 765.This whole process, while do-able, is clunky. And not seamless. A couple of times I found myself looking at the same screen I thought I had already executed instructions from, but the process didn't seem to know I had. Eventually I stumbled through but as I say, NOT seamlessly.So plan on a half day or longer of your time, and loss of use of your high speed connection while you are at it.During the course of all this you are asked at least 6 times (I lost count) to agree to the license conditions.But here's the real kicker: The map data base has severe omissions! I couldn't find my nearby Super Walmart, which has been there for 5 years. So I wrote Garmin and here is what the responder said:"I tried looking for Wal Mart in Glen Falls, Queensbury, and even Albany. I was unable to find the point of interest by multiple methods of Point of Interest searching. It appears this particular point of interest was left out or forgotten in our latest 2010 mapping revision.I'm unsure why this point of interest was removed from the mapping, but I will be forwarding this to our mapping supplier Navteq."So after spending the better part of a day getting registerd I am left wondering what other "particular points of interest" (like gas stations?) might have been left out of the database.there are places on line to download POI files but I haven't found any which are totally thorough. Plus if your custom-loaded POI duplicates a built-in one, your get a duplicate listing. Seems like the programmers at Gamin should be smart enough to eliminate that.Short battery life:Apparently this is a common complaint. I tried completely discharging and recharging and it appears 2 hours is the max battery life. Still, this is long enough so I can take the unit into a motel at night and select the next day's route or do some searching for restaurants. (If they haven't been left out of the database!)Bluetooth:I am not a big bluetooth user but I had no problem pairing with my cell phone. Though I did learn that I could not use the bluetooth connection with my computer for the loading/upgrading process, unlike my PDA, which syncs with my computer via bluetooth. Thus for the 765 you have to use a cable or the updating software does not "see" the 765.wanted to add a couple of more points after using the unit a bit more:1. the 765t lacks a remote. However, the screen seems pretty responsive to the touch--a bit more so than the 2610. Still, a remote can be important in two situations:- it you have big fingers, or- you have a larger suv or truck and the unit is sitting pretty far forward on the dash, and/or the user is in the rear seat, etc.2. The 765t has a significant higher speed redraw/recalculate than the 2610. Aligned with this is the better reponse in approaching an intersection.....it is more accuate in terms of distance-from than the 26103. For the 2610 I had a bean bag mount. The 765t is so light it does not have the mass the 2610 had, so I am happy so far with the suction cup mount. Plus, wanting to cut down on weight, for take-along to use in rental cars, not using the bean bag is a huge +++that's all for now......

First off, I am impressed with how rugged and durable this holster is. The Kydex is extremely thick, thicker than any holster I have seen in fact. The leather is also very thick and durable, however it is rough looking and unfinished, which may not necessarily be a bad thing depending on your tastes. The rivets also appear to be high quality. This holster is clearly made to last, and I might also say that it is extremely comfortable while worn. And $35.00 is a hell of a price!That being said, it is impossible to get a comfortable full-firing grip on a Glock without trimming the leather back to expose the thumb indentation, and filing/cutting the Kydex near the trigger guard away from the middle finger indentation on the frame of the pistol. For the leather I simply used a box cutter with a sharp blade, and for the Kydex I snipped away at it with a pair of diagonal pliers, then finished it up with a file.I should also mention that the retention was perfect when brand new, but after much wear is a lot looser, and is also almost completely controlled by how tightly you wear your belt - there is no indentation on the Kydex where the trigger guard fits into that "snaps" it in place. This could probably be easily remedied with a heat gun to tighten up the Kydex a little.Now... the clips. They are too long, period. They are made for a belt that is 1/2" wider. It doesn't translate really to much up and down movement of the holster while wearing it, but they simply don't fit regular belts. Also worthy of mention is that the tabs on the clips that you use to bend open and get your belt in there stick out too far! Far enough that your t-shirt will catch on them when drawing. Not confidence inspiring. They may be able to be snipped back then sharp edges be filed away.In conclusion, although this holster is very durable and made of quality materials, it requires a couple slight modifications to the leather, which covers the thumb indentation on the pistol, and the Kydex, which covers too much of the trigger guard, interfering with middle finger placement. These modifications took about 20 minutes and were very simple. I only noticed these flaws when I got my Galco Kingtuk in the mail and noticed the differences between the two. (to be fair, the Kingtuk creaks like a pair of old shoes...)

I've been addicted to frothy, foamy lattes and cappuccinos for well over a decade, but my DIY efforts at home have been somewhat...deflated. Then there was the scant and quickly dissipated foam produced by our kluged arrangement of heating the milk in the microwave and using the battery operatedAerolatte Milk Frother, Satin.  My first use of the Capresso Froth TEC Automatic Milk Frother made me feel like Dug, the dog from the movie "Up" - it's MY FAVORITE THING!When I received the Capresso, I unpacked and washed the pitcher, lid, and frothing disk.  It couldn't be easier to take this apart for cleaning.  The disk pops out of the pitcher and can be thoroughly rinsed.  The glass pitcher has a coated base and the lid is a heavy plastic, so I would recommend washing by hand, or at least don't use the "heated dry" cycle on the dishwasher.Frothing the milk couldn't be easier.  Pour in the milk to the desired fill marking (MIN, FROTH, HEAT), with 10 oz being the max; place the pitcher on the base and choose from cold, warm, or hot. Now I'd like to start off by saying that I'm not a tech or video geek, so I'm coming from the point of view of a buyer is who looking for a product that is easy to set & use and has a decent amount of versatility.  This is the first digital camcorder I've used, let alone an HD digicam, and I was a little concerned about the supported file format, in particular how hard it would be to get the video off the camera and onto my computer.First off, I was surprised at how quickly I had the JVC Everio GZ-HD300 set up and was ready go to.  It was out of the box and ready to be charged in a matter of minutes, and in the time it took to charge the camera I'd easily installed the included software for viewing and backing up/exporting video from the camera.  I was shooting my first video in just over an hour.  The camera interface is pretty straight forward, with most of the work done through the LCD monitor arm, in particular the laser touch scroll bar.  I've had a handful of touch screen mp3 players and am used to the sensitivity issues of some touch screen interfaces.  The touch scroll bar on this camera has a nice midrange sensitivity that makes navigating through most of the menus pretty easy.  My one complaint was scrolling through the video playback menu, as the up and down on the scroll bar is very unintuitive for skipping though rows and columns.As for capturing video, again, the design of the camera is pretty intuitive.  Not only is the camcorder small, but the placement of the stop/start and zoom buttons seemed perfect for me.  There is a separate button for shooting still images, which is a little weird (I'd figure it would work of the record start/stop button on the back), but it is located right next to the zoom toggle switch on the top so it's not that hard to get used to.  The 20x zoom is very nice, though for handheld shots it the video can get very shaky.  I also liked the power on function coinciding with opening the LCD screen, as it takes a step out of the process and gets you shooting video a few seconds faster, and from my experience those few seconds can really matter.  It also has a sleep mode for when you close the LCD without powering off the unit, again, saving precious time when trying to conserve battery power and shooting video on the go.  As I've mentioned the camera is also capable of shooting stills as well, though it's almost impossible to get quality shots when using the zoom without a tripod.The largest gripe I had with the camcorder, and the reason why I can't give it more than three stars is the horrible proprietary Everio MediaBrowser software that's included.  First off, it's Windows only, which is sort of limiting (and weird considering it has a built in export function for iTunes.)  Second, it's very confusing.  I've played around with it a few times and from what I can tell the interface is split up between the camera and the software.  You have to initiate the backup/export function from the camera and then take over in the software.  There is no drag and drop functionality from the camera to your computer, instead you have to use the software.  On top of this, and for the life of me, I couldn't get the video playback to display decently in the software player included (it was very herky and choppy, and I'm not referring to my handheld skills.)  The video playback on the camcorder's LCD is beyond beautiful, as well as playback on my old Sony Trinitron TV (with the included Audio/Video cords), but it really stank on the software.  I noticed that there are some freeware programs like Media Player Classic that can handle the .mts video files, but there are a bunch of codecs needed to get the video to display.  As for exporting to iTunes, this wasn't that hard, but the converted m4p video files were almost unwatchable with mass amounts of pixilation and discoloration from the conversion process.Though I really like the design and ease of use of the JVC Everio GZ-HD300, I would give up all of the bells and whistles for an easier way to get the video off the camera and onto my computer.

The dictionary defines the word "BIG" as large or great in dimension, with bulk, large or great in quantity.  Well makers of this "Big Boss Grill" need to look up the word Big and redesign a product that properly reflects the description.  This grill is suited best for one, maybe two people at most.A product like this should be versatile, convenient, somewhat rugged, and easy to clean.  Unfortunately the Big Boss Grill misses virtually all of these traits.  Sure, it can be considered versatile, but at the expense of making quite a mess.  They give you a lot of cooking plates; so many that it takes a stand to hold them.  Who wants that sitting on their counter?  This grill has no method of draining grease and oil away from your food, except by allowing it to pool up in the channels of the cooking plate.  What happens when the channels start to fill up?  The grease and oil starts to run out the ends of the grill, making a horrible mess, and even creating a potential electrocution hazard to the operator.  The construction of the product is mediocre at best, with a weak hinge design, and not even so much as a power button or switch.  That's right; the power plug is your on/off switching method.  I don't like anything that instantly tries to draw a high current while you are plugging it in.  That is just dangerous.  Almost as dangerous as when the grease from the cooking trays starts running down the side and into the opening where the power cord enters the grill.Results of the food I grilled varied a great deal, depending on what I was cooking.  Sandwiches grilled up nicely and rather quickly.  Burgers took much longer, were rather dry, and the amount of grease all over the grill and counter top made me decide to never use this grill for burgers again!  Grilling chicken breasts was slower yet, and they came out extremely dry.  I did make an omelet, but found the process and cleanup to be much more tedious than just getting out a pan and making it the old fashioned way.Overall there is very little, if anything, that impresses me about this product.  For the money they are asking, there are so many better choices to be had; such as the bargain pricedCuisinart WM-SW2 Dual-Sandwich Nonstick Electric Grill.  I'm not saying that the Big Boss Grill is completely useless, but they have designed and constructed it in a way that clearly reflects bottom shelf quality and manufacturing standards.  If you are single and want a simple grilled cheese sandwich, when you may want to give this bad boy a whirl.  However, if you are cooking for two or more people, and/or don't want to have an awful mess every time you decide to use your portable electric grill, then invest your money in a higher quality product.  It's small, poorly designed, and extremely messy to use.  I guess maybe including the word "Big" in their product title is not a reference to physical size, but rather the mess it is capable of creating.  Sorry folks, a 2 star rating is rather generous for this "As Seen On TV" contraption.  I hope my review will save some frustration and money for someone out there.  =o)

I wouldn't purchase this item if I had it to do over again -- it just doesn't remove much water from the air.I bought this to keep the humidity down in my bathroom after taking a shower.  Despite having to empty it every few weeks, the mold kept growing and the bathroom didn't seem any less humid.  So I bought a hygrometer to measure the humidity.  Sure enough, it doesn't drop much with the dehumidifier running.Unsure about air circulation, I decided to get a reasonably large cardboard box (perhaps 1' x 3' x 4') and run the dehumidifier inside with a wireless hygrometer.  I sealed the edges of the box, and ran the dehumidifier with a wireless hygrometer inside.  What I found was that the temperature inside increased 5-8 degrees and the relative humidify decreased, but the due point didn't change (hotter air can hold more water, so the best way to compare the total water in the air is to use the due point).In sum, other than occasionally emptying a few cups of water, I have no proof that this dehumidifier is doing much of anything (but I do now own a pretty nifty wireless hygrometer :)  ).Also, as others have noted, the voltage converter does get hot and it does run quietly.
