Note: My preferred rating is three-and-half stars, but I don't have that option.Personally, I'm not a fan of cookware sets. That's because they often tend to be a bit of "something for everyone" but not necessarily exactly what you need. Many people buy a set because they get one or two pieces they really want and the set price is comparable to, or less than, what they would pay for the one or two individual pieces they want. Sets also make good gifts for select audiences (see below).This seems to be the case here as well. I showed the contents to a friend's 20-something son (who is just setting up an apartment and having never cooked much at all) to get his opinion (His mother wanted to know if I thought the set would be good for him as she was thinking Christmas gift potential) and he said, given his and his friends cooking routines, and the size of their apartment kitchen, the only thing useful was the small fry pan and the two smaller sauce pans. (SO, no go for her on this as a gift for him.) This may be the case for others who don't cook a lot beyond the basics of heating up stuff and frying an egg or two.I've been cooking for years and my kitchen is pretty much set up in terms of what I need and use. So, to be fair, I'm not the target audience for this set and my comments should be taken in the context of someone who already owns exactly what they need in terms of what I cook each week and for special occasions.That said, here are my overall comments, based on item type, etc.We don't put pots in the oven so I can't comment on how these will stand up to high oven heat. But it says they should only be used at up to 350 degrees, which means you can't use for high-heat cooking, such as roasting. Even our frittatas in fry pans require higher oven heat. That's a limitation in my mind for some cooks.But for use on an electric stovetop, which we have, they're fine and seem to respond as we need (neither too hot, too slow to heat up or such that food is easily burned or overheated as compared to what we now use, which is a combo of Calphalon and Le Creuset pieces, saute pans, skillets, frying pans and dutch ovens).Appearance: It's a good-looking set for its price point, with a nice finish (have no idea how it will hold up but it was easy to clean by hand; we don't have a dishwasher.)on both the stainless steel and aluminum pieces. You won't be ashamed to have them out and on display.Lids: Kudos for making them all glass. Also liked the way the handles were configured and that decorative touch of  copper. All tops fit securely and stayed in place during cooking.Sizes: I really don't get including three  smallish step-up pans so close in capacity. To me, it'd make more sense to have just two, the one or two-quart and one 3-quart, or larger. For frying pans/skillets, it would be more useful to have the 10-inch (which is really small in terms of what you can fit in it even for one person) and a larger-sized pan. The 8-inch barely fits a large egg and would never be used in our house even though we're only two people.The six-quart covered stockpot is a great item for soups, stews, chilis, roasts and other things that a lot of people make regularly. Great size for both cooking and storage.The two, slotted plastic utensils? I don't get those being included unless they felt someone was getting this set and may not have any utensils on hand to use the Teflon-surfaced frying pans/skillets out of the box.Weight: I would disagree with those who say these are medium weight, especially the frying pans/skillets. When using lightweight plastic utensils with the saute pans and the frying pans, I frequently had to grab the handle to stop the pans from tipping over or going off the stovetop. And it wasn't as if I was furiously scrambling or sauteeing something in the pans. Sauce pans were a bit more stable, depending on contents. (THe stockpot was fine but then it was always at least half-way filled with food.)Longevity of Teflon-coated pieces: These days, this is always a concern to me. But there's no way to know how well these will do as we've only used for a couple of weeks, not months or years. Only time will tell.Value: Given what pots and pans cost these days, if someone will actually use at least half of the items, it's probably a good buy for a starter set for those who don't do a lot of heavy-duty (or pan-specific) cooking. It's probably very good for small spaces (dorms, studio apartments, rec vehicles, etc.)too.I haven't done a comparison of similar sets in terms of contents and prices so I really can't say.The "Brand" Name: As for it being by Paula Deen, well, really who cares? What does she bring to these products that differentiates them from others on market? Honesty, I don't see any added value. What makes this a "signature" collection? I really dislike this type of marketing. It's one thing if someone creates a new product, meets an unmet need or offers something of particular value or relevance that can't be found elsewhere. But when that isn't the case, what's the point of putting a name on it?I know who Paula Deen is but having her name on this doesn't make this a better or unique product. (And in fact, will turn a lot of people off.) And it doesn't make me think this product is better or more desirable.

I know ND filters can get up there in price, but I'd never used any before and I was SO excited when I remembered they existed! I set out to find the most affordable filter or set, just to try them out and see if they were the answer. I LOVE shooting wide-open with my 50mm 1.4, but in New Mexico sun it's a joke if you expect to also use flash (which limits my shutter speed drastically). These puppies certainly allow for more bokeh, but the cost is MUCH higher than the price tag. These cheap filters soften the HECK outta my images. The close-ups were MUCH less terrible, but there was still a vague softness which required MUCH more sharpening than I am interested in using. The full-body shots were incredibly soft, and MANY shots were just out-of-focus and unusable. This was mainly due to my inexperience with ND filters I imagine, as I had trouble finding my focus points since the lens was so dark... but I somehow doubt it should be this hard. Either way, I don't shoot slowly and calmly enough to waste my model's time and ruin their groove by having to constantly pause to check my focus and re-shoot things I didn't get in focus. Shooting at 1.4 already has it's issues (getting boobs in focus instead of the face, which I HATE and try to NEVER do...I never edit those shots, regardless of how nice they are), so adding this level of darkness just makes it more of a challenge.A challenge I'll gladly accept if it is the only challenge, not one of many :( I've only used them for two separate model shoots so far, both times deciding to remove them and just sacrifice my aperture instead of sacrificing my mood and photo sharpness.With my beyond-low-income status, I am excited to save enough money to hopefully get either a Tiffen ND filter or a LCW filter next time. Fingers crossed I'm not just overreacting about ND filters in general, hopefully they only get better with more money! Maybe someday I can blow five hundred dollars on one, and NEVER regret it!I will not be tossing these in the trash, I plan to play with them when I don't have clients and have no need to produce images that are perfect. Despite my rage when I see 4-6 out of 10 amazing shots are out of focus, I still think they are a great introduction if you really only have fifteen bucks. Just be ready for a big need to get better ones immediately after these arrive.The seller was GREAT, however! These were not eligible for Amazon Prime (bummer!!!), but they still arrived in two or three days! Which was great, because I nearly had a heart attack waiting. My impatience coupled with excitement is deadly :) I gave this a 3-star rating because I don't think I had a good expectation in mind. I was expecting something MUCH more awesome than what these were, and I think it was my own fault for lack of experience with these types of filters, both cheap and expensive. In my own mind, I'd give these a 1 or 2 star rating. I mean....photo filters should enhance my photos, not potentially ruin them.Still thankful I know what to shoot for next time! Just wish I could use my fifteen bucks toward the next time.

Shaving is an annoying fact of life but as much as we dread doing it, shaving is still an important part of the daily grooming routine. Manufacturers continue to make changes and enhancements to razors so that the task will be less irritating, smoother, easier, more comfortable, etc. This Schick razor, with its five blades, is one of the latest enhancements that is supposed to make shaving less annoying and more trouble- free than usual.Taken from the package, this razor does score some immediate points. I like the larger handle with its textured surface and rubberized grip. This provides more confidence that the razor will not slip, even when used in the shower. The overall look is nice, even though the large head, with its five sharp blades, does seem a little intimidating.Next comes the shave and here, the Schick Hydro 5 scores some hits and misses. The lubrication is good and it does help relieve irritation. The lubrication system is designed to last longer, too, and it helps to extend the life of the razor. However, the shaving experience itself yields mixed results. It does remove the hair and it works fine on the neck, but because there are five blades and the head is so large, the razor has a difficult time reaching certain areas, particularly close to the nose.  You can maneuver the razor any way you like, but there is a good chance you will not be able to shave these areas of your face with the degree of closeness you prefer.One unique feature of the Schick Hydro 5 Razor is that it has a built- in trimmer that is accessible with the press of a flexible plastic extension. This certainly sounds interesting, but once you use it, you realize it isn't quite as impressive as it leads you to believe. It is nothing more than a plastic extension that locks into the head, preventing it from pivoting. The idea is that, minus the pivot, the blades will be better capable of trimming because they will be better locked into place. My experience shows that this feature does little to improve your shave and the razor still cannot reach certain areas of the face.With several good points and some not-so-good points, my final verdict on this razor is that it is good enough to try, but perhaps not good enough to purchase again. I agree that the lubrication is good and the cutting ability on the neck and other large, unobstructed areas is above average. But five blades is truly excessive and the razor's inability to reach certain areas of the face lead me to rate it average overall.

I ordered this charger because of a combination of good ratings and its relative low price. The charger itself is "alright" - there are a few things I'd have preferred, like a not-as-bright LED and some sort of non-slip surface (on top AND bottom), but overall it does its job well (and does not go BEEEEP when you set a device on it. This is definitely a plus).What shocked me, though, was a note included with the charger saying (amongst a few other things) "Would you please leave a positive (5 stars) feedback to us? If yes, we can send you $5.00 amazon gift card to you free by email. In addition, if you can write a customer review (product review) will be much appreciated. Thanks in advance". (Please see the "Product Images from Customers" section for a picture of the note). It's one thing to say to a customer "If you like our product, please leave a good review!" but it's another thing entirely to offer bribes in exchange for doing so. I don't know if that is the entire reason that it had 100% 5 star ratings when I ordered it, but it sure seems suspicious. Bribing customers for good reviews skews the real rating and defeats the purpose of having product reviews in the first place. I don't have time or finances to try out every product on the market, so I rely heavily on the user reviews to help make purchasing decisions. I can't help but feel suckered by this company's actions.As I said earlier, the product itself is pretty decent and deserves maybe 3 or 4 stars. However, I'm taking it down to 1 star purely for the conduct of the company itself. I only wish the LED wasn't so bright that it lights up the room at night, and that the top and bottom both had some sort of non-slip rubber feet or something. I fixed the LED problem by applying some darkened stickers made just for this purpose, but it would be nice to not have to. I suppose I could dig up some non-slip dots to use on the bottom of the charger, but again I wish I didn't have to.So now, I'm on the fence as to whether to keep this or return it. It does its job, and in the meantime I've found another Qi charger that is much more to my liking (check out my review of the PowerBot PB1020 if you're interested). The only advantage to this one over the Powerbot is its size, which makes it easier to line up with my Nexus 7 than the 2.7" diameter "puck".

Silicone baking pans are extremely cool.  Light and flexible, they store easily and don't deform even if you accidentally leave something heavy on them, and you can just peel them off your finished baked good.  Since they cool down quickly, you can lift them without potholders after ~5 minutes out of the oven.  Plus, I get that thrilling "the future is now" feeling whenever I use them, and sometimes I bake solely in order to be able to use the pan because it's just so cool.Unfortunately, this pan and its sister, the 9x9 cake pan don't get clean --- whatever you bake leaves stains behind.  No matter how many times I have soaked them in hot soapy water, put them in the dishwasher, or scrubbed them, there are white splotches from flour that has spilled and brown splotches from cocoa and a shiny oil film.  Even with the stains, they work perfectly well, but I just try not to let my guests see them since they look somewhat questionable.  Also, I would be wary of using them with foods with strong flavors like onions or garlic, so that I wouldn't end up with garlic flavored brownies in the future.One reviewer noted that they get clean if you grease them, but I don't think that could prevent the oily film, since the problem there seems to be too much fat, not too little.  It's possible that they have improved since I bought them last year, but you may want to look elsewhere to the silicone pans with shiny insides like the Roshco.

I didn't take an actual measurement, but by ear that is close enough to get an idea of what all these people are talking about when they say they cant hear anything.. This ear piece is very loud, but because all the sound is focused in a narrow and sensitive frequency band the ear rejects it as an irritant. Turn it up louder and drive yourself nuts. What I have to do is move the ear piece so the sound hits the area near my ear. Plantronics does a great job in this department, they sound much better. But the last one I had the ear bud didn't fit right or something and I dropped it somewhere and never saw it again. The Mac Mini was updated on June 15th 2010. There are some upgrades and minor changes between the 2010 Mac Mini and 2009's model, detailed below.UPGRADESHDMI audio/video output (HDMI version 1.3 and supports up to 1920-by-1200 resolution and multichannel audio.)  Allows you to connect the Mac Mini to your HDTV easily.Nvidia Geforce 320 M integrated graphics processor. More powerful than last years Nvidia Geforce 9400 which was in the 2009 Mac mini. Useful for content creation.320 gb hard drive - Last years base model had a 160gb hard drive.Secure Digital (SD) memory card slot - Useful for transferring photos and videos from Cameras.Unibody aluminum body.STANDARD FEATURES - from last years model (minor changes noted in brackets) areCore 2 Duo Processor ( 2.4 ghz - up from 2.26ghz )2 GB 1066 MHz DDR3 Ram8x slot-loading SuperDrive DVD burnerMini DisplayPort video output with support for up to 2560-by-1600 resolutionCombined optical digital output/headphone outputFour USB 2.0 ports (1 less than the 2009 Mac Mini)One FireWire 800 portWi-Fi - 802.11n specification; 802.11a/b/g compatible, Bluetooth 2.1 and Gigabit Ethernet -10/100/1000.Software included is OS X 10.6 Snow Leopard and the iLife 09 suite of content creation tools. A 1 year warranty on parts and 90 day telephone technical support is standard.As one can see, not much has changed. Apple is still using outdated Core 2 Duo processors while the rest of the computer industry has moved on to using Intel's "i" series of processors and it's still shipping the Mac mini with 2gb of ram which is completely inadequate for multi-tasking effectively.However, whatever little has changed, is for the better.Apple has finally acknowledged that people connect their Mac Mini's to HDTV's and use them as media centers. So it's added an HDMI port to the machine. This makes hooking up your Mac mini to a HDTV really easy. No Blu-ray drive though.It's also included an SD card slot at the rear (Which also supports SDXC cards) - so you can transfer your photos / videos / data directly from an SD card without having to connect your camera / card reader to the machine.Also, new in this year's Mac mini is a removable panel on the bottom of the Mac mini which allows you to easily upgrade the ram. This is a welcome addition considering that accessing the ram slots in earlier Mac mini's was a tedious and time consuming process. And since the Mac mini only comes with 2gb of ram, a ram upgrade should be one of the first things you choose to do.Kingston Apple 4GB Kit (2x2GB Modules) 1066MHz DDR3 SODIMM iMac and Macbook Memory (KTA-MB1066K2/4GR)for [...] currently. The operating system STRUGGLES with multi-tasking when there's only 2gb of ram present. Note to Apple. Stop skimping on the ram. Thanks.Unfortunately, there are some negatives too.First up is the power supply unit. In the 2009 Mac mini, the power supply was an external power adapter, which meant if anything went wrong with it, you'd take the adapter for servicing, not the whole machine. However, the power supply unit is now inside the June 2010 Mac mini. This may look better / cleaner from a design / clutter point of view but it also means that if it ever malfunctions, instead of the power adapter, you'll have to take your Mac mini in to an Apple Store or Apple Authorized Store Provider and leave it there for repairs which may lead to more downtime.The SD card slot is at the back of the machine, and reaching behind to insert a card gets tedious fast.Also, the machine is STILL not designed to not let users access the hard drive easily (or without voiding the warranty). This forces the customer to be dependent on Apple for servicing, replacing or upgrading the hard drive. Considering the amount of confidential data customers store on their computers, they should be allowed to take out the hard drive when they need or feel like instead of being forced to take their machines into an Apple store if there are any issues. This is definitely a privacy / security risk for many customers and Apple should address this in the next iteration of the machine.Also, because of the closed design of the Mac Mini, Applecare will always be a requirement, since you can't replace anything in the machine if something goes wrong except for the ram. Power supply goes bad - no Applecare - pay Apple big money. Hard drive dies - no Applecare - pay Apple big money. So Applecare becomes a  $ 150 requirement to protect yourself from Apple's exorbitant repair costs. It's like a hidden cost, You don't see it until you realize you're probably going to need it.The price has also gone up by $ 100. Cost is an important aspect to consider. If you decide to upgrade the ram and also need to purchase a LCD monitor, keyboard and mouse, once you total it all up, the Mac mini will end up costing almost as much as a Macbook(which is more portable) or the entry level iMac (21.5 inch screen, 4gb of ram, dedicated graphics and bigger hard drive). If that's the case, you better off examining those machines as purchase options instead of buying a Mini.The Mac mini is a capable machine for general tasks such as watching videos, working on documents, listening to music and surfing the web. It's small and occupies very little space. It's also very energy efficient which is good for the environment and your energy bill. I would have loved to rate it 4 stars but I can't ignore Apple still including only 2gb of ram which is inadequate for multitasking, not including a Blu-ray drive, STILL not allowing customers to access the hard drive AND increasing the price by $ 100.If the issues mentioned above don't affect you in any way and you want a small, power efficient and capable machine (After upgrading the ram) the Mac Mini may be the machine for you.Hope this helps!NOTE - Mar 18 2011. The Mac Mini is now  extremely out of date compared to other computer makers current products. C2D processor, 320 GB 5400 rpm hard drive, 2 gb ram (stutter stutter). In 2011, these specs for $ 700 +  $ 150 Applecare = very bad value for money.Forget about the superficial things like how small it is. Instead buy a  $ 700 dollar  HTPC(Home theater PC), Excluding the operating system (which is always a matter of personal preference) you'll get a lot more bang for your buck with regards to hardware. IF you must buy a Mac Mini,  wait for Apple to update it so that the hardware will justify the cost.

The more I shoot, the more I've grown to understand how much camera straps and bags will always force uneasy compromises. The SLR form factor simply offers too many lens / accessory combination possibilities of too many different sizes, shapes, weights, centers of gravity, etc. for any single solution to hold it all at the ready with stability and security in every situation.  Ultimately, the best SLR accessories embrace the systematic, modular nature of the gear; but the R-strap, I've found, is decidedly anti-system.For the first month or so I used it, I thought the Black Rapid RS7 might just be the only and best camera strap I'd ever need.  As advertised, I found the R-Strap system highly secure, comfortable, and absolutely capable of holding my gear at an instant quick-draw ready.  Better, the R-Strap system actually works best with the largest body/lens/flash combination you can hand-hold--it's frankly amazing how well it tucks a D3 + 70-200/f2.8 combo in the small of your back--keeping your system protected and at the ready while offering you complete hands-free mobility.But if you carry anything more than a single SLR body and lens, the R-Strap won't play.  If you take a shoulder or sling bag with your camera (in my case, a Boda lens bag via the shoulder strap), the R-strap's beefy, bandolier design either gets tangled and fussy with your bag strap or it'll simply block access to your bag.  It'll also prohibit you from working with two bodies (though Black Rapid does make a goofy-looking and expensive suspender-like double harness, if you really don't mind being so conspicuous on the job).  I found the R-Strap ultimately uncomfortable with vertical shots, given that framing these pulls the strap loop slightly further from your body; if you size the strap even somewhat close to your body, you'll end up fighting it to position your eye.  Worse, the R-strap's use of  your lens tripod foot to hold your system with larger telephotos or telezooms--the very same engineering innovation that gives it such balance with big lenses--makes swapping lenses to your smaller wide zoom or prime slow and delicate work.  You'll need to unscrew the carabiner, un-latch it from the tripod foot, and, while making absolutely sure you're now supporting your otherwise unsupported camera body, re-hook and lock the carabiner to the body before mounting the smaller lens.  If that sounds like a three or four-handed juggle impossible to perform quickly or while standing up, you've got the right idea.  (And this procedure works only if you have a "Fasten-R" attached to both your telezoom's lens foot AND your body.  If you've only got the single Fasten-R that comes with the system, factor in unscrewing it from the lens and screwing it into the body before starting your carabiner dance.)  I've heard some pros warn that it's all too easy to forget that the R-strap doesn't actually support one's camera body when affixed to that all important lens tripod foot, and you might therefore drop the body on lens swaps.  Things get even slower if you carry a tripod: you'll have to unscrew the system's (necessarily) tight "Fasten-R" from your body or lens foot before locking in.In short: if you're climbing a mountain with your Nikon D3 / Canon EOS-1 + 70-200 f/2.8 and nothing else, it's perfection.  Want to carry a bag of anything else as well, swap lenses, or use a tripod? Get ready for the awkward--the Black Rapid remains black, but loses all the rapid.  I've seen some pros working Rapid straps well with waist-belt bags or fanny packs, but that limits your gear and doesn't solve the R-strap's big-to-small lens swap or tripod mount issues.Where does that leave us?  Maybe the typical top-mount SLR strap suffers less from any functional deficiency than it does from bad PR--too many obnoxious tourists with SLRs hanging from their necks.  My advice?  Think of that stock strap as a body strap or a wrist strap, not a neck strap.  When you wear your camera, either:(a) sling your strap around your neck _and_ shoulder, bandolier style, with the lens pointed _toward_ your body rather than away from it.  As you'll see, with lenses both large and small, wearing your SLR this way will force the lens downward and tuck your system close to your body--an even better position than the R-Strap's hold for hands-free security and system protection, especially in large crowds or in tight spaces.  Or,(b) put the flat section of your strap over your wrist, twist two or three loops, and pull tight.  The strap will hold your camera tightly to your wrist should you loose your shutter finger grip, and you'll be able to "quick draw" to any shooting position even faster than the R-Strap slingers.Used either way, your factory strap will secure your system with any lens, during any lens swap, with any bag, while mounting or unmounting from any tripod.  And it's free!

basically, the 70-300 ED is the perfect complement to the 18-70 kit lens for the nikon d series. it's worth having because of the 1.5 mag factor which means it's actually a 105-450mm, which gives you plenty of reach. add a teleconverter and you can get to 900mm (!). general consensus is it's also better than the 70-300 G lens, although if you're on a budget or don't plan on using telephoto that much, the extra $250 might be better spent elsewhere (like the 50mm 1.8 prime and/or a flash). this is a mid-level nikon lens with ED glass and decent build quality--not cheap, but not tank-like either. the lens extends way out at 300 mm, and you have to twist the manual focus ring (which is a bit stiff) to get it to fully retract. the plastic lens hood is big and has a cheap feel (not lined with velvet like tokina), but reverses for carrying around.still, it's nice and sharp with good bokeh and a reasonable value--if you want better bokeh, go for a long prime. no macro capability like the cheaper sigma APO variant but sometimes lenses are better if you don't ask them to do too much.optical quality is pretty consistent through the entire zoom range, which is a good thing; definitely a nice piece of glass, although not a head-turner. it's not a quick lens at 4-5.6, but what did you expect for $400? a 2.8? yeah right.with a steady grip, it's usable handheld out to 200mm; beyond that shake is noticeable. the rubber grip ring balances nicely on objects without worrying about scratching the finish for braced shots. if you plan on using it handheld fully extended, consider the VR version, although you'll still want a tripod for longer exposures. 70mm is a bit tight on the wide end, but passable for portraits. for a non-macro, it lets you get reasonably close with a shallow depth of field. no noticable lens creep. not super lightweight, but not too heavy either. doesn't take up much more room in the bag then the 18-70. middle-of-the road in most categories, except for optical performance, which is above average. good for nature or wildlife w/tripod, or for law-enforcement/private detectives, handheld "stakeout" surveillance shots (which don't require perfect clarity). if you plan on using it for sports or action in low light, good luck -- use a speedlight and a tripod/monopod, set up at a spot, lock focus, and wait for subject to come into view. wouldn't recommend it for tracking quick-moving objects beyond 200mm.the 70-300 ED is super-sharp stopped down to 5.6-8, beyond that performance didn't really improve; the images just got a bit more resonant. bottom line, you can get some nice long shots with this lens, which should be good enough for casual enthusiasts and prosumers. it's not a pro lens, but then again, it doesn't cost what a pro lens does. you might be able to find it used for a fraction of the price, but it might be worth it to get the warranty.

Update 7/10/2011:Sadly Toshiba has not released any firmware updates to fix stability issues and with Tron 3D crashing the player it seems this is not the greatest 3D Blu-ray player.  I predominantly use the player as a Netflix player which it has functioned nearly flawlessly.=====I purchased this player with a 3D bundle three months ago and though it has missed the mark in a couple areas(mainly stability and speed), I have not been tempted to return it.  I would however compare this to other players before blindly buying this one again.  That being said I want to give a fair review of the product to help others make a decision.I experienced the same lockups that many did, even after the software upgrade, but after extensive testing(can't help it if I'm an engineer!) I found a couple things.  The first is that if I turned the player on before my TV, it would lock up the player most of the time.  I noticed two things happening when the lockups occurred so I changed the following settings and I have not had lockups since:- Under the "System" settings, turn "Optical Disc AutoPlay" off- change the Resolution under the Display setting from "HDMI Auto" to a specific resolutionOther than that, I actually like the interface.  It is simple to use and intuitive, but could definitely be more responsive.  Disc play is as I would expect it to be on any DVD/Blu-ray player.  The built-in wifi is very convenient.  The Netflix interface is very nice, allowing you to access your instant queue, suggested content and has a name search.  When streaming a movie you can fast forward and rewind with the remote's regular controls.  The Pandora app is nice too if you like playing music through your television.Sadly I have not had a chance to try out a 3D movie so I can not attest to the quality level.  Just remember you'll need a HDMI 1.4 cable to view 3D in full 1080p resolution.  And of course though it seems obvious, you'll need a 3D capable TV along with glasses.Overall it's not a bad product, but I marked it lower because of the aforementioned slow responsiveness and lockups.

Until the Logitech mm50 came to market, you had the choice between cheap and very portable folding speakers that made your iPod sound like a transistor radio and $300 devices from Bose and Klipsch the produced wonderful sound but didn't travel well. The Logitech mm50 is in the middle of this spectrum, with a fair degree of portability, and good clock-radio-quality sound that doesn't distort at higher volumes.One of the unit's strengths is in it lithium-ion battery that, when fully charged through the AC adapter (which charges the iPod as well), last about 6 hours. You'll more battery life if you play your music softly, less if you blast your tunes. It's tempting to crank up the volume, because I experienced no distortion on either the high or low ends of the sound spectrum at volumes that I needed to shout over to talk to someone next to me.At 13x4x1.5, you can't put the mm50 in your pocket, but it's been portable enough for me to listen to my favorite music of the moment in any room of my apt., including the bathroom while I shower (no shorts so far). The semi-soft carrying case made taking it to work and a party a relatively safe proposition.I chose the mm50 over comparable products because of the reviews praising its sound as well as its portability. On this score, I've been disappointed, given the price of the unit (even with Costco's discount). Mid-to-upper range sounds are good, but bass and percussion sounds have very little resonance, sounding flat. The result is like a good clock radio, but not a rich sonic experience.There are also some first-generation design quirks in the mm50. When you dock the iPod, you control the speaker volume with the iPod, even when you use the mm50's volume control. When the iPod is out of the dock, you control the speaker volume through the mm50 itself, but you can't tell what the effects are, because there's no built-in display to show you how loud the speakers are set. So, if mm50 is set to be soft, turning the volume on an iPod all the way up has little effect. Conversely, if you increase the volume setting on the mm50 before you dock the iPod, you could blast your eardrums, even if you had set the iPod volume on low. A small volume-setting display in the mm50 would fix this.The mm50's infrared remote is poor, having a very limited range and requiring exact line of sight to the IR sensor on the speaker. Would it have killed Logitech to increase the range and put in a multi-IR-beam transmitter to let you control it from anywhere within a 45-degree angle to the unit?The case also needs some design re-work. There's no handle or shoulder strap on it, and there are no compartments for your iPod itself or for the AC adapter. I'm not an industrial designer, but I think these features should have been obvious to include.Using the Ipod's sleep timer and alarm clock, I'm thrilled to be able to go to sleep with my RelaxTracks playlist and wake up to one of a few custom music sequences instead of the crap on the radio or a jarring alarm. I love having my tunes with me in the kitchen, the bathroom, and the yard. I will, however, be on the lookout for the next-generation speaker from Logitech.

I purchased this camera from a local store while visiting in Arizona in January 2014. The trip was supposed to be very short, only a few days, and I was 'traveling light'. The only camera i had with me was my iPhone 5s.As the trip time stretched out to over a month I decided I wanted another camera to take 'better' (i.e. zoomed in) pictures but I didn't want to break the bank for a temporary camera.  Thus the choice of the 510 HS.  The local store agreed to match the Amazon price otherwise I would have ordered it from Amazon as I'm a Prime member.I didn't expect a whole lot from this camera (I own a Canon 5D Mk III and a Canon 7D) but I was surprised in how well it does work if held in a stable manner.  Except for a little bit of softness (described below) one can get very good images using manual mode. I even managed to get a very good image of the moon using 30x magnification--hand held no less--and manual mode.The system is not really sensitive so one has to be careful if not using the flash.  Watch out for the orange symbol indicating camera shake as that indicates the exposure time is below 1/20th of a second.  Anything below about 1/125 is going to give considerable blurring when handheld in a caviler manner.  I suggest using the flash, if possible, whenever the exposure time grows larger than 1/60.Even when taking flash pictures, the images are a bit soft but they usually become 'good enough' if given a little sharpening.  I'm not sure if this softness is native to the 510 HS or if it's my particular unit.  I'm used to the incredibly sharp images I get from my 5D Mk III or 7D so it may just be the softness one can expect from an inexpensive camera with a huge zoom range.  In other words, I'm being too critical of an inexpensive camera with respect to softness of the image.To sum thing up, I'm not sorry I purchased the camera.  It will be used quite a bit for quick snapshots--my wife already prefers the 510 HS to her S95.

I originally purchased the Mitsubishi HC1500 DLP projector, but had some problems with it. Ordered this one from amazon and put them side by side. This isn't a review so much as a comparison between 3 Chip LCD and SINGLE CHIP DLP (which tend to be in the same price range). I actually liked the HC1500 a lot, but ended up keeping this SONY VLPAW10 for a number of reasons. It's not perfect, and in some areas underperforms the DLP. Here's the comparison.Single chip DLP projectors create images by having a "chip" filled with thousands of tiny mirrors (1 per pixel on the screen) that can tilt up and down. When they tilt, they send light to the screen, when they don't tilt, the light stays in the projector. This ends up creating wonderfully bright and brilliant images. The only  problem with this setup is that there's no color (just the white light is being directed) so the color needs to be introduced by spinning a color wheel in front of the chip. (in this case it's a 7 segment red-green-blue-white-red-green-blue wheel. The problem is that the colors are therefore being created via an optical illusion, which for some people creates a "rainbow" effect  where they see color rainbows in the white areas of the image. It's very pronounced when there are credit rolls at the end of movies, or any other times there are high contrast black/white (or light/dark) areas. In a certain percentage of cases, the rainbow effect causes headaches and eyestrain It did so for me. (google "DLP rainbow effect" if you don't believe me. There are such things as 3 chip DLP projectors that don't need the color wheels and don't create this effect, but they aren't even close to being in the sub $1000 price range (they start at SEVERAL thousand dollars)Three chip LCD screens actually have 3 panels (red green and blue) so they don't need the spinning color wheel, they just project the light through the panels, and the colors line up on the screen if calibrated properly. They are not as bright and brilliant as the DLP images because the light is going through the panels, and not being reflected by mirrors which create more direct light. The LCD projectors also need more space between the pixels than DLP, and this ends up giving you a more visible "screen door"effect where you can actually see the faint black lines of the pixel grid if you sit close enough to the screen (as if you were looking through a door or window with an insect screen on it, hence the term "screen door".So that's the background, here are the results of my side by side tests (accompanied by the media manager for a major lecture hall at an Ivy League university) who is a specialist in these kinds of things (I myself teach video production, so have some expertise here as well).The Mitsubishi HC-1500 (1 chip DLP)Advantages+ about half the physical size of the SONY.+ Image is brighter+ colors are more saturated+ no need for air filter+ less screen door effectDisadvantages- potential for rainbow effect- noisy (the spinning wheel makes a high pitched whine which is louder and more annoying than the fan)- If you have a small room, you may not be able to fill a large projector screen with an image because this projector cannot throw a large image from as short a distance as the sonyThe SONY VLPAW-10 (3 chip LCD)Advantages+ no rainbow effect+ quieter+ can throw larger image from shorter distanceDisadvantages- Much larger than the mitsubishi- Bulb not as bright, need darker room- colors are less saturated- has an air filter than needs to be changed periodically- more screen door effect- HDMI input on the rear has a bezel around it that will make it impossible for some of the cables with thicker ends to fit in. I had to change cables to get this to workCONCLUSIONI went with the SONY. It's not perfect, but for my needs it beats the Mitsubishi. I know there are a lot of die hard fans of the HC1500 and I'm sorry - but this is a fair assessment of my needs.Some ways to mitigate the SONY's disadvantages:Neither tv will perform great in a bright room, so both of these are really best suited for rooms where you can control the light.In  terms of the saturation, if you're watching DVD movies, then I think you'll prefer the LCD since it creates more natural colors. The DLP is better for watching HDTV shows where the colors really pop (like CSI Miami). I use it mostly to watch movies, so don't mind the less saturated and brilliant colors.In terms of the "screen door" effect, I find this is minimized by defocusing the image just a hair. Yes the image is more soft, but this looks more like a projected image in a movie theater, and this is the effect I'm going for when watching movies on my projector, so it works great. It does not work as well to watch sports or news or other material that has lots of CG text up on the screen.One last note, if you decide to buy it, the price of the sony does fluctuate on Amazon wildly ($799 yesterday, $999 today !!!). But I see it go up and down on an almost weekly basis. So time your purchase carefully!

It performs v-e-r-y s-l-o-w-l-y !!!Unfortunately this negative feedback is coming from someone who really likes Iomega products. I've had their Zip products for years, really like their Zip USB 1.1 250MB drive and the 128MB USB 1.1 Mini Drive, both acquired recently, yet this one is going back.The problem, I'm pretty sure, is WINXP SP1's support for USB 2.0 disk devices when attached to USB 2.0 ports. Other combinations perform well. I have written several articles on USB 2.0 mini drive products here on Amazon giving those products great reviews, but NOT until I formatted those devices as "NTFS".There's something about FAT and FAT32 formats that's in conflict with WINXP.Nonetheless, I was optimistic about buying the ZIP 750 because I figured that if it runs slow like the 2.0 mini-drives, I'll just format it as "NTFS". However, six hours after buying it, it was back in its box; I had given up in frustration.My benchmark was a web site that weighed 120MB, containing 2899 files. No point starting small given my experience with USB 2.0 mini-drives. Well, it took 10.5 minutes, which was an awfully long time for a 2.0 device on 2.0 ports on a fast Pentium 4. So, I tried to format it as "NTFS" and Iomega's software didn't support anything but "FAT". Not even "FAT32". I saw articles on Iomega's web site indicating that they don't recommend "NTFS" for Zip products, yet they provide instructions on how to use WINXP to do the formatting instead of their own software. It's not point and click, folks ... but never mind, because once I formatted it as NTFS this benchmark ran in 12 mins 50 secs. 10MB a minute is not good!Before I packed it up to return it to OfficeMax, I ran this benchmark on my 5+ year old computer which has WIN98 and some seldom used USB 1.1 ports and it ran my benchmark on the Iomega 750 in 4 minutes or so, but not before hanging me twice. Not one to give up without a fight, I reinstalled my Iomega 250 USB 1.1 on the WINXP computer and the benchmark data ran at 4+ minutes. I was not at all surprised. By the way, since you asked, the benchmark ran in 1 min 25 secs on my PNY USB 2.0 Attache mini drive (NTFS, remember). Using that as a standard, the Iomega USB 750 should have run this benchmark in less than 2.5 mins ... if it did, I would have kept it.In summary, if your computer has WINXP SP1 and USB 2.0 ports, you are extremely likely to have the same miserable performance I've had. Please buy the product from a dealer who will take it back. And ... don't be beguiled by reviews that say it was really fast when they copied a single 120MB file in only 1.5 minutes or so. That might be true, but it's not the way we use computers.Thanks for your time.

A little about my background.  I've had bad skin with a lot of acne and scars.  I've been using aha products since the early 90s when Alpha Hydroxy products came to market, along with other exfoliation methods.  I've gotten TCA peels (in the doctor's office), 2 rounds of laser treatements, etc....just wanted to explain where I'm coming from in this review.  Let me be very clear about this product.  It's a fantastic product with several different "peel sources" used in the product.  Smells great, and gave me skin like glass.  And what is amazing is that only a thin layer is needed per application, which means it will last a very long time.  I want to give a very strong caution to people in terms of expectations.  If you have serious hyperpigmentation, age spots, etc....using this product alone will probably not do anything in terms of fast fading.  You have to use a lightening product along with exfoliation in order to get a good result to treat problems like that (many great lightening/vitamin C products on the market). For example, I exfoliate much more aggressively than the average person because I've been doing it for 20 years and have tough skin.  I do two major peels a week and use much milder exfoliation products during the week (Shea Terra black soap).  I use a product like this, and then do an AHA peel right behind it.  It helps products penetrate much better, and you get a quicker result that way.  However, not everyone can do that.  But the point I'm making is that for TOUGH PROBLEMS, you will need to do more than an exfoliation like this provides because it will take a very, very, very, long time, to see results.  Depending on what you want to treat, you need to use topical serum lightening products, maybe some plant stem cell products, etc.....Dr. Gross' retinol plus ferulic acid product is phenomenal and quite mild for those with sensitive skin but wonderfully effective.  I use quite a few natural products (you can see my reviews), as well as other products (matrixyl, plant stem cell products, etc....).  I rotate my products quite a bit.  Hope this helps the reader.

If your battery is less than 50% full capacity, the charger will initially charge at very high-amps to give it a quick charge and then when it reaches 90% capacity, it will tone down to a lesser amp. The problem here is that during the initial high boost charging, the unit gets very hot. Even  the 8 gauge cable gets hot. Though of course, it cools down when the charger lessen the amps as the battery gets full. I think it just gets too hot during the initial charging.Secondly, once the battery reaches 100%, the charger goes into trickle-charge mode. However, the cooling fan still goes full blast. During trickle charge, the charger runs very cool and the fan should also turn down. This will avoid the obnoxious loud fan and also the fan motor will last a lot longer.

Update April '10: I like this a lot more then I did originally. Now I only use it in the kitchen, and I use it once or twice a week. It's not worth it on the hardwood floors, which we usually just vacuum, but it's perfect to maintain a clean kitchen or bathroom floor. I found a practically(used probably once) new scooba at a thift store, and bought it, since my remanufactered battery had stopped holding a charger. I figured if nothing else I could use it for parts -- but it actually worked better then the other one, and gave me more positive overall opinion of the scooba. The battery is much better and it doesn't seem to let out so much water when it powers off. But, the virtual walls from both scoobas I've had are crap, and the scooba eventually starts ignoring it.Original Review:I have a roomba 530 that I absolutely love. My worst enemy is the kitchen floor -- I HATE it. It always seems dirty and I really just despise sweeping and washing it.  So for xmas, my parents got me the scooba which I'd been wanting(VERY BADLY), and it was a good choice to get the remanufactured one here on Amazon being it doesn't seem as loved as the roomba is if you look at reviews. For $150, I think it was a fair price. Having used it now, I wouldn't pay more.I got the 5800(they say you'll either get the 5800 or 5900 when you order one remanufactured). Totally fine with me as its the model where you can use either the scooba Clorox solution mixed with water or white vinegar mixed with water. Once the solution that came with it runs out, I'll definitely be using the white vinegar not only for the cost effectiveness, but it's 'green' and also probably healthier for my cats.A couple of things that bug me. I realized when you power it down, the suction stops and therefore leaks a bit of the dirty water it was in the process of sucking up. but it does make sense, so that's not a big deal. I usually just swiffer up the stuff it leaked when I'm done. The other thing that's not great is that it is not as intuitive as the roomba. It seems to have issues when a room is not completely square. It either ignores an entire area or if you block it in a small 3x3 space(in my case the area it was ignoring in the room) with the virtual wall it just becomes confused and rams itself into the same corner over and over looking for a way out. That was a bummer for me, as I love how the roomba can get in and out of anywhere on its own and never leaves any reasonably reached area untouched in my opinion.Also the battery life isn't very long. It usually does my kitchen and then makes the "I'm so done and out of battery juice" booping and beeping. It's pretty easy to clean when it's done and things clip in and out of place for washing. You can submerge the tank but not the bottom part of the unit, but the little brushes to pop in and out so you can wash them as well.So all in all, it does wash the kitchen floor so I don't have to do it, which is amazing. I'm happy to have it and really feel accomplished when I'm 'roomba-ing' my bedroom and 'scooba-ing' the kitchen while I read a book haha As long as you don't expect it to work wonders and have realistic expectations, it's definitely a fun and useful gadget to have.

I've been a commercial photographer for over 25 years and I know a lot about polarizing filters, filters in general and camera accessories. This one is poorly designed with vague instructions and takes advantage of people.You don't have to be a brain surgeon to figure out what to do with this but the instructions tell you to take it outside and mark the top after rotating it. Fine, we can do that but that could easily have been done in the manufacturing (stamping circles out of a sheet) process. They know what the orientation of the polarizing lines are at that time and know what is exactly the top. Then the instructions say to "center in housing with mark to the top." Well, it's undersized and it just lies there inside the domed lens. Once the camera is in it's possible that the lens keeps it from spinning but I won't know that until I've ruined a shot that I thought was polarized. Because of the darkness you can't see the mark from the front so you have to keep taking the camera in and out to continually check that it hasn't rotated. Being undersized makes it removable but it also makes it susceptible to flying away forever if you open the housing and wind catches it.This is literally a piece of plastic stamped out of a sheet of Roscoe Polarizing material or similar. You can buy an entire 36" sheet of the stuff for $12 and make 100's of your own which is what I wish I'd done. If it weren't for the fact that I have Amazon Prime and shipping was technically free, I'd be sending this back.I expected a small glass filter and got a piece of polarizing sheet that's maybe worth 25 cents retail.Very disappointed.

Hope you have better luck with HP than I have. I just bought an HP dv6. Upon setting it up, I noticed that the wireless dropped frequently and the notebook would then be unable to find the network. I called HP and spent the first two hours of the call following instructions from their "award winning" help desk. Near the end of that part of the call, the rep took over my machine and attempted a bios update. It failed, and the machine will no longer even boot. He then routed my call to a "warranty rep" (or something like that) who came on the line a half hour later. He said HP would arrange to have the machine repaired, as they had determined it was a defective motherboard. I told him I wanted the machine replaced, as it was brand new and defective out of the box. Repairing it and sending it back to me would have me in the position of paying full price for a refurbished machine. He felt there would be a means that HP would leave me satisfied and said I would be contacted the next day. The next day I was contacted and told there was no way they would replace my machine, though they acknowledged it was defective out of the box and that their representative had "bricked" it.HP quality control is poor. They appear to have reached a corporate decision to send out defective machines and then repair them under warranty. This allows them to sell what would ultimately be "refurbs" as full price machines. They would have to repair them anyway, but this way they capture a higher price. I am not an HP basher. Of the half dozen laptops in my home, three are HP products. I am running four HP printers. HP until now had been my preferred brand. Going forward, the HP name on a product will inspire suspicion rather than confidence. Finally, I should mention that the last printer I bought (three months ago), also HP, was also dead out of the box (they sent a new one). It appears that quality control and cultivating customer good will are considered poor business practices by HP.

I bought the current (version 2 revision) model of the 1GB DAP to replace an older version 1 DAP that I broke. (Note: do NOT let these things fall off a top shelf onto a tile floor.) Because I  use an MP3 player almost exclusively for podcasts and audiobooks, I'm disappointed in changes they've made to the user interface in V.2. So far as I can tell, they've made two kinds of changes: to simplify the GUI a bit (for users who don't want to read the manual), and to organize folders/playlists better. But they have eliminated three features of V.1 that I relied on heavily for spoken-word listening: (1) you can no longer adjust playback speed (V.1 let you increase to as much as 130%, nice for zipping through a lecture); (2) during fast-forward you don't hear any sound, meaning you can't identify program breaks, etc.; (3) with V.1, if you paused playback of an audio file and switched to FM listening, then returned to file playback, you'd be at the same place in the file, but with V.2 the file goes back to the start.It's possible that SanDisk will offer a firmware upgrade to address these things, but since they've moved on to the new m200 line they may consider the DAP to be a legacy product.

When the drive works, it works well.  I had issues with the drive not spinning up, though this was due to power limitations on the hub I had it plugged in to.  Even USB Hubs that advertise USB 2.0 Compatibility do not guarantee that they will supply the amount of power required by USB 2.0.  This means that this hard drive will not work for you.  This hard drive requires 1 amp at spin up, most USB hubs provide at most 500mA per port, or half of what this drive needs.  I had other problems where it would spin up for a few seconds, long enough for windows to recognize it as a drive and ask about autorun, then shut down.  It would go through this cycle for hours if left unattended.  This would result in hundreds of autorun windows open on my computer.  Other issues I have seen with this drive are transfer rates dropping to 0 and clicking sounds.  I have yet to lose any data and it still works so I can't complain too much.

Over all I like the build quality and the value I get for the price.The biggest thing I disliked, and no one has mentioned here is the touch pad scrolling. MSI didn't want to license the right side scroll on the touchpad from Synaptics, so they chose a different touchpad vendor, who implements the scrolling differently, by assigning two areas on top right and bottom right corners to scroll up and down. These two areas are basically like two buttons, you don't actually drag your finger on the touchpad, you just touch the scroll areas to scroll, and hold it for continuous (kinda choppy) scroll. It's no where near as intuitive, predictable, and responsive as Synaptics touchpad's side scroll, where one can control the scroll speed/amount pretty accurately by varying the scrolling gesture. I ended up using arrows more often, and having to move back and forth between the touchpad and the arrow keys, while not a big inconvenience, is definitely much more tedious.Given the small screen and especially the small height of a netbook screen, scrolling up/down is needed a lot, I think MSI really made a bad cost saving choice here. There is also no horizontal scroll on the MSI touch pad, but it's not a big deal for me.Update: decided to return it after 3 weeks of usage, the touch pad is a deal breaker.

There are a lot of love it/hate it reviews here and complaints about a formula change. I have a middle of the road view and can't address the formula change since I've never used the lotion until a week ago. So here's my take...for whatever it is worth...I don't generally buy "drug store" lotions. There are a lot of ingredients I like to avoid and I gravitate towards brands that at least make an effort to use organic ingredients and skin/body friendly formulas. I came across this St. Ives Skin Renewing at my local grocery that was restructuring their store and had this on clearance for two bucks. The ingredient list is largely inoffensive and contains no parabens or pthalates and I was in the middle of a battle with prickly winter skin so I bought it. I've been using this almost daily for a week now and I am *so* close to absolutely loving this lotion. I'm not wild about the scent...it isn't bad, but a little strong for me even though it does dissipate in an hour or so. This healed my winter bumps within 24 hours, something my slew of natural and organic lotions can't seem to do unless I religiously slather it on twice daily. So, hooray...my legs have finally stopped itching. This lotion also leaves my skin BABY SOFT up to and including the keratosis pilaris bumps on my upper arms. The bumps are still there but are significantly less red looking and scaly feeling.Now, this is all very wonderful but not ultimately what compelled me to write a review. I have a couple of cats. One of them has an annoying issue referred to as "petting induced aggression". You'll be sitting there with him in your lap, he's purring while being loved on and then suddenly he turns into a flailing bunch of claws and teeth and your forearms are mincemeat. Mostly I can see an episode coming these days and can avoid being scratched but once in a while he still gets me.What is the point of this little story? Well, as I've gotten older (I'm 37) the little kitty scratches, even shallow ones, take longer and longer to heal and are more likely to scar. Our most recent session of "hey mom, meet my claws" ended with quite a few scratches on my forearms. This happened right about when I started using this new lotion. Now, just a few days later, the scratches have all but disappeared!!! There are some almost imperceptible red lines, but they are just about gone. In less than a week! This is absolutely unheard of for me and I will definitely keep this lotion around because it is clearly doing some good.I'd like to address one more thing: the texture of this lotion. Setting it up: This OMRON has the most sensible settings menu I have ever used. You select menu or mode to choose the category, beginning with lb or kg, and then ending with hours and minutes. When you have the right number, you select SET. That's it. With all of my watches, I have settled on the method of just pushing buttons until I see what may reasonably be my heartbeat. I have found it is best not to get too stressed out by trying to figure it out, unless I want my heartbeat up.Online set up. The online setup of this was also really easy. I admit that I'm not likely to use it because I don't much care about graphs of my activity. I'm the type that just likes to check off that I did it. Did it and done. :DWearing it. Pedometers generally only work when you are wearing them. One of the things that I especially like about this is that it just needs to be on me, not clipped to my waistband. That makes it much easier to see what I am doing on any given day, not just days when I happen to be wearing pants. I also tend to wear roll top yoga pants to the gym, so pedometers won't clip then anyway. This OMRON is small enough to be able to put in a pocket or even inside your clothes.I have been testing this against an old Radio Shack pedometer, which was to date the most accurate I have ever found, and this is the first modern accurate step counter I have found. It is better than accurate because it also counts calories for aerobic exercise, which I think is amazing. Not all steps are the same.A couple of Mac things: Needs OS 10.7 (one of the Lions). I have not upgraded because I wasn't sure that PhotoShop would be workable yet. PLUS I DON'T LIKE CHANGE. Size of the plugin: it fits but the other USB port on my MacBook Pro becomes unusable. Not a huge problem for me because I found a new way to avoid change. I just switched to a PC -- the one without Windows 8.

Wow. Hamilton Beach needs to take this machine back to the drawing board. I understand what they were trying to do. But in the process of trying to make a product that did 3 different types of brewing, they failed miserably. I already own the single-serve HB pod brewer and I love it, so I thought this would be great. I have a large Keurig brewer for K cups, but found it impractical for brewing coffee just for myself (great for company and guests). So.....I bought this. A HUGE MISTAKE.First, even though I ran clear water through it 3 times before brewing my first cup, my coffee smelled terribly of burning plastic (this is with a K cup). I also noticed a film (oil? plastic?) on the top of my coffee. When I called HB's customer service, they said to run straight vinegar through it, let it brew for a few seconds, then turn the machine off for a half hour to let the vinegar sit in the machine. I did this once. Still smelled and tasted plastic. I did it again, and again (3 times total). While this diminished the plastic taste/smell some, it was still there. So was the oily film on my coffee. Then, I noticed that after brewing, the k cups I used (about 5 different brands), were coming out all warped, as if the plastic had melted on the cups. Well, it turns out they were actually getting way too hot with this slow drip brew method. They were melting. Also, I noticed the burning plastic smell was coming from the insert (where you actually add the pod or filter or k cup), and that portion of the machine would not and could not be improved with all the vinegar baths in the world. So I believe the plastic in that insert portion is also not made to handle the heat of the water that pours through it.Bottom line: This is a poorly designed machine made with cheap plastic products. I can't imagine the amount of harmful BPAs that I drank, even for the short time I used it (It went back to Amazon after 2 weeks of messing with it). (If you aren't aware, plastic, heated to the point of melting--as this machine does with K cups--leaches out toxic and carcinogenic chemical BPAs.)I finally decided to spend the extra money and purchase the Keurig K10 mini brewer, and it has been worth every extra penny I paid. It works like a dream, and has from the first cup. You are welcome to take your chances with this Hamilton Beach coffee maker, but I would definitely wait until HB gets all of the kinks and problems worked out before spending your time and money on it.I suggest:Keurig K10 MINI Plus Brewing System, Purple(it comes in several different colors, including black)

I bought this on 11/11/2012  after reading reviews.  I won't say it sucks because that would be a good thing for vacuum cleaners. Since we only used it on carpet, I "fixed" it by wedging it in place (beater-bar-on) with a cardboard shim.  In the 385 days I've owned it, I've had to dismantle it three times to unclog a right-angle air flow path design in the base - a definite design flaw.  We have no kids, no pets and live in a clean low dust area. The unit was definitely not being used in a challenging environment.  The final blow was that we bought new carpet -- slightly higher fiber than our old carpet.  The unit apparently has no mechanism (automatic or manual) to adjust for carpet density type (only "carpet" or "bare floor").  With our new carpet using this vacuum was like pushing a plow through thick mud.  No thanks.  Life is too short.  Yes, it looks good on paper but my wife brought home a new vacuum from a local store today. .....just in time to save me from a fourth dismantling and unclogging.  The first time I had the clogging problem I had taken it to a distant repair depot complaining of a short circuit.  It would power off after some initial use.  After being in the shop a couple week, the repair depot told me this was a "design feature" to keep the motor from burning out in the event of a clogged air flow.  Although I later found a statement in the manual which hinted at that, it was anything but clear and prominent.  Moreover, the repair depot said they wouldn't unclog it for me under warranty.  It would cost me quite a bit out of pocket.

This thing looks great and I enjoy using the glass because it's well insulated and whatever you put in it looks cool. Unfortunately, after about a dozen uses, I've noticed that the upper edge has a crack in it. It's as if I hit it from the top with something. Maybe I bumped it with another cup or mug while I was hand washing it or something else. The crack looks to be internal, so it's still smooth and probably safe to drink from as long as I don't put my mouth on the cracked part. I have used this cup with beer, but have been afraid of freezing the cup before using it for that purpose. Mainly, it's because you can thermally shock the glass and I'm concerned that the curve portions can't take the stress. Also, if the cup is cold on the outside, it takes away the point of having something insulated.The infuser is disappointing. It looks neat, but the holes are fairly large. I use nice whole leaves of green or white tea most of the time, so the dust that gets through is bearable, but when I use it to make ice tea, there is so much of the bits that fall through that I don't drink ice tea using a straw made with this infuser because of the sediment at the bottom. The best thing about this infuser is that it fits well into all the cups and mugs I've used because it tapers down at the bottom.The lid is also something else that looks neat, but can be a sanitary hazard. It doesn't work well flipped over so when you place it like in the photo, it collects condensation, which means that when you put it on the table, that wet tea gets on your table. Even worse, if you want to reuse the lid before washing, you would want to make sure that the surface you'd place it on was clean to begin with. I tend to not use the lid as a lid and only as an infuser holder. It's also a little annoying to clean because of the sharp edge. It hasn't cut me yet, but it's tough to get a good hold on when I'm trying to clean it with elbow grease.In the end, there are better tea infusers out there on Amazon like the one from ForLife with the silicone wrapped lid (though this one doesn't fit well in smaller mugs/cups or one from Kuchenprofi) but I do like the cup. In spite of that crack, I will probably pick up another cup (sold separately, of course) and hope that it holds up better.

I received my Tassimo a few weeks ago and have used it extensively since.  It's fun, it's quick, it couldn't be easier to use.The bad news?  The milk in the cappucinos and lattes tastes funny to me (the UHT milk factor).  Those two drinks and the Gevalia crema have a chemically taste.  The Gevalia coffee and decaf coffee are great.  But I mainly bought this to make it easier to have a quick cappucino, so I am kind of disappointed.Yes, I knew the machine was expensive.  And I knew the discs were too.  Do the math: 10 cappucinos is $10.  But one is 1/2 the size my regular mug (i.e. it's one shot of espresso and a small amount of milk).  You probably never drink a cappucino this size.  So you're likely to have two.  You're up to $2 now for what is essentially about a 14 oz cappucino.  (They say one is 11 oz, but this is really not true; two together do not fill my 16 oz mug.)  So I just saved about $1.50 over buying a Starbucks Grande, but the latter is MUCH better. More to the point, I saved myself only about 4 minutes of cappucino-making and clean-up, using my traditional espresso maker, which is awesome and cost the same as the Tassimo.  If I had known how small and how so-so the Tassimo cappucinos would be, I would have stuck with that, and maybe bought a cheapo one-cup pod maker for my coffee drinking housemate.  He prefers Hazelnut anyway, and Tassimo can't provide that yet.Other comments?  The noise is brief and no big deal.  (You should hear my banshee of a real espresso machine frothing milk.) Cleanup is easy but like the other reviewer, I have had messy milk issues: after EVERY cappucino, there's milk around the area where the disc sits; I run the cleaning disc and there's some milk here and there.  Not good.Bottom line: the t-disc prices need to come WAY down; bring my faux-cappucino down to under $1 for 15 oz. and we'll talk.  The ease of use and variety are a plus, but don't get too excited.  You don't _quite_ get what you pay for.

The Sabrent USB graphics adapter will use make heavy use of the CPU instead of delegating most of its graphics processing to its onboard GPU. On my 2.5 GHz computer, which admittedly is a little antiquated by today's standards, the display is choppy, but tolerable.By choppy, I mean the mouse movement across the screen is a tad choppy and videos played in full-screen mode is a stop and go affair. The adapter will, however, handle videos in a windowed mode quite competently. Videos played in a windowed mode is quite smooth. The color rendering is also superb.A little information on my setup: I have a 3-monitor setup. I use the Sabrent for a a third monitor, anHP Envy 23-Inch Monitor. I have another twoDell S2440L 24-Inch Monitorshooked up to aGeForce 8400GS Graphics Card. The GeForce handles graphics admirably by comparison, acting up only occasionally with a flicker on a isolated part of the screen when complex graphics is changing too rapidly.Despite the Sabrent being CPU intensive, it will relinquish CPU cycles for other processes that need them, so it is by no means a CPU hog. It is unobtrusive and won't interfere with (or at least have minimal impact on) other programs running both in the foreground and background. I use the Sabrent for additional screen real estate for displayng relatively static content like photoshop content overflowing into it, browsing Web pages, checking email, and (like I mentioned earlier) playing videos in a windowed mode. For all these tasks, the Sabrrent handles them quite well.FYI (and I'm going on a tangent here), here's a helpful tip: To prevent a program from being a CPU hog, press Ctrl-Alt-Del all at the same time, on the window that pops up, right-click on the offending program, and on the popup menu, mouseover "Set Priority" and click on "Low."---All in all, the Sabrent USB graphics isn't bad. Just be aware that if you have a dated/slow computer, graphics performance will be a little choppy.

This monitor is good if you plan on sitting on a desk and look directly at it. Its viewing angle is poor - even for a TN panel. You have very little tilting capacity, so if you're not sitting right at your desk, you may not find an accommodating angle. I had wanted to watch movies or youtube on this screen from a couch that sat slightly below my seat level at my desk, but I found I needed to prop the panel stand up with a book to give it nearly a 90 degree angle with my desk which still wasn't enough to allow me to see the picture well.

If you want your LCD to look like there's a lighting scrim over the screen, then this is for you.  It's very grainy to my eye.  Put a white background up or anything not completely black, and it looks like a permanently-fixed chemical photo of the image.  There is no texture purity here.  Watch a 1080p movie, and fleshtones shot with 35mm get this motionless grain added on top of the film's moving grain.  The screen on my $299 Compaq laptop doesn't have that issue at all.  Even if you like the grainy still photo look applied to everything for some reason, it reduces the effective resolution of fine 1080p textures and actually corrupts them.  You are not seeing the actual textures in the image.The blacks are also not incredibly deep unless you turn down the brightness, and I'm not sure you actually have full control over that after all.  It's decent in blacks rendition, though.I do have a little flashlighting in the lower left screen, but it's not too bad.  The left side of the screen is slightly brighter than the right overall, though.  It's a gradual progression across, as if the corner LEDs need to be adjusted.  That option is not available, though.Also, as I type this the screen is wobbling visibly side to side.  It's just not a very rigid stand.  Pretty and simple to attach, but the stem could have been wider at the top where it connects to the monitor or used multiple connection points.So the notable aspects are indeed grayscale & color contrast, no dead pixels, and excellent viewing angles.  With the glowing professional reviews for this display, however, I can only think they either didn't use it with bright images or other budget LCDs must be totally awful.Edit: According to someone on simhq.com, the grain is caused by the anti-glare coating.  A plastic film that is rough and textured for scattering the light.  Very different than, say, eyeglasses polarized treatments.  I can confirm there isn't much glare, but I can tune glare out easily.  And I can turn the lights off if that was a problem.  This IPS AG coating is awful and will probably cause me to return this purchase.Edit: Overdrive is up, not down.  Too high causes a different set of visual issues.  Too low causes ghosting.  40-60 is the recommended range.  It is probably not capable of rendering 60fps quite as artifact-free as a TN display.

Although I've always been interested in juicing, I've never owned a juicer before, relying on my blender the odd times I would actually want to make a smoothie or shake. I bought this router without thinking too much about it.  I had to replace my old Microsoft router that stopped working (after about 5 years of non-stop use).  Without a reliable network connection, I didn't bother to shop around, just figured whatever I got would work well enough.  I was wrong.The first thing I noticed was that I can never log onto the router to change settings, it just hangs, unless I unplug the router to reset it first.  (The reset button on the front of the thing seems to have no effect whatsoever.)  Then, if you save any settings on the router, a screen comes up informing you that you will have to wait 30 seconds before being returned to the page you were on.  Why is that?Nevertheless, I did get it working, connecting two Vista desktops via ethernet and two XP laptops wirelessly.  But when I tried to connect my daughter's Vista laptop, that is when the real trouble began.  After configuring the connection on her laptop, the router would hang whenever her laptop was turned on.  It was absurd. I tried to find the user manual and guess what --- it's on line!  no copy of the user manual on the cd and no help on the router itself.  HELLO Linksys! If I need to troubleshoot my wireless router, maybe, just maybe, I can't GET on line.One thing and the next, I figured out that I had to shut off her pc and recycle the router to get back online.  Once online again I finally saw a post here on Amazon that linked to a forum article that said if you want to use this router with a Vista laptop you need to downgrade to a prior version of the firmware.  Since I am an IT professional, this was not a daunting task for me.  But I sure would hate to have to walk my brother-in-law through it over the phone... so I won't be recommending this router to him!After the downgrade, I got the Vista laptop working too.  So I guess everything is working now, but it still hangs when I log into it (unless I power cycle it first.)  And the range is NOT as good as my 5 year old MS router.  AND, by the way, don't try to use it with WEP security.  I was planning to switch to WPA anyway, but one of my old wireless adapters only supported WEP, so I was going to use WEP with mac filtering until I could replace the old adapter.  I found that my newer adapters kept dropping the connection using WEP, which worked without problems on my old router.So, shop around.  Surely you can find one better than this.UPDATE:  Final straw today.  I can no longer log into it to change any advanced settings.  I used to have to turn it off and on again in order to log into it; but now that doesn't even work.  It just hangs when I try to log in, no matter what I do.Router technology is NOT rocket science and Linksys been dong it for years.  There really is no excuse that I can think of for such an awful product.I'm going to go buy something else, don't know what yet.  But for sure I'm going to do my homework this time.
