I've had this vacuum for 3 months, and got it off of QVC with more attachments than on here, but I never use the microfiber mop anyway. I'll put brackets around reviews for the attachments that don't apply to this amazon package but for someone who was wondering about the extra pieces (which you can see here on the QVC website [...]This vacuum sucks a lot of stuff out of our carpet. With a dog and two cats we have a lot of pet hair around, and every time I'm done vacuuming the canister is full of dirt and hair.The cord isn't a long or short length. I use a vacuum extension cord anyway, but if I don't then I need to change the outlet once or twice while vacuuming my main floor.[I use the bare floor attachment for my kitchen. It works okay, but when you run it parallel to the wall, it won't get any dirt or crumbs against the baseboard. Instead, you have run it at a perpendicular angle, so that's a little annoying since I have to often run over the same floor twice in two different directions just to make sure I get all the dirt/crumbs around the edges, and it forces you to slowly make your way down the wall a foot at a time, only as wide as the nozzle. It's irksome to say the least. I think I'll just start sweeping before I vacuum, which is pretty annoying.][I haven't used the dry dust mop attachment (microfiber pad) because I haven't had any real use for it when I have the bare floor attachment. The kitchen is high-traffic area and for the amount of crumbs from food and dog food that land on the floor, I'd rather use the bare floor piece rather than the dust mop. If I had a wood floor without as much traffic I might use it, but the rest of my house is carpeted!]The regular "motorized floor brush nozzle" works well. I have to cut out the hair from the spinning brushes every few uses--it's amazing how much of my own long hair ends up on the carpet (gross, I know). I don't think it gets the edges of my carpet very well either, but I didn't seriously expect it to.I wish the turbo brush could have somehow been motorized, but it wasn't with my last vacuum either so I didn't really expect it to be. I use it on my carpeted stairs, and it works ok but could definitely work better and more efficiently if it was motorized.The vacuum is very tippy, [especially with the bare floor attachment. It almost can't stand up on its own with that attachment], so I always lean it up against a wall anytime I need to stop vacuuming (that goes for both floor attachments I use, [but the bare floor one hardly stands up at all without tipping over).]My biggest issue with this vacuum is the "stretch hose." On the vacuum itself, it is 22" long. When fully extended, it's as long as 65". They want you to detach the floor attachment and use just the handle with stretch hose (with other attachments), OR you can detach the extension wand and use it with a floor attachment (like the dust mop piece in the pictures on QVC, turning the vacuum into a canister vacuum rather than upright).However, the resistance of the hose is so strong that you can't extend the hose without holding on to the vacuum itself or else the vacuum gets dragged along with you (or tips over at the very least). If I wanted to use the vacuum as a canister vacuum rather than an upright, it'd be nearly impossible to do so since you can't tow the canister along with you. I have the biggest problem while using it on the stairs. I wish I could leave it at the top or the bottom of the stairs and use the handle with the turbo brush, but I can't go more than one step without the vacuum falling over because the resistance is so strong on the hose once you stretch it in the slightest. Instead, I detach the canister from the floor piece and extension wand, and just try to hold it in one hand while using the nozzle handle in my other hand. It's a big pain that I wasn't prepared for with this vacuum.Overall, I don't think I'd recommend this vacuum just because of the inconveniences I have with it. I'm not very excited that I know I'll be stuck with this vacuum for a least a few years before I can try something else. All of the attachments make you excited about it, but I don't think they make up for the cons. The high ratings really made me think it'd be fantastic, but unfortunately I just don't think it's all that it's worked up to be.11/7/2012 Edited to Add: I forgot to mention that this thing is a pain to empty. The bin holds very little until it is at is "max full." But if you have any sort of pet hair then it gets all clumped up in the top of the bin instead of the bottom. The bin is shaped so that all the hair/dust/dirt gets caught way up inside it and you have to reach your fingers up to pull it all out. I can't imagine this being possible for anyone with bigger fingers than I have, and my hands are fairly small. Another reason I'm very disappointed with this vacuum. Cannister vacuums are supposed to be easy to empty--just tip the bin upside-down and everything pours out. This vacuum is the opposite of that scenario.

This is a beautiful mirror that has a large bright surface and is lit with "natural daylight" full-spectrum LED's. It's powered by a lithium battery that is charged via USB and an ac adapter, so it operates cordless on your bathroom counter or vanity table. It has 5X magnification, just enough to see for tweezing eyebrows but low enough to apply makeup effectively. The claim of "full-spectrum" or imitating daylight is true. I brought it into the kitchen where we have southern exposure, and compared it with light on and light off. The colors were true to life.What comes with the mirror:The mirror, assembled on its standA USB cable and AC adapter for charging the internal battery.A scratch-free cleaning cloth for safe cleaningGood points:This is a BEAUTIFUL mirror.It is sleekly styled, with a heavy base that incorporates a light (green or red) around a ring to indicate charged or needing charging. It truly is elegant.It has no cord, holds a charge for weeks, stays off until you approach it, then it turns on automatically. Goes off when you back away. So you will be keeping soapy hands off the mirror, no fumbling for a switch.5X magnification is good for applying makeupThe size is large enough for the full face and neck, again, perfect for makeup.The light is truly daylight.No batteries to install, doesn't take up an outlet in the bathroom.No hot bulb behind the mirror to eventually burn off the mirror coating. This is what happened to my current magnifying mirror; the incandescent bulb installed behind the mirror eventually caused a burnt spot and ruined the center of the mirror. No fix for this. I have to discard it and that is a shame.Even lighting; the LED's are spaced to provide even, diffused light.Bad points:No optional wall mount. A bracket and mount on the back or an option to purchase a wall-mounted unit would have been great. I like a mirror by the sink that is at eye level. I'm tall and to use this mirror, I have to bend over in half or I have to sit on a vanity chair to use this mirror. I suppose I'll have to find a vanity chair for the bathroom--there is a space under the counter for a vanity stool but I don't own one. I like this mirror well enough to change my ways but I prefer to stand to do my makeup and I can't do that with a counter mirror.No 10X smaller mirror-in-mirror. These are helpful for fine work like tweezing those eyebrow strays. Sometimes you need a bigger magnification. A small quibble--I can live without it.It does take up counter space; which for many people can be an issue. My previous house had only one bathroom and a very tiny counter. This would not have fit on it at all. That counter had room for a toothbrush mug and that was it.LEDs have a finite lifespan (100,000 hours? Not sure) but eventually, they will burn out. Maybe years, but ultimately, they are not replaceable. Also, how long will the internal battery take a charge before needing replacing and can it be replaced? I am not certain if it can be.Bottom line:This is a beautiful mirror, the finish and styling are superb. It is superior to my previous mirror in many ways. The lighting is wonderful. The cordless operation is slick and clutter-free. Only a wall mount would make this better, and that's a personal preference. Overall, if you want a counter-stand mirror, I can enthusiastically recommend this one.

I switched from a high quality IPS panel to this mainly because I wanted to run 120fps in driving simulators. You might want to pick up a 2nd high quality monitor if you're tweaking photos.The next generation game consoles are capped at 30FPS which is probably a good thing for PC gamers.  We'll be able to run console ports at 60 or 120 FPS with the inevitable hardware upgrades that become available.It would be interesting to see how different 120hz interpolated from a 30FPS game compares with a game running at 120FPS on a native 120hz monitor.In short, I'm not sure it's worth it because a 60hz monitor is still double what the next gen consoles will support and you get to keep color quality.

One of the reasons my general philosophy has been you can never have too many of these cords is because the ends tend to break. Now I certainly know enough people who fix that with a few tools and just replace the plastic end, the tab, frequently breaks off. Once that piece breaks off, you don't get the snug connection that you come to expect. There are plenty of DIY yourself guides out there that teach you how to take large spools of cable and bag of Ethernet connectors and have at it. OR you could get cables like these and just have them handy. What I really like about the Micra Digital cable is that it protects the tab so you are less likely to snag that end and break it off as so many of my other cables experience. 5 feet is plenty long for typical set-ups, longer cables might be needed for multiple devices, assuming you like the speed and stability of wired over wireless connections. We do a lot of home canning and preserving and purchased this mill to help with some of the chores associated with putting away pumpkin butter, grape butter, pumpkin puree and other foods. The handle seems to have the same coating and is pleasant to hold.--also with the legs, they fold for storage, but I have found that folding them down around the sides of a 4-cup pyrex measuring cup also helps to hold it stable while using it.--I like the white enamel (I think that's what it is) coating on the outside of the pot. Very attractive.--Easy to clean. If I clean this immediately after using, I can practically just rinse it in hot water and let it dry and it looks great.--handle assembly is cleverly designed and feels sturdy and secure when using it.--comes with 3 disks for different jobs. We use the most coarse disk for pumpkin and apples and it works beautifully. (Note, we do take the seeds out of our pumpkins before cooking and straining). We used the medium disk with our grapes this year and it did a nice job, but a few seeds did sneak through. Next year we will try the fine disk.My ONLY quibble with this piece of equipment is that it is not bigger. As I mentioned above, it fits nicely over a 4-cup pyrex measuring cup. I'd be thrilled if it was larger. The pot itself probably doesn't hold more than 4 cups. You *can* use it over a large pot, the legs will simply hold it there for you. It's the size of the pot itself I am talking about.

This is a summary of my experience with the Canon 1DX.  Skip to the bottom of this review if you want final impressions of the camera after the honeymoon period.  My previous camera was the 5DII, mainly for weddings and portraits.  I look for low light performance.1st Day 7/20/2012  I took several photos of my 13 year old daughter in dark incandescent light at 6400 and 25,600 ISO with an 85/1.2II lens at f/2.0.  I ran both photos through LR4 with +10 noise reduction.  I shoot in RAW.  Here's what I noticed.  At 6400 ISO,  I could see the downy blond baby hairs on her forehead and there wasn't much noise in the dark areas, just grain.  At 25,600 ISO, the dark areas had grainy noise and those little downy hairs disappeared.  But, the image was totally usable.  My wife really liked it.  I noticed that at these high ISO's underexposure results in a significant increase in noise in the dark areas.  So, overexposing a little minimizes noise at the higher ISO's.  The autofocus is blazing fast in good light, and in dim light it slows down, taking 1 to 3 seconds to focus.  This is a 1/3 stop improvement over my 5DII, which was a solid low light focuser (because I had sent it in to have AF tweaked).  I was expecting more improvement, but I'll take it.  One deficiency is that in Manual mode, the exposure indicator does not show up on the top LCD, only when looking into the viewfinder.  It does so on the 5DII and 40D.  I called Canon and it turns out this is unique to 1D's.  I relied on this as a quick light meter check without having to look into the viewfinder.  Customers expect me to start snapping photos once I start looking into the viewfinder.7/26/2012  I did an experiment to see how quickly the camera buffer might fill up using a high speed UDMA card.  I held down the shutter and took 200 images without letting up.  The camera quit working and showed error code 30, which was a locked shutter.  I returned it for a new unit.  Canon CPS said I should have been able to take as many images as I wanted without the shutter locking up.  I won't try this again.7/30/2012  I received the replacement and snapped photos for a half an hour.  When I put the lens cap back onto the 85/1.2II I mistakenly pressed the shutter button halfway and got an error code 80.  It went away after taking the cap back off.  Canon said error code 80 was software-related.8/8/2012  I photographed my daughter swinging using the 85/1.2II lens. This is probably Canon's slowest focusing lens because of the way it moves the entire heavy internal glass. It's meant for portraits, not for sports. With my daughter coming toward me, the AF tracked her in AIServo. To give some perspective, this is something I have never been able to do with the 5DII and 40D. The glass takes 1.5 seconds to move from one end to the other.  Looking at them in LR4, I had a 50% keeper rate, which is excellent given that the 5DII would have had none. This camera has more power in the AF to move the glass faster.  Very nice.  What I'm not liking? The AF point doesn't light up when I press the shutter halfway down until it locks focus. That means in very dark conditions, I have to guess where the AF point is.  I could press the AF selection button to light it up, but that's a delay which defeats the element of speed and it also lights up all the AF points like a Christmas tree.  It took several calls to Canon CPS for me to realize that this feature, which was on the 5DII, is now gone.  Some of Canon's CPS techs were convinced it was there and it just needed to be turned on.  It's really gone.8/13/2012  Two weddings.  One was very dark and went late into the night.  I did some portraits of the couple walking around the gardens in the dark as I experimented with off camera flash.  These images are usually my clients' favorites because of the dramatic light effects.  But, it's usually the end of the day and clients are tired.  I have to work fast.  The AF not blinking with a half-press of the shutter button was a problem.  It took nearly 10 to 20 seconds to lock focus versus 3 to 5 seconds with the 5DII.  After a few of these, the couple wanted to head back.  With the 5DII, I half press the shutter button and the AF point blinks to let me know where it is.  Then, I move this AF point to focus on a high contrast area of the face or edge of the white dress, recompose, and take the shot.  Then, it's off to the next pose or location for another shot or two.  With the 1DX, I was unable to locate a high contrast area without knowing exactly where the center AF point was.  It was grayed out.  As a workaround, I tried using the AF point selection button on the back.  It lit up all the AF points and blinded that eye to the dark.  Using this camera in low light slows me down compared to the 5DII.  I'm baffled as to what Canon was thinking when they decided to eliminate lit up AF points.8/28/2012  Another wedding in fairly good light.  I did the formals at 1600 ISO, as I generally do with the 5DII, using a tripod and dragging the shutter.  This gives images that are sharp, yet with balanced light.  At 1600 ISO the 1DX was 1/2 stop ahead of the 5DII in terms of noise and detail rendition.  I expected it to be 2 stops cleaner, like 400 ISO on the 5DII.  Also, 4000 ISO images weren't much different than at 1600 ISO.  Noise was fairly constant in this range.  Auto white balance was very accurate.  Only a few images got overly yellow due to mixed light.  After 1200 images the battery was still at half charge.  New issue:  Three separate times, the AF froze and quit working with the 85/1.2II and 16-35/2.8II lenses.8/29/2012 Installed new firmware.  Canon's bulletin said it fixed error code 80 (which I experienced on 7/30/2012).9/4/2012  Two more weddings.  The wedding party had very dark skin.  There were 16 groomsmen.  I used f/11 to get adequate depth of field with a 35mm/1.4.  I used 8,000 ISO for the first time (for a paying customer) and these looked fine with +25 noise reduction (in LR4).  Conservatively, I would not hesitate to blow these up to 11x14.  I bumped it to 12,800 ISO, which came close to looking like 8,000 ISO with more noise reduction applied.  Another photographer thought they were clean enough to blow up larger than 11x14.  I overexposed these images by 1/2 stop for the darker areas, then brought exposure down by 1/2 stop in post processing and dodged exposure back into the groomsmen's dark skin.  This helped a lot with noise.Conservatively here's how I see the noise levels on the 1DX compared to the 5DII (for example, noise at ISO 4000 on the 1DX looks roughly like noise at ISO 1600 on the 5DII).  These comparisons are AFTER noise reduction was applied in LR4 on RAW files.5DII  1DX800  1600-20001600  40002000  64003200  12,8001DX noise looks more like film grain and cleans up better than 5DII noise.  At times I can get ISO 6400 on the 1DX to look like ISO 1600 on the 5DII by overexposing and bringing it back in post processing. The 1DX's noise performance is very impressive.9/24/2012  Wedding this past Saturday.  AF froze twice, once with an 85/1.2II and the second time with the 35/1.4.  With the 35/1.4, the bride threw her bouquet and I missed it completely.  The only way to get it working again was to turn the camera off twice.10/3/2012  Two more weddings.  Off-center AF points are 1 stop less sensitive than the center AF point.  In dim light, they tend to hunt, so I use the center AF exclusively, and then recompose.10/13/2012  Three more weddings.  AF froze twice.  It happened very reliably with the 70-200/2.8 IS II, right about the time the bride was coming down the aisle.  This is also my slowest lens in low light.  It will simply not work on low contrast areas, so I have to aim it dead center at the hairline on their faces.  I now rarely use the 70-200/2.8 IS II except in good light due to its AF locking up on the 1DX in addition to it already being a sluggish lens in low light.There is an issue with AI Servo in low light - it lags the action by 3 seconds.  AF will not lock onto people dancing in reception low light unless I go back to one shot mode.  No AI Servo until it gets fixed.Another issue is that about 20% of the time, when pressing the playback button the image flashes for a fraction of a second and then goes away.  The only way to get the playback button to work again is to turn the camera off and on or hammer the playback button multiple times.  This makes it difficult to show images to the client on the back of the camera.10/21/2012  Canon released firmware update v1.1.1.  This fixed the grayed out AF point for AI Servo , but not for single shot mode, which is what wedding and portrait photographers use.  I called Canon CPS and they said that AF on all their new cameras is being grayed out.  This has me contemplating switching to another brand.  It really slows me down with just slightly darker scenes.8/8/2013  I had to take it in for its second shutter cleaning at the local camera store in Indianapolis.  Oil gets onto the shutter.  This cleaning cost me $75 because the tech had to spend extra time getting the oil off.  There was a lot of it.  Even after this cleaning I can see spots when photographing blue sky.2/9/2014  Upgraded to firmware 2.03, which fixed AI Servo sluggishness in low light.  AI Servo is snappier in low light now and I can use it like I could on my 5DII.  The new firmware also improved the image playback locking up issue I was experiencing.  It still locks up occasionally, but it is better than it was.  I also sent the camera in for a recall that was related to the AF freezing up.  Turns out that this issue was specific to a range of production serial numbers that included my camera.  This improved things somewhat, but AF still freezes up once in awhile.  In the future, I will rent a camera before purchasing it.  This is a great camera for sports, but for weddings, I doubt I will get my $6700 worth from it.  My 5DII was a much better value for the money.

The SD images from BB will not run on BBBK (Beagle Bone Black). I was looking for a bag that can accommodate a gripped body with heavy zoom lens and 17 inch laptop.  This bag fits the bill. It is rugged looking, well-built, well-padded and durable.  It is tad on a heavy side but that's expected with all the padding and size-wise, slightly big, but not too big. The shoulder straps are comfortable and can accommodate a bigger person.  I like the fact that the waist strap is also present but unobtrusive if I don't want to use it.  On some other bags, it gets in the way.Since the bag is divided into 2 separate compartments, the lower compartment is not as roomy as the bags that are dedicated to carrying equipment only. Unless you are going to carry another bag for secondary stuff, it forces you to think and pack carefully what you really need for your task. You cannot open up or convert upper compartment to accommodate more dividers.  Therefore, if you are looking for a bag to cram only the photo gear, this bag is not for you.  I have other bags that are better designed for that purpose. Still, if you need to carry more stuff, I have put extra lenses and flashes in their cushioned pouches in the upper compartment without any issues.  However, the upper compartment is not as well padded as the lower compartment; therefore, you want to be careful not to put anything too fragile there. The upper compartment has two small and a medium compartment as well as an elastic strap and a detachable, small, zippered pouch to secure filters, SD cards and other accessories. There is a small pouch between the shoulder strap to carry an iPod.Although it may make the bag feel unbalanced, I prefer to carry tripod attached to the side of the bag than in the middle of the pack.  The tripod holder extends out from the side of the bag and tucks back in neatly if not used. However, when the tripod is attached, it will get in the way of carrying water bottle in the mesh pouch. I have a Cullman Magic fold-flat tripod that I can carry in the laptop space if I decide not to lug the 17 incher and still have space left over for an iPad and accessories.The rain cover is built into the bottom of the bag so it is unobtrusive and can't get lost - a nice design detail.  You can take this bag as a carry-on on the plane and it will fit in the overhead bin no problem.  Just be sure to leave out your expensive Leatherman multi-purpose tool.  TSA in their infinite wisdom, in the name of reducing terrorist threats confiscated my mini Victorinox key-chain pocket knife, nail clipper and my Leatherman ($65 - ouch!), but lest I digress ...No bag is perfect, and choosing one is a very personal process.  Even if you can't find one locally to check out, this bag merits consideration for the reasons given above.

I've owned this monitor for 6 months now, and it has been a mixed bag for me.Good:  The colors are very bright and vibrant, much more so than my previous Samsung 2333HD.  I am not a professional reviewer and don't have any calibration tools, so it is a huge plus that the out-of-the-box color accuracy is great, and better than most monitors.  I am also happy with the blacks: they look deep while dark details are not crushed.  The whites are nice and bright, but unfortunately the white detail is a bit lacking.  This is one of the most responsive monitors with the least input lag, and ranks as one of the best 60hz gaming monitors.Bad:  As with other TN monitors, the viewing angles are not great, especially when standing above the monitor.  The monitor is also light on features, only containing a single DVI and HDMI for input.  The only ergonomic option is a slight backward tilt, and the stand lacks height or swivel options.  The stand is built in, and there is no option for VESA-style mounting.  This leads me to my biggest complaint...Ugly: It drives me nuts that the monitor is extremely wobbly, and I don't mean just when I bump the monitor.  My keyboard is about half a foot away from my monitor, and typing can cause the screen to shake, which is very distracting.  Another annoyance is that when I am using the headphone output, there is a very loud buzz if the brightness is not set to 100%, which is too bright.  Lastly, the monitor only stores one "custom" setting.  This definitely felt limiting, especially since the HDMI presets are not usable since the blue pumped up for no good reason.Overall, the monitor's performance makes this is a great PC gaming monitor.  However, lack of flexibility and the nagging issues hurt its overall value.

It's tough to provide a review for me, as the product rates a 5 for it's intended purpose - but that's mostly do to a great app and not so much the iPad itself.We are an Android family and have the latest Galaxy phones, plus a Transformer Prime tablet and even a Samsung Slate (Win 7 tablet). As it turns out, I'm a pilot and use it for Foreflight/Stratus.  For that purpose it's fantastic, but that's because Foreflight is awesome, and could be just as awesome on Android.  So the iPad doesn't deserve all the credit - but maybe some.My girlfriend loaded her Danish newspaper website, and it didn't display well at all, everything was a mess and all the flash elements were obviously broken.  The same site loads perfectly, flash and all, on the Transformer tablet.This is my first experience with iOS and it just feels really dumbed down and overly simplistic, but in a bad way.  Missing flash is a very real problem and I kind of think anyone honest with themselves would freely admit that Android is far superior at this time.The battery life is fantastic and will last for a couple days of flying without a recharge, that's a big bonus. I use this filter in a Winix 9500 and it is identical to the filter initially shipped with this product.  Changing the filter is easy but the filter design is not optimal and the cost is very high compared to prices for filters for other air purifiers of similar functionality.  The Winix 9500 is claimed to have a filter sensor that activates a light when the filter needs to be replaced.  No criteria is mentioned for how the the air purifier determines when a filter needs to be replaced but the fact that the filter change light needs to be manually reset suggests that the filter change interval is being determined merely by the period of time the air purifier has been turned on (or possibly by the average speed setting over that time period) rather than the being determined by the condition of the filter.  My replacement light came on after 11 months of use although it is being used in a fairly clean environment, which also suggests that run time is the only criteria being used. The filter consists of 4 components: a washable prefilter, a decent quality HEPA filter, a modest amount of activated carbon, and a silver mesh. The weakest component is the prefilter, which only catches very large particles and lets lots of sizable dust particles that would be filtered out by many other types of prefilters pass though to the HEPA filter.  The Winix 9500 has air intake slots that sit very close to the ground and thus it picks up lots of dust that is too heavy to be a significant source of air-bourne contaminants; this fact, together with the low-quality prefilter, means that the HEPA filter can get clogged very easily.  I have four different brands of air purifiers and this is the only one where the HEPA filter gets clogged with large amounts of dust even though this is the air purifier with the lowest air flow rate.  The carbon filter component weights a little over a pound but once one accounts for the frame the filter contains less than a pound of activated carbon. This is not a large quantity (by contrast my Aurpura filter uses 18 pounds with a suggested replacement rate of 2 years and my Blueair filter uses 2 pounds with a suggested replacement rate of 6 months) so many users will find that the activated carbon component would need replacing long before the HEPA filter would.  Ideally, one would be able to replace each component separately but the all-in-one nature of the product does not permit this, which is a very significant limitation.  I have no way to evaluate the usefulness of the silver mesh.  Silver nano-particles are known to have antibacterial properties and the silver mesh is called a "nano-silver" mesh, but I am skeptical of the effectiveness of this particular component, especially as the mesh has a fairly large gauge and thus most particles will pass though it without coming into contact with the silver.This filter does adequately filter the air, but the relatively high cost and need to replace all the components at once means that it is not a particularly good value for the price.  Unfortunately, there are apparently no third party vendors for the Winix filters so one either has to use this filter, jerry-rig something, or replace the air purifier.  Thus, it only merits a three star rating.

Updated 11/8/12:Down from 5 stars to 2.Like so many other people, I experienced the heat issue. You'll get careless or cocky and pour a hot liquid into it, if only to make that iced tea or coffee which is ultimately cold anyway.This would be such a nice jug if they just tempered the glass. I have a Dell E1705 laptop hooked up to an external monitor in addition to the laptop screen, so that the ms desktop spans across both screens. I haven't noticed any  degradation of the picture quality with this switch in the middle, and I simply flip to A when I want to use my smaller desktop monitor and B when I want to use the 46" TV monitor.You'll also need 2 M/M monitor cables if you are trying something similar:Tripp Lite P502-006 SVGA Monitor Gold Cable w RGB Coax HD15M/M - 6ft. Whatever you get just make sure they are male on both ends, as all the monitor inputs on the TV/switch/computer are Female.You'll probably also want a stereo cable to connect the pc sound to the TV:Cables To Go - 27412 - 12ft 3.5mm Stereo Audio Cable M/M PC-99 (Beige)And a reliable remote keyboard/mouse so you can operate the computer from  the couch when you've switched to the TV monitor:Adesso 2.4 GHZ WIRELESS SLIMTOUCH TOUCHPAD MINI KEYBOARD SILVER W/BLACK KEYS ( WKB-4000US )The mousepad on the above keyboard works well, but there's a few games that I prefer to use a normal mouse with. I just ordered a Logitech bluetooth mouse for that purpose, but haven't tested it out yet:Logitech V470 Bluetooth Cordless Laser Mouse for Notebooks - BlueThis setup works for me for switching between my TV and another monitor on the same computer.A more traditional use for this AB switch would be sharing one monitor with two computers, and I noticed a couple reviews mention that application as well. I didn't see anything specific on using it to  switch to/from a HDTV and an external monitor on the same computer, and that's one reason I wrote this review.The Switch itself is a very simple device and it's hard to imagine much going wrong with it. One minor issue I had was with the screws inside the box unraveling instead of the monitor connection screws. I wound up having to get a phillips screwdriver out to  open the box and reseat the screws that had fallen off inside.Edit 5/27/2008: After writing all this about using two monitors via one connection on the PC...my son pointed out that a vga splitter would be simpler and allow the tv and pc monitor to display the same image simultaneously.Cables To Go - 29550 - 2-Port UXGA Video Splitter Extenderseems like it should do the trick, eliminating the AB switch from the equation. I had the Harmony H659 which is one of the more simple remotes out there.  Well, after several years of great service, we found out just how not-toddler friendly it was. No matter what you want to do, you have to swipe a hard to find area beneath the touch screen to advance to the next screen where you can then select your activity.  Once you have selected your activity, it spins into the "these buttons work for this activity".  Well, if something isn't right, it takes several button presses to get to a semi-helpful screen.  For instance, if I am getting no picture because my reciever is on the wrong channel, the only way the remote can help is if I tell it I have no sound (it'll then change the input to the right one)  Anyway, I'm not new to electronics nor am I sheltered from the newest and greatest things... okay, I haven't gone to 3D TV yet... But hey, this remote ALWAYS is 3 to 4 button presses from what you need to do.  The old one that I was replaceing was at most 2 button presses from any action.  When you are done for the night and want things turned off,AR AARX18G --You have to wake it up, press the "activity" button, slide to the right to the next screen, press the "Goodnight" spot on the touch screen and you have turned it off.Harmony H659 - press "Off".For christmas, I got a brand un-new Harmony H659 from the Family.  Apparently, 4 months wasn't enough to endear us to the remote.We had no issues with the charger as some had said.  For a rechargeable remote though, it'd be a lot better if you could actually use it while it was plugged in.  3 times in the four months, I found myself over by the wall with the entire charging stand in my hand trying to get things to turn on.  I mean, remotes are just dead... they don't linger... they work or they are dead...I hope this is helpful to someone.  I really thought the touch screen would be a bonus rather than a detriment.

I tested this with and without a loaded OS with the same results under three different benchmarks.Sequential Read:  ca. 180-190 MB/s average 183.Sequential Write:  ca. 80 MB/s or so.I can get near this performance from the new Kingston V+, with better write performance overall.  And it is less money (2.30 gig vs. 2.80 gig).I do not understand how review benchmarks put this Intel drive at 250 MB/s, since I am using the same software (on an i7 2.60 gHz).I have the latest firmware, and as I said, I ran the benchmarks both on a partition-aligned Win 7, a formatted drive with no data, and an unformatted drive with variance of only a few percent.Win 7 Experience with Kingston V+ = 7Win 7 Experience Index with this Intel X25 = 7.2 (I do not see how anyone can get 7.8 or 7.9)Win 7 Experience Index with Kingston V = 6.5  (there are serious write issues with this drive, and you will get a warning from the detailed log of the win 7 index run).I note the screen shots from another buyer showing 200+ rates.  I suspect that there may be chipset issues or variability of manufacture.  My experience with the Kingston models and this Intel strongly suggests there is variability of manufacture, and not just the firmware.  As far as I know, there is no product specification range, which makes it difficult to judge the acceptability of a given performance.My computer is a Dell Studio XPS i7 2.66 with 8 gigs of RAM with Intel 5 3400 Series chipset.  I ran tests with each drive independently and paired with my Caviar Black...there is no difference in these various contexts < 1.5%.If I scan the reviews for the retail and for the oem versions here on Amazon, I note Win 7 experience benchmarks (which are nearly always the value of the disk test) varying from what I got, a 7.2, all the way to 7.9.  That is large range, ca 10%.Win 7 Experience Index with WD Black Caviar boot drive = 5.9.I note the previous reviewer who found not a big difference on boot times.  This was not my experience..boot times are very much faster with SSD, no matter what brand I use, in Win 7 Prof, (SSD vs. Caviar Black 650 and two 650s in RAID 0).  The 2+ min boot time with over 150 start up processes, various gadgets (weather etc) that must connect to ethernet, etc went down to 22 seconds total.

I have both the 4" x 2" and the 5" by 2" round cake pans.  These are very sturdy and high quality pans. I baked them for about 30 minutes - the small diameter did not make the cake bake any faster.  I originally thought that I would stack them for a layer cake, but each layer rose pretty high.  I ended up cutting each one in half horizontally and making four layers for a total of 2 little layer cakes.  So cute and people loved them!  People don't really want to have so much cake; they just feel guilty throwing most of it away.  I just made a half-recipe of a homemade red velvet cake recipe and used the 4" x 2" size - I had quite a bit of batter left over - enough to fill up 3 of the mini-Wilton tasty fill mini cake pans.  I recommend those too, by the way.  I love making the mini-cakes; the presentation is so superior to handing over a quarter of a full size cut cake to someone.  I also recommend using parchment paper to line the pans in lieu of buttering and flouring the pans.  You place the pan right side up on the parchment paper, circle around the base with a pen, and cut just inside the circle.  You don't have to grease anything.  When the cake comes out, cool for 10 minutes, and run a plastic knife around the perimeter of the pan and the cake should fall out easily.  Very little mess to clean up.  Have fun!

(This review is not small, but neither is the price of the knife. If you want my overall impression, skip to the last paragraph)This is my first Spyderco knife, and, it's everything I expected it to be. Given that this cost me more than twice as much as I'd ever previously spent on a knife, that's a bit of an accomplishment. To be entirely honest, I regretted the purchase shortly after I placed the order, and was ready to find a fault with it so I could return it and have the money back - but I like it far too much. I'll eat eggs for a few weeks. Worth it.This is a big knife. Yeah, "XL" kinda gives that away, but even looking at the measurements and being given rough size estimates doesn't quite tell the whole story. I've submitted pictures (with some annotations) that should help.Ergonomics:Herein lies my biggest complaint: The handle's jimping. It's a little uncomfortable. My ring finger gets the worst of it, but it's really not too bad. It might start to make your hands a little raw after extended use. It will not, however, slip out of your hand....Ever.The handle is very well formed, whether held in a standard or reverse grip. Even the pocket clip helps fill the hand and give extra purchase on the knife. No real complaints, but (perhaps notably) no praises.Portability:It's a little hefty, but the weight is evenly distributed. Given how large the knife is, the weight is admirably low. It sits in the pocket very well, and takes up much less space than my previous every-day-carry knife, theCold Steel Voyager Lg. Clip Point Plain Edge Knife(shown in the submitted pictures). The texture of the G10 is perfect - rough enough to give a good grip, but not so rough that it will fray your pants. I wear cargo shorts most days of the week, and, while this stays firmly in place, it can be removed or stored with ease. Thicker pants (jeans) may make it less easy to remove.Deployment:Buttery. Smooth. This opens up so smoothly that it's unreal. All of the linerlocks and lockbacks I've used have nothing on this. The large hole in the blade makes it very easy to open, even with gloved hands. Due to the lack of a thumbstud, thumb-flicking this open takes some practice. It can be wrist-flicked fairly well, and, if you hold down the lock mechanism, it can require almost no effort whatsoever.Sidenote: Shortly after getting it, I put a ziptie through the hole to give it a DIY Emerson Wave, which works astoundingly well with this knife. The handle sticks out about an inch above the pocket because of the clip placement, and that allows you to get a very good grip on the knife before pulling it out - while leaving your fingers entirely clear of the path of the blade. I went with a larger size zip tie that also serves as a surrogate thumb stud, allowing me to open the knife without touching the blade whether I wave it out or not.Appearance:It's a very plain knife. While the wide leaf-shaped brushed blade is certainly impressive, it's not going to win any beauty contests. Function over form. I'm cool with that.Durability:I haven't used this knife for long, so I can't say much about the edge retention or the lock's long-term durability. I can say that it feels extremely sturdy, locks up with no blade play, the blade is evenly ground and is almost exactly as thick as the blade on my aforementioned Voyager. (Research shows the Manix2 XL to be 0.5mm thinner. Not visually noticeable.)HOWEVERThe tip and edge are crazy thin, thus this is not a beater knife. Hacking down trees and prying are entirely outside the workload of this knife. From everything I've read, S30v is an extremely durable and corrosion-resistant metal. It is not, though, indestructible. This will cut, slice, and serve as a self-defense tool, but using this to hack and chop will almost surely leave you with a broken blade.Overall, this knife seems to be designed perfectly for everyday carry. It will work beautifully for all of the cutting tasks one typically encounters in a day, at work or otherwise. Trim fingernails, prepare food, open boxes, cut straps, impress knife nerds (like myself)... All with little worry about rust or rapid dullness. If you can afford to drop the cash on this, or even if you can't (like me), you won't regret it.

I bought this camera mainly for taking videos.  There are a lot of things that I like about this camera, but my biggest beef is that the video quality isn't as good as I expected it to be.What I like:The form factor- The size of this thing is great.  It easily fits in your pocket.  Because it is so portable, I think will use it more often.SD Memory Card Recording - This is great!  No tapes to mess with.  Just remove the card and stick it in your PCs card reader.  For me, this makes it really easy to edit/delete the videos.  I also noticed that there is a mode where you can save your videos directly to a USB hard disk and play them back thru the camera to your TV.  No PC required!Lots of adjustments - There are tons of adjustments to help you fine tune your videos.  I have found that I get the best results by running the ISO at 100 to 200.Decent Zoom - A lot better than the Aiptek A-HD I also own.Very Good Sound Quality - Again, a lot better than my A-HD.In Camera Editing- While I wouldn't want to edit a long movie in the camera, it is fine for cutting out segments while sitting in the hotel room at night.What I don't like:Video Quality -  Maybe my expectations are too high.  Indoors under typical room lighting the videos are passable, but they won't wow anyone.  The ISO should be above 400 but if you do that, there is a lot of video noise.  In brighter lighting, the video quality is much better. I also think that the video could be much sharper.  Running the videos thru sharpening in Premier Elements helps a lot. Now don't get me wrong, the video quality is significantly better than the A-HD, but I would have expected better, especially when you see that these things are selling for $500.  I paid $100 for the A-HD.  The HD700 DOES NOT give you 5X the image quality of the A-HD.Editing - It seems the videos from my A-HD are easier to edit. I have a 3GHZ P4 with 3GB of RAM.  The A-HD videos play smoother in Premier Elements and much smoother in Quicktime.  The HD700 videos have a very strange cyclical jump when played in Quicktime.  I have been converting the videos to AVI with MP4CAM2AVI and then editing or playing them in Windows Media Player.Lens Cap - OK, maybe this is a little picky, but for $500 I would have expected something more than a flimsy snap on piece of plastic.  The lens cap on the A-HD is very similar to a Canon DSLR lens cap.I got the HD700 for $300 and I think that it is worth that much.  If I paid $500 for this camera, I would return it.

The specifications on these drives are outstanding. I bought a pair April 25 with the intention of creating a mirrored RAID in a content creation workstation I built last year. When they arrived I checked the box labels and both said 3 TB Enterprise drives. There was no sign of damage to the boxes, and the drives looked pristine inside their static packages, identical down to the yellow label, at least identical to the naked eye, because the static wrap is partially opaque. Nor was there any damage to the plastic suspension carriers that were to protect them from dropping. I repacked them into the carriers, with their static protection intact and unopened, to rest until I could get time to insert them into the workstation and perform the steps necessary to create the array. Normally, that is the smart way to store hard drives. You just don't mess with hard drives until you install them. They come wrapped in static protection for a reason, and I honor that reason until it is time to put them to work.Unfortunately I did not get time to perform the installation until more than a month later. When I opened one of the static packages I discovered the drive inside was 2 TB, not 3TB. If I used it as part of a mirrored RAID it would reduce the capacity of the final array to 2 TB, wasting 33% of the capacity of the larger drive. Generally speaking, this is also considered unwise. The most stable arrays are created with two absolutely identical drives. These were not, despite the fact I had purchased them under the assumption they were.Amazon clearly states returns are limited to the first 30 days after purchase and I was taking a chance when I had to delay installation. My thinking was if something went wrong with the drives it would simply be between me and Western Digital, which is always the case after the first 30 days anyway. I just did not consider the possibility either package contained the wrong sized drive. I suppose I could have taken it out of the static container to check the fine print, but the safest way to store drives is to leave their original static wrap alone until you are ready to use them. There is some irony here because the procedure I selected was the one that provided the greatest safety to the drive itself, thus maximally ensuring no harm would come to it that would invoke the provisions of the warranty. In so doing, I exposed myself to the possibility that someone in the chain of custody put the wrong drive in the bag and I would not see that until it was too late.The meaning of 1-star is "I hate it" and that is the rating I initially gave this purchase. To be honest, my solution is to bite the bullet and order - once again, and at my additional expense - what I ordered in the first place, a 3 TB Enterprise Western Digital drive. They appear to be very good drives.UPDATE June 3, 2014:I ordered a replacement drive from Amazon which arrived today, June 3. It was the correct size, 3 TB. However, when I registered it with Western Digital they granted 666 days of warranty, not the FIVE YEARS promised in Amazon's advertisement! The label on the drive says it was manufactured Feb 25, 2014.I have contacted Western Digital about the warranty problem and the original mis-boxed 2 TB drive sold as a 3 TB. I will post what they have to say and do about the situations.UPDATE June 4, 2014:Western Digital informed me the 3 TB drive offered as new on Amazon was re-furbished and has but a 6 month warranty. This is considerable variance with the 666 days cited when I registered the drive, raising another question in this questionable process. Amazon has referred my request to return the drive to Aeon Micro, the "reseller". Obviously there are, at minimum, extra complications when one buys from "resellers".Update July 11, 2014:I intend to raise my rating to three stars, if all issues are settled. One has. Aeon Micro sent me a replacement drive, also labelled as "new, factory sealed" but, according to them, had set on a shelf longer than normal and therefore would register at 3.5 years warranty instead of 5. But, Aeon said, WD would restore the full 5 years if I filed a support case. I filed the support case, but WD ultimately said the drive was a "replacement drive" they had sent someone else and they would not increase the warranty. At first, Aeon offered to accept both drives back, shipped at their expense, with full refund to me. Since I had invested considerable time in building my RAID array with the 3.5 year drive that was supposed to be extended to 5 years, I countered that I would accept both drives which, combined, had a warranty of a little over 5 years, and thus salvage all my effort at building and loading the 3 TB RAID. Aeon agreed, so the issue with them was satisfied.But the 2 TB improperly labelled as a 3 TB has not. After photographing the 2 TB drive, its box, and the packing slip and uploading them to WD, the "higher ups" ruled that packing the wrong drive in the box was not their doing. This after coping with a fairly rude customer "assistant" who did not read English that well, as he confounded the 2 TB support case with the "refurbished" 3 TB case, and made a few too many snide remarks as if he knew what he was talking about when he did not. So, when I filled out the "customer satisfaction" survey I let them have it, both barrels. I got a response from someone who had real authority. That person repeated the assertion that the 2 TB problem was Amazon's, not theirs, but asked why I took "3 months" to notice. He too had not read my communications that well, but was perfectly able to understand them when I pointed out I had waited slightly less than 2 months, and that the reason was simple, I was building a workstation and constructing the RAID took place at the final stage. At that point he decided to pursue making an exception for me, and provided a RMA and shipping label at their expense to return the 2 TB (which was, after all, brand new and fully qualified for the 5 year warranty) while he overnight shipped a refurbished 3 TB with a 5 year warranty. 5 year warranty not to be implemented until they received the 2 TB back. I checked today, several weeks after I returned the 2 TB drive, and the warranty has not been extended and has but 97 days left!So, for now, I am leaving it at one star. This has been an incredibly twisted journey.

My friend has an electric burr grinder that cost a couple hundred dollars. It doesn't take me that much longer to leisurely grind beans by hand than it takes his electric grinder. We both brew with French presses. His grinder produces quite a bit of dust and sediment. The Kyocera produces barely any at a medium+ grind. Admittedly at that setting it does allow for some uneven grinding, and larger chunks inevitably manage to slip through, but that's not a big concern at a larger grind anyway and at fine grind settings, those larger chunks just don't make it through until they've been pulverized. It took a bit of trial and error to find the grind that's right for my process, but once I got it, there's been no more fiddling or adjusting, and I've used my grinder nearly every day since purchase.The hopper holds exactly 1 cup of roasted beans which is equivalent to 80 grams or just under 3 ounces. It takes about 3 to 3 1/2 minutes to grind that much, and it's enough to brew a ten cup batch.I've noticed that some reviewers complain about, "flying beans." I put the rubber sleeve on top of the grinder with the handle protruding through it, and that keeps bouncing beans from flying about. I grind while I hold it with my other hand rather than on the counter top. I suppose you could just place a kitchen towel on the counter to protect the glass if you prefer to use it on a stable surface.I have absolutely no complaints about this grinder and highly recommend it.

New shortened review to summarize:After using this product for 30 days and in three completely different locations and environments, I can no longer recommend this item. It is simply not worth the effort to get it to work, it does not handle some network configurations and it has not proven reliable even when it is working.- Configuration is needlessly difficult, requiring connecting via ethernet, setting up static IP addresses on your computer.- iPad doesn't connect unless you enable WMM in advanced settings. Even with it on, the iPad can have trouble connecting sometimes requiring multiple attempts before it succeeds.- It has not proven reliable. In two situations where i have successfully used it, I've had to power cycle it every few days when the network stops working.- It has issues as a repeater in some network situations. I worked with support who was very pleasant, but ultimately unable to fix it. This was an environment with multiple access points on the same SSID, typical of larger network deployments.Overall, it has the feel of an abandoned cheap product. Looking back, it has not been worth my time to try and troubleshoot various issues with this device over the last month. In contrast, I've used multiple Linksys RE1000 in multiple network environments with no trouble. Setup is incredibly easy and it just works. Hard to realize how big a deal "it just works" is until you try another one what doesn't just work and you spend hours debugging it. My caveat with the Linksys RE1000 is that the first one I bought failed after a week, as in wouldn't even power on.Detailed previous review:Read the reviews, ordered it with high hopes. Unfortunately I've spent all day trying to get it to work. My network consists of Appleproducts, Macbook(s), iPad(s) and an Airport Extreme Base Station. It has all been problematic.Bottom line, I have experienced extremely inconsistent results being able to use this device as a repeater. Rarely does it work, more often than not I have some connection issue. I'm not sure I've sorted out all the issues.1. The setup CD only includes a Windows program, although after eventually running it, it doesn't do much that isn't reasonably clear through the menus accessing the device directly.2. Part of my problem was that the AEBS (Airport Extreme) by default is configured to pick a channel automatically. Every time it reboots a new channel is picked and the configuration on the Edimax needs to reflect it. I changed the AEBS configuration to use a static channel.3. I have had extensive and persistent problems connecting to the iPad in particular. Reading Apple docs, they indicate that an iPad/iPhone/Apple TV may not connect if WMM is disabled. The Edimax by default has WMM disabled under the advanced settings.4. Apple also indicates that the "channel width" should be set to 20mhz, Apple devices don't use 40. I'm not sure if this has helped with connection issues to the iPad or not but I've changed it.5. Early on I configured a static IP address on the iPad. This configuration may not have been cleared later and may have caused some failures. It helped to run Settings, General/Reset/"Reset Network Settings", then configure it new.Despite all these changes, the iPad will still not consistently connect. Best case it requires multiple attempts to establish a connection. Typically it says "failed to join" then the network name. Worst case you spend all day trying to get it to connect with no success...Once connected, it seems reasonably stable. Performance seems good (not great). Latency is low, with ping times <50ms all the way through to internet sites.The device itself is very small, lightweight. Even the power pack is almost cell phone charger sized.At the end of the day, I'm not sure its been worth the trouble and I'm not confident I've figured out what the issues have been. I've spent most of the day flipping settings throughout and doing searches on Google. I have it working for the first time 12 hours later, but I have no confidence it will survive anything rebooting. I'll update this review if I either find out more about what the problems were or it turns out to be a stable environment.Update:A couple of days have passed. The configuration I've setup seems pretty stable. iPad(s) have trouble connecting at first, typically requiring multiple tries. But once connected, it stays that way even waking up from sleep. I haven't had issues with other devices. It may be that the primary problem was #2 above, that the Airport Extreme kept changing channels every time I changed a router setting and didn't realize it was doing that.Performance has been very good for internet access, low latency, low jitter. It is much slower than a direct 802.11n connection. The Macbook is reporting a connection speed of 65mbps vs. 300mbps if it was using the primary network.Range has been good. I move the repeater halfway across the house. I'm now able to get full speed internet in every corner of the house and well into the back yard.The only flakey behavior remaining is that bonjour (a cool Apple technology), sometimes works and sometimes doesn't. Its used to find the Airport Extreme which is acting as a file server and my excellent Brother printer. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't find any devices.BTW, this repeater works fine with SSIDs that have spaces in them. I had tried a ZyXel that could not handle that.Update 6/23/2012I've tried it in another couple of locations. I used it as an access point in a hotel that only had ethernet. Worked fine, although for some reason I had to recycle it every day.Unfortunately, I went back to a rental condo where I had originally intended to use it and much to my dismay it does NOT work. Not sure what the issue is, having multiple access points broadcasting the same SSID? It is unable to act as a repeater. I had to run out and buy a Linksys RE1000 which works fine. WIth the Edimax I get an error from my Mac saying that my IP address is already in use. Its as if the DHCP request/responses are getting scrambled.

I thought I would try a pistol grip as I have never had one before, and this seemed to have some nice features.  I am not a convert.Supposedly the benefit is you can move quickly by squeezing the grip then release to lock in a new position, this would allow you to pan quickly and smoothly while also providing fast adjustments and end point stability.  I have to say that the Vanguard does a decent job achieving these goals, but it doesn't do a better job then my Markins ball head, nor than the Really Right Stuff ball heads I have used.A good ball-head, if properly friction adjusted will allow you to move the camera in any direction with a relatively small application of force and then when you stop moving the camera it stops moving.  The one I have has zero creep and I only rarely have to readjust the tension if I am using a particularly heavy or light lens, but I only have to make one adjustment, then I don't have to squeeze move release ever time.I would highly recommend a top quality ball head over this, essentially it accomplishes the exact same thing, but with a smoother action and less work.  Moreover because you don't have to hold a trigger to move the camera you can use the camera's shutter release, even while zooming.  This also means it is easier to change camera settings on the fly.The shutter release on the Vanguard is a nice feature for a pistol grip style head, but the fact that it only comes with cables for lower end cameras is annoying.  I did not purchase the additional cables, I just went back to using my ball head, as I said I prefer access to my cameras controls, even while zooming, so the release while helpful would have been insufficient to my needs.Conclusion:If you like pistol grip heads this seems to be a good solid options.  But if you never used a high quality ball head I would recommend trying that before you actually buy this one, I think you'll never want to use a pistol grip style head again.

Breadman BK1060S Two Pound Professional Bread Maker is a good bread machine for making creative loaves of bread, hot and fresh, right in your own kitchen. This bread maker offers a nice, professional- looking appearance with its metal exterior and it has many extras like fourteen different settings for specific types of bread; a fruit and nut dispenser; a built in memory that stores your settings for up to seven minutes in case of a power failure; and the ability to program the bread maker to start up to fifteen hours ahead of time.All of these extra features are nice, but what matters most is the performance and quality of the finished product. My experiences here have been mixed, but they have improved. My first attempt resulted in a compressed block of bread that was inedible and had to be discarded. I followed the instructions presented in the included recipe guide, and later discovered the problem: The recipe book contains several errors. The recipe I consulted did not have an accurate measurement for the liquids and after looking through the guide, I noticed others errors in other recipes. One recipe, for example, calls for a tablespoon of raisins, which is obviously incorrect. I am a little surprised that the manufacturer hasn't realized these glaring mistakes and made a greater effort to correct them.Beyond my first experience with this bread maker, I have enjoyed positive results. My more recent attempts with this bread maker have resulted in good, fresh loaves of bread and my confidence in the machine has improved. However, there are still a few areas of concern. One is that the loaf of bread, once removed, often has a patch of flour on one of the corners. This is because the paddle doesn't always mix the ingredients as well as it should and you end up with a flour- coated corner. Another area of concern is the metal paddle. When you release the loaf of bread, the paddle often pops out with the bread and lodges itself in the bottom of the loaf.Breadman BK1060S Two Pound Professional Bread Maker is generally good, but I have noticed other peculiar qualities that are misleading at first. There are multiple points in the process where the bread maker will go several minutes without making any sound. You will think there is a possible problem with the machine and will be tempted to open the lid, check the settings, and possibly even reset, but you need to resist the temptation. The machine is fine and needs to be left alone. And, I have also learned that if you open the door early on and you have ingredients in the fruit/nut dispenser, it will often drop the extra ingredients into the bread as soon as you close the door. Again, you have to trust that everything is okay and resist the temptation to open the lid. And you need to be careful where you touch- the metal exterior looks nice, but it also conducts heat very well and can get quite hot to the touch.Hot, fresh bread is a great addition to any meal and the Breadman BK1060S Two Pound Professional Bread Maker is a good small appliance for the purpose of making tasty, creative loaves of bread just like a professional. If you use the included recipe book, make sure to examine the recipes closely for typos and above all, exercise patience. The lack of noise and other distractions are not cause for alarm. Just let your Breadman complete its process and enjoy the finished product.

You know that great picture their plasmas come with?  Those dark blacks and great contrast?  Well, by this time next year your expensive new HDTV will look worse than sets that sell for half the price at WalMart.  Panasonic, you see, has programmed their tv to "gradually" increase their black levels.  ([...])They didn't let us know before we ponied up all this cash that they had irrevocably programmed our expensive TVs to degrade in quality.  There is no fix in sight and they're now being sued. I ride street motorcycles (Buell XB12R) and I have been looking for a good headphone solution to use while riding.  Most motorcycle riders use earplugs due to loud exhaust and high levels of wind noise, and many use noise-isolating headphones to provide a little boredom relief on longer rides.  The purpose is not to block out ALL ambient noise, but to block out the harsh, loud sounds of the wind and motorcycle.These earbud tips are made from a foam that is SIMILAR to earplug foam, but that's where the problem lies.  It's only SIMILAR.  the foam on these earbuds is much firmer than earplug foam, and it bounces back very quickly.  You can't really mush them down and put them in your ears, allowing them to expand for a perfect fit.  I don't have exceptionally tiny earholes, but only the smallest of these foam tips fit in my ears comfortably.  Even the second-smallest size was uncomfortable and caused mild pain after 30 minutes or so.The photograph of the kit is a bit misleading as well.  The kit includes one set of small tips, two sets of medium tips (in black and white), a set of large tips, and a set of tips that are meant for Andre the Giant.  Seriously... why these tips are included in a generic set is anyone's guess.  In the photo, the small gray and small white tips appear to be the same size but they are not.  The description says there are 5 different sizes, but after comparing them, there are 4 different sizes.If the foam were a little softer, the medium size would work perfectly, but as is, only the smallest ones are useful to me.On a positive note, the sound quality with these tips is excellent.  Though uncomfortable, with the medium tips in I got crisp, clear bass and a nice sweet treble out of some very cheaply-made earbuds.  With these tips, my cheap earbuds sound at least as good as the $40 Sony earbuds I normally use.  Too bad I lost the Sony earbuds or I could try these out on them!Overall, if you usually prefer the smaller silicone earbud tips, you're only going to be able to use the smallest of these tips.  If you like the larger silicone earbud tips, then this kit will be perfect for you because the medium or even large sizes will fit you well and you'll get excellent sound quality and slightly better sound isolation than the silicone tips offer.

I purchased my RX-V773 locally at a substantial discount ($200 off list price).  The place I bought it from offers their own 30-day in-store return policy, although I would not hesitate to purchase from Amazon.I would rate this unit 4 1/2 stars if I could.  It's a very versatile receiver--2 of the 7 amplifier channels that can be assigned for something like a second zone (stereo only, obviously).  The 5 HDMI inputs and dual oututs are a nice feature at this price point.  I upgraded to this unit from an older model Marantz that did not have any HDMI inputs.I had no problem with the Wi-Fi setup on my receiver.  I followed the instructions using the push-button on the adapter and router.  On the second try, it connected and has not dropped connection since.  I enjoy the network features a lot.  The receiver found my network hard drive (Twonky server).  I was able to use my computer to quickly create some playlists and then play them flawlessly with the receiver.  I also followed the instructions for creating a free internet radio account for the receiver and set up a dozen or so bookmarks for free internet stations.  That feature also works very well...but once in a while the receiver will switch to another of my bookmarked stations.  I suspect that is caused by the internet service (vTuner) that provides the bookmarks, not by the receiver itself.  The bookmarks are stored on the vTuner site, not the receiver, so it just about has to be at that end.  It's not a big deal since internet radio is mostly for background sound.  Right now there is no support for any internet service other than vTuner.  That could change with a firmware upgrade.  SirusXM over the internet would be great.Onscreen setup menu is very easy to use.  I tried the automatic speaker setup (YPAO or whatever they call it) but did not like the results so I set the speakers up manually.  This takes a few minutes.  You can independently set the crossover point for each set of speakers (main, center, and surround).  That's a nice feature that my older Marantz did not have.  I'm very pleased with the sound.  Right now I'm using a Definitive Technology sub and surrounds, and Polk mains and center.I can read the front display of the unit from across the room.  That makes it easy to select internet radio bookmarks or server playlists without having the TV on.  I like that feature.  The receiver has a built-in Web server so you can use any computer on your network to control BASIC functions, like volume, source, and bookmark/playlist selection.  There is also an Android app that allows more control and works well.  The remote control that comes with the receiver works fine but is nothing fancy.  I use a Harmony remote for the whole system.The only real fault that I've found after about a month with this receiver is that it does not appear to support the older Yamaha dedicated iPod docks. Had the Tomtom 920 for one week for a trip from Los Angeles to Mammoth Lakes. Found 2 of my friends homes which Nuvi 650 had located on the wrong sections of streets. It did not find 2 business addresses correct though which really bothered me more as it drove me a mile away. Also had funny routes going back to LA that were not ideal. I bought it mainly for the voice recognition feature which does work well but as others found does not really save time, just hands on. I'm willing to give that up as I'm returning the TomTom 920 and getting another Nuvi 650 (had 2 stolen in a year!) for the following reasons:1. Screen is not as bright/readable during daylight vs. Nuvi. Also TT has more stuff on the screen that takes away space from the map. This is a big complaint among many reviews I read. It helps to change the text to vertical so it's on the side but still bulky.2. Too difficult to CANCEL Routes, I had to start a new route to find a Cancel button! Nuvi takes 2 taps to cancel. It was VERY annoying that Tomtom would not shutup when I made a detour...I had to shut her off.3. TomTom's only included "computer voice" that speaks out street names sounds quite unpleasant, like a computer. Nuvi has a very pleasant voice, it has a big effect on a long drive;)  TT's other voices are nicer, but don't read streets, lame. All of Nuvi's voices speak names.4. Zoom out function is limited, could not zoom to see my whole state.5. Cannot scroll map using finger like Nuvi, similar to google maps. That is a very nice handy feature I loved to use to see where my route was headed from the big picture perspective.6. Maps/graphics just don't look as nice on TomTom as Nuvi, especially the night maps. Hard to say exactly why, but I miss my Nuvi after a week of TomTom.7. After entering your destination, it asks if you need to arrive by a particular time. That is so lame, and I doubt most will use it, yet this step cannot be disabled. Nuvi is lame to ask which State each time so I guess they are even on having a forced wasteful step...8. Estimated time of arrival is WAY off, way later...even my Grandma could make it earlier.  Not just a by a few minutes but by over 2 hours on a 5 hour drive. Does it assume I am having dinner and stopping for bathrooms 5 times? Even within 20 minutes of arriving home it still estimates 30 minutes...Nuvi is VERY accurate given light traffic, and usually I arrived within minutes of the ETA.9. The mount sucks, fell off once after a short while indicating I had not installed it properly.  It's more difficult to remove vs. Nuvi, the angles of the unit are more limited, charging cable is in the way of dashboard.I strongly suggest removing any MOUNT as well as GPS unit as my car was broken into in San Francisco just from leaving the mount on the dash, and hid the GPS which was found and stolen as well. The Nuvi mount is much nicer and easier to deal with.I find it interesting that others called the Nuvi operating system "dumbed down" as I find it just right with a good balance of features, decent mapping/directions vs. others I've tried, nicest screen, mount, charger, hardware=a quality product. Not to mention significantly lower price recently at big warehouse stores and online auctions vs. TomTom.In conclusion, if you have not used a Nuvi before you would not have another standard to compare TomTom with.  Most of my issues would not be as relevant as you wouldn't know what you're missing. I actually really like the voice recognition feature and it worked really well for me. It's a big deal to give that up to go back to Nuvi 650 for now, until the future Nuvi's with Voice Recognition come down in price.  The 650 is nearly the same GPS as the much more expensive 660/670/680 but without Bluetooth and Traffic which for me is a gimmick anyway as Bluetooth cannot pull out the ADDRESS of my contacts and I don't use speakerphone or need another device to control my phone...I see google traffic on my phone (PocketPC XV6700) so I don't need to pay the extra yearly fee for Nuvi Traffic. The 650 just dropped significantly and is one of the nicest GPS Navigation systems I've seen and used. I have had experience with 5 other brands and none were as nice as the Garmins. If you intend to just use a GPS for GPS use, the Nuvi 650 is a great choice.  Physically they look/feel nicer than Tomtom.

It looks very simple when opening the box; two pieces of plastic that snap together. I first tried it in our Caravan. It hooked onto the headrest arms just fine. While this would be understandable if it gave the tablet a good bit of left/right pivot ability, there is very little. With it hanging out a good bit, it makes the tablet much more susceptible to shaking and wobbling, not to mention accidentally hitting it or scratching yourself -- which happened to us multiple times.When I did try to use it in the car while sitting in the back seat, I found that the glare was too much in the daytime, so I had to put it on my lap to be able to see.
