Something strange has happened to me over the last few years.  There was a time that I thought that coffee should come in an IV-drip. Consuming an entire pot before noon was no great feat.  When a new doctor asked how much coffee I drank, I simply replied "lots." When she wanted to know what "lots" was I asked her if she remembered medical school.  End of subject . . .  and then one day I noticed that the first pot didn't disappear before noon.  Before long it wasn't the "first pot" but "the pot" and it still wasn't all disappearing, so eventually I gave in and switched to a 4-cup coffee maker, but after a bit I noticed that even the 4 cups, really only enough to fill my mug twice, was not all disappearing either. And then one day I woke up and realized that I hadn't had a cup of coffee since . . . .  so long ago I didn't remember the last cup of coffee!Since then I've satisfied my coffee urges, when they strike, with some sort of little gizmo that sits on top of the cup or maybe a little French press.  The 4-cup coffeemaker went into the tag sale box.  Meanwhile, my daughter has been trying time and time again to give me a Keurig machine, but frankly, I have a bit of a penny-pincher streak and the cost of those K-cups as  regular source of coffee just rankles me.  And then along came theHamilton Beach 49999A FlexBrew Single-Serve Coffeemaker. . . .Now admittedly the FlexBrew sat in my kitchen for several weeks before I actually felt like having a cup of coffee. (In all fairness, I've been in and out of the hospital. It really wasn't the fault of either the coffee or the machine.)  Eventually however, the mood struck and I must say, the FlexBrew makes a darned good cuppa.I particularly like the flexibility of the machine.  You can, if you are of of a mind, use K cups or the version made by Melitta.  Remove the K-cup holder and add 2 tablespoons (level) of regular grind coffee to the basket underneath for a dynamite brew with your usual grounds - or remove the stand you set the cup on and you'll find a smaller (1 tablespoon capacity) basket to set inside the large one if you want to use a fine or espresso grind coffee - a great way to discover extra flavor notes.  (8 O'Clock "red bag" on espresso grind tastes much like chocolate.)TheHamilton Beach 49999A FlexBrew Single-Serve Coffeemakeris flexible in another way too.  The stand raises a coffee cup high enough under the spout of the machine that the coffee does not go cold on its way to the cup, as the coffee did in one particular Keurig machine that my daughter has had.  Remove the stand and the machine will accommodate a travel mug.I did find one minor drawback.  The water receptacle is on the small side - confusing because the machine is so tall.  I got around that by putting the water in a different cup than the one I was using to catch the coffee, leaving the lid open and adding the remainder of the water as soon as there was room in the water receptacle.Grandma's $0.02  - TheHamilton Beach 49999A FlexBrew Single-Serve Coffeemakeris great for the occasional cup of coffee without locking you into expensive special coffee delivery systems.  If you're looking for a coffee maker for a college student, just buy a 12-cup model in the first place!Recommended

I don't like it.Really. I don't like it.Having made that perfectly clear, I will say that I have owned previous to this MP3 players made by Sansa, Sony, Microsoft, and Memorex, and this is honestly the worst on of the bunch. If only I'd spent a couple extra dollars.In what ways does this product fail? Let me list them:Low volume - compared to previous MP3 players I have owned.Poor audio quality - again, compared to the previous players.Bad menu layout and controls - the buttons don't always work, and trying to get anywhere is a chore.Inconsistent track sorting - I loaded it up with nearly 8GB of MP3s, and can't even find a few of the albums on anything other than the directory listing. Not under Albums, artists, or genres.Shuffle, isn't so much - I would think that shuffling through the entire 8GB would actually do that, but it seems to play multiple songs from the same album before moving on. Every single time.Inconsistent track sorting - Yeah, I know, I already had this one, but even the songs that do show when browsing through artists - don't always show up under the right artist. Remember, the exact same songs have worked correctly before on three devices from three different manufacturers within the last year.Album art (sometimes it's there, sometimes it's not) - I bought this as a replacement to a Sony player for my four year old. She's not the best reader in the world yet, and depends on the album art to determine where she's at. Not on this player she doesn't. I would guess that 3/4 of the album art doesn't populate for whatever reason.Poor battery life - It seems like it needs to be charged every other day... and it only gets played an average of 1-2 hours a day.Ok, that's enough negative. I could go on, but it's ruining my day thinking about wasting money. Some positives... yes there are a few:It has a sleep timer - again, this is used primarily for my four year old, as a sleep aid. So it's nice to be able to set a 30 minute sleep timer. Of course it's counter intuitive to get there and turn it on (I've got to stop all music playback just to turn on the sleep timer???)It was cheap. Yep, just a few dollars more than the generic no-name brands.It's blue. I like blue.Ummmmmmm, that's about it. Bottom line, when my daughter's Sony Walkman MP3 player died, I thought based on my small bit of research that this would be a fantastic replacement, considering her bare bones needs. Once I loaded it up and tested it out, I was a little ashamed to give it to her.

One of the biggest improvements I've when it comes to hand and wrist pain came from my Microsoft 4000 Ergonomic Keyboard.As such, I figured "well, if they can do the keyboard so well, why not the mouse?"I'd been struggling with a Logitech mouse for a while, so this one seemed like a good try.Don't get me wrong, it'll help...IF you know how to use it. I get lazy and just grab it sometimes...no joke, it hurts WORSE than any other mouse when I do not use it in the manner prescribed by the directions. When I'm holding it correctly, and I keep my elbow at 90 degrees, I can rock this mouse out all day. Because of those requirements, I had to install a pull out on my desk that was lower. I can see how it may be foreign to some, but really it only takes about 20 minutes of using it to forget about the strangeness.Overall, it probably does what it is supposed to do. I purchased this to use camping, at the lake and when traveling. Upon opening the package and allowing it to inflate for several hours I noticed that it was no where near the thickness the description boasts of. The memory foam was crushed and discolored and there was a rip in the seam of the machine washable cover. I called Thermarest and was told that both the air pad and memory foam need 24 to 48 hours to fully inflate the very first time it is used. This is due to the fact that both have been stored rolled up since production and wont retain the fullest potential until they have been stored fully inflated. I was told that after the initial inflation, if it is stored unrolled and inflated, it will inflate to its potential much quicker. I then left it stored unrolled and inflated for a few days. I still do not think its as thick as it says it is. I wouldn't have been so mad about this but before buying this I watched a YouTube video review of the product done by BackcountryEdge (a gear review company). The Dreamtime XL in the video looks so thick and comfy, no where near how mine looked after being left out for days. I tried it out at home for a few nights anyway. I would say its moderately comfortable. Now I am a stocky guy (under 6ft/over 200lbs) and I could feel the hardness of the floor beneath me (especially at the shoulders and hip). I sent it back because of the rip at the seam and considered a replacement but decided this product is definitely not worth this kind of money. It is a 2.5 inch(according to them-I think that's being generous)self inflating air pad and a 1 inch memory foam pad inside a cheaply made cover (not only was there a tear at the seam but all straps were frayed-you could tell this thing would fall apart in no time). For this price, I would expect something better made and more comfortable. For about the same price (or less if you shop smartly)you could buy the 4inch air pad made by Alps Mountaineering, a  memory foam mattress topper and make a cover giving you more than twice the thickness of the Dreamtime XL. All you are purchasing for this much money is the name Thermarest. I'm not saying its horribly uncomfortable, its just not worth the price.

Please note that a large part of my rating is based upon my using other (Magnavox MDR 515H and 535H) DVRs for many years. In comparison to them the Philips loses in several areas.First the good:  I use an antenna and the Philips and Magnavox digital tuners both work very well.  If I understand correctly the Philips is true HD while the Magnavox units upsample. This is not a big deal to me but it may be for some.The Philips can record to an external drive or internal drive.  It does not have a disk player or burner.  Magnavox units cannot record to an external drive but can record to their internal drive or a recordable DVR.  Magnavox units can play a DVD while the Philips units cannot play any disk.I much prefer the user interface of the Magnavox units but it is too hard to describe the differences. I like the display on the Magnavos units.  It has a clock and the units can be turned on, tuned to a channel, and instant recording started without using a TV.  The Philips has no display but it does have a super-bright white power-on light that is blinding to anyone sitting in front of it.  I had to tape a piece of colored plastic over it. Extremely poor design.  Someone was not paying attention.Setup on both the Magnavox and Philips is very easy.My major complaint is the horrible remote for the Philips.  It seems like they sold out advertising space on the remote. The buttons for Netflix and Vudu  are so large and prominently placed it is hard to reach the power button.  It is even harder to use the Play, Pause next track/previous track and FF/FR buttons because they are dwarfed and crowded by the Netflix and Vudu buttons.  I use the control buttons a lot and never use Netflix or Vudu.  I suspect anyone using Netflix or Vudu only needs to hit the button once.  There is no need to make them such a nuisance.I was going to make the Philips my main DVR due to its capacity but changed my mind due to it being a major pain to control (play/stop/FF/FR etc) while watching. This is especially true in a dimly lit room.Finally note that the Philips is much smaller than the Magnavox due to no display and no disk drive.  Each brand has advantages.  Each user will have to decide what they prefer.  I can say I have only had the Philips about two months so I cannot report on longevity while I have had Magnavox units for many years without problems.  Good luck on whatever you choose.

So far so good. I installed it an hour ago and have yet to hear my CPU fan spool up.Four years ago I bought a Dell Studio XPS 435MT, an infamously noisy desktop. That first time I turned it on sounded like a jet was taking off in my house. I replaced the case fan (which was the culprit, per Dell) and the noise level went down considerably. Still, from time to time it would get a bit loud and that was due to the CPU fan, especially when under load.I finally decided to get a new fan, coinciding with an upgrade to SSD. I like that this new fan is considerably bigger than the previous one and the fins feel cooler to the touch (which means they are a better conductor of heat and can thus dissipate heat better). My old one had the only benefit of a really stout metal base with screws that were additionally held down with springs. This Freezer 7 Pro has these really cheap plastic clips with expander inserts (sort of like expanding drywall screw sleeves). Luckily for me (and this may apply to you, so, buyer beware), my motherboard already had metal inserts so that the CPU fan would secure to the motherboard. Well, at first I didn't feel so lucky when I realized the new cooler's base wouldn't attach to the motherboard. The metal insert/sleeve prevented the new fan's plastic clips from being inserted properly. As I was doing this swap along with a Samsung SSD drive install, I happened to have 4 spare screws for mounting hard drives to the chassis. These screws fit perfectly in the metal inserts AND the base of this CPU cooler. I went ahead and secured the base, then mounted the CPU cooler to the base (make sure you orient the base properly so that a) the CPU cooler can be attached to the mount using the two long screws, while b) the fins point toward a case fan that vents to the outside.I have to note that this new fan, despite being intended for LPGA1366 CPUs, has a footprint that is a tad smaller than my CPU's and even that of the previous fan. Let's hope that doesn't come back to bite me.As soon as I turned on the computer, the BIOS complained of a CPU fan failure. I wasn't happy at all. I did confirm that the new fan was spinning so it wasn't like what some other users had experienced (that sometimes led to CPU failures). So I went into the BIOS, made some updates relating to the SSD (boot drive sequence, etc), and restarted the machine. The second time there was no BIOS error relating to the CPU fan and Windows started promptly.Computer upgrades almost never work right off the bat. Anything that can possibly go wrong usually does. I am very satisfied that I was able to readily circumvent the snag I hit with the plastic clips.

Connect your NAS, follow the instructions, then setup your basic software from the CD that comes with your ReadyNAS Duo( RAIDar, and NTI Shadow );amazingly, if not deceptively , easy.I deliberately tried to give this unit a working out on a home network, and found that if you have a fully configured ( and configurable ) Firewall, then you need toset up trust relationships with the firewall.If your Parent PC  ( in the case of the network I have running) is an XP Pro OS, then you will need to start the necessary network services, which is usually a little more advanced than a basic setup procedure.I deliberately pushed this into non-recommended areas, and found that this will run under a secondary PC  running Windows 2000 and does it beautifully, if you mainly want to transfer files ( say, if one machine does one task well, and another machine does a second task well, like when my main PC had its CD burner die during my tests , and I needed a unit with good software and high burn rates with files using high bitrates... all the reasons a network exists).After the basic setup, you register the unit, then you get to advanced mode in the file server.After setup you are forced to change the password, so the idea of good security is there, however the details of a good password are not really stated.Installation in a home network environment places the icons in the sys trays and in the network world  of other PCs on that network( Windows 2000).In some PCs, the network will just show the NAS as available.After this, You can then start any one of many services, FTP, HTTP, STREAMING.Time to put the file server to work !!BitTorrent is brilliant; finally organised legally , it shows all you can rent or buy as well as a massive range of free downloads and its all legal.The client for this seemed annoying, and without the full setup I describe above on a secure network, the downloads fail consistently.This runs counter to what I had thought to be one of thebig selling points in the bittorrent client on the file server, that it could run with the PC shut down ... well, not that I found, since everytime I attempted to start the firmware download client, not a thing happened, and only with the settings as described, and with the PC on could I download with the Server.I tested the streaming of a digital file from a wired part of my home network to a wireless part, and the file streamed beautifully, no wow and flutter, full video consistency, in fact just like the base video file.With all the other services on the File Server, I found no problems.I tested these as much as I could over a 7-12 day period.I made comments on services that I found to be either a problem, or extremely good.The Hard Drive is consistently temperamental.Whilst  I was consistently getting the "Blinking disk" error, the only utility available to me was a check disk and bad sector check done after a reboot of the file server itself when done in the firmware admin mode.I found no way to get to the SATA drive to run any kind of rudimentary utility, which I think is a potentially bad thing for preventative maintenance.The Hard-drive can and does spontaneously reboot, with no option to cancel out of the reboot.Whilst this File Server looks like a mini version of a large scale server, and has many features in the firmware of fully fledged, it also has some of the quirks of a first generation version of a product. There is probably a lot I have yet to learn about this machine, but I put this little server through a lot of tests to see if it has the content.Its part of the way there.

I jumped at the chance to try out the 7-port USB 2.0 hub via the Vine Program, as I wanted to replace the two old USB 1.x four-port hubs that were taking up a lot of real estate on my computer table.Pros:The hub has a very small footprint. In fact, it is very small all the way around, being roughly the same size as the power adapter. It can be used  either in an upright or flat position.I have the usual sorts of peripherals plugged into it:  two printers, scanner, card reader, backup drive, and camera battery charger.  Nothing that I have plugged into the hub draws a lot of power to run, so I have not run into the insufficient power issue outlined in older reviews.  I searched around for an item that needed a full charge to test the charging ability.  I found a very old Kindle that has not been charged in over two years.  I plugged it into the hub, and it charged up just fine.  Please note that the product description states that this hub is not designed to charge tablets or iPads.All of the ports work.  Older reviews indicate that some of the ports failed after a very short time. I have had the hub less than a week, so only time will tell if all of them remain working.Cons:The cord for the power adapter is insanely short!  Amazon, what are you thinking???  Basic is basic, but the thing needs to be usable, for heaven's sake.  Because of the short cord, I was not able to position the hub in a convenient location.  I will have to daisy-chain together a couple of power strips, which is just silly. Some people might find the cable that plugs into the USB port on the back of the computer to be too short also.The hub is "graced" by a red power indicator light that is far too bright.  It reminds me of HAL in '2001, A Space Odyssey.'  Amazon, if you are trying to be economical with your AmazonBasics components, try putting in a wimpier light, and make the power cord longer. It doesn't take much in the way of lumens to simply show that the device is powered.One of the ports seems to be slightly "off," misshapen or otherwise flawed - it resisted being plugged into, so I didn't force it, and simply don't use that particular port.  I would have been really ticked off if I needed all seven ports.Summary:The hub is small, and it works.  The major drawback is the short power cord.If ports start to fail, I will update this review.UPDATE:  January 22, 2014No failures, so far at least, I am hoping that this hub will make it for the long run.

I bought this for my wife, who listens to a lot of podcasts and web streaming. The speaker on herGalaxy Nexusis not optimal for listening in anything other than a quiet room.The speaker is very well built -- it's already been dropped on the tile floor on day one, and is no worse for wear. The size is just right, and its appearance is understated and refined, with the exception of the overly bright blue LEDs that everybody else has mentioned.The sound quality is good, but not great. It's about on par with many clock radios we've owned, which is actually a bit disappointing, considering they usually have a single rear-facing, undersized speaker, versus the Monster's two front firing units and the subwoofer looking thing under the lid.Setup is a big of a pain. There's a slider on-off switch on the rear, and it's the "master" power control. Then there's the push button on/off on the side, which needs to be long-pressed to bring the speaker to life. But for pairing, the power button must be longer long-pressed, but only just after turning the slide to on. So basically, it's not so obvious like with most Bluetooth devices, so it may be good to keep the instructions handy. And I'm still unsure of the reasoning behind two power switches.Speaking of pairing, it only pairs to one device at a time. That's a bit of a disappointment, because now I can't hijack it to use on occasion without the hassle of pairing to my Nexus, then re-pairing to my wife's when she next wants to use it. It seems that even the cheapest Bluetooth speakerphone and audio devices are capable of pairing to at least two devices, so for the money spent, this is a let down.On the second day of owning it, it no longer played audio from my wife's phone, yet phone calls went through OK. Pairing with my phone worked a-ok (phone calls and audio both worked), but re-pairing with my wife's device yielded the same problem. It wasn't until we deleted the speaker from her phone, the paired it again (basically from scratch) that it worked. I don't know if this was a fault of the speaker of the phone, but be aware of this in case you run in to a similar circumstance.The product manual states that this unit supports AVRCP (audio/visual remote control profile). Other Bluetooth devices that support this profile directly control the volume of the source, i.e. a car speakerphone volume + key, when pressed, will cause the volume slider icon to pop up on my phone's screen and reflect the volume change, as if I had pressed the volume + key on my phone. Not so with this device, which does it the old way of maintaining its own volume, while the Bluetooth master volume from the phone is set separately. This isn't a huge deal, but it means balancing the volume settings of two devices when, in principle, either one should do the trick and act as one.The speakerphone seems to function just fine. Audio is relatively clear in both directions, no worse than what I've heard from just about every other hands free Bluetooth speakerphone device.It's not clear on the product page that there's a difference between the two models being sold, other than color. The black model has a total of six buttons: soft power, phone (dial, answer), Volume + and -, and FFWD / RWD. The silver model appears to only have four buttons, probably missing the playback controls.It would have been great if Monster could get on board with the industry trend of micro (not mini) USB ports for charging. It doesn't help that they include the USB cord only, not a complete AC power pack, because we have a bunch of micro USB connections floating around the house from various phones, speakerphones and headsets, any of which are available for charging, and this device relies on the connection standard that the industry moved away from two or three years ago.The 3.5mm audio jack is nice for quickly plugging in non-Bluetooth and non-paired devices, but beware that the onboard volume controls will have no effect over the output flowing through this jack -- all volume adjustments must be made at the device.In summary, the sound is decent for music and talk at low levels -- certainly better than any phone's speaker -- but struggles at louder outputs. Setup and charging could be more user friendly. It's a nice unit, but for the price, I expected just a little more, especially multiple device compatibility.

It's a great monitor for my mac mini.  The only thing I have to compare it to is an Apple monitor. Paired to her macbook, my wife has a 27 inch Apple Cinema Display (which I gave to her after buying it for myself and deciding a month later that it just wasn't for me). The Apple display produces images that look slightly more beautiful than this Asus display, but I'm still happy with my purchase of this Asus for several reasons. Let me explain why:First, you're going to think I'm crazy for saying this if you haven't had experience with a huge monitor, but 27 inches is completely too big if you're at all sensitive to screen brightness.  Every time I get on Safari or open iTunes on the 27 inch, I feel like I'm being blasted with light from the white background on the window.  It's really fatiguing on your eyes after a while. Turning the brightness down isn't a valid solution because it only makes the colors look less accurate since everything just looks grey and washed out.  And if you push the Apple display back on the desk to compensated for this "background whiteness" problem, it makes most words impossible to read since the pixel density of the display is so high and fonts and letters are rendered so tiny as a result.  So ironically, you end up squinting at your huge 27 inch screen because you have it pushed back so far on your desk that you can barely read words.  The command and + button combination became my friend when working under these conditions, which is really ridiculous when you think about it. I have a friend with a discontinued 1080p 24 inch Cinema Display, and that's really a much better size and pixel proportion, so I wish Apple would continue to make a Cinema Display in that size too or at lease a 21.5 inch (which is the size used for the smaller iMac panel) as an alternative.  27 inches looks awesome in the store, but when you get it home and start using it for hours, you realize that it's not really ideal.  You'll probably doubt my advice on that until you experience it for yourself.  A smaller screen size with a pixel presentation that does not make text look tiny is much more ideal.  Apple made a mistake discontinuing the 1080p 24 inch.  For me, I think a 120hz retina 21.5 inch Cinema Display would be a dream come true (assuming that Apple made OSX 120hz-ready at some point).  I'm happy with this 24 inch Asus, and I would even venture to say that it's a bit big for my tastes too.  I think maybe the sweet spot for a comfortable, ergonomic monitor is somewhere around 20-22 inches.Anyway, the second reason I'm happy with this Asus is the price and configurability.  It's way cheaper, obviously, than a Cinema Display.  Of course, that's always nice.  Also, besides the tilt, it has an adjustable height and it can be rotated 90 degrees if you want to view in portrait instead of landscape widescreen.  It seems very well made for the price.The third thing that's nice about this Asus is that it is matte instead of gloss screen.  It's a tradeoff though because I feel that gloss screens can produce more beautiful and accurate images than matte screens, but they do it at the cost of glare.  I forget all about glare until I leave my man cave and walk into my wife's lady cave and notice it on the 27 incher.  This Asus doesn't produce quite as beautiful images as the Apple, but there's no glare.  So if glair is an issue for you, then consider getting a matte screen, but if you mostly view in a dimly lit room without lots of light sources behind you, then getting a gloss screen like the Apple one would be the best idea.Anyway, for what it is, this Asus is a good monitor.  I'm happy enough with it for now until Apple gets around to making a smaller alternative choice in their monitor category.

4.5 starsAfter decades of trying every cooking material there is, and doing A-B tests with all of them, I am absolutely convinced that for taste, quality and ease of cooking, they go in this order: glass, ceramic, stainless steel, cast iron, copper, and everything else such as aluminum and non-stick is to me unacceptable, not only for health but simple taste reasons.Comparing coffee made in this ss french press to my glass presses, I definitely do note a very light metallic edge to the ss coffee. Which is only logical, as coffee is very acidic, and will leach whatever container it is in. No matter what anyone says about steel being completely inert, it is not. Simply leave water in both this and a glass overnight, then pour them into glasses the next morning. I can taste the metal every time. Likewise with the coffee. It's very subtle, but I notice it enough to prefer using the glass press.Aside from that, however, this is a very nice press and at 30 clams, its present price, it's a real deal. It is all steel, even the filter, which is vital as some cheaper presses (and even some costly ones) use a petrochemical screen that not only stains over time but also melts a tiny bit in boiling water. You want a steel screen, and this press has it.It also has a more insulated wall than glass, so this will keep your joe warmer longer...but that also causes the mild leaching I mentioned, and besides, I make one cup at a time because even five minute old coffee is inferior to completely fresh. There's a reason serious espresso cafes in Italy and Vienna etc give you that cup right off the machine in seconds.If you're deeply serious about coffee and won't even consider drinking anything but Blue Mountain or Kona or even Luwak (you crazy freak!), then stick with a glass press with a steel screen. But considering how solid and all-steel this steel press is, and its good basic design, I would price its worth at about 40-50, so 30 seems a true bargain.

My overall impression of the 12-50mm lens is that it's pretty good. Many people give it a low rating, but it depends what you compare it to and your expectations.Most kit lenses for m4/3 and DSLR's are 28-80mm (in 35mm format) affairs, usually made of plastic. Images are usually adequate, but not nearly as sharp as more expensive zoom and prime lenses. Aperture is usually 3.5-5.6 - nothing special at all. Pentax adds weather sealing, Canon has USB focus motor. That's about it.In contrast, this 12-50mm has a great deal of ability:- weather sealing. This is important to me as I hike and take a lot of photos. Areas I hike may be very misty, damp and humid, suddenly rain, be rocky or have both sand and mud (ie- normal outdoors away from the city). It's nice to know I can just hang onto this regardless of conditions.- very stylishly designed. It looks high end. Most kit lenses, and many more expensive lenses do not look as sleek and well made- 24-100mm (in 35mm format) is vastly more useful than 28-80mm. It never ceases to amaze me how much more you can fit in at 24mm, than 28mm. At the very least it is easier to take a selfie and larger groups of people. 100mm is a noticeably greater reach than 80mm.- I have only used kit lenses for DSLR's for Pentax and Canon, but I'd say images from this 12-50mm lens are sharper, and there's no obvious distortion at 24mm. I do not magnify images to 1000% to check so maybe I'm missing something.- Related to sharpness, bokeh is very smooth and creamy. Only primes are better, imho.- Fast focusing.- 3 modes- manual zooming, electronis zooming, macro modes. Takes a bit of practice to work out how to switch between modes. Olympus is one of the more user UNfriendly brands I've come across. But having these options is good, and the electronic zooming means you can produce better videos.- aperture...ok, it's not fast. But then, no kit lens is. In fact, you have to pay hundreds and thousands more for f2.8 lenses. They also weigh 3 to 4 times more too.The main disadvantages are:- cost. Less of an issue now that the EM-10 has come out and the EM-5 price has come down.- length. There are several 28-84mm kit lenses for m4/3 which are between 50-70% shorter in length, making them lighter and easier to carry around.Overall, I feel the 12-50mm is a fine lens, and there is no reason for me to spend money for a smaller lens of reduced range, nor hundreds more for a faster lens which is 3-4 times heavierI bring both this lens and my 14-150mm lens when I travel and often when I hike. The 14-150 has far greater reach which is very useful, but I do notice the 28mm being not as wide as the 24mm.Sorry for being wordy. I like this lens.

I've owned a wide variety of 30-pin Apple cables.  I have never bought an Apple-brand cable, but I've had several that came packaged with my various iPhones, iPods, etc. They've all been pretty good, and lasted years of indelicate treatment before failing.  I've also owned several name-brand third-party cables, from the likes of Belkin, Griffin, etc. Likewise, these have survived a considerable amount of mistreatment (winding them up with tight corners, and stuffing them unceremoniously into a bag to be knocked around all day).  Then I started buying cheap (on par with a 20oz soda) Chinese knock-offs. I figured why pay $10 for a Belkin-class cable when I can get 6-8 DealExtreme specials for the same price? Well, it turns out those bottom-of-the-barrel cables are true crap, and only survive about 1-6 weeks of mistreatment. I've gone through at least a dozen of them, and not one has gone more than two months (on the desktop, not even in bags) before giving me "Charging is not supported" and "Not Charging" errors.So, having been very satisfied with Amazon Basics products in the past, I decided to spring for this pricier option to cure my CCC woes.  I used it in the car to charge my iPhone on the go.  And I was very happy with it... for about six months.  Then it stopped charging my phone. And yes, I did confirm that it was the cable, not the charger.  So, bottom line:Cheap Chinese: .5mo-1mo (sample size: 12)Amazon Basics: 6mo (sample size of one)Name Brand: ~12-18mo (sample size 3)Apple: ~12-36mo (sample size 4)

My old Linksys WRT54GS finally died after maybe 8 years of faithful service so I bought this one.  Here are my simple observations:1. The Cox online automatic setup does not work.  I got a Cox technician on the phone and within 15 minutes was up and running.  The Zoom 5352 is on their approved list.2. This is a combined modem/wifi.  I really like it for that reason.  Really, in this day and age I'm surprised this isn't yet the norm.  It looks nice too.3. Range is very good.  HD Netflix streaming to the living room and far master bedroom is no problem at all.  Buffer load times are faster now.4. My upload speed more than doubled from 5mbs to 12mbs using this new/updated modem.  It probably could go faster but this is the service tier I pay for.  I get 30+ download speed and 15ms ping here.Now for some negatives:5. The power cord is 5' or less.  It can be too short if you have it on a bookshelf.  I had to put my battery UPS on a pedestal in order to reach the shelf the modem is on.  What a stupid thing to cheap out on.  That extra few feet of cord length is very useful if you need it.6. The biggest negative for me is DNS configurability.  If you use an alternate DNS server like Google DNS or OpenDNS...this modem/router will NOT work.  I researched this issue, found no solution. If you've never heard of OpenDNS - check it out.  It's a great way to filter out all the porn/adult web sites automatically that you don't want your 6 yr old getting into.  Another advantage can be better speeds and incredible reliability with no downtime.7. The firmware cannot be flashed.  If you're a DD-WRT fan forget it.  I never bothered flashing my old router but some folks love to tinker.Install tip:Have the S/N and CM MAC # ready when you call the ISP for the install.  No need to flip the unit over - there is an identical sticker right on the box.I give this unit 5 stars for doing it's mission and 4 stars for overall configurability.

I am quite pleased with this product; I did find a few flaws in the design, though.When I assembled it to my Nikon D60, there was a noticeable (about 1/8") gap between the battery pack and the bottom of the camera on the battery side. I removed it and examined the battery pack, and discovered that there were two 3/16" plastic nibs that were preventing it from seating all the way. It did function properly in this configuration, it was just aesthetically whack.After measuring the camera's battery compartment to make sure that it would fit all the way in if given a chance, I decided to fix the problem. I took a micro Phillips screwdriver and detached the "tower" from the top of the pack, then trimmed off the nibs (I used a jeweler's nipper and an Xacto knife). After replacing the 4 tiny screws and re-attaching the battery pack to my camera body, the fit was perfect. The product looks great, and the finish is decent (it's splatter painted, so no idea how well it will hold up after a lot of use) - it's not a spot-on perfect match for the Nikon's body, but I think I'm the only one likely to notice.The second issue: the instructions state that you can store the camera's battery cover (which must be removed in order to install the product) in a compartment in the base - no you can't, it doesn't fit. Maybe a D-40 cover, but the D60 cover definitely does not fit, so I have to make some previsions to keep up with it.Favorite feature: a second battery housing allows you to insert and power the camera with AA batteries. Sweet.All in all, I'd buy it again and recommend it to a friend that is comfortable tweaking plastic. I probably would NOT recommend it to someone like my mom who would prefer things to be perfect out of the box.

I haven't used the Big Boss fryer for steaming or sauteeing, the Big Boss comes with a cookbook that includes several 'non fried' foods, such as, Italian Sausage with Peppers and Apple Turnovers, so I can't really comment on the efficacy of using this product as an oven or a steamer, yet.So I will just tell you what I know about the Fryer from the four items I have cooked in it.Frozen, breaded mushrooms - I didn't care for them, but I suspect they would have been chewy and flavorless even if I'd deep fried them.Sweet Potato Fries - Oh my fur and whiskers, these were tasty.  Just the right amount of crispy fried foodness, but you have to be super careful, some of the fries burnt and some were barely browned, might be worth it to give the fries a stir halfway through cooking (which was three minutes longer than I'd planned for).  Best of all, they didn't stick to the tray and were crispy all the way around, instead of being soggy where the fries come in contact with a cookie sheet like they usually were.Taquitos - These were much better than I'd hoped for ('specially considering I bought them almost two months ago).  The tortilla took on a fresh crunchy texture, much better than when I bake them (they kinda taste like tortilla flavored dirt then.) I think it is the all around cooking that seals in the flavor.Fried pickles - These were not great.  I followed a pretty standard recipe (homemade of course) and thus, never prefried and froze the pickles.  While the pickle was tasty, the breading (a three step traditional way of making breading, first into seasoned flour, then submersed in egg dip, then rolled into breadcrumbs for the final coating, the breading didn't really stick or brown.So I threw away my first tiny batch of pickles and started a second batch, this time I covered each pickle with a fine mist of oil after finishing the three step breading.  While this batch turned out an appetizingly golden brown color, an improvement, aesthetically speaking, they were still not right.  The breading fell off as soon as you bit into a pickle, giant shards of crunchy, crackerlike breading fell onto my plate, a crisp reminder of the pickle failure I was experiencing (don't mean to be so melodramatic, I just really, really wanted a fried pickle). So disappointing.  I think if the pickle was prefried, in a deep fryer, the results would be much better, more edible anyways.Now for my thoughts on the device itself;1.  It's big.  Really, really big.  The Big Boss fryer is bigger than my crock pot, bigger than my food processor and much bigger than my kitchen Aid toaster.2.  It is not hard to put together, so you won't have worry about last minute setups being a pain, but it  definitely is not something you'd set up to make a few fries to go with your lunch.3.  But for all its parts (more than my crock pot; crockery pot with lid and heating element pot thingamajig. it was easy to clean.  Unlike my crockpot, the inside of the main cooking chamber is clear glass, making it easy to see whatever food stains might be there.  It also seemed easier to scrap up all those baked on bits of food.5.  It lights up your kitchen like that scene in E.T., the part where the spaceship comes back for E.T., picks him up and then lifts off, lighting the dark, dense forest with an alien glow.  There is so much light, that I turned off the overhead and waited for the timer to dink.All in all this was a surprisingly useful kitchen appliance, but not one I'd reccommend for everyday use.

The Flip MinoHD is the kind of camera you either love or hate. If you're a videophile and analyze specs and features then this camera isn't for you. Using the Flip MinoHD reminded me of why I was skeptical about buying an iPhone when Apple first launched it and why I ultimately bought one and why I feel the iPhone is a fantastic device despite all of it's limitations. Now on to the Flip...There's not much in the box (camera, soft case, strap), the battery can't be changed, and the memory can't be expanded. There's no CD included (the software is on the device) and no cables are included (or needed for most users). There are almost no settings to play with: set the date, time, beeps on/off, recording light on/off and you're ready to go. The ergonomics are ok. It's tough to make a small device easy to hold and use and the display is small but that's to be expected of such a tiny package.For many products this kind of simplicity would suggest that the manufacturer tried to cut costs (e.g. Apple not including an AC Adapter with iPods). In the case of the Flip the message I heard was clearly different: you don't need any of these things. Since there's not much fiddling to do with settings you're left with actually using it!I tried it outdoors and indoors and took videos of the kids and of scenery. It perform wells in all lighting conditions including low light. Based on on my experience low light is the weak point for the HD Video Mode in my Panasonic P&S; as well as in the mini-DV HD Cameras that I own. The Flip outperforms them all. The audio isn't bad at all and the picture quality is better than anything I've seen in a P&S; and is very comparable to what I get with my Canon mini-DV HD Camera.Overall it's easy to pocket and a pleasure to use for making small video clips.

I'm torn in reviewing the Sony MDRHW700DS headphones.  If I had to boil my experience down to one sentence it would be that this is an incredible-sounding headset burdened by complications in the setup and the use that ultimately limits it to a very narrow audience of ideal users.  Simply put, if you determine that you need headphones enough to bear with the prospect of completely redesignining your home theatre wiring and control scheme, then the sound payoff for the MDRHW700DS is more than adequate. However, given that high initial price in terms of complexity (and actually dollars), I wonder how many people will actually fit that bill.If you're familiar with wireless headsets for gaming consoles, the Sony starts with a similar premise:  a processor/transmitter box that connects to your system (the sound source) and then sends sound to the wireless headset. However, the Sony processor pretty much requires that it become the HDMI hub for all sources (it has four HDMI ports), supplanting that role from your A/V receiver.  For myself - and most out there - the A/V receiver is the undisputed king of signal collection and distribution and I don't want to upset that balance.  I also don't want to reprogram my universal remote controlIf you're familiar with wireless headsets for gaming consoles, the Sony starts with a similar premise:  a processor/transmitter box that connects to your system (the sound source) and then sends sound to the wireless headset. However, the Sony processor pretty much requires that it become the HDMI hub for all sources (it has four HDMI ports), supplanting that role from your A/V receiver.  For myself - and most out there - the A/V receiver is the undisputed king of signal collection and distribution and I don't want to upset that balance.  I also don't want to reprogram my universal remote control.  I don’t want to make room on my power conditioner for another device to plug in (particularly with a large, odd-shaped plug.  Finally, I don’t want to purchase additional HDMI cables (the MDRHW700DS comes with none) in order to support all of this change/disruption.While testing the headset, I didn’t notice any apparent HDMI degradation due to the processor box, but I believe that any additional links in the signal chain (even a digital one) can’t be good.  And again, my overarching concern is that the processor is an unnecessarily obtrusive additional component in a typical home theatre setup.  This leaves two main use cases that I could think of for this headset:1. People who live in apartments and/or have roommates/family members whom they don’t want to disturb while watching TV and therefore need to have some way to isolate sound from others around them2. People who use a laptop as their sole source for watching content.In either case, the MDRHW700DS has a price point high enough to likely scare away most buyers, particularly given some of the other notable head-scratchers in the overall offering, e.g. lack of included stand or cables, the plastic build quality, etc.In use, the headset really shines.  Its sound it absolutely top notch in all regards – a dynamic range that goes from sharp highs to immensely powerful bass; rock-solid wireless throughput with no dropouts that I encountered; separation between channels that really is amazing for something resting directly on your ears.  The headset cups are comfortable and the sizing adjusts to a wide array of head sizes.  The headset is light enough to support lengthy periods of use (the relatively brief battery life will limit you there well before).It’s a shame that Sony didn’t give more thought to the overall design of this product and particularly in how it would integrate easily into the existing system of a user considering a headset in its price range.  The exceptional sound quality of the headset should have been the hard part, but they really nailed that and instead stumbled on the easy part of the transmitter/processor design.  For those people willing to (or who need to) put up with the disruption to their existing design, the sound is more than good enough to recommend the MDRHW700DS; however, that is a decision that should be carefully evaluated before proceeding with the purchase.

I have a couple of different ways I can tomatoes - either quartered in juice (hot pack) or crushed in juice (hot pack). But skinning, coring, and prepping the tomatoes for packing takes awhile, and sometimes, I would look at my bowls full of tomatoes and think, ugh. Then I saw an Internet tutorial from someone who used this food strainer to make tomato sauce and I thought, aha. Maybe this would make processing bushels of tomatoes a little faster.Setting up the strainer takes very little time and learning how to use it takes even less. Once the machine is assembled, you take washed, quartered, unpeeled tomatoes and put them into the hopper and then crank them through the strainer. The strainer separates out all the skins, seeds, cores, etc. What comes out of the strainer is an extremely smooth, seed-free, thin tomato puree, and out the other side comes a nearly dry mash of the "leavings." I take the puree and simmer it down into a thicker sauce, which I can in quarts. I take the "leavings" and put them in the compost pile.The worst part of using the strainer is cleaning it, which takes some work. The instructions say not to put parts in the dishwasher, but I don't see much harm in putting the plastic parts through, on the top rack. Cleaning the metal cone filter takes some effort and I wish they included a stiff conical brush to assist with this. Also, the small steel spring that you need to make the strainer work is easy to lose - we've already lost one, and had to order a replacement.All in all, though, this is a GREAT tool and makes processing tomatoes into cannable product fast and easy. I LOVE not having to skin tomatoes, my least favorite task of canning them. I got the salsa screen as well, and while the screen allows for a few more seeds to get through than I would like, it produces a nice, chunky puree that is great for both fresh tomato sauce and for salsa.If you have a lot of tomatoes to can, I highly recommend this item. I plan to put it to use making applesauce from baked apples later this year - apparently you can core and bake the apples and then toss them into the strainer almost whole, which will be a big improvement over the multiple hours of cooking down my current recipe requires.

First the good:I wanted a bluetooth headset that I could use with my phone for music and making calls. This unit does that very well. The music reproduction is strong in the midranges, but tinny in the treble and muffled in the bass. Turning on the SRS function improved the sound significantly.  No complaints from callers about hearing my voice, and I could hear them very clearly. With my droid phone I was able to control volume easily. For music playback you have track skip capability right from the headset. Using the android vlingo voice app I had full voice control of my phone. I REALLY wanted to like this headset. But....Now the not so good:The headset is on the small side of compact. The ear cups are not suited well for adult sized ears and were too tight. The headband fully extended was still very tight on my slightly larger than normal sized head. The unit has a lot of cheap feeling plastic in its makeup, and the ear cups are just not comfortable for me to wear.The noise cancelling function is very important to me since I spend too much time on airlines on a weekly basis. I found the noise cancelling characteristics of this headset to be very very weak. Firstly because the headset fits so tight, some outside noise is actually AMPLIFIED as it resonates through the body of the headset itself.  Secondly the level of active noise cancellation is very low compared to other sets I have used. Active noise cancellation is supposed to blank out external noises that are constant and steady. It works best on low frequency noises. This headset only eliminated a small amount of the very low frequency noises. With the amplification of the non-constant outside noises (conversations, television audio, etc.) wearing the headset is actually noisier than having it off.I have just spent a week airlining around the country using a Nokia BH-905i headset. The Nokia headset is everything that the Sennheiser MM550 was supposed to be but is not.  The Nokia sits on the ear instead of around the ear. The Nokia is not too tight and very comfortable. Phone calls are easily heard and callers have no complaints.  The music reproduction is very good. But the active noise cancellation function is far and away better than the Sennheiser.  Flip the switch and most external noise (of a constant nature) is practically erased.  The price point for Nokia is around $189 and ( in contrast to the Sennheiser)  it is worth every penny.For $499 the Sennheiser MM550 headset is a complete disappointment. If it retailed for $200 - well that would still be too much to pay for what you get.  There aren't many headsets out there with both Active Noise Cancellation and Bluetooth functions. I have only tried this one and the Nokia. The Nokia wins by a mile and this one is going back to Amazon.

I love doing product reviews. I like to think, while writing one, that I am actually talking to someone, telling them about the product in question. And as a reviewer, there are some companies whose products I love to review. Hewlett-Packard (HP) is one such company. I have had a long and happy relationship with every HP product I have used and reviewed over the last decade. So it saddens me when, after testing the HP Photosmart 435 digital camera, it came time to write this review.The Photosmart 435 is a 3.34MP digital camera that you can also use to take small Quick-Time movies with. While not a large camera, the Photosmart 435 is by no means tiny. It fits easily in a purse, but not in the pocket of your pants. (Unless you are wearing cargo pants.)The camera is not stylish, but rather plain and boxy. This works for me, as I don't always want to call attention to my camera. It does not look expensive, and at $149 (US) it is not. If anything, the design reminds me of a 110 Film camera I owned in my teenage years. It has that feel in my hands, very familiar.Operation is simple. Slide the lens cover, which doubles as the on/off switch, and take a picture. There are a variety of options, from picture quality, shutter speed, flash, red-eye flash, zoom, and most of the other features every digital camera sports. So far so good.The Photosmart 435 has 3.34MP resolution at its highest quality setting. As I already own a 3.1MP camera (The Kodak DX3900) I had an idea what to expect in image quality. In fact, I was expecting somewhat better looking photos with the Photosmart 435, being a higher resolution camera. I was sorely mistaken. The image quality, most times, is decent to good. However, the quality of the pictures is not at all consistent. I found that out of ten pictures taken indoors under normal lighting conditions, eight of the ten photos would be of decent quality, while the other two would be very poor. I don't know why the image quality is so unpredictable with this camera, but after extensive testing, I would personally not use this camera.Also like most digital cameras, the Photosmart 435 has an image display viewfinder. The 1.5-inch LCD is used to set options, review pictures or movies, and can be used instead of the optical viewfinder. For those who hate looking through the tiny optical viewfinder when taking pictures, the image display viewfinder is a much better choice.The problem here is the quality of the Photosmart 435's 1.5-inch LCD display. It is far and away the worse I have ever used. In live mode, the display is a green and blurry mess, all but unusable. In picture review mode, it is somewhat better, but still far and away sub-par to any other digital camera I have used in the past.One of the biggest disadvantages is the zoom. There is no optical zoom on the Photosmart 435, but rather digital. A digital zoom is always sub-par than a optical zoom, and that is true here as well. The 5X Digital zoom works as advertised, but any picture zoomed became pixilated and not at all sharp. After playing with the various settings, I found that if I had to zoom up on an object with the Photosmart 435, it simply was not worth taking the picture.Taking photos of objects in motion, even a slow walking cat, really showed the Photosmart 435's shortfall. After taking pictures of a cat in both normal and action shutter speed mode, the pictures were blurry and unusable.The big test, however, came when I gave the camera to our eight-year-old daughter, Brittaney, and told her to take pictures around the yard of anything she wanted to. The conditions were very cold, around thirty degrees and frosty, but the sun was very bright and the fall colors look beautiful. Brittaney took a total of 17 pictures. One of the first problems I noticed was that every other picture had a nice close-up of a finger. Because the lens on the Photosmart 435 is receded, it is very easy to block the lens with your hand while taking a picture. Camera's that have a lens housing that sticks out some, extends from the camera body itself, usually prevents this. The pictures she took, about ten, that was unobstructed by a finger, came out blurry or the camera had too much light. Different setting made no difference.The Photosmart 435 does come with 16MB of internal memory, so you will not have to run out and buy extra storage. However, today, 16MB will quickly prove too small. It is nice, though, that the 16MB is internal, not a card that you will toss out when you upgrade to a 256MB memory card. This is great if, by chance, you fill your memory card up and still need to take a few pictures. I wish more digital camera's would have internal, built-in memory. Unfortunately, you can use one storage device at a time. If you have a memory card installed, the internal storage will not work. The Photosmart 435 takes the smaller SD / MMC Memory cards, not Compact Flash.The Photosmart 435 ships with its own software solution, HP Director, which you can use to store and transfer pictures. While the software does work fine, I preferred using iPhoto. The Photosmart 435 works perfectly well with iPhoto, as expected. But if you use the Photosmart 435 to take video with, you will need to use the HP Director software to capture that file from the camera, as iPhoto will not work. Also, the HP software does not find the Photosmart 435 when running Mac OS X 10.3 (Panther) but does under 10.2. If you do buy this camera, look for an update to their software if you are running 10.3. As I type of this review, there is no update for the HP software. In fact, I have not seen anything on the HP website that indicated you can download updates. The only option I have found is to order a CD-ROM.The video capture feature is more gimmick than anything. The clips are small, grainy, and not worth using to record your important memories with. But it is fun! My kids liked the ability to capture video and audio using the Photosmart 435. I have less worry letting them practice being the next Spielberg with this camera than I do turning over my Canon Camcorder to them. All the video recorded can be used in iMovie, so this is a neat and fun way to let kids learn the basics of shooting video and editing in iMovie.Unfortunately, the Photosmart 435 is a sub-par digital camera. The price, at US $149, makes it inexpensive. Simply reading the specifications in its documentation would sounds like a great deal: 3.34MP, internal 16MB of memory, able to capture video and audio, a 1.5-inch LCD, the ability to use an optional dock, and an optional AC adapter, and more. The reality is that the Photosmart 435 has horrible power consumption (I used three sets of batteries in one week of testing, a total of around 100 pictures!) sub-par picture quality, and a near-useless LCD display.I am disappointed with the Photosmart 435. I expect much better from HP. I am hoping that the next HP camera we review will better meet my expectations of quality HP products. The Photosmart 435 does not feel or operate at the expected quality of an HP product.MyMac Rating: 2 out of 5Tim Robertson

The first MP3 CD players were picky about what discs they would play and lacked any features beyond  bare-bones playback. But these products have matured quickly, and after seeing Sonicblue's Rio Volt, we're  ready to say that MP3 CD players have arrived. Aside from an awkward carrying case, we were hard-pressed to  find anything wrong with this player. Best of breed To put this device through its paces, we burned a number of  test CDs, which included MP3s and WMA files with a wide range of bit rates. We used CD-Rs, CD-RWs, discs  with everything in one root directory, discs with songs organized in folders, and a number of different burning  preferences within the included Easy CD Creator Standard 4 (for PC) and SoundJam (for Macintosh) software  packages. Much to our surprise, the Rio Volt handled every disc that we threw at it with aplomb. It's also only  the second MP3 CD player we've seen that reads ID3 tags (the Pine Technology D'music SM-200C being the  first). Without ID3 tags, you have to plod through 150 songs on each CD using only track numbers as a guide, so  we consider them a necessity. It's also the only such player to play WMA files as well as MP3s and audio CDs.  But there were many other reasons to be impressed by this newcomer. The +10 button, which lets you jump  ahead ten songs, makes navigating more than a hundred songs much easier. You can also group your songs in  folders, since the Volt lets you navigate within directories, unlike the other players that we've seen. A Shuffle  mode lets you skip around between all the songs on the CD-R, while the A-B mode is useful for looping any  section of audio. We were as impressed by the player's form as we were by its function: The understated,  rounded design is starkly modern compared to those of other portable MP3 CD players, which often look like  prototypes. Skip the skipping The Volt collects 120 seconds of audio from MP3/WMA discs and stores the sound  for playback in a flash-memory buffer. When playing back standard audio CDs, you can choose between 10 and  40 seconds of antiskip protection (40 seconds consumes more power). While walking around with the device in  a bag, we encountered an occasional delay when fast-forwarding between songs on an MP3/WMA CD.  However, once the music started playing, skipping was not a problem. If we can single out one problem with the  Volt, it would have to be the carrying case, which must be threaded through your belt if you want to attach it to  your hip. (The player itself doesn't have a belt clip.) While the player is in the case, you can't tell which song is  playing or whether the player is on or off, since there's no display on the remote control. But at $..., the Rio Volt  has to be one of the best portable audio values around. Unless you really need a very small, light MP3 player for  exercise or travel, multiformat CD players such as this one are the way to go, since they're cheaper and hold  many more songs on a single CD. I have the 'Platinum' round version of this but I would imagine it's the same since it also lists 15 functions. I don't even know if these are still being made because I think mine had been sitting around for sometime, meaning the batteries were too weak to work right. After installation, it would cut-out a lot, so I replaced 'both' batteries with known fresh ones, and it then seemed to work okay.But it was only after screwing around with it for hours. Be forewarned, making sure you have fresh batteries for both the speedometer and sensor is only half the battle. The sensor has to be mounted so it is nearly touching the magnet, the magnet has to located near the 'exact' part of the sensor that reads the magnet (and it's not the middle of the sensor), and the sensor has to be as close as possible to the speedometer unit but still mounted on the fork in a way that's it's as close to the magnet as possible, too. IOW, you can't have the sensor mounted high up on the fork (even though that gets it close to the speedometer) because having the sensor high on the fork takes it too far away from the spoke where the magnet is mounted.Because of sensor/magnet mounting, the wheel size adjustment leaves a lot to be desired. I had to play with it for hours, constantly readjusting the wheel setting, until I finally got it to where it's reasonably accurate for where the sensor/magnet have to be mounted to get the speedometer to read. Although it defaults to '2174' for 700c tires, because of where the sensor has to be mounted on the fork, I had to keep resetting it with different values and ended up using '2055' as being as close as I could get it to match the distance traveled. Essentially, you have to use the 'distance' measurement and keep fiddling with it until the distance on the speedometer matches what you know was how far the bike had traveled.In short, I think I'd try something else for a wireless bike speedometer. Better still, I'd go with a wired unit, and one that was from a different (i.e., better) brand, too (and not a cheap Schwinn speedometer, either, which I think are just as bad). I have wired Sigma and Cateye speedometers on other bikes, and they weren't half the trouble setting up as the Bell wireless.

The neat thing about this roller is that some of the most common moves are imprinted on a sleeve that has been fitted over the roller.  However, once you have exhausted these moves,  the internet has many sites with videos. Try bodyspex.com and youtube for starters. It wasn't applied in the neatest way.  It hangs off a bit at the ends and after rolling around on it, these ends are a bit floppy.  I haven't had the sleeve come off, but it would have looked a touch more attractive had the ends been trimmed.Again, if you are new to foam rolling, please give it a go. It may not cure all that ails you but it may be a good start to treating pain and tightness on your own. I've seen people with tight IT bands and tight hip flexors use a foam roller and feel like new people after ONE rolling session.

It would be even more awesome if it allowed more than one block (for example, you can set it to turn on at 8am and off and 10pm, but you can't set it to be on from 6am to 8am, and then 6pm to 10pm, so that you have pictures before work and after work, but the frame isn't on while you're out and while you're asleep).You can also upload pictures directly from a memory card/stick to the frame, but here you get back to the utterly horrific frame UI. (Did i mention that you have to type in your wireless router password every time it connects, but the on-screen keyboard is alphabetic instead of qwerty? If you're not a computer user, you're not going to be connecting to a router, and if you are a computer user, you'll find it nigh on impossible to type on an abcde keyboard.)If you want the frame to just play a slideshow of the pictures on the memory device, great, because that's what it'll do without asking. If you want to upload the pictures onto the frame, that requires jumping through flaming hoops. Once you can even decrypt the pictograms that serve as buttons (no helper text, that would make it too easy), you get the option to upload the current picture or all pictures on the memory device. Again, allowing the user to select a subset would be just too easy, or too useful.Once you finally slog through the set-up, the picture quality is pretty good. The default brightness is perfect, the colors are true, and it just plain looks good....until it transitions to the next picture. The website gives you a bunch of pre-set options for how long pictures should display, but you can't independently select how the photos transition. If you want the pictures up for 3 seconds, it can do a wipe transition, but at 30 seconds your only option is fade. Which would be fine, except the fade is more of a sickly-flicker.And, lastly, if you upload a portrait-oriented picture, it just shows it with big black rectangles on the sides. There's no (apparent) way to either tell it to fill the frame, or to select which part of the picture to show.So... if you can make it through the set-up, and don't mind the flicker between pictures, and have only landscape-oriented photos, you'll love this frame. Oh, and don't mind that there's no battery option, so it always has to be plugged in.(Edited to add: i had no compatibility issues with my MacBook. All the troubles i had were entirely within the kodak frame's UI or product presets.)

As a lover of classical music and jazz who travels a lot, I wanted a pair of high-quality headphones that would not break the bank. Sure, one can find audiophile headphones with fantastic specs that sell for thousands, but I could only manage a few hundred. The AKG K 701 is one of the most highly rated headphones in that price range, so I bought a pair. I am extremely happy with the sound quality. The first time I listened to something through these headphones, namely Collin Walcott's albumCloud Dance, I was gobsmacked by the subtle sound of fingers moving over strings, a detail that I had never before heard in headphones. While that might not be a specifically musical pleasure, the capability to offer that level of detail does endow the music you hear with more life, more richness, more body and other effusive adjectives.The complain I have with the headphones is not the sound quality per se, but the construction. These are extremely bulky headphones, more than I could guess from the photo of the product here, and they take up a huge amount of space in one's luggage. They are also of a very open design, doing nothing to block out ambient noise. Now, I didn't intend to walk down the street with these, but even within the privacy of a hotel room, if there is a trafficked street nearby (or even loud crickets), even that amount of noise will shatter your ability to appreciate the music.Thus the AKG K 701 is a flawed product for what I would imagine are a significant portion of headphone buyers: those who want to want to hear music away from their home, where they presumably own a decent stereo system with speakers. Consequently, the only demographic that will be entirely satisifed with these headphones are those who live in a block of flats (which must necessarily be a very quiet one) and don't want to disturb neighbours who would protest at the noise made by a speaker setup.

This allows me to prep 200 rounds at a time, before I move on to seating the bullets for 200.  These took a bit to get used to (compared to the thinner universal trays), but now are the only ones I use, and will probably buy a few more.For someone loading with a single stage press, they are an indespensible item to have, and you can't have too many.

Iron is an element so all pure iron is the same. However, not all iron pans are the same. They vary by weight (mass) and how that weight is distributed.Greater mass means it needs more heat to heat up, and will retain the heat longer. My expensive Koblenz enamel-glad iron Dutch oven has thin walls so even though it can stand high temperatures, it doesn't retain heat for very long.I decided to compare this T-fal skilled with my 12" skillet by the brand LodgeLodge L10SK3ASHH41B Pre-Seasoned Cast Iron Skillet with Red Silicone Hot Handle Holder, 12-Inch.Weight:T-fal(this product) is heavier at 8 lb 5 oz. Lodge, the other product, weighs 7 lb 15.25 ozThe two skillets'dimensions are similar except for the handle length and surface texture. At 5", the Lodge's handle is shorter than the T-fal's by 2.5 inches. A shorter handle makes the pan easier to handle (less leverage). Surface texture might be IMPORTANT because it is likely to affect how non-stick the pan is. Both were 'pre-seasoned' but it seems intuitive that the smoother one would be more 'non-stick.' Maybe how well-seasoned the surface is, makes a bigger difference than the texture?Aluminum pans, even with copper bottoms, don't heat up as hot as iron, don't retain the heat as well as iron, can't be used in the oven over 400 degrees (e.g. braising meat) and the food tastes not as good to me as when cooked in cast iron.Cast iron is so heavy that I cannot carry it with one hand, I must use the helper handle. It can scratch the countertop, glass or ceramic cooking surface, sink, cabinet shelf (I put it on a paper towel so that any moisture that might remain in the groove on the bottom of the pan can be absorbed). Iron needs more care than other metals. After every washing, I dry all surfaces then spray with veggie oil, then wipe to distribute the oil evenly. It rusts if left wet even for only a few hours. I think the food tastes better so it's worth the trouble.Astronomy fun fact 1: Once a star starts to make iron, it's the river of no return to death. Point to ponder: Does cooking with cast iron pots put iron in the food in a form that our bodies can absorb?

This drive is fast, quiet and has a very generous cache.  Unfortunately the reliability of the ST31000528AS (at least of the drive I got) leaves something to be desired.  After 4 days it developed its first error as indicated by a "1" for Current_Pending_Sector.  This is a real pain because this pending reallocatable sector won't be reallocated till something writes to the sector.  The only way I know to do that is to move all the data off the drive and then zap the drive by either writing zero's across the raw partition or by using the security erase to do the same thing.  I've done this a couple of times now and after 179 days the drive has 17 reallocated sectors and has also starting making clicking noises once per second.  Back it goes to Seagate for a swap.  This isn't a good deal because they end up sending one a refurb in exchange.  It is a bit annoying that one pays top dollar for a new drive and one ends up with a refurb after paying for an extra shipping and digging up a Seagate approved mailing container.

Although I use the regular chopper and the grater blade most (the latter's indispensable for making cole slaw although it's a pain when food gets caught between the blade and the feeder), the slicing discs are great for French fried potatoes, etc. Still, it's a myth to think you can use a food processor to cut up or prepare every and any food. I figured they would sound even better with my system the way I had it adjusted. Boy was I disappointed. I have the Pioneer VSX-1020 AV receiver that puts out 80 watts plus per channel. I hooked them up and played them about 6 hours at a medium to low volume setting. I noticed the upper mids to highs were very clear but the lower mid range was almost non-existent. I have a sub that was delivering the very low parts of the music but there was a gap at the lower mid range. With the sub off they sounded like small bookshelf speakers. I thought they might sound better after a few more hours of listening but the sound wasn't getting any better. I bought some better quality speaker wire and bi-amped them hoping for an improvement but there was little if any change. I tried making adjustment on the receiver but I could not get them to sound like what I thought a speaker of that size and reputation should sound or the way they sounded in the store. I hooked my old cheap Sony speakers back up and they sounded better to my taste so I returned them. A week later I go into another store with the same speakers hooked up and they sound great, lots of bass. For some reason those speakers do not perform well on my system or maybe I didn't break them in long enough or I had a setting wrong. Real bummer.

Digital camera-wise, I started with a Fuji S304 seven years ago after a couple years with a DSL camera Canon 50E. In 2005 I moved ahead with a DSLR, Fuji S2 Pro, probably because of good exprience with the Fuji colors(espeically skin tone). Since then, a number of DSLRs obtained from ebay have came and went, including Canon D30, Rebel XT, Nikon D100, D1H, D50, D40, D80, D300...You know, the gear fever for most photogs.My purchase of a Fuji F40fd is actually an upgrade from a F20 I got a year ago. I use them as a backup that always stay in my pocket, coming handy when I see an interesting scene in the streets, but not so big a deal to take out my DSLR in my backpack. But thank goodness, it's these "backup" little cams that helped me record most of the candit street shots in the everything-can-happen New York City.You'll have a better idea what a Fuji F40fd performans if I compare it to other cameras I've used.Warning: Don't compare it to any DSLR, the small CCD can never be on par with its big brothers. A F40's ISO 400 is only close to a Nikon D40's iso1600. Also, don't expect much from a lens small like the pocket cameras', the worst DSLR lens (including Sigma's or Tamron's) is much better than a point-and-shoot's.Compared with its earlier version, F20, the F40 has advanced in everything but iso performance.1. thinner body. Now it really feels like a pocket cam, as the F20 is still a little bit too thick.2. Larger and better LCD. I don't want to talk about numbers, but the F40 has a larger LCD. And most importantly, the number of pixels is much more than the F20's, and the view angle is much wider. Result, no more low-definition picture like that on a F20, and you can chimp from all angles now.3. Faster response in starting, focusing and reviewing pictures. You just feel it's a lighter and swifter camera.4. At last, the cons. ISO performance is a full stop lower than F20. I tested them side by side with the same settings, and the F40 with more mega-pixels (which I hate, I don't need that many pixels crammed into such a small CCD) just showed more grains and noises. F40's iso 800 is close to F20's iso 1600. This is the biggest disppointment for me, because at first I was exited to see F40 be equipped with Auto ISO 800 and 1600 (F20 only has Auto iso limit on either 400 or 1600, missing the 800 step that I consider the best compromising spot between speed and picture quality)Anyway, though F40 is not as good as F20 in ISO, it's still better than many cameras of other brands, including Canon and Nikon. My friends' Canon SD870 and SD1000 show worse noises on high iso.Conclusion: good colors consistent of Fuji taste, relatively good iso, an affordable foolproof pocket camera for candit shots. But if you are serious with photography, try any entry-level DSLR of Canon, Nikon, Olympus or Sony, you'll see a difference wider than from heaven to earth.
