This is a well-assembled and high-quality product as far as cables go, typical of a Cables Unlimited product, but it was useless and will likely be useless to you.  I have a two-monitor setup on my PC and wanted to duplicate the output of one my monitors to an LCD HDTV.  The product comes with no real instructions, no support whatsoever, and the manufacturer hasn't bothered to tell people about the many limitations of this product. The result for me was many frustrating hours trying to get it to work. I have decided to return this product and purchase a powered DVI splitter from Monoprice.If you are even considering this product, here are some things you should know:1) The product will only work for splitting a DVI signal from a "Dual-Link" DVI port. What that means is that if you're using it to split the output of a DVI port on your PC, for example, your PC's video card must output Dual-Link DVI through that port. Now Dual-Link doesn't mean that your card has two DVI ports. It is a special output mode for DVI digital signals where the video signal is sent through two sets of pins on your DVI cable.  This passive (non-powered) splitter essentially relies on the redundant signal transmitted through the second set of pins to be able to output the same signal to two displays.Many video cards only output Single-Link DVI, not Dual-Link, and it is not always easy to find out if your video card supports Dual-Link DVI. Some cards claim "Dual-Link DVI," but they're mistakenly referring to the fact that the card has two DVI ports. Finding out whether your video card supports true "Dual-Link" DVI is a challenging task, trust me, especially if your video card is a couple of years old. I ended up replacing my nVidia video card with an ATI card to gain true Dual-Link DVI support, but it still didn't work for the reasons explained in (3) below.2) This supports only DVI-D, meaning it works only with digital devices. The DVI standard can support analog outputs (to a VGA-type device), but that doesn't work for this device.3) Even if you get a true Dual-Link DVI-D output through your video card, it still may not work. This is because your PC may not be able to deal with the fact that you have two devices connected through one DVI port. When you plug something into your PC's video card, the computer tries to figure out what type of device it is talking to so it can determine the available resolutions, refresh rate, etc., for that device. On my system, this identification step fails when I have the splitter plugged in, presumably because the computer can't figure out what the device actually is, so it determines that nothing is there. (The only way to get it to work on my computer is to plug in just the monitor without the splitter and then hot-swap the splitter, which fools the video card into skipping the identification step so it thinks it's still talking to just the monitor.)The mere existence of this product is misleading in that it suggests that splitting a DVI video signal across two displays is simple and straightforward.  For most people, it isn't.  A powered DVI 1x2 splitter from [...] will cost more ([...]), but will actually work.

OK, for everybody who are bashing these glasses, calm down. Its apparent you had your hopes way too high. If you're going to be cheap, then you can't expect the best. I say cheap in relative terms because playing games with a proper 3D TV with active shutter glasses is way more than I can afford, even working for a major electronics retailer.But for anyone who bought these thinking they were going to get 3D like in the movie theaters, you're acting silly. Anaglyph 3D has never been the best and it never will be. However, what these glasses can accomplish for you provide depth into the picture. It's not going to blow your mind or anything and nothing is going to pop out of the screen very far, because that is the limitation of the technology. At best it looks like the "simulated" 2D to 3D conversion you would get on a real 3D TV. It's good, but not great. I will say though, the added depth seems to help me judge distances while I'm zipping around as Batman in Arkham City.Inficolor is a moderately successful way of bringing 3D to those of us who are too cheap or who cannot afford a proper 3D system. I give it 3 stars for the technology, how it performs and for the fact that the glasses are a little over priced. I mean, you can by active shutter glasses for a real 3D TV for $20 nowawadays.

I bought this motherboard to upgrade my 6 year old computer system.  I wanted to go with high end components and didn't mind paying a bit more to get them.  This motherboard was part of that purchase.  The specs were great and reviews of ASUS have been great as well.  This motherboard was paired with 32GB 2400MHz RAM, 1TB SSD, Intel 4770k processor, ATI R9 290x video card, and Corsair AX860i power supply.  Everything was purchased from Amazon (I love Amazon Prime).  :)The motherboard worked great until just over two weeks ago.  I turned on my monitor one Saturday afternoon and my system rebooted itself bringing to a "BIOS is updating...." screen.  I did not tell it to do any BIOS update and after 20 minutes, I had to try resetting the computer and getting things working again.  Everything I tried resulted in the same "BIOS is updating...." screen.  Even after flashing the BIOS from a flash drive.So now, I have to call support.  They aren't open on the weekend so I have to wait until Monday...no big deal.  I call Monday and after being on hold for 1/2 hour, I talk with a technician and explain what the issue is and everything I have done up to this point to try to troubleshoot it.  He says there isn't anything else he can suggest to do and says it appears that the BIOS chip has gone bad.  He says I can send in the motherboard or for expediency, I could purchase a replacement BIOS from their site and have everything done quicker (I had already said I really wanted to do this fast in order to beat the x-mas shutdown).  So I go on the website, and find the BIOS chip I needed with the help of the tech who stayed on the phone with me and paid for overnight shipping (which was more than the chip itself).It was two days before ASUS finally got around to shipping out the BIOS chip.  I did not like how slow they were but that would be forgiven when I was back up and running.  I put in the BIOS chip, turn it on and it immediately shuts back off then a few seconds later the fans come on but nothing else happens.  I try to flash the new BIOS and it fails.  There is something wrong with the chip they sent or they sent the wrong one!So I'm back on the phone and they offer to send another BIOS chip but I don't want to deal with what could be a bad batch or mismarked batch of BIOS chips.  After all, the one I received was in foam wrapped with paper and scotch tape.  The manufacturer was also different.  I express an urgency to try to get my motherboard replaced and working before x-mas and the technician was trying to be helpful in trying to make it happen.  He called me back later that evening to tell me I should have received an email to get the RMA started.  I checked and it wasn't there.The next day, the email also isn't there so I call again and now the story is that it will take up to 48 hours to receive the RMA email because they have to do a stock check (why a stock check takes 2 days is beyond me).  There is nothing they can do.  Now I have to wait until the following Monday.Now over a week has passed since the board stopped working and I am no closer to getting it fixed and my frustration level is climbing.  I call and they have no status for me and don't know what is going on.  There is nothing they can do but to initiate another stock check which would take up to another 48 hours to do.....and btw, they will be closed on the 24th and 25th for the holidays.  I'm right where I did not want to be.I call back after receiving nothing on the Thursday after x-mas and am finally told I will receive the email for the RMA within 30 minutes.  I receive an email but there is supposed to be a form I have to fill out that isn't there.  I have to call back AGAIN!  After another hold time, I tell them what is going on and they said they would notify the RMA department but that is all they can do.  After about an hour, I finally receive an email with the attachment needed.  I fill it all out and email it back.  I opt to pay $40 for overnight shipping of an advanced RMA and to have a hold placed on my credit card for the replacement cost in case I don't return mine.  I still have hopes of getting the computer running before the end of the year.On a side note; every time I call support they verify my name, address, phone number, email, etc.  I have no idea why they do this because the RMA paperwork has me fill everything AGAIN.  Why can't they verify it once and use it across the board?So I send in the RMA for an advanced replacement and even though they said they have a motherboard on hold for me, it will take up to another 48 hours for them to ship it out (even with overnight shipping).So now it is the following Monday and I have not been notified that they have shipped it and I call once again.  They confirm that it doesn't appear that the motherboard has shipped and they have no way of telling me anything else but suggest I call back tomorrow to see if they can tell me something then.At the same time as I'm getting the replacement motherboard, I have to do a separate RMA for the bad BIOS chip.  I called a week ago and was told I would receive an email to get that process started......nope.....didn't happen.  I called today and they don't even have a record of me calling about this but said they would start it again.  I did finally receive that RMA email today.So after over two weeks, I still have ZERO progress on getting my computer system back up and I have now thrown $85 at the issue to try to expedite the process.  But at every step, ASUS has failed to do what they said they were in the time frame they said.  I have made so many calls to them and every person has been friendly but at the same time they can't get anything done.  Who knows when I will finally get my motherboard.ASUS can be the best hardware out there but if they can't support their customers when failures happen, they get moved to the bottom of my list in the future.UPDATE 12/31/2013-----------------I received an email that my replacement motherboard should be shipped today.  It took 3 days for them to ship out a motherboard they had on hold for me and I'm still paying $40 for overnight shipping so should get it in 2 days.  I am so livid with the quality of the service with ASUS.  My computer has been down for over two weeks because they can't get their act together.

I always get these drives from elsewhere but figured I'd try Amazon this time.I have not received them yet but have put more than a dozen of these drives into play for clients without any failures whatsoever. Oh, ALL MACINTOSH so I don't even know if this driver/firmware business is relevant or if it ever was. I've been using these for about a year or more.They are 2TB but run "slower" at 5400rpm... so I would use these for back ups of videos, large photo collections, movies, or scheduled backups of multiple computers. I do have some of these in pretty active day-to-day access that hasn't bothered me personally but you're better off using a 7200rpm (or even a 10,000rpm or SSD) drive as your main boot drive.I don't see anywhere mention of the typical 3-5 year warranty for these so I'll have to look to see if it mentions it when I get them. I'll report back then.I think I heard Samsung hard drive line was purchased by Seagate so I don't know what this will do to branding or cost...usually you can get these for 75-80$. Seagate is a good hard drive company too, good warranties (again 3-5 years) and minimal/no-hassle returns/exchanges.There was a good period of 8 years there where the most important thing about a hard drive was how easy it was to exchange for a replacement! If you look on some other sites, you can see that a 70% success rate (30% fail rate) is still pretty good! Luckily now the quality rates for big drives are in the 80%-90% ... at least according to reviews at the tech site.The trick is that you really don't want to be buying the newest biggest drive.... I don't mess around with 3TB+ yet personally.... it was a long time before they got 500GB stable! Then 1TB! Now 2TB.... For now, my limit is 2TB for 3.5" drives but laptop drives I'm still afraid to go above 500GB!The nice thing about the slower RPMs with this 2TB drive is that less mechanical motion should translate to longer drive life and reliability. Fast RPMs are fun, don't get me wrong, but they're likely to bust up sooner. So this is a good workhorse.... highly recommended.Oh, if you get a DOA, dead drive, etc, don't sweat it... it used to happen ALL THE TIME and we're not out of the woods yet. It's still only 2011 and things don't always "just work."UPDATE: Punching in the model number Samsung reveals 36 months (3 years) warranty on these puppies. Good!

I'm a long-time Garmin Forerunner user.  My first was the 305 and I now use the 310XT as I do ultra-distance marathons and Ironman distance triathlons.  I got the Forerunner 10 for my wife, which is about perfect for her.  She's under 5 foot with small wrists so the size of the Forerunner 10 is perfect.  The simplicity is also very welcome.  Nothing fancy, just start, stop, just as she wants.  The lime green color is also a huge bonus for her.I used her Forerunner 10 a couple times and she's had it for a couple weeks now.  Now for the problems, which there are only two.First, the missing lap pace and average pace display.  While the current pace is fairly accurate, but it doesn't replace the need to know your AVERAGE pace over the entire run and your average pace for the current lap.  This is really vital information for any runner doing say a half marathon that's looking to finish at a certain time.  I figured the virtual pacer would solve this problem.  But, it still only shows your current pace vs. what you set for your virtual pace.  It should show you how far ahead or behind you are compared to your virtual pacer.  Basically, the virtual pacer is useless, as it just shows your current pace, just as the pace field does.  The only time you can actually get an average pace is at the end of a mile (lap) where it displays the average for that mile.  This dove-tales into the second problem...Secondly, the beeper is VERY quiet.  My wife cannot hear it at all while running unless she puts the watch against her ear.  This is important because to know your average pace for the last mile, you need to catch it right at the time the mile (lap) ends.  It only displays the lap time for a few seconds.  If you can't hear it beep, you can't really get your mile pace.  My hope is that she'll become accustomed to the beep frequency and be able to hear it.  But, it's still really quiet and at a high frequency which is much more difficult to hear than my 305 or 310XT.My hope is that Garmin will realize they missed a few things and a firmware update will address it.  As it is now, I can't recommend this to anyone looking to run in any type of race where you're trying to hit a goal time.  Or even training where you're trying to run at a specific average page, as you have basically no clue as to what your average pace is.  And even with the Virtual Pacer, you have no idea if you need to slow down or speed up to hit your goal.  All you know is your CURRENT pace, which is about worthless when trying to hit a goal time or pace.  I'll change my review and rating if Garmin fixes things with firmware update.** 11/27/12 UPDATE **Still no firmware update from Garmin to fix the problems with this.  Wife is okay with the limitations, but hopeful that Garmin will fix things.  I've received many firmware updates to my other Garmin GPS watches, so I'm hopeful the problems will be addressed in fairly short order.  Garmin, if you're reading this, here's what your new firmware should fix:1) Beep for lap needs to be more like the beep for the Virtual Pacer.  The lap beep is just too quiet to hear while running.  The Virtual Pacer beep is obnoxiously loud, so I know it's possible.2) Virtual Pacer is worthless.  It doesn't show if you're ahead or behind your pace plan, just if you're CURRENTLY running faster or slower.  This is the same information you get if looking at your current pace.  The Virtual Pacer needs to show your current AVERAGE page from the start, and if you're behind or ahead of this AVERAGE pace.  This is the way the Virtual Pacer function works for every other Garmin watch.3) You can set to display pace on the display panels, but both of the pace options are instant pace.  There's no lap pace or average pace option.  You really have no idea what your average pace is till you're done with your run.  Works fine for training, but try hitting a goal time in a half or full marathon if you have no idea what your average pace is till the race is over.  Just a few quick water stops and you're never going to know what pace you should be running at.  This dovetails with the Virtual Pacer, as that also doesn't show what you should be doing to hit your goal finishing time.I'm a long time Garmin owner, owned the 205, 305, 310XT, and now the 10 (my wife's first Garmin).  I'm an ultra marathoner (up to 50 miles) and Ironman, who does around 8 marathons or longer a year.  I always wear my Garmin and have for several years.  My point is that I know what I'm talking about.  I've always been very happy with all my Garmin watches.  This is the first time where it appears that whoever designed the watch software wasn't a runner.  They added all the features requested, but not correctly.  Feel free to contact me if you need any clarification.** 04/17/13 UPDATE **The software update adds the much needed average pace!  However, the watch still is faulty in the following two areas:1) Lap beep is still super quiet, so much so you can't hear it while running. The Virtual Pacer beep is obnoxiously loud, so it's possible to fix this.2) Virtual Pacer is still worthless.  It doesn't show if you're ahead or behind your pace plan, just if you're CURRENTLY running faster or slower.  This is not how a virtual pacer should work.  It should compare against your average page, not instant pace.If Garmin can fix these broken features, it will be a 5 star watch.

This is an excellent solution to a sticky problem. If you are reusing a K-cup, you have to have a secure lid or you get leaks.  I tried foil, but it can't seal tightly enough.  I've tried the one-cup inserts, but they are a real pain to rinse and use each time.  These lids fit almost all the K-cups perfectly.  There are some that don't work very well, but that is the cup, rather than the lid.  The filters inside the K-cup are glued just inside the rim of the cup.  If the filter isn't trimmed or properly aligned during original manufacture the lid is very difficult to get on.  It still works, but it is a pain.  Donutshop is one cup that is like that.To re-use the K-cups, first, buy these lids.  Tear off the foil cap on the cup - it doesn't have to be perfect, just make sure there is no foil that can bend down into the cup itself.  Empty the used coffee - I recommmend putting it through your disposal unit, it actually helps keep the blades sharp and helps keep odors away.  Rinse the filter thoroughly - I use a tooth brush to gently pull the stuck grinds.  Just lay the tooth brush on the filter and turn the K-cup all the way around once and all the coffee will come out.  After they are rinsed, I recommend drying them, but it is not a required step.  Then, fill them up and pop this lid on top.  When you make a cup of coffee with a used K-cup, make sure to align the bottom hole with the bottom needle so you maintain pressure.  Two holes cause leaks and weak coffee.The lids themselves can be reused as well, as long as you don't break off the tab that gets created when the top needle punctures it.  I've been through 100 lids once with no issues and about a dozen reused lids with no issues.  These things are a great solution.  Plus, the seller sent them out right away and packaged them well so they didn't get damaged.Give it a try, it is a cheap solution and you can use your own coffee blend!

The pace/distance tracker is a great idea but I was surprised by its large size and complexity.  I have solar pedometer and it is 1/3 the size and much easier to use.Because of its many features you will need to read the instructions on the booklet provided.  It basically has 2 modes.  Workout mode for set amount of times and continuous mode where it tracks you all day for up to 7days.  I did like how it tracks your movement and has a memory to store your information for the past 7 days/7 sessions.  It is certainly more than adequate for people who are serious about their workouts, want to know how many calories they burn and/or check their pace and exercise time.  Plus it also includes readouts for step count, distance, and even fat burned.  So it is particularly useful for someone who wants to compare their workout.  Plus I found the clock was very convenient.  I also liked that it can calculate your stride by inputting your height and weight but it really is for one person to use since if you want to input data for a new user you have to reset everything for that new person.However, one of the big drawbacks for me was that it did not have an on/off switch which I thought was strange.  Neither workout or continues mode take into account an exercise routine when you don't know when it will end. You must set the time you want before you use it to track a workout!  This can be a bit frustrating.  For example I wanted to turn it off after I finished a lap around a track and check the calories I burned.  But since I didn't know how long it would take me to finish the lap and it only calculates for specific amounts of time I couldn't store the information accurately.  Another drawback is that it also needs a more specialized battery to store your information which could get expensive over time.  The instructions note to remove the battery if it isn't going to be used for 3 months or longer.This is a handy and multi-featured tracker that serious runners or people who really want to compare their steps/burned calories from day to day will find useful.  If you have a set exercise routine and love gadgets you will find this a worthwhile product.  But for casual use it is probably not worth the effort.

I've had a chance to run the Samsung N310 against another laptop (MSI Wind U100) and had a few comparisons to make:Pro:-- The outer shell of the Samsung is nice. I made sure the WiFi had the latest drivers, but still it was only average.  Given the a netbook is built for portability and use on trips, this poor sensitivity would limit the usefulness when you're in a hotel and the access point is way down the hall!  The Samsung would not hear WiFi signals that the MSI could hear and connect to.  The Samsung needs a fairly strong WiFi signal to keep connected.  With only one or two bars on the Windows wireless utility, I could connect but would disconnect and reconnect sporadically.--  Nowhere near a 9 hour battery life.  Seems to be on par with other laptops.--  Power adapter gets quite hot during charging.  Makes one wonder how long this charger will last before the circuitry fails from thermal issues.--  Lots of preloaded junk software.  You can uninstall what you don't want. MacAfee blocks the Samsung update utility until your uninstall MacAfee.I guess if it weren't for the weak WiFi performance, I could give this unit 4 stars.... but since WiFi is such a critical piece of a portable netbook, this makes the unit only "average" in usefulness.  Putting the MSI against the Samsung, I can see more signals with the MSI and can connect to WiFi access points that the Samsung can't even hear.  I would be at careful taking this along as my only computer, as many times I may be in a hotel where the wifi signal just isn't very strong, and the Samsung may be borderline in connectivity.If you want a stylish computer that looks good, this netbook meets that criteria.

I decided to try out the iSport in-ear headphones from Monster because I always seem to have to re-adjust my earphones as I'm working.  I wear them most often while I'm doing things like cutting the grass or otherwise working in the yard. Every other pair I've had, except a pair of Sennheisers that went over the ear, would work themselves loose.  I find myself constantly pushing them back into my ears- especially as I get sweaty.  Just the weight of the cord pulled my prior pair of Monster DNA's out of my ears.  The iSport comes with three sets of SportClip (TM) adapters, small medium and large.  Putting the iSport into your ear is a bit tricky and is different from any earphones I've used in the past.  Getting the right sized adapter is probably more important on these than any as there is a piece that fits up into the curve above your ear canal and holds them in place.  Initially, I wasn't thrilled about the fact they don't block outside sound as well as the earphones I have with full sound isolation.  Monster describes these as "Isolation Factor:Partial". That is wise for people wearing them while doing things like biking or running on the road, but you compromise sound quality.  They are however not so great for tasks like cutting the grass.  I find that I have to turn the volume up pretty loud to hear the music and even then, during the quiet parts, it's inaudible. If you're looking for earphones that block outside noise, these are not the ones for you.  Noise isolating earphones not only give you better sound quality, they allow you to listen to your music at lower volume, saving your hearing.I once again have to complain about Monster's lack of documentation.  Inside the from panel of the box (a nice box, as always from Monster), there is a nice diagram showing you how to put on the "SportClip" and how to insert the buds into your ears.  However, the manual has  nothing about the product itself. There's some legalese concerning the warranty, some information on the anatomy of the ear and warnings about hearing loss.  It's not an owner's manual as far as I'm concerned.  It's 80 pages of worthless, generic information repeated in several languages.  The only thing customized about it for this product is the "iSport" on the cover.This is the second pair of in-ear headphones I've had from Monster with Control Talk.  Again, not a word on what Control Talk is or how to use it is included in the box. What I have figured out from experimentation is one click starts your music.  Another click pauses it.  A quick double click fasts forward to the next song.  A triple click skips back one song.  If you get a call, a click answers.  Another click hangs up.  On my iPhone 4S, a long click will launch Siri.  If you want volume control, I think you have to buy the iPhone version (which then I guess doesn't work with Android devices, I'm not sure about that).Sound quality is good, not the absolute best. These are not Monster's highest end in terms of price and the lack of full sound isolation means you're not going to get the absolute best quality.  However, the snug fit is amazing.  The SportClips seem to be sturdy and are easily removed to exchange or to wash.  The box says "Sweat-proof and washable, with antimicrobial eartips".  I'm pretty sure they meant the eartips are washable, not the headphones themselves.The look and feel is great with a aqua color cord and tips and a shiny silver driver.  I like the flat, non-tangle cord.  Overall, I give them four stars, deducting one star for sound and for the lack of documentation either included in the box or on Monster's website.

I have been wishing for an Android compatible docking speaker for a while, so I was super excited when I saw this one was available from Philips. The sound really is fantastic for such a small speaker.PROS:*I LOVE the bluetooth feature. I can be checking my e-mail on my smartphone and jamming out to my favorite music through the speakers at the same time. I've even used it when I'm watching movies on my phone.*It's a great size. Perfect for nightstands, shelves, or entertainment centers.*You can adjust the volume from where you're sitting. It turns your phone into a remote control for the stereo.*The nightlight provides the perfect amount of light.CONS:*I seriously dislike the Fidelio App. It made my phone act spastic and so I finally uninstalled it. It kept searching and trying to connect via bluetooth even when I did not want to be connected to the speakers. When I would log in to try to "disconnect" from the speaker it would start running the app all over again. It seemed like the App would start of it's own accord. Maybe it's user error on my part, but I got irritated with the constant issues with the Fidelio app. I just started using Pandora or Amazon Cloud and connecting to the speaker through my phone's regular Bluetooth connection. That worked just fine. I think there are a still bugs they'll need to work through.*The actual docking station doesn't seem especially sturdy. It does allow you to adjust the "supports" on either side of the micro-usb, but due to the small size of the micro-usb it doesn't seem quite as sturdy as the iPod models. It doesn't really seem to cradle my phone especially well (I have a HTC Inspire).*FYI - if you use a super hefty protective case for your phone (like an Otterbox) you will have to remove your case before being able to dock the phone. It was a bit of a hassle to constantly take the phone cover on and off, but it's not Philips fault that I have to use a tank to protect my phone from my two-year-old.To sum up, this docking speaker has fantastic sound, especially for it's small size. The Bluetooth feature is fantastic and I love that it's compatible with my android phone. I'm not currently a fan of the Fidelio app, but I'm hopeful that they'll continue to do updates and work out any current bugs or glitches. I wished my phone could dock with the protective case on, but again, that's my choice to have the cover and isn't Philips fault that my phone is wrapped in tank-like fashion.

If you purchase this, make sure to read through the reviews for tips on using it! My first effort, I used fine grind because I assumed that would be best for slow drip - wrong. It was awful. After reading the reviews more closely, and discussing the problem with a local coffee shop, I tried coarse ground Kenyan (Trader Joe's AAA) and it worked like a charm.Pros: Easy to use. Directions fairly clear (though directions on box were actually better than directions IN box). Once I switched to coarse ground, coffee itself is very flavorful without the bitter undertaste Starbucks iced coffee has (for instance).Cons: The carafe is plastic, and not great plastic at that. Worst part is it's impossible to clean - something about the way the neck is shaped means it also doesn't dry, even after leaving it upside down/aslant for two days in the drainer.They only include one filter, which is pretty cheap given what the product costs. I don't know if they've changed the filter manufacturing, but mine are only lasting two uses, although I rinse them well and store them correctly.As other reviews mentioned, the detachable handle comes off very easily - not good when you're standing in the middle of your kitchen and it's full of water and cofee grounds.The entire thing feels cheap, which might just be a design issue. The dark brown doesn't help.Over all, I'm wishing I hadn't purchased this, because the cons really outweigh the pros at this point. I think I'd have done better with a large Bodum press or the like.Tips:Use good water - that's key. Here in Nashville our tap water reeks of chlorine, so I buy large jugs at Trader Joe's specifically for making coffee. (And it's still cheaper than Starbucks or other coffee shops.)Let it sit for a full 24 hours, not 12. If you have a press, use it to push down on the grounds for the last half.You DO need a paper filter, because otherwise the grounds get bogged down on their woolen one, and what should be slow drip becomes one drip every 30 minutes.I personally didn't find the nut bag helpful. The grounds collected at bottom and it was almost like not having a filter in there at all, except it made emptying the grounds easier.Last, if you order filter or other replacements, order them direct from Filtron - shipping is free over a certain amount, service is fast, and it's a lot less expensive than the Amazon vendors I've seen advertising the plugs and filters.

This monitor looks great in daylight. Mine came with a dead pixel right in the middle. It's not a big deal if there's anything with detail displayed on the screen, but whenever there's a sheer color displayed, it glares at me, laughing.In darkness, there is some backlight bleed. Turning down the backlight helps a bit, but only so much.The biggest problem with this monitor is the low quality power supply. If you do audio production and have audio equipment, this will bother you to no end. it makes buzzing noise, and whining noise. The noise responds to the backlight brightness setting of this monitor as well. I spent a whole day trouble shooting, plugging in and out of things, etc, etc. Turns out there's some sort of ground loop created right in the electronics of the monitor, and then that noise transfers over to the computer over DVI, and can go to your audio interface over firewire, then to your speakers. While clearly, such noise shouldn't be passing through at either of these stages, the most obvious fix is to get rid of it at the source: This Crossover monitor's cheap power supply.The quickest and easiest fix is to remove the ground(This monitor is all plastic so no need for a ground). The best fix is to get a cleaner power supply - but I can't verify 100% that that would solve the problem.Also they confusingly write in the description of this monitor that it doesn't work with MacBooks, but this isn't entirely true. If you have a pre-unibody macbook pro, (mine is a 17" 2008), it has a dual link dvi built in as the only video connector - perfect for this version of this monitor which comes only with DVI.

My relationship with Tech Armor Screen Protectors started when I first purchased the matte version of this protector when I first got my S3. The installation was quick and easy and I was quite pleased with the product but the reason I bought the matte version was due to the anti-glare and anti-fingerprint which I felt would outweigh the HD clarity provided in this version. What I didn't expect was that the matte version dulled down the screen brightness and color and had a sort of newton effect (although small) on white and lighter colors. For more information about the matte version, you can read my review for it here: http://www.amazon.com/review/RP3T0LK9A608G/I wrote to Tech Armor and they were very helpful and sent me these HD Clear Screen Protectors as a replacement free of charge. They get an "A" in customer service, I can tell you that much.The installation process was the same, although I had a bit more trouble and was forced to trash the first protector I tried to apply--once lint and debris gets on the protector, you can remove it using some tape but if you do it too much, it gets impossible to remove all of it.The HD Clear version, however, does not disappoint in screen quality and color; I haven't seen my screen this bright since I first got my phone.I give this product 4 stars out of 5 because it does what it's supposed to do; however, do be warned that this screen protector will be primarily used to keep tiny and small scratches away from when you put your phone in your pocket. It WILL NOT protect it from larger scratches like wet-application screen protectors like ZAGG's InvisibleShield.Since I removed my old protector and had the first failed application protector to spare, I ran some "test" on them. The first was the "pen/pencil test" in which you try to impale the screen protector with a pen or pencil. It gave little resistance. The second test was trying to cut it with both a dull and sharp blade of a pocket knife. The dull blade damaged the protector but didn't cut through or damage the surface below it but the "sharp" blade, or rather the not-as-dull blade, cut through it fairly easily. The third test was the rip/tear test in which you try to rip the protector in half with your bare hands. This and the dull blade test were the only tests that it was able to pass.By no means am I saying this is a bad screen protector; the pen test and the sharp blade, to me, are extremes. I just wanted to point out the durability of the product to potential buyers. If you're careful with your phone, like I am, and only want a protector that will protect it from smaller hazards like the car keys in your pocket, then this product is definitely recommendable especially with their wonderful customer service. However, if you're looking for an extremely durable screen protector that will protect your phone from greater hazards, I suggest you look elsewhere.

I'd read the other reviews before purchasing, but had such good luck with other Belkin products over the years, "assumed" this would just have to be a great product too.This is not the 1st wireless router we've had.  Our most recent was a Linksys Simultaneous Dual-N Router - WRT610N.  Unfortunately, it wasn't grounded properly and took a hit by a nearby lightening strike.  I wasn't worried though - there were definitely places in the house where I was unable to get a signal (mostly where I would normally sit).  So was excited when the Belkin reviews over and over were all about its amazing 'range'.  CNET had glowing recommendations of the product.The Good:  range on the Belkin is really amazing, actually.  All the places I would normally sit and, at best, get a Fair signal from the Linksys - I get an Excellent signal from the Belkin. I really appreciate this attribute of the product.The Bad:  where shall I start?*  When laptops are first powered up or are brought up after being 'asleep', it takes a lot time for signal to be re-established.  We have 4 laptops in our home, and experience this on all of them.*  Fairly complicated programming.  Yes, it seems to work perfectly right out of the box - very easy set-up.  Problem is that part of the default programming is to shut a 'sleeping' laptop out of the system overnight each night.  The only fix we were able to find was to re-start the router.  Until we finally figured out how to change the programming.*After bringing a 'sleeping' laptop back up - even a wired laptop, we often get errors saying there are duplicate IPs on the network.*  Router loses connection fairly regularly.  We have to re-start it probably every 2nd or 3rd day.  Frequently I can't even access router's IP address from my computer.  We walk upstairs and unplug it.*  Does not act as a print server.  When I saw the ports in the back, I 'assumed' the router would look at the printer as just another attachment (like the Linksys did).  I was wrong.*  Does not 'see' our 2GB external hard drive we were using as storage.  The only 'fix' to this appears to be to manually make a wired connection to the hard drive and copy and paste from laptop to hard drive from time to time.Since range was my original complaint from the Linksys, I would say that the Belkin definitely relieves that problem.  However, we now have a whole host of problems we never had with the Linksys.I'm already looking for another router.

The original "French White" Corningware was made of Corning's famous pyroceramic glass, which could be used on the gas stove, put directly in the freezer, put under the broiler right from the freezer, and oh yes, also used in a microwave. And it was very unlikely to shatter if dropped. If you pounded on it with a hammer and nail you might have gotten it to break.When World Kitchens bought the license from Corning n the late 90's, they decided to halt production of a line of cookware that would take anything and last forever, and dupe customers, especially brides, into thinking the stoneware "French White" was the same thing as the wonderful French White pyroceramic cookware previously available to their mothers and sisters.The pattern is very attractive and can be used with any decor, and they  do offer many sizes, but this stuff is not, repeat, really not, what people mean when they say "Corningware."Le Creuset can do most of the above mentioned, but it being metal you cannot use it in the microwave. Stoneware cannot go on top of the stove, and repeated trips from the freezer to the oven will eventually cause it to craze and crack. And stoneware will also chip, and break if dropped, etc. Pyrex glassware cannot go on the gas stove although you can take it from the freezer to the oven, and also microwave it.The only product which could do anything was pyroceramic, and World Kitchens has chosen to remove it from the market because it is "too good."They have recently brought back a few of the old square shapes, with the Cornflower, or plain white, calling it "vintage," but the French White shape is not making a reappearance yet. If you want it, email them and ask for it!Meanwhile, don't buy this stuff. Get Le Creuset for cooking and roasting (yes it is expensive but it lasts forever and cooks beautifully), and reheat things in Pyrex in the microwave.

I have used this serum a total of 4 times-- 3 nights, and 1 morning, on both my top and bottom lash line.The first night I used this on my lashes, I woke up with bloodshot red eyes and the surrounding eye areas were red and puffy. My boyfriend said I looked like a racoon that got into a fight, haha! Seriously, I looked like I was up all night doing god knows what. I thought I had a bad reaction due to it seeping into my eyes. I stuck it out for the second night, and swept it on my lash line carefully. I woke up with the same side effects, although my eyes weren't as puffy. I figured it just gets better, so I tried it out in the following morning. It didn't really work out for me because it made my eyes dry and itchy, which I had to deal with for the whole day.After just 3 days, both me and my boyfriend saw a difference. My eyelashes definitely look darker and longer already. I still wanted to take a break since I don't see the point of having long beautiful lashes, if I have to deal with a bigger problem of dark red circles around my eyes.My eyes looked a lot better when I skipped a day, and since I figure the side effects aren't permanent, I went ahead and tried it for the fourth time last night.This morning I woke up with no side effects, whatsoever. No dryness, itchiness, redness, and no bloodshot eyes. I think you just have to be extremely careful that this product does not seep into your eyes.Make sure the serum dries completely before you go to sleep.Overall, a promising product, but there ARE side effects. It just depends on what you're willing to put up with. I will most likely keep using this product, however, if I see that there are worse side effects, I will discontinue use, and inform everyone through review.

I wish I could compare these to the Bose IE2 sport ones, but I was very disappointed with my original Bose IE2 earphones.  If they are anything similar, these iSport Victory's must beat both of them.  I recommend these for people who are active at the gym or like running long distances.  They will stay put and won't disappoint.  Are they worth $150?  Probably not exactly that much... I had them on in the gym yesterday and I was blown away.  The bass from these is amazing and you really feel it.  Also, my previous assessment of the mids being a little low is probably wrong. UPDATE: after a couple of months use, I find this unit great.  Other reviews mention some cons such as short battery life and slight delay in GPS position vs. real position.  Neither of these are serious.  I have found several nice features that are not mentioned in the manual.  For example, on any screen if you see a "map" icon at the bottom right or bottom center, click on the icon.  If you are doing route options the icon shows a map of the possible routes.  If you have selected a route note the screen with the big red go to button has a map icon at the bottom right.  Click this icon and it shows your route.  With POIs after the list is generated there is a map icon at the bottom center.  Click this and you can see location of POIs.  Also you can delete a saved route by deleting each of the routing points and intermediate points.  If you do, you will get a window asking if you would like to delete the route.  Click yes and its gone.  Nice feature to clean up old routes.Some report charging unit or not thru the USB cable.  Mine DOES charge through the USB.  Not sure why but when charged this way it has longer battery life.  As for microSC, I purchased one and didn't seem to make any difference on unit.  Note there is an option for "Added features."  You need a code to activate.  If you type in "DEMO" you will see a demonstration video.  Be aware that DEMO is still working.  If you go to a saved route and click "Go TO" the DEMO will begin following your saved route.  This can be great to help you preview a route.  To cut DEMO off, go to the Added feater screen and type in DEMO again. IT will ask if you want to turn DEMO off.  I checked with Magellan and the only added feature you can purchase is additional maps that come with a feature code.I am enjoying my Magellan and recommend it.Previous: I purchased this unit due to size of screen.  No complaints about accuracy or ease of use for most travel.  The user manual is very bad - just not enough detail about features of unit.  For example, you can delete a saved route but no where in manual does it describe how.  I happened on to the way to do this by trial and error.  Two features need improvement.  Battery only works for about 15 minutes.  My guess is the large screen just takes too much energy.  I can live with this given the other benefits.  Second problem common to most GPS units is that this unit will not save a route traveled.  If I leave a point and drive to a destination without GPS guidance, I would like to save that route.  Can't do that.  I am impressed the the AAA trip points.  You can search the data base easily.  Yesterday I was looking for a restaurant and found it easily in the AAA data base.  Then the Magellan took me right to it! One day manufactures will set these things up to interface with a PC making trip management easy.  That day I will trade up for another GPS.  Until then, if you like the larger size unit - go for the Magellan.

I picked this up from the local bestbuy after a lot of searching and trial and error for my setup because of my unique requirements: should have a num pad, and dedicated arrow keys, yet be small enough to fit in my keyboard pull out with space left over for the mouse. My computer desk came with a very small keyboard holder, and is skewed to the right, so a larger, more normal sized keyboard does not work very well, because it crowds out the mouse.I tried several other compact keyboard options, but they were all geared towards the HTPC market, so none offered a dedicated num pad (absolutely essential for working with spread sheets!), e.g. IOGEAR's GK trackball keyboard, which i love for my HTPC, but couldn't work with on my desk because of lack of num pad.what i like about this logitech keyboard:a) very nice form factor (suits my needs as mentioned above)b) num padc) dedicated arrow keysd) dedicated home/end/pageup/pagedown buttons (no need to fiddle with fn or alternate function keys)e) full row of function keys (f1-12)f) dedicated ins / del keysg) ctrl, win key, alt, arranged in that order on left and alt, fn, ctrl on right. i cannot stress how important this is when you're touch typing. I find it difficult to work with keyboards that place the fn key as the left most or where alt normally ish) caps lock indicator light right above the num padi) dedicated on/off switch right above num pad, but nicely tucked away so that you won't accidentally toggle it while workingj) volume control keys (up/ down/ mute)!g) installation with vista was a snap! plug in usb key, pull out yellow battery tab (nicely indicated arrow) and you're good to go. no kidding. 30 seconds or less. came with installed duracells, and in the "on" position with battery tab keeping the batteries from being consumed. very well done Logitech! Btw, works with Linux as well, no monkeying needed. Also works via my IOGEAR KVM.now on to what i don't like:a) spacing of keys: because the keyboard is smaller, they've had to compromise on the layout a little bit, so if you're used to typing (not looking at the keyboard because you know how to type), you'll find yourself hitting an unintended key occasionally. I guess you have to sacrifice something to get the form factor, so I guess i'll just have to get used to it. I would still give kudos to logitech that they did a good enough job with the "main"keyboard keys: letters and numbers appear where they should, as do most of the symbols and you can type well for the most part once you get going. but still, things are a little more compact, so some slippage will happen till you getused to it.b) odd placement of home/end / pgup/pgdn keys. this is a frustration not directed at logitech or at this particular keyboard, but at the keyboard industry in particular. since there isn't a "standard" (which is perhaps good in some ways) almost every compact keyboard (laptops included)has a funky layout. this keeps me from using muscle memory, or rather typing the wrong key due to muscle memory most of the time. for this keyboard, the home-end etc. keys are horizontally *above* the numeric keypad, in a location / orientation i've never seen them before. Again, this is a sacrifice for the form factor, so i guess i'll get used to it in some time (switching between this and laptop keyboard and my office setup and HTPC IOgear keyboard, will be an added pain though)barring those two concerns above, i'm perfectly happy with this little champ. I've owned it for only a day now, so will probably update this review if i find something else noteworthy.cheers!

I bought this for my two and a half year old daughter to use with a new-for-her eMac. I was pleased that this keyboard looked like an adult keyboard (insofar as it had the QWERTY layout with a separate keypad-lookalike on the side) as my daughter routinely shuns the miniature iMac-type keyboard that I had originally set her up with, in favor of my full-size keyboard.Out of the box, the first thing that surprised me was the size of the keys. This is purely my fault. I had assumed that the keys on this keyboard were normal sized but they are not. Each key is easily 50% larger than a standard key. In addition, the rows of keys aren't staggered as they are on a normal keyboard; where the "A" key would be sort of between the "Q" and "W" keys on a normal keyboard, it's directly below the "Q" key here. At first I was put off by this but after thinking about it I found I liked the arrangement better. Smaller, less coordinated fingers can touch the larger keys easier, and directing children's hands is simpler ("it's under the Q" versus "it's under the Q and W").The tactile response (how the keys feel when typing) is a little soft but seems like it'll stand up to a fair amount of abuse. There are two plastic feet under the keyboard which angles it up. I suspect these aren't quite as strong as they may need to be for energetic children. One of my daughter's first actions was to stand on the keyboard (it was on the floor) and it held up fine, though she didn't jump on it or anything like that. Speaking of structure, the keyboard does feel very solid. Not "IBM PC/XT"-solid, but solid enough to survive a few drops to the floor, maybe even a small macaroni-and-cheese spill or two.One small shortcoming should be noted for Mac users: There are only three modifier keys rather than the Mac-standard of four. You get a single SHIFT key, CONTROL key, and ALT key (known as OPTION for Mac users). There is *no* COMMAND key. What I did was, using the Keyboards & Mouse preference panel in OS X, I remapped the ALT key to be COMMAND and remapped the CONTROL key to be OPTION. I lose the CONTROL key but very few Mac apps, and virtually zero apps that are designed for kids, use the CONTROL key so that's not a big loss.Another Mac user note: When you plug in the keyboard and start up the computer, OS X will go through the "identify your keyboard" process by asking you to tap the keys to the right and left of the SHIFT keys. Since there's only one SHIFT key on this keyboard you have to think ahead. The left SHIFT key is easy enough, but when it wants you to press the key next to the right SHIFT key just press the ?/ key (since that's what would normally be next to the right SHIFT key) and you're golden.As an aside, some people may think that it's unfair to detract points for Macintosh issues because this is a Windows keyboard. In fact, if you go to the manufacturer's web site and look up this product, you'll find that they explicitly support Mac OS X 10.1 and higher. Unofficially, because it is a USB keyboard and mouse, it should work just perfectly with any version of Mac OS from 8.1 onward (provided, of course, there's an available USB port).There are no USB ports on the keyboard so when you connect the mouse you need a second port on the computer. This is annoying but I can see the rationale for it. Since it'll be near small hands - often within ready reach of things like finger paint and Play-Doh - you don't want to put a USB port within range of things like that. So, while inconvenient, I understand it and agree with it.The mouse is optical rather than mechanical, and longer than I thought it would be but just about as wide as I figured. My daughter can manipulate it far easier than she can with my adult-sized Microsoft mouse, but not quite as easy as she can with a miniature notebook-style mouse that's found on the local library's kids computer. The buttons are firm but not too firm; my daughter can click it easily, and it takes a deliberate motion to do it so there's no accidental clicking as the mouse is being moved. The scroll wheel is reasonably grippy and responsive. If it weren't for the liquid-filled palmrest with the really bright tri-colored LEDs reflecting through it, this would be a reasonably sized mouse for a small-handed adult.Yet another Mac tip: This mouse has three buttons (left, right, and clickwheel). Small children, such as my own, will not understand this and a lot of problems can result from an errant right-click or two. The excellent shareware utility "USB Overdrive" (Google it for the link) allows you to assign all three buttons as a standard left-click which makes things much safer for the young'uns.The mouse pad is nothing really to write home about, particularly since optical mice don't actually need mouse pads. The transparent plastic surface lifts up so you can insert a photo below it. My daughter could care less about this but that may change when she gets older.

The iPod has so far been one of the most advertised and populated MP3 players so far. I'm still figuring out why. There isn't much features on the iPod at all, except games. My friend has this unit while not experience it much, I look at other reviews on this site and tried out the unit at Best Buy, and it's definitely the most overrated gadget in history.SOUND QUALITY: The iPod's sound quality is pretty good. The Creative player sounds a bit better, but not anything to worry about. It has an equalizer, but the iRiver H10-20GB has a lot more presets than the iPod. The bass is deep and the treble is clear.DURABILITY: Not good. First problem, if you haven't seen the news recently, the iPods are being recalled for battery problems and not lasting the advertised 18 months. This is really stupid to me. 18 months for a battery isn't good, actually, it's medicore. iRiver's battery lasts four to five years. Also, the battery's AREN'T USER REPLACEABLE. However, the Creative and iRiver players are (Rio's isn't), and they only cost around $30 to replace, while iPod charges shipping and technical support. The iPod's battery, 1.5 years. Yeah, pretty weak. Another thing you should know, the metal on the flip side of the iPod is very tacky, and scratches very easily. While all MP3 players are easy to scratch, the iPod is the worst of the Creative and iRiver. Also, not liking the gel case. iRiver's seems a lot more sturdier than the iPod's.FEATURES: Really, there aren't any features, unless you call the games a feature. There is no FM tuner, while there is no FM tuner on the Creative Zen (on the micro version of the Zen there is a tuner), the iRiver H10-20GB, the Rio Karma, and the iAudio X5 have FM tuners. There is also no voice recording, something most if not all MP3 players have that the iPod doesn't. There is no photo viewing option, however, there is a 20 GB photo iPod, but it costs $20 more. There is an alarm and timer, but most MP3 players have this feature.EASE OF USE/DESIGN: The iPod is a very easy to use MP3 player, and if you can't figure this out, you shouldn't even own one. The Click Wheel is a great design, something no one else came up with (however, the iRiver has a touchpad). I'm probably the only person that dislikes the iTunes software. I just don't like it, the weird thing is, I don't know why I dislike it. Maybe because it doesn't have a lot of skins to choose from like WMP, but then again, I dislike WMP as well because it's slow on my computer. Anyhow, adding music to the player is easy.BATTERY LIFE: Pretty medicore at 12 hours, the Creative, iAudio, Rio, and iRiver players last longer.CUSTOMER SERVICE: Awful. Listen to this one, remember the battery statement I made earlier. If your battery dies and it's still under warranty, guess what, you're out of luck, because Apple doesn't cover the battery in the iPod warranty. They have the nerve to charge you $30 for a warrantied iPod. There technical service isn't helpful either; they just read what's on their website and charge you $50 (+ toll fees) to do it. At least Creative and iRiver's only charge toll fees like most companies.OVERALL: I highly dislike the iPod, even though the sound quality and design is above-average. Maybe in their 5th generation they'll add features to the iPod. But for now, pleases don't buy this, and buy a Creative Zen or the iRiver H10-20GB instead.

I really like the design and layout of this hub, and it worked great with my 2013 Mac Pro (both Mac & Win8) and all my devices...for about three weeks.  Then, four of the seven ports simply died.  Plug something in and nothing.  Fortunately it died within the 30 day return window, so it's going back.  Replacing it wasn't an option, as they're now backorded for months.  Still giving it two stars since the port arrangement was so nice.  The power/input jacks face the back (towards the wall/computer), most of the USB ports are on the side (towards your peripherals), and the charging ports are on the front (towards you).UPDATE: I did a quick autopsy on the unit before sending it back.  Typical board-in-a-box, you unscrew the bottom cover by peeling back the rubber feet a bit.  It has two four-port VL811 USB hub chips daisy chained to each other, with the downstream of one VL811 fed from one of the other VL811's ports (BTW, this is why USB hubs always have N*3+1 ports).  Now, you would think, with four ports out, that the downstream port chip circuit is what failed.  But that's not what happened - tracing the circuit, half the dead ports belonged to one VL811, and half the other.  Very strange.  See diagram at saccade.com/export/ABusb.jpg

There are 2 versions of this speaker sold on this page, and this review is for the Logitech Wireless Boombox with Bluetooth.Super easy to set up, I had this up and running with an iPod touch in a just a few minutes time. You can either wait for the internal battery to be fully charged and listen wirelessly, or keep the power cord pluged in and start listening to music right away while it charges.Syncing with the iPod touch is simple, just turn on the Bluetooth on the iPod, press the sync button on the speaker, then when the iPod sees the speaker, touch the name of this speaker (Logitech Wireless Boombox) on your iPod and it will activate the connection. With the press of just a few buttons, you are able to instantly play all the music on your iPod through this speaker.The sound is WONDERFUL! I have an almost identical speaker set up (with Bluetooth as well) made by Creative, which is also in the exact same price range and the sound is not nearly as nice. There is a huge range of sounds that come through on this Logitech speaker, where as the Creative speaker seems to have a bit less. Side by side, this Logitech wins hands down.The speaker has a pop out stand on the back for propping it up on flat surfaces. There are volume controls on it, however you can also control the volume through your iPod. It comes with a 3.5mm cable adapter, so other MP3 players and tablets that have an earphone jack, but that do not have Bluetooth can still be used with it. Just plug one end into the players ear phone jack and the other end into this speaker/boombox and you can play all the music without the need for Bluetooth. I was able to hook this up with my Kindle Fire tablet with no difficulties.The speaker has a rechargeable battery inside, so you don't even need to be connected to any wires to listen to music, perfect for taking with you outside where you wouldn't have any outlets. The Bluetooth and the rechargeable battery make this speaker a truly wireless setup.With wonderful sound and easy syncing to Bluetooth devices, this Logitech Boombox is a stellar device for listening to all your music stored on any music player or tablet.

I own this unit,  the DEZL 560LMT,  the 465LMT Garmin trucking GPS,  and as of yesterday,  the DEZL 760LMT.If you're looking for a basic GPS,  no frills,  but routes you well,  with a large address database,  get the 465.  It acquires satellites and calculates routes quickly and fairly reliably.  If you're a company driver for a large trucking company and aren't required to log state by state mileages and roads used,  the 465  is a great value.  The 560LMT doesn't acquire or calculate  nearly as quickly as the 465,  most noticeably on the longer routes,  or when adding a midpoint location to force recalculation along a more desirable route.  It can  also be sluggish in recalculating if you miss a turn or exit for any reason. It routes differently than the 465 does for many longer trips,  and I usually prefer the 465 routes as being more truck friendly. I have been using it primarily as a backup for the 465 as a second opinion, and for my IFTA logging. But if you're interested in the 560 for its features,  I would strongly recommend that you go ahead and spend the extra $100.00 and get the 760. It routes at least as well as the 560 if not better, has more features,  a much more detailed screen of information and surrounding roads in your immediate vicinity as well as having a big easy to read screen and much more loud and clear voice prompts. ( To be fair the 560 was clear and loud enough for me,  but the 760 turned up all the way is really Really loud,  while still retaining its clarity.

This extender ends up as a SECOND wireless network, with a different SSID than the network you're extending. This wasn't obvious (at least to me) from either the product descriptions or the the documentation. Hawking should be more clear - it's as simple as stating "this product works by creating another wireless network in your home, and that network has a different SSID". Why does this matter? Because I am unable to get either my laptop, running Windows XP Pro, or my PDA, running Windows Mobile 2003, to smoothly transition from one network to another when moved about the house. In both cases manual intervention is required, and in the case of the PDA I actually have to delete the network settings I don't want to connect to and add new settings for the one I do. Perhaps there's a better way to configure these devices, but I haven't found it. If you end up connecting only to the extender you should be fine, but I find that if I'm too close to either the WAP or the extender, I have to connect to a different SSID for reliable communications.

I got one of these adapters with the purchase of a MacBook Pro about 3 years ago. The MagSafe feature is really handy. It probably saved my computer from a crash to the ground at least five times because someone tripped over the cord, bumped into it, etc. In each case the cord came unplugged from the computer (as it is designed to do) without pulling the machine down with it.Unfortunately, the cables on this power supply are not very durable. A little over a year after I bought my Mac, the outer insulation on the attached cord separated from the power brick, exposing a few inches of the wire inside. I was able to put electrical tape around it. The adapter still functioned in this state for almost two years, but eventually the exposed wires shorted out and the adapter failed to charge the laptop reliably.My girlfriend, who purchased her MacBook Pro at about the same time, experienced a similar problem, except it was the insulation around the AC extension cable that came apart. I replaced my faulty power adapter with a cheaper, generic model (MAGSAFE 85W Power Adapter for Apple MacBook Pro) that is still working fine after four months.To increase the longevity of the power adapter, I recommend that you avoid winding the cord very tightly around the built-in winder clips.

Also, a single pump is generally more than I would use so when I take too much by accident, it makes it worse. We tried the cheaper model from the same brand and returned it.  This one works perfectly, especially for cooking very small quantities of rice.  Couldn't be happier, and yes,it does employ fuzzy logic when cooking the rice.  Don't buy a cooker without that feature.And everything from this brand is usually very high quality.  This one is no exception.  If you are a serious cook, this is the entry level.  Don't go any cheaper.  Note that it only cooks 3 cups.  Perfect for those who like rice but may not want so much of it.  For two people, we've found that 1 cup is enough to satisfy our craving for rice dishes for two, without pumping up our waistlines.It's very easy to use.  They give you a measuring cup and you measure the rice with the lines on the cup (we use 1/4 cup per person, but most will probably want 1/2 cup per person), then dump it into the bowl that is included in the thing.  Next, add water (some people will stir the rice with their fingers) and pour the water back out to rinse the rice.  Some of the hulls from the rice will float off when you pour the water out.  Rinse twice, then fill the water back up to the mark corresponding to the amount of rice you have in there.  Yes, you add water to the mark with the rice inside.  Put the bowl in the unit and close the lid.  Next you push menu to select the type of rice you have (white, brown, sushi, etc., use porridge for steel cut oatmeal) and push start.  If you want to use the timer, instead of pushing start, push timer, use the arrows to set the time (it starts with the last time you used) and then push start.The only knock I have is that it takes a *long* time to cook 1 cup of rice.  40 minutes just seems like it's twice as long as it should take.  However, because I don't know whether that is longer than other fuzzy logic rice cookers, I didn't take a star away from the product.  Just be forewarned, it takes a LOT longer than cooking rice on a stove.  Is it underpowered?  I don't know.  The flip side is that it only takes 450 watts to run the thing, and so it is less likely to pop the circuit breaker if you have something else going.A little off topic, but if you are looking at a rice cooker, you may want to learn about rice.  Here is what we have learned so far.  There are three basic grain sizes of rice: long grain, medium grain and short grain, also known as sweet rice or sushi rice.  Each kind has its place.  Long grain rice is best for fried rice and pilafs - where the rice shouldn't stick together because you want every grain to be coated with a flavoring.  By itself, long grain rice is not that great tasting.  We Americans are used to long grain rice, but wait until you branch out into other types.Medium grain rice is for serving just plain rice, like as a side dish with Chinese dishes.  It is easily the best tasting rice by itself.  It clumps together to a degree, making it easier to eat with chopsticks.  If you want the most delicious rice you can find, and you won't be flavoring it, buy medium grain.  It's so much better than that long grain minute rice we grew up with.Finally, sushi rice is very short grain and clumps like mad.  It is generally limited to sushi, where you would be willing to sacrifice flavor to get better clumping, and sweet dishes, because of its high starch content.  This rice cooker has a special setting for short grain rice.  But I find short grain rice to be too artificial tasting, and so even for sweet dishes, I use medium grain rice.Next, there are two basic types of rice: brown rice, which is how all rice starts, or white rice, which is brown rice with essentially all of the nutrients removed.  With no nutrients, white rice doesn't spoil like brown rice can.  We've found very little difference in taste between brown rice and white rice.  If you don't like brown rice, you were probably thinking of an exotic variety that had a deeper taste.  Regular brown rice you buy in the store is very nearly the same taste as white, so we've stopped buying white.  Find Botan Calrose brown rice in an asian market, look at the health advantages of brown rice on the internet and you'll never go back.  Note, there is a special setting on the cooker for brown rice, and different water marks for brown, and brown rice takes about 80 (not a typo) minutes to make one cup.I'm sure you can find more detail on line, but that should give you the basics.  Ditch your long grain rice: you'll be amazed at how much better medium grain rice can be.  And try brown rice: you'll be shocked at how close it is to the nutrient-less white rice.  This cooker makes all kinds of rice really well.  I've had it for about three years and we use it nearly every day.  It's still working like the day we got it.  The nonstick bowl looks and acts like new.  The battery keeps all of the settings and the current time, though my understanding is that the battery is not easily replaceable without sending it back.

This is Western Digital's entry level SATA RAID drive. It generally costs about $10 higher than the AACS even though the specifications look exactly the same. What the extra $10 buy is special software engineering going into the firmware, which makes sure that the drive will not go incommunicado for longer than a few milliseconds. Ordinary drives have no such safeguards and the RAID controller can possibly mistaken the temporary lack of responsiveness as a drive failure. Once the controller marks the drive as failed, it has to be reformatted and everything on it is as good as gone. This is an inconvenience in RAID 5 or RAID 1, and a fatal blow in RAID 0.I bought two of these and put them in RAID 0 configuration. This RAID array serves as the only storage system. The setup is rather risky and therefore necessitates frequent backups. On the other hand, the performance is phenomenal, approaching that of the 10k RPM drive while costing a fraction of the price.

This Corsair case was purchased for that purpose.The case and other parts arrived yesterday (3/24/14), and I proceeded to install the components. The ASUS motherboard went in without any problems... or so I thought, until I tried installing the video card and noticed that, with the card seated all the way into the PCI-E slot, the top of the mounting bracket was about 2mm off the case. My first thought was that the motherboard was not screwed all the way down, but I verified that it was (the connectors at the rear of the motherboard lined up correctly with the backplate).To verify that the video card's mounting bracket wasn't out of spec, I test-installed it into my primary PC that uses a Cooler Master HAF 912 case; the card seated all the way down with the top of the bracket contacting the case, and the screwholes lined up correctly.Additionally, I had an old Sound Blaster PCI card in my spare parts box, and tried installing it into the Corsair case. Same result: the top of the mounting bracket was about 2mm short of the case.Cranking down on the bracket screw is not an option as that would press the video card into the motherboard, distorting and possibly damaging it. My interim solution was to superglue 3 washers together to use as a shim between the video card's bracket and the case, thereby allowing the mounting screw to be tightened without distorting the motherboard.The entire rear of the Corsair case is obviously out of spec, as the ledge where the tops of the mounting brackets screw onto is about 2mm too low. Hence my one-star rating for this product.
