Hamilton Beach Big Mouth Juicer / B000FHQJ6CI bought this juicer back in 2009 and have used it less than I'd hoped (more on that in a minute) but often enough to feel that the purchase was worth it. When aKuvings NJ-9500U Centrifugal Juice Extractorcame up on Vine, I figured I was well-placed to review an expensive juicer and contrast it with the cheaper stuff on the market, and post the same essential review in both places. But I'll just cut to the chase right here: as a hobbyist juicer who just wants to whirl the juice out of a handful of fruits, I cannot honestly tell that much of a difference between the expensive Kuvings and the half-price Hamilton -- the Kuvings is better in some ways, but it's not twice as good in proportion to being twice as expensive.* Parts: Both the juicers have mostly the same basic parts: base (with cord and buttons), whirl-er (where the mesh screen sits and the juice comes out), pulp-bucket (where the waste goes), top (where the fruit is fed), and piston (to help jam the fruits through the top and to the whirl-er. But I was surprised to see that the juice pitcher that came standard with the Hamilton is NOT included with the Kuvings; you have to supply your own bowl for the juice to pour into, and since our bowl was wide and uncovered, the new juice pouring in caused the existing juice to splash lightly all over the nearby counter, which I found quite annoying.Advantage: Hamilton.* Weight: The juicers take up about the same footprint on the counter, in terms of width and height. The immediate obvious difference is that the Kuvings is plastic and lighter, whereas the Hamilton is heavier and uses stainless steel clamps. The lighter Kuvings is easier to carry, but I don't know how sturdy the clamps will be over time. Personally, I care more about weight than about sturdiness (we tend to 'baby' our appliances in general).Advantage: Kuvings* Assembly: The Kuvings is more fussy at assembly time; the pulp-bucket has to be sort of tilted up and in and snapped into the top before then being tilted down and sideways to snap into the bottom. The Hamilton, in contrast, just has the pulp-bucket sit flush to the side and the top secures it in place.Advantage: Hamilton.* Speeds: The Kuvings has two speeds, regular and turbo; the Hamilton only has one. Since I only use fruits with my juicers (and therefore only use the regular speed on the Kuvings), I can't say whether the turbo speed is worth the extra cost. That's something to look into if you're planning to use really tough veggies in your juices.Advantage: Neither / Depends.* Noise: The Kuvings boasts a 350-watt motor while the Hamilton uses an 800-watt motor. I do think the Kuvings is less noisy, but not proportionately so and not so much that it doesn't still mightily startle the cats. What I am saying is, when you are using the Kuvings, the rest of the house is aware that you are using the Kuvings. And when you are using the Hamilton, the rest of the house is aware that you are using a slightly louder version of the Kuvings. Neither of them are so loud that the neighbors will hear, nor so soft that you won't disturb your napping husband.Advantage: Kuvings.* Cleaning: Cleaning is the major reason I don't juice more often, and it's an area where I think improvement is possible. The only thing that doesn't need to be cleaned after juicing is the base (unless it got dripped on, which does happen); the whirl-er, piston, pulp-bucket, and juice pitcher will all need cleaning. (I did see recommended in another review that the pulp-bucket be lined with a plastic bag, which is a good idea I will try next time.)This means that if you want a quick juice on your way in to work, you have to assemble the juicer, run the juicer, unassemble the juicer, and either wash everything or at least put all four parts in the sink to soak. If you skip the unassemble-and-wash steps, you will come home to a sticky caked-on mess that will be a nightmare to clean. And since none of this is particularly fast, it means that your 'quick juice' is going to be a 20-minute proposition. No, that doesn't mean that the juicers are "hard" to clean, but it does take time -- or at least it does for us. (Maybe the rest of you have super-speed powers. If so, please come wash my dishes?)Both the Kuvings and the Hamilton use the mesh-screen whirl-er and that little guy is a fright to get clean. Husband -- who does the dishes in our family -- has declared after a great deal of consideration that the Kuvings mesh is slightly faster to scrub clean than the Hamiltons mesh, so I will award the advantage on his say-so but with the caveat that the Kuvings mesh still took several minutes of scrubbing to clean. (Husband also registers a concern that the Kuvings cleaning brush doesn't seem very sturdy. But we'll cross that bridge when we get there.)Advantage: Kuvings.* Juiciness: Both the Hamilton and the Kuvings juiced the heck out of a collection of apples and clementines, and in both cases the pulp was very dry afterward. And in both cases there was a lot of flecky foam that can either be strained with a cheesecloth or can be stirred in and drunk. We saw no difference in actual juicing performance between the two juicers.Advantage: Neither / Identical Performance.---I'm pretty sure that if you add everything up mathematically, the Kuvings comes out as better than the Hamilton. But the advantage overall is pretty slight -- the Kuvings is lighter, but seems more in danger of breakage; the Kuvings is less noisy, but not super-noticeably so; the Kuvings takes a minute less to clean but a minute more to assemble; and so forth -- and for twice the price I'm more than a little irked that there's no juice pitcher included because it means that if you don't have a bowl or glass that can fit under the juice nozzle, then you'll have to make another trip to the store.If you're a first time juicer and aren't sure how much you will use your new appliance, I would recommend starting with the Hamilton and seeing how you like it and whether the excessive clean-up process is a turn-off for you. But I would recommend buying the Kuvings over the Hamilton if:* You have strict weight-lifting limits. (I have a bad back.)* You intend to pulp a large volume and/or tough veggies. (Turbo speed!)* You need a less-noisy motor for medical reasons.Otherwise, I think both juicers are very good and do the job they're meant to do.~ Ana Mardoll

I'm not a big fan of diamond stones, and the triangular rods that Spyderco sells are made pretty much for sharpening on the flat sides. The diamond particles on the edges will come off fairly easy and that, as they say, is the rub. One can take a standard diamond stone (or your choice of flat stone) and simply lean it against one of the two Spyderco rods. Then you can use the same downward strokes with your knife and the angle will be correct. When you're done making, say, 10 strokes, you simply move the stone over to lean against the other Spyderco rod and do the same. The angles will be correct and it will be cheaper.The Ultrafine rods are an altogether different proposition. They last forever and they put the equivalent strop on a knife. I recommend those. But not rods that wear fairly quickly.In sharpening, the angle is everything. After using a Sharpmaker for awhile, many people will instinctively pick up the correct angles and go for just flat stones. Getting a mirror polish with the Sharpmaker is almost impossible.

I purchased this video card to upgrade my XFX Radeon HD 5770 that I've had for two years.  I admittedly did not do enough research in video cards before purchasing this card.  Although this HD 7770 is a good video card, I actually saw a decrease in overall performance compared to my HD 5770.  After doing more thorough research, I learned that the HD 7770 is supposed to be an almost direct replacement for the HD 5770.  It turns out that the HD 5770 is basically the same design as the HD 6770 and the new HD 7770 is a more energy efficient, cooler-running version of the same basic design.  I wish that Radeon's chip numbering system for their video cards was a little more clear, I naively thought that the bigger the number, the better the performance.  I was also surprised that ATI Radeon hasn't significantly increased the performance of their video cards in the last two years.  Basically, the new models are just that, the models for this year's line-up, and do not represent a general increase in overall performance.  This is where I didn't do enough research.  But, I know now and, if you read this review, you will know too.Pros:o Good basic design.  A very good bargain as an entry level gaming card at this price point.o Runs very coolly and quietly.  This card is much more quiet than my HD 5770 and you can hardly hear the fan, even while gaming.o Neat packaging and card design.  Looks cool.  Came with a metal label you could afix to your computer case for bragging rights.Cons:o Equivalent performance to an HD 5770/6770.  It performed slightly better in 3D graphics and slightly worse in 2D graphics benchmarks. (This is a con because a HD 6770 can be purchased for a whole lot less money.)o I saw many video glitches when playing games.  I don't know if it was a faulty card, faulty driver or inherent product flaw.  The lack of a tangible performance increase over my HD 5770 led me to have no desire to troubleshoot what the issue was.  This cost the review a star.Because there was no overall increase in performance with this card over my HD 5770 and because of the video glitches I noticed while playing games, I decided to return this card and shop for something better.  At the moment, the HD 6850 cards would give me a slight 25%-50% increase in performance over my HD 5770 for ~$175 and a HD 7850 would give me about a 100% increase for ~$275.  (There are a freakin' lot of Radeon video cards out there and figuring out which is the best price/performance is not an easy task.)If I were to purchase my very first gaming video card today and I were on a very strict budget, I would purchase this HD 7770.  It's a good entry-level gaming card for the budget conscious.  I would have rated it higher if it were not for the video glitches that I saw.  Hopefully, that's just a driver issue and Radeon will fix it, turning this into an excellent video card for the price.  But, as I noted in my review, for just a little bit more money, you could get a slightly better HD 6870 card, so you should consider that option if you have the money.Update (5/16/2012)I ended up purchasing a Sapphire Radeon HD 6870 video card.  It has twice the performance of this card at only ~$30 more.SAPPHIRE AMD Radeon HD 6870 1GB GDDR5 PCIE Graphics Card.  Tom's Hardware and Legit Reviews websites both had good things to say about this card.  I expect that the HD 6870 will be noisier and less energy efficient than the HD 7770 because it is a generation older design.Update (6/22/2012)Just a follow-up: The Sapphire Radeon HD 6870 is wonderful.  No problems with performance and the fan noise is negligible.

I'm on my second Onkyo AV receiver (three, if you count the replacement of the first), and a characteristic of Onkyo is becoming apparent.  These products are shipped before they're ready.  My first unit, theOnkyo HT-RC260 7.2-Channel Home Theater Receiver (Black)suffered from an under-designed HDMI board.  The complete unit had to be replaced, and some-time later the HDMI board was swapped in the second unit.This second model also gives me the feeling of being not-quite ready.  Much is made of the network interface--wired and wireless.  It's there alright, and it works.  But it doesn't do anything useful.  You can stream music, but you can't stream video--not from a local server and not from any internet service.  It's strictly a radio.  It can play music, but it can't play video.  Almost every device connected to my TV can stream network video (my TV, my DVR, my 2--year old BluRay, my WD TV-Live).  But not this brand-new receiver.  That's just not acceptable.  The same deficiencies are apparent with USB: audio only.  It's possible that a firmware update will resolve this.  The receiver is supposedly updateable from network or USB.  When I check for a new version, I'm told it can't check.  Is it a brick already?The user interface (which I found just tolerable in the older version) is still something of a mess.  There are two primary menus, accessed by two different methods.  The assignment of features to different menus follows no logic I can ascertain.  This was clearly designed by engineers who never give the user a thought.  One nice feature of the older unit has disappeared.  In that older unit, I could set it up in such a way that turning on my TV would also turn on the receiver.  That works now, but the receiver input is forced to the TV input (rather than the satellite or cable input).  In the older unit, the input would stay where you wanted it.  It's a small, but persistently-irritating quibble.It's not all bad.  The unit sounds quite nice, especially when you take time to do the audio setup properly.  A small microphone is provided which is placed at the primary listener positions.  The unit then calculates levels, delays and corrective equalization.  This whole process takes perhaps ten minutes.  Most receivers provide this process nowadays, but the Onkyo EQ works particularly well in getting the best possible sound for your particular speaker setup.There is also a 4K passthrough.  I, like nearly everyone else, do not have a 4K screen.  While quite lovely to behold, they're still in the multi-thousand dollar price range and there's very little material to play on them.  If you DO have 4K, you're simply not going to put it through a $500 receiver.  This is empty specsmanship.  They'd have done better to work on the things that matter.I'm afraid I like the idea of this receiver much better than the receiver itself.  With appropriate updates, it may grow into its claims.  But not yet.EDIT: One more thing. Many aspects of program material may change when going from one channel to another, or even from commercial to program.  Forgive a little technical talk, but often the sample rate may change or word-clock may be temporarily lost.  Unless managed carefully, this can cause ticking noises to come from the speakers during the transition.  While not likely to damage speakers, it's a distraction to say the least.  Most receivers are smart enough to briefly mute (just a fraction of a second) so this noise isn't heard.  My earlier Onkyo was smart enough to mute, but this one isn't.  The ticks happen with regularity.  Just one more aspect of a system that wasn't ready to hit the stores.

My first and biggest pet peeve is the auto-numlock feature which the keyboard defaults to every time the PC is restarted. My computer requires every user to sign in when the PC is restarted, re-awakens from sleep mode or when it is interrupted from screen-saver mode. When I first restarted the PC, I could not sign in. After multiple attempts, I had to use the old keyboard to sign in. Once signed in, I opened up Notepad and typed in my password with this keyboard - that's when I discovered the middle set of keys were defaulting to the num-lock feature. It is a pain in the arse to have to unlock the numlock everytime the PC is restarted. The instruction manual does not indicate a way to turn off the num-lock feature, but does indicate that the keyboard defaults to numlock and to use the FN and Numblock key to turn it off. Horrible design.My second pet peeve is the lack of dedicated media keys. My old ioGear keyboard has dedicated media keys for Windows Media Player or any other playback software. I use this a lot, because I'm often listening to my MP3 playlists while surfing the Web or working on the PC. Having to use the FN key again with the function keys in the top row requires two hands to play media, instead of one hand with my old ioGear keyboard.My third pet peeve is the location of the touchpad. Having owned 6 laptops in the past 9 years, 3 laptops currently, navigation on the touchpad often requires 2 hands - one hand for moving the cursor and the other hand controlling the button(s). This is fairly easy on a laptop, because the touch pad is centered and at the bottom of the laptop, under the keyboard. On this keyboard, it is on the right, upper corner, where it is almost impossible to use two hands. Plan on becoming extremely dextrous with your right fingers and if you are left-handed, then good luck.I am still giving this 3 stars. because it is a full-size keyboard. I will keep and use this keyboard when I am doing extensive typing. However, for navigation on the Web, playing music or videos through Netflix and Amazon, I will continue to use my ioGear cordless keyboard with it's problematic, but much more intuitive roller, thumb-ball. This keyboard will also back up the old, ioGear cordless keyboard in case that stops working. Wireless keyboards become essential when one is sitting 6 feet or more away from an HDTV, my 37" Vizio in this case, which I am using as a high-res monitor.

Since this item has been reviewed pretty extensively, I'll just summarize my likes and dislikes when it comes to the Belkin FastFit Bluetooth Keyboard with cover:Like:* Good keys, nice tactile response, decent size for an iPad-sized keyboard.* Easy pairing, no trouble getting it to work.* Attractive as a screen cover. Matches the back of the iPad.* Magnetic latch is pretty cool.* Multiple grooves allow multiple positions.* Battery life is excellent.Dislike:* Provides zero protection for back of iPad, and not very accommodating to various types of back protection.* Doesn't actually secure the iPad into the groove, like the Logitech version does.* Provides no actual connection between iPad and keyboard/case. Someone could just walk by and grab your iPad easily in public while you're typing.* Keyboard layout is a bit strange, and really not made for touch-typists; Most notably the tiny right-shift key.* Belkin doesn't advertise a back protector to go with this, making the quest to protect the iPad's back a blind one.* A little bit on the heavy side when compared to other keyboard cases.My overall impression is that this is a great idea, but Belkin fell short of what I'd like to see in a keyboard case like this. I adore the actual keyboard, but without anything to protect the back of the iPad, and no suggestions from Belkin about how best to go about this (i.e., what back covers would be compatible with the FastFit), I feel less secure using this to travel because a slip could mean my iPad hits the ground with no protection on one whole side. It also means the iPad is vulnerable to scratches from normal use.I think any keyboard screen cover like this should come standard with some form of back protection. The reviews for Belkin's own back protector (which may or may not be compatible with the FastFit) are terrible, but at least if Belkin included it with the FastFit, I'd have something to keep my iPad safe on both sides. One-sided protection doesn't really impress me; Especially when the side being protected is the sturdier Gorilla Glass side, and not the vulnerable aluminum side.Will I use it? Sure, from time to time at home I think I might... But I'm not eager to go out in public with this thing as the only protection for my iPad. It's just not enough.Three stars for general build quality and the nice keyboard keys. I docked two stars out of the five total for the "don't like" reasons above.UPDATE: I picked up the Logitech Ultrathin Keyboard Cover, and for those wondering how the Belkin compares... Well, I hate to be unkind, but the Belkin is bulkier, doesn't attach magnetically to the iPad when in landscape view, and doesn't have the nifty magnetic connection at the hinge like a Smart Cover. In short, Logitech simply out-thought Belkin on this one. It doesn't mean the Belkin is bad by any means, but that when compared to the Logitech it just falls short in key areas that Logitech nailed. HOWEVER, the Logitech is typically thirty bucks more expensive than the Belkin, so if you're on a budget the Belkin's a great alternative to the Logitech Ultrathin. If you can swing the extra cash, though, you may want to compare them before jumping in.

First of all, the Belkin Petals Standing Cover is identical functionally to the Belkin Glam Tab Standing Case. The only significant difference is the appearance, with the Petals cover having a colorful fabric and pleather surface, while the Glam Tab covers come in more subdued solid colors and full pleather surfaces.Initially, I wasn't a fan of the newer-style Belkin Y-frame plastic yoke that holds the Kindle Fire, preferring the older style leather corner grips, but after using the Glam Tab for the last couple of months, I'm confident that it will hold the Kindle Fire securely in place, so I'm happy to see it in the Petals cover.The Petals folding mechanism is well designed and allows the Kindle Fire HD to be propped up in the landscape orientation at angles from about 45 degrees to almost vertical. It's an effective design that prevents the tablet from slipping if it's bumped. When using the case as an easel, the tab folds back out of the way and magnetically sticks to the back of the case. For hand-holding, the front cover folds easily against the back. When the case is closed, the magnetic tab sticks to the front of the case and keeps it securely closed, a feature I really like.The magnet in the cover activates the Kindle Fire's AutoWake switch. This is a really nice feature that keeps you from having to fumble around for the Kindle Fire's tiny on/off switch. Also, the magnet in the cover and the magnetized tab keep the Petals cover closed more securely than any other closure system that I've seen except for a zipper.Overall, I like the Petals case very much. It's an impressive-looking, showy case that gives good protection for the Kindle Fire, and it functions nicely as an easel. The magnetic switch works perfectly with the Fire's Autowake feature, and the tab keeps the case securely closed when the Fire is not being used.

I recently bought a '93 4runner and didn't plan on any crazy stereo equipment.  I just wanted something that offered good sound quality, enough volume to hear my music clearly when riding with all the windows down and the sunroof open at highway speeds.  As a bonus, this cd player is user friendly, plays mp3's, and has 2 auxiliary jacks.  This head unit also offers very usable features regarding the tailoring of the sound.  It delivers ample power for loud and clear listening that will satisfy all but the most die-hard audiophiles.  The unit also comes with a single pair of pre-amp coaxial outputs for running an external amplifier.  I think that this cd player offers the best compromise of cost and performance for those that just need a head unit to cover the basics, or for those that will add upgraded coaxial speakers and an amplified subwoofer.  Obviously, this unit will not in any way compare to a high-end Alpine head unit, but at the price point that this player sits at, it is easily the best value in a head unit for under $100.Don't be afraid to setup a modest sound system with this head unit.  In my 4runner it sounded much better than the factory unit, even with the factory speakers.  However, I was only so pleased, so I installed a pair of 4" replacement JVC and Cerwin-Vega co-axial speakers and a 10" jl audio subwoofer with a 150 watt RMS kenwood amp.  I did the install myself in about 2 hours, and by looking for deals online, I have only around $200 invested in the whole system.  By utilizing the cd player's high pass filter (HPF), I am able to get accurate midrange and treble reproduction, while letting the amplified subwoofer handle all the low frequencies.  I am thoroughly satisfied with the setup, and the heart of it has been this JVC head unit.  At these low prices, you have no excuse not to put one in any car you own.

I workout at the gym at least three days a week and drink lots of protein shake supplements to help me reach my caloric goals.  Shaker bottles are almost a requirement at this point for convenience alone.  My current shaker bottle uses a metal BlenderBall which mixes well and adds frothiness.The Rubbermaid 20 ounce/600 ml shaker bottle, made in Malaysia, is constructed of a tinted BPA free tritan plastic.  The screw top lid provides access to a 2 5/8 inch diameter opening and includes a twist-lock drink cap.  Plus a rubber finger loop makes carrying easier.The bottle includes volume guides, ounces on one side and ml on the other, for accurate measuring.  Once the contents have been added and the lid tightened, a quick vigorous shake readies the contents for consumption.  The five-sided paddle ball blends the shaker’s contents with little frothiness.  The BlenderBall blends better, however the paddle ball does a decent job.Rubbermaid makes this shaker bottle in four different colors, all seemingly chosen to appeal to women.  Even at Rubbermaid’s website, the pictures imply matching the bottle’s color to her workout wear.  There is nothing wrong with that approach; however some masculine color options may broaden this shaker bottle’s appeal.Since I only have one shaker bottle, I drink a prepared shake after working out.  I would consider mixing my own shakes in an effort to reduce costs and have better control of consumed macronutrients.  However I would rather use a shaker bottle with a BlenderBall for my protein shakes.  I will still use the Rubbermaid shaker bottles for other beverages.  If you're looking for a good shaker bottle, the Rubbermaid 20 ounce/600 ml shaker bottle may work for you.  Although, a BlenderBall shaker bottle may be the better choice.PROS:Resists stains and odorsMade from BPA Free TritanDishwasher safe1 year limited warrantyCONS:Doesn't blend as well as a BlenderBallFeminine color options

I have been using this UPS for about six months. It keeps my computer alive during brief outages, and seems to do a good job filtering electrical noise. I basically really like this UPS. My only harware-related criticism is that there seems to be no way to keep the cool display lit permanently while the UPS is on mains power. Maybe there's a way to set this through the Cyberpower Software? Maybe...but I'll never know.What I hate about this product is that the software that comes with this UPS is deficient. In point of fact, it does not work for me at all. I have uninstalled and reinstalled the original and the newest version of the CP software on my PC (Windows 7, i5 64 bit quad core processor, 8G of RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 460 video card), but it never works. The icon appears in my taskbar, but the program will not open. Process Manager shows that it's running, but the GUI never shows up. Each time I reinstall the program, the first time I try to start the GUI, I get a small white window in the middle of my screen. All subsequent attempts to run the GUI result in nothing at all.What I wanted to do was set actions to be taken when the PC is running off the UPS battery. For example, I wanted to set the point at which the PC would shut down, what the max CPU percentage would be, the cooling policy, etc. And oh yeah, set the blinkenlights to stay on. My last UPS was an APC, and their software was really nice. In addition to a user friendly GUI to set when the PC should perform an orderly shutdown during a power failure, it showed me a history of power failure or line noise incidents. But the APC had no blinkenlights at all!I called CyberPower support, but was told they had no idea what was wrong, and they didn't seem to care much about my problem. It's possible that my PC's hardware specs are uncommon (it's homebrew), but it doesn't seem all that arcane to me. It's not overclocked, everything is running vanilla. Personally, I think it may be a compatibility problem with the video card or drivers. This software may work for everyone but me, however I can only rate a product based on my own experiences, and I am dissatisfied with at least this aspect of the product, and seriously irritated by CP's lackadaisical tech support.What especially frustrated me was the inability to set the shutdown point for my PC when the UPS battery gets too low. The "Power Options" in the control panel didn't seem to know about the UPS, and--oddly--no "Battery" options were present. I now think the CyberPower software took control of the UPS from the OS. However, I did figure out how to fix this: I just now uninstalled the CyberPower software (for the last time), and found that the Windows 7 Control Panel power options now permit me to select actions to be taken on low battery conditions!I think that if CP is not going to support their software, they should just sell the UPS with directions on how to set the power options through the Control Panel, and forget about distributing the software at all.

I had a Asus VivoTab RT but my frustration with Windows RT finally convinced me to return it. It was a really nice tablet, but I definitely needed full Windows 8. I also have a HP Pavillion dv7 laptop and it is pretty much the exact opposite of these new Windows 8 tablets: it's heavy (6 lbs), it's loud, the battery life is terrible (from 100% to practically 0% in only 2 hours) but it has a core i7 processor. I was interested in the Envy x2 for quite sometime and bought it on eBay because Amazon did not sell it at the time. Finally got it and WOW I am totally impressed with everything!Screen: Just like theASUS VivoTab RT TF600T-B1-GR 10.1-Inch 32 GB Tablet (Gray)it is an IPS display and the crispness is just terrific! Compared to my HP pavilion dv7 laptop, which I bought for $750, the Envy x2 just blows it out of the water, period. Vivid colors, sharp display, all around great. I have a little minor complaint though: the dummy micro SD card that is inside the tablet is extremely difficult to put back in without breaking your nails, so I have just left it out since I don't really need that anyways.Keyboard: I have not encountered the keyboard issue yet (though it has a fix via a BIOS update, check HP's website) since the keyboard is small enough that I usually don't type too fast. However, I am really glad I considered an 11.6 inch size, because the Asus VivoTab's keyboard was just CRAMPED! I had to curl my fingers and still had to look at the keyboard to know what I was doing! Not the case for the Envy x2, as I am typing this and have had no issues with it. If you are a typist, go with an 11.6 inch size because a 10 inch is just too cramped. HP really wants to emphasize using this as a laptop, as this is not sold separately which to me is a good thing. It does have all of the essential ports: 2 x USB 2.0, Full size HDMI, headphone jack, full size SD card slot. The tablet only has a microSD slot and a headphone jack for ports.Responsiveness: Here's what I usually do on this tablet: Read websites, stream HD videos (Crunchyroll), RemoteJoy (projecting my PSP's screen onto the tablet, since my PSP's screen is cracked big time) and using online educational tools such as MyMathLab. All of these work responsibly well with the Envy x2, and I have yet to encounter anything major such as a crash or BSoD. Everything from swiping back in Metro IE 10 to go back a page, to streaming full 1080p video and using Flash-heavy websites, the Envy x2 does without a problem. In fact, I wonder why I even bought a $750 Core i7 laptop, when this little guy for about $200 less does it just as well and doesn't run out of juice in less than 2 hours!Battery life: I have been using it for two hours now, on 40% brightness (the brightness levels are in intervals of 10%) with Bluetooth and NFC off and it's still 85% battery! By this time on my dv7 laptop, it would likely be around 20%!Minor issues:Using headphones connected to the dock, the sound is a lot less loud then if I were to plug them in directly to the tablet itself. Not a major issue, but something to note. Actually, now it starts to make a loud popping sound when I watch YouTube videos which actually hurts a little bit. Could be my headphones, but for now I will use the tablet's speakers for laptop mode.The Wi-Fi is at 2-3 bars, but strangely everything still loads quite fast. Apparently lots of people have issues with the Wi-Fi, but I am using one of my ISP's slowest internet plans, so I guess it doesn't really affect me.Overall, I am absolutely in love with the Envy. The tablet itself at least to me doesn't have any plastic, though I think the keyboard does but everything about the Envy x2 is so sleek and professional looking! If you are in the market for a tablet with a keyboard dock with full Windows 8 experience, you got to give the Envy x2 a try.

Ok so I purchased this Roku because it was on sale, and I figured since it was the "elite" version that it would be worth my investment. I did research prior to purchasing the device, and the 600 + channels that are available is the reason I decided to pull the trigger and purchase it.So why three stars? I will tell you why. This device does what every other device in existence does: it streams Netflix and Vudu movies. I think that consumers should know that if you are expecting high-end content from this device that you will be disappointed. One of the few channels that I was interested in, and one of the reasons I bought the Roku, is Crackle. Sure it has commercials, but on the whole it is a good station. This is where great content ends.Don't get me wrong. This device works well and I have never had streaming issues. As an incentive to buy it also streams Amazon Prime content, which is great if you have the Prime membership. However, in my expierence, the vast amount of content that this device streams is very retro. Sure, if you love old movies and commercials from the 1900's-1950's then this device is for you.  Also, if you love B movies and, in some cases even worse (I dub them "C" movies) then by all means purchase the device. Another good reason to own the device is if you speak a multitude of foreign languages as the Roku offers tons of Bollywood content. But, if you are like me, and all you want is a cable alternative, DO NOT BUY THIS DEVICE.So three stars. The device works wonderfully well and has a simple interface. The fact that it streams from Amazon is most of the reason it even has three stars. But five stars? No way. Not until they give me a true cable alternative and not 150 channels of religious programming.I hope this has been helpful. I am not trying to discourage anyone from purchasing the Roku. The above review is just my personal opinion on the device and what I personally expected it to do.Thank You.

I originally purchased the Poetic Slimline case for my new Fire HDX, sure it didn't have all the fancy folding ability of the Origami case but I learned awhile back that all folding cases sort of suck when it comes to actually holding up your device, especially if you're using it on a soft surface (watching in bed), or trying to touch it (stylus, finger) as they all tend to fall over... so I use a Anker standAnker Multi-Angle Portable Stand for Tablets, E-readers and Smartphones, Durable Aluminum Body, Compatible for Apple iPads iPad Air, iPad Mini / New iPad Mini, iPhone 5S 5C 5 4S 4; Samsung Galaxy Tab 2 Tab 3, Note 8.0 10.1, S4, S3, S2; Google Nexus 4,7...which is the best $10 you'll spend as it holds all devices and folds up tiny... but I digress. The issue with the Poetic was that it didn't work well with the camera, even though it had a hole cut for the camera everytime you'd try to use the camera the kindle would insist you slide it up, but the Poetic isn't a sliding case, and it clips in the kindle securely, which means I'd have to snap it out of the case to take a photo. It simply wasn't working.This case arrived and initially I was really happy, sure it was a lot more money than my other one but it was real leather and looked/felt nice. The magnets were a bit annoying in that the lid sticks to itself and takes a bit to straighten back out, but it surprisingly held the fire well on a table, if at a bit of a weird angle when standing up. When I first got it the feature of it activating the camera app when slid up worked perfectly, but about a week later my HDX did an auto update and now that doesn't work. If I slide up my HDX nothing happens, I still have to manually click on the camera icon which isn't the end of the world but was one of the main selling features in my opinion, no response from support as to why this happened and I don't want to ship back my HDX if it's an issue with a software update or a failure of the magnets inside the case.The big deal breaker for me, and why this is still the case I use but one I promptly switch out for the Poetic if I am leaving the house or my kids might touch my HDX is that it's not secure. The ability to slide it up, well that's because it's not clipped in to anything... your expensive Fire is held in the case by nothing but magnetics! If you give it a shake (over a bed only please if you're testing this) it's going to fall right out of that case... I don't know about you but if I'm guessing that if my fire falls, it's going to do it with some force, and any force will knock it right out of this case thus making the protection 0. It'll keep it from being scratched sitting on your desk or besides your bed, but it's not protecting anything from a fall, or a child trying to slide it up to take a photo... heck I've almost even slid it right out of the case myself and I know to be careful. I much prefer the Poetic case because it clips onto the edges and holds the Fire securely.I'm hoping there is a redesign that allows it to be held in by more than magnets and I also hope the camera application autostart upon sliding magically comes back, but I'm not holding my breath for either. All in all not a horrible case if you know what to expect, but it could (and in my opinion should) be so much better.

I am a keyboard snob. There, I said it. As a touch typist I've gone through (and worn out) quite a few keyboards in search of the perfect keyboard. My current keyboard of choice is theMatias Products FK202SB Tactile Pro 2.0 USB Keyboard - Silver and Black, though it will never replace the King of All Keyboards, the original Apple Extended Keyboard. So when I set aside my Tactile Pro and started working with the Microsoft Wireless Keyboard 3000, I was immediately reminded of why I love the Tactile Pro so much.I'm getting ahead of myself. If you want the basic summary skip to the bottom of this review. If you want to know exactly why this is only getting three stars, read on.The keyboard and mouse combo arrives in a single box along with a USB dongle, four AA batteries (two each for the keyboard and mouse), installation CD and owner's manual. The keyboard is advertised to work with both Macintosh and Windows systems, though like most keyboards the modifier keys are designed with Windows users in mind. Since OS X can remap modifier keys it takes only a moment to "Mac-ify" it. You can also install Microsoft's software which enables all of the special keys and key combinations.The keyboard itself is reasonably attractive. Glossy black plastic surrounds the matte black plastic key caps, and the keys are silkscreened in white for easy reading. A nice touch is the addition of silkscreened "tips" on the face of the key (the part that faces the user, not the part that faces up). So the Z, X, C, and V keys have UNDO, CUT, COPY and PASTE on the faces, respectively. Veteran users won't need those reminders but it can be helpful for newcomers.The keyboard also sports a rubberized wrist rest that runs the width of the keyboard and about 2 1/2" deep. It's smooth and pleasant to the touch, but it's still hard plastic underneath. I wouldn't have minded a bit of soft padding below the surface. Still, it was comfortable to use.The underside of the keyboard sports the battery compartment (which requires no tools to open) and a pair of cheap but effective flip-down feet to elevate the keyboard at an angle. I actually found the elevated position to be less comfortable than the flat position, a trait that I also found on virtually every low-profile keyboard (like this one) I've ever used.Like virtually all keyboards these days the row of F keys (there are 12 of them here) doubles as application macro keys, so you can set them up to do things like create a new email message, check your spelling, save a file, etc. Mac users will see them used as standard Apple shortcuts such as volume adjustment, screen brightness adjustment, Exposé, etc. One disappointment: The actual F numbers (F1, F2, etc) are printed in medium-dark blue on the shiny black plastic above each key, not on the key itself. The combination of the blue color, the shiny black plastic, and the slight curve on which the printing is placed makes the markings virtually unreadable in anything other than office-type lighting conditions. If your desk lighting is, like mine, perhaps less than ideal, you'll miss these markings completely.Above the F-keys are yet another row of keys, seventeen in all. These are yet more user-definable keys, by default set up for things like volume control and music playback controls (pause, play, stop, etc). On the Mac the volume control keys work as you'd expect, meaning that Mac users get two sets of volume control keys out of the box. Happily, this is easily changed through Microsoft's software.There are a few other "random" keys as well. To the left of the keyboard are four buttons arranged vertically (yet more user definable buttons), there's the PrtScn/ScrLk/Pause triumvirate above the Page Up/Page Down cluster, and (very odd, IMO) a special calculator key above the NumLock key on the numeric keypad. In practice this calls up the Calculator app on your computer, but I find that to be a particularly odd speciality.Finally, in the upper-right corner is a battery replacement indicator LED to let you know when it's time to change batteries. I cannot comment on battery life as I haven't used it long enough for the original batteries to wear out.But the verdict is: How does it type? Well, on my Tactile Pro I average between 90-95 words per minute. After a few hours of using this keyboard I was averaging about 85 words per minute. The biggest problem I found is one which all low-profile keyboards share: They're all basically repackaged laptop keyboards. The key height is very low so there's not a lot of rebound on the keys. Any seasoned typist will tell you the same thing.One particular annoyance is the CAPS LOCK key. Unlike every other key on the keyboard, this one is "double bezeled". The key is rounded like every other key, but then there's a sort of raised-up section on it as well. When you're typing, your finger feels the edge of the CAPS LOCK key and you THINK your finger is no longer above it, but the "A" key is actually about 1/4" to the right so you wind up having to correct yourself while typing. I would have much preferred the CAPS LOCK key to be just like all the rest.The mouse is unremarkable, styled in the same glossy black and rubberized plastic as the keyboard. It has four traditional buttons (left and right click, plus one button on other side in the "squeeze" position) and a clickable scroll wheel that also leans to the left and to the right. I found the two "squeeze" buttons to be reasonably placed but too high, forcing you to adjust your grip on the mouse whenever you want to use them. I find this to be a common design flaw on all Microsoft mice, including theMicrosoft Laser Mouse 6000that I commonly use. The mouse is universally shaped for left and right-hand users. The action on the wheel is smooth but weighted and is comfortable to use. The side-to-side rocking action of the wheel takes a little getting used to at first but, once mastered, lends itself well to tasks like switching between browser tabs, moving amongst applications, or using OS X features such as Exposé or Spaces. The optical mechanism uses a blue LED; I prefer my less obvious infrared LED of my Laser Mouse 6000, but either way I detected no anomalies in tracking or using the mouse.It's worth noting that this set is NOT for Bluetooth. It includes a small dongle, low profile and suitable for laptops (where USB ports are often crammed tightly together). When plugged into my Mac mini, OS X immediately asked to identify the keyboard and it worked perfectly after installing the software. Wireless range for both keyboard and mouse was tested up to about 12 feet without any problems or difficulties.Finally, the software. Microsoft includes Microsoft Desktop v7.0 on CD. It installs without a problem and demands a restart afterwards, and (on the Mac, at least) is accessed through a pair of preference panels within System Preferences. Here's the set's biggest flaw. In typical Microsoft fashion, the software is not particularly elegant or intuitive but it does get the job done. The key settings are set up in two columns; the name of the button on the left, and what you want it to do on the right. The problem is, Microsoft's icons may not be that readily identifiable for new users. I see no reason why Microsoft couldn't have also included an image of the key cap icons; it would make things a lot easier.One small detail caught my eye; when I checked Microsoft's web site for a later version of the software I was told that version 6.41 was the most current version, even though the set shipped with version 7.0 and several web sites indicated that 7.01 was the most current version. I was unable to download anything past 6.41 from Microsoft, and the internet-update function with version 7.0 that I installed from the CD indicated that version 7.0 was the latest version. Go Microsoft.SUMMARY: On the plus side we've got attractive styling, a LOT of customizable custom keys, out-of-the-box *supported* Mac and PC compatibility, crystal clear white-on-black markings, tool-less battery replacement, and a reasonably pleasant wrist rest. Taking away from that is the mushy laptop-like feel of the keys, the CAPS LOCK key that is a textbook example of What Not To Do, poorly designed software, and a questionable update process. The most impressive thing about this set is that it excels at absolutely nothing. Given the amount of keyboard and mouse sets that gets more right than wrong, I therefore bestow three stars on this set as it is, overall, perfectly mediocre.

I've always thought Monster products were snake oil, now I'm sure.I'd been reading about the value of isolating the incoming power for digital and analog components in high end audio. Nothing. Even the faint 60Hz hum one of my subwoofer amps produces was still there. So much for conditioning power...More important: the first (and only) time I powered it up remotely from my preamp (using the correct trigger ports) my power amp's right channel fried. Mixed feelings. In many ways the TX55 is a tiny marvel. When it came, I was excited that the look and feel were wonderful. I love the slide-down panel that covers the lens and flash. It make the camera feel secure, and the sliding action is smooth with a nice tactile bump at the end. The action is precise, like fine machinery. I didn't have any problem opening it, as some have said. Needs to be started from the middle.The IQ (image quality) looks very good. Although little is adjustable, the automatic modes appear to do a nice job, in daylight, low light, flash on/off etc. Color rendition was excellent. The noise reduction at higher isos was very nice too, compared to some I've seen. You'll never get noiseless pix with this size sensor, but the CMOS and the processing probably get close to the best you can get (combined with the Zeiss lens).The big 3.3" OLED screen is impressive for brilliant colors and detail. Background defocus mode works nicely to simulate the shallow depth of field normally obtainable only with larger lenses (eg DSLR etc). However, one does have to be quite close to the foreground object for this to work--about 30cm or 12" is recommended. Dynamic focus and many other features make this a very modern camera, although many bells and whistles are things I'd probably never use, like 3D and some of the picture effects. The "clear image" digital zoom actually does work quite well, bringing usable zoom to 10x, and is far better than the typically crappy digital zooms offered on most point-and-shoots.I found the manual controls (just on/off, shutter, and zoom) fine. For someone with big fingers, I suppose it would be a problem. After a few times of turning the camera off instead of the intended shutter press, I learned the trick. The zoom stick was fine for me.So why did I return it? I suppose part of it might be a defect, but it could also be a design flaw--and one that could have had several work-arounds that would have made it irrelevant.The touch screen is too darn sensitive. This has been mentioned by other reviewers, so it may be a design thing, but it was so irritating that for me, it was a defect. On a camera where the touch screen is a huge part of the user interface, I find it simply amazing that Sony didn't do a better job here.First of all, the screen was so sensitive that often things would happen with the finger hovering an eighth-inch above the surface. This could have been solved by including a sensitivity adjustment in the settings somewhere! Of course one couldn't operate the screen with gloves on, in the winter for example, but I'd have been willing to wear cut-off finger gloves for this otherwise marvelous camera. But the basic problem, is this:A big part of a digital camera, for me, is showing people pictures in the camera. The 3.3" screen should be great for this. BUT, when you start reviewing pictures, there are all sorts of icons and readouts cluttering the screen--making the picture almost secondary. If you wait about 4 seconds, they go away. But 4 seconds is a long time when you're trying to show a picture to a friend, on the fly. Now after the icons go away, you can swipe to the next picture, and the next, without them coming on again. Which would be GREAT, except that if you tap the screen while swiping, the icons come back. And for me, 80% of the time a swipe turned included a tap in that small computer brain. So the next picture would come up, but it would again have all the icons, and you'd have to wait another 4 seconds for them to go away to see the darn picture! Unacceptable when trying to show off your recent accomplishments. Swipe--4 seconds to see it clearly. Swipe--4 seconds before it's clear. etc.Now maybe I just have a strong aura or something, but others tried it with similar results. Sony could have EASILY put a couple of things in there to make this problem moot, not counting a sensitivity adjustment. Among the icons are left and right arrows, which you can tap to make the previous/next picture come up. But they aren't there in the icon-free viewing mode! If Sony had left just tiny arrows you could tap, instead of swiping, then that would be an acceptable way to go through pictures without having all the other icons around. Another solution would be to have a mode to switch to that just didn't have any icons! Then you could swipe/tap to your heart's content, moving among the picture showing up on that big beautiful screen.Interestingly, there is an icon that, in shooting mode, does turn off the icons. But that same icon, in viewing mode, only turns on/off the exposure info, eg iso etc. All the other irritating icons remain!Another minor niggle is that in shooting mode, you only see the picture in a reduced format, not using the full screen. The icons are outside that area, but you don't really get full use of the screen for seeing your target. Also, even at max brightness, the screen is pretty weak in sunlight. It's not bad in just bright light, but it doesn't automatically adjust, so if you go from shooting outdoors, where you want the screen at max, then go indoors to look at pix, you have to navigate a few menus to turn the brightness down for pleasant viewing.I really did want to like the camera. I loved, or could live with, pretty much all of it EXCEPT the 4 second wait for icons to go away. I really really like the smallness of it combined with the big screen, and tried my best to imagine that I could live with the viewing problem. But in the end, I knew it would not work for me. C'est la vie.

First, let me say that I have been a very happy owner of the EF-500 DG Super for over three years now. Besides its tendency to underexpose for about 1/3 of a stop, it has proven to be a reliable and functional unit, very much worth the money. Recently I decided to add another one of these to my collection, primarily to be able to use it in E-TTL wireless mode. Since EF-500 was hard to find, I ordered EF-530 DG Super f/Canon (this was not an Amazon purchase). The first impression was fine. Sigma definitely fixed the underexposing issue, making it very consistent, as many of the reviewers have stated so far. All the other features seemed to be more or less the same as of its predecessor. Then, I discovered a major issue. When I tried to use this unit as a wireless master to my EF-500, I found that Left/Right Power Ratio function was not completely available through its menus. I was able to make adjustments from 8:1 to 1:1, but not any further than that, although the owner's manual clearly stated that it should cover values up to 1:8 as well. This flaw made it completely useless as a master unit. Needless to say, this function was perfectly usable on my EF-500. When I tried to use the EF-530 as a wireless slave, it worked properly. For a moment I considered keeping the flash, since it functioned OK as a slave, but eventually I decided to return it for a replacement, hoping that the new unit won't have the same problem. Unfortunately, I was wrong as the second flash I got not only had the same issue, but it performed terribly as slave as well, having a totally inconsistent output. In the end, I decided to return it and take my money back.Having heard about not-so-great Sigma's QC before, my experience with the EF-530 seemed a perfect example of it. Apart from this Master/Slave issue, this flash performs as it's supposed to, so everyone who plans to use it as a single unit should experience no problems. Also, I would like to hear from other EF-530 DG owners if their units have the same type of design flaw as mine did.

If you are new to mesh filters, there are a couple things to know:1. There will be some grounds get through to the pot.  NONE of these filters will filter as good as paper.  They all let grounds or coffee dust through.2.  The water moves through these faster than paper.  The idea is that they don't remove any coffee oils like paper does so you still get great tasting coffee.  You'll have to judge that for yourself.If you still want to go mesh, consider the following:1.  Will the filter last long enough to justify the cost?  The cheapest of these may fall apart within a year.  I suppose thats not bad for a $5 filter, but I would like it to last several years.2.  They all have plastic that comes into contact with hot water. Do they say they are BPA free?3.  Sentences like "Reusable stainless steel golden mesh filter; enhances flavor." should make you press your back button.  First off, gold plating is supposedly used in most of these products because gold is non-reactive--it doesn't react with the oils in the coffee and pass on old taste. So why does this one say "golden mesh"?  To fool people.  Secondly, NONE of these filters "enhance" flavor.  That is in fact the opposite of what they do. They are supposed to allow the flavor through.  If they enhance it, then the question you must ask is "with what"?

After seeing reviews on-line suggesting that this cradle worked with a naked Verizon Samsung Galaxy Nexus, I decided to give it a shot with my Verizon Galaxy Nexus plusDiztronic TPU case. After removing the plastic insert, the phone appeared to fit well inside the cradle. Unfortunately, it would only intermittently charge if the phone was pushed down far enough onto the USB connector. Unlike other docking cradles, this cradle's USB connector is not very long. If the connector was made slightly longer, I think it would make a consistent connection. The cradle is definitely marketed for use with the Samsung GS3, and so maybe the situation is slightly different with that device. Having said that, Galaxy devices are designed to be able to uniform in much of their interface with accessories. So I'm surprised that my Galaxy Nexus isn't better supported by this Galaxy accessory.The other problem I had with this cradle (which will apply to GS3 users as well) is that it did not come with an AC adapter despite being a phone+battery charger. Other combo chargers include AC adapters with at least 7.5W (i.e., 1.5A at 5VDC) output capacity. Instead, this one's instructions indicate that the phone and battery can be charged together but you should not use the phone's data features while charging. In other words, because you are forced to use your own AC adapter (which likely has 5W output capacity), the 500 mA your battery might require to charge coupled with the 1A your phone might require will be out of your adapter's capacity.Otherwise, it's a good-looking cradle with lots of vertical support for your phone. Its short USB connector may be a challenge for some cases, and you might get a slow charge if you try to charge both a battery and a dead phone at the same time.

I think the trick to stainless steel is that it has to be primed.  The first time you drink or eat from a porous metal like steel or titanium, it will taste like metal.  Eventually, the metal will take on the taste of the items you put into it.After reading the complaints about these glasses having a metallic taste, I bought just one to test.I 'wasted' a glass of Two-Buck-Chuck and let it sit it the glass for about 24 hours, then rinsed and dried it before packing it.  (I did not use soap on it.)A set of four, heavy-weight glass wine goblets cost about the same as this.  I brought both the GSI steel wine glass and the glass wine goblets (Libby Catawba Footed Goblet) on a car-camping trip for comparison.After having been primed, I did not taste any difference between the GSI wine glass and the glass wine goblet.The GSI wine glass is very light weight and the stem unscrews then snaps securely into the cup so that it packs small and other small things can be stored in it.The GSI wine glass is theoretically unbreakable, although I'm sure I'll end up finding a way to break it someday.  The glass wine goblets did not break when dropped on the ground but they are very heavy and take up a lot of space.Stainless Steel would not have to be re-primed when going from white wine to red wine but it might need to be re-primed when going from red back to white.I think that I will eventually get a full set of these and keep the goblets for home use.

Design:  2 StarsFeatures:  3 StarsPerformance:  4 StarsThe Creative EP-660 earbuds are the latest mid-level offering from Creative.  I have a pair of EP-830 that came with my Zen X-Fi mp3 player that I will use for comparison in this review.  I was impressed with the sound quality of the 660's compared to the 830's which retail for $20 more.  In listening tests that included rap (K'Naan), hard rock (Guns `N Roses), and blues (Beth Hart and Joe Bonamassa) I found little to distinguish one from the other as far as reproducing sound across the full spectrum.  I don't think you can ask for much more in terms of sound quality at this price point.However, there is a catch.  I have a number of durability concerns for the 660's.  First, I wish that Creative would start to design angled plugs rather than the straight ones that both the 660's and the 830's share.  The straight plug makes strain and bending much more likely when using with an mp3 player.  In addition, the 660's seem even more fragile than the 830's. My hair is mid-length, colored (at home), medium thick and wavy/curly (depending on humidity!). I've used a LOT of conditioning products and hair "masks" over the years so I have a fairly broad frame of reference to products that are out there. Some are better than others at keeping hair smooth (at least for a few hours) and unfrizzy. In my experience, shine comes from adding a glossy spray (after drying and styling) or something like a Frizz-Ease silicone-based serum to wet or damp hair. Not via a rinse-off or leave-on conditioner or mask.Had heard a lot about the "authentic Moroccan argan oil" ingredient in this and other products and wanted to give it a try.Out of the package, it's a bit more liquid than a cream. I guess I had been expecting a firmer, cream-like consistency but no matter. The key thing I found is to be very careful about NOT putting too much on your hair. Followed instructions and found myself spending extra time to rinse it off (it just seemed like it wasn't rinsing out).Scent is highly personal and subjective. I personally did not like it while using in showr (it smells good at first, in the packaging) and really did not like it when my dried hair also smelled like it (I don't like products where the scent isn't washed out. I don't want scented hair.)I did not use the matching shampoo and I wonder if the mask works better AFTER shampooing with the specific shampoo. (double dose of argan oil?)I let my hair dry naturally (curls/waves), blew it out straight and also set hair to dry to see difference in impact the treatment had. In every instance, my hair was softer to the touch and seemed smoother to the eye. However, there was no increase in shine.Having used no other hair products with this argan oil ingredient, I can't say how this product compares to others in terms of features and performance. Given the price, it's probably worth a shot to see if it works for you.However, if you are definitely looking for shine (as in the company's description of "Shine Mask"), I think you may be disappointed with this product.FYI: I wonder how much of the argan oil is actually in the product as it is listed pretty far down on the ingredients listing.

The Archos AV504 wins by price in a big way, with Epson a close runner-up, and edging out Archos for picture quality. For my two cents worth, I'd buy the Archos and use the money I saved on a Nano.

I've owned this camera for 3-months and waited until now to write a review because it was a gift and I really wanted to like this camera. But the more I've used it the less I like it. To be fair, it can take a descent picture under optimal conditions if you are careful, but so can a 1968 Kodak Brownie in the right hands. I really expected more from Nikon and modern electronic technology.Let me give you a little more background... I'm 63 years old and I've been taking pictures since I was 8 years old. Last winter I suffered a stroke which affected the coordination in my left hand and I found it difficuly to operate my Nikon D50 SLR. My wife, trying to be nice to me bought an S6100 for my birthday because she assumed that a point-and-shoot would be easier and less frustrating for me to use than my D50 SLR. I was excited to get it and try it out. The Nikon S6100 was smaller, lighter and easier to carry. As far as being easier to use,it is NOT! A person would expect an automatic point-and-shoot camera to be just that, point it, press the shutter release and get a fair picture most of the time. That's something this camera can't do with any regularity. A pox on Nikons house for the damn touch screen controls! Why have a touch screen shutter release function that duplicates the function of the shutter release button? While you try to hold the camera with your right hand you are almost forced to touch the screen while trying to frame the image and push the "real button". This more often than not activates the shutter resulting in a picture of the ground, your pant leg, or shoe. Then while you wait for the exceedingly slow electronics to store that image on the memory card, you miss several oportunities to try for a good shot. Would that this was the only problem with the touch screen. Nikon designed this cameras controls so the ONLY way to control various camera functions is through a menu system controlled using the touch screen. If that were not bad enough the screen itself is not sensitive enough to respond well to a finger touch unless you use a long finger nail or the little stylus hung on the wrist strap. This almost insures that you can't make any sort of quick option changes while you try to shoot. You may wonder if that screen does anything else. Yes, it shows a fairly bright image to use as a viewfinder or to review pictures of your shoes taken by mistake. Of course it is constantly smugged and dirty because you have to be touching it all the time.How about the overall function? The S6100 is as functional as most of it's competitors in the crowded point-and-shoot field. It's a snapshot camera at best loaded with difficult to control features and totally unecessary post shooting editing functions that are much better done on your computer after you download the pictures. I expected better from Nikon and I certainly thought that a 16 megapixel sensor would capture better quality shots. Again I was disappointed. My 6 megapixel D50 captures better images and it's over 5-years old. In anything other than optimal light, the automatic functions of the S6100 bump up the ISO a few clicks and once that's happened the image quickly gets grainy without gaining good exposure. Again I sure expected better from the newer class of sensors and software. The S6100 can also take Quicktime movies with a single press of the movie button on the back. This would be a nice function if the movie button were not small  placed directly below the right side thumb grip, almost ensuring that you will take some short movies you didn't want, again usually of the ground, your shoe, or the sky.Oh, and then there is battery life. Not too good. I can get maybe 200 shots and a short movie before the "battery exhausted" message pops up on the screen, and then you are done since the only way to recharge it is to plug the whole camera into the charger or a computer USB port, you will be out of luck in the field unless you invest in a second battery, keep it charged and in your pocket while you'r out shooting.Do you think I've been be too negative about the S6100?Here are the good things about it:1. System: Macintosh OS 10.3.9 on an iBook G4I bought way more GB than I needed (I only really needed 60-80GB, but at the time the price difference between the sizes was minimal with a huge discount on this device) in purchasing this item. My Macintosh is getting older (almost four years) and I have not been responsible in backing it up and decided to begin that process in case it spontaneously combusts at some point in the near future.I bought this one because it seemed simple, straight forward, and not space consuming. Also, for about $10 more I got three times or more the space (hard drive ~$70 when purchased). Even if I didn't need that space now, it seemed like a good idea.When it arrived, my first impression was that their marketing design folks are geniuses. The box is simple and clean and each little bag is taped with an orange sticker that reads "hello." The instruction manual is streamlined and candid and I had the first impression of a friendly down to earth company. Installation involved plugging it in.And I waited for it to show up and be recognized by my hard drive.And waited. I double checked the connection. The hard drive was recognizing that it was plugged in but my laptop was not recognizing the hard drive. I went through all the steps in their trouble shooting information on their website, and still nothing. So I contacted them through their online chat service and they told me to return it to the store. So, back to amazon it went.My new one arrived and was recognized by my laptop. I backed up my system and went to dismount it. Three or four different methods of dismounting were attempted, and each time I got the notice that it could not be ejected because the disk was still in use. I quit every program I thought was running and it still wouldn't eject. Half an hour later I realized that Norton was still running in the background even though I thought I had turned it off. The disk ejected once Norton was switched off (again).While that latter part wasn't strictly Seagate's problem, with nearly every computer being protected by Norton or something like Norton, you would think that something would be said about turning Norton off. My trust is also shaken of this device's long term abilities because of the defunct one that I received before. I also really wish that the software that Windows users have access to was accessible to Macintosh as well, from what I can tell they would be convenient in managing my back up drive.**Clarification**No, I don't give Seagate a low rating simply because of the software problem. And if this is a Mac problem, perhaps they shouldn't advertise the hard drive as useable on both Windows and Mac.Months later, even with Norton turned off Seagate regularly freezes my entire system, causing me to have to restart my computer, which then messes with the external hard drive. The only time my Mac has ever frozen has been when it is plugged into the Seagate hard drive. It kind of defeats the point of having an external hard drive if I've had to reformat it four times because of this problem.

I used to have the 'standard' blenders you can buy in every store and I was never happy with how they worked. After the last one broke, I decided to invest in a better blender. Reading some reviews including ConsumerReports, I kind of got my focus on this one for several reasons: price - i was not going to pay >$100 for a blender, performance and rating, and the fact that I already have a food processor so don't really need a blender that is designed to be a food processor too.I got the Ninja at $40 during a sale which was really a great deal. I have used it a few times now so this is really a sort of a first impression rather than a long term review however I believe there are already some good and less good things that are pretty evident.The good:There's a lot of good here. Price is the first one - this device is very reasonably priced. You get 3 different sets in one which is nice. I expect to use the 'pitcher' container and blades the most - they are kind of the "traditional" blender I was looking for.Power and blending/crushing performance is excellent comparing to other blenders I had. fruit and ice blend quickly and smoothly.Noise level is very reasonable too.Assembly and operation are very simple. It really takes a few seconds to "figure out" how to assemble the device and it's ready to work.Operation is pretty simple - there is just one "button" to push which is equivalent to the "pulse" button on other devices. The device is not designed to work for a long stretch of time - it is designed to work in 20 sec intervals.build quality seems to be excellent too. All the parts look robust and though they are plastic, it looks like very high quality material (and they're BPA free too).Parts are dishwasher safe and cleaning is easy.Some of things I found that were not as good:FIRST - none of the points below are a deal breaker. Not even close. These are all things that would be nice to improve (if they ever have something like a "version 2" of the device) but definitely not things that should scare anyone away from buying this device.So first, the power cord is very short. It would be nice to have a slightly longer cord.then there is the way the device is built. As you probably noticed, the device motor is on the top and the container is on the bottom. I'm not sure why it was built this way but what it means is that opening the container to add ingredients or to check on the contents (sometimes it's hard to just see through the container what's going on inside of the container. If you ever used a blender you'd know that) is a little more complicated than in 'traditional' blenders. Not a big deal though, but still worth mentioning. There is a small lid that can be opened for adding ingredients while the lid and top are still on but it's a small lid and is not too convenient to use.Bottom line is i'm very happy with this blender and highly recommend it.

For the past couple of years I've been dreaming of a pocket size Internet tablet in order to replace my outstanding but aging HP 2415 PDA.So far, LATTE folks seem to be the only manufacturer smart enough to put in the market a 5 inch Internet tablet that is more than a simple MP3 music player!When I saw this five inches machine with Android 2.3, Android market, USB and HDMI connections (BUT NO Bluetooth, NO Adobe 10.1 flash and NO GPS), I thought this would be the replacement that I had been yearning for.  Unfortunately, it is NOT!Maybe I was unlucky and it's my machine that was defective but here are the lacks and issues that I encountered after two weeks of very moderate use.1) LOOOONG TO TURN ON (800 MHZ).  Unlike my good old PDA, which turns on in a fraction of a second as soon as I hit the button, the Latte Ice Smart needs MORE THAN TWO MINUTES before you can reach the home page.  When you turn it on, it takes more than a minute before you see a first screen with a big clock and 2 messages ("No service") and a brief message on the toolbar saying: "Preparing Nand memory", followed later by another one that says "Scanning SD memory".  At this point, you press the "menu" key and wait another minute to see the home page which otherwise will never open!  Now you can open your files except video.As for the video, it won't even open the "Gallery" until it has scanned the micro SD card containing all photos and videos.  This will take another 90 seconds or so.  That's AT LEAST THREE MINUTES AND THIRTY SECONDS TO OPEN THE GALLERY from the time you turned on the machine.  As long as you see a wheel turning in the toolbar, it won't open it.  Once it has scanned your card, you may open the Gallery but then you have to wait one more minute until it "loads" your files.  You are now almost FIVE MINUTES since turn on!2) NO INFRARED, NO BLUETOOTH.  This means that you can't use portable keyboards like the excellent PALM Infrared folding device, which is a full keyboard when open but folds down to only 3 1/2 by 5 1/4 inches and therefore fits in your pocket!  I bought a USB IR key from Tiger store on Flagler Street that I hooked to the OTG cable but it didn't work either.NEITHER will it take a BLUETOOTH folding keyboard similar to my IR from Palm, even if you buy a USB Bluetooth key as I did from Amazon.  The manufacturer sent me an e-mail clearly saying:"Our device doesn't support IR. So it will not work with IR keyboard nor Bluetooth keyboard. It will only work with regular 2.4 Ghz wireless keyboards which have wireless adapter (which will connect to OTG)"The only problem is that those who make 2.4 Ghz keyboards are NOT smart enough to make a full keyboard that folds into 3.5 by 5.25 inches like the Palm IR, so that you can put it in your pocket!  They are all huge desk keyboards!  Please gentlemen!  How about putting your brains to work?  Try a fish diet; sometimes it helps!You can therefore only use a USB keyboard BUT the smallest I found is 5.5 by 9 inches, made for 7 inches tablets and therefore won't fit in your pocket.3) AVERAGE BATTERY ~ I ran TWO BATTERY TESTS:First, for music.  With Wi-Fi and screen off, it ran continuously during nine hours before turning off at 10%, which is not so much: all my Chopin and Lily Laskine CDs went through.  That's slightly more than my HP PDA, which uses 9% of power per hour of music when I walk along the beach listening to Nana Mouskouri or Sarah Brightman with the PDA in my pocket.  That's with a Compact Flash 32 Gb card.  If I use a Seagate or a Hitachi microdrive, which is the size of a CF card type II, then my PDA uses more power (about 12% per hour)Secondly, I ran a test with video concerts.  I could see the first two concerts of Celtic Woman (3 hours for both) plus the first part of Andre Rieu in Tuscany.  Grand total was almost four hours, which is not so much either.4) Finally, I had PROBLEMS WITH VIDEO PLAYING after ten days of very sporadic use.First, I could only hear the sound but there was no image.  The screen showed all my DVD files but as soon as I pressed on one of them the screen suddenly became black and I could only hear the sound.I ran a reset by inserting a paper clip in a little hole next to the micro SD card and it worked again.But then the film stopped after a few minutes (with a full battery) and I had to turn it on again.  After it happened three times, I requested an RMA from Amazon, which sent me the label to return it for free, as usual.Amazon's outstanding returning policy makes me buy more and more from them.  I started with a few DVD orders the first year and now I have placed more than sixty orders in eleven months.  HONESTY PAYS!Maybe I had a defective device?  I don't know but I didn't want to take any chances and requested a refund from Amazon, which I usually get in a couple of days, unlike some Marketplace merchants who need ten days after they receive the merchandise!GOOD POINTS: I deeply regret these lacks and failures of the Latte Ice Smart 5 because, although slow and imperfect, I loved this little machine a lot due to the size, small enough to fit in a shirt pocket.  Furthermore, unlike my Archos 604 and other machines, which don't read the real thing unless you convert it to AVI, it reads both MPEG 2 AND MPEG 4 files.  See more about this in my Skypad review.On the other hand, it has a USB + an HDMI ports, which is very convenient because you may hook a second memory SD or USB jumpdrive (works like the Skypad Alpha for which I detailed the mechanism) and also allows you to watch your videos on a big TV, although I have never seen a hotel TV with HDMI yet.  Maybe they do have it at the Sheraton but since I'm a simple professor working almost for free, that's not the kind of place where I usually go...  I'm already happy enough when I find a composite connection in my usual budget hotels over three continents!After I returned this machine, I discovered and purchased a SAMSUNG GALAXY 5" MP3 MEDIA PLAYER that has Android 2.3, Bluetooth (therefore possible folding Bluetooth keyboard) and GPS BUT NO HDMI or any possibility to see a video on a big screen.  I hoped I could use my Archos 604 cable that plugs into the headphone input with a composite connection at the other end but it didn't work. I took it on my trip to Montevideo for Thanksgiving weekend and I am quite happy so far.  I'll write a detailed review in January, after I will take it on my trip to Paris next week, then again to Montevideo at the end of December.
