The Max Burton 6200 lets you get the performance and control of a good gas cooktop, but do so anywhere you have an electrical outlet. It works well, but the marketing literature promises FAR more than this unit can deliver. However, if you know what to expect before you buy, you can be quite happy with this purchase.I originally rated this with a five star rating, but reduced it to three stars after I realized that the unit does NOT contain a real temperature control that actually measures the temperature and then adjusts the energy being supplied.Like any tool, you need to understand it completely in order to get the best results. The manual is quite basic, and doesn't tell you everything you need to know, and the marketing specs make you think it has certain features which, in fact, it does not. To help you out, I did some extensive testing, and these tests should provide you with some important insights into how best to use this appliance.Let me share with you what I have learned.To keep things simple, all of my tests were done with a four quart All-Clad saucepan, filled with exactly one quart of water. I used a Thermapen thermometer to make all my measurements (in Fahrenheit). This thermometer is quite accurate, and gives the same results every time. To measure the power consumed, I used a Kill-A-Watt power meter.My first test was to put the saucepan with one quart of water onto my Thermador 11,000 BTU/hour cooktop, using the largest burner set to the highest setting. I measured the water temperature before I turned on the burner, and then let the burner run for exactly two minutes, without stirring, and without a lid on the pot. I immediately took the pan off the heat, stirred the water a few times, and then took the temperature.I then repeated this same test with a new quart of water, but this time on the 6200 induction cooktop, with the control set to level 10, the top level. When you press the on/off button, the unit always starts with the power level set to 5, so I had to press the button five times to get to the top level.My gas range raised the temperature by 60.5 degrees in two minutes, and the Max Burton 6200 raised the temperature by 63.4 degrees in the same amount of time.So, very much to my surprise, this device heated the water faster than the largest burner on my gas stove! I knew it would be faster than a standard electric stove, but I had not expected these results.This is VERY impressive.My next test was to see how well it can hold a given temperature. Unfortunately, the model 6200 only provides a few temperature settings below 212 degrees. Most of the temperature settings seem to be designed for candy making, deep-fat frying, and searing.I set the temperature to 150 degrees (by pressing the function button until the display showed a temperature), and then took temperature measurements every few minutes. The water quickly came up to 150, but then kept going ... and going ... and going. After fifteen minutes it was still inching upwards, eventually reaching 173 degrees. I had the sense that it might continue to get a little warmer, but I didn't wait any longer.Later in the day I did some more thorough tests using the temperature control while measuring the power used by the unit. What I found out is this:The temperature control does NOT use a temperature sensor!!What this means it that you can heat the water to boiling (212F), and then set the temperature control to 100 degrees (Farenheit) and the unit will still supply EXACTLY the same on/off cycle as it does when the pan contains 50 degree water direct from the tap.I was not willing to believe that the marketing literature would promise temperature control, and yet not actually provide a product that sensed temperature and then modified the power setting based on what was sensed. I thought, perhaps, that the temperature sensor might only work for the higher settings. So, I put my Lodge cast iron skillet on the burner and set the temperature to 350 degrees. I monitored the skillet surface temperature with an infrared "point-n-shoot" thermometer. Once again, the power cycling, measured by my power meter, was exactly the same at the beginning of the cycle, when the pan was dead cold, as it was when the pan reached 400 degrees (well past the 350 degree setting) and began to smoke a little.So, bottom line: you should forget that this unit claims to have a temperature control because IT DOES NOT!Fortunately, it is still a very useful cooktop. In fact, not one range or cooktop I have used in the past sixty years has had a temperature control. However, if you buy this unit because you were hoping to have a closed-loop temperature control unit, then you will be disappointed and angry.The people at Aervoe Industries (they manufacture Max Burton appliances) should definitely be taken out behind the wood shed and given a lashing for promising something in their marketing literature that is not true.My next step was to measure the electric power consumption for the ten different power levels, and also for the ten temperature settings. It was these tests that gave me a lot of insight into how the unit functions.First, here are the power measurements at each of the ten power levels. This was done with my four quart All-Clad. I should point out that the highest power I ever saw on the meter was 1580 watts. However, I later did a few tests with a very large Dutch oven, and measured a much higher wattage, close to 1700 watts. So, the amount of power delivered (and used) depends on the cookware used.Level  Watts1  0 - 580 (cycles on/off)2  0 - 770 (cycles on/off)3  8964  10505  11206  12007  12808  13709  142010  1520I learned several important things. The first is that levels 1 and 2 are quite different from the other settings. They are MUCH lower power than the other settings, both because the maximum power is less, and because the heat is cycled on and off about every 5-8 seconds. However, as soon as you bump up the power to level 3, the cooktop heats with a wattage that is more than half of what is supplied during full power, and the power stays constant at whatever level is set, with no on/off cycling at all. From that point (level 3) upward, every increase adds about 80 watts to the previous setting.I then did a similar test for the temperature settings. What I found is that the power being supplied is the same as what you get at each of the ten power levels. What I mean is that each temperature setting operates at a different power level. I think these power levels are the exact same levels as when you set the power manually. I realize that the numbers I show here are not exactly identical, but when I repeated each of the tests (I'm an engineer, and we're taught to do that), I never got exactly the same results, both for the power and for the temperature tests. It appears that the power supplied may be modified by the internal temperature of the cooktop (there is a fan that cools the interior of the cooktop).Whatever the reason, each time I did the tests, I got wattage readings that were sometimes different by as much as 100 watts. This is no big deal because the controls on even the most professional cooktop are not all that precise.So, here is what I got for each temperature setting:Temp  Watts100  0 - 540150  0 - 740210  890250  1090280  1160320  1245360  1325390  1410430  1455450  1560So, given that the unit clearly does NOT contain a temperature sensor, here is the big discovery: the power settings and the temperature settings are exactly the same thing!! So, don't even bother with the temperature controls because they don't do anything useful.So, now that I know all this good stuff, how do I use it?Well, I see no reason to use this device differently than I have used any other cooking appliance for the past sixty years. If I want to heat something fast, I'll crank it up to the top setting, and then if I want to slow down the cooking, I'll set it lower.  Duh. However, when I need lower heat for simmering, I will definitely be using the lowest settings (1 & 2), and will be very conscious of the rather large "bump" when going to level 3.Before I finish, I should make a comment about the size of this unit. The measurements given in the specs are quite accurate, but somehow it didn't sink in how large it is. For instance, I have a 12" Lodge cast iron skillet, and it fits on this unit with very little overhang. I think I read several reviews that suggested that a 12" skillet went over the top of the controls, but this is most definitely not the case. You can use a 12" skillet with no problem.Another thing I should mention: someone said it took a long time to set the timer because after you have pressed the function button to enter the timer mode, you have to press the up button 120 times to set the timer to 120 minutes. Well, there is an easier way. All you have to do is press AND HOLD the button, and while holding, the timer increments up (or down) by 15 minutes every half second. Thus, you can set the timer to any time you want in only a few seconds.I'll add some additional notes to this review after I've made a few meals. One thing I definitely want to try is deep fat frying some french fries. My plan is to take this unit out to my gas BBQ and use that as a no-cleanup enclosure (i.e., the BBQ will be turned off). I'll put the induction cooker on a flat baking sheet to protect the bottom from the greasy cooking grates. I'll then be using a trick I read about, namely I'll put a sheet of parchment paper between the pan containing the oil, and the cooktop itself. I'll let this sheet cover the controls and the cooktop, making sure to leave the fan intakes and exhaust open. So, the combination of using the BBQ enclosure, using the parchment paper, and doing the whole thing outdoors will make deep fat frying a no-cleanup proposition. I'm really looking forward to that.As for cooking tests beyond boiling water, as others have pointed out, the unit only heats about four inches in the center of the pan. You need a pan with excellent heat dispersal (like my All-Clad) in order to avoid hot spots. If I end up using this a lot, and if hot spots become a problem, then the obvious solution is to purchase the induction disk. While this is designed primarily as a way to use non-induction cookware with this unit, it also will spread out the heat across its 8" diameter surface. When using it with an induction pan, I would heat the pan without the disk and then when I need to simmer something or do cooking that requires more even heat, I'd insert the disk. I guess this is a little like using an insulating trivet with a gas stove in order to get really low simmering temperatures (most gas stoves don't have a flame that is low enough to simmer without burning).I did try it with my Lodge cast iron grill skillet, and it heated up MUCH faster than on my gas burner. However, it did heat quite unevenly, as measured by my infrared point-n-shoot thermometer. My traditional gas cooktop also creates hots spots, although these are around the edge of the pan, where the flame hits, whereas the induction cooktop creates the hot spot in the center. I was a little surprised to see this on a thick cast iron skillet. the solution, of course, is the same as what I do on the gas cooktop: move the skillet around every thirty seconds, so that the energy goes into different parts of the pan.So, in summary, I am very pleased with how fast this unit heats water, and how simple it is to use. The two things that would make it better would be to have an actual temperature control rather than a fake one, and have a larger heating area when larger pans were detected.

I recently had a kid so I wanted a camera for taking indoor, low-light shots.  I bought both the Canon S90 and the K-X because both are top-rated for low-light shots.  Surprisingly I give the S90 a slight edge over the K-X for low-light snapshots.  S90 has a fast f/2 lens so you ISO setting is much lower.  Typical indoor night shot on the S90 is 1/30 @ 400 ISO, whereas K-x is 1/30 @ 1600 ISO.  I'd say the S90 at 400ISO is slightly clean than the K-x @ 1600ISO.  With a fast prime lens (not cheap unless you buy manual focus), the the K-x would win easily.  If you're buying a camera primarily for quality, indoor snapshots of kids, then I'd recommend the S90.  However, if you really want the features of a DSLR then you can't go wrong with the K-X.  Good all-around camera.  I like the ability to use any k-mount pentax lens.  HD video is a nice bonus.I can recommend NiZN batteries for this camera.  I've been using them for a month with this camera and they seem to work almost as well as Lithium and better than NiMH.

UPDATE: DEC 2010 - As was recommended in comments,  I updated the firmwear.  Mode dial sensitivity and roller bar problems are gone. I give this camera now 5 Stars.Previous review BEFORE firmwear update:The TL-350 has more features than most equivalent cameras, and takes decent photos even at higher ISO levels (ISO 400 is quite good). But it needs some attention.  I purchased it to replace a dropped LUMIX DMC LZ5, which was a great travel workhorse. The Samsung takes reasonable RAW, processes them quickly, and has a very usable zoom range. Lens is fairly fast. 1080p video is great, panorama stitching is great, takes both raw and jpeg simultaneously, takes jpegs while in video mode, and has reasonable battery life.The good: Small, and feature packed. Feels very well built. Takes nice travel quality photos ONCE you figure out how to press the forward-angled shutter release without touching the mode dial. The two analog battery and memory storage capacity dials actually are a nice touch.The bad: The top mode dial is extremely sensitive. Will shift you in and out of mode just by touching it. Caused ghosting of images, much like double exposures. Keep your shutter finger away from it.The rear "roller" selector for adjusting bracketing fps and shutter timer is another weird one. You have to keep rolling it like a low res pc trackball to select what you want. An annoyance. ISO 80 is not as noise free as I would have expected, but noise does not increase significantly at higher ISOs.Bottom line: I came close to returning it due to the undocumented "double exposure feature", but took the time to work through it's quirks's. A professional photographer friend claimed my pictures were of "average" quality, which I took as "pretty good" for the sensor size and camera cost.  If you want to play with high-end camera features, but are not willing to go to the larger form factor and cost of a micro 4/3 to get better quality, this will do it for under $300.October 2010 Update: one month later - the high speed video recording is a blast - playback in slo-mo shows you a whole new set of micro features of your world you never appreciated. Worth buying for this feature alone, especially if you have children or pets. Re: picture quality - as stated above, high ISO photos are very good, and now appreciate that the dual anti-shake mode works so well in low light. I have not owned a camera yet this versatile. Would go five stars if it had just a bit better picture quality when shooting at "optimal" settings (e.g. ISO 80) and did not have the roller bar control mentioned above.  Analog dials are now addictive. Give this serious thought if you are a looking for rewarding "play with" camera.

I have seen a lot of reviews complaining about the touch screen of this device, and I must say that was the major drawback to this device. I would touch an L, but an S would appear onscreen. I'd try to erase a letter or number, and the number 7 or a p would show up, etc. Very frustrating and time consuming. Well, I CALIBRATED the touch screen, which I was instructed to do by a Garmin rep (and there are instructions way in the back of the instruction manual, which is available at Garmin.com as a PDF file). The difference is AMAZING. The screen is now responsive and accurate, and inputting directions is quick and easy. So much better than before, struggling to type in numbers and letters in the driveway, erasing a few and starting over, all while getting later and later for your destination.My previous model was a StreetPilot III, which I purchased for a mere $700 just 8 years ago or so, so I am VERY happy with this newer model's sensitivity to satellites, accuracy to position, and information available. However, I did have to take some points off for some quirks in the software. I did a firmware upgrade, and I did purchase the lifetime map updates on Cyber Monday sale (which is kind of a rip off but they've always been this way), but I still get some funky directions I know to be wrong: I was told to take a right onto a side street that didn't exist (after the update); I was told to leave a street, go a half-mile west and then come back east to the original street and continue on. I was told to go one block north of a major road and struggle on the side streets with much slower speed limits on one occasion. Once I was told to take a large road with dozens of traffic lights instead of the highway with none, for a rather long drive of about 12 miles, and another time I was instructed to leave a major highway and suffer through rush-hour side streets in the wrong part of town for 10 miles to get to my destination. Fortunately I was only "tricked" into the last joyride. But it shows that the map service is still pretty unreliable, because these are a pretty large percentage of the times I've used this device, as most of the time I don't need it in my hometown. And by the way, I live in suburban Kansas City, ONLY ABOUT 10 MILES FROM GARMIN'S HEADQUARTERS, so it's pretty unforgivable that I should have so many mapping errors in their hometown. I've had to cross-reference my directions with my iPhone's FREE navigation app.So the touchscreen is infinitely better these days, but I had to deduct for unreliable mapping and having to pay for updates to a device I've already purchased.

Although this sharpener is lightweight and simple to use, it actually seemed to further dull our Wusthof Classic chef's knife.  It also scratched up the sides of the blade about an inch from the edge.  Obviously, we won't use it for that knife any longer, and are back to our diamond sharpening stone for now.  Maybe it'll work on our other knives.  Cook's Illustrated magazine noted that Asian knife blades have a 15-degree angle, whereas Western knives have a 20-degree angle.  They seem to like the Chef's Choice 110, which is an electric device at around $80, though they don't specify for which type of knife. For the Asian knives, they like the Chef's Choice 463, or the electric 130, 315S and 1520, pricey from $100 to $150.Update: We bought another sharpener, the Wüsthof 2-Stage Knife Sharpener, for $20.  We happened to see it at Williams-Sonoma, so we bought it there, but it's almost the same price on Amazon.  The Wusthof is a far superior sharpener, and I highly recommend it over the Chef's Choice, especially for high-quality knives.  It is also light and easy to use.  There are some 140+ Amazon reviewers who gave it high marks.  As some have added to comments about it, you shouldn't sharpen your knives every day or after every use.  Use a steel (that textured rod that comes with most knife sets) instead to re-align the blade edge, and only sharpen (which actually removes metal from the blade) after the steel no longer helps the edge stay sharp (maybe once a week or every other week).  On the Wusthof sharpener, one slot is for coarser sharpening, and the other is for finer honing. There's also a sharpener in it for scissors.  One test for sharpness is holding a piece of newspaper up by the edge and running the blade down into it from the top edge.  If it slices cleanly and easily, it's sharp enough.

I've tried a lot of different iPad cases that work with keyboards and this one came up short. But first, what I did like:I do like the keyboard. The feel of the keystrokes was solid and mechanical, not soft and squishy as even laptop keyboards are now. And of course, having an on-off switch so I can switch off the keyboard rather than turn off Bluetooth on my iPad to keep it from phantom typing in my bag is just common sense. (Hear that, Apple?) And it charges through USB instead of with batteries. I always have a mini-USB to USB cable for one thing or another in my bag, but my rechargeable batteries are always at home where they don't do me any good if my Apple keyboard dies when I'm out. (Talking to you, Apple!)Now for what I didn't like. First, the case does not have the Smart Cover magnets so it doesn't turn off when you close the lid. You have to remember to manually switch it off.Second, unlike previous Belkin keyboard cases like this in the past, this one does not have a way to fold the keyboard safely out of the way when not in use. At least as far as I could figure out. Instead, you end up with the keyboard face down on whatever surface you put the iPad on which can be awkward or even damaging.Third, I never could get the magnetic flap that's supposed to keep the cover closed to stay out of the way when I was using the iPad. It's supposed to fold under and stay in place with a magnet, but the connection was never strong enough to hold it.Fourth, the case is just so bulky and yet it's such a struggle to get the iPad in or out. I didn't like the exposed seams or stitching or the overall styling. The bit of the case around the screen was substantial enough that it got annoying trying to drag things to the edge. For the same $100, there are plenty of other folio-style keyboard cases that are sleeker and more stylish. The Logitech keyboard cover comes to mind, although it's not a full coverage case.So I can't recommend this combination, but if Belkin sold the keyboard by itself for about 40% of the price, that would be a real good deal. (I'm talking to you, Belkin!)

Half the time these bunny ears work well, but the other half of the time we have huge reception problems. I took the unit apart and this is what I've been able to figure out so far.* The flat PCB is about 1x1' and poorly constructed.  Low grade PCB, weak solder points as well as improperly soldered points, and materials were starting to oxidize.* Coax cable going from the antenna to the amplifier, as well as the coax from the amplifier to the end you plug into your receiver, is un-shielded coax that is highly susceptible to local electromagnetic interference.Since having an antenna (even a bad one) is usually better than no antenna at all, I'm going to use what's left of this unit until my non-RCA replacement arrives early next week. I got this camera because I wanted something lighter than my K-5, with a larger sensor and greater resolution than my FZ150.  I wanted decent burst speed and depth, good tele capabilities, and good IQ.  In theory the G5 fit the bill, although the burst function wasn't as good as either of the above cameras.  But I was willing to accept that as part of the trade-off in size, weight and sensor.Initial impressions:--The body is synthetic material, but feels strong and solid.  Kevlar is synthetic, too, and it stops bullets.--Much lighter than a DLSR like, say, the K-5, or even the K-r.  With lens attached, heavier than my FZ150, but not enough to really notice.--Made in China (lens made in Japan).  China makes the world's fastest bullet train, the world's fastest electric-powered car, and a lot of other good stuff.  So the "made in China" label doesn't worry me and I'm not going to blame anything on the supposed inherent defects in Chinese manufacture (something often seen on Amazon camera review pages).  They get the specs from Pany.--Not flat like, say, the NEX cameras, but for me the curves make it easier to grip and use.--From the rear and from the top (or from the bottom), amazingly similar in size and profile to the FZ150.--The location of various switches (On-Off, exposure toggle) is a little odd compared to previous and current cameras I have owned/own, but I imagine I'll get used to it.--Eyepiece is very nice size.--Fully articulated LCD screen is good, although a bit small.Bad:--Lens cap works well, but no string or thread to attach it to the camera with?  This is basic.  Charge me another 5 cents and give me something truly functional.--160 minimum 1SO will require forgetting all the situation & exposure settings that I've learned from years of working with cameras with ISO 100 as the baseline.--The control dial and buttons look cheap and tinny, and the control dial feels that way.--The 4-way controller (ISO, WB, Macro, Burst/Timer) is chrome on chrome, which makes it impossible to read.  Every other camera I've ever owned was white lettering/icons on black.  There is absolutely nothing good about this distinctive approach.--Exposure via a lever instead of a wheel is going to take some getting used to.  Also the display is counterintuitive and will take more getting used to.  Not sure what Pany thought could be accomplished by this approach.--Minimalist approach to info display (exposure, etc.) is hard to read.So far, I don't find it very easy to work with compared to most (all) of the other cameras, from old Canon P&S;, a variety of bridge cameras and DSLRs of various brands.Functioning and IQ:I should make it clear that I push cameras in terms of using maximum zoom, shooting in very high-contrast situations, and action.  For someone who does other things, this camera may be totally different.  For example, I rarely shoot in low light and this may be a strong point of this camera.  So far I haven't tested the low light capabilities.--Burst depth at high speed (SDHC Class 10 card) was 16 frames before slowing down.  RAW burst depth at any speed was 8 frames.  This is a bit less than expected from online reviews (18 and 9 frames)Images:-- "Easy" shots (no extremes of contrast and lighting, well-defined edges, not a lot of detail) are very good.--Images with the 45-200 lens are pretty bad.  Not only soft, but edges in areas of fine detail and high contrast are choppy both in JPEG and RAW.  Foliage tends to have a paintbrush effect.  My FZ150 does better, to say nothing of the 55-300mm kit lens on my K-r, an APS-C 12mp camera.--In many ways I was more impressed with the ZS15 and the LF1.So now I have to decide if I want to return the lens, hope that was the problem, but still end up with a camera that is in many ways less comfortable and effective than my FZ150, to say nothing of the K-5.  I may wait for the Fuji X-E2.-----------------------------UPDATE 11-17-2013I decided to go for a major upgrade.  I returned the camera and lenses (best to start clean) and ordered a GH3, which is due to arrive in a couple of days. Also ordered a 14-140mm for a walk-around lens and a 100-300mm for long-distance surfing images. Both Panasonic. For video I have my eye on the power zoom 45-175mm, but we'll see about that one.After a lot of research, I went with the GH3 because I'm getting more into hybrid photography and want solid video capability as well as good IQ in stills. Burst speed is only 6fps (which I find is minimal but acceptable for most action that I shoot) but the JPEG burst depth is somewhere around 100 frames (depending on the card used) and the RAW is about 18 (one test achieved 24 with a super-fast card) so I think I'm winning on that score.

This is my second 5n. My first was returned before being aware of the Service Call issued by Sony for the clicking issue. I sent the first one for an exchange and then found out about the call. Immediately upon receiving my exhange I sent the body in for the click repair. Approximately 10 days later I had the body back in hand and while the clicking sound was resolved there was a new sound problem that was even worse. My revised rating and review is based off the poor experience with Sony Technical Support and the repair of the issue.I contacted Sony Service using the repair number of my Service Call repair, after receiving my "repaired" 5n and noticing the new sound issue. A day later I received an email advising I would receive a response soon.Two days later I receive an email from a Tech stating they would overnight the body and expedite the repair. I am excited at this point thinking I would be able to get this resolved. I respond with information about lens used and what I have noticed as well as a link to a video that exhibits the problem.The next day notice a missed call but no voicemail. I later find out they tried to call but I was not avialable. I call Sony Service and reference the email about the expedited return and repair as well as my original repair #. I am told the person that emailed me is out of the office for X amount of time and that a new Tech would contact me. Again they do call but not when Im available, but do leave a voicemail that I should call back. I call back and Im told that I am already in line to get a call from a Tech. I explain that he tried to call and left a message stating I should call back. The person again states that the Tech is already set to call me.The next day I get the call. The tech apparently is unaware of the issue as he immediately starts explaining that Sony has a Service Notice for the clicking. I have to explain that the camera has already been sent in for that issue and that the problem is something else. I offer to provide links to two videos that exhibit the problem. The Tech instructs me to hang up and respond with the links in an email he will send me. I get the email shortly after and respond with the links to the videos.Two days later and I do not receive a phone call nor an email response. This puts me just 4 days of my return window with Amazon closing so I am forced to return the defective camera for refund. I simply cannot risk missing my return option to only find out later that Sony does not fix the issue with this body.PROS..Exceptional IQ >JPegs from camera match the 7D IQ in most situations including high ISO. The 5n seems to be a little more particular about lighting though.Features >List of features is nice like Panoramo, HDR and other effects.Manual Modes >Camera gives you plenty of control.CONS..Clicking Sound >Its well documented that the 5n has a clicking sound during video recording caused by an internal part moving around. Sony has offered a free update but even the info on their page states thatit REDUCES the noise. Apparently the fix involves placing grease or something on the part to dampen the noise ? This sounds temporary to me and as stated there is no guarantee it will fix theissue completely. This is a big CON in my opinion since HD video is a very big feature of this camera and it was marketed as such.10 FPS >Yes this sounds like a PRO but not when you only get about 10 shots before the buffer is full.The clicking sound ruins this camera for me. It amazes me these days how products make it through production with these issues and are not recalled (Asus Transformer Prime GPS ring a bell?). To me this is an unacceptable flaw.

I have both this speaker system and theAltec Lansing VS26212.1 Speaker System.  I will use this review as a comparison between the two systems.  Hopefully that will you a good idea of relative strengths and weaknesses of this Logitech system.This system's PROS:1. This system is fairly attractive looking to have on display; both the speakers and subwoofer.2. The wire that runs from the subwoofer to the speakers in just a stereo headphone cable, which is terrific, since it means you have the flexibility to extend it (however see CON 4 also).3. I love the fact that the power button is on a little wired remote control device with the volume control also.  (The Altec Lansing system has the power switch on the back of the subwoofer and the volume control on the right speaker.)This system's CONS:1. There are no equalization controls whatsoever, not even subwoofer controls.  That means that you are stuck with the EQ settings from the factory, like it or not. (see CON 2)2. I don't like the sound...  When the volume is down, there is very little bass, so it sounds tinny and too high-frequency weighted.  When turned up loud, the bass is better, but still too much high and not even low for me.3. There just isn't enough amplification to get very loud.  The loudest setting isn't impressive, especially when compared to the comparable Altec Lansing system.  There is a noticeable difference in volume when switching the headphone jack from system to system.4. The way the wires run, you don't have a whole lot of length for the farthest speaker from the subwoofer.  Uniquely from the systems I've seen, this has a stereo headphone cable from the subwoofer that directly splits to each speaker.  Many computer speaker systems will have a cable going to the right speaker, then the left speaker plugs into the right speaker, giving lots of flexibility in putting the left speaker far from the subwoofer.  Since you could extend this with a common cable, it isn't a terrible thing.What I care the most is the sound quality and the "boom."  This system doesn't have either that is up to my expectations.

Well, I tried out my Dad's VM4 for a few weeks, thinking I wanted something a little more ergonomic and nicer than the mouse I have now, even though I don't have joint pain. I spend a lot of time in front of computers though, so I wanted to take preventative measures. I tried to like the VM4. I really did. But there's no chemistry between us. There are just too many problems.The deal breaker was this: my hand is too big for it. I don't think my hands are big; they're standard size for piano playing, and my fingers stretch to the length of an octave. Still, the fingers between my pinky and thumb are too long for the mouse. So I have to change how I handle the mouse, which is no good because it just makes my fingers and hands hurt, thus defeating the point of the VM4.One unique issue--easily fixed with a software patch--is that it crashes my computer when I plug it in. I use a MacBook Pro from 2010 with Mountain Lion and haven't heard of this happening with people who use them on PCs, so most users may be spared from this frustration.Another detriment is that there's no side scrolling. I like to enlarge the text on webpages when I read news. I didn't know how much I missed side scrolling until I didn't have it, and started using my trackpad all the time.Finally, the lights on the mouse are bright in low light and there's no way to turn them off.For the people who like it, they LOVE it, which is why I give this three stars instead of one. I've never heard anyone talk about a mouse the way the fans of the VM4 do. Gamers who have serious gaming mice with more buttons and variable weights that you can add or subtract don't care as much about mice as the VM4 users care about theirs. You may want to give the VM4 a try if standard mice simply don't work for you, or you have serious tendonitis or joint problems. Otherwise, I'm afraid I can't recommend this mouse without trying it out for a few days first.

I bought this to use during our kitchen renovation, in which I am replacing a gas range with an electric oven and a separate gas cooktop.  I waited to order the cooktop until I tried out the induction hot plate, and after using it a while chose to stay with gas.Other people have listed the pros, which I won't quibble with.  Here are the "cons" I found, having now used it for a couple of months.  First of all, my husband and I find the electrical hum (varying from almost inaudible to quite loud) quite annoying, and absolutely hate the alarm whenever you lift the pan off the plate, no matter how briefly.  Contrary to other reviews, I find the choice of compatible cookware too limiting--I don't really want to have to use a cast iron griddle whenever I want to cook bacon.  I also dislike being apparently limited to smaller diameter pans than I often like to use, but even if a multiple burner unit handled my large pans, the noise (induction hum and alarms) ruled it out for our household.I do have one usage tip.  When pan-searing food that does not cover the entire pan, even on a low numeric setting the pan overheated in areas, and the hotplate alarmed and error-coded. As the pan overlapped the margin between the unit and the control panel, it resulted in cosmetic damage to that seal/interface.  Since then I discovered that if I use a temperature setting instead of a numeric level, I get no overheating alarms, even when pan-searing meat or fish. This also works well for eggs, and other things that need to cook at lower settings/temperature.So, the hot plate is serving the purpose.  Once our renovation is complete, I will loan it to my neighbor for her kitchen update, then give it away, or perhaps store it for occasional use.

Now I'm stuck with a crappy phone, proprietary HDMI adapter that I can't use with another phone, and several charge cables which are likewise specific to this phone.I will never buy another HTC device again. A week or two after discovering this, I bought a Nexus 4 and put this in storage with the battery removed. When HTC/T-Mobile release an update I tried powering it back up ... the battery wouldn't charge at all, the phone wouldn't start. At all. T-Mobile sent a replacement (manufactured circa April, 2012), and this phone charged up the battery and started fine. With the fully charged battery back in the bad handset (the third one I'd received from T-Mobile, by the way), it would power up, but wouldn't charge at all (yes, with HTC chargers and cables, not third party accessories). This case is excellent value for money, and fits the Supernova really well. I finally found the solution !  Listen up guys and avoid heartache. All Pandigital Supernovas run on Android Gingerbread but WILL work with an external USB keyboard, like the one built into this tablet case.  I had tried several USB to mini-usb adapters and none of them worked. This was frustrating as I had seen online that some people were saying that their external keyboards worked fine and some insisted that they didn't.  The secret is that you MUST use an OTG (On The Go) USB to mini-USB adapter. This allows your adapter to work as a host for your passive keyboard, which acts as the client.  I purchased mine as part of a set of 5 adapters from here: [...].  This cost about $12.00, though you do have 4 other types of cable that you may be able to use elsewhere.  There are other places which sell these singly, and maybe cheaper, but they have to come from China, may not be as reliable, and may take a month to be delivered.  But just make sure that it is OTG and that it is a USB to mini-USB one.  Hope this works for you...I think you'll find it does.

I got this antenna because I live midway between Ft. Lauderdale and West Palm Beach, and so all the HDTV broadcast stations are either 20 or 30 miles away.  This antenna did a good job at receiving most of these channels, although I can't pull in a reliable ABC station.  In short, the antenna works, although I don't know how well it works relative to other antennas.  The Pinnacle HDTV-USB tuner I use this antenna will came with a simple, collapsable antenna, and even that thing is good enough to pick up some stations 20 miles away.  The Terk did better, but that comes with a fairly high cost.My gripe is with the design of this antenna.  The antenna cable comes out of the bottom of the base of the unit, and it can either be bent to exit the base either from the front or the back of the base.  Problem is, the cable is fairly stiff, the antenna is fairly light, and the base has a small footprint.  Put that all together, and you have a wobbly antenna caused by the cable pushing the antenna off the flat place you've set it upon.Worse, though, is that the amplified signal is a AC transformer that plugs into a little black box that attaches to the end of the antenna cable.  For me, this is a bad situation.  I'm trying to use this antenna with a laptop, and now I've got to mess with two wires -- the antenna cable + the AC transformer electric line.  Why didn't Terk just include the circuitry that amplifies the signal inside the antenna base, and have the electricity flow directly into the base?  This would make it easier to use. Although the Harmony One remote works well for "pre-programmed" devices and activities, attempting to custom program the device is a mess.First, instead of writing "real" software to run on Windows, Mac and Linux computers, Logitech opted to write a web-based application. This application starts out by requiring the user to log into the Harmony One site. Only God knows what is sent back and forth across the Internet, but the process is sinfully slow.Second, although the device is touted as being infinitely programmable it is not. You tell the software which devices you use and, if they exist in the database, their programming is added to the remote. If you need to custom program a device, you're in for a nightmare. Instead of providing a page that shows all of the Harmony's buttons and touch pad areas you are presented with a list of "commands"; those commands are based on the "type" of remote you selected: TV, VCR, DVD, etc. If you have a device and remote that don't neatly fit into one of those categories you are out of luck: choose an inappropriately titled and probably incorrectly defined device and then TRY to have the software learn the infrared commands from the original remote.I bought the Harmony One to replace an older programmable universal remote control. The older remote, which also plugs into my computer, allows me to put ANY command on ANY button or touch pad area; it even allows me to create custom graphics for the touch pad areas and then downloads those graphics to the remote.All in all, if you truly want a completely programmable device, the Harmony One isn't it. Keep shopping for other company's devices.

This is my second and last LaCie external drive.  Both had power failures after the year mark.  On this one, I noticed the drive disappeared one day recently when I received an error message to properly eject drives on the Mac.  Looked at it and saw it was powered off.  That was a little weird.  I powered it back on, and it appeared again.  In a moment of foresight, I had ordered a WD replacement external drive.  Sure enough, the day the replacement arrived the LaCie drive died never to be seen again.  It would not power on any longer.  I had to pull it apart to get the drive out so that I could recover the data.What did I find?  Well, it was a Seagate Barracuda drive, part number ST2000DL001, a metal enclosure, and a small circuit board for the power and USB interface.  I hooked up the drive to an adaptor kit I have and recovered all of the data.  I have no idea why LaCie has a hard time with getting the power circuitry right, but having seen two failures now, there is definitely something not right.At least I was able to salvage the drive and will have a spare for my Drobo in the event I have a drive fail on that.  The rest of the junk goes to the trash.

I thought with how immensely popular this router is I would be 100% completely satisfied and not encounter any problems.  But I was wrong.  About a week passed by before I started experiencing random connectivity problems.  It all started when I began using uTorrent, a popular bit torrent peer-to-peer software.  At first the software would connect and download fine but it would eventually lose connection and I wouldn't be able to connect to the Internet at all.  The only resolution was to cycle power to the router.  But it would keep doing this over and over as I continued to use uTorrent.  However, the problem disappears when I connect directly to my cable modem, I can connect and download just fine.  And yes, I properly forwarded all the ports on the router.  So I narrowed it down to being this router and after further research on the Internet I find that I'm not the only one with this and other issues with the WRT54G line of routers.  See for yourself, just Goggle search "WRT54GS connection problem."  You'll discover that this router has numerous issues with any peer-to-peer software and dropping connections for apparently no reason at all.  There are other shortcomings with this router as well.  First, you cannot log out of the router after you have logged in.  This poses a security issue and should be a no-brainer feature that every router should have, even the cheap ones.  Second, there is no feature to create a MAC filter list for wired clients.  Third, you cannot assign static IP addresses to connected clients and exclusively associate a certain client with a certain IP.  People claim there is a work around to this by assigning those machines IPs that are out of the DHCP range.  This seems more like a simple fix more than an intended function.  Fourth, you don't have to type a user name in order to log into the router.  The only thing that is authenticated when you log into the router is the password.  Seems like another security issue since requiring a user name adds another layer of safety.  I guess that I'm too use to my old D-Link DGL-4300 router which has absolutely every feature you could want.  I just figured that the popular Linksys WRT54GS would have these otherwise standard features.  I am less than impressed with this router.  Sure it might be great if you want to install an aftermarket firmware on it but straight out of the box with the default firmware this router leaves a lot to be desired.  A lot.

Overall, I would rate this a 3.5 for construction and 2 for the game itself.  This is strictly an outdoor game. The instructions proclaim it can be played indoors or outdoors but unless you have a room at least 25' feet long with nothing else in it, I do not see how this could work.I opened this box as soon as it arrived, looking forward to another yard game.  Currently, we are fans of a tossing game called Corn H.  The instructions state that the ladders should be placed 20' apart.  When we tried to toss the bolas (two golf balls filled with sand and connected by a string) onto the ladder, we failed miserably.  Getting the knack of throwing the bolas and getting them to wrap around the colored poles in the ladder took some doing.  I would not recommend this for a family game with younger kids.  The top colored pole ladder (blue) is worth 2 points, the middle (orange) is 3 points and the lower one (yellow) is 1 point.  The first team to get to 21 points wins.  The instructions tell you to keep score with the numbered poles on each ladder but I have no idea how since there is no mechanism included to help keep score other then the numbers 1 thru 21 being printed on the pole.Constructing this game was a little time consuming but easy enough.  The directions were not great but looking at the box helped.  FYI: the numbered poles are placed between the orange and blue rungs in the ladder.  The poles must be pushed together hard in order to form a more stable ladder; otherwise, the poles come apart too easily.  It will not be perfectly level when you are done but it works.  The instructions are in english and spanish only.  Very basic rules are provided.  Instructions on techniques to throwing the bolas would have been appreciated. The construction of the poles is lightweight but not so cheap that it fails to work.  Also, mine did not come with a carrying case as advertised.So far (understanding I have only played it a couple of times), I am not a big fan.  If tossing games appeal to you, this would be worth a try.  The construction is sound enough for the asking price.  My issue, the skill level is too high for young kids, not to mention hard balls being whipped about raises all kinds of red flags for this mom.  I have been hit with errant bolas and it hurts!  So stand far, far away from ladder when playing for the first time.

What a huge waste of my time.

I own the Dir-825, hardware version A. When I got the item with firmware 1.01, connections dropped tremendously. I upgraded to firmware 1.11NA so as to solve the problem but this made it even worse. Connections dropped even more and other persons were complaining since they also shared the internet connection via the router. I always had to keep on physically powering off the router and plugging it back on. It got so bad that I installed an electrical switch on the plug that connected the router to an electrical outlet. So instead of pulling out the router's charger and then plugging it back on so as to reboot the router, I could now switch off the power supply.However it has been a week thus far and I have not had to reset the router. This is  of course a world record for me since I had to reset this router every 2 days or so. I'm not sure if it's a fluke or what but I'll tell you what I did. I first saved the router settings to my hard drive. Then I upgraded the router's firmware to version 1.12NA. Then I upgraded to firmware version to 1.13NA right after.I then reloaded the router's settings that I saved on my hard drive. In the advanced tab of the router's webpage I went into the Qos settings. I unticked "Automatic Upload Speed" and I set the manual uplink speed to 360 kbps. My acutal uplink speed is 256 kbps but I just set the uplink a little higher to see what would be the effect. Thus far there has been no ill effect of doing such. In the end the router has not dropped connections or stopped being accessible via it's webpage.A great feature about this router is that when wireless clients log onto the router you can actually see who logs on as well as the percentage strength that the wireless device is receiving. Also the router respects the commands that you set in for port forwarding as well as port blocking. Port blocking is very essential for my use as well as the website blocking.

I had unsatsfactory results with Philips' earlier recorders, so I bought this with some reservations. Earlier recorders had a lot of problems with short laser lifetimes, and minimal editing ability. This one, however suits my needds. Let me state my mission first - I have a collection of about 1500 old fashioned laser discs that I want to back up before they give way to laser rot. About 20% have not made it to DVD, so recording them to digital format is the idea. So far I have recorded about 2/3 of them and here are my observations. 1) Editing a video stream from something that looks like a TV remote will be challenging under any circumstances. 2) 120 GB is a decent size for a working buffer but not for a collection 3) To do a better job you need a computer with a nonlinear editor like iMovie. Here is the way the unit works: The video stream is acquired from one of the inputs and programmed by time and channel. The video stream is compressed to MPG-2 and stored on a hard disc. The resulting stream can be editied to delete scenes like commercials, unwanted trailers, etc. (You can edit the video stream more than once.) You can then archive the edited stream on a DVD inserting titles, chapter marks etc. The DVD has some basic menu stuff, and the recorder does not provide for editing background or other cosmetic changes. (I wish it did.) A DVD can hold 6 hours of video without much degredation, and the image is quite watchable.  You can edit or archive a movie while you acquiring the video stream to the hard disc. It takes about 15 minutes to record a 2 hour movie DVD, and about 3 minutes to finalize the DVD after it is recorded. The editing of alpha information is much easier than the Panasonic and Sony systems and is a big step up from the earlier method Philips used. You can record one movie in a low quality mode and another track in high quality. A-to-D is pretty good, and loss is minimal. Remember that the quality of the final product is limited by the source quality. Some of my laserdiscs, like the Godfatehr collection were really good, and made super DVD's, while some of the B-movies made only fair copies. C'est la vie, I guess.I don't see this recorder on the Philips website any more, so they my have stopped production. If I were to make a suggestion to them if they are considering an upgrade, it would be: 1) Include a keyboard jack, 2) Put in a bigger hard disc, 3) Make disc editing (especially title menus) more robust, and 4) beef uup integration with digital cable. These things aside, I don't think there is much wrong with the recorder. Face it, this is a transient technology, one we need to record our old VHS movies of the kids' birthdays, and occasionally the Knicks game while we are at work. To do these things, this recorder more than admirably does the job.

I had to return this product in the end, even though I really liked the concept of the product. It just was not fully thought through.I've tried several of the dedicated streaming boxes, but they all (for now) are pretty horrible. Their media center software is, for lack of a better description, lame. I want an organized media center with fan background art, DVD covers, movie synopsis, television series organized by season and episode with information, a listing of music in a variety of ways with CD cover art, artist information, etc. I want to both stream content off the Net as well as over my local network and last, but not least, surf the Net. The only way to do all these things is with a PC and media center software like XBMC, MediaPortal, or the like. When I say "PC", I am using the term in the general sense, the way it was originally intended, so this could refer to a computer running Mac or Linux as well. The streaming set-top boxes just don't cut it.So I was pleased when I received the Zotac Zbox as to it's compact size, not much larger than some dedicated streaming boxes, but I could install whatever I wanted. I had purchased a 60GB SSD and memory for it and installed Windows 7 with MediaPortal at the time. It runs quiet with only one small fan so I had no qualms about leaving it on 24/7. I connected it to my Hi-Def Sony 42" television and it looked good, but the deal breaker was the Intel graphics it uses. Now this system is not powerful enough for gaming and I would not expect it to be. It's real purpose would be for a Home Theater PC, which is fine up to the point of where you connect it to a television. You see, most televisions (as opposed to computer displays) overscan to prevent fuzziness near the edges. What this results in is that your computer display will be larger than the screen. In Windows, you will be lucky if you can see the START button and the task bar at the bottom. Pretty much everything gets cut off that's near the edges. This is very common. With most Nvidia or ATI graphics drivers, this can be compensated for by adjusting the overscan in their control panels. Unfortunately, the Intel graphics control panel does not have any overscan compensation, so there is no way to correct the problem. As I stated, this computer begs to be an HTPC and that means it will most likely be connected to a television, not a computer monitor, so an overscan adjustment in the graphics software is crucial. I'm sorry, but Zotac missed the boat on this one.Aside from that most major issue, the Zbox really has to struggle to stream Hi-Def material. The CPU process while trying to stream 720p will typically run between 85-95%. I ended up spending a bit more and building a Mini ITX system using on of the new AMD APU's (graphics built into CPU) and I'm happy. Though about twice the price and size, it performs 10 times better than the Zbox. If anyone wants the specific hardware list I used, let me know.

At first I thought this was defective, but after investigating, I realized it was a bad knockoff of the real thing.  It took some effort to figure out that this power adapter was not an original Apple Power adapter. (like the one that came with the iPad) But if you look closely, it's pretty obvious.  The plugs don't flip out and recess like all of the apple plugs I've had over the years.  The printing is of much lower quality, not sharp, kind of blurry compared to an original Apple Power adapter.  The weight is even slightly different, this one is lighter.  I didn't notice any of that until I started having problems, and got an original Apple power adapter to compare it to.Here's the Mythbuster-style science that I used to figure this out:The thing that tipped me off is that the iPad would make the plug in noise over and over.  The battery would show charging, then not, then charging then not.  I found this odd.  It acted like a typical power supply acts when it's faced with an overload... shut down, start up, repeat.  So I tried a different Apple cable, and the results were the same.  Then I tried a 3rd cable, that I ordered along with this power adapter and it worked!  Could it be that both of my original Apple cables were bad?  They seemed to work fine!  I was perplexed, so I turned to my old friend, Science!I put a Kill-A-Watt on the wall, to measure the actual power draw of the adapters, and got the original Apple power cable, and original Apple power adapter, and it charged the iPad at 9 watts.  Out of a 10 watt original Apple power adapter, this seemed about right.So then I used this new (knockoff) power adapter, with two Apple cables, and it would draw 4 watts, then 0, then 4, then zero.  The iPad kept chirping over and over.Next step was to use the new cable (also a knockoff) I got on the same order as this adapter, and it charged the iPad at 4 watts.  AH HA!!!Next, I tried the new cable (knockoff)  with the original Apple adapter; 4 watts!So I read a little about Apple's high power USB, and it all started to make sense...........here's how it works;The iPad draws 2 amps, (10 watts) from the USB cable, and the Apple Power adapter using an Apple cable because that's a "high power" USB cable.  The Apple power adapter is a "high power" (10 watt) adapter.This knockoff adapter is only 1 amp (5 watts).  If you use it with an Apple cable, it overloads the knockoff adapter, and it constantly toggles on and off.The knockoff cable I had was a low power cable, so it acts fine with the knockoff low power adapter. If you didn't measure the power draw, you'd have no idea it wasn't supplying enough power to the iPad.

I bought this sight for my youngest son's Ruger 10/22, mainly because of the price ratio between this sight and that rifle. In other words, I wasn't about to spend 300 bucks on a sight for a 250 dollar rifle.The sight has one knob that turns 360 degrees, and allows switching from red to green dot with adjustable levels of brightness. I shoot in the day and always use the brightest setting, so I have not found a need for the adjustable feature, but I guess it's nice to have. The dot is not as crisp as other reviewers have seemed to suggest. The dot, while bright and highly visible in the day is not close to a perfect dot. It has a ghost of a dot overlapping the center dot, that gives it a slight resemblance of a pear shape. While it may not be that noticeable to novice shooters, it will throw you off, because the diameter of that tiny little dot you see in your sight translates to a few inches down range.The lens covers are fine for covering the lens while stored, but are not practical to use in the field. First, they slip on and off relatively easy. That means that every time you try to flip open the cap, they slide around and sometimes fall off. It's easier to remove the cover completely so you don't have to fuss with it. Second, the entire cover, including the transparent lens, is made of famously Chinese plasticky material that you can't really trust to hold up. I bought a cheap 40 dollar red dot sight at Walmart with screwed on hinges with glass sights, so I can't imagine it would have cost more to produce these with a better cap.The sight has stayed zeroed in through 500 rounds, although it was almost impossible for my son to hit a 25 meter target consistently inside two inch groups. Again, I attribute that to the quality of the dot.  Also, after buying it here, I found this identical sight selling for as little as $29 on other sites, but I didn't want to go through the hassle for a few bucks, and it's decent enough for an entry level accessory for me to keep it as a back up. However, if I had to do it again, I would have found something else.

This is a mechanical keyboard that uses Cherry MX brown switches.  These keys aren't as "clicky" as the blue switches, it allows for a more smoother keypress and isn't quite as loud as the blue "clicky" switches.  Still, keep in mind that it's not super quiet either (although quiet by mechanical keyboard standards), so if the sound of keypresses will annoy you or someone else in the room, pretty much any mechanical keyboard will be noisy.The blue backlight is user controllable from off to super bright and a couple steps in between.  As mentioned by others, if you reboot, this keyboard seems to forget its backlight setting and most of the time turns it off.  You'll have to turn it back on each time (by pressing a special function key combined with a corresponding key on the keyboard to increase the brightness.)The media control keys are the F-keys and are activating by holding the special function (Fn) key down, so it's a keystroke combo for volume up/down, mute, play, pause, etc.Integrated mic and headphone ports are convenient, and work as a pass-thru to the back of your PC with stereo cables (note that this doesn't act as a usb sound card, it just passes-through to your existing sound card).The USB ports work, and have had a Logitech MX518 connected to it, but sometimes when I've rebooted, it will stop seeing the mouse connected.  I've had to disconnect the mouse, reboot and then connect the mouse again for the OS to see it.Aside from the backlight and USB quirks (which is why I can only go 4 stars), this is a great keyboard for typing and gaming, and comes with a detachable wrist wrest.  If you're looking to switch from a "rubber dome" keyboard to a mechanical, this (or other Cherry MX Brown KBs) provide a balanced experience without having to press too hard and without the loud clicks.

Motorola has a newer version called the Roadster, but I'm seeing the same reliability issues in the reviews.How does it compare to other devices I've researched?=======================================================1. For about $20 more, the Jabra Cruiser2 seems to match the Motorola T-325 that I used to love, but the Cruiser2 does not have perfect reviews and no auto on/off.  The Cruiser2 does do caller-id-NAME-announce though. If the reviews were more consistently better, I would've considered the Cruiser2.2. The Motorola Roadster is a little more, but I am hesitant because of my T-325 reliability issues also, a lot of 1-star reviews...3. The Jabra Freeway is brand new, but 3 times the price!  If the Jabra Freeway drops in price by 60% I would consider it - it also has caller-id-NAME-announce, auto on/off, etc.  Does not have exactly perfect reviews.So until the next perfect device comes out with really good reviews, I decided to save money and get the SuperTooth Buddy.  In the pursuit of hands-free, it gets the job done, minus some of the nice frills of more expensive units out there.[Update 9-6-2011]I have now returned my SuperTooth Buddy for several reasons:A. The first time I needed to charge it, I charged it for several hours until the "halo" light turned green.  The next day I used it fine.  The second day, it would not turn on at all. I charged it up again and it seemed to work fine for a few days....B. With my phone in the cupholder, it did not auto-pair for another 10 minutes, this has now occurred 3 times.  Sure, I can turn the unit on/off and or toggle my bluetooth and make it pair, but I shouldn't have to, it should automatically pair when in range.  For battery-savings, perhaps *MY* phone defaults to checking every 10 minutes if it doesn't find a device for a long while, or it could be the SuperTooth, who knows, but other devices like the T-325 (and BlueAnt S4 and Jabra Freeway) automatically turns itself off and on, so this was never an issue before.C. I decided to return it when it wouldn't turn on again 2 more times.  The second time it happened, it worked on the way home after a short trip doing errands.  The third time, I got a little Sherlock idea, and put the device on the a/c vent to cool it off (even though it was not too hot to touch).  After just a couple of minutes, the device then turned on and auto-paired and worked fine since. So my assumption is that if it gets too hot in your car, that the device won't power on.  (You can test if it is on by hitting the "Up" volume button, when it reaches max volume level, you should always hear a beep, regardless of being paired.  Holding down the power button should also beep on/off, too.  In my cases, the device would never turn on or beep, etc.)Final Parting Summary:=======================With the 30-day warranty period almost over, I decided I needed to return it ASAP given the reliability issues I've seen related to Texas Heat so far.  Too much finagling involved to make it work; things should just work out of the box. I still think 3-stars is fair because those of you in a much milder climate, might have great luck with this.  When it works (and turns on) it is a pretty decent no frills bluetooth speakerphone, especially for the price.  Like another review mentions, if you're sitting on your couch one day and go to use your phone and hear nothing, it is probably because the bluetooth is still connected in your car! hehehe. This is probably why the other manufacturers added *motion-sensing* auto on/off...

Pros:- The sound is good- Setup is super easy- Tons of stations to choose from- You don't need to hook it up to a computer- Unit is very small and portable- You can add stations to your favorites list.Cons:- Finding stations you like can take a while; there are just a ton and using the remote to sort through them is kind of awkward.- The time it takes to load a station can be kind of annoying when searching through stations.- You can only control the unit from the remote (if you loose that remote you are out of luck).- The unit does not have its own speakers; you must connect to something (speakers or headphones or computer)- No way to rate the stations; although you can add stations to favorites list- Doesn't tell you what song or artist is playing.- Descriptions of the stations are very limited; hard to pick a station based on its description.- Some stations still have commercials (you can't complaint too much since you are listening for free).Over all this is a nice unit.  I have wireless speakers throughout our house that I can move around, and matched with those this is a really nice way to listen to all different types of music from anywhere in the house.  The remote is IR which means that the radio has to be controlled with line of sight.Setup to my network was really easy, when they say that it can be connected in a couple of minutes and playing music they are not lying.  I had this up and running in about two minutes.  The longest part was entering in my network key, which is kind of a pain on the small screen.  It found my network right away, and a bunch of other ones in my area.  I currently do not have the SSID hidden like I use to on my router, so I am not sure how hard that would be if you were in that boat.  I have WPA2 set up on my network, though since it didn't ask, it seems like it was able to figure out the encryption for my connection even though I didn't have to enter it.  I know some other devices do this, but most computers you still have to enter what type.  They basically have all the letters and numbers listed for entering the network key, but with all the moving around for was a little clumsy with the remote.  Also there are NO buttons on the unit, you have to use the remote for everything, which is ok, but you hope you never loose the remote or this will be worthless.I liked the selection of music when I first turned it on.  It didn't take too long before I found a station that I liked. It stays on that station when you turn it off and on, so if you really like one station, that is pretty nice.  Also the unit has a favorites list that you can set, and a recently listened to list, in case you didn't save a station and you wanted to go back to it.  The one thing it doesn't have is a way to rate each station as you listen to it.The unit comes with a RCA cords for connecting to whatever you want, but it also comes with a 3.5 mm jack for connecting to a computer or something like that.  The RCA cords could also be used for a stereo system, which is pretty cool as well.  There are NO speakers on the unit, which is fine for me as I mentioned our wireless speaker setup up above.Overall the build quality seems great, and the number of stations is really amazing.  The biggest problem is finding stations.  The Ira breaks down the music by genre, with some sub menus were needed. It ends up being a huge list though, so it is hard to sort through.  Also once you pick a station it does take a few seconds to load, so that can be kind of annoying if you are trying to find a station you like.  The one nice thing about choosing new music, is that it will keep playing the station you picked while you are looking for a new one.Another annoyance for me is that some stations still have commercials.  I know that the Ira is just playing everything it can find, but still you pay so much for a device, it is kind of irritating that you have to listen to commercials.Overall I like the Ira, but I am not sure if I will replace my computer playing music with the Ira.

This is a class 10 SD memory disk with WiFi capability. To use it, insert it in the memory slot of a compatible digital camera and take photos as usual. You can then download the photos onto a WiFi device such as a tablet or camera using the free FlashAir app. (You can also download the photos using a standard card reader if a WiFi device is not available.) Once on your WiFi device, the pictures can be shared with the world via Facebook, Instagram, etc. This card is a relatively inexpensive way to add WiFi capability to almost any digital camera currently on the market. Since the disk is class 10, it is capable of a very fast write speed, and is suitable for cameras that produce pictures with large file sizes.I tried this card in both a Nikon 7100 and a Canon Powershot SX210 IS. It seemed to store photos well. But I had a lot of trouble getting the WiFi to connect to a Samsung Galaxy 2 tablet. I downloaded and installed the FlashAir app without problems. Then I turned on the power in the Nikon 7100 camera and tried to connect to the Samsung tablet. The FlashAir card did not show up in the list of WiFi connections. It also did not show up from the Powershot camera with the power turned on. I placed the card into a SanDisk card reader that is attached to my desktop computer, and the FlashAir connection flashed by briefly on the Samsung tablet and disappeared. I tried looking up support for the FlashAir card through Google but kept landing on a Europe-only support site. A few days later (after I needed but couldn't use the FlashAir card for a professional photo gig), I tried the FlashAir card again in the Powershot camera. This time the WiFi connection showed up after a 20-30 seconds on the Samsung tablet. I switched the card over to the Nikon, and the connection showed up on the tablet after 5 minutes. I switched the power off on the Nikon and tried again--no dice, no connection. I'm not sure if the issue is with the Samsung tablet or the card. I also tried the card in a Nikon D90. No luck. To be fair, the Nikon 7100 and D90 are not on Toshiba's list of compatible cameras (although the Nikon 7000 is). The list of Nikons compatible with the card is surprisingly short. In any case, I did not have such problems with a similar Mobi Eye-fi card--the connections with that card worked immediately and without problems with the same equipment I have tested here.In any case, if you can get this card connected, it does have some nice features. It is fast. You can set your own password for security. The app for managing downloads onto devices appears to work well. So, if you can get it to work, it will probably work well.

I am an avid coffee drinker and a particular fan of Tim Horton's coffee.  I buy their 2lb can of fine grind but never got the same results brewing at home as when I bought a cup from their store.  I struck up a conversation recently with a young lady who worked at my local store asking her why it just never tasted the same and she told me she was going to let me in on a coffee brewing secret.  She said most all home brew coffee makers don't get the water near hot enough to thoroughly extract the oils from the coffee properly and that after all, that's where the good coffee taste comes from. She told me that I might consider an old school stove-top coffee percolator and guaranteed me I would taste the difference.  She emphasized a stove top and not an electric percolator because very few of the popular electric models brew the coffee long enough and that with a stove-top model I could experiment and find the right brewing cycle time for the perfect brew to my taste. She also said to just buy the most economical one I could find inasmuch as the more expensive models are no better than the less expensive ones. I bought this model from Amazon but opted for the addition cost of the glass top over the plastic one that was on this model and it took me just 2 tries to get that taste I enjoyed when I bought a cup from the store. I'd gone trough Mr. Coffee, Melita, and Keurig machines in the past couple of years and this cheap little metal pot is the best coffee maker I've used in recent years.  The Mr. Coffee was just OK at best, the Melita lasted 6 months and really made lousy coffee anyway so it didn't bother me too much when I threw it out, and the Keurig at over $100 that I sold on craigslist made dishwater tasting coffee and looked like a Hummer SUV on my counter top. I hated that thing. Lesson learned... It's not the machine that makes the best coffee, it's the process, and just like many things; the old ways are very often the best ways.  If like me you find good coffee one of the great simple pleasures of life get yourself a stove-top perk and get back to good tasting coffee.

I bought this griddle to replace myPresto 07039 Professional 22-Inch Jumbo Electric Griddlewhen the Teflon coating wore out after years of use. There are some things on this Hamilton Beach griddle that are better than the Presto, and some that are worse. I just received it yesterday and tested it out with a batch of bacon. If I come across any problems or revelations in the future I will come back and change my review.PROS:Splash guard - This is a great innovation and it was the selling point for me. My old Presto griddle would leave a big mess on the counter and wall behind it when I cooked anything greasy. Since I used it for burgers and bacon more than anything else, there was always a mess to clean on the counter after using it.Warming tray - I must confess that I haven't used it yet, but I pulled it out to see how hot it gets. It just stayed "warm," as it should. I am looking forward to making pancakes for guests with this griddle so I can test that drawer. With the old Presto unit, I would have to leave pancakes wrapped in a couple layers of aluminum foil to keep them warm.Large cooking surface - It seems to be about equivalent to the Presto.Large grease trap - It looks small, but for the amount of bacon I cooked in my test run the Presto unit's grease trap would have been full and this trap was only half full. I do think that it might turn into a problem if I am cooking a large amount of burgers or bacon on it, and in those cases I will just remove it and put a disposable pie tin under the griddle, just like I did with the old one.Strong handles with lock washers - This is better than the Presto unit by a long shot. They are sturdy cast aluminum handles with lock washers and I expect them to last a long time. The Presto unit had cheap "bakolite" style plastic handles and they constantly had to be re-tightened. The only down side to metal handles is that they heat up, so you have to use oven mitts to move the unit while it is hot.Great non-stick surface - It is very slick, and seems to be well applied to the unit. I don't foresee it peeling or cracking any time in the near future. The Presto unit had more of a textured Teflon coating, and things did stick to it. Nothing is going to stick to this griddle.Very secure thermostat housing - It really locks into place, whereas the Presto one just slid in and didn't really lock.Fully submersible - Just like the Presto unit, everything but the thermostat unit is fully submersible, which makes cleaning very easy.High edges all the way around - I thought the edges were pretty good on the Presto, but these are even higher. That helps when picking up food, and keeps stuff from spilling onto the counter.CONSUneven heating - I put bacon across the entire cooking surface, and I could literally see stripes on the bacon where the heating elements are. Eventually, the whole batch of bacon cooked evenly, so perhaps I should have preheated it longer. On the Presto unit, I preheated it for just a couple of minutes and it cooked evenly every time. This unit is definitely inferior in that regard. It also took a lot longer to cook a batch of bacon than the Presto unit did at the same temperature setting, so it could be that the Presto unit's temperature indication was high or this one is low. It is going to require some adjusting either in the temperature or preheat time.Cooking surface not tilted - This might make it easier to cook eggs, pancakes, or anything else that might run, but it also keeps grease from running into to grease trap. To get grease into the trap, you have to tilt the griddle. If you read my comments above, you know that it has nice metal handles, so you need an oven mitt to grab the handle and tilt it. Also, if the grease trap already has some hot grease in it, tilting the unit could cause that grease to pour out of the grease trap. I will get by this problem by just setting the grease trap on the counter below the holes, rather than sliding it into the drawer slides.Overall, I think I will be happy with this griddle, but there are a couple of areas that could have been improved and a couple of things I will need to get accustomed to.
