Nobody will ever claim that a Zalman cooler is pretty, nope this is one of those ugly pieces of technology. On the other hand, this cooler does a great job of cooling with virtually no noise. The cooling is amazing - stock very loud cooler, folding at home running 85 degress C, with some really horrible fan noises. The first day of the Zalman cooler, 75 degrees on the highest fan setting. Just outstanding. Construction is rock solid on this. The GPU contact plate (where heat transfer occurrs) is mirror shiny copper - kudos Zalman for a job very well done!February 21, 2009 Update. After a week it seemed like the cooler wasn't doing it's job (the 8800GT was up to 80-85 degrees C). I ordered some MosFet heat sinks. And sent an email off to Zalman. Didn't hear anything for a long time. The MosFet heat sinks didn't help. Then at three weeks I sent another note to Zalman. This time, almost immediate response that this cooler is not compatible with the 8800 series of video cards. Well it took about two weeks, and Zalman made good on their product. They swapped this cooler for a VF1000 - the correct cooler for the 8800 series.I have to give Zalman huge thanks for standing behind their product, and getting me exactly what I needed. Thank You Zalman. Customer Service does really exist.And one addition to the installation instructions - after you remove the original heat sink from the memory modules - clean them with alcohol and a cotton swab. When they are dry, rub a pencil eraser over each one. This will roughen up the finish a little bit and give those purple heat sinks with adhesive some bite.Back to the Original Review:This is not a hugely complex job, but you do need a bit of careful reading and work slowly. I installed this on a BFG Nvidia 8800GTGeforce 8800 Gt OC2 512MB, this is a single slot card about a year old. So the fan has gotten a bit worn in and gotten noisier than I liked. My computer case is a big roomy well ventilated Antec P182 on a standard ATX Asus P5QPro motherboard. All that to say, there is a lot of space inside my computer to add this cooler.Be aware, this cooler, as will any aftermarket cooler, takes up the slot next to your PCI or AGP slot - you are basically building a 2 slot card now.Zalman's website is awesome at telling you all about compatibility for this cooler. Make sure you take note of the "nipple" number for your specific card - my card was not listed in the instructions. In my case I had a first generation of these 8800GT cards (read single slot, small noisy fan). Later generation cards might not need this upgrade.Disassembly of the original heat sink was the worst part of the job. I had to remove about 10 screws on the back side of the card. The heat sink and fan then came off as an assembly, along with a ton of heat sink compound and some dust. Be sure to clean all that old residue off your card, don't miss the memory in a circle around the GPU. I used rubbing small amounts of rubbing alcohol on a Q-Tip. Just be sure everything is absolutely dry before you proceed.From here, the assembly went exactly as written. I did dry fit the cooler to the card before applying the thermal compound. I just wanted to be sure everything would line up and Zalman didn't give me a bum nipple number. Sure enough, it all worked exactly right.Running the fan controller wire is kind of strange, but you'll figure it out in your case. It's just a lot of wire.I set the controller to max cool and I can just barely hear the fan over the other fans in my case (a very quiet case). The nasty graphics card was silenced!!!!Not pretty - but it sure does do what it's supposed to do, cool your graphics card.

Right out of the box I instantly fell in love with this set - it's beautiful to look at and touch which you can't always say about cookware.  Each piece feels sturdy and well-made. I wasn't surprised that these are hand-wash only - I would never put any nonstick cookware in the dishwasher even if the directions say it's ok to do so, it just helps preserve the life of the nonstick coating to wash them by hand, that just makes sense.  I wasn't surprised that it is only oven-safe up to 350 degrees - many stove-top sets are the same way.  What did surprise me is the specification that you should not use these on the stove-top above a medium heat.  Say what?  What's the point of having pots and pans if you can't use them to their full potential?  I'm sure this specification has something to do with protecting the nonstick coating or keeping it from leaching chemicals into the food at high heats, but it's just not practical at all.So far I've used these for sauces and soups, pasta and rice, omelettes and pudding and all have come out beautifully - everything cooks evenly, the pans heat quickly, no sticking at all. When it came to boiling the water for the pasta and rice - I did set the burner to high to get a good strong boil even though it was above the medium setting, but then turned it down once the high boil was achieved.  I didn't notice any issues with sticking or anything like that.  I also (out of curiosity) seared a steak in the skillet on a high heat (hi-low), and it seemed to come out just fine.  I did use a dab of butter in the pan - nothing burned or stuck.  I'm not sure if this would be the case if I continue to use the pan on a high heat, against the manufacturer's instructions, but so far it seems fine.Overall it's a very nice set and a good price considering how many pieces you get.  I'm not sure about the stipulation of only using up to a 'medium heat', if I were going to buy a good non-stick set I would definitely pick one that didn't have this 'restriction' and pick a set that I know can be used for anything and everything.

I think what I really wanted this lens to be was a true fish-eye lens but without the barrel distortion (yeah, oxymoron, I know).What I got is "OK."  The extra wide isn't that dramatic on my video camera (the Panasonic HMC150, which has a pretty wide lens to begin with).  I would say I get about %30-%40 more image with this lens.  A far cry from the %55 I thought I was getting.  I'm sure it really is giving me a true .45x wide-angle, but that's just not as wide as I thought it would be.There is some noticeable vingetting around the corners at full wide (zoom 0) up to about zoom 30.  So to put it another way, the corners are always going to be vingetted when this lens is used to go beyond my camera's widest angle. That said, the vingetting isn't horrible, it just makes the shot look more like a special effect and less like I had a camera with a shorter lens.  If you frame your shots carefully I'm sure most people won't notice it though.This lens also comes with a Macro (which I think is necessary to focus the wide-angle lens).  The Macro is decent...probably a +12 or so.  Lots of distortion on this lens, but who expects a +12 macro to be free of distortion?In closing, I do want to say that the image quality of the wide lens is flawless at full wide, but has some vingette-like blur when zoomed in past 30.  The effect is pleasing, but also impossible to avoid.  The Macro lens has such a narrow focal length it's hard to judge it's image quality, but I'd say it's near perfect as well.Ultimately, a fair lens for the price.

SEE UPDATE AT BOTTOM:This was fun item to review! With so many people looking down instead of the road, the Monster Cable iMotion is a smart idea to play music.  This item makes hands-free obsolete.  Now we are hand waving!  First, it is black and sleek looking with an auxiliary cord that wraps and hides. The directions were simple, plug and play.  Me and my BFF tried it with both a iPhone 4S and iTouch and we had no problems getting the adapter in with our otterboxesOtterBox Defender Series Hybrid Case for iPod touch 4G (Black/Red).  (We would have tried it on an iPad but Sam didn't trust us with his iPad or the keys to his BMW.)We only saw two problems: One, you have to have an auxiliary outlet in your car. The device is powered by a cigarette lighter, but you have to have an auxiliary outlet for the sound.  Second: Any object will set it off or stop it including movement of other cords and objects around the scanner. This also includes the sun.  When turning in your car, the scanner mistakes sun and shadows as a hand wave.  You definitely don't want this if you drive a manual transmission.All-in-all, I think it's a great product. I do feel it is a little overpriced, ($30 would be a better price) but it does look durable and adapts to several music devices.UPDATE:  After two months of use, it can't even be used as a charger.  Anytime a shadow crosses the path of the screen/sensor, it changes the Pandora or music app by pausing it, or changing play mode, or stopping it, scanning channels at will.  The theory of it is good if you are in a room with no shadows moving, but in a car, it is frustrating.  Tinted windows don't help. You can't even trick it and put something over it. The iMotion will just shut down.Plus after the excitement of having a hands-free device the audio output road noise becomes more noticeable to the point of unbearable.

I got this to review through the Amazon vine program.  The product comes in a very nice case, it is faux white leather with a nice zip closure.  There is a nice little mirror in the case as well.  In there you get two cylinders of product.  One is the Extreme Repair Plus and the other is the Extreme Eclat Instant.The instructions that are included with this are tough to use.  There are in super tiny print and you have to search through four or five languages to get to the English instructions.  Even once I found them I had to read the instructions a few times to figure out what to do with these two products.I have combination skin that is sensitive and breaks out easily.  My current skin care regiment involves usingSmashbox Photo Finish Foundation Primerunder my makeup for moisture and staying power andBoscia Enlivening Amino-Ag Eye Treatmentaround my eyes.  At night I moisturize withCetaphil Daily Advance Lotion for Dry Sensitive Skin.The Extreme Repair Plus is meant to be an overnight treatment.  You are supposed to apply to areas susceptible to wrinkles and leave on overnight.  This applies with a roller ball.  You basically push the button on the bottom to pump out product and then roller ball it out on problem areas.  I am not all that keen on a roller ball application because all the dirt/oil from you face is just being rolled back into the product.I used the Extreme Repair Plus for three days and had a lot of problems with it.  When I applied to my forehead and wrinkles around eyes it burned. My eyes also burned and watered even though the product wasn't that close to my eyes.  I ended up with red swollen eyes that burned and felt dry.  I finally stopped using after three days because the discomfort didn't fade or go away.The Extreme Eclat Instant is supposed to be worn under your makeup for an instant face lift.  This is pumped out from a button on the bottom of the container and comes out through a brush at the end.  It is an interesting application method, but the brush is pretty coarse so you end up having to rub the product in with your fingers to even it out.  I used this under my makeup in place of mySmashbox Photo Finish Foundation Primer.The Extreme Eclat Instant was even worse for my skin than the Repair Plus was.  It was very oily and caused my makeup to look glossy and smear easily.  After using it for three days my skin started to breakout everywhere.  A week after using it I am still trying to recover; my skin it red and blotchy and dried out. In addition to all of this it has a flowery scent to it that gave me a headache.So while the packaging is very pretty and the application methods are interesting; this product was a disaster for me.  The Extreme Repair Plus made my eyes and skin burn.  The Extreme Eclat Instant was very oily, caused my whole face to go red, blotchy, and break out, and in addition to that had a sweet floral scent that I had trouble with.I know skin products work differently for every individual.  I would just caution those with sensitive skin prone to breakouts against trying this product.  It was pretty much a painful disaster for me.  Mainly I am grateful I received this for free through the Vine program, otherwise I would be really angry at wasting so much money on this product.

The Kindle Great Shield 3-pack protective shields arrived stuck together in a clump with plastic leaves in-between.  The packet arrived with a 4-step instruction printed on the back of the package.  Step 1 is to clean the surface with the provided cloth - the cloth does a good job of removing lint, but couldn't remove dirty spots.  Step 2 is to "locate the `Step 1 Remove Me!' label and slowly peel off the mask."  However, there are three `Step 1Remove Me!' labels stuck on various surfaces, including one of the shields.  So when the shields were separated from the protective plastic, and the "Step 1 Remove Me!" label was removed, it left behind an adhesive strip an inch long stuck to shield's surface.  According to the directions, removing the `Step 2 Remove Me!' label should have been the final step.  Sounds easy, but the protective shields on both sides of the shields had these step 2 labels.  By the time I got the mess sorted out, I had one usable shield.  After thoroughly cleaning my Kindle screen, I applied the shield, which does in fact have a matte surface - pretty much the same matte surface as my Kindle screen.  But try as I might, I could never get all the air bubbles out from between my Kindle and the shield.  I thought this step would be relatively easy because the shield doesn't reach the edges of the screen, but no - that part of the process didn't work very well either.  This product earned one star because, on a positive note, the shield removed easily and cleanly when I gave up, took it off and threw it away.

While on a smaller level, the Klipsch ProMedia 2.1 system rivals home theatre systems in sound quality.My out-of-box experience was slightly unnerving, but the problem seems to have fixed itself.  The subwoofer driver sounded as if it was blown or had a short of some kind.  At low volume levels, the system sounded great, but as the volume was increased to mid-range, the subwoofer became garbled and poppy - never a good sign.  I notified Klipsch of the problem and they were ready to ship a replacement immediately.  Fortunately, about 2 days after the problem started, the problem stopped.  All I had to do is leave the speakers on.  I'm not sure if it was a moisture problem, or the cold the system was exposed to during shipping, but once it warmed up, it was fine.The clarity of the sound is the best I've ever heard from a computer speaker system.  There are elements I've never heard before in songs I've listened to dozens of times before.  The mid-range has a strong presence, and isn't drowned out by the low and hi-ranges.  The THX technology is effective and well-utilized.  When positioned properly, you'd swear there was a center speaker hidden somewhere.While pricey, the sound quality is hard to beat.  These speakers have been around for awhile.  That being the case, Klipsch could benefit from updating the housing of the speakers in both shape and color (silver would be nice).  However, looks aside, I don't think better 2.1 speakers can be found.

What occurred to me after wasting half an hour with this thing is that what is needed is an iPhone app to control your television and stereo, not a single freaking light bulb and a long, long list of codes printed in mouse type.See photo. The buttons are not what you might expect, the volume and channel buttons are flabby feeling and weak, not definite-feeling. The center "OK" button is kind of clicky, like cellophane. There's a whole array of buttons, but it's not worth my time to try and program each one. And I grew to dislike the hard plastic feeling of the remote. There are other plastic materials that feel better to the hand. LOOK AT SONY PRODUCTS, RCA, LOOK AT SONY PRODUCTS FOR A FREE CLUE.I'm annoyed and frustrated. This seemed like such a neat idea. But sitting on my couch juggling three differently-sized manuals AND this remote and wondering why none of these instructions were doing anything was really frustrating, just not how I want to spend my free time. I'll happily continue to exist with my TV remote, my surround-sound remote, my AppleTV remote and the AT&T; cable box remote, you know? BECAUSE THEY WORK and they work without frustrating me.Here's my idea: RCA hires an  app developer and somehow figures out how to have your devices tell the app what their codes area. Something like that. Because the notion of combing through a manual full of codes in tiny type is worse than doing your income taxes.THE WORLD HAS MOVED ON, RCA and you are apparently living in the 1970s with burgundy leisure suits and avocado-colored kitchen appliances.STAY AWAY FROM THIS REMOTE, IT WILL ONLY FRUSTRATE YOU and dig in the skin under your nails. It turns out if you plug an external cd/dvd drive into a usb 3.0 port it wont work; this is because Windows 7 and older os's do not ship with a usb 3.0 driver.  So while the drive does work it doesnt work sufficiently to install Windows.  So while the error says it cant find the cd/dvd drive its more the problem that the usb port the drive is plugged into isnt fully supported with a driver.  MS likely will fix this with Windows 8. It seems like the duct tape thing is never going to go away. I remember being in 7th grade in 1997, and one of my friends made a wallet out of duct tape. I thought that was the stupidest, but also most brilliant thing ever. Only months later did I find out that people have been making things out of duct tape for a long time. Unfortunately, this Kindle Fire cover is not made out of real duct tape, though it's pretty dang close. The material feels a lot like your standard duct tape and should offer just as much protection as if a regular Kindle case were coated in it.This cover follows the standard Verso Kindle case formula. It features 4 elastic bands on the inside to hold the Kindle on each corner, and has a microfiber interior to ensure that the screen doesn't get scratched while covered. The elastic bands hold the Kindle perfectly too- they're not too tight or loose. There's also a pocket on the inside of the front flap to hold any papers you may need. I got this case for my daughter since pink's her favorite color, and I ended up liking it a lot for one main reason. The pink is so bright that you -can't- miss it! I always look right past my iPod since it's in a black case, and there's no way that'll ever happen when the Kindle's in this sucker. Another nice touch is how the duct tape design feels like a bunch of pieces were stuck over it, and it's not just printed on. At first, I tried to peel one of the pieces off before I realized that it wasn't the real thing.The only downsides to this cover are that it doesn't have a more secure closure like a clasp, and there's no holster for a stylus, which a lot of people are using these days from what I see. The lack of a stylus holder isn't a big deal, but for people like me who want as much protection as they can get with a case for something expensive, a little more protection would've been nice. The case closes with light magnets, and should be enough for most cases, though if it's in a bag with a lot of room, there's a good chance something's going to end up within the case. If you use your Kindle mostly at home, this shouldn't be a problem.For the price, this is a pretty good case. They also make this same design for the Kindle Fire HD too.

This is the best choping block I've ever owned.  Notice I didn't call this a board, as the brawny thickness of this product with the substantial feet(with rubber bottoms to prevent slipping) brings this up quite a few notches from mere ordinary cutting boards. This is a chopping block to end all chopping blocks.  I can only compare this to butcherblock, but made from Green, eco friendly, self renewable bamboo.  You're doing the environment a favor by going with bamboo over synthetic boards/mats, and even over traditional wood such as red maple.I love red maple, don't get me wrong. Aside from the green advantages, bamboo is 16% stronger than Red Maple.  Its not going to dull your knives significantly faster, at least nowhere near the extent of the fools who cut on glass or marble as a cutting board.  I still can't believe some people preach using infinately harder surfaces like marble to cut on.  Sure its a snap to clean up, but you're going to be cutting with a popsicle stick after all the sharpening sessions you're going to have to perform on your knives.This block has a good feel when chopping on it.  it doesn't move, it's not too high when set on a counter top, and its so darn beautiful I leave it out all the time.To get the maximum life from your block, keep 3 things in mind.1) don't intentially try to damage the board.  with enough effort, sure you can impale your blade and make it stick.  Why oh why would you want to do that?  also I wouldn't put a hot pan on the board.  unlike countertops, bamboo burns. :P2) treat your board with mineral oil right after you buy it, and before you use it!  Any food grade mineral oil will do, you don't have to stick with something that is "certified" for bamboo.  Food Grade mineral oil is what you should use, and you can get it in the supermarket or drug store.  I use the mineral oil designed as...don't laugh...a laxative.  It's 100% food grade, and is safe to treat your bamboo or any wooden board. It's also a lot cheaper than wood treatment mineral oil.  Simply apply some oil to a soft lint free cloth and rub it in, leaving a thin layer behind.  go away for a half hour and come back.  repeat.  keep doing this until the board doesn't soak in anymore.  Wipe the excess off with a dry cloth and you're ready to use it!  Every few months apply the oil again to keep the wood from drying out.3)  Cleaning!  some people use mild soapy water.  I like to use distilled white vinegar applied with a soft sponge (not a scrubber) and then wiped dry with a towel.  Vinegar kills bacteria and does a fantastic job cleaning, as long as you don't mind the smell.  I water down my vinegar a little bit (a little stronger than 50/50) and keep it in a spray bottle.  Clean your block using vinegar(or mild soapy water) after each use.  Its easier to get the food off when its not dried on the surface (and in any cuts that may be on the surface).If you follow those 3 steps I bet this block will last you a lifetime.  I've had mine only a week and I love it!  Yes, it is expensive compared to other alternative products. you can get a similar sized cutting board made from bamboo for $15 and be happy.  I personally think the manufacture and quality of this product merits the price tag.  This sucker is not going to be splitting or cracking anytime soon.

For years now Ultimate Ears has provided my personal benchmark for the best sound in-ear headphones can produce.  I listen to music on my own favorite headphones, theirTripleFi 10s, every day, and whenever I am testing a new headphone I always compare it against both the TripleFis and a friend's older pair ofSuperFi 5 Proswhich are still the best-sounding things I've ever put in my ears.  So I was excited to test the new top of the Ultimate Ears consumer lineup, the UE 900 -- the first really new high-end earphone UE has produced since the Logitech acquisition, and a make-or-break model for the brand.I'll go into more detail below, but here's the short version: the UE 900s passed the test with flying colors.  These are simply fantastic headphones.  They deliver just what they should: truly excellent, best-in-class sound quality (though it's arguably not much of an upgrade over the already fantastic-sounding TripleFi and older SuperFi models), a few key improvements in build and form factor, and a premium feel in keeping with the high price tag.The unboxing experience is entirely commensurate with the UE 900s' price tag.  A store-shelf-friendly advertising wrapper protects the outside of the real box, which is a heavy black cardboard enclosure stuffed with protective closed-cell foam.  Inside its lid, a cardboard folder protects the manual and warranty information, along with UE's traditional photo booklet, full of interesting concert images.  Below this you find the headphones themselves, easily removed from the foam along with their plastic hard case, an extra cable, a soft pouch, and all the usual accessories (different-sized fam and silicone tips, airline attenuator, 1/4" plug adaptor).  The new hinged, shiny plastic hard case has a magnetic closure and neat little built-in storage for extra tips and the 1/4" adaptor, but it's also larger and heavier, less pocketable and more vulnerable to ugly scratching than UE's bulletproof former aluminum clamshell case -- so despite the cosmetic appeal, it's not a perfect upgrade.The UE 900s are a big improvement over their predecessors in form and fit.  I found the shape made it far easier to achieve a good seal with the 900s than with my TripleFis, and the earbuds pivot on their cables, making both untangling and fitting easier (though I fear this may make the connection more vulnerable to damage, as only time will tell, and the cable is not backward-compatible with TripleFis or SuperFis due to the new round connector).  The new lightweight braided cable is a huge improvement; it both resists tangling and transmits much less handling noise than more rigid cables.  The bendable, semirigid over-the-ear portion of the cable is not as useful in achieving a solid, tug-proof fit because of the pivoting earbud mounts, but overall this cable is a huge upgrade (and it's very nice to have a backup, remote/mic-less cable included in the box in case of damage or wear).In any case, the sound is what really matters here, not the package.  And there, the UE 900s simply deliver; this is the best, clearest sound I've heard in any in-ear headphone I've tried.  The clarity and separation of the sound is amazing, even compared to the TripleFis and SuperFis; the individual instruments, even background players, pop out of a jazz ensemble or orchestra -- or even a multi-guitar rock band -- with clarity that I never knew my recordings even allowed.  And the human voice seems unbelievably clear -- though many pricey headphones call themselves "IEMs" just as a buzzword, these really do deliver the vocals-to-the-front sound of a studio monitor, almost to a fault (e.g. I found myself cringing at an occasional hissed "s" or popped "p" sound in tracks I never knew had this flaw before!).  I ran a series of direct comparisons against my beloved TripleFis and my friend's SuperFi Pros, and found it very hard to pick a winner; the UE 900s are undeniably clearer and crisper, with a broader separation between instruments and stunningly rendered vocals, but the SuperFi Pros win on warmth and have a more rounded and atmospheric (if not as crisp) bass response, and the TripleFis a brighter treble.  It's simply a matter of taste whether the UE 900s are worth the significant upcharge over the already excellent-sounding TripleFi 10s, but in any case, their sound quality is excellent enough to justify their fairly exorbitant price tag.I did notice that the UE 900s initially needed a lot of power -- they had to be driven much louder, at a higher volume setting, than other earphones to achieve a similar loudness.  While I'm usually inclined to dismiss the idea of "burning in" headphones as a superstition, it does seem like the power my 900s need has significantly diminished after a few hours of dedicated listening, as has the 900s' initially almost harsh high end.  It might be a good idea to give a new pair of 900s a bit of time to settle down before passing final judgment on their sound quality.When people ask me to recommend the best-sounding in-ear headphones in existence, this is where I'll point them.  Ultimate Ears has once again justified the name.

Recently I had a need to replace my Logitech G35 usb headset. I saw the p3 and p5 models on amazon and chose this this px5 refrub since it was both wireless and bluetooth. I was excited when I got the package, hooked the product up and then the strange, almost surreal problems began.This product is not PC compatible. The px5 can work with a pc, yes, but PC or smartphone is not the main focus of this product. The PX5 is designed to work only on ps2/3 and xbox consoles. So once you turn the Bluetooth on, the Motorola becomes no less then Three devices - a wireless headset, a bluetooth hands free device, and a blue tooth stereo headset. In enabling the bluetooth you will rapidly increase the headset power demands.To be honest, this would have worked out pretty well for me since my pc sound card has a toslink output (fiber optic) which is needed for the core transmitter to work. Please read that again - this wont work with a pc that lacks toslink output. You can get a anaolg adapter but this will disable much f the dolby processing.However getting this to work not just as a set of speakers but as a skype head set required that I add a bluetooth transmitter to my pc and pair the headset to my pc. I would go on about this, but lets not beat a dead horse - the process of getting this to work with a pc is strange and results in much aggravation.Alone, the pc oddness is something I can get past. Because these headphones are just that good. It's worth a little oddness for sound this good and this light on the ears and wallet.Except for the core flaw in the ps5 design. The PX5 uses AA batteries. Two of them. I should say the PX5 EATS AA batteries. You see, the PX5 will exhaust a set of AA batteries every 20 hours (per the docs) if used as the manufacturer expects. If you use the PX5 in both wireless and Bluetooth mode, well a fresh set of energizer AA lasted me just over 6 hours. I cant understand why they did not use a usb rechargeable pack like my other stereo headsets.I can only caution the reader to be ready with a AA NiMH battery recharger, and have a few sets of batteries ready. You will need them. If this is not a problem you will just love the quality, lightness, responsiveness and ability to tweak the head set sound profiles.regrettably I am not willing to feed this thing batteries. I have to return it. IT makes me sad to send this back, but I simply cant justify buying a set of rechargeable batteries and a charger just to use this headset.

The DNS-321 has the ability to send email alerts. What is NOT disclosed in the manual or in the configuration pages of the device is that the email alerts use port 25 to reach an SMTP email server. (This may also be true for the DNS-323.)For many thousands, maybe millions of Comcast users, this is likely a problem, because Comcast (and other ISPs) is increasingly blocking port 25. Email alerts will not work even when trying to use Comcast's own SMTP servers. After an all-night investigation with Comcast and a non-Comcast network, we were finally able to conclusively pin the email alerts problem on Comcast blocking port 25.1st Major Defect:There is no way to change the SMTP port in the device, unlike the ability to change the port for FTP. It's beyond comprehension why there is no ability to change the SMTP port. Major, major, oversight, given the increasing clamp down by ISPs and hosting companies to abandon port 25.2nd Major Defect:D-Link staff simply does not know how this product works, therefore if you need help, you wold be wasting your time getting in touch with D-Link. D-Link's support staff could not say what port the device was using to reach an SMTP server. After several phone calls and a submission to their trouble ticket system, I have yet to have a D-Link person be able to tell me what port the device uses. They are clueless and reflects a complete lack of knowledge about their product.

The password-protected screensaver works fine: type password, hit enter, done. I figured I was getting a good product, but I never expected to be so surprised at how REALLY good this one is.  It's very easy to use, and the screen is plenty bright to be seen even in the sun.  It's about the size of a pack of cards, making it very easy to travel with - you don't feel like you're lugging it along with you, it just tucks away.We took this on a trip from Central Illinois to Kentucky, including several stops and detours along the way.  The directions were very good, and in the one instance where a road no longer went through when Garmin thought it did, the device recalculated the correct route in seconds.  It was equally good when we hit a detour on the way back home. I pressed the Detour button, and immediately had a new, very efficient route that only added three minutes to the total estimated time.The Points of Interest feature works well. It helped us find several restaurants and parks that we wouldn't have known about otherwise. It obviously doesn't know about *everything*, but it is still very helpful.  When searching for POI's, you can look for locations near where you are at the time, along your route, near your destination, or near a different city.  The POI's are also very nicely categorized so you can quickly find exactly what you're after.You can store locations in a "Favorites" list.  These and other locations (such as but not limited to the POI's) can be inserted as "waypoints" on the way to your main destination, which is a nice feature.The most helpful feature is how much time the device gives you to make your next turn.  You get about a mile on the Interstate, which is generally plenty of time even in heavy traffic.  Unfortunately this time is cut down when you're driving in town, and sometimes you don't get enough notice to make the turn on time.  However, the device compensates for this somewhat by giving directions such as "In .3 miles turn right on Main Street, then turn left."  In that case you at least know what you're going to have to do next and can be ready to do it quickly if you need to.I also like that it tells you which side of the interstate your exit will be on.  It will even tell you when you need to "keep left" or "keep right," so often you don't even need to watch the highway signs.The text-to-speech feature works well and provides audible directions that are loud enough to hear easily even over an older vehicle that has a lot of road and wind noise.Accuracy on the open road is usually about 9 or 10 feet, which is shorter than most cars and therefore plenty good.The device will tell you what time you can expect to reach your destination, which is very accurate. It tallies the amount of time you've spent driving and the time you've spent stopped. It also tells your current speed, your average moving speed, and your overall average speed including time stopped.As far as the "extra" features go, the MP3 player is remarkably full-featured (browse by album, artist, etc.) and easy to use. The speaker isn't really good enough to get great sound, but it's nice if there's nothing good on the radio.  The bluetooth feature is also pretty good, although not outstanding.  I can hear callers well, and they can hear and understand me okay, but they do hear some background noise. (I don't know how you'd avoid that in a moving car.)There are a couple features that I'm not sure are mentioned in the owner's manual that are worth pointing out:1.) From the menu screen, you can tap the GPS signal strength icon for a report of current positioning accuracy2.) While traveling to a destination, you can tap the "Turn In..." icon at the lower right to have the next turn read to you, or to scroll through the rest of the directions for the trip with a map and mileage and time estimates for each step.3.) You can get a short list of remaining turns by tapping the green bar at the top of the map that displays the current information.4.) Tap the "Estimated Time" button in the lower left to pull up your current speed, average speed, distance driven, etc.I am highly satisfied with this unit.  I can't imagine going back to traveling without it.  This makes trips so easy.

It's no secret that I am partial to my Roomba. I've had it for over a year and it still impresses me several times a week. I guess I could say that maybe my expectations were a little high when I received the LG HomBot.I'll start off on what I did like about the LG HomBot. It's quiet, very quiet. When you compare the two this one is the hands down winner, BUT since I have mine programmed to run when I am away from home I never hear it anyways. So that really isn't a selling point, at least not for me. It's styling is much more attractive than my Roomba, but like I said before looks aren't everything. It does do an acceptable job of cleaning in the areas that it runs over (slightly better on my wood floors than the carpet), but again not as well as my Roomba.Okay now on to the problems.  The dock has some pretty specific needs on where you can set it up. Putting it out of sight under an end table in the family room wasn't an option, plus Roomba didn't want to move.  The slanted top edges caused it to get stuck all around my home; under cabinets, couches and beds.  It's just low enough to start going under, but then gets wedged in and isn't always able to remove itself.  The cleaning cycle is way too short.  My Roomba goes for 2+ hours, three times a week around my home. The HomBot returned itself to the dock in 38 minutes on average which left areas uncleaned.  I also do not care for the non-specific scheduling that it has.  With my Roomba I have the days of the week and hours programmed, with the HomBot I have to remember the day of to set it for a couple hours later and hope it doesn't get stuck while I'm gone.  Pricing is more than the Roomba, but unless looks and noise are of utmost concern, then you're paying too much.Overall while the HomBot is definitely a better option in some features, it doesn't have enough to convince me to make it my main squeeze.  For now I let it run around the upstairs of the house and leave the real job downstairs to Roomba.If you are interested you can check out my video review on the model I have hereiRobot Roomba 770 Vacuum Cleaning Robot for Pets and Allergies.

I purchased a first gen Panasonic recorder (DMR-ES10) about two years ago and gave it extremely heavy use until it started acting up recently.  Bought the ES15 as a replacement, figuring the newer entry level product would be at least comparable.  Boy, was I wrong.I was extremely happy with the ES-10, and between recording movies off of digital cable and using the 'chasing playback' feature to watch a bunch of sports while skipping commercials/halftime, etc. recorded shows had to be more than half of my TV time.My comments are in comparison to the first-gen ES-10 I loved:ES15 is the same:Same outstanding picture quality.  Even LP mode is almost DVD equivalent on an HDTV, and SP is DVD quality.  The most important feature, for me at least, wasn't decontented on this model.ES15 is better:Smaller size, probably 1/3 smaller.Time slip function is simpler.Chasing playback feature now blocks the recorded feed while it gets ready to start from the beginning.  On the ES10, the 'live show' would show for a few seconds while the unit was kicking in.  If you weren't careful you could catch the 'live' score of a game you wanted to watch from the start.  This is no longer a problem and is a great improvement.Scheduled recording no longer requires the unit to be powered down to begin.ES-15 is worse:This model is unbelievably sluggish.  Functions take three to four times longer to kick in than on my ES-10.  Don't let this slug take its time, and multiple instructions cause it to freeze, necessitating a power-down.All functions, even simple playback, must go through the 'direct navigator' screen or stopping play will freeze the unit.  You can no longer just pop a disc in and hit play---truly a stupid change.The remote has less features than the ES-10.  Since the ES-10 remote, and its extra functions, work on the ES-15, I'm using it.  One example of cost cutting stupidity---the ES-15 remote has no 'open-close' button for the disc tray.  My office mini-stereo system (60 bucks) has an open-close button on the remote.The unit display is less informative when recording or playing back content.In summary, the ES-15 is a very frustrating product.  Ultimately, because the picture quality and chasing playback functions remain outstanding, I'm OK with my purchase, but its clear that Panasonic decontented to hit a price point with this unit. The unit's sluggishness has to be seen to be believed.  This is the first Panasonic product I've ever purchased that has left me unsatisfied, and it might be the first second generation electronics product I've ever purchased from a name brand that is noticably poorer than its first generation counterpart.My advice, since Panasonic has the best recording quality and features amongst DVD recorders----wait for the new models due out this summer and see what Panasonic, and others, have to offer.

Since perhaps 2004, I've been an enthusiastic fan of the Sangean ATS 909 radio.  Naturally, then, I was excited to hear the company would be releasing a new version of the 909, and ordered one shortly after it was available. I'm very happy with the 909X, with just a few exceptions.Unlike many shortwave enthusiasts, I consider audio quality to be an important feature.  I keep this particular radio at my desk and regularly use three bands - AM, FM, and shortwave - and I listen for about one to three hours per day.  Therefore, I'm not going to tolerate poor audio.  In this department, the 909X has to be one of the best portables.  The speaker tone is crisp, clear, and well-rounded enough for both voice and music.  Compared with the older 909, the newer model is brighter - better for AM talk and shortwave.  But this brightness can be a little too much when listening to music on the FM band.  It can be somewhat mitigated by switching the filter or adjusting the tone switch.  By comparison, the older 909 sounds warmer and darker, but after an hour or so of the AM or SW bands, this quality can become wearisome.  For FM, though, I do prefer the tone of the old 909.The sensitivity off the whip antenna is good, and it's greatly improved by using the included reel antenna.  Try to stretch it out full length in a straight line near a window.  This substantially improves the radio's shortwave reception.The selectivity is also very good.  In fact, I methodically compared the 909X with the Sony ICF-SW7600GR, and found the sensitivity of both to be about the same, but the selectivity of the 909X was superior.  And of course, the audio quality of the Sangean is far superior to that of the Sony.  The comparisons are unavoidable, since these models have probably been the two leading portable shortwave radios for about ten years now.  In my opinion, the Sangean is in an entirely different league.  The Sony might suffice as a back-up or travel radio with effective synchronous detection, but I'd honestly rather have two 909Xes than one ICF SW7600GR!A complaint sometimes made about the older 909 concerned the display window: it was relatively small and poorly lit by a dull olive green light.  With the new 909X, Sangean has done a fabulous job.  The new window is large, well arranged, and beautifully lit by a bright white light.  It gives the entire radio a sharp new appearance.  I would add, though, that the digits indicating the time are still rather small for easy middle-of-the-night viewing.I'm pleased with the 909X radio, but I would still add two qualifiers.  First, on some units the buttons do not function as well as the older model's.  You have to press them firmly and deliberately, and often they require a second or third press.  This is probably going to be an issue that Sangean will need to fix in future production runs.  In fact, the first unit I received was entirely spoiled by this problem.  Some buttons just would not register, no matter how firmly or repeatedly they were pressed, and eventually they would trigger other functions.  I finally ordered a second 909X.  The newer unit is better in this regard, but the buttons still require a firm press, an occasional repeated press, and at times malfunction as well.  It seems to be a matter of quality control at Sangean.My second reservation concerns the tuning wheel.  I actually like the old 909's wheel better, but the newer one is still good.  However, because it's detented, it can get a bit jittery.  Between clicks, there can be a little give that allows the frequency to change by one step without the wheel actually moving to the next physical step.  By lightly jiggling it back and forth, you can make the radio jump a digit.  When dialing through the frequencies slowly, it's possible for the wheel to skip over frequencies.  As with the button issue, Sangean will need to refine this feature in future runs.  I think the problem might be resolved by returning to a non-detented wheel.  The old 909s came with one or the other type of wheel, and I personally prefer the non-detented, which maintained the audio as you scrolled through the frequencies.In spite of these two qualifiers, I still consider the 909X to be my favorite radio - alongside the 909.  My older unit is seven or eight years old, and it continues to function flawlessly in every way.  That said, the 909X's ergonomics are logical, so that it's a cince to operate.  It sounds crisp and looks sharp, performs well on SSB, and includes a power adapter and an external reel antenna that can be connected either by a jack or a clip.  It also comes with a well written and fairly large-print operation manual.  The radio is on the expensive side, but that's the way it goes.  I'm giving it a full five star rating on the presumption that the two units I had were part of a bad batch, and not the norm.Both the 909 and the 909X are superb multi-band radios with many features that make DXing and SWLing both an ease and a pleasure.[Update: I finally bought a new 909X (the standard model) from Radiolabs, and it's 100% free of the troubles I had with the previous units bought from Amazon.  I believe they examine each unit before shipping.  An absolutely superb radio!  I highly recommend buying one from Radiolabs.]

It may not seem like much, but a MacBook Pro weighs about 5.6 pounds, so this case increases the weight on your MacBook by 18%. I knew the specs before I got it, but it is amazing how much I feel the additional weight. Combined with the added thickness, it transformed a svelte laptop and made it "chunkier." It also made it harder to fit in laptop bags with padded compartments such as the laptop sleeve in a Timbuk2 case.Since all I wanted was to protect my MacBook from scratches, the added bulk is not a compromise I was willing to settle for. The case simply did not meet my needs, but it is a very good case that can be a great fit for the right need especially if it is your primary protection such as carrying it around without a bag/sleeve or using in a travel bag with minimal or no padding.

I'm a knife guy...it's been our universal tool for so long I wouldn't be surprised if its embedded in our DNA somewhere. Anyway, I'm also a great fan of Spyderco, having owned several and my favorite carry is the Endura 4 with the wave. The place I work had decided we shouldn't have knives with blades over 2.5 inches in length, so I'm in the hunt to replace my beloved Spyderco Endura. My collection has no small knives that meet my needs, so I scour the internet, looking for the suitable replacement and chose the Ambitious. This is a nice knife overall. 8Cr13MoV is a nice choice of steel, with a pleasant blade shape making the blade strong and useful. As with any Spyderco knife I've bought it arrives out of the box scary sharp. G-10 scales are a mark of a well crafted knife, and steel liners to keep the body stiff. It's screwed together so I can maintain it, and the trademark spyderhole is perfectly placed to allow for a quick & secure opening. Like most quality knives, it has a clip that can be moved to accommodate the owner. I like to carry "Tip up", but the knife is configured for "Tip down", no problem...I'll move it. This is where the problem begins...the holes for "tip up" don't line up. I'm sure Spyderco would fix it if I ship it to them and pay five bucks for return shipping, but I'm not likely to invest that in a thirty dollar knife. OK, I'll see how I like" tip down", not so good either. Somehow the width of the knife kind of hogs up more space in my pocket than I like, and the g-10 scales are so rough that it's hard to get at stuff like car keys that fall below it. I'm starting to like this knife less.Looks like it will go back in the box and become a present for a nephew or friend who isn't so opinionated about what a great knife should be like, and as for me? Back in the hunt for a pocketknife with a blade length of not more than 2,5 inches, that pleases me.

These were given to me as a promotional incentive (to try to get me to give the company a rave review on another item) and, at first, I loved them.  However, it didn't take long for me to find out what other people were complaining about.  The glasses are NOT truly sealed on the bottom.  It took a little while before I noticed but I discovered that what I thought was a finished 'plug' from the blowing process was actually nothing more than a very thin, very clear sticker covering the hole at the bottom.  With use and even the most careful of washing, those stickers degrade or fall off, resulting in a small but troublesome hole that allows water in between the walls of the glass.  And, believe me, that water does not come out easily.  The first time it happened, I kept the glass upside down on a sunny windowsill for MONTHS before it slowly evaporated out.  Now I have two glasses trying to dry out and a third will probably join them shortly.  If I had paid the amount of money they ask for these glasses, I would have been irate that they basically literally used a band aide to fix an issue with the blowing process.  I would not recommend these at all until they fix that issue.  They're lovely and comfortable to hold but if you want to actually wash them, those little stickers will eventually fail.  I might have given them two stars but the fact that Ozeri bribes people for good reviews made me less inclined to be generous.  Those who own them already, I recommend only the most careful of hand-washing for as long as you own them.  Do not immerse them.  Do not wash them in a dishwasher.  Do not run water over the bottom of these glasses.  If you can avoid that, you may be able to avoid their flaw.

Generally I'm not a fan of ear bud headphones, least of all for rigorous activity such as running, but these Bose headphones are a rare exception to a grocery list of qualms I tend to have with the style.Firstly these actually stay in my ears without requiring periodic adjustment.  I regularly run long distance at a fairly aggressive pace and haven't encountered a problem with these slipping around even slightly.  Perhaps I lucked out but the default buds fit me perfectly; it goes without saying that your mileage may vary in that respect but the box also includes a couple more sets.  Calling these buds is slightly misleading I suppose as they're more ergonomic to the inner shape of your ear compared to simply jamming a silicone nub in to your ear hole.  All things considered exceptional design for extended wear particularly in light of their designated purpose.Secondly the sound is completely respectable.  Buds can lose a lot of sound quality to poor fit in my experience so going back to point one these already had a leg up in the nice snug fit but outside of that they produce surprisingly rich and full sound.  I generally run with my volume just short of maximum with 'lesser' headphones (Sony MDR-J10, cheap, fairly secure on the ear, get the job done) to curb the inevitable distortion I tend to see at peak volume but these also jump right up to maximum while maintaining the sound quality.  I wouldn't go so far to call these audiophile headphones by any means so perhaps the price is somewhat suspect in that regard but they are still good easy listening headphones to be certain and hands down the best set of sport headphones I've ever had in terms of audio quality.Last but not least is thoughtful yet simple features.  The cord is splittable which at its shortest is pretty much the perfect length for an armband phone/mp3 player while at its longest will reach my waist (5'10" dude) without an excess of cable tangling up.  It also comes with a shirt clip which plenty of headphones come with but worth mentioning.  It's good for tethering the cable in place to avoid raking your hands on the cord and yanking them out while running or what have you.  All of the materials inspire a fair amount of confidence in their weather and wear resistance but that isn't something I can confirm just yet.The headphones also come with a pretty decent Reebok armband.  While I can't really give credit to Bose for the armband I will say kudos for throwing it in there.  The armband itself, despite a lack of adjustment aside from its elastics, features numerous entry points for headphone cables depending on the design of your device, a velcro cord wrap, and enough room for smaller phones (iPhone 4, HTC Aria...).All things considered these are easily my new favorite running headphones.  They really deliver on all fronts in really sensible ways as a de facto sport headphone unlike any number of things with 'sport' tacked on as an afterthought.  The price is a little up there but even still I'd recommend them in spite of that when I stop to think about the oodles of other headphones I've purchased over the years.

After two attempts, I was able to get what I wanted.  And I feel lucky since each was under a buck, costing me less than $2 total.  It's misleading and wrong to bundle many different products under one title.I was looking for a standard 3 contact adapter as shown in one of the pictures.  The pictures showed both 4 contact and 3 contact connectors with straight or right angles.  Description didn't bring any additional clarity either.  3 Contact connectors are standard stereo connectors with tip, ring and sleeve.  However, 4 contact connectors have 2 rings and use the extra contact for the microphone (or for some other specialized function).  Depending on the brand you're dealing with, the microphone might be the first (tip) or another contact.Unfortunately in both cases, I received 4 contact adapters from two different suppliers.  But luckily, in the second order tip was connected to the tip of my input connector, and the extra contact ended up harmlessly unused in my configuration since my input signal was mono (actually an antenna).Since these connectors are priced so low, it might be worth gambling if you have time and patience.  I wouldn't pay more than a dollar under the circumstances though.By the way, the quality of the connector was fine in both cases.

I had one cabinet devoted to containers with lids--mostly Pyrex with lids--and decided one day to dump the whole pile and start over. I purchased 2 of these packs and was so pleased with how little space they take up. We've had them perhaps 3-4 months now and they've been working well. I could perhaps use a few more mid-size ones as we rarely use the tiny ones and my husband is always using one that's way too large for the amount of food.We've put them in the microwave and haven't had any trouble--but we don't do this a lot as I've found that things reheat better on the stove anyway. As for staining of tomato-based foods, I've been doing 2 things: spraying the container with Pam first and then also putting a layer of Saran wrap in the container before adding the food. So far these have kept them from staining.My only annoyance with them is all the grooves in the lids that make them a little difficult to clean and dry--but I guess you need those grooves in order for them to to stick together as they do (the lids stick together and the bottom of the containers can stick to the lids too). Just try not to have food all the way to the top or on the edges--like when you wipe off a spatula--you'll find it all over the inside of the lid when you open it next time.UPDATE Jan 3, 2014: I removed 2 stars because I've had quite a lot of trouble with these containers getting...well I'm not sure what the white marks are: are they dried-on food from the dishwasher drying cycle, or are they scratches/melted spots from the dishwasher drying cycle? But what I've concluded is that I have to wash these by hand if I want them to last. It appears that if you put them in the dishwasher with even the tiniest amount of food on them, you'll get these unattractive white marks all over them--and at least from what I can tell, they can't be removed in any way. I've already thrown a couple out because of this.As for stains: I now keep a squeeze bottle under the sink filled with bleach and will squirt a little bleach into a container and add some soapy water and let them sit a little while. In no time, there's not the least trace of a stain.So these containers do save a lot of room in the cabinets but they've become rather high maintenance to keep them in good shape.

This is the second Oppo product that I have purchased; the first being the DV981 DVD player.As others have already mentioned, the BDP 83 is a very classy unit - from the packaging to the weightiness, appearance and operation of the unit, it exudes a level of quality that very few, if any, mass market consumer electronics possess.  The Blu-ray playback quality is very good, although I can't honestly say that I notice a significant difference between it and my 2-year old Panasonic BD35.  What IS noticeable is the improved IQ of upconverted DVD's played on the OPPO.  I suspect that this is where Anchor Bay's VRS techology pays diffidend. Audio performance is also well above average, with a well-defined soundstage, smooth mids and trebles (ever so slightly on the darker side of neutral) and, most importantly for me, a full bass that serves to underpin any sensibly recorded music.  Moreover, this player has the ability to play Super Audio CD's, something valuable to me and other audiophiles but perhaps not for most consumers.The main issue with this product for most prospective buyers comes down, rightly and inevitably, to price: $500 is quite a bit of money in the here and now marketplace to pay for a Blu-ray player, even a quality one such as this.  For most consumers on a budget, I am afraid it may well prove too much - the current line of demarcation for an average BD player being somewhere in the $200 pricepoint.  In terms of the Oppo's video performance (the reason for being for most people considering buying it), one can have 85-90 percent of it in another Oppo model (BDP-80) or other name mass market players costing half or less.  The audio performance, fine as it is, is almost a throwaway; most consumers between 18-49 (the target demographic for a tech product like this) nowadays listen to their music at home on portable devices connected to inexpensive docking stations/speakers.With all that being said, it seems clear that Oppo rolled out this product with a 500 dollar pricepoint for a niche group of potential buyers - those who are currently looking for high(er)-end BD players that are not being sold at your local Best Buy, who appreciate quality video AND sound performances and don't mind paying more for incremental improvements.  If that is you, then your search can end here.

Having owned a lesser Garmin model (which I gave to my dad when I bought this), I am very familiar with the wonderful functionality of the Garmin Nüvi.  I decided to upgrade to this model because I wanted to have "hands-free" cellphone capability (bluetooth) with on-screen caller ID.  Voice-Recognition also sounded like an AWESOME safety feature (not to mention 'cool').  The additional features that my previous Garmin did not have that attracted me to this model were Lifetime Traffic, Speaks Street Names, Lane Assist, and Junction-View.Here is my report after 1 month of ownership:PROS:VOICE RECOGNITION: AWESOME! Works even better than I expected!  FANTASTIC!  Such a breeze over having to type everything on the touch screen. You can speak any word you see on the screen and it will navigate there.  Shortcut voice commands allow you to do things that a regular garmin can't!  What can sometimes take a series of screen touches to accomplish with a regular Garmin can be accomplished with a single command (the 3 most useful voice commands are 'View Map', which takes you back to map view from any other screen, 'Hands Free' which takes you directly to the bluetooth phone call screen, and 'Find xxx', which basically locates a POI in your area by name. Saying 'Find Bank of America' will result in a list of Bank of America branches in your area from closest to furthest.SPEED LIMIT ICON: This is perhaps one of the most useful features on this Garmin that I didn't even know was offered when I bought it!  Whenever you are driving on a highway or freeway, the Garmin displays an icon showing the speed limit of the road you are driving on. So far this has proven to be VERY accurate and VERY useful!  The moment I pass a new speed limit sign on the freeway, the icon changes to reflect the new speed limit.  Whenever I see a cop on the highway, the first place I look is the Garmin screen to verify that I am not speeding!MORE GREAT NEW FEATURES: 'Speaks Street Names', Lane Assist, and Junction View all seem to work GREAT!  I don't know how I lived without them before!CONS:DEVICE VOLUME!!!:  This is the most glaring flaw of the device!  The maximum volume of my previous, bottom-of-the-line Garmin was TWICE as loud as this one!  Even with the radio off you have to strain to hear what this Garmin is saying when traveling at freeway speeds.  Why Garmin?  WHY??  Before buying this, I had read several other reviews here on Amazon that complained of the same problem but just assumed they didn't know how to adjust the volume of the device correctly in settings.  WRONG!  This device has an inadequate speaker.  One work-around is to use the FM transmitter feature (built in to the device), but it is not something you can quickly turn on and off, while driving, and unless you want to listen to ONLY the Garmin while you are driving (and not the radio), then this is not a viable option.  Also, as you travel around, you need to keep changing the FM frequency due to interference.  Another problem is that due to the inadequate speaker, it is also difficult to hear a bluetooth phone call using the Garmin while driving.  My Jabra is TWICE as loud as the Garmin.  Unfortunately it looks like I will have to continue using the Jabra due to the inadequate volume that this Garmin is capable of.  What a bummer!POWER DEFECT: This device, even when turned off, doesn't seem to be fully off.  Unlike my last Garmin, which could be left unused in a car for over 30 days and still have plenty of charge in it, the battery in this device will become fully discharged in about a week!DOESN'T COME WITH LIFETIME TRAFFIC!:  Don't let the 'T' portion of the '885T' model number fool you as it did me! This device does NOT come with lifetime traffic!  Instead, you are given a brief trial subscription to MSN Direct, which is not only not available in my area, but is being DISCONTINUED on January 1st, 2012!  Garmin should give the user a choice between lifetime traffic and MSN Direct, but sadly, they do not.  If you want a lifetime traffic subscription, you have to pay extra for it.MY FAVORITE VOICE DOESN'T SPEAK STREET NAMES:  I have found that the included American voices on all the Garmins are weird, sometimes too quiet, unclear and "computery sounding", On the other hand the 'British English' voice is fantastic!  It speaks clearly, loudly, elegantly, and human sounding.  Unfortunately that voice doesn't speak street names on this device!  There is another Female British voice offered that is not quite as easy to understand (but still better than the American English options) that DOES speak the street names, although overall it is not as loud or as clear as the "British English" voice is.DISCONTINUED!:  According to the Garmin site, this model has been DISCONTINUED!  Why is Amazon still selling them, and why is this not mentioned when you are buying it?  Most importantly, WHY has Garmin discontinued this model, and not released a new model with all the same features (that all work properly)??  If it weren't for it's glaring defects, this would be the BEST GARMIN EVER!Overall, I LOVE the features of this device, and I still use it everywhere I go.  I just wish Garmin had bothered to test this product before they sold it!

I wanted something that I could take with me on hikes that was light, compact and something that I wouldn't fret over getting damaged (inexpensive).  This just fits in my day pack, so it qualifies.  You can certainly tell that its an inexpensive piece from holding it, but I think it will do the job.  Just cant beat the price!UPDATE:  Now after using this for a couple weeks, I have something to add.  My main reason for getting a tripod was to do more long exposure shots, not for setting up the camera for me to be in the shot (i.e. quick shutter speed).  For this, the tripod is mediocre at best. To the naked eye, it appears still, but I get blur on > 50% of my shots 1 sec or more.  I even set the timer for 2 seconds to make sure the movement isn't from hitting the button.  Its either still moving slightly after 2 seconds or even the slightest breeze will cause it to move.  Note that this is with the center shaft extended.  If resting strictly on the legs of the tripod, I've had better luck.  I'll also add that I'm not trying to mount some monster camera on this thing... I have a Sony NEX-5n (a whopping 16.4 oz w/ lens).  This will still serve its purpose for the time being, but I will be looking for a more robust tripod that does not move at all.UPDATE 2:  I have found this tripod to be way too limiting for what I need it to do.  When you mount it with the level facing front to back, as most do, you will be able to tilt up and down, but then you have to eyeball if its level (horizontally) by adjusting the legs and/or fix in post when you crop (crooked horizons are the worst!).  If mounted with the level oriented left to right (to make sure you have a level horizon), there is no way to make incremental increases in the forward facing angle, only straight ahead or looking up towards the sky.  You need to fold your strap over and tuck it underneath to get the right angle if you mount it this way.  What you really need is one with a "ball head" that allows you to maneuver the camera into whatever position you need without endless fiddling with the legs.  I have also found it nice to have a quick release, as when I'm shooting, I see a shot that I want to capture off to the side and then resume using my tripod.  If you are looking for an affordable tripod that has these features, check out theDolica AX620B100 62-Inch Proline Tripod and Ball Head(around $40 at the time of this review; you don't have to spend $100+ for a decent tripod)

I've tested and used many pedometers over the years, including the BodyMedia and SlimCoach systems which are both full blown metabolism / calorie usage trackers. This Omron HJA-312 purports to be an intelligent pedometer that provides extra features. It just compare with the many other options out there which do the same job in a far more reliable manner.First, the basics. It's fairly small, about the size of my iPod Nano. about 1 3/4 inch square. It comes with a clip to hook on your belt. When you press the large START button it first shows you the date/time and then shows you today's progress with your step count and mileage covered. When you go into the memory you get the last seven days of data, to compare it.But - and this is extremely odd - when you buy this unit there is no way to get more than 7 days of data and no way at all to plug it into your computer. There's a screw-off cover for the CR2032 battery and that's it. Just about everyone I know who is tracking their health does so with a computer program of some sort, not with a physical spiral notebook. So to have to look at one computer, and then hand-enter those values into another computer, feels fairly archaic.Also, we always test our pedometers against other pedometers that we've verified against physical walking tracks with mileage spots, if we can't take the pedometer out to that track directly. Most pedometers are quite accurate at this point, with all the technology and research that's been put into them. This one, not so much. Sure it comes up in the general range of the other ones, but it's never quite right. Which on one hand you might say is "good enough" - but on the other hand it's not like this is the only option out there. It's one of hundreds! So why would you buy a not-quite-right pedometer, with no cable connector, and with a short-term memory, when there are other things that you can do very well with.I do adore our Body Media system and highly recommend it - that can track all types of activity you do including biking and so on. A pedometer CANNOT properly judge biking motion - it can only track walking and jogging because of its design. It can't even properly figure out "walking in place" because your body sway isn't fully there. So it's important to realize just what a pedometer can and cannot do. But if you're only currently looking for a pedometer, and understand its limitations, I still wouldn't recommend this one. Go with one of the others that connects with your computer, has a longer memory, ideally tracks activity in hour breakdowns, and is more accurate.I received a review copy of the Omron HJA-312 activity monitor via the Amazon Vine Program.

I bought the B60(Special Editon) last Christmas and was surprising pleased with the product.  It brews quickly, there's minimal clean up, and the coffee tastes great. It also has five cup sizes instead of three.  The width of the B70 is narrower although it has a deeper depth.  I considered the compact version of the Keurig, which is everywhere, however the reviews on this item appear mixed and at a price of $100 I wasn't willing to risk purchasing it.  I know the K cups are pricey but break down to about $.65 per cup which is still much cheaper than buying a cup of coffee.  Also, you can use grounds in the optional reusable K cup.  I love both the B60 and B70 machines and will use one at work and one at home.  This is the best home coffee machine I've ever owned.1/29/13 UPDATEI saw this earlier review and thought I'd update it. I am now on my second B60 and second B70. I found that after about a year these machines became non functional. It appears there is a problem with the water pump of these machines. I used only filtered water and descaled the machines religiously. In spite of this they both stopped working at about a year. Luckily, Keurig has wonderful customer service and was willing to replace both of the machines. However, I am seriously disappointed that a machine costing so much would break after only a year and since this happened with two separate machines, it does not appear to be a fluke. Given this, I would not buy another Keurig and I have lowered my overall score from five stars to three. Keep in mind that the warranty is only good for a year (and you have to register your machine when you buy it). If your machine happens to break at one year and two months, you're out of luck.

I just wanted to leave a brief review.I purchased the third Nexus mouse for my wife in March of 2014 and by May it was already non-functional.  My wife is a professional who needs to use a mouse during frequent daily meetings.  The silent buttons were a welcome feature, since loud clicking during presentations can, obviously, become a distraction.Of the two previous Nexus mice I purchased, either the sensor has stopped working or the USB dongle broke.  Unfortunately, the manufacturer does not sell parts, like dongles, so you will have to replace the entire mouse if you break that piece.  The sensor, as per other comments left on Amazon, seems to be a frequent complaint. This third unit, which is the one I've chosen to finally leave feedback on, stopped working altogether and will not power on.  It seems that there is probably a bad solder in the battery compartment since multiple new battery pairs make no difference.The idea of a silent mouse is terrific, and in that department these devices deliver like no other.  I just wish that a company like Logitech, known for quality, would develop their own silent mouse.  As it stands, this product seems to be shoddily built and cannot withstand the rigors required for business use.EDIT: Thanks to another review, I found out that the battery diagram inside the mouse (both on the housing and the battery flap) are wrong.  As you insert the batteries, place the first battery with the positive end (the bump) to the right, which is where the spring is.  Place the other battery in the direction pictured on the flap (to the left).  That is the proper battery orientation.  That doesn't address the other durability issues, and brings up quality control issues of its own, but it's nice to know that at least one mouse hasn't died yet.

These are tiny, cute sized guest soap hearts.  Perfect for making little sweet smelling guest bars!!!  The ease of a silicone mold in soapmaking--NOTHING compares. (I guess it is also perfect for candy making and possibly for ice cubes as well)Also...if you actually plan to bake with this--the carton stated that it is safe up 500 degrees!UPDATE--This could have worked fine for what I bought it for but my rating is being lowered from 5 to 1 star because I just learned it is not pure silicone.  I just learned about the "pinch test"...basically when you fold/pinch a silicone mold, if it is pure silicone and not made with fillers it should be consistent in color.  If you pinch something made with fillers, it will turn white.  When I pinch this, I see white.  Seeing white is also the mark of a low quality product.  For that reason, I would would not purchase this again nor recommend it to anyone.  The use of fillers means that flavors/odors may transfer between your baking/soaping projects.  Even the safety of fillers (will it leach into your food) is a question.  At the very least, I would read more about silicone made with fillers especially if you plan to use it for food purposes.  As for me, this will likely remain designated solely for my guest lotion bars.

I was quite fond of my previous Logitech keyboard (a "wireless desk" set), which I'd used for last five years. But the markings on that keyboard were wearing off and it wasn't part of the "unified" system that Logitech has been using in their wireless devices recently, so I figured I'd upgrade to this K800. I've only been using it a few days but I can already tell it was an excellent purchase. On the up-side, the keys are much quieter than my previous keyboard, and have nice travel and a comfortable feel. They're a little softer than the previous keyboard I used, but I'm getting used to that. The keys are laser-cut, which means the markings will never wear off, and they're backlit which means it can be used easily in low-light situations. I don't know how much I really need backlit keys, but I have to admit it is very cool looking - the backlight automatically shuts off when not in use to save battery, but turns on when your hand gets close (even before touching a key) which is a very cool effect. The backlight can be adjusted from never on to very bright, depending on your preference, and I believe there's an ambient sensor that adjust automatically depending on the light in the room. The function keys are nice, with dedicated volume controls and some FN features for launching the usual apps (mail, media player, fwd/back track, etc). One button I particularly like though is the dedicated calculator button at the top of the number pad - it's very handy for launching the calculator and doing some quick sums without having to mouse around. Using the latest version of the Set Point software downloaded from the Logitech website, all the function keys can be customized at least to a certain extent - programmed to launch particular programs or perform a keystroke combination. Unfortunately there are some limitations such as keystrokes that use the Windows Start button don't seem to work, but it's still pretty useful. The Set Point software also adds some nice interface enhancements as well, for instance displaying an on-screen overlay that shows brightness settings or volume settings, which are very handy.On the downside, there are just a couple of things; the wrist-rest area is shorter than my previous keyboard, so I find my palms rest half on and half off the keyboard. I find the keyboard feels a little shifted to the left - not quite centered in some way, which feels a little awkward. Maybe that's the result of my previous keyboard having a separate function button area on the left that made the keyboard seem wider. The keys themselves are sort of halfway between a "chiclet" style and traditional keyboard, so they feel more rounded and easier to slip from one key to the next - not quite as easy for touch-typing. I'm sure these are things I'll get used to. I do wish there were more hot keys and that the Set Point software allowed for more "power user" controls for both mouse and keyboard, but it's pretty good as it is.Overall it's a great keyboard that I think will last for many years, and it's worth the somewhat higher price for the wireless option and extra features offered by this keyboard over cheaper ones from Logitech or other companies.
