Pyrex has two product lines, Storageware (of which this set is a part) and Serveware, that really should be combined.  As others have pointed out, this set could be improved by having some larger bowls.  The Serveware line features larger bowls, made of textured glass, that look nicer on the table than these plain glass bowls.  But the Serveware bowls don't come with lids; you need to use disposable plastic wrap for refrigerator storage.The bowls in this set have mostly straight sides.  While this is more efficient for storing things in your refrigerator, it's less so for stacking the set in your cupboards when not in use.  A bit more taper in the sides would let the same-size bowls stack better.  The Serveware bowls have quite a lot of taper in the sides, so they stack together well in the cupboard but don't use space in the refrigerator efficiently.Here's what Pyrex needs to produce: a set of bowls, mostly larger than in this set, with the attractive texture of the Serveware line.  The sides should have a moderate amount of taper so they'll stack together in your cupboards.  They should have lids that fit the bowls.WATCH OUT for mismatched lids.  My set came with the correct assortment of bowls, but 5 small lids for the 4 small bowls and only 1 medium lid for the 2 medium bowls.  Of course I didn't check this until I'd already run the full set through the dishwasher and torn the box apart for curbside recycling.  I would have rated the set 4 stars without this warehouse goof.

I heard a lot of great things from the Sandisk extreme 32gb SD card, but I just felt like it was overpriced. I bought this SD instead after reading that it was great for the Canon T2i. Sure enough, it's true! It handles what I need it to do (I shoot 1080 25p video and take the occasional photo).Update 1: Lately I've been getting sporadic flickers in my video when I use this card. Re-formatted and still doesn't solve the flickers. Even when I remove Magic Lantern and turn off all auto adjustments and custom funtions (auto focus, auto white balance, auto exposure, highlight tone priority, etc), I still get them. It's very annoying.I've tested the card with CDM3's software and found out the read speed is a bit over 19Mb/s and the write speed is a bit over 16Mb/s. I think the flicker is due to the card's slow write speed. I'm going to buy a Sandisk Extreme and see if it gets rid of my problem. I will write an update when I get my Sandisk card.Update 2: Turns out the flickering was because of Apple's preview window (the window that pops up when you press space bar on a media file). The Transcend captures 1080 25p video without any hick-ups. That's at the standard stock bit rate though, if you use Magic Lantern to crank it any higher, it'll frequently stop your recording. The Sandisk Extreme that I purchased can handle 3.0 CBR with audio on (at least for me it does).

I held off on buying a case for my Kindle Fire in the hopes that Vine would offer me one for free.  After both November newsletters came and went, I ordered one, ultimately settling on thePoetic (TM) 360 degree Rotary Leather Case for Amazon Kindle Fire (Landscape / Portrait View) Black.  Then in the short newsletter in December I was offered this case, and thought about trying to return the other one and get a little money back.  I waited for the new case to arrive, of course, just in case it turned out to be vastly inferior to the one I was using; but since it was made by the very same people who make the Fire, what are the odds of that?Well, it's worse.  And let me add that the Poetic case is really nothing to write home about; it's a very mediocre piece itself, and I would happily snap up a better one of the price were right.  But even that blows this Amazon case out of the water.By the way, I know that no one reading this is likely to be choosing between just those two cases, so I'll avoid direct comparisons; but let me add that the Poetic case, which has all the features of this case and then some, is also cheaper.  I bought mine for $12.95, and it looks like it's gone up to $18.95.  It's fulfilled by Amazon, so if you use Prime you'll pay neither tax nor shipping.  This inferior product is also fulfilled by Prime, but its price is $25, making it even less attractive when so many better products are selling for less.I do like the elastic band which holds the case closed when not in use, a feature it shares with my other case.  I don't like the little elastic pieces in the four corners that hold the Fire in place.  This is very much a matter of personal preference, but I prefer the Fire encased in leather all the way around.  (My other case does it that way, which has the added benefit of giving me something to which I can clip a pen or stylus--no such feature here.)  Furthermore, getting the straps on over the Fire's corners is a real pain.  You really need to stretch them out and draw them over the corner of the device, while at the same time maneuvering the device into position.  Slide it too far, of course, and the other little straps you've already gotten over the corners will pop off.  I know this thing is also advertised for the Samsung Galaxy Tab.  I've never even seen one of those, maybe that's a better fit for it?  Even if so, I can't believe it's this hard to fit a tablet into a case when both are made by the same company!Once you've got all four corners strapped in, they hold the Fire in place all right, but of course that's such a bare minimal expectation of something like this that it doesn't count as a virtue.  It's hard to come up with anything positive to say about this product, though, so maybe we do need to fire off this talking point after all.  Hey, put your Fire in this case and it won't spontaneously pop out on you!One thing that can be said in this case's favor is that it gives three options for angles at which to prop up the Fire, and holds all three positions quite sturdily--so much so that it has a slight advantage over my other case, which sometimes requires a little delicate balancing to keep the Fire in place.  (By the way, if you do go straight from here to the Poetic product page, know that, while the Fire in Landscape orientation usually holds up as it's supposed to, don't even bother trying to prop it up in Portrait orientation.)  That stability plus the elastic strap that holds it shut earn it a two-star rating and save it from being called a complete and utter one-star train wreck, but they don't overcome its flaws.And I haven't even mention the biggest flaw yet.  As others have mentioned, when you shut the case you're left with a huge bulge on one side and a downwardly-sloping cover.  Think of a three-ring binder that only has a few sheets of paper in it and you'll get the picture.  Unbelievable!  The main reason there are so many tablets in this seven inch size is that people love how compact and portable it is, and this stupid mismatch of thicknesses goes a long way toward neutralizing that advantage.  In the closed position the Fire in this case takes on roughly the dimensions of a 400-500 page hardcover book, which is WAY bigger than the Fire needs to be if kept in a more form-fitting case or no case at all.  I can't even begin to imagine what they were thinking when they designed it this way.  I can't imagine a reason someone would choose to use this case when there are so many other options available, either.  Keep looking.

When that cable disconnected yesterday, I got a brief frustration but after a few 'f words' to the manufacturers I found a way which is to de-skin the thin cables, connect the metal ends and tape it as well as I could. First off, let me say that the marketing claims of "total body workout" are exaggerated. You may have seen these ads on TV. This machine will work your chest, back, arms and shoulders. While effective for these specific regions, this is not your entire body. It most certainly will not provide "the same incredible body sculpting benefit as a gym full of machines in your house". This machine does not work the quads, forearms, calves, lats, glutes, or deltoids, for example. I also don't see how this would help give you "rock hard abs", as the product description claims. For sketchy marketing claims, I deducted a point.ASSEMBLY:The machine comes mostly assembled, bound in about a dozen zip-ties for shipment. The only thing to do is cut off the zipties, unfold the arms and string a bolt through each of them, then screw them back in with the 2 included wrenches. The wrenches, unfortunately, aren't very good and would've been much better if they had been closed wrenches. Lastly, attach the bungee cords for the desired resistance. It took me about 20 minutes to unbox and set up, mostly due to the clumsy wrenches. Construction felt sturdy.. certainly well adequate for my 155 lb weight. I did have a similar issue with the red pad peeling off the plating as other reviewers.COMFORT AND USE:At its core, this is an assisted push-up machine with hinges. It can be uncomfortable if you put all your body weight on the "bicycle seat" (because I think that's where the parts came from!), especially if you're a beginner and do not have a lot of upper body strength. The chest support could stand to be wider and more padded. If you are resting between sets, you'll probably not want to lie on the seat for too long. If you're in motion and using the machine properly, however, this is not a problem as most of your weight will be supported by your arms or other muscles. The height of the seat is not adjustable.On my very first test of the machine, I thought it was a bit wiggly, but that problem went away on my second set as I got used to the machine and moved in a smooth, controlled motion. I also tightened the arm bolt more which may have increased stability.STORAGE:The arms don't fold back in unless you uninstall the bolts again, so this product can take up quite a bit of space. The instructions say to just slide it under the bed. I found this to be a lazy suggestion. Just how much exercise equipment can be crammed under there?CONCLUSION:I work out regularly at the gym with free weights and treadmill or elliptical, but always hated push ups because of difficulty maintaining my posture and changing up the hand positions. With this unit, I can concentrate on my range of motion instead of worrying about proper form. The 3 grips help isolate specific muscle groups. I tried a workout with all 3 bungie cords attached (supposedly 65 lbs of resistance) and really felt the muscles in my arms and chest being worked. If you ignore the "total gym" nonsense and intend to use this for assisted push-ups, this product may be for you. Just don't expect to look like the guy in the product photo or on the box art. They did not get a body like that using this product. If you are looking for something less expensive, there are push up bars. At $100, this is overpriced.

I got this very cheap, but I got it to use as Wireless N Access Point. There are problems with the original firmware but you can fix that by upgrading to the most current one at this time it's 1.10.8. This is very basic N with 12X coverage area, so you're looking at 2 rooms about 150mbps at excellent signal range. The 3rd room would be 120mbps at very good signal. The 2x 2dBi ANT are okay the higher you place this device the better signal you'll get. You don't need to buy additional ANT for it.Now the true story about Wireless Draft N 2.0.. Remember this is still experimental so true Standard N would be 600mbps. Draft N is 300mbps. Based on chipset not real time.Okay so let's see:300mbps = 150mbps (real time) but in the router it can be 130M270mbps = 135mbps (real time) but in the router it can be 115M260mbps = 130mbps (real time) but in the router it can be 110M240mbps = 120mbps (real time) but in the router it can be 100M130mbps = 65mbps  (real time) but in the router it can be 45M120mbps = 60mbps  (real time) but in the router it can be 40M60mbps = 30mbps  (real time) but in the router it can be 10MThese are the speeds you'll can get, but you want to have about 150mbps that's close to the chipset speed which is 300MB.This router has Atheros AR9130 400MHz CPU and 32MB of RAM plus 4MB FlashNot bad faster than DLINK DIR-655 which only has 276MHz, 16MB of RAM and 4MB Flash. Except the DIR-655 has USB port and Gig ports. TEW-652BRP doesn't have USB or Gig ports.If you're going to use it as wireless access point in N or G then you don't have to worry about the 10/100 ports only for connecting it to your network.Now some programmers online have come up with a way that you can turn this Router into DIR-615 C1 3.01 using mod firmware which is just changing the last HEX entries to work the DIR-615 firmware that's all. Once you flash the router to a DIR-615 you'll have more features, but it won't be easy to use. You'll have to read the DIR-615 manual. Then you might find you want to switch back the Trendent Firmware you can do that but editing the firmware or modding it. Still I've tried both and found going back to Trendnet because the DIR-615 firmware not there yet and is prone to disconnections.OpenWRT has firmware for this router but it's in Linux so you'll need to know the Linux code more like Telnet dos text session. Most users were waiting on DD-WRT another firmware you could use but doesn't at this time support TEW-652BRP.Today I am using the latest Trendent firmware and the Router is used for as Wireless N Access Point.  I also own 3x Trendnet TEW-641PC/A Wireless N PC Cards with this device. I don't have problems using those cards.If you need any network tweak head over to DSLReports.com under DLINK forum more there about how to mod an etc.Still this router isn't bad, if configured right you would have something just as good but for less the other expensive ones.I am only rating this router 3 out of 5 because of the lack of features in the firmware, but most of the features are good for the basics plus it's easier to configure!

I have several HDMI to mini-display port adapters littered throughout my house.  In fact, I have one hanging from each of my HD TVs "just in case" I ever need to hook up my Mac laptop.This adapter has a special advantage over the old ones: if you have a 2010 or later MacBook Pro, it carries the audio feed as well as the video feed!  In my testing, this feature works exactly as advertised with one major caveat- the sound is in stereo, not 5.1 Dolby Digital!!!On a 2009 MacBook Pro, the dongle provides a perfect HDMI conversion with no audio present (this is expected behavior).  With a 2010 MacBook Pro, my attached Sharp Aquos TV showed up in the sound settings control panel as an audio output device.  When I selected this device, the sound came through perfectly with no additional cables!  This is a great feature and one that I greatly appreciate for new MBPs.  Saddly when I tried this same test on my Denon AVR, all multi-channel sound was lost and squashed into stereo sound.  Disappointing!If you have a 2009 or older MacBook Pro, it would be foolish to spend this much money for a mini display port to HDMI adapter.  And truth be told, for half of the price of this adapter, you can have a 5.1 optical audio cord and mini display port to HDMI video adapter.  For those cases where you need the sleekest/easiest setup and are playing through stereo speakers (like on a TV), this is definitely the way to go!As with other minidisplay port to HDMI adapters I've used, the video connection works immediately when plugged into the TV.  I'm always impressed by how well my Mac handles this type of thing.  I plug it in, and up pops Mac screen on my TV.  Once I setup audio the first time, that too worked when I plugged the HDMI cord into this adapter.This product would be 5 stars if it carried 5.1 audio.  Instead, it is 2 channel audio and gets only 3 stars.

I bought this CPU as part of a new system to replace my older Core 2 Duo router that was beginning to show its age. This newer CPU performs much better than the older C2D part, but it's still not going to win any speed award.Despite AMD claiming this is a "quad core" APU, it really isn't. It has two Piledriver "modules" that have some duplicate core functionality that allows each core to process two threads. It's very similar to the Hyperthreading scheme from Intel used on the older Pentium 4s. In certain multi-threaded scenarios, the APU performs well, but single thread performance isn't that great.I did some brief testing with the 7550D IGP and it performs well for what it is. It will run older Source engine based games at medium settings well and float between 40-80 FPS at 1280x1024 depending on how much stuff is being rendered. I haven't tested any newer games though; But using the Hybrid Crossfire with a discrete HD7xxx card should improve performance, especially on newer games.The two problems that I've had with this APU are the high heat output and the awful heatsink/fan. While the APU is idle, the included cooling solution is fine, but under a moderate load and above, it can't handle the heat output and the APU quickly starts overheating. The heatsink is this awful poor quality and fragile aluminum and weighs about as much as a small stack of paper. The fan is equally bad and is really noisy, even at low speeds. It reminds me of mid 1990s era SCSI hard drives with bearing noise. It also barely moves any air through the heatsink, further exacerbating the overheating problem.While this APU has its flaws, I'd recommend it for building a cheap machine for the kids, office machines or media machines. Though I would recommend trashing the included cooler and getting something like a Hyper 101a/TX3, or a slim cooler for smaller cases. I'd also make sure you have plenty of airflow in your case, especially slim cases.

I usually stay with Canon accessories for my Canon cameras, just for the 'peace of mind' I can expect from the same manufacturer. But in this case, I see no reasons to choose this package (Canon CBK4-300 Battery and Charger Kit) just because of the brand name. Consider the following facts:1. Canon is not a battery manufacturer. So those 2500mAh rechargeable NiMH cells are simply re-labeled from other vendors.2. All 2500mA NiMH cells in the market are plagued by the problem of high self-discharge rate. That is, if you charge up a set of those AA cells and leave them in your camera for a few weeks, they may become completely drained before you can take any pictures.For the price of this Canon battery and charger kit, you can buy an equally good 'smart' charger (for example, theSony BCG-34HE4), plus eight of the latest generation LSD (low-self-discharge) cells such asSANYO eneloop, Rayovac Hybrid, or Kodak Pre-Charged. Even though their stated capacities appear lower at 2000-2100mAh, those cells can hold 80% of their charge for 6 months or longer. So you don't always have to recharge your camera's batteries the night before, and you can keep another set of charged batteries as standby. This makes LSD cells much more suitable for digital camera applications.Personally, I have retired all of my old-genreation (2500mAh) NiMH cells, and am using only LSD cells in photo equipment now.

I make movies of my kids all the time, and like to share them with family.  I've tried different methods to make that work - but usually it's kind of a pain for them to figure out how to get things.  In most cases I've found that in the end the easiest way is to burn them a dvd and send it.  Not anymore.The Seagate FreeAgent GoFlex Net Stak provides an easy way to set up online file sharing.  Anything you can put on a USB 2.0 external hard drive can be shared with anybody you like.  You just send an email link and they can access, preview, and download the file directly.  Plus, it's a cinch to set up - this is designed for simplicity.  You don't need to be a power network user to make it work.  Think of it as a private server, where you get to decide who has access to what, and that you don't need to be a sysadmin to run.  Or think of it as a local version of a filehosting site for files of any size and where the only storage limit is the size of the external hard drives you decide to plug in - and where there are no advertisements, and no annual fees, and the "hard copy" of the files stays with you.You plug it in to the wall, then plug it in to your network router, and plug in either one of the GoFlex ultra-portable drives (with the adapter removed so it connects via the SATA connetor) or a USB 2.0 cable from any external harddrive.  Then all you do is go onto Seagate's GoFlex Net registration site and register.  The site detected my GoFlex Net setup right away, and in a minute or so I was signed up and onto the Pogoplug site.  It has a very simple and straightforward interface that shows all the files on your drive, and allows you to arrange them into playlists and slideshows.  More importantly, it allows you to share either the entire hard drive or individual files with anyone you like.  They'll get an email with a link to the Pogoplug site - where they can preview or download the file or files you've shared with them.You can plug in one USB 2.0 drive, and there are also two ports designed to fit the Seagate GoFlex ultra-portable drives (like myFreeAgent GoFlex 1 TB) - though it might also fit other drives with 2.5" SATA ports.  There's a little adapter in there that makes it ready to accept a plug-in 2.5" SATA port, but the adapter slides out, allowing for a snug fit when you drop in one of the ultra-portable GoFlex drives.  So, it allows you to have three separate external hard drives connected at any one time, and any one of them can be changed out.  They recommend ejecting it through the Pogoplug site before removing it from the setup.  One thing I like about it is it doesn't seem to matter how the drive is formatted.  It recognizes drives formatted for PCs or for Macs (or, either NTFS or HFS+ formatted drives).This is a very simple networking solution for ordinary users.  Advanced network users may want something that's more flexible and that they can set up for access in other ways than through a free account on the fairly straightforward Pogoplug site.  The site allows you to do some basic things with files on your drive: create slide shows of photos and video, arrange them into folders, preview them, upload new files to your drive remotely, and share them.  It doesn't serve every need - it won't allow you to setup your drive as a remote system backup, for example.  While the GoFlex drives can be used with Mac's TimeMachine program, for example, the GoFlex Net setup won't allow you to run TimeMachine remotely.  It's ideal, though, for sharing memory intensive video files, or as a way to have access to files you need occasionally but don't want to keep stored on your harddrive or your networked iPhone.  Perhaps its a bit of a tradeoff between flexibility and ease of use, but it is very easy to use and does very well what it's advertised to do.

I just got done spending over an hour unpacking and putting these together for the first time.  This isn't going to be a thorough review of the product itself, but rather a word of warning for what you're getting yourself into, and a few tips.  I'm also doing this partly because the manual is ABSOLUTELY WORTHLESS.First, I'll start off with my thoughts on the assembled lights.  They feel moderately sturdy.. the piece that lets you adjust the angles feels pretty weak, and as others have mentioned, the plastic tightening knobs are flimsy.  The tripod is thin steel, but seems to stand well.  The lights are pretty bright, I have no complaints there.  There IS a little bit of a blue tint to the light, but it's very minor.  It's not pure white, but close.  I love being able to switch on and off all bulbs separately, it gives a lot more control. Each fixture has a removable fuse and came with a spare fuse for both.  The cords are a good 10-12 feet long.  The diffuser material and reflector housing don't really straighten out when everything's put together, there's a lot wrinkles in it.. not a big deal, but it does make them look a bit cheap.  There's a very faint hum emitted from the lights, but it's nothing that's going to get picked up by a microphone if you're doing video, you have to have your ear right up to it, and even then it's hard to hear.  Overall, I'm content with them.  I don't love them, I don't hate them, but they work well and do what they were designed to do.  Would I buy them again?  That's a tough call.  Only time will tell how long they're going to hold up.Now for the fun stuff.  As my title reads, if you want a portable continuous softbox kit, look elsewhere.  There is so much involved in setting these up and breaking them down, it's insane.  It's a lot like setting up a tent.  Each softbox consists of 15 parts, all of which need to put together and taken apart each time.1x Slip-on diffusing material1x Clip-on (4 clips) diffusing material, goes under the slip on4x Tension rods5x Bulbs1x Fixture assembly1x Reflector housing1x Stand/tripod1x Power CordThe reflector housing goes over the fixture assembly.  The fixture goes into a small hole in the reflector.  There's a slit in the reflector held together by velcro to make the hole big enough for it to fit into.  The four tension rods are what make the reflector pop open.  Before installing the tension rods, make absolutely sure the fixture is rotated the right way.. you're not going to want to have to do this again.  There's a large end and a small end on each rod, the large ends go into the 4 corners of the reflector, and the small ends go into the sides of the fixture.  There's actually 8 holes around the fixture, just skip one each time.  There are also little white loops that each rod must go through on the way.  If something doesn't seem to fit right and the reflector is sliding off the fixture, one of your rods didn't go in far enough to the fixture (this happened to me twice). The holes go about 3/4" deep, you really have to work at it to get them to go in all the way.  After all 4 rods are in, wiggle everything around a little to make sure one of your rods doesn't pop out.  If they're not all the way in, you're going to wind up with some broken bulbs.  After the reflector and rods are installed, put all the bulbs in.  Now is a good time to make sure they all work, so plug it in.  The small white diffuser fabric with the clips on the corners gets clipped to the white loops that the rods go through.  The fabric is GOING to make contact with the bulbs, there's no getting around this (which has me a little concerned it may be a fire hazard).  After that, just slip on the outer diffuser material and affix the velcro on all 4 sides.  Once that's all put together, it should feel pretty sturdy and is safe to lay diffuser-side-down.The only thing left to do is screw it on to the light stand and plug it in.  Oh, and then do the next one. ;)While that may not sound terribly hard, keep in mind that every time you put it together or take it apart to transport, you have to do ALL of that again (everything must come apart), and you also need to put all the parts into their bags, and safely store each bulb.  You're looking at about 15-20 minutes to disassemble and 20-30 minutes to reassemble.. each (including packing/unpacking).  The styrofoam that the bulbs came in is very brittle and isn't suitable to reuse.. so I advise wrapping each bulb in a cheap rag and putting it back into the bulb box it came in.What I'm personally doing, is storing the softboxes preassembled, and keeping the light stands and power cords in the big tote bag that came with it.  This way it's quick setup and take down.. only problem is storing them, since they're pretty big.  There's no way I'm ever going to mess with putting these back together.Hope this helps someone.

Item arrived on 4/30 at 6pm (practically 5/1) rather than 4/28. The case is fine, though "you get what you pay for" kind of applies here. The sides are still pretty slippery despite other reviews. I am satisfied with the experience - but definitely nothing higher than that. So, 3/5 stars. More details on the case below:The people who claim the sides give the phone a nice grip are exaggerating a bit; or, perhaps they've never had a case above $10? I understand the Galaxy Nexus bare is very slippery, but this case doesn't add much more "grip" at all concerning the sides. Yes, I admit it is slightly better - but that's as far as I'd go if I were putting my word on it. To say it adds a nice grip is nonsense. The case is easy as all get-out to put on. You simply put one end of the phone in first (whether top or bottom), and then push the rest in. It fits snugly, so that's good - HOWEVER (all caps for a reason, this is important) - if you'll notice in a couple of other reviews, it is mentioned that the case kind of covers up the headphone pinhole, and/or mic, or some other part of the phone that shouldn't be covered if this case were made for this phone. I can attest to the fact that my case definitely almost covers up the bottom headphone jack pinhole. It's so close to not allowing headphones to be plugged in, it's kind of upsetting to think I spent money on it - it feels like it's not made for my phone because of this. Again, "you get what you pay for" applies here. However, headphones do still fit - and it's not difficult to get in and out or anything - so the functionality is still there. It's just concerning. You've been warned. Moving on - the best part about this case (and all of them, no matter the color), is it looks great. Come on, admit it, the main reason you clicked this case on Amazon is because of the huge Android ("Bugdroid"/"Andy") on the back - you want that on your phone! And, you should - it looks great and is a nice addition to any Android-powered device! Protection-wise, I don't know. It definitely doesn't feel flimsy in the least; it feels nice and solid/sturdy. At the same time, I know it's not the toughest case out there...brands like Seidio and Otterbox come to mind as tough cases I've had experience with.Despite my neutral review, I am contemplating picking a new color up. This "Smoker" color looks great in the Amazon photos here, but in person, honestly it's hard to see and looks more black than anything. I am wondering how the "clear" color shows up in person. Why would I pick another one up? - come on, this case is obviously a case for looks more than protection - I want one that I find the most aesthetically pleasing!Edited To Add: By the way, the item description on Amazon has a lie in it. It claims that it has "Precise cutouts provide easy access to all ports while buttons have been covered for protection from daily use", however no buttons are covered on this case for the Galaxy Nexus, at least. It's completely untrue. There is a cut-out for the volume rocker (button), and another cut-out for the power button (button)...I realize it says the ports have cut-outs, but it claims the buttons don't, and that's a blatant lie. If you're looking to buy this case but are concerned about this part, I'll be more specific: the charging port has a cut-out, as well as the mic, headphone jack, and speaker on the back. Even the 3-pin connectors on the right side of the phone below the power button, for the optional dock, has a cut-out. All have cut-outs. Do NOT buy the case if you want your stuff covered. DO buy it if you want everything to have open cut-outs, and a nice-looking Android guy on the back of your phone. :-P

CRKT M16-01KZThis is the 3rd CRKT knife I have tried, and it is the third knife that I have returned due to lackluster design and quality. This blade is advertised to be 8Cr15MoV, but it is not stamped or engraved anywhere on the blade. The blade quality wasn't all that spectacular. The black EDP coating looked and felt like cheap paint.It came out of the box almost dull. It would tear apart paper. Every Spyderco that I've bought has come out of the box almost razor shape and fully able to shave paper. The dull blade has been almost a trademark of every CRKT M16 and even M21 that I have tried. Straight out of the box, the blade sharpness is not consistent and would tear apart paper versus slicing through it. My Spyderco Tenacious and Ambitious would shave paper and slice through paper effortlessly even after being used for shop duty.The CRKT M16-01KZ liner lock, just like the other M16 and M21 liner locks, is very thin and felt flimsy. The Auto Lock mechanism is cumbersome to use and also equally flimsy. Even my tiny Spyderco Ambitious has a beefy liner lock with a very positive engagement.The M16-01KZ uses Zytel Nylon for the handles, which was fine, except CRKT designed the handles to be short/thin at the tip of the blade. While trying to release the blade using a single handed motion, I almost sliced open my palm because the tip of the blade pops out of the handle as soon as the release knob is touched. Luckily, the blade wasn't very sharp so I just got a tiny imprint on my skin. Had it been my Spyderco, it would have been a bloody and painful mess, but Spyderco designed their liners and handles to be wide/thick enough  to give decent coverage before the blade is released.I realize the CRKT M16 and M21 line of knives are very popular and inexpensive, but their "tacticool" appeal from the desert tan or black EDP coatings, Auto Lawk and single handed release features should not be considered their selling points. This is the third CRKT M16 and M21 that I have tried, and I won't be trying anymore.  The two other M16/M21s I used were the M21-14DSFG Special Forces Desert Big Dog and the M16-14D Desert Big Dog Combo Edge Blade Knife - these are easily twice the price of this M16-01KZ. Those blades were all rubbish (8Cr14MoV or AUS 4 or AUS 8 or whatever was the flavor of the month), as was the liner lock, Auto Lock mechanism, and release method/technique. I would choose the Spyderco Tenacious or Ambitious G10 any day of the week.Overall: 3/5 stars. Dull out of the box. More tacticool than useful.I felt this particular model was unsafe, I almost sliced my palm open trying to release the blade due to an insufficient amount of liner/handle material at the tip of the blade. Essentially the tip is exposed as soon as the release part of the blade is touched. There is no tolerance, and coupled with the small size of this knife , it could be fairly dangerous to the user. The Big Dog CRKT knives are at least larger, but the blade quality was just as bad as this M16-01KZ.

After a year and a half of occasional use, my TLR-2 lost its ability to hold zero for windage with the laser. Fortunately this product has a lifetime warranty and can be sent back to Streamlight for diagnosis and a fix, though that has yet to happen yet. On the list of things to do, however.That said, I decided to investigate picking up a new unit and ultimately settled on a Surefire X400, albeit at a significantly discounted price thanks to an employee purchase program. Still it wasn't chump change for the X400, especially when considering the fact that I still have a TLR-2 that, in theory, will be as good as new after it gets back from its 'spa treatment' at the factory.Unfortunately for the Streamlight, by picking up the X400 I learned first hand a thing or two about a firearm light/laser combo SHOULD be made. The controls of the Surefire are worlds away from the manner that the Streamlight does things, and even on the nastiest, most ornery kicking guns I own it just keeps working exactly like it should. Of course for its normally five Benjamins price tag (again I paid far less than that), it had better.But what the Surefire REALLY did was spoil me, and made me look at the TLR-2 in a vastly different light. The Streamlight, when working correctly, is still a capable unit. But the switchgear that it uses is far less convincing a solution than how the X400 handles things. And the TLR-2's overall bulk doesn't score brownie points with me given the X400 slightly smaller size and especially in light of new designs from Viridian and others now on the market.The reality is that I paid less for the X400 than I did for the TLR-2. While the Streamlight is serviceable, it's not the pinnacle I initially thought it to be, and given the windage pot breakage it's fallen down even more spots on my own 'hit list'. While it worked fine in all conditions that I used it in, I find that it's really HARD to regain that faith that was shattered when something breaks, particularly when it comes to one's firearms and related equipment.3 1/2 stars...with adjustments as needed after the unit returns from Streamlight.

Why don't they just turn off automatically after some period of no signal? Some people use these with no sound source for quiet, but a lock button/switch could easily solve that. I purchased this monitor to be used with a laptop as a second screen. It was a bit above my limited budget, but I sprung for it on seeing reviews celebrating its colors. I believe I may have set my expectations too high. The colors are not bad, but I do not feel that they are worth the extra over a lower-priced monitor, even after some adjustment. I liked the picture, but do not have a good enough eye for colors and detail to say much more than that it provided a clear image with fair reproduction of colors in a variety of lighting conditions.I found a good range of options in the OSD for adjustment, though. Some people dislike the OSD buttons on the back of the screen, but I think it's a great design touch. The OSD appears in line with the buttons, making use very intuitive. The rear buttons were very responsive, but the touch-sensitive power button in the center of the screen is surrounded by a large ridge, making it difficult to use.On the whole, I was disappointed by the monitor's design. The images make it appear more square, but it has many rounded touches. I do not like the clear edge on the outside of the bezel that Samsung uses on its monitors, nor am I a fan of the rounded power button and circular base. I recommend looking at one of these monitors in a store if possible, as they look quite different from the pictures. I do love the impossibly thin design of the monitor, though, working in an enclosed desk, it's impossible to see. The monitor is also extremely light, to the point where a swivel mechanism is not needed. Some reviewers reported wobble on this monitor, but I saw more wobble with other monitors than this one due to its stiff hinge. Unless your desk is very flexible, I don't anticipate this being a problem.For the time I owned this monitor, I had no issues with broken or stuck pixels, which was my biggest concern. In the end, though, I wasn't completely satisfied with this monitor, and returned it for theASUS ML248H 24-Inch 1920x1080 LED Monitor.

This is a really great screen protector for the iPhone 4. Once properly applied, it is crystal clear and feels better than the iPhone's glass screen.  You still get fingerprints on the screen.  However, I haven't seen any crystal clear (as apposed to the matte finish) screen protectors that truly are oleophobic.  Very happy.Now the application is a bit of a challenge, as is with any screen protector.  I installed it in a laminar flow hood (i.e., dust-free cabinet), and I stilled managed to get 2 piece of dust near the outer rim (These must have been transferred by the nitrile gloves I was wearing).  No biggy; I was able to peel up the corners and pull the dust off using the sticky sheets included with the screen protector.My advice, use the wet application method. I used wet solution included with another screen protector.  However, you can make your own by adding a tiny bit of mild soap (unscented, uncolored) to deionized water (buy some distilled water from the grocery store) and putting it in a spray applicator.  You can read instructions on the wet application method elsewhere online.  But by application a liberal amount of solution to the screen and the iPhone, you can slide the protector for a few seconds to position it properly before it adheres.  Also, I think it helps prevent dust.  Don't freak out if it looks like there are tons of bubbles.  These dissipate within a day or two.

===== Update 03/26/2013 =====I own this AP for almost a year now, here's an update  .....- As an access point, it's super reliable. It's always stable whether it's in 70F or 95F environment (24/7 operation). (Wireless connection is much more reliable than much-hypedEAP350)- VLAN support is broken. You can put an SSID into a VLAN, but tagged wireless traffic never show up on LAN side. (Used wireshark to verify that). Zuni Digital wasn't able to provide any useful support.- Never tested it with radius server. Never used it as a router. Therefore I can't comment on 802.1x, QoS, bandwidth throttling.===== Original Review =====This is a newer generation of a pocket router that has many great features that standard routers may not even have. As you may have read from other reviews, this router is tiny.There are three modes that you can use with this router :1 - Wireless Access Point or Router :: Allowing you to create a wireless connection from a wired network2 - Wireless Extender/Bridge :: Extends your wireless coverage and/or make your wireless connection available on both ethernet ports, allowing devices without wireless adaptor to connect to the wireless network.3 - WISP Hotspot :: You can share a wireless network with several devices. (Imagine having several devices accessing one paid hotspot account at the same time.)But that's just what about every pocket/travel router can do these days. What's special about it? Not everyone wants these features, but many will probably appreciate them.1 - You can create an extra wireless network (SSID).2 - For both SSIDs, you can put one or both of them on specific VLAN.3 - For both SSIDs, in addition to conventional WPA2/WPA/WEP security, you can even authenticate your client against a radius server. (802.1x)4 - There's even a basic QoS service that allows you to shape traffic for each devices connecting to the router.It's basically a full-blown wireless router in a very tiny package. Most of wireless routers on the market don't even have these extra features.Wireless coverage from this Zuni pocket router is just about the same as my other pocket routers. It runs hot, but that's to be expected from such a tiny device. Be sure to give it enough space for ventilation.If you are not a road warrior, and want a set-and-forget router/access point/bridge/repeater/etc., this router is an excellent candidate. I have been using it instead of my primary access point for 24+ hours and it's still stable. No network drop at all.On the other hand, if you travel often with just your wireless device (e.g. iPhone/iPad/Android) and expect to use this Zuni Connect to extend hotel's weak wifi, or share a paid wifi connection with your friends, you will be sorely disappointed as a wired connection is REQUIRED to configure Zuni Connect under these modes.If you are interested, keep on reading to find out why 3 stars instead of 5 ::1 - It doesn't have separate Wireless Router and Wireless Access Point modes. If you want it to work as an access point, you have to disable DHCP server, reboot, switch uplink cable to LAN/SETUP. :: And to revert back, you will have to configure your adaptor manually to router's subnet and enable DHCP server on the router -- OR -- just lose all the configs and reset it to factory setting.Under this mode, you can either configure Zuni Connect via wired or wireless connection.2 - Switching from Access Point/Router mode to other modes require A RESET. It means that your wireless name, wireless security and all other settings will have to be wiped out. You lose all your settings when you change operation mode.3 - After the reset and router rebooted, to continue configuring the router, a wired connection MUST be used. If you are on the road, and you do not have a device with wired connection with you, you cannot extend or config WISP Hotspot at all. Some may say otherwise, but I would categorize this as a MAJOR design flaw for a pocket/travel router.4 - Once the router is on Wireless Extender / WISP mode, the only way to get it back on AP/Router mode is to reset the router, and losing all your settings once again.5 - Since all your security settings gets reset every time you change operation mode. Until you complete  Wireless Extender and WISP Hotspot setup process, your new wireless network will be wide open, and vulnerable for attacks.- - - - - - - -I, as a road warrior/network geek, personally prefer Tenda W150M/W150M+ pocket router over Zuni Connect.Sure, Zuni Connect is smaller, sexier and has even more features. But the advantage of Tenda W150M over Zuni Connect is that the settings ALWAYS stay intact when you change operation mode, and if you know what you are doing, you can configure/control Tenda W150M from pretty much any wireless device (Android Phones/iPhone/iPad/etc.) without the need of wired connection. This can't be done with Zuni Connect.You can change Tenda W150M's operation mode by pressing a button a few times, and that's it. For Zuni Connect, you have to plug in the cable, launch a browser, put in new security settings, etc. Yes, Zuni Connect's web interface is light-year better than Tenda W150M's. But to me, it's just a cosmetic and it's not worth a hassle to use Zuni Connect on the road.Oh, and did I mention Tenda W150M is almost half the price of Zuni Connect ZR301F?

Scenario:  Had a wireless workstaion running Vista that would not connect to a OKI printer via USB.  By acquiring this Linksys device WET54G(hardware version 3.1) I successfully got the job competed for the client.  Attached the WET54G to the Linksys WRT150N router.  From a wired workstation configured the WET54G to talk with the proper SSID, WPA security and setup the proper gateway.  Move the WET54G to the Wireless workstation and connected the LAN port of the printer to the LAN port of the WET54G.  Pinged from the Wireless WS the IP of the WET54G and Printer 192.168.1.103 successfully.  Installed the printer under Add printer and chose NETWORK printer.  Vista found the printer but received a Sub Spooler error message.  Time to think out of the box:  Deleted printer from Printer section and set it up as a LOCAL printer using a Standard TCP/IP port with proper IP address of .103.  All successful.  This product saved the client as she wanted the OKI printer to work in her WiFi environment at her desktop.  Linksys support was oustanding to say the least using their Tech 2 Tech line (we are a VAR for Linksys).  Can't say enough good things about their staff in assisting in getting the job done.

Had huge hopes with the Bissell steam mop. My mom really likes hers for use in her small vinyl floored kitchen. I have about 1600sf of hard surface floors, mostly tile with one room of Pergo.  I've used this twice and it will be going back ASAP.The contraption is pretty simple. Steam pours out the bottom, goes through the thick pad on bottom, and wipes/loosens the dirt on the floor. But that dirt has to go somewhere! I didn't think about the fact that when I mop with my sponge-on-a-stick, the water is nasty long before I'm finished. But the dirt is pretty much going back in the bucket with that method. With the Bissell steam mop, there's no place for it to go. The first time I used it, I noticed dirt puddling outside of the grout before I'd even finished through the first round of water. I thought maybe my floors were dirtier than I thought. I am giving this product 4 out of 5 stars.Positive Aspects:* Product is wireless, with the ability to use multiple frequencies within the 2.4GHz range. If you encounter issues with conflicts between your wireless phones or networking, you can change the ID that the keyboard uses. I have found that compared to a bluetooth wireless keyboard I also have, this one has better performance and better "distance" from the system.* Plug and play. All I had to do was plug in the wireless USB adapter, put the batteries in the keyboard, sync'd the devices and it was up and running in less than 20 seconds.* Integrated trackball mouse with multiple left-click options. You can either use the left/right mouse buttons on the upper left of the keyboard, or for one hand mousing there is a "trigger" style left click button on the upper right near the track ball. This is very handy and a nice feature.* Integrated scroll wheel. Just like normal mice, this keyboard also has the scroll wheel available, and it's located in the "trigger" spot on the upper left near the mouse buttons.* Soft-click keyboard is not too loud, and the keys feel good when using them. Since it's a mostly full size keyboard, you also don't feel like you're having to smoosh your fingers together to use it.Where it looses points for me:* No visual indicators for numlock, scroll lock, caps lock. The only light on the keyboard is the low battery light. This means that if you have accidentally engaged one of the "lock" keys, you won't know it until things stop working. I accidentally had the numlock on and half my keys became numbers vs. letters. I would love to have a more visual indicator, even a low powered led would have been nice.* Moving the trackball doesn't "wake up" the keyboard. If you haven't used your keyboard in a bit, it seems to go to sleep. You can wake it up by hitting a key or clicking a mouse button, but not by moving the trackball. I'm not sure how negative this is, but it doesn't function like a normal mouse would to wakeup your screen-saver/etc.* Not rechargeable. Yes you can use rechargeable batteries (two double A), but in this day and age it would be much more convenient to make this thing rechargeable by plugging it in - even to a USB port on the computer. In this fashion you could alternatively have it plugged in and charging or unplugged and wireless.Overall for our media centre PC, which requires the ability to be anywhere in the room and control it, this keyboard is a great form factor to sit on the coffee table and be out of the way when not in use.

If you are a serious gamer and don't want to disturb others -- without sacrificing the overall experience -- then you will love these headphones.Steel Series Spectrum 7xB Headset for Xbox 360 was very easy to set up. It took less than 5 minutes and I was ready for some Call of Duty action.The headphones are well made, are comfortable, and they look great, too. The retractable microphone is a nice feature, and you can dial down chat altogether in case you are playing solo and end up in a room full of loud or irritating people.I am a veteran Turtle Beach customer (have purchased several generations) and up till now had been using the Ear Force X41 headphones. My main complaint about the Turtle Beach headphones is static and random pops and clicks - it can really ruin the gaming experience when it kicks up.I've noticed no hiss, static or pops with the Steel Series Spectrum headphones. And while not in true Dolby Surround Sound, you can indeed tell when someone is creeping up behind you to the left, for example. You can hear shell casings falling to the right. So it's surround sound, and it sounds good.My only major ding for the Steel Series Spectrum 7xB Headset is that you cannot "hear" yourself talk very well -- for example, when you are on the phone, you can "hear" a little bit of your voice through the earpiece part of the phone. Your own voice is muffled and if you are not careful, you can get LOUD in the heat of battle. Earlier generations of the Turtle Beach headsets also had this issue, but then they added it with the introduction of the X3s.Like Turtle Beach headphones, the Steel Series rely on an IR base station to wirelessly transmit the signal to your headphones. The base station for the Steel Series is very small - vastly smaller then the Turtle Bach base station, which is a tower of sorts that includes a hook to hang the headset on. The Steel Series base station is smaller than a mobile phone.Unlike Turtle Beach, however, the Steel Series only has the option of using traditional red and white connectors to connect the base station to your TV. Turtle Beach offers that option along with a digital optical cable connection. The difference is sound quality is noticeable when compared side-by-side, however, the frequent popping and clicks and constant hiss of the Turtle Beach makes the SteelSeries the preferable headset for me.A couple of fast tips for the Steel Series:* If you play on Xbox Live (especially Call of Duty), choose the "Performance" setting, which is excellent for directional sounds footsteps and gunfire.* Turn on the "LiveMix" option, which automatically lowers the volume very subtly to enable you to hear your teammates better when they talk.

OK, lets get started. First of all, the company that makes the Drobo call it the first storage robot. Let's make one thing clear, this is no more a robot than a laptop, printer or coffee machine. There is no mechanized anything with the Drobo. It's an electronic device, that's all. The video ads floating around the drobo website are also somewhat misleading, it is NOT as simple as unpacking, pluging a couple drives in and that's it.Here my personal experience with a recent model Imac 20", the new firewire drobo and 3 drives (2x500, 1x750)Inserting a drive into the drobo will erase any and all data contained on it!Be sure you read the instruction carefully and think through how you want to format and partition the drobo, yes, it does not do this crucial step for you! You can have one big partition or several.This is done with the mac osx disk utility. Also, you can format the partitions in any of several osx flavors or even fat32. If you are thinking of hooking the drobo up to an airport extreme via USB to share it over your network you MUST FORMAT THAT PARTITION in Mac OS Extended but NOT JOURNALED. Otherwise the drive will never show up in the airport utility shared disk window.I created a 700GB partition just for time machine and the rest as one big chunk. [Update:  On July 5, 2012, this drive failed catastrophically after being in service for 2 years 3 months. As this seems a bit short, I'm docking this drive a star and going back to a mechanical drive for now.]I recently put together a low power Ubuntu (actually MythBuntu) server for my home. The server has two drives: a large traditional hard drive which will keep media files and version control repositories, and a smaller laptop sized drive which will just contain the operating system and a few databases. The hope is to spin down the large hard drive to  save electric usage during the bulk of the time when the server is just waiting.I've wanted to jump into the SSD game and I finally saw an opportunity where the size I could afford--this 30GB drive which Linux formats to 29GB--would be useful. In fact, this drive size is more than plentiful for the purpose under Linux, if I could have found a non-junky 16GB drive it would have been fine. A full install of Mythbuntu only uses 2.3GB.Impressions. I don't believe I'm saving much power with this SSD, at most it's using a Watt or so less than the Seagate Momentus laptop drive it's replacing--according to my Kill-A-Watt. This was a bit disappointing, but it speaks to the energy efficiency of laptop drives. The drive, of course, is dead silent and that adds value as my previous server was intensely loud and I'm going out of my way for quiet. I have hopes that the solid state nature of this drive will make it long lasting; the laptop drive it's replacing was probably not meant to be spinning 24x7 for years on end. Time will tell.It's rocket fast. My boot time dropped from 58 seconds to 18 seconds. But I don't reboot very often. Still it's fun seeing how the various boot screens pop in and out  so quickly.My drive shipped with the well regarded 1.5 version of the firmware, so in the end I didn't have to go through the process of making a FreeDOS CD and running the firmware updater off a thumb drive.I purchased this particular drive because it reviewed well from many many satisfied users at the places I shop for computer components. Not quite as good as an Intel SSD, but still well regarded compared to lesser brands. Also, it was comparatively inexpensive where I bought it after a rebate.In the end, I got it because I like buying new tech. Probably, the re-purposed laptop drive I had been using would have been fine. Still this is sweet and if it gives me many years of reliable service it will be worth it.

So, I have been buying New Trent external batteries for awhile now.  I am an emergency responder / incident commander - so having my electronics work for long-durations during extreme conditions is very important to me.  Just having a way to keep charging my blackberry and iPad for hours (days) is crucial.So... I have a collection of various external batteries that have different power capacities, abilities, and sizes.Before now, my iCruiser was my best, all-purpose, go-to charger.  It's still phenomenal (with 11000mAh and the ability to completely recharge my iPad to 100% from dead), but there were two things I didn't LOVE about it:  1) it only had one USB port for charging; and 2) it is shiny - and fingerprints get all over it.So, it would seem that New Trent in their development of the iCarrier has fixed these two issues...  The iCarrier is a 12,000 mAh powerhouse.  Like the iCruiser, it has the blue LED light that blinks to let you know that it's either LOW, MED or HIGH in the charging/power supply - but this model is black mat plastic.  NO FINGERPRINTS, and it has TWO USB ports (both are 5V, but one is a 2.1A and the other is a 1A output) that allows me to power my iPad in one output and my blackberry (or ipod, or GPS, etc..) in the other.ONE QUESTION - and I will follow up with an answer when I get it:  My iCruiser had a technical direction in the paperwork that informed me (the user) to not use the device as a pass-through power supply (i.e., don't use the external battery as a powerbrick for your iPad) - and this iCarrier doesn't carry the same warning.  I wonder if that is also true of the iCarrier, or if it's not a problem anymore to do that with this upgrade?  Here is what I found: if I have my iPad charging with an iPad USB cable already plugged into the 2.1A output port of the iCarrier, and THEN I add the AC power cord - the iCarrier continues to power my iPad AND the LED light blinks on the iCarrier which makes me believe that it's recharging***.  HOWEVER - if I have the iCarrier plugged in with the AC adapter first, and THEN try to attach a device to the USB output, it prevents me from being able to charge the device, but still continues to power the iCarrier.  Since there is no technical direction in the iCarrier paperwork that warns me to not use the device as a passthrough powerbrick I wonder if it's not big deal.... or, did I accidentally figure out a way to bypass a safety feature that they installed...?  I will write to their tech service department and get an answer... (***I only tried this for about a minute... just in case...)Still - absolutely a 5 + star review.OUTSTANDING device.p.s.  these are NOT teeny-tiny external batteries.  I can still fit it in my one hand, but it's not exactly a device you would put in your front pocket (or side pocket, for that matter).  It's a good fit in cargo pants pockets.

I purchased a Soundtouch 30 and added a 20 after just a week with the 30.Set up was relatively simple with the first one, however, it locked my Mac up after the initial setup when the application says its now safe to disconnect from the USB port.  A call to Bose customer service was extremely helpful and they walked me through the remaining steps and remained on the line while I tested it.If you intend to add additional Soundtouch devices to your network, upon setup, when asked to name your device, I would recommend changing the default to reflect the room it will be placed in.I love being able to simply touch a preset button and have my favorite radio stations begin to play.  But it's also convenient to play anything from my iPod, iPhone or iPad through Airplay.Cons:* I added the second device thinking while in radio mode, I would have continuous music room to room.  However, the radios do not play synced . . .and if the volume on one is turned up loud enough to hear in the other room, the delay between the two is extremely annoying.  Hopefully this is something that will be fixed with a future firmware update.* Provided my Mac, which houses my iTunes library is in wake mode, the iTunes music library is accessible.  From within iTunes, I can send synced music through multiple Soundtouch devices via Airplay.  After experimenting, I discovered iTunes Radio can send synced music as well via Airplay . . .so there is at least a workaround.  However, it somewhat defeats the convenience the devices would otherwise offer.Overall, I couldn't be happier with my purchases and plan to add a third device once more features become available and the sync problems are addressed.  I'm also very much looking forward to the soon to be released Soundtouch Controllers that will work in conjunction with the devices.***UPDATE***. Feb. 1, 2014Thanks to the helpful advise from Bose, I am now able to listen to radio streaming everywhere and it flows together perfectly.  I'm purchasing a third unit for my bedroom to replace a Bose SoundDock Air which, unfortunately, doesn't integrate.***UPDATE*** Feb. 6, 2014After now having the ability to fully sync my SoundTouch 30 & 20, I added a Portable today which replaces a SoundLink Air that could not be synced with the SoundTouch systems and I plan to pass on the SoundLink Air to my son.I had to call Bose tech support because I just couldn't get the portable on my network.  After walking me through a number of options, the very helpful tech determined the wifi card on the Portable was defective and offered to ship another or I could simply return.  I opted to exchange the Portable locally.I now have the Portable connected to the network and it works just as I expected it too.  All that to say, sometimes, there's a faulty manufacturing problem but exchanging is simple and connecting truly is extremely easy.All in all, I'm very pleased with all three devices.  The Portable sound quality isn't quite what the 20 is, but it's still quite good and I have portability when working outdoors.For those having difficulty setting up while tethered to a computer . . .or would prefer not to set up using a computer, there is an alternative method (I used the method successfully while setting up my Portable)Actually, there is an alternative setup route.Hold down the 2 and minus button simultaneously.  Continue holding until the load bar is full.  Release, then hold the 2 and minus button down again as a countdown comes on the screen . . .continue holding and you will see instructions to go into your wifi settings on any device using to access your network via wifi like a tablet or phone or laptop, etc.Select the Bose Soundtouch network that appears . . .then pull up your browser and type in the URL address the Soundtouch display says to go to.Follow onscreen prompts as it automatically connects you to your home network.***UPDATE 2/14/14***For anyone wondering if the Bose SoundTouch will work with Logitech's Harmony Touch Remote, yes it will.  We use the Harmony Touch on the bedroom TV which is where I installed the SoundTouch Portable.  So I currently have that one set up on the Harmony Touch with very little effort.  I'm curious if I can set up an action to play a specific favorite radio station "everywhere" on the other two SoundToich Devices in the house.  Will update if it works.In the meantime, we're enjoying the features and wait with eager anticipation for other features to come.***UPDATE April 30, 2014***With the recent updates to Bose SoundTouch devices as well as their iOS App, I'm now able to listen to my stored music library via NAS drive using Western Digital's My Cloud.  I'm not sure which other NAS drives are compatible with Bose SoundTouch but certainly My Cloud is.  I also noticed, using the iOS App, I can selectively listen to different music on all three of my devices.  Both features have greatly enhanced our enjoyment of SoundTouch.

I've started with Sony changers ever since their first 5-DVD spinner, to their 200 then finally their 300.  I eventually dropped Sony and went with the Kenwood Sovereign Faroudja progressive scan DV-5900M 400+3 daisy-chainable integrated system (HR-1 Entre Entertainment Hub, VR-5900 receiver and two DV-5900M 400+3 changers as I peaked at about 700 DVD's).  I truly loved having all 700 DVD's in one comprehensive library launching point that was able to download cover titles and information from the internet (OpenGlobe).  And the library interface was much more robust and allowed more title information than any of Sony's offerings.But with the march of time and technology, Blu-Ray was the future and my BR collection was reaching 200.  Having to squint to read the side labels of all the BR cases when trying to pick out a movie to watch in the bookcase they were stored in became too tedious for my old eyes, I realized it was time to invest in a BR mega-changer and put my PS3 to rest (I already burnt out the BR player in it, but luckily it was still under warranty and repaired for free).  And the only one out there right now was this Sony BDP-CX960.Setup went smoothly loading my 200 BRs, though the slots don't have as much support as my Kenwoods, so the discs tend to have more wobble and play.  So far, this hasn't caused any jamming issues, unlike my Kenwoods which are now beginning to jam with alarming frequency, requiring full disassembly to pull out all the DVDs and reinsert them.After about an hour of having it load title information from Graceote, I was left with 7 unidentified BR's, of which I was able to manually reload 3 and select the best option from multiple hits.  The remaining 4 I had to type everything that I was able to myself from scratch.Benchmarking:1) Cold power-up times average approximately a minute before I'm able to manipulate the interface.  Compare this to 15 seconds for a PS3.2) Loading the movie "2012" from halfway around the carousal and getting to a usable DVD interface was almost 2 minutes.  The PS3 took 45 seconds, but keep in mind there was no spinning a carousal involved; just slipping in the disc and letting it take over from there, but you have to include the time it took you to find the disc on your shelf, retrieve and open the case, then sit back down.  Don't forget the post-time required to unload and safely secure the disc back in your library shelf.3) My Kenwood would usually take 30 seconds to a minute longer than the new Sony in similar tasks.PROS:1) FINALLY a beautiful 1080p playback CD/DVD/BR mega changer, 400 to boot!2) On screen library that loads title information from the internet (Gracenote).2) Overall, much more responsive and faster in every category than my older Kenwood Sovereign system.3) Familiar and fairly intuitive media library interface based on the PS3 interface.CONS:1) NOT daisy-chainable.  A big let down as it forces me to keep my Kenwood system to handle just the plain DVD's.  And with my voracious appetite for BR DVDs, I'm bound to push past 400 soon enough and will dread the day of having to manually switch between multiple BR changers just to see all my titles.2) If the title information is wrong on Gracenote and there are no alternative suggestions, you are limited to editing the title, genre, MPAA rating, director, actor and release date.  You can NOT edit nor add your own custom thumbnail picture nor assign a category (roughly 10-15% don't have thumbnails from Gracenote).3) You can't jump alphabetically within the library; you must always scroll.  And scrolling through a couple hundred movies can be tedious.  If you hold down the advance button, the titles stop displaying and you only see the thumbnail view blur by, thus forcing you to release the button to see where you currently are in the library.  Though the library does scroll very fast so it's not that bad to scroll through 400 titles.4) The onscreen keyboard is painfully slow to use, and its different than the virtual keyboard of the PS3.5) No optional keyboard input available.  Heck, even my Kenwood INCLUDED a WIRELESS keyboard (though, switching between upper and lower case on that thing was awful as there was no CAPSLOCK and the default was always uppercase).6) Unlike the PS3, audio output via optical is only Dolby Digital and DTS.  To truly get the best audio experience from this, now I have to invest in a multiple-HDMI receiver (as I have DirecTV, PS3 and Xbox 360 HDMI audio to handle).  Even though HDMI Monitors/TVs may have multiple HDMI inputs, all of them pass STEREO ONLY out through either its HDMI or optical out.7) I was expecting a big machine as my Kenwood DV-5900Ms were 21" deep, but this monster is also 1 inch taller than my 8.5 inch tall Kenwoods!8) The jog-wheel feels very flimsy and flexes on the lightest touch.FUTURE UPGRADES SUGGESTIONS:1) I don't think daisy chaining will ever be possible as there are no inter-changer interface ports.  Alas, that means a whole new design.2) Allow jumping alphabetically within the Library.3) When fast scrolling, display the title as well, even as its blurring by in super fast scroll, I can attempt to ascertain approximately where I am in the library.4) When viewing the library there is too much wasted space to the left of the listing (which is reserved to show the Photo and Music library icons).  If they can shift to the left while providing larger thumbnail pictures, this will make it easier to identify titles, especially ones with long titles.5) Allow for adding custom thumbnails and editing the category field.Sony seems to have been keeping this machine updated as I have been getting rather frequent monthly updates since I bought this at the beginning of the year, though I haven't noticed any notable interface changes.  I can only hope they will be listening to customer feedback and incorporating new features instead of just bug fixes.UPDATE 2011-Feb-16:It seems one firmware update that I can't recall introduced the ability to change Genre's; unfortunately, they removed the ability to change the MPAA rating.  Not sure why Sony did that.I have now bought an HDMI AVR and after getting useless and wrong answers from different reps in the Sony chat technical support trying to get true audio bitstreaming via HDMI instead of PCM, I discovered on my own that you have to set the "BD Audio Setting" to "Direct" instead of "Mix," otherwise the changer will always decode audio internally and output PCM via HDMI.  The Sony tech support staff kept telling me that bitstreaming via HDMI was not possible (though the product descriptions even on Sony's website states explicitly that HDMI bitstreaming is supported); they even suggested I connect a digital audio cable (which my AVR doesn't allow a separate coax/optical audio connection in lieu of the audio via HDMI as HDMI is designed to handle both audio and video signals) to get bitstreaming, however, they don't realize that HD audio (DD TrueHD and DTS-HD Master Audio) can only be sent via HDMI as SPDIF does not have the bandwidth to handle the higher data volume of HD audio.On a separate note, my little 3 year old niece was playing with my changer unbeknownst to me and threw in several Wii discs on their side inside the carousel.  I kept hearing a grinding sound when playing movies but otherwise everything worked fine.  One day I decided to investigate the source and to my horror discovered the door wouldn't open all the way and would automatically close.  I had to force the door open and reach in and manually pull out all the discs while trying to get the carousel to turn.  Long story short, after discovering the cause and examining all my discs, there was no damage to anything to my amazement.  Reinstalling all discs and reloading all Gracenote information (I mistakenly closed the door after pulling out all the discs leaving it empty and the changer deleted all disc information), everything worked as before.  All I can say is that I've heard of other reviewers claiming their changers physically damaged their discs.  In my case, even with "loose" discs jamming up the system, the changer did not damage any of mine.

It's probably unfair to write a review after only one day's ownership, especially a work day, but here are a few thoughts.12x zoom in a pocket camera is an amazing thing. Whatever other camera(s) you own, this is the one you can take everywhere.And while the 65x zoom available with combined optical/digital doesn't produce pictures that you'd want to show anywhere, it's certainly fun for spying on people. I was even able to see people at the top of the Empire State building taken from the street, 10 blocks away.Polarized sunglasses can make the screen disappear in bright sunshine. (Do wish this camera had a viewfinder.)27 scene modes cover most conditions, but they're on 2 separate screens, and the first has modes such as "baby" and "pet" (which I don't need) while "burst" and "flash burst" are on the second screen Wish one could move them around.Tried flash burst in a pretty dark room and didn't work very well, pictures were much darker than with normal flash, though the camera's flash refreshes fairly quickly so you can take a series of pictures with full flash almost as fast as in burst mode. Didn't try burst flash in a room with some lights on, yet. One of my reasons for wanting this camera is to be able to take candid pictures in a party situation and my old Sony H-5 just takes too long and I'd miss more pictures than I'd get.I'll add to this review after I use the camera a bit more.UPDATE: I've had the camera for about a month now and just returned from a weekend in Wash DC. The weather was gorgeous, not a cloud in the sky, and that was the problem. Without a viewfinder, I ended up taking lots of shots just guessing because I couldn't see the screen because of the glare. You want to take pictures with the sun behind you, lighting up the subject of your shot, but that means the sun is shining onto the screen, thus making it almost useless. It actually turns into a mirror. If you focus, you can barely see through the picture of your own face and see a dim outline of what you're shooting and hope for the best. This is not really acceptable. Otherwise the camera is great. The wide angle allows you to get shots that would be impossible (the whole dome of the capitol from underneath it) and the 12 x zoom is great and the HD movies are great, but taking pix in sunlight is what everyone needs to do. I did not try making the screen brighter, and I will play around with this next time I'm in sun and not with family, but the glare off the screen was so bad that I can't see that making a difference. I have a protective shield on the screen. Maybe they make one that acts as "sunglasses." I'll have to check. I don't know why Panasonic chose not to put an EVF but this was a major blunder and while there aren't a lot of point and shoots with 12 x zooms to choose from out there, you might want to wait for one that has an EVF.
