I've owned a number of portable devices over the years, and am on my 5th IPOD. (All still working) I've purchased many different headphones of different designs, styles, manufacturers, and wide array of price points. These are by far my favorite sounding earphones to date.Many people have commented on the bass, and admittedly, I'm not a bass head.  I've been a rock and roller attending hundreds of concerts over the years. (I just joined AARP the same month I went to see Petty and CSN&Y; and on my way to see The Who next. I've stood on the field level during the last Pink Floyd tour while the speakers were actually blowing us backward they were so loud and bass filled. I've also had the luck of seeing Jimi, Janice, Zepplin, Tull, U2 and countless others) This has led to my beginning to lose my "highs".  Therefore, bass is not an issue for me.I spend an awful lot of time writing at my computer and doing research in loud environments, so the noise isolating feature is very important to me. I've owned noise canceling headphones, but the battery packs reduce mobility, and require carrying batteries  when you travel. These earphones do the job nicely, without any bulk, and allow you to lower your volume thus increase your IPOD's playing time.I've toned down my music taste a little over the decades, and find myself enjoying Mark Knopfler's rich bluesy style over the hard rocking sounds of my youth, however, early Clapton live boots, and The Who live stille rock my world. Remastered releases of my youthful favorites still draw me to that old time rock and roll. The ER6i transmit the sound equaly as well regardless of who or what style I'm listening to. I've invested in the silicon triple flange ear pieces as I've smaller ear canals and these fit much better for me. You will need to try out the spongy foam or the silicon for your own ear's shape.My main complaint is the silicon triple flange go deeply into the ear canal and due to the thinness of the wires, you must be careful when removing the earphones. Do not grab them by the thin wires to remove them, or you will start to experience what other reviewers have mentioned, an intermittent cutting out of sound in one ear or the other.  This design flaw, the thinness of the of the wires,is a design flaw I find fault with in regards to the ER6i. For to get the full effect from the sound, you must firmly insert the ear piece, but removing them can be difficult, especially if you have thick stubby fingers as I do.Etymotic's instructions tell you that if you purchase the earphones from another seller, you must register your Er6i on their website, under "warranty registration" within 90 days of purchase to receive the full year warranty.  You will find yourself unable to locate this section on their website.  However, a call to Etymotic's toll free number will get you in touch with some very helpful staff eagerly willing to resolve your problem without any proof of purchase date.  I know this because after suffering with the intermittent cutting in and out of my left earphone, (it's the one I would remove when someone wanted to speak with me) my right earphone finally went out completely.  I called the toll free number, explained I hadn't registered the ERI6 prior to the expiration of the 90 days.  I was told I couldn't because this feature was not enabled. The staff member was apologetic, and without any argument at all, I was given an RMA number, no questions asked or proof of purchase date requested or required.  I expect a replacement pair within the next ten days. This was very impressive to me in this day and age.  I've read from some reviewers that SHURE does not have good customer support, though I can't personally attest to that.  I had considered replacing the ERI6 with a pair of SHURE E3's but after dealing with Etymotic, I've decided to stay with them for the time being.Oh, initially, when I first purchased my ERI6, I was so impressed with the sound that when I saw them on sale for $80 with free shipping, I purchased a second pair. (I was going to be selling them on Ebay and going with the SHURE E3 after the right ear went out, but I'm glad I didn't. I will be using my second "spare" pair, while waiting for the replacement from Etymotic.My advice, these are great sounding earphones and at what you can find them priced for through Froogle, they are also the best priced quality earphones for the money.  I can live with their design flaw of thin wires knowing Etymotic stands behind their product. A rare feat these days.  Also, the customer support person spoke English, and actually lived in this country.  Another bonus.Also of note, some people have complained about the length of the cord. When I bought my second IPOD, I found a company out of Australia that sold a cord wrap.  They've since been bought out and are easily located under the name "Sumajin SmartWrap". They come in many different colors.An update on the replacement pair: Sure enough, customer service came through for me.  They sent me a new pair and this is hard for me to believe, but I think they sound better than the first pair I sent in for repair.  (though this might be because of a difference in the 2nd generation Nano?)I did use my Shure E3's for a while and thought the sound was superior on those compared to the Etyomics. Now, I'm not so certain.  With the Nano the thinner cord of the ER6i is a definite plus over the Shure E3's.  And the difference in price certainly make the ER6i a better deal.

A great duvet cover should be as lightweight and soft as the duvet itself, in my opinion, so that when I'm sleeping under the duvet I don't feel as if I need to add a sheet to protect myself from a harsher linen fabric or that I'm being pinned to the mattress by heavy velvet. In that respect, this duvet cover really is ideal -- it's a soft cotton, just high-enough grade that you can feel there is some quality there, and the seersucker-style pattern isn't overwhelming, running in wide bands the length of the item. The white would be a good choice for someone who is looking for a plain/minimalist cover, but wants some texture in place of a pattern.One caveat, and the reason I haven't given this the full five stars. The cotton is very sheer, which when the duvet cover is white, becomes an issue. If your duvet or comforter isn't also pure white, be prepared for some of that to show through. I mention this because my duvet has a kind of cream tone to it, and it's obvious that it isn't the same color as the cover. It's not glaring as the colors are too similar, but you will notice it. Going forward, the thin cotton also makes me slightly anxious about how well this will stand up to wear and tear, and to routine washing. All cotton wears thin over time, and the thinner it is the greater the prospect of rips & tears down the road. I'll keep an eye on this and post in a year's time, by which any problems should have become evident.All in all, a good, simple style of duvet cover for those looking for an alternative to the endless stripes and flowers.

Great concept but with major functional issues... and so far - terrible support from Belkin.Sometimes auto-connects, sometimes I have to hit the button to get it to connect to my phone. Sometimes auto-answers calls without any prompt (!), sometimes I have to hit the button or the answer button on the phone. There are no support documents at all for this product on Belkin's website. In fact it is exceptionally difficult to find any information at all about this device unless you know the model number. Even then, it took me ten minutes of digging through all of their product categories to try to find it. I've emailed Belkin support with these issues, but after a week of waiting for a response, I've had no reply other than the automated "we've received your question and you should receive a reply within one business day" email. I've had similar issues with Belkin support for wireless routers in the past, so big thumbs down for Belkin support.Auto-connecting would seem like a neat feature- IF the device were not dependent on the aux-in input. On factory and aftermarket head units with Bluetooth support, a Bluetooth paired phone's audio will over-ride the other input signal during calls. But for this device and other aux-in adapters, there is no way to do that. So your ringer will need to be turned up when paired with this device if you are not on the aux-in on your head unit.Now, add in the auto-answer "feature" to the auto-connect "feature" and you've got a real vexing problem. If you don't hear your phone ring and it auto-answers while the head unit is on another input, you may not ever know it. The caller will be able to hear you (via the belkin mic), but you won't hear the caller! This has the potential to be extremely embarrassing let alone annoying. Auto-answer is something I would NEVER want my phone to EVER do, let alone do it without me knowing it! I could live with auto-connect if it did it every time. Auto-answer? Not so much.The device looked promising. I've tried a couple of other Bluetooth adapters with aux-in for music, but both required keeping an internal battery charged, and neither had a built-in mic (so hands-free wasn't an option and made answering calls awkward). This one powers on and off with my car, and will even charge my phone. The price seems a little steep, and the charging current is fairly low- seems to take a very long time to charge my phone- so long that I'm not sure it's actually charging my battery. Some phones may not charge at all with too little current. Again, there are very few details or specs for this product on Belkin's website, so I cant say what the charging current actually is.Caveats: The auto-connect and auto-answer issues could be the phone, which is a Verizon HTC Droid Incredible. However there do not appear to be any settings in Android 2.2 to control whether calls received while connected to a bluetooth headset will be auto-answered (nor for whether to auto-connect). Nor has my phone auto-answered with any other bluetooth device or headunit. Additionally, I have yet to find reports of others experiencing this issue with Android or HTC phones in particular. Perhaps the next step is to email HTC, or email Belkin an update to my question with a copy of this review attached. However, even if it IS an issue inerrant with Android, Belkin markets this device as compatible with "All Phones". Android phones make up a large percentage of "all phones", so if there is a known flaw which prevents this device from working properly with Android, it would behoove Belkin to provide such information at the very least on the product support page.

I realize it has very high marks per the user reviews, but I haven't seen any of those reviews comparing the unit to either of those which I am comparing to here.  So, I must assume those reviewers have't had the luxury of listening to either the Harman Kardon or the imt800.  Additionally it lacks treble and bass controls on the device itself.  Its sound is a bit flat and lacks crisp highs and deeper bass.Harman Kardon - I got this for my wife for Christmas in 2008.  It rocks, has incredible volume with no distortion.  Is portable with 8 D batteries, but doesn't charge later ipod/iphone models.  Nonetheless, sounds better than the Pioneer by far and is portable and durable; well made.Altec Lansing imt800 - I've had this since December 2009.  It has by far the best sound, perhaps due to its dedicated tweeters, mid-ranges, and subwoofers.  The bass on this device is unreal, and I usually have it turned down to a +7, which is even by far more bass than I can get out of either of the other two devices compared here.  My music is high bit rate and my comparisons were fair.  I might even  ask that this be buried with me in my coffin someday... :)  It has separate bass and treble controls.  Plus, this unit even sounded better when running on batteries.  Not to mention the FM tuner which i don't use when at home but comes in handy when camping.  This comes with two adapter cords for alternate music device connections which was very considerate of Altec Lansing.  If I could get on a call with Oprah, I'd ask her to add this to her list of favorite things as is continues be mine even after a year and a half.  Not sure why or how it can put out so much more bass than the pioneer or Go Play since they all have dedicated 30 watt sub woofers, but it certainly does.  BUY THIS!  Definitely worth the $200.

We live in a three level townhome with a 65lb dog that loves to shed.  Our current vacuum is theBISSELL 5770 Healthy Home Bagless Upright Vacuumwhich does an admirable job keeping our house clean.  However, it weighs in at 35lbs and it becomes quite tiresome having to constantly haul it up and down multiple flights of stairs.  Therefore we've been in the market for a lighter vacuum we could place upstairs and leave theBISSELL 5770 Healthy Home Bagless Upright Vacuumin the basement den.  We decided to try out the Dirt Devil Vigor Cyclonic Pet Bagless Upright Vacuum Cleaner.  Here are my thoughts;Pros+ Lightweight (see Cons below).+ Easy to assemble.+ Bagless cyclonic technology.  Twist out inner cyclone filter makes cleaning easy.+ 5 levels of height adjustment.+ Powerful suction with a 10 amp motor.+ Multiple attachments.+ Washable filter.+ Affordable.+ Compact size.Cons- So lightweight it tips over with even the most minor pull.  Not really heavy enough to hurt you but can give you a bruise or two if you're not careful.- Power cord could be longer.  It also doesn't stay attached to the clamp on the handle.- Extremely small dirt canister.  Not ideal for a pet household despite the vacuum's name.- Some of the attachments fall off of their holding clamps very easily.- No power button on the handle, only on the base of the unit.- Vacuum extension hose consistently pinches the hairs on my arm when using it.The Dirt Devil Vigor Cyclonic Pet Bagless Upright Vacuum Cleaner is an inexpensive and powerful little vacuum that does its job and does it pretty well.  It had no problems picking up dust, dirt and pet hair from the carpet, beds or other furniture.  This vacuum is perfect for our smaller upstairs and laundry room.  It's versatile, lightweight and compact which makes for easy use and storage.  The 10 amp motor provides good suction and it will pick up just about anything.  Unfortunately, this isn't the perfect vacuum for a pet household, at least not one with a large dog or multiple pets.  The small size of the dirt canister alone rules this vacuum out completely unless you enjoy emptying it after every 5-10 minutes of use in heavy pet traffic areas.  The lightweight construction while convenient comes with the problem of the vacuum constantly tipping/falling over when using the attachment hose.  This can be quite dangerous on stairs.  Overall I found this vacuum rather capable despite my concerns.  However, if you're willing to up your price threshold to the 150 dollar range you'll find there are many more options to choose from that will offer you much better performance for your money.  I would recommend this vacuum to people living in apartments or smaller sized condos or homes but nothing larger, especially those with pets.

I have and normally use an Oreck XL21 and thus found myself comparing this vacuum to that one.First of all, the PROS:I love the attachments. Besides three different floor sweepers--power brush for hard floor and carpet, a blanket brush, and a flat dust brush, this thing comes with a little brush and a wand for those hard to reach corners/crevices, areas between furniture that the regular vacuum won't fit into. My Oreck did not come with attachments. You have to buy a separate vacuum for that stuff and I've come to regret not having attachments the last few years. The brush and wand really came in handy, especially for doing the blinds. I also like that you merely disconnect the big brush, slide this part forward, and flip or hit a button and you have your wand or brush. You don't have to go search for the attachments or retrieve them from storage.I like that this vacuum reaches many hard-to-reach places. It's way more versatile and gets under the bed and stuff. With a regular stand-up vacuum, it only goes so far under furniture, like, not at all really.I love the retractable cord. I no longer have to worry about winding it back up and getting the kinks out from it. Just hit a button and the canister just sucks it up.The canister is not too heavy. You can carry it easily.It has filters that are washable. It's bagless.It has a quiet mode and as a deaf person, this is really hard for me to judge...so I watched my pug as I turned this thing on and off and used it. My pug hates vacuum cleaners and barks and attacks and just protests as much as her little dog body can. And while she at first reacted badly to this--keep it in mind I hadn't even turned it on yet and she was belly-aching--after I hit the quiet mode button, she no longer reacted but for the first few seconds it was on. She didn't attack or try to bite it either, and this telling me this vacuum is indeed a lot quieter.The cons:I really can't say this sucks any more dirt or hair than the Oreck. If it seems to have more stuff in the canister, it's because I was able to REACH more with it, but as the instructions say, you have to go over a spot many times from different directions, slowly...and when I was cleaning a maroon rug, I paid close attention to the fawn-colored pug hairs on it and realized I had to go over the same spot like five times to get a single hair. So....this does not clean any better than my other vacuum. Matter of fact, it took me twice as long to vacuum. It's def not as good as my Oreck and NOT worth 400 bucks.While the big wand itself is adjustable and that's awesome, the hose part is NOT adjustable and when I had to take off the big wand to use the hose to do my blinds, I was not able to reach the very top of them. A longer hose would be nice, as you cannot put the brush or the tiny wand on the big wand.I said the canister wasn't too heavy and you can carry it around... the problem is you sorta have to, especially if you're doing a big room and this was inconvenient for me as I need one hand free to pick up dog beds,  move taxis or chairs...The +/- button that controls the suction power... I think it should be two separate buttons. You can't really tell if you're increasing or decreasing the suck.The dust sensor...I didn't try it. After twenty minutes, I gave up on trying to get the battery door off it to install the batteries.Aw. You'll have to keep some triple-A batteries handy for two parts of this.Conclusion: I will keep my Oreck but use this for the blinds, get under the bed, get the hair off the dog beds, do the stairs... It has many great features, but the suck isn't as good.

I tried a pair of these for about an hour and could hear no earth-shattering difference between them and a pair of $70 Sony Extra Bass or $140 Bose TriPorts. The P5s are also less comfortable than either, and the Sonys actually have a larger range (4-24k Hz vs. 10-20k Hz) which gives them clearer bass.Overall the P5s are nice but in my opinion worth one third to one half their price. And people say Bose is overpriced! I'm not an "audiophile" but I'm not deaf either. Also worth noting with the P5s is that if you wear glasses these can cause them to dig into your temple and get sore after an hour or so. They also tend to get a little sweaty.I suppose I should say some good things about the P5s since they're actually pretty good headphones, price notwithstanding. They're certainly no slouch when it comes to sound. They're also very sturdy and well-constructed. The sheep skin feels nice but not amazing. Magnets hold the replaceable cups in place and the cord is also replaceable and includes an iPod controller and standard cable (though the iPod cable wasn't working with my stereo; only my iPod). I could see Bowers coming out with different types of cups later on (like around-ear, etc) which would be a blessing for additional sound isolation and comfort. Overall the P5s are designed to last even if various components break down or wear out, which helps you get a bit more for your money.In conclusion, I would really only recommend the P5s in two cases:1. If you're an audio engineer requiring the most accurate sound for your work. While these do sound accurate they don't sound as "colorful" and "bouncy" as other sets and I don't think I would care much for them for day-to-day listening unless I only listened to classical and jazz.2. If classical and jazz are your two favorite types of music I would get the P5s right away since they really showcase the richness of the P5s. I haven't heard jazz sound better on any other phones, even Bose or Sennheiser don't come close. Very crisp and alive. It's just that the P5s lack a bit of character and "oomph" when it comes to pop, rock, techno, and metal and for the price the P5s should be absolutely outstanding in most cases and not just great in many cases. Especially when there are so many other options out there. You can pump up the bass and treble in your EQ to get some more color but what's the point when you can just do the same thing with a much cheaper pair?I don't mean to be a buzzkill but these are just my opinions and observations. Go to the Apple Store and try a pair out if you want to; they might be worth the price to you. Anyway, hope this review helps.

The Incredicharge I-5000 is an external power source which will extend the period you can use small electrical devices for or recharge them up to a full charge.  At a capacity of 5000mAh it is most suitable for small devices such as mobile phones, ipods, cameras etc.  For larger capacity devices such as an ipad it would be better to use the I-10000.The I-5000 is charged via a USB cable which can be plugged into a laptop or indeed, into a mains source with a USB adaptor plug.  On receipt I was surprised to find that the device already had about a 50% charge. The device has four blue lights on the front, one lit shows that it is 25% charged, two 50% etc.  Whilst charging some of the lights will be on and one will be flashing eg if one is on and the second is flashing it will show that it is 25% charged and the next stage will be 50%.Charging another device from a charged I-5000 is quite straight forward.  The USB cable is connected to the Incredicharge and an appropriate connector is chosen from those seven supplied to fit the power input of the device to be charged.  This goes on the other end of the USB cable.  Just press the on button and off you go!The instruction booklet is clearly suited to a user with 20/20 vision as it is in tiny printing.  However, the operation is so easy that this is not really an issue.  It also appears to have been written by someone who, perhaps, did not have English as their first language.  However, despite the sometimes rather stilted phraseology the meaning is clear.This is a well designed, easy to operate device. It is aesthetically attractive and measures a compact 3 inches by 4 inches by  inch. It appears to be robust.  We have all been in the irritating position of having a mobile phone or other electrical item fail at an inconvenient time when there is no mains power to hand, or the charger is elsewhere.  Hence I can see the Incredicharge being an essential item, particularly when travelling abroad.  Very impressed!

My mother raised me to know how to separate eggs.  There were some dishes we cooked together back when I was a teenager that required a lot of separated eggs.  Imagine my shock when Mom told me she now uses an egg separator.  So, I decided to try one for myself.  This is the only one I've used, so I can't compare it to other egg separators.The surface on which you can crack the eggs works well.  It has fit on the various bowls I have tried and cracking the egg has been an easy process.However, it's not as easy to get all of the yolk separated from all the egg white.  The device allows for the egg white to slip through the slots in the bottom, but not all the egg whites slip through those slots.  And, when I have tried to get more through the slots, the yolk has broken and it has been easy to get some yolk mixed with my egg whites.  Given that I was raised to never, ever allow yolks into the egg whites, this has been a major negative for me.  Maybe people who are less klutzy than me don't have these issues.For me, it has been a neat experiment and, I'll probably try to use it when it's not critical that no yolks go into the egg whites.  In that case, though, I'll continue to do the process manually.

My floors in my dusty town are SPOTLESS. I love my robot. It cleans the whole house faithfully at 9AM each day and then goes and recharges.PROS: smarter, more powerful, faster and more robust.CONS:  misses some areas each day but overall cleans everything -- claims of super precision are exaggerated.Note:  I have mostely bare floors with a few area rugs.  Single story small house.My roomba could not handle my area rug with dark patterns.  It acted like a cat with a paper bag on its head.  xv-11 has no issues with it.Roomba wanders randomly around, bumping into everything obnoxiously and moving stuff around.  xv-11 makes roughly one pass over the floor in neat strips, after mapping the house with a frickin' laser beam.  xv-11 does not bump into things very much, since it has "eyes."I notice that XV-11 does not get as close to walls and corners and does not have a side brush like the Roomba, but the much more powerful vacuum on the xv-11 seems to clean them anyhow.  I figured I'd have to start sweeping the edges, which would have sucked a bit but still been OK.  However, there is no dirt build up.Similarly, on my area rug, there is only a rubber brush on my xv-11 so it does not dig the dirt up like Roomba would, but the vacuum is powerful and the rug is getting very very clean after a few days.  Since I do pushups on that rug, I do notice!xv-11 can cover more house per minute than Roomba.  Roomba takes FOREVER to clean my small house.The reviews for XV-11 show perfect parallel stripes covering your house -- not for mine -- it seems to not do perfect 180 turns.  I'm going to call and see if I can get it replaced as another reviewer did.  This is  bug I think.  So quality control at Neato might be a bit lacking in this first wave of units.  I'm on the bleeding edge, I know.Both robots park themselves when out of battery -- but xv-11 starts up again from where it left off after recharging!xv-11 is supposedly slightly louder, but it's at a lower frequency, so I haven't noticed it.xv-111 does not have "dirt detect" but I don't miss it.  In fact, Roomba seemed to imagine dirt that wasn't there.xv-11: much easier to clean and maintain, no mess or spills. Neat little box traps the dirt and is easy to empty.  Roomba was a mess to emptyand constantly needed attention for its brushes.  Keep in mind that I don't even have carpet or a pet!With xv-11, I don't need to move any of my area rugs, except one flimsy one in my bedroom that I just threw away.  xv-11 still can get stuck, but it's way less frequently, and each time it was due to an easy to fix quirk in rugs, cord, or furniture placement. With Roomba, there was no way to Roomba proof my house and keep it the way I wanted it.  I had to do so much roomba prep I literally stopped using it and my house was getting dirty.  xv-11 is on auto-clean and works daily, and my floors are immaculate.xv-11 figures out where the doorways are automatically. No more virtual walls!  With Roomba, I had to devise a system of virtual walls to tell it how to clean the house.  xv-11 figures it out automatically.Having said all that, if you have a roomba and it's automatically cleaning your house, then keep it as it's cheaper and if it ain't broke, you probably won't notice any benefit. I stopped using my roomba due to the prep required for my house. Roomba just couldn't handle my big area rug, so I had to fold it in half and put a table on it!  Obviously a huge hassle to fold, and Roomba got stuck on my little ones all the time, so I had to go around rug cleaning all the time. xv-11 no problems.UPDATE:  I have replaced the rubber squeegee on the front of my XV-11, which they shipped to me.  The  XV-11 is acting weird now, the clock is resetting, it's missing strips in the middle of the room, and it is really starting to malfunction, claiming to be unable to find its base, running out of charge, and basically being broken.  I'm going to call customer support tomorrow but the bleeding edge sucks.  If you can, wait a bit before buying one of these.  I'll update this when I get a replacement, which I believe from reading other reviews will be forthcoming.UPDATE 2:  Neato tech support noticed this thread and asked me to call them, which I did.  They were very helpful, friendly and polite and sent me a "new" (refurbished?) unit and told me to ship the old one back, all free of charge and all happened within two days (I live in California, which probably helped a lot).The new unit is working well, except that it had some "RPS error" messages.  I called Tech support and they told me to shut the unit down, which is a special command, not the same as just powering off.  This made it forget what time it was, but it remembered my schedule.  It has only run a couple times since then but does operate correctly now I think.  I'll revisit this review in a month and let you know.  I know I'm on the bleeding edge and am OK with the problems as long as their tech support remains responsive and helpful and friendly.  When it's working, this robot is awesome.  It's possible that if you buy one now they've worked through the bugs and you'll have no problems.  I'd give that a 75% chance right now.UPDATE 3:Well, I'm on my third unit now, and this one also has problems.  The second unit would randomly stop and think it was lost or stuff was in its way but nothing was.  The current unit cannot find its charging station now.  My house is clean but I'm spending a lot of time on the phone with Neato.  They are a nice bunch and keep replacing my unit, so I'm still happy, but cannot honestly retain a 4 star rating for a product that keeps failing.  I'm hoping to get one that really works as advertised pretty soon!  Time to call AGAIN for unit #4!  Sigh.  Keep their customer support number handy!

You have to be real picky to notice this first one but I am so here we go. Although this is a good case and well worth the $20 I paid for it, its not perfect. The first issue I wont take any stars off for because its something the manufacturer dosent even claim and thats water resistance. It seems that with just a couple extra additions this case could be water resistant which would make it great rather than just good. As it is this case isn't even moisture or humidity resistant. If i keep it in the holster the heat from my body will cause enough condensation for it to get under the screen. A drop of water anywhere near this case and it somhow seems to make its way right insid the protective film. Real annoying.The second issue is what I am deducting 2 stars for though. The case at first glance appears to be well constructed with good attention to detail. Upon closer inspection however you will notice the rubber gasket that surrounds the hard shell bulges out in some places and over laps in others. I guess with this kind of manufacturing its hard to stick within exact tolerances. There are places all around the case where it just dosent fit perfectly. There are even a couple areas where there is just a bit too much plastic on the hard case. I't probably wont keep the case from functioning but it is bothersome. Again, for $20 its a solid purchase but for the $50 the brick and mortar stores are charging for it I would have taken it right back.Edit 8-11-12:The day after I received the case I returned it for another one. The fact that it didn't fit just right was annoying me. Although it didn't really interfere with the case functioning it just bothered me when i looked at it. The replacement case came quickly. The box was the same but the case inside was anything but. The fit and finish of the 2nd case was well beyond the first. No bits of hanging plastic or bulges in the rubber covering. The screen protector was clearer the rubber fit tighter all around (especially near the openings) and the case felt more solid. The colors were noticeably different. The original looked as if it were faded. Lastly the spring in the belt clip of the 2nd one is much stronger than the first.If I had not received the first case I would have given the 2nd one at least 4 stars. However, for Amazon sending either a fake or poorly manufactured one to me I'm giving it a 1. Hopefully anyone who gets a sub-par one will see my review and know to return it.

Purchased this MacBook (MC516LL/A, 2.4 GHz, 250GB HD) on 8/1/10 for the second daughter.  This is the third MacBook our family has purchased in the last 2.5 years.  Hopefully everyone will have their own one day.  This one, like the older two (purchased at an Apple Store), just plain worked right out of the box.  The shipment from Amazon was fast- got the MacBook in 4 days- and that was with free super saver shipping!We are definitely not rich in the monetary sense and MacBooks are more expensive than *seemingly* "similar" windoze laptops, so, the decision to buy the first MacBook (a late '07, 2.2 GHz) was a tough decision.  When we used windoze, I spent untold hours maintaining them- e.g. complicated and buggy "updates", the tedious and untrustworthy back-ups, the anti-malware/etc apps I never trusted, difficult networking and firewalls.... ad nauseam.  With the Macs, setup (especially networking!) is easy and maintenance is almost a pleasure- easy updates, no malware of concern, Time Machine does a constant, almost unnoticeable, backup and it's almost fun to retrieve files, great out-of-the-box firewall.  Then there's the ~$30 third party apps that'll do a full hard disk clone to an external USB drive which one can then boot and run (although slowly) from to help ensure the clone will work if you ever need it.  It absolutely blows away windoze with Ghost or True Image.  Startup is 20 to 24 secs,  shutdown is 3 secs. (that's not a typo).  Target disk mode is great if you've more than one Mac.  If you learn the basic keyboard shortcuts in one app, they almost always work in ALL apps!  The menus are much more standardized than on a windoze PCs.  The dictionary/thesaurus/wiki  works seemingly everywhere.  I could go on and on...As for problems with the MacBooks: 1)  The first Mac has the widely reported cosmetic cracks on its keyboard face plate.  It's reported that Apple will replace the face plate without charge since I bought Applecare but it is not worth a 100 mile trip to the Apple Store.  2) The plastic exterior on all the MacBooks scratches a bit too easily for my taste and the white keys show dirt easily.  That's it!  Absolutely no hardware or OS problems!  The few third-party app problems were easily fixed by a bit of googling.  So, I can't rate Apple's service after the sale, but consumer reports rates them significantly high than other laptop mfgs.  Then again, that's not saying much given my past experience with some of the other mfgs.As for issues with the latest MacBook:  1) Apple dropped the firewire port.  Beware if you've a "must use" firewire device and get the MacBook Pro instead.  2) The video port is different that that on the older two MacBooks and hence requires purchasing  another adapter if .  Pluses are the much better display (I thought we might hate glare from the shiny glass), it's faster, has more touchpad functions and it seems to run on battery longer.Although this is a glowing review of the MacBook, seriously consider a MacBook Pro if you need or even if you thing you'll need the added horsepower or if just like the added fancy/flashy features.

I had purchased this router to upgrade from a Linksys Vonage wireless router (Wireless G). I was having trouble in streaming content over my network using a PS3. I also had a external 500GB hard drive (Iomega) which i thought would be cool to be able to connect to the router directly than connect to my PC and then share. I also purchased a Dlink DAP 1522 Accesspoint/ bridge to utilize the N speeds since PS3 has a G adapter and not N.I had run some baseline tests on my network prior to changing the router.My Wired LAN was providing me 51-56 Mbps (one PC to my laptop). Wireless from my PC to PS3 was between 3.4 to 3.2 Mbps (using Tversity). Internet d/l speed on my PS3 was 2 Mbps.After getting the router i redid all the connections and followed instructions for installing the router (The s/w install on my XP PC took a very long time ~ 45 mins) but after that setup was a breeze. My DAP 1522 setup took time as I had to reset it twice becuase i kept on messing the Static IP settings.KEY NOTES:1. My PS3 is first floor about 20-25 ft away from my router which is on second floor. 5 GHz was poorer signal and SLOWER speed. I used 2.4 GHz and i got a 70% signal and BETTER throughput.2. I ran new tests. PC to Laptop now averaged 64 Mbps (~12% improvement due to Gigabit). PC to PS3 about 19 Mbps. So, a substantial improvement. However, please note- PS3 gives DLNA and media server and protocol errors if you use any encryption on the wireless network. I had to use Mac address based authentication and use static IP to secure my network.3. The speed of USB drive access is about 39 Mbps on a wired connection. If i connect it back to desktop PC, i get the same wired speed as i get for my PC (64 Mbps)All in all, I feel that in my setup, I wasted money in paying for two features:1. 5 Ghz- evidently it works very well on short distances but for longer distances, 2.4 is a better deal2. USB connect - Not worth it. Loss in performance is too great. Also when using the web admin utility, it takes a long time to load up that page when the device is connected...very irritating.Wirleless N - Boasts of 300 Mbps, but i got only 1/15th of it, however, a 6X improvement over the wireless G speed and solved my problem.Please note that my setup is different from what you may have and results I have got may not be similar to what you should expect. I just wanted to share a guidance on how things actually change. For example 300 Mbps is really a myth and the reality for me is 20 Mbps!!!

DV tapes cannot be played anymore once the camcorder dies. And the Sony DVs do die in numbers, for example with the dreaded C:32:11 error code. So very reluctantly I just ordered a used replacement for my dead DCR-HC38. The loading mechanism no longer works, and I need a working camera so that I can get our entire video material off the tapes one last time. I am looking forward to no longer having to deal with this technology.If for some incomprehensible reason you actually consider buying this camera new today and paying close to $600, run!

I don't usually write a review, but I am compelled to do so with this product in hopes of making others aware of the product and aiding in their decision to purchase.I have been wrestling with trying to get internet from my second floor to my first floor.  I have an expensive wireless AC router that is supposed to offer better wifi ranges.  Even with the greater range I can not get good enough speeds to stream full HD files.  I tried a wifi range extender - these don't work well in my experience.  I tried an Access point, still did not resolve my issues.I then ordered a powerline kit.  The ones you plug into your outlets.  This was the worst solution I tried.  Speeds were barely registering.  My electric is fairly new, and both outlets were on on the same breaker.I was about to give up and called for an estimate to run cat6 cabling. This was expensive.  And not something I wanted to do taking into consideration how the wires needed to be run.I was searching the internet for answers when I stumbled upon an article that offered solutions for the predicament I was in.  And this article mentioned the MoCA solution.  Skeptical, I decided to give this solution a try before I committed to running the Cat6.The items arrived quickly and I was excited to give this a go.  Set up was extremely easy.  Disconnect your existing coax cable from the wall, and connect to the coax out TV port.  Connect the included coax cable from the COax IN on the moca device to your wall.  Connect an internet cable from your routers LAN to the LAN port on the Moca device.  I immediately tested to my TV to make sure I still received Cable TV and in full HD.  I did.  I then connected the MoCA device on my first floor the same way.I fired up my Oppa BR player and browsed to my HDD attached to my PC on my second floor.  Previously, the Oppo was not able to stream my MKV full HD files because of my bandwidth issues and being on wifi.  The files would stutter and pause every millisecond rendering the files useless for streaming.Not this time.  The files streamed beautifully without any stutter, or pause and played my DTS HD MA without any issues. I had finally found a solution that offered me enough bandwidth without having to hardwire with Cat6.I am amazed that such an inexpensive and easy solution is not readily more popular.  The units boast 190MBPS, but I am actually receiving about half of that.  Which is more than enough to stream HD.  My only regret with the MoCA devices is that there is no gigibit connections.If you find yourself in a situation like mine, I implore you to try this solution.  It works.  And works well.

I'll preface my review by saying that I am the owner of a Panasonic TZ5, and my opinions on this camera are based on a comparison of the two.First off, if you don't own a TZ5, then you may really love this camera.  It has tons of great options, an excellent 12X zoom lens that was very smooth (and quick), and a variety of modes that are easy to set.  If you understand the many adjustments that can be made in taking a picture, then you will really enjoy the manual modes on this camera.  It comes with several levels of manual picture taking, with each level allowing more and more customization, with the highest level leaving it all to the photographer.  This allows someone with the know-how and experience to get the most from the camera.  I did play around with this a bit, but for the most part I want a camera that takes good photos with as little adjustment as necessary.Things I found to be negatives:Pop up flash - I always had my finger right where the flash pops up.  Eventually you may get used to this, but it did annoy me.Lower quality LCD - Was grainy even when outdoors, and indoors it was very grainy.Bulk - The camera is a big larger than the TZ5, and didn't really feel comfortable in my hands.  Canon made one end of the camera larger in an attempt to give you something to grip, but it just felt a bit awkward to hold, in my opinion.Speed - A bit slower than the TZ5 overall in processing the picture after taking it.Some thoughts on the modes:Outdoor mode - Makes some odd choices with the exposure - In comparison to the TZ5, a blue sky would come out much whiter in some areas.Auto mode - Pretty good at selecting the right ISO, flash strength, etc.Indoor mode - Better than the TZ5 - Good white balance, still a bit grainy.Macro modes - Offers two versions - One "regular" macro and one for extreme close ups.  Took some nice close up shots that were very clear, even when zoomed.All in all, I found the camera to be mostly on par with the TZ5, with the TZ5 having the edge on overall PQ and ease of use.  For a next generation camera at $350, I would expect better performance.  You can get a TZ5 for $100 less and similar performance.  However, if this is your first experience with a larger Point and Shoot with extended optical zoom, your likely to be pretty satisfied.  I'm sure next years model will be much improved.

You can set alarm, trigger "night mode" (softer contrast), and even get a preview of the weather, among a few other minor passive functions. You *could* make it also play music in the background (yes, the built-in MUSIC app has a jukebox mode), so I guess it's more of a clock-radio with alarm.If I really want a clock radio with alarm, I would buy one in my local Walgreens (or whatever) for $10, not pay $20-$30 for a fancy piece of shaped plastic with a charger tip.As many others have pointed out, the dock is designed for an UNPROTECTED NAKED PHONE. It is not compatible with cases. If you have a case slipped on, you cannot put it in the dock.While, technically if you don't want the BOTTOM half protected, then you can remove *THAT* and put the phone in the dock with the keyboard exposed, but that rather defeats the aesthetics of the dock. Doesn't it?There is ONE good thing about the dock though... The AC adapter you get with it can be used WITHOUT the dock. Yes, you can plug that tip straight to the phone, skipping the dock altogether. Since a spare AC adapter cost the same as the dock on the Verizon website, you may as well get the dock.If you already have alarm clocks and such, then this accessory is superfluous, except it looks cool. But then, looking cool is not always a good reason to spend money.

The Microsoft Touch Mouse is very well built and it is a bit heavier than other mice, so you might take this into consideration if you are accustomed to using light mice. Unfortunately, the quality of the mouse does not carry over to the software. The first major stumbling block I ran into is that Microsoft IntelliPoint software consistently failed to install with a very cryptic and unhelpful error message. A quick search of the internet revealed that many people were having the same problem but nobody seemed to have a solution. Even digging through the installation log files wasn't very helpful. After a lot more digging around I finally discovered that the usb.inf file was mysterious missing from the C:\Windows\INF folder. Fortunately I was able to restore a good copy of usb.inf from one of my backups stored on Windows Home Server.After installing the IntelliPoint software, I quickly discovered that Microsoft has pretty much shot itself in the foot with user account control. The basic issue is that the IntelliPoint software runs as a normal user application (instead of as an actual driver) to interpret all of the gestures into the various mouse commands so none of the gestures work with applications (like Microsoft Visual Studio) that run with administrator privileges. This means simple actions like left click and right click work across all applications, but the scroll gesture does not work with any application with administrator privileges. One workaround is to run IntelliPoint as with administrator privileges, but you'll have to run ipoint.exe manually each time you logon.Several people have complained that the scroll gesture doesn't work very well and I've found that it seems to depend on where you perform the gesture. If you place your finger where the left or right button should be and slide your finger back, the scroll gesture seems to be recognized primarily in the back half of the mouse. Performing the scroll gesture in the middle (where the scroll wheel or middle button should be) seems to work a lot better. Unfortunately, it also seems to depend on the application for some reason. Scrolling in Firefox for example seems to work fairly well, but scrolling in Visual Studio seems to be less than reliable.I also have a huge issue with the Microsoft Touch Mouse/IntelliPoint software mistakenly thinking I'm performing a gesture when I reach for the mouse. The biggest issue is that when I move my hand from the keyboard to the mouse, the active window (e.g. Firefox) will snap to the left half of the screen and occasionally it will minimize the foreground application. This also sometimes happens when I'm moving the mouse normally.Finally, the Microsoft Touch Mouse occasionally confuses the left click gesture from the right click gesture. You should be able to left click just by clicking with your index finger (even if you're middle finger is touching the mouse) and right click by lifting your index finger off the mouse and clicking with your middle finger. Every so often when I use the left click gesture the mouse performs a right click and "sticks" (every click thereafter is a right click) until I move my hand off the mouse and start over.Overall, I like the weight and feel of the mouse but the software needs a lot of work to interpret the gestures reliably. If Microsoft can finally resolve all of the gesture issues, the Microsoft Touch Mouse could be a fairly decent mouse. Until then, I recommend sticking with a non-touch mouse.

My next airplane ride is not for another year. However, due to a recent power outage in the New England area I was able to use these earbuds on a long 5 hour car ride to borrow a family generator. While these earbunds don't completely knock out the radio or tv it does knock out all the white noise. Which is exactly what you're looking for on an airline. To use this feature you need to use the AAA battery that is provided with the headphones. You can use these earbuds without a battery but there would be no noise cancellation feature.Most earbuds that I have used are very uncomfortable and I usually end up going back to the wrap around headphones. I did find some Skullcandy's that worked well but I have to say, I like these, but they're a little too pricey for what you get.The volume control with the TalkThrough feature and mode buttons is a bit bulky. However, It never seemed to affect me. It hangs low enough that it never pulled the buds from my ear. For me it wasn't too bulky and didn't bother me at all. I suppose it's a matter of opinion.These have a nice TalkThrough button that you can push when you want to hear when someone is talking to you without the hassle of taking out the buds. It tunes out the audio device you are listening to and seems to magnify the person speaking. It's a wonderful feature that gets a good amount of use from me, as I always seem to have something to say.The earbuds came with a few adapters for a receiver and an airplane jack as well as a large carrying case. Also three different sized earbud covers.All in all I'd say since I'm not very familiar with noise cancellation headphones that my experience with these was mediocre at best. I feel if the price was not as high they might be worth it. However, since they are so pricey I expected something I probably can't get. I'm not completely disappointed with these. They do have some features that amazed me, like the TalkThrough and the comfort.I mainly listened to an Audiobook which came out very clear. I must say I was satisfied with that aspect. My first reaction though when I plugged these in and turned them on was disappointment that I could hear outside voices and noises still fairly clearly. I just turned the volume up on the headphones and had no trouble listening to my audiobook, but I could still hear the muffled voices on the TV as well as the loud war video game that was being playing in the background.

I bought one of these for my brother and was pleased with it at first.  Setup was surprisingly easy and we had wireless access throughout the house for his Windows machines.So when I wanted wireless access in my apartment I bought one for myself.  I tried skipping the installation CD since I have a MacBook and figured the default setup should be fine.  Unfortunately I could not get an Internet connection working.  When I tried accessing the router's configuration through my Web browser, it was in Italian!  Apparently the router autodetects your language and if you have a Mac it thinks that you speak Italian.  With no way to fix the configuration, I returned the Linksys and got a Netgear WGR614 which worked fine and is better looking.When I visited my brother again with my new MacBook I couldn't get on his network.  After much tinkering and research I found that a bug in the Linksys router software prevents Macs (and presumably Linux or Wii) from getting IP addresses.  I was able to fix it by installing an outdated version of the software, but that kind of problem is unacceptable.  Do not buy this router if you'll be using anything other than Windows.

ok folks here is my experience with this print server.IT WAS A PAIN TO SETUP - but once I got it working it worked fine with no troubles so far.I read the poorly written documention ( doesn't make any suggestions for trouble shooting ) as I followed it to a tee. My router could not even find the darn print server at all.When calling the outsourced techsupport I had a hard time being patient with them as they answered my questions as if they were dancing around them. I don't expect tech support to know everything and I caught one not admitting he didn't know the answer. after I made a few more calls I got someone who actually spoke english well enough and knew what was happening. She was a much more pleasant experience. if you're having trouble with your router I would suggest doing the following before calling tech support.1. turn off printer2. unplug power from print server3. (first time setup) Plug in an ethernet cable to server and plug in the power.4. turn printer back on after about 10 seconds. (gives a little extra time to acquire an IP from the router, it helped)5. run setup wizard from CD and follow your documentation from this point on.6. after you tested the setup with your ethernet cable, turn off printer, turn off print server, unplug ethernet cable, plug in print server, turn on printer, test print, and Viola all should work fine.if you have WEP settings be sure to have it handy before going through the process of setting up the print server.if you need info about the print server itself (like the mac adress). while the printer is on you can hold down the reset button on the back of the print server to get additional info. the info will be sent to your printer and printed out.Last, even though tech support sucked they all managed to slip me more info about problems with their hardware. I would suggest calling them if you don't get your product working within a reasonable amount of time.my setup worked with WEP 128 and no trouble so far. Though I should point out that tech support did mention they are having trouble with multi function printers ( as in those that take pictures from your cameras and/or memory cards to print from.) and linksys is aware of it. She could not give me an answer as to why and pushed me to find current drivers for the printer.I took the whole after noon to rebuild a wireless network for my parents. ALL linksys/cisco products. Personally I would go with a competitors products next time. Though I will give cisco a thumbs up for trying hard at staying in the home market.I hope this at least helped a few people after readying this.TTFN

A really bulky knife to be carrying around as a "survival" knife. The best knife for survival is the one you have on you and you won't have this one on you everyday. This is a tool best left at camp for batoning wood or hammering into trees for whatever reason you can think of. It will stand up to a lot of abuse (I wore the coating off mostly from batoning but not much sign of rust and no other signs of failure) but it's simply too large to be a practical knife. I think the Cold Steel SRK is a pretty good size benchmark because personally it's the largest knife I can carry on my person comfortably and do work with and I'm not a small guy at 5'11 180 athletic frame. This knife is at least two inches longer and about twice as heavy. Additionally, the sheath is not as modular and convenient as a kydex type and is certainly less robust. The BIG upside to the package is the small removable pouch on the front of the knife sheath that could conveniently house a ferro rod and a small stone or a compass or whatever you need! This could be moved onto a new sheath, say you made one out of kydex or something... so that's a big score in my opinion. But this whole "survival" bandwagon needs to be derailed I think. People simply aren't using these knives and others like them for real wilderness survival because they don't do that job well (and by "job" I mean a multitude of jobs in a true survival situation). The only thing this knife does exceptionally well is split wood and even then, you have a swept blade that is not ideal for the batoning application nor is it particularly easy to sharpen; two strong marks against this knife's ability to be a "survival" knife. I think one would be much better served by a smaller knife because it is foremost easier to carry and wield. Because if you need to chop you should have brought an axe, if you devote your knife to a job it wasn't intended for you sacrifice what it WAS intended for. So by making this knife a hulking behemoth it simply undermines itself. For the price, it's a fine peice of steel but be ready to get a workout just strapping it on and you might want to consider a custom sheath option.

The SpokeGrenade SG-1000e is probably my fifth bike light, each one better.  I started out with a discount store cheapy, and gradually moved up.  My last light was a 1000 lumen flashlight, which was plenty bright, but had no battery life.  Before that, I had twin 80 lumen lamps which were adequate, but nowhere near the SpokeGrenade.  This light meets all of my needs and expectations, so no need to go higher up the chain even though I know brighter lights exist.Far and away the best feature of this light is the lens.  It has a spotlight in the center, which I focus maybe 40-50 feet in front of the bike.  Surrounding the spotlight is a huge halo of light that's maybe 40% as bright.  That halo illuminates tree branches above you, the trail immediately in front of you, and a goodly part of both sides of the trail.  I can corner on the darkest trails without a headlamp, because the halo lights the turn.The "rubber band" mount actually works quite well.  I might make 1-2 adjustments on a 20-mile ride, each takes 1 second.  I actually prefer this mount to many that are hard to adjust up or down, and this light can be put on or taken off your handle bar in 3 seconds.  The battery also attaches quickly and nicely to my front fork post.The only negative at this time is I wish the mount had a full-motion swivel.  You can turn the light slightly, but it really isn't designed to swivel.I cannot speak to battery life, as my average night ride is 2 - 2 1/2 hours, and then I recharge.  I generally use a mix of full and one-half power, depending upon conditions.  The lamp is rated for 3 hours on full power, but I can't verify that.  But battery life has been adequate for my needs and I have not noted any tail-off in brightness.I have seen nearly identical looking lights available by direct shipment from China for about 1/2 the price of the SpokeGrenade.  But in reading their reviews, I was concerned that corners may have been cut that would make those cheaper lights less reliable.  I can't identify any "cut corners" on the SpokeGrenade.  It appears very well made and has a one year guarantee.

This review is for the newcomer to DSLR's and not the advanced user. So we don't need to hear the experts bashing on how someone doesn't know what they are doing and shoudn't get a camera like this. I am speaking for the person who needs a camera to capture their kids in the school play, soccer game etc. and can't capture the moment with a point and shoot. You can't expect awesome pictures if you do not learn how to use all the settings, features, and purpose of an SLR camera. You might even get worse pictures than your point and shoot. Sure an SLR has an auto feature where it will figure what is the best settings to use for a basic picture, but you also end up with a basic picture.But even all said I would still recommend an SLR and a good zoom lens that you can afford. It is worth spending the money because you can never recapture that moment of your child or whatever your trying to capture.  How many pictures have you taken with a point and shoot that were horrible because they were too dark or blurry? Sure they are fine if the lighting is good and you are within 10 feet or so away. Any further than that well, why bother. The larger zoom type cameras are better but are still limited when lighting is an issue. The pocket type point and shoots usually have a lag time between shots or flash charging up again. So forget about getting off several shots in succesion. Hard to capture a picture if the object is in motion also. The larger zoom types have mimimal lag time and some can even fire off bursts of 3 to 5 in a second with one push of the button and better at capturing something in motion. But they still can't beat an DSLR. I have gotten shots of my children with an DSLR with low lighting and no flash from many rows of seats away and they were great. The image quality was even good enough where I can crop it and still look good. People using their camera phones crack me up, but that's another story.I am not going to get into all the technicalities of this camera. You can read the other reviews for that. I just want to mention that if you are one of those people who need to step up to an SLR because the point and shoot couldn't do the job but don't want to become the serious photographer then this inforomation might be what you are looking for.I find the XSI pictures are soft and not crisp. Some photographers prefer this. The new Nikon DSLR's take crisper pictures, and they are less expensive.The main con of the XSI is the focusing points. If you use the camera in auto mode then it will focus on the nearest or most identifiable focus points it can focus on. So it might focus on an object in front of the actual thing your trying to capture that is behind it, or on a purse or print on a shirt for example instead of the persons face or what not. If your trying to get a group picture with the guest of honor in the middle of it, you might not have that person in full focus but instead the preople around because the cameras focus is focusing on the most vivid or closest points. You can set the camera in one of the manual settings and pick one focus point of your choice, like center, top, left, right etc. but you can't pick all on. In auto it will focus on more than one but like I mentioned before, not excactly on what you want. you can press the shutter button half way and it will try and refocus on different points or you can get closer to your subject and press the shutter button half way and hold it so it keeps that focus point and then you step back and snap the picture. Well you don't have the luxury of time on your hands for those kid or spontaneous shots.So this is where I recommend the newer Nikon DSLR's. Their focus points I find tend to focus on more points and usually on the center also where my subject tends to be. The XSI was here and there. If the area your focusing on is busy, the XSI will pick a few focus points here and there were it thinks are the best. But with the Nikon, I found it to focus on more points which is nice because the whole image will be more sharper instead of certain areas of it when cropping or zooming the image on a computer. Unless you are going for the "bokeh" effect in which the subject is in focus and the area around it is blurred.A camera of this size isn't always convienient to carry around to all occasions because of it's size, accessories, worries, or whatever the reason. If you already have a pocket point and shoot or zoom camera, don't get rid of them. I keep them for when I go on vacation because I don't want to carry a big DSLR around on vacation. I use the pocket one for when we go out and I don't want to carry anything bulky and for those you never know shots. I use the zoom one for the amusement parks. Joby's Gorillamobile Ori for iPad cover is revolutionary in its design and capability, but its not for everyone.  I decided to get mine as part of a quest to find the right set of accessories for the iPad.  I found other cases, including Apple's case to be less than useful as they did not stand up well, nor protect the device to the degree I was looking for.  This is not the case in this case and perhaps its too much for some people.If you need a case like the ORI you will think its a 5 star.  But then you are more likely a heavy users and road warrior who values function over style.  If you are someone who uses their iPad sparingly, values it as a cool look and likes to carry it around for appearances as much as its applications, then take a pass on this one.I give this case a three star review in the hopes that people will read this to see if its the right one for them.'When Joby defined this as a Gorillamobile, they used the term to capture both the strength of this product and some of the personal muscular requirements for using it.  The cover is more than a cover, it's a three position case that is truly remarkable in its design.  However, the Ori for iPad is clearly meant to be used as a stand rather than a cover as the weight and bulk that makes it a very stable platform reduce its portability or use as a traditional `book type cover'.Its a clever design from its flexibility, to the padding on the inside cover that also provides a pad for your desktop. But this much flexibility comes at a cost.  The cover does not close neatly as the top is slightly agape when the device is closed.The strength of this case almost mandates the use of a separate keyboard to make the device useful.  Here is why, the piece that holds the iPad rotates meaning that its not locked into the rest of the case.  In every mode this means that the iPad 'bounces' in response to your finger tip touch.  This is acceptable when you are choosing apps, etc but is annoying if you want to type using the soft keyboard.The case is highly recommended for users who need a stable stand because they place the iPad on their desks rather than carry them around from meeting to meeting.  It is also recommended for people who are frustrated by the Apple iPad case and its inability to stand up properly, then you will really enjoy this product.  Its flexibility, stability and quality of the materials are all positive factors.I chose it because i am looking for something that is rugged, a good stand and will protect the device.  The Ori does all of that well, but it is not perfect for everyone.Positive Points'The quality of the materials is exceptional as the case is brushed aluminum with multiple hinges that all work well despite their complexity.The folding process is easy to learn, after a few attempts you quickly learn how to make the case perform well.Flexibility is a main reason for purchasing this case.  You want to hold your iPad stable in different positions.  The ability to rotate the iPad is unique and very cool.The case holds the iPad securely and makes all of the ports available.Challenges and negative pointsThe case is heavy.  It is much heavier than other cases and therefore people may be surprised by the weight and find it less usable.  Personally, the weight does not bother me so much but others may find it a distraction.  The device is clearly meant to be used as a stand rather than holding it in your hand.The case is thick almost doubling the width of the iPad in your briefcase.  If you are relying on having something sleek that slides in and out of your briefcase or hand bag, this is not the case for you.The case is not pretty.  The cover front is dominated by one of the aluminum fold outs so there is no smooth cover giving the device an industrial look.  Other cases concentrate on their appearance over functionality.  This is all function over appearance.The case, at least initially, smells a bit of machine oil.  That may be a factor that the case is new, but the smell adds to the industrial feel of this product.The case has to be put down with care.  The sides and edges are aluminum and while Joby has polished them, putting the case down with any force -- including that last few inches from your hand, can and already has created gouges and scratches in tables.  Eliminating this would be hard since its a metal case, so you need to be careful.I can see people wanting to get a cloth sleeve ala a shoe bag type thing to protect the device from scratching as well as scratching the rest of the stuff in your briefcase.Every case has its compromises, something I have learned by looking at the Apple case, a simple aftermarket case, the DODOcase and the ZAGGmate case.  These other cases were lacking the ability to provide a solid base for the iPad that would facilitate its use in standard office work.  The ORI overdoes the stability part to the detriment of a few other aspects noted in this review.  So is not for everybody but for right now it looks to be the best for me.

The main challenge---and experience and experimentation will resolve this---is the choice of CDR and RW formats. I chose the CD-RW and have found it quite manageable, although I have not tried to finalize and play the recordings on other DVD players, since the purpose of our buying this was to time shift and play back with the same device. Loading has been faster than suggested by other reviewers and the quality of the recording is very good!The manual is clumsy and should be accompanied by a condensed version.The creators of the remote need a bit of supervision: small, light-gray letters on a dark gray instrument must have been the work of some apprentices! Others have commented on this.Since I believe than few pieces of equipment merit 5 stars, I would give this one 4.5!Updated review:Since writing the above, a few comments are in order:A few days after using the timer recording function, I encountered problems with the stability of the clock, which began to reset itself. After many attempts to correct this, I called Toshiba customer service and was rapidly connected to a helpful person who suggested a reset to factory defaults. This was completely successful; but, I observed that attention must be paid to doing a manual setting of the time and checking the correct time zone, since the default is Atlantic time!Using DVD-RW discs for recording TV programs has worked well. They play on my PC's new and old DVD drives if finalized, but not on a 12+ year old Samsung DVD player.I have also tested the DR570 on an older JVC CRT TV using component cables, and it worked very well. The next test will occur when Comcast gives us a digital adapter (DTA), since I intend to use the DR570 to record programs with the older system to play back on a Blu ray player which will be installed with our new HDTV. (one of the reviewers encountered some problems with the HD Motorola tuner. Theoretically, this should work since the coax goes to the DTA and then a coax connects the DTA to the tuner and the component cable connects the tuner to the TV.)Stay tuned!

i picked up one of these refurbished routers off a deal-of-the-day site for about $30. it looked brand new when i received it, and worked right out of the box. after making sure the unit was functional, i installed DD-WRT to really get the most out of the router. i stream from an nas device to a roku, a sony media center, a ps3, a wii, and a raspbmc client, and all of them pick up the 2.4ghz band with no problem. i also use the 2.4 and 5ghz bands for internet access on phones and tablets. the throughput with the router is always enough to max out the internet connection at 10mbps, even with only 1 or 2 bars.the only downside i've found with this router is that the range is lacking. i can't get good enough signal to stream hd content off the nas from more than about 30 feet away on the upstairs level. i had to set up my old router as a bridge behind the entertainment center upstairs to pull enough signal to get lag-free streaming on the ps3 and raspbmc. i know it's supposed to perform better than that. even cranking up the antenna power within DD-WRT yielded only slight improvements. i would guess that this is the reason the item was a refurb, because someone else had the same problem with it and returned it.i have been running this router for almost a year now, and it still performs quite well (with the infrequent need for a reboot, about once every other month). however, it's about to be replaced with a gigabit router, and moved to the garage as a bridge for out in the backyard. if you are comfortable installing custom firmware, this router does a pretty good job for <$40.

Although the box clearly says "Supports any drive capacity" this is not true. It may have been true at the time it first came out, but it isn't true anymore. Unfortunately, all Goflex bases convert 512 byte drives to 4k byte drives. After taking the Goflex apart and removing the included Barracuda XT I placed that drive inside the Sabrent enclosure.The good news is that the Sabrent enclosure correctly reports the drive has having 512 byte sector sizes which allows me to use it properly with legacy hardware. Unfortunately, only 1.6 TB is visible even if I convert the drive to GPT. Normally I should at least have the option to create to partitions, but it doesn't even see the 2 TB maximum that the MBR should be able to handle. It's a great enclosure for all my old 1 TB drives, but this enclosure is clearly obsolete.
