I have had this item for nearly three-weeks.  I agree with nearly all other reviewers in as much as quality and durability is concerned.  However, note that the length of the cable will introduce considerable resistance between any charger (needs to be at lease 10-watts for ipad 3)and your device.  Copper, at a resistance of 27-ohms per/ft, one can expect an increase of charging time, especially with an iPad 3.  There will not, however, be any negative effect on the charger or ipad. This will occur simply because some of the voltage is being dropped/lost within the cable.  Apart from measuring, one can easily "feel" the difference (by touching the charger case) when comparing charging with and without the extension cable.  Whether charging via a wall charger, of via a PC USB port, the cable affect will be the same.So, I recommend the cable.  Especially, if you are used to charging your device overnight.  Otherwise, you can expect no appreciable increase in percentage of charge while charging and using the iPad 3.  Otherwise, it's a great deal.

...there is a whole lot of marketing hype to this product and most don't need to purchase it. Unless you roast your own beans you would be better off putting your beans into a $5 sealable ventless kitchen canister and using the $10-15 you save to buy a nice cup or some really good coffee.Unless you roast your own beans, the coffee beans you buy likely no longer release any CO2. CO2 release usually is maximal within 1 week of roasting and dwindles down to almost none after 2 weeks. Most of the roasted beans you probably purchase are many weeks to many months old. They were stored at the factory under vacuum to maintain freshness or shipped in a one way vent bag to purge the air from the beans. Even if you bought from your favorite coffee shop it is still likely several weeks to a month old or more....unless you purchased directly from a coffee roaster who roasts on site. So think about saving your money, buying a regular kitchen canister, and then buying some good coffee or a fun looking cup.Now if you roast your own coffee like I do, you will need a container that has a release valve of some type (a one-way valve is better). I cracked my cheap plexiglass kitchen canister in half because the gas could not escape....lol. Not sure about the little filter valves on this...not sure what good the filter does except make me continue to spend money. I see no reason why the valve can't be permanent.Also, there are people here who are under the mistaken impression that CO2 is bad.....you are incorrect. CO2 released by the coffee is good!Why CO2 is good for your coffee!Fresh roasted coffee beans release CO2 for 1-2 weeks after being roasted. During the roasting process, essential oils are also released from the beans and contribute greatly to the wonder fresh coffee flavor. In a canister like the Friis, the CO2 that is released helps protect your coffee beans. CO2 is GOOD, while air/oxygen is BAD.The oxygen in the air is very reactive. It will quickly chemically react with the oils released by the coffee beans (much like oxygen will chemically react with your vegetable, olive, or canola oil). The reaction, called "oxidation" results in coffee going stale or your oils going rancid over time.Thus, in the Friis, the CO2 that is released by freshly roasted beans, purges/displaces the air/oxygen in the container and protects the beans from oxidation and maintains the bean freshness. Yes, CO2 can react with moisture to form carbonic acid which is not good for the beans either (hence, don't put your beans in the frig or freezer where moisture is high). But the main culprit to beans becoming stale is oxidation, not carbonic acid. The CO2 helps to prevent the oxidation from occurring. An alternative would be to place the beans under vacuum or to purge the air and CO2 with nitrogen which is very non-reactive --- and both of these methods aren't too practical.So for the home coffee roaster or if you buy direct from a local coffee roaster (and get freshly roasted beans), this is a decent product (just not sure about having to keep buy a new one way value all the time). But for the person who purchases their beans from the grocery or even a coffee shop like Starbucks, you don't need this to store your beans or to maintain freshness - a regular kitchen canister will do the exact same thing.

Pros:This is a great mid-range video card in the ~$200 range.  I bought one in August 2011 and it still handles everything I throw at it.  I might not play the most demanding games though - I often play games like Unreal Tournament 3, Duke Nukem Forever, Portal, Portal 2, Civilization V, and Minecraft.  When I bought this card, my PC (at the time) had an Intel Core i7-2600 CPU, 8GB of DDR3-1333 RAM, and an ASRock P67-Extreme4 motherboard, and with Unreal Tournament 3 I got about 62fps at 1920x1080 and 63-64fps with Duke Nukem Forever.  I've since put faster RAM in my PC (DDR3-1600) and a faster processor (Intel Core i7-3770K) and this video card is still chugging along with the high frame rates.If you're into scientific computing (for BOINC projects such as SETI@Home, Milkyway@Home, etc.), this card is compatible with some of such projects.  Running SETI@Home v7 7.00 for Nvidia, this card can go through a work unit in about 6-15 minutes.Also, the card is quiet, even though it has 2 fans. Its temperature seems good - Mine runs at around 37C when idle and 57-60C when under a load.This card also has 2 DVI ports, which is nice if you want to use 2 monitors and have a high-quality picture on both. With the DVI port, you could probably also use a 3rd monitor.This card is also capable of SLI.  I recently bought a 2nd one of these cards to work together with my first one in SLI mode for even more video power.  Installing the 2nd card was a breeze - After I put it in and powered on my PC, the Nvidia driver automatically detected it and configured itself to use both of the cards.  Now I can run 2 Nvidia-bound BOINC tasks at the same time, and games run very fast as expected.Cons:The HDMI port on the card is a mini-HDMI port, so you need to use an adapter (included) to plug in an HDMI cable.The card is a bit longer than a lower-power card. You'll need to have adequate room in your PC case and no parts on your motherboard preventing this card from being installed. Also, even though the card uses up just one slot, it takes up the space of 2 slots due to the cooler. These things are normal for high-end video cards though.

I bought this because everyone was giving it rave reviews for TV's 46" and below.  My TV is a Samsung 46" LN46A650.  Previously, I was using my PS3 to play all DVDs, including Blu-Rays.  I decided to buy a standalone up-converting DVD player in hopes that my standard DVDs would be "enhanced" to a level fairly close to Blu-Ray.  Blu-Ray discs look incredible!  I realize the term "up-convert" means that the DVD player takes the DVD's native resolution and "smartly" blows it up to 1080p (or whatever resolution you so choose).  But, people keep saying that there is no need for a Blu-Ray player because up-converted DVD's look just as good!FYI:  All HDMIs are connected direct to the TV, not through my audio receiver (which I find unnecessary considering it's an audio receiver and does nothing with video).  I say this to clarify that there is no issue with my HDMI-switching receiver - I don't use that feature.  Also, I'm using top-quality, and overpriced, Monster HDMI cables.  (I doubt even the cheapest cable would make a real difference anyway so long as the gauge of wires are the same.)I first started with a Pioneer unit for $89 because all my home theater equipment (except for the Samsung 46" TV) is Pioneer.  The standard DVD playback at 1080p with it looked no better than when I played my DVDs through my PS3 and the picture actually looked darker and noisier, as if someone aged the picture in Photoshop.  I spent an hour with different DVDs (e.g., Ronin, Kill Bill, American Gangster) attempting to notice a difference, especially one worth spending $89 for.  I decided to return it to Abt.com.I then typed in "Best Up-converting DVD Player" into Google and the Oppo line came up.  I decided to go with the least expensive one because all of them were extremely expensive relative to the Pioneer I had.  I figure just over double the price of the Pioneer I just had should get me an up-converting DVD player I'll be satisfied with.  Boy was I wrong!Just like the Pioneer, this thing doesn't up-convert any better than my PS3.  It certainly up-converted better than the Pioneer, but not by much and certainly not enough to justify its price relative to the Pioneer.  I consistently felt as if standard DVDs looked better coming through the PS3.  I tested and tested and tested, same feeling.  I also consistently felt that DVDs played through the Oppo had a subtle green hue where dark grays and browns were.  Through the PS3, everything was natural and normal looking.  Not to mention this weird issue: title credits and moving text would actually skip around or get all discombobulated for a quick second everyone once and a while.  This never, ever happened with any DVD player connected to any TV I've ever had (including my PS3 and the Pioneer I tried first).  My TV checks out fine.I'm going to try, just because Amazon.com has a fair return policy, the more expensive Oppo 981HD with the Faroudja chipset and see if it will finally satisfy me.  If my standard DVD's don't "enhance" to near Blu-Ray quality with the 981HD, I'll stick with using the PS3 and keep my money for something worth it.  As far as I'm concerned, if standard DVD's don't look "better" by using this Oppo over a PS3, then it isn't worth two-cents.Also, just so you know, when the laser eye is moving about the disc, this thing makes more noise than my dust buster, I swear.  It sounds like Robocop moving.  This isn't a quiet machine.  I'm sure it's built well with high quality parts, but it's loudness doesn't reflect that.  Plus, why the blue screen text?  What home theater set-up uses blue text?  Most are green or amber.  Blue is hard to read in the dark because there are less blue receptors in the eye than other colors and therefore causes eye strain.  (This is why I always wonder why VW still has that blue interior!)Am I going to say don't buy this?  No, because you may not have a PS3 or Blu-Ray player and/or Blu-Ray discs.  Nor would you want to pay for either if you don't.  (I rent Blu-Rays from Blockbuster Online!)  I'm going to say, if you have a big 46"+ TV, I have a feeling you and I will be sticking with Blu-Ray discs only and skipping the whole "up-convert" thing because it just ain't good enough.

Sportcraft Anywhere Table Tennis set is a handy way to enjoy some instant, spur of the moment fun. With this set, you don't need to worry about pulling out the large tennis table stored in the garage and finding a place to set it up. With Sportcraft Anywhere Table Tennis set, most any table can be quickly turned into a tennis table for immediate fun and entertainment.This set consists of everything you need to play table tennis, except for the table, of course. All you do it anchor the two posts to a table, remove the balls and paddles, and the game is on. The posts can be attached to the edges of any table up to six feet, three inches in width and no more than 1.75 inches in thickness. The net itself is spring- mounted and the bases of the posts are rubberized to protect the table surface beneath.We have multiple tables in my house and the one we tend to use for this game is our game room table. It is a little small (a larger, closer to regulation size table would be better), but the posts fit and it works just fine for my family, which includes two children who are still too young to play on a lager table anyway. One of my other tables isn't usable for this purpose because its edges are too thick, but I have two tables in the house that work just fine and considering that a table can be up to 1.75 inches in thickness and fit the posts, most households will likely have a table that works for this purpose.This set comes complete with a pair of paddles and three balls. You need to keep track of the balls- they are small and will get lost if you're not careful. The paddles are not the greatest quality, but one has to remember that this set is intended more for the casual table tennis player. It isn't meant for the serious competitor and will likely not suffice for that purpose.A good, physical, indoor game makes a nice change of pace from the usual board game and for this reason, I am glad I received the Sportcraft Anywhere Table Tennis set. It quickly turns most any table into a tennis table, saving families the space problems and expense of buying a regular table tennis set.

I bought this along with another, larger, battery to figure out if size/weight was more important or if power and connection options were more important. It really is about the size of a large lipstick tube so it'd fit great in a bag or purse of the like.  It comes with a cable as well with an assortment of plugs to charge stuff with from iPhones to android phones and a few random ones.The size and capacity, while impressive, appear to be a limiting factor here.  It's not as easy to tell the charge state of the device as there's only a single LED, unlike the typical 4 or so (for % base) on other chargers I've seen.  This also limits the charging options - you're limited to a single device and only 1A/5V.  Not a huge issue really and it's to be known when buying the device - not something I was surprised by.Charging over a wall outlet tends to be a little faster, but may not be depending on the outlet you're using (if it's just 1A/5V out, it'll be the same from your computer - about 6 hours).  All in all it's a handy device but the limitations and inability to know exactly how charged it is, along with missing features I've come to enjoy on the larger unit I bought (integrated wall outlet and integrated USB cable) leave it a little short.  I've given it to my girlfriend to keep in her purse for use when her battery is dying.  She seems rather happy with it and it works well.Pros:++ Tiny!++ Lightweight++ Enough battery to charge most phones+ includes charging cableCons:--  Poor charge level indication- Limited to single 1A/5VIn short you trade some features for size/weight.  If all you need is a portable backup battery this will do the job amazingly well.  If you need more features look elsewhere.  The only thing I can really knock it for is the lack of a better charge level indicator.

I first will start off by stating that I have a lot of respect for the Klipsch brand and have previously owned a set of home tower speakers and a powered subwoofer.  The subwoofer is still going strong at 17 years.  The towers, I sold a long time ago, but had great service; I blew the horn tweeters and Klipsch sent me a new pair within a week.I had been wanting some new earbuds that were going to sound much better than the standard cheaper earbuds that most of us use.  I've had a couple of $10 Sony earbuds, a Philips, and probaby a bunch more.  If you go to Best Buy and sample all of the over-the-ear phones they have as samples: in my opinion, the Klipsch pair sound the best overall.  I can't stand Beats as they are way too bass heavy and they sucker people into buying their expensive products because of artist endorsement.  So I used some points to buy the reference S4's and ended up only actually paying about $15 for them.Sound Quality:  I'm only going to rate these as being better than those priced say below $75-80 or less.  There might be some comparably priced Shure's or Seinheisser's that might sound just as good or better.  Since these are single driver earphones (like most are), they are only going to do so much.Comfort/Fit:  I've never liked isolating rubber tips and this continues.  I have always simply preferred the basic cans that just sit in the ear.  Using these rubber tips never really feel like they are secure in my ears, and most of the ones that come with these are the same and fall out of my ears.  I have since ditched all the tips that came with the S4's and am using some custom DIY tips I made out of foam plugs that mold to your ear canals after you squeeze them.  This was the best idea; the plugs only cost $2 from Lowe's for 4 pair and are (1) comfortable, (2) near complete noise isolation, (3) and fit perfectly and don't fall out.Uses:  I've used them occassionally on my DJ mixer and at work. Some people can't use in-ear headphones, and I am apparently one of them.  That's somewhat funny considering as a kid in the '60's, I spent countless hours listening to my little portable radios using the little white earphone included with all little portable radios.  As a teenager in the '70's, I upgraded to headphones, and have owned countless pairs of Koss, Sony & Panasonic over-the-ear and on-the-ear headphones.  For the last 10 years, I've used nothing but the Panasonic RP-HG10--an incredibly cheap foam headphone with unbeatable sound.  My pair from last Christmas aren't working right at the present time, so I thought it would be interesting to try these in-ear headphones.My first experience with in-ear ones was a cheap Koss pair that was included free with a pair of Koss headphones.  They were so painful, I couldn't keep them in for more than 5 minutes.  Then, with my iPods, of course came Apple's in-ear headphones.  I found them way more comfortable than the Koss pair, but still only used them for a few minutes. just to see how they sounded.  These Denon in-ear headphones are totally comfortable.  I tried all 4 ear piece sizes-the extra small was too small, the sound was strange; the small were okay; the medium and the large sounded the best to my ears.  Only, I couldn't use these in-ear headphones for more than 20 minutes.  Although, I found a good EQ sound to make these Denons sound good with my iPod, I just could not stand having the music playing directly in my ear! Music playing directly in the ear affects the brain differently than music playing a bit away from the ear.  Seriously, it seems too close . . . not too loud . . . just too close.  I feel like I'll go deaf with the music so close, and thus cannot enjoy the music.  Also, and this was very strange--at times I could hear myself breathing!  And no, I wasn't breathing really hard, because I was in a panic about going deaf! :)  I had a slight sinus problem while trying them out, but I don't know if that caused the problem.  I just know I'm obviously one of those people who can't use in-ear headphones.Afterthoughts:  I gave these earbuds to my 15-year-old nephew to try out, since I couldn't use them.  He thinks they are the most comfortable and one of the best earbuds he has ever used.  And he has owned a lot of earbuds, including Bose.

The device also displays the best lane to be in (in terms of your next turn, not in avoiding bad motorists, unfortunately).One very nice thing about the Magellan is that it has the maps loaded in when you receive it. For my Garmin (which I do very much like, I admit), loading the maps took hours before the first use. This one was ready to go immediately. I got in the car, plugged it in, and within a few minutes it had found the satellite and I was up and running.One complaint for this is that it does not come with a protective slipcase. That's true of that other brand, too, but I still feel it's noticeable. This product should last a very long time, and part of that is my ability to keep it protected. It would have been a nice final touch to include that.Overall, I have found this easy to use, it functions well, and it matches the standard set by Garmin in every way that's important to me. GPS devices are wonderful things (nothing stresses me out quite like getting lost), and this is as good a GPS as I've ever used.

I own way too many cameras as I love to try them out to see if a particular one is "it" - the perfect small camera.  There are a lot of nice things about the ZS7.  Like many have mentioned, it sports a terrific range in a small form factor (25-300mm).  It offers complete manual, automatic, or anywhere in between shooting options.  There are a host of nice scene modes that are fun to experiment with ranging from common ones like beach, snow, candlelight to more artistic ones such as dynamic range and pinhole photography.  Just about every bell and whistle on the market, are on this camera and then some.For me, however, the bottom line is image quality.  Now you must have realistic expectations.  After all, this is a small point and shoot camera with a small sensor and there is no way it is a substitute for a dslr, or a micro 4/3 camera.  The trade off is you don't have to change (or pay for) expensive lenses, the camera is tiny and can go everywhere.  Basically your investment of time or money ends at the purchase price.  But I gave this camera 3 stars because I felt even within the peer group, the image quality is noticeably poor.  Noise is evident even at the lowest ISO setting of 80.  Because of this, the noise reduction within the camera is heavy and the details get smeared and hence, lost.  You can lower the noise reduction setting but you cannot shut it off.  And shooting Raw is not supported, so there is a limited ability to even work around this issue.Now, many people will not notice or care.  If you are looking for a snap shooter, convenient, latest technology, and that long zoom range this camera deserves serious consideration. But for me the poor image quality overwhelms the many positive aspects of this camera.

Canon's TS-E 17mm f/4L is a fantastic lens for architectural photography; especially interiors with smaller tight spaces. I am often asked which Canon wide angle tilt-shift lens to purchase (first), so here are some thoughts:1. The TS-E 24mm f/3.5L II is slightly sharper and better corrected against chromatic aberration. Another asset for the 24mm is that is much easier to use with filters (I use the Lee Foundation kit with 4" x 6" gradient neutral density (GND) filters). The 24mm is my go-to tilt-shift lens and I prefer it for landscapes. But, when I need a wider field of view, especially for architecture, I regularly reach for the TS-E 17mm f/4L lens.2. Although the 24mm tilt-shift is in some ways better, the TS-E 17mm f/4, might be the best tilt-shift to start with for any one of three reasons: 1. You plan to shoot interiors, 2. You plan to shoot cityscapes with tall highrise buildings (shooting downtown NY or Chicago for example), 3. You supplement your purchase with a Canon 1.4x EF Extender III. Extenders work beautifully with Canon's tilt-shift lenses, and a TS-E 17mm f/4L used in conjunction with a 1.4x extender will produce a 24mm focal length.One final note to those considering this lens: The bulbous nature of the front element makes using filters a challenge. But, thanks to Fotodiox, you can use a circular polarizer and neutral density filters with this lens with their "WonderPana" filter system, which they have made custom fit to this lens (they also have WonderPanas for other bulbous lenses, like Canon's excellent EF 14L f/2.8L II). The WonderPana simply attaches to the TS-E 17mm f/4L exactly the same way the lens cap snaps on. A brilliant design by Fotodiox! I still can't use GND filters with the lens, but between the the 1.4x Extender III and the WonderPana system, I can mostly replicate the TS-E 24mm with the TS-E 17mm. I still prefer having and using both, which I do, but knowing these things might be helpful for those struggling with the dilemma of either starting with a TS-E 17 vs the TS-E 24mm.

I will review this bed from two perspectives. One from an overall quality perspective for the average consumer. The second perspective for California consumers or those who are concerned about chemicals in their home.First Perspective:I would not describe the quality of the product as "solid", from what the top reviewer has described it. I would describe the product as "stable enough". The actual product design is much nicer than the pictures depict. I had really low expectations and was surprised.This is good for a child 3-8 years. The manufacturer recommends for ages 6 and up so this bed should really be used by a 6-8 year old. I could see where a 3-6 year old could easily destroy the bed with rough use like jumping on a bed, hanging/swinging from the ladder, and bumping into the bed too much while playing underneath. The bed has a slight "swing" to it but nothing different than one could expect from an IKEA type bed. I bought this bed for temporary use so it should hold up for the time being. The manufacturer includes a one year warranty & I would say that is pretty accurate. You may get two years out of this product if you the child is careful.The ladder is probably the most stable piece of the unit. I honestly had the opposite expectation. The bed is a lot shorter than I had expected also. This was after measuring, before purchasing. The space under neath is only suitable for a child's play. As a short adult I wasn't able to sit underneath without crouching. There was a suggestion from a reviewer that maybe a small adult could sleep with the child. I wouldn't recommend it. In fact, I think only one child by themselves would be safe. Overall, it's a $200 bed & that is the quality you should expect.Second Perspective:This bed should include a Prop 65 warning on the description page. There are HIGH levels of formaldehyde used in this bed. My child touched the ladder & can not get the smell off of his hands 24 hours later. I originally was going to buy this bed Thuka Low Loft Bed with Angle Ladder and Slide but given the price for something we only need for a year or two I decided to go with the cheaper model. They are both similar in size & look similar in structure quality. Not buying this bed was a HUGE mistake. I will now have to pay for a UV-C air filter putting my costs at about the same price of the FSC, non-toxic bed. The bed has been quarantined for 24 hours & the smell is still very strong. It is spreading through out my whole house & making us very dizzy. I am VERY careful about the products I buy & make sure that we buy products with little or no VOC content. Perhaps we are not used to those types of chemicals & that is why it is affecting us. Regardless, I have bought a lot of new things & nothing I have bought has EVER had a smell this strong. I am seriously concerned about the smell & if it does not go away in a week I may have to give this bed away. Saving money is not worth my family's health.

The BUILT cover for the Kindle Touch, Kindle Latest Generation and Kindle Paperwhite is lightweight and functional while providing protection from drops or while in a bag. I tested this cover with both a Kindle Paperwhite and a Kindle Touch, and found that it fit both of the Kindles equally well.The run down:- The outer cover's gridlock design is black and grey but in some lighting the grey in the design looks purplish.- The outer cover has a protective inner foam padding encased in a neoprene type material. Like most cloth type covers, I found while using this cover, it does attracts pet hair but it's easy to remove with a few swipes of the hand.- The outer rubber edges provide grip on most surfaces if using the cover as horizontal stand, to read in landscape mode. The cover will not stand stable upright/vertically, easily falling over.- The outer strap is easy to maneuver to keep the cover open or close. While using the strap to keep the cover open, I slide my hand between the strap on the cover and use it as a holder while reading.- The grey interior is a suede material that's soft to the touch while providing protection for the Kindle's screen when closed.- The corner mesh holders are very stretchy and form fitting, holding the Kindle snugly in place along with the help of rubber backing in each of the four corners. A possible downside to these snug mesh holders is through repeated removing and inserting the Kindle into the holders, the material could rip since they are so snug. The second time I placed my Kindle into the holders, I heard a small tearing noise but I couldn't see any holes in the mesh holder. I have removed and inserted my Kindle several times since and I haven't heard any more tearing nor seen any holes or tears but after hearing the tearing sound, I have a sense of unease about the longevity of the holders.- The bottom ports for headphones and the charging/data cable are easily accessible.- Does not add any noticeable weight to the Kindle and feels good in the hands while reading.- There is no magnet built into the cover to take advantage of the Kindle Paperwhite's auto wake/sleep feature.This cover is overall a comprehensive design and a universal fit for the Kindle Paperwhite, Kindle Latest Generation or Kindle Touch. I own several BUILT NY products and this cover resembles in form factor and feel what I'd come to expect from a BUILT NY product.

I received these headphones for review.  Overall, there is a lot to like about these headphones.Pros:1. What's in the box: Headphones, carrying case, and adapters.2. Aesthetic: First off, these are very nice looking headphones.  They are much smaller and less bulky then I expected.  The earpieces are a combination of shiny plastic cups that are covered by faux-leather ear covers on the outside and comfortable leather ear muffs on the inside.  The cord is about four feet long (I do sometimes wish it was longer), with a shiny control piece at the conjunction of the speaker wires coming from both ear pieces.  Overall, I liked the appearance.3. Sound:  Well, obviously, this is the major point of the headphones. I believe these largely succeed.Sound environment: I found the sound of these to be quite excellent.  The sound is vibrant, and very clear.  These are far better than Ipod earphones.  Response seems quite expansive, with crisp highs.  The bass is somewhat muddy, however.  I think this is due to the ability to really get sound pumping through the headphones. As such, sometimes, the bass can be 'thumpy' and not as clear as one would hope for the truly superior experience.  On the other hand, drums and percussion are as clear as one would hope to have. Listening to jazz and rock was pretty revelatory in terms of hearing a clear sound.  Often, because of the percussive range I hear using these headphones, I believe someone is knocking at the door - it is the music, not the door. That is cool!The sound is really quite a bit livelier than I have heard in other headphones I have purchased. So, I would judge these as being superior headphones.  The music overall does seem to come through quite clearly.  And, in fact, I have heard things from 50 year old recordings that I have never heard before after hundreds of listening sessions.I have used classical music, rock, jazz and some rap music to judge the sound.  Overall, I am more than pleased at the sound of these headphones, and I prefer these to a just purchased Sennheiser HD 555.  I get a much more livelier overall appearance of music and the music is louder.For perhaps a first time, I have had to actually not use full volume on my Ipod when listening to music because the music is too loud. To me this means that the response on these headphones is excellent and does not require to many ohms to drive the speakers.4. Comfort: As mentioned above, the ear muffs are a bit smaller than I expected.  So, if you have larger ears, then perhaps you might look elsewhere. However, I have worn these for a few hours, and they are quite comfortable.5. Noise isolating: One of the features that attracted me to these headphones was the noise isolation quality. I have a previous pair that requires a battery and uses active noise-canceling to filter out `white noise.' While those work well, two issues always happen.  First, I have to keep a constant stream of batteries going.  Second, there is the occasional buzzing during music play. Since these headphones require no battery, there is also no buzzing.  As for noise isolation, I have found that the quality - particularly with music - is quite excellent.  I do not hear any white noise at all, and I can barely hear other noise when using these headphones.  Overall, I was quite pleased with the noise isolation quality. I have yet to use these on an airplane, so I wonder how these compare versus noise-canceling headphones and when the opportunity arises I will leave a comment.6. Build quality: The construction of these headphones seems pretty solid except for a sole exception. It does feel I am using a quality piece of work when using these headphones.  The faux-leather covers on the outside of the earpieces are nice-looking and also would prevent scratches from being placed on a table.  The cord is also a hair larger than I am used to with Ipod earpieces and that is always reassuring.  It doesn't feel as though I am going to be able to accidentally rip these apart.  However, I do feel the sliding part is less substantial than I would hope.  On the other hand, the trade off is these headphones are not bulky, so perhaps that is a worthy excuse.7. Phone:  one nice touch is that these headphones are anticipated to be used with a Ipod or Iphone.  The controls all for volume and advancement of the songs being played.  This is nice.As for being used as a phone, a microphone is available so you can use the phone. This is not a primary use, but for taking calls it is handy and quite adept.  I have had no complaints about sounding distant when taking calls using these headphones.Case:  The case provided with these headphones comes with two adapters for a large size jack (default is for the Ipod, etc.) and one for airplane use.  I think the case is of good quality and enhances my belief that I am receiving some quality for the money.Price: These are not cheap.  A quick and dirty approach might be for earphones, rather than these.  However, the sound is pretty darn superior, and these are rapidly becoming my choice for using during listening sessions.  I don't like paying for headphones, because I always think it is so expensive, but these are pretty impressive. And since I own a speaker system made by Klispch, I do think they make quality products.Conclusion:I really have grown to like these headphones.  The controls and the ability make these a winning product and making the use of an Ipod/Iphone really fun.  They are expensive, but I think I would feel comfortable in purchasing these if given the opportunity.Update:After using these headphones for some months, and having a second pair of headphones from Logitech/Ultimate Ears, I have to confide that although the Klipsch are nice, I often prefer using the cheaper headphones to this model.  The sound just isn't quite the same.  Also, having used these on a few plane rides, I have found that the noise-canceling ability of these headphones are just okay, and not great.  So, overall, I have become less impressed over time with these headphones than I was initially.

Like everyone else, I refuse to turn my wifi off, Everything in the house is connected to it.I knew when I bought it that the camera was in the same frequency range, but I saw the tuning knob on the receiver and thought I could dial it in clear on the back of the camera as well..The problem is that their are two switches on the rear that allow for a total of four frequencies. My wifi is set to channel 11 to avoid interference from the neighbors who is on the standard channel 6.I tried all the channels the camera had, and they all seemed to be the same, interference, stuttering, and a maximum of ten(10) feet range. Channel 1 had the broadest fine tuning range of all the channels, but being the perfectionist I am, I still would settle for a little static as long as the image quit jumping.All of a sudden on channel 4 my reception came in nice and clear and moving the camera around had no problems whatsoever even from across the house through 2 walls.Satisfied, I sat down to write a review on the camera, and boom.. no wifi detected. Turn wifi back on and camera went out, but I've found a happy median while sacrificing video quality and range, Camera channel 1, wifi channel 11, fifteen feet away looking out a window onto the porch and driveway.I placed a bit of aluminum foil onto the receiver antenna and laid it down onto the metal casing and got a little better signal.If you are using this camera to record while you are away and not using wifi it is great, but if you are monitoring it from a computer or while sitting around surfing I would suggest you find a camera in the 900Mhz -  5.8Ghz range.

UPDATE 10/2013:My second adapter of this model has started to die again after moderate use (at the jack-cord connection) just as my first did after heavy use. So I do have to acknowledge shoddy construction quality, unfortunately.---------I have purchased most of the styles and brands of this kind of inline mic+button+clip adapter available on Amazon over the past few years, and despite the other negative reviews here, it is probably the best of those available. Monster (mic/button dongle) and Griffin (mic on male plug) make better products, but their design and function is different because of the mic placement; if that fits your need, buy those instead.I use this for seamless music control and call receiving/talking while working a job that requires me to wear gloves constantly; with my smartphone at my waist, I clip the mic on my pocket/pleat and plug a high-quality pair of earbuds into this unit.Better than the rest:- compared to others, I find the material and construction superior (I think the flat cable is tough and classy)- sleeker appearance than most- right-angle male plug feels less stress than straight plugs (in my own setup, may be different for others)- clicker is large, easy to find without looking, and has a consistently tactile "click"Bad:- still relatively poor construction (my female jack is failing after several months of heavy use)- the clip is quite weak (mine snapped after the cord was caught on something, taped it to a carabiner instead)2 Important Caveats from other reviews here:(1) Claims of poor audio quality are bogus - there will be no effect on transmitted quality unless the jack connection is poor/failing(2) The responsiveness or delay between clicking the button and having your phone respond is NOT the fault of this unit (or others like it unless they're broken). This is a software issue, where the phone OS often has a delay between sensing a click and doing anything about it. There are some apps for Android (I don't know about iOS) that improve this problem on some phones, but it requires some trial-and-error. If my current phone (Galaxy S4) is not responding, tapping the power button will immediately fix the issue.If a company like Monster or Griffin or Belkin made the equivalent product with better materials and aesthetics, I would immediately switch products exclusively. But until then, this one is better than some of the reviews imply.

I did extensive research to decide between this and the Sandisk e260R.  I knew that I wanted a player that could take full advantage of Rhapsody channels, and at the time, these were the only two available.  After comparing features, I went with the iRiver Clix2 (as seen on this page).At first, it seemed fine.  It is lighter than you might imagine, and quite small.  Worked alright with my FM tuner (also iRiver branded).  However, the battery life wasn't even close to what is advertised.  They say it can get about 20-24 hours, and mine lasted barely 6.  Perhaps it was because, using the channels, I was skipping songs often, which meant lighting up the screen, which drained battery life.  But still, that's one of the main features it was made for.  I tried it for two weeks, and all told got maybe 8 hours from a full charge, playing only music at moderate volume.Second, and the final nail in the coffin.  The batteries died on it while I was trying out the e260R (which I'm very pleased with).  I had to recharge from scratch (3.5 hours), and found that all of my music had vanished from the player!  This is a serious problem.  Flash drives shouldn't wipe clean like that just from running out of batteries!So, back it goes.  A shame, lovely screen.  I still give it 2 stars for the potential to be a great player.  Perhaps mine was buggy, but I'm not willing to give it another chance with a new one.  If it worked correctly, I'd give it 4 stars.Good:-Screen (it is quite nice)-Very customizable (skins, wall paper, etc...)-SizeBad:-No accessories for it.  I had to use a generic camera case to keep it safe, and screen protectors cut down from a bit one meant for a PDA.-Battery life (6-8 hours!)-Buggy OS (I'm guessing)-Very difficult to use one-handed (if you are driving, for instance).I'm sticking with the Sandisk e260R.NOTE : Amazon was excellent throughout this, and offered a full refund as well as paid for the shipping back since the product is faulty.  I will absolutely buy from Amazon again, just not this product.

I frequently rent a GPS when I travel, so I figured I'd finally get my own.Started with the nice price point- $80 for a Tom Tom Go 125. Loved the personalization and customization options...didn't like the fact that a quick test couldn't find my work address that has existed for 40+ years, but I could find it by browsing on a map, so I just figured I could deal with it. What I couldn't deal with was that the unit wouldn't power on unless I did a soft-reset EVERY TIME (hold power button for 15 seconds...not acceptable in my opinion). So I took it back and got an XL 340. Nice price point for a big screen, this one connected to the satellites much quicker, and turned on like it was supposed to. Still couldn't find my work address, but at least I had a working GPS, I thought.Then, I installed the latest updates and charged it all night. The next morning, it turned on to a big flashing red 'X'. No amount of resetting or updating would fix it.I called TomTom support. To their credit, the TomTom support reps are very polite and knowledgeable (and US-based- a great plus these days...) However, it took a good 20 minutes or more to get someone (possibly due to holiday increases?). That wouldn't have been so bad, except their reps aren't allowed to stay on the phone while you run through their recommended fixes. I had 4 reps, 3 of which gave me a few steps, then told me to call back. 3 1/2 hours later, they set me up with an RMA. Hmmm...don't think so. The thing was 2 days old, I wasn't about to wait weeks to get a replacement, fight for a new one vs. a refurb, etc. So I got a Magellan. Not as flashy and friendly, but there's something to be said for a unit that just 'works'...What I liked:Beautiful screenCustomization options (voices, car symbol, all able to be changed yourself, or upload your own!)What I didn't:-Map discrepancies (if it didn't have the address, you're just out of luck! No navigating to 'nearest option', it just won't do it. TomTom's suggestion: submit a correction. Don't think so. I want accuracy out of the box.-Unclear operation (how do I 'cancel' a trip? You pretty much need to add a separate trip in order to cancel out the first one-No car power off/battery operation warning or indicator. You could turn the car off, and forget to turn off the GPS as well.-Unclear how to get TTS (Text to speech - speaks street names). Box claims it does it, but you need a less pleasant computer voice set for this to work)-No easy POI searching. Any search pulls up random locations, no clear categories (gas, grocery store, etc). POI entries are very abstract...and NO, I don't want to manually enter a bunch. If I'm in an unfamiliar place, I need a good search tool!-It broke after 2 days of VERY minimal use.

This version of Roku seems to do everything well. While that is just fine if you are only going to connect to the TV, what about those other Roku channels available, like Pandora, Tune-in Radio, and the other music or audio stations?  Now you must listen to them through your TV, unless you happen to have a newer-type audio system with a digital HDMI input AND with a pass-through, so you can still route to your TV.  If you happen to have a perfectly functional, high-end audio system without an HDMI digital input, then Roku 3 will not work for you.  This is extremely disappointing from such an otherwise great product.Sure, you can get some add-on equipment to split the signal, but that seems to be going backwards.  Who wants yet another bunch of cables, another wall-wart transformer, and something else to fail, stuffed behind the TV, with the additional expense of more equipment.Maybe they will redesign the next version, and add the audio output back.  Until then, I'm digging my old Roku back out and returning this one.

This review is about a PANASONIC DMR-485V DVD/VHS RECORDERAll the stuff everyone else said... locks up, won't read a disc it just recorded, timer just forgets? It's a lot like a teenager that just won't listen. But they're ALL like that! Actually, it seems all digital stuff is like that... "IF I feel like doing it at all, I'll do it when I'm good and ready." It's as if you don't even exist sometimes. I can't believe that nobody can (is it can't or won't?) make a reliable DVD recorder.I recently bought a Magnavox MDR515H with a hard drive and sent it back it was such a frustrating POS. I then got a Toshiba DVR670 DVD/VHS Recorder. Looks to be the same lousy firmware as the Magnavox by the menu screens and horrible channel selection method, but I kept it anyway. (I can't keep wasting money on return S&H;!) At least it only records a black silent screen on some of the channels as opposed to most of the channels like the Magnavox, and 5 to 10 seconds can add up when you have to wait that long between every channel change. It can literally take several minutes just to go from a channel at the low end of the tuner like 4-1 to one somewhere in the middle like 20-2. And yes, you have to wait for every single one in between. The Panasonic isn't nearly so bad and the channel selector (especially for timer recordings) is so much easier to use. Also, you can preview the channel you are programming as you set the timer so you know there is actually a channel there. Not possible with those other two units which, btw, don't let you label channels. The Panasonic does. Oh yeah, DVD-RAM discs... GREAT! You can pause live tv then fast forward like a DVR and play back recordings at 1.3x (You think "Bad Brad" is fast at normal speed?) with sound and captions, although the video quality can be a little squirrelly depending on the original record speed. Also, some other players read DVD-RAMs (like the Toshiba) so you can move them without having to "finalize" the disc. A big disappointment is not being able to record to VHS from a digital signal, especially since we have no analog channels provided on our cable system anymore.So, the Panasonic has some problems, but it is so much better and easier to use than the others. It's too bad when an unreliable unit is the best "go to" option you've got, but it is what it is and it ain't gettin' no better. I would hesitantly recommend it keeping that in mind. Also, I found a firmware update a few months ago and it worked reasonably well for a while. Lately it's has become very problematic again so I will try to find a newer update.I threw out a Sanyo D1000 not long ago that I used to think was a PITA, but after dealing with these SOBs I miss it. (Although, I missed a lot of shows that didn't record and threw out a lot of unreadable discs with that one too.) It only had an analog tuner, but I could have at least used it to record off the cable box. Now, Comcast... THERE's a topic for disgruntlement! (Some other time and place.)

PLEASE READ BEFORE ORDERING if you are planning to use with AppleTV. The product will convert a 1080p or 720p digital signal to a 1080/720 analog RCA component video signal.  In order to view video, your "old" TV must be capable of displaying video in one of these resolutions. For example, in my case I have Sony WEGA (circa 2000) tube TV with square display, which does not support either of these resolutions.  Since this device will not downconvert the video signal from widescreen to the old square resolution, this is product is useless for me.  Before ordering, verify that your old TV is capable of accepting and displaying signals in either the 1080 or 720 resolutions. Whatever signal resolution is sent to this box, will be converted to the same resolution except in an analog format.This product will not work with Gen 3 AppleTV, since Gen 3 now uses HDCP encryption.  You may get some signals to convert properly, however any video from your iTunes or Apple Store library uses this encryption, preventing the convertor from functioning properly.

I received the the PS4 from Amazon yesterday.  Mine was not a preorder, I ordered it at 12:02 AM on launch day.  I don't have any games yet, the first one will arrive on Monday.  That being said, I installed the 1.50 update right out of the box.  When I change resolutions or display settings, the TV would go blank and no amount of button mashing or turning the console on or off would fix this.  The PS4 would blink on top.  I tried holding the power off button until it would rebate, changed the resolution via safe mode, etc.  It would start up again, and I could repeat the process by changing resolutions.Then I tried playing a DVD or blu-ray.  Every time it would go to play the movie, I'd get the same behavior.HERE'S THE WORKAROUND!!!  At least for me so far.  The problem has to do with the handshake between the PS4 and TV.  All I do when the screen goes blank is turn off the tv, wait five seconds, turn it back on, and everything's fine!  In the case of the movie, turned the tv off and back on, the movie was loaded up and playing just fine.  BTW, the same thing happens when you exit the movie and go back to the main ps4 menu.  Again, turn the tv off, back on, and you're back at the menu.  The same when changing the display settings.Since the PS4 is going right where it should and isn't actually crashing, I don't believe the unit is broken or that mine is an isolated incident.  If I never would have turned the TV off and on, I too would say that my unit is bricked.I'm trying to get as much feedback on my workaround as possible from other owners.  If it is truly the widespread issue, then my unit isn't broken, but perhaps something Sony can fix with a firmware update.If you go to youtube and search for Noah Bershatsky (my name, I'm typing this on my wife's account), you'll see a video I made of this workaround.*** Update late on Sunday, November 17th.  I have the PS4 now working properly.  I changed the hdmi cable to a different input on my TV.  After much research about 120 hz, 60 hz, handshake, hdmi trouble shooting, etc.  The manual of my TV says to have gaming systems on inputs 4 and 5 (I had it on 1).  Moving the cable to another input and now everything works as it should!  Still haven't played a game, I will be doing that tomorrow when I receive Assassin's Creed.

After using this product on it's own several times with lackluster and quite frankly, piss poor results, I think I've AT LAST gotten the hang of using the Raw Shea Butter Deep Treatment Masque. The first several times I used this product I was VERY dissapointed. I ended up with straw-like hair, and I think that has a lot to do with the Shea Butter as a main ingredient. I can't use Shea Butter on it's own in my hair-it dries it out something awful. I have to use it in combination with a lighter oil like Jojoba, Grapeseed or Olive. Since the base for this product is Shea, it would likely leave my hair feeling dry and stripped after I used it. This was exactly what happened whenever I used this product on it's own.I have 3b/3c hair (so I believe). I do not use coconut oil outside of deep conditioning for my hair because I find that it is much too heavy and on me, leaves an oily residue that is impossible to remove outside of washing. I have fine hair, so this may be why coconut oil and I do not get along. The only reason why I decided to use this masque was because I was pressed for time, lacked several of the main ingredients to make my own DIY Dry Hair Treatment Masque, lacked the money to BUY said main ingredients, and didn't want to leave my house because I was too comfortable and it was cold outside. At the time, my hair was very dry due to winter weather and prolonged heat use. I had been sitting under a bonnet dryer and doing wet sets for probably 2 months. Wet sets with perm rods and an hour or so under a dryer were not making my hair happy. I needed moisture, and it was the one thing I lacked.I decided to mix this masque with some unrefined, organic coconut oil I had lying around. I divided my hair into sections and ran coconut oil through each section and followed it with a good cupped fingerful of the Shea Moisture Organic Raw Shea Butter Masque. The oil gave the masque more slip than it had previously, and the oil seemed to allow the masque to actually sink into the hair and penetrate the shaft, instead of just sitting on top of the hair and coating it, which is all that I feel that this masque does when used by itself. I twisted each section into a chunky bantu knot and covered my hair with a plastic shower cap. I left the masque on for probably 2 1/2 hours, maybe closer to 3. Then I rinsed out. Rinsing out my hair felt moisturized, and I seemed to shed a lot less hair than I normally do.Afterwards, when I styled my hair, it seemed to help my curls define themselves (they have trouble with this normally) and my hair felt MUCH more moisturized than it had been for months.Three days out, after a no heat styling regimen, I'm pleased to say that my hair seems to be doing a good job of retaining the moisture that the masque seemed to put into it. I'm just now seeing the effects of dryness, but it's by no means as bad as it was before I started. Spritzing my hair nightly with some water and tea-tree oil mixed in and rubbing jojoba oil through my hair before bed seems to help too. For dryness, the Raw Shea Butter Deep Treatment Masque PLUS added coconut oil seemed to really do the trick. If i'm out of everything I'll use this mixture again but I won't buy another tub of this masque when I run out of it.I plan on making my own masque for dry hair when I run out of the Shea Moisture one. Less expensive than spending $10.00 (don't buy this for $23 on Amazon, in my opinion it's only worth about $7 and you can find it at Target for $10.00) but IMHO, not worth it unless you have nothing else. You can find so-easy-it's-painful recipies for DIY Dry Hair Treatments on youtube or on any other curly girl website or blog that will cost less than this to make and will last longer. The fact that for me it only works with the coconut oil added is also another 'meh'.Another dissapointing Shea Moisture purchase. I'll see if I still like the Curl Enhancing Smoothie after winter's over and then do a review on that one.

I ordered this camera "Used- Like New" for $40 less than retail. No complaints there. It was like new and it worked great right out of the box. The reason I bought this camera was because of the 1080p video in stereo, 16mp, the non-exposed lens, and all of the durability features. I was anxious to get it because I had a 4 state trip to go on and I wanted to make a photo journal of the trip. I should have brought the charger. The battery in this thing is weak. It is a 3.7volt, 1050mAh rechargeable battery that wouldn't make it past 150 shots in the daytime with no flash. The camera takes great photos and good videos, but it almost seems to me like its affiliated with Apple because it records video in .MOV format and nothing else. It almost makes me think that Nikon is Apple's un-official line of digital cameras. I am absolutely, 100% against the Apple regime, so this is a problem for me. I had to buy a video editing program that accepts .MOV format files. The program is slow on most computers, even on my higher-end desktop. Another problem I've had with 2 of my computers is getting the computer to recognize the camera. Connection via USB is time consuming and slow. And something about the way that this Nikon formats memory cards prevents me from viewing photos and videos straight from the card. It would be nice to have some alternate firmware that would allow this to be more of a Windows camera. File formats and connections aside, the video quality is up to par. The waterproofing is a pretty neat from what I've tested so far. I pressed record and dropped it into my friends fish tank and it made for an entertaining video. I've read other reviews since then, and I think I'll reserve that feature for when I might really need it.  Many of the 1 and 2 star reviews said that the camera leaked upon firs submersion. Scary thought. Other than the battery life, connection issues, and the .MOV format, it is a great camera, but these three things really limit what I can do with it. I sell used equipment so it is absolutely necessary that I have a durable camera, which this is. It is great for taking photos in the rain, and the fact that there is no exposed telescoping lens helps to prevent things from breaking when it gets bumped on steel and such.1-30-13 - UpdateThis camera has grown on me. I've used it underwater, in snow, dropped it, and it's still working great to this day. I've been able to work around it's formatting faults once I began experimenting with other video editors, and the SD card issue was resolved by using a better card reader. The battery life isn't as bad as I first though, but I recommend spending an extra $20 on a cheap set of 2 extra batteries and an additional charger.I've upped the rating to 4 stars, but I'd almost consider giving it 4 and a half. ★★★★

I have never built a computer before so finding the right case was based on reading lots and lots of reviews and looking at lots of videos.Fortunately I read and saw enough to come to the realization that a full tower case would be way too big for my needs so I went with the mid tower, which is still a lot bigger than my old Dell, but not too bad. There is plenty of room for the wires behind the mobo so there is not a single wire running through the case for excellent airflow, plus it just looks good.As with all cases it was a compromise between what I wanted, what was available and what was affordable.Pros/likes:*The case is all mesh on the front and top with filters on the intake fans to catch the big chunks.*Right now the case is on the floor until I am sure everything is working good. The front of the case is actually cold to the touch and it moves enough air that it makes my feet cold!*There is room for 10 fans and it comes with 3 that are very quiet. If it weren't for the stock cpu fan it would be silent. The fans can be variable speed as controlled by your mobo.*There is a hot swap sata dock right on top for quick access to a bare drive.*Excellent wire management, all behind the mobo. Smooth edges everywhere, not a single scrape when installing wires and mobo. Holes everywhere you need one.*Simple to install drives and disk players, tool-less.*Blue fan light can be turned off and on with the push of a button.*There is a huge access hole to the back of the CPU for easy cooler upgrades without removing the mobo.*One big fan blowing across the hard drive bays. That helps a lot.Cons/wishes:*All the front panel ports are on the top. If you keep it on the floor this is OK, but I will have it on a shelf above me and they are hard to reach. I will just add a USB extension to get around it. They probably will fill up with whatever is floating around the house, too.*I would have liked all the hard drive bays to be hot swap. I remove the data drives and put them in a safe when we are away for extended periods and that makes it much easier.*The hot swap dock on top won't "eject hardware" so I can't just pull the drive out of it without shutting down. That may be a mobo issue, though.*The drive in top hot swap dock gets hot. There is nothing but ambient air on the top to keep it cool, no airflow at all on the bottom, so it is not for extended heavy use.*Throw away the "instruction" book and go watch YouTube videos. The book is an abysmal joke. I still haven't gotten the top off.Overall I really like this case and I am very happy with my choice. I would buy it again. The price to feature range is really good. The mount itself is great.  I have a 39" LED-based HDTV mounted on it (40lbs), and it doesn't droop.  However, the supplied bolts for concrete or stud mounting are a cause for concern.  The bolts are extremely long and big, bigger than the standard six-sided drivers that come with American drill bit sets.  I had to use a Japanese drill bit set that included a huge adapter that would fit the head of the bolt.  However, the bolts themselves are made of very cheap metal that shears and breaks under pressure.  If the instructions are followed, the bolts will shear in normal wooden wall studs.  The guide hole made using the recommended size drill bit is too small and does not give enough guidance/relief to the weak bolts, which will shear and break.  Since the bolts snap in the middle, there's no way you can bolt in the wall mount.  After two bolts snapping, I went with bigger guide holes to relieve the friction on the lag bolts.  The mount itself is solid and great, but if you can't mount it to the wall, then it serves no purpose.  It's unfortunate that the company decided to cut corners on the crucial components.

After hearing my first dac some time ago and understanding more about what is involved with converting digital bits to analog sound, I have a nice home setup with a dac (not something one travels with!)  I also have Dragonfly (which I do like) for my laptop. I'm not an audiophile, but I really love great music that sounds fantastic.But- what to do when you drive or travel a lot...that's the question. If you've spent any time at all listening to music on your iPhone (even with really good headphones), you'll know that the sound quality is pretty terrible. You can slap a few EQ apps on it, but at best, it drowns out the sounds of the airport. And plugging it into the audio jack in the car? Forget it. It makes even good speakers sound bad.Since I already own the latest Dragonfly, I gave that a go on my phone. The Dragonfly must require a lot from the system that it's connecting to because it won't even flicker when paired with a phone. So, that option is out.However, the Microstreamer is the perfect solution. You can use it with your iPhone and it works! You'll need  to pick up the camera connector from Apple to create a USB to lightning connection. They'll tell you at the Apple store that it won't work for anything but a camera, but what they really mean is that the iPhone doesn't handle external devices that require a lot of power very well. Now that the firmware was updated on the Microstreamer to address that issue, it's all good. Mine shipped with the latest firmware (Out of curiosity, I checked. There are instructions on their site). Of course, the fact that it worked should have been answer enough. I didn't have to do anything to make it work.As someone mentioned, it's smaller than a Zippo lighter and you can just throw it in your bag and go. Or, hook it up to the phone and plug into the audio jack in your car for your commute. Then plug it into your laptop when you get to work.I do notice that the phone battery drains faster when using this (not unsurprising). There are designated connectors for headphones and for speakers. Be careful to connect it to the proper one. It's marked on there pretty clearly, but it's easy to mess up if you aren't paying attention. They both put out sound, just a little differently. It's nice that they have both.Believe me, once you give this a try, it'll be really difficult to listen to music without it.

This machine is a nice gadget that makes pretty good coffee, albeit somewhat expensive.  However, if you decide to purchase one of these machines, be aware you may only get about a year of good performance before trouble sets in.  I bought 2 of these machines, almost a year apart.  The first one I used myself, usually brewing only a cup per day.  Even though I followed all the maintenance recommendations, and even used the charcoal filter, the machine started acting up about a month after the one year warranty ran out.  It started giving only partial cups some of the time.  Descaling and cleaning the needles helped for a short time before the machine reverted to short cups.  As the next few months wore on, we got used to having to lift the handle and re-brew the same K-cup to get a full cup of coffee.  With a little more time, the machine started refusing to work at all.  We'd turn it off and on, try descaling again, and cleaning the needles, but the problems just got worse.  Now it refuses to brew at all.  It just sits there and makes strange noises, but gives no coffee.Unfortunately, before my problems started I bought another of these machines for my daughter.  Hers seemed to work okay, except for the occasional short cup, until it was 11 months old.  At that point it broke down completely, spewing water all over her counter.  Since she had one more month to go on the warranty, she was able to get a replacement.  Hopefully this one will last longer.In my opinion, you're rolling the dice on just how long one of these machines will last.  Just remember that it can be an expensive gamble.UPDATE *****A lady named Angela posted a comment to my review and said I should have called Keurig about my problems.  I did, in fact, call them prior to posting this review, and should have mentioned that.  I've copied and pasted my answer to Angela here:Angela, thanks for your reply.  I should have noted that I did indeed call Keurig to try and resolve this problem.  Almost 2 weeks ago I emailed them and detailed everything that went on with my brewer.  I received an email back from Amanda in customer service advising me to call a number she gave me.  I spoke with a man in Customer service.  After listening to my tale of woe, he took my name and promised to have tech support call me.  Shortly thereafter a man named Rick called and we went through all the steps he could think of to get the brewer working.  Nothing worked.  In fact, the brewer had reached the point where it would literally only give a cup of fluid once every 20 or 30 tries.  Once we did everything tech support advised, it absolutely refused to work at all any more. So, as bad as the situation was, it was now worse.  Rick put me on hold.  When he came back on he said I was too many months past the warranty expiration and they wouldn't give me a new brewer.  They would only offer me a discount on a new brewer.  I told him that with the problems people all over the web were having with their machines, not to mention my own, I would not buy another Keurig even at a discounted price.  I bought my brewer later than you, and registered it it January 2009.  Apparently, besides building a lesser quality machine, Keurig also doesn't treat customers equally.  I find this very disturbing to say the least, and one more reason why people should stay away from Keurig.  Good luck with the machine they're sending you.  I have a feeling you'll need it.Another update:After seeing how Angela got a replacement brewer with a machine older than mine, and the prodding from family members, I decided to call Keurig customer service and complain one last time about the apparently unequal replacement policy.  This time they decided as a 'one time courtesy' to send me a replacement brewer after all.  The lesson to be learned here is to be persistent if you feel you've been treated unfairly.I thought about increasing the one star rating, but decided against it since so many people are having trouble with this particular model.  If you decide to buy a Keurig, I'd buy something different than the Platinum B70.  And make sure to call customer service the first moment anything goes wrong.  You want to be on record in case a replacement is needed.

I have been searching for years for a cheese slicer that rivals the ones I used while I lived in Sweden. Thank goodness I brought one back with me, but it has a wooden handle and is perhaps not quite as sharp as it used to be. You'd think a replacement would be easy to find in the land of plenty, but not so. I've bought several, even one from IKEA, but none of them came close.I became excited about the Boska because of the positive reviews, but was soon disappointed. While it is definitely better than any other slicer I've bought in the US, it still doesn't quite make the cut, haha. Its best point is that it doesn't skip across the top of the Tillamook medium cheddar we love so much, as other blades have done. But the Boska doesn't cut smoothly, and that's the rub. It leaves a funky textured path in its wake, and it's also rather a hard pull compared to my trusty Swedish souvenir (actually made by Spar, a Norwegian company).I compared the blades visually. I think the difference between great slicers and so-so ones is the angle of the cutting edge. Many make the mistake of trying to slice too much cheese at once; i.e., the cutting edge lies at too sharp an angle from the plane of the slicer. My older slicer cuts smooth, thin slices because its blade tilts ever so gently from the straight of the plane.Which leaves me still searching. Thank goodness my old Spar still has some life left in it, and this Boska will certainly do the job, if inelegantly.Perhaps this slicer would work better for softer cheeses, such as havarti. Haven't tried it on anything softer than the Tillamook cheddar mentioned above. Hope this helps.

I received this as a reward from my health insurance provider fulfilled by Amazon.  I didn't want a huge, space-consuming 20-quart monolith in my kitchen as I only intended to can 4-ounce jars to give as gifts this holiday season so I thought this was perfect. When it arrived, the instructions were vague, mostly a few recipes tailored to this pressure cooker and that was it. I wasn't really even sure how the pressure valve worked. The instructions are pretty much useless--just twist on the pressure gauge deal and throw them away. I am guessing that if you twist it all the way to the side marked "pressure" then it's pressurized, and if you twist it to the side that says "release" then you won't have pressure. I checked the Presto Web site for more guidance--more useless recipes. NOTHING about canning. I clicked on over to amazon to read the trusted reviews of other users, and lo and behold, apparently this is not to be used for canning. Crud. Wish I would've known that prior to choosing this as my "reward."Not to be deterred, I continued my online research into why this particular model cannot be used for home canning. Turns out, there's really no good reason besides that there are no specific, lab-tested and approved times for canned goods using this model. Apparently, the powers-that-be decided people would only like to can in large models so they did away with testing for smaller pressure cookers. What's a girl to do? I decided to be bold and try it out anyway. I was canning a savory jam that contained bits of meat, so I looked at recommended times for other pressure cookers to can meats and just went with that. (The USDA recommends pressure canning for pretty much everything but tomatoes these days, something to do with the temperature inside a pressure cooker being hot enough to kill botulism bacteria along with other harder-to-kill microorganisms...) I began timing after steam started coming out of the pressure gauge doohicky, turned down the burner to a medium-low setting, and left it alone for 45 minutes. Then I took the cooker off the burner and let it rest about another hour before attempting to twist the release valve (didn't want a hot-steam thermofacial at that point). I then took the lid off and checked the jars--sealed tight. Hooray! I have since opened a jar of that jam (it's been a month) and detected no strange odors, growths, flavors, etc.I am going to keep on using this for small-batch canning projects, as I don't have the time, patience, or kitchen space to undergo a large home canning experiment. I haven't used it for anything else yet--those included recipes seemed pretty bland--but I might venture into meal pressure cooking eventually. The stainless steel pot seems sturdy enough to last for many, many years, and I cleaned the inside where I had a bit of a spill last canning go-round with some Bartender's Friend (or is it Barkeep? Anyway--that scouring powder for cleaning around the kitchen) and it shined right up like new.The product itself probably rates 4 stars, but the reason this gets only 3 stars is because the manufacturer really ought to have better instructions on regular "approved" use of this thing. I also don't understand what prevents them from testing canning times and letting the rest of us know. Other than that, I like it just fine and will continue to use it for my unapproved canning activities!

Initially, I assigned it 3 stars for the "mixed bag" of pros and contras. Now, having used it for a few days, I have to drop to 1 star (since there is no option for zero stars). I am no longer in the mood to list the positives, as this thing is just too temperamental to be used as a CD writer.Here is the growing list of boo-boos:Upon arrival (in undamaged double box), the little toned "plexiglass" plate that covers the display had fallen off. It's held to the body with a few drops of sticky-note-like glue, only stronger. Oops. Oh well, glued it back. Not sending back for this.CD COMPARTMENT: It takes disproportionately long time to open it ... even when it's empty. You'd think, press 'Open', and it shall open unto thee? Nope. First, there is some noisy activity inside. Then the display tells you 'No disk'. Keep pressing the Open button, and it may open. Or not. On two occasion I thought it was going to keep toggling between 'Reading' and 'No disc' messages forever without ever opening it. If there is no disc, what exactly was this pile of trash reading?ON/OFF: You'd think if there is a remote, you should be able to turn the unit on- and off, using the remote? Nope.REMOTE (CONT'D): Tried using remote ... if you are further than even 10-12 feet from the machine, it won't work. Changed the batteries - no difference.STOP FROM RECORDING: Either works, or not. This is especially fun when you are trying to rip a vinyl LP: you reach the end of side A, press a button to pause or stop it, but the Teac keeps soldiering on regardless, recording lovely 10-second tracks of silence instead of going into standby.AUTOMATIC TRACK DETECTION: Near impossible to set correctly. It has several incremental pre-set levels of signal drop (-60, -50, -40 and -30 dB, with -50 recommended for LP's) that would be recognized as intervals between tracks, but it ends up either making 20+ tracks from 4-5 songs @ -40 dB setting, or writing the whole side as one track @ -50 dB. And this is on brand new, once or twice played audiophile LP's (very little noise).RECORDING LEVEL INDICATOR: Kind of doesn't like to move (too much damping)? In the old good 1980's those luminescent read-outs used to "pulse" with music ... the indicator on this TEAC just sits at 2 or 3 bars for the whole duration of a song.PROBLEMS WITH FINALIZING/FURTHER USE: Out of probably dozen CD's I have recorded, 3 (three!!!) were either missing tracks, or wouldn't play even on the Teac itself.The good news is that it hasn't blown up or burnt the house yet.

If you read the negative "technical" reviews on this voltage regulator, most of them are fair and honest, yet disappointing. I put mine up against a meter where the voltages were low and high.I called the customer help number for APC and ended up talking for a loooooooong time to a person that repeated everything I said to him, back to me, and most times getting it incorrect...and not my fault.He was patient and earnest but alas yet another company hiring "triage" help desk clerks with very little knowledge armed with only a pre-written script.He eventually had to place me on hold several times so he could ask a higher level tech for answers.Here is what he explained to me:The unit actually is a small boost or cut in voltage. It will not, nor does it act as what most people would think of as a "regulator."This unit will either boost or cut the voltage by a factor of 6%.If you are in America and have it set to 120 but have a low voltage service coming to your home, say 90 volts for example. This unit will only boost it 6% or approximately 5.4 volts If you are at 95 volts, then you may get close to 100 volts using this "booster". 10 volts will go to 106 volts...and so on.Likewise if you are experiencing high voltage service at your home, this unit will reduce it by a factor of 6%.130 volts will be reduced to 122 volts. Still running a little hot, whereas in the USA most voltages are 110-120.This may help minor power surges or low voltages, and may keep your computer or TV from "messing up", but it only does 6% either way.If you are unsure of how "hot or cold" your devices can safely operate, consult the manufacturer or owners manual. (or a friend who knows about this type of stuff.)I play loud guitar at a place that has "dirty" electricity. This devices will not help with "dirty electricity." If there are other machines, coolers, air conditioners, heaters, washing machines, dryers that use a lot of power and may have a bad ground or poor circuitry, this APC unit will not "condition" the line, though there have been honest reports of some devices that "no longer hum" or don't shut off & restart when the air conditioner kicks on, etc.A really good quality Voltage Regulator/Power Conditioner will cost well over four bills. (Benjamins.) There is no way of getting around it, yet I decided to keep this unit as I cannot afford the expensive ones in hopes that any help will be better than nothing. Try it...if you hate it...send it back!
