The latter turned out to be true, the former not.I knew a real weakness of the Nook HD is its battery life. I had measured it (100% charge to powered off) and got only a little over four hours. I was hoping the HD+ would do better. B&N; claims 10 hr life for both devices, and a search of the Nook HD+ reviews showed no reviewers complaining about its battery life, so I was expecting it to be better. It isn't, in fact in a fair side by side test the Nook HD+ and Nook HD batteries discharge at almost exactly the same rate. The HD+ might run a few minutes longer, but essentially these are both four hour tablets, and 4 hours is a long, long way from B&N;'s 10 hour claim.Wierd DifferencesI knew before buying HD+ that B&N; had not put the switches in the same place on both devices, which as a design engineer I find to be an odd engineering decision. And in fact going back and forth between the two tablets I find having the power and volume switches in completely different places on the two tablets to be annoying. Also the switches are nearly impossible to see in the HD+ as it is black on black.Pleasant surpriseThe max volume is much better in the Nook HD+ than the Nook HD, where it is too soft.Unpleasant surprisesHowever, I ran into two unpleasant surprises in the Nook HD+. Operated alone the HD+ screen doesn't look half bad, but in a side by side comparison with the Nook HD the quality difference between them is obvious. With both set to max brightness and displaying the same material the Nook HD screen is beautiful, its white very bright and colors that pop. In contrast the Nook HD+ white is more off white and not as bright and its colors are somewhat muted and dull.But worse the HD+ appears to have a nasty thermal problem, an over-temperature trip, that I have never seen on the Nook HD. Without warning up pops a triangle warning screen, and the device begins a repeated reset that only stops when it has a chance to cool down. This has happened to me twice, most recently while using HD+ in the sun. (Note we are talking the sun in Maine in Oct, not Florida in July!) Whether the over-temperature trip threshold is set in hardware or in software (which in principle would allow it to be raised), I don't know. A battery utility that displays temperature shows the HD+ runs 5-8F hotter than the HD, and its back feels hotter too. This smells like a thermal design problem, and it should not be happening. I am not using the device under unusual conditions.----------------(update1) I want to scale back a couple of my negative comments from above, and I have increased my rating one star. Rereading my comments above on the screen brightness and color, I think I was too harsh. I used the HD+ today for a couple of hours looking carefully at the screen quality (color and brightness), and it looked fine. It is only in a side by side comparison with the Nook HD that the HD+ screen suffers a little.Also a couple of commentors have objected to my saying that the Nook HD+ might have a thermal design problem. They report having no problem like I had, and one commentor said he has used it in the sun and hot car. That's good to hear, but the fact remains that my HD+ does have occasional thermal shutdowns, while it otherwise runs fine.-------------------(update2)The over temperature problem on my Nook HD+ is pretty bad. I now have installed a battery app that shows battery temperature and status (labeled 'health'). Using it indoors at normal room temperature I find that after 10-15 min of use the battery temperature rises from room temperature to 105-110F. When it goes above 105F, the health status display changes from 'Good' to 'Overheat', which is just a warning because Nook HD+ continues to run.However, I had a 3rd thermal shutdown using it in the Oct sun for 15 min. As soon as the HD+ recovered, I ran the battery app and the first temperature was 121F, with a little time in the shade it dropped to 110-115F stayed in the "Overheat' mode and continued to run. This confirms the cause of the shutdown is a component running too hot and that component is apparently the battery.I like the HD+ and use it a lot, but still this is annoying. At home my main use for a tablet is sitting on my balcony in the sun, and of my three tablets (Nook HD, BB Playbook, Nook HD+) only the HD+ has a thermal problem.

I got this clock radio/iPhone dock as a Christmas present and overall, I give it a "meh" rating.First the good - the sound is pretty great for such a small package.  I'm able to pick up both FM & AM radio without issue at all.  The sound is crisp and loud enough to fill the bedroom.  The bass response is also pretty decent - with the option of adding Sony's "Megabass" for a little more oomph.  Also, it charges my iPhone 5S without issue.  For that, I like it.Now for the bad - there is VERY little customization when it comes to the alarm.  You can wake up to the standard buzzer, the radio, or the iPhone.  I'm the type of person who likes to wake up to a different song each day.  On my old Philips iPhone dock, I was able to create a playlist specifically for the dock, and the songs would shuffle with each day.  It was a great feature.With this dock, you MUST have the music app going in order to wake to the iPhone.  Otherwise, it just defaults to the buzzer.  Quite the unpleasant surprise if you forget to get the app going before you dock your phone.  It's an annoyance, for sure.  I always have to make sure the app is launched before I go to bed.  The second major annoyance is that you have to set the app to whatever song you want to wake up to.  You can't just select a playlist - you have to have a song queued up.  This may seem like something minor to a lot of people, but it's 2014.  There is no reason I shouldn't be able to wake up to a shuffled playlist.One option is to download Sony's app for your phone.  It is a completely non-intuitive app and, just like with the music app, you have to have it running in the background in order for your dock to take advantage of its features.  (If you're looking for it in the app store - search for "D-Sappli" - I know, it's just as intuitive as the app itself...)  This app does add some features, but unlike with the regular music app, you can't just have it running in the background.  The app has to be launched and front and center in order to use it.  This means your iPhone screen will be on in the middle of the night - you can't put the phone to sleep while using this app.All in all, if you're looking for an extremely BASIC iPhone clock radio/dock, this is not an awful option.  I would argue that it's a little overpriced for what it offers, though.  For the same functionality, you can get something at half the price from a competing company.  If you're looking for the latest and greatest - with the most current features, look elsewhere...

i made the mistake and bought this motherboard for a brand new cpu setup with a 8320 cpu. Asus should have never listed support for 8320 and 8350 as it simply does not have what it takes to support these beasts. I have a 7970 video card and 8 gb ram along with this motherboard and 8320 processor. While at first i did notice a slight performance boost from my ancient intel q9550 build, I knew I wasn't getting the full potential with intermittent choppiness in games and benchmarks not on par with reviews. After LOTS of research I quickly learned that the VRM chips on this motherboard run extremely hot with these chips due to not having any heat sinks along with only 4+2 power. When loading OCCT on full load i noticed occasional cpu throttling after 5 minutes even though CPU temps were perfectly fine. Any attempt to overclock to the rated turbo of 4 ghz would result in serious throttling after only 2 minutes of benchmarking.Almost ready to eat the costs and buy a new motherboard, i decided to buy some heatsinks for the VRM chips (cosmos 20 pc aluminum heatsinks) as well as point a fan right above them and the difference is night and day. I can now run OCCT at 4ghz with NO throttling and the gaming performance is butter smooth as it should be. To think I almost blamed it on a mistake in trying AMD over Intel when really the fault was Asus misleading that this motherboard is fully supported to achieve optimal performance.

At various times over the years, I have owned an iPad, iPad 3, Kindle, Kindle Fire HD, Nook, Galaxy Note 10.1, Microsoft Surface, and a couple of models that were literally forgettable. At this point, I think I have a fairly refined sense of what makes a tablet great, and my bar for a five-star model is set extremely high.What makes the Samsung Galaxy Tab Pro 8.4" my favorite--and first five-star--tablet?1) It's size. 8.4" is the perfect size for a tablet. Given the extremely high resolution of the Galaxy Tab Pro, the fact that it's a little smaller than the "standard" large tablet (10" or so) doesn't seem to make any difference in terms of reading or viewing. Where the 8.4" form factor really shines is portability. Whereas I used to hesitate when deciding whether to carry along my iPad or Galaxy Note 10.1, the Galaxy Tab Pro 8.4" goes everywhere with me. That kind of "no brainer" portability is worth a lot these days.2) The quality of the camera. I have been slow to embrace cell phone and tablet photography because the cameras that are built into these devices are generally crap, no matter what the hipsters and hype machine tells you. I have enough experience with SLRs and DSLRs to appreciate a good camera and a quality lens, and what passes for a camera in many portable devices is a far cry from what you get from a real camera and lens. Having said that, portability is still the critical factor when it comes to tablets, so having a surprisingly good camera in the Galaxy Tab Pro 8.4" makes me very happy and expands the range of things I want to do with my tablet.3) Android 4.4. In a word, Android 4.4 (Kit Kat) is superb. It's stable, smooth, and reliable. I have access to virtually every app worth having, and I know that my device is not going to become obsolete in a few months.4) Price. Yes, I know the Galaxy Tab Pro 8.4" costs more than competing models, but when you add up the list of features--along with some mighty nice extras like the $25 Play Store credit and the 2 years of 50Gb Dropbox service, the price seems downright competitive. Factor in the incredible build quality and the overall user experience and you have a home run. I couldn't be more pleased.

Update 2: It took Yamaha Customer Service 6 weeks to email me an RMA number so I could return the defective tuner to them. They never explained why producing a number takes a month and a half. I shipped the unit back to them about two weeks ago and haven't heard anything about it.  If nothing else Yamaha is proficient at chipping away at the two year warranty.*****************************************************Update:  It is now nearly a month since I contacted Yamaha customer service for help with my broken receiver.  Ken at Yamaha has made predictions about when Yamaha will issue an RMA but it never happens.*****************************************************Original Review:I've had my Yamaha receiver for about six months.  At the four month mark the audio failed completely.  Yamaha customer service provided the name of the nearest authorized repair center, 50 miles from where I live.  The repair center told me the unit needed a new main board.  After two trips to the repair center, 200 miles and four hours of driving, I set up my receiver again only to find that while the audio was again functional the HDMI connection was not.  Blu Ray video was snowy and produced persistent flashes while playing; running the HDMI connection directly from Blu Ray player to TV showed a perfect picture, so it was obvious the repair center bungled the job.  At the minimum they failed to fully test the unit before giving it back to me.  Rather than deal with the repair center all over again I contacted Yamaha customer service by email.  While they were fairly quick in replying they were not particularly candid about what they would or wouldn't do.  After repeated inquiries Yamaha finally wrote that they would send an RMA number so I could return the receiver to them--and only after receiving my return would they send me a replacement.While it worked the receiver was satisfactory.  The various digital sound options offer a variety of choices for mimicking different acoustic environments.  Setup isn't any worse than other AV receivers.  One of the main reasons I went with the RX-V573 is the two zone function.  Unlike other receivers that have a dedicated volume control for Zone B, the Yamaha controls the second zone through the main volume control; in order to adjust the Zone B speakers you must change their basic setting in the speaker setup menu.  (Zone B on these and other brands' units just takes two of the 7.1 surround channels, changing Zone A to 5.1 surround when Zone B is active.)  This works OK, but it's a corner they cut designing the receiver that doesn't speak well of the brand.My experience with this receiver confirms my general suspicion that AV receivers in this price range are plummeting in quality as the manufacturers use cheaper and cheaper component parts combined with questionable Asian quality control.  The receiver has a two year warranty, another big reason I chose it, and I'll have to see if the replacement unit--should I ever actually get one from Yamaha--will last more than four months.The bottom line is even though this is a likable receiver when it works I can hardly recommend it.  I'm sorry I bought it.

No, the SD10 is not perfect.  For one thing, it could use some optical zoom.  There is *always* a situation that arises when you do need to zoom in just a little bit.  Digital zoom never does it for me.  So Canon, please add optical zoom (even if a paltry 2x) and this will be a 10-out-of-five camera!That said, the SD10 is perfect for the snap-happy.  Count yours truly as one.  It's a take-anywhere-snap-anywhere-view-anywhere-hide-anywhere kind of camera.  The four megapixels are nice, and the picture quality is nothing short of astonishing, at this super compact size or at any size.  BTW, the number of pixels usually does not translate directly into picture quality, just as a CPU's megahertz rating doesn't correlate directly with a system's overall speed.  But Canon engineers are a bunch of smart monkeys, indeed, and every Canon digital camera out in the last three years has just been totally fabulous in the picture quality department.What makes a digital picture top-quality?  The colors have to be natural-looking and balanced, preferably both indoors and outdoors.  There shouldn't be any digitized artifacts (like glowing edges of your new kitchen knife or pixelated pimples on your kid's face).  The white should be white and the black black.  Above all, one look at the picture and you go, "wow, this is one nice shot!" (assuming it's meant to be one nice shot).  The SD10, happily, delivers in all these aspects.  One could wish for a longer flash range, but, alas, that's why serious photographers like me have to keep an old-style SLR film baby around with a hotshoe on it.  If you want serious flash, man, you have to use an external flash.  The SD10 does well what it was designed to do.I really don't want to talk to you about the tech specs.  They are meaningless in the real world anyway.  To sum it up, the SD10 is a camera you'll be happy with and you'll probably fall in love with -- a gadget freak like yourself likes all nice gadgets but we don't fall in love easily, but the SD10 deserves to be loved.  If you are anything more than a casual photographer, I recommend you *also* buy a "more serious" model like the Canon S410 or Minolta Xg which has more controls and does come with optical zoom, and use the SD10 as a candid shooter.  But, seriously, this is a great camera for all kinds of photographers -- and gadget freaks.

Simply amazing espresso. If you want world-class coffee every morning, consider this machine.  I use an organic bean dark roast that has the shimmer of oil on the surface.  When the bean looks to be coated in oil, it will produce a rich flavor that I feel makes the best espresso; not too sweet or bitter (lighter roast) and not too flat (darkest dry roast).  With poor quality beans even the most expensive machines will produce poor coffee.This being said, the Ena Micro 1 creates a noticeable even grind which allows the espresso to gain the most delicate hints of flavor from the bean.  Go ahead and inspect the ground beans and you'll see the same size pieces throughout.  All beans crack at subtly different temperatures/times when roasting; each bean will also vary in fragility during grinding.  A quality grinder will keep the piece size even throughout, whereas a cheap grinder will leave large chunks mixed in with fine grounds.  The Ena Micro slowly and quietly grinds the beans to produce a top-quality finished product.This brilliant machine allows for 2 aroma/strength levels to suit the palate and preference of the drinker.  Or you can add variety to your life by selecting the setting anew each day or cup.  Also select 3 serving sizes: single, double or triple shot.The operational process is simple and fast, and the machine even cleans itself.1) Press the on/off button.  Then watch as the Ena Micro 1 rinses clean it's chambers and heats up - which takes less than one minute.2) Press one of three icons to select your serving size and one of two icons for your aroma/strength.3) Watch as your beans are ground and tapped. The coffee is then brewed and your cup is filled. ***the macintosh g-4 i have is about 8 years old and is used to store, under itunes, and edit, under amadeus, a large collection of music files. i also edit and create video files using imovie hd.the original internal ide drives are 250 gb western digitals.having read reviews from other mac owners about their successfully adding a bootable drive via firewire, and being concerned that i would soon run out of room on the wds, i decided to install a capacious external drive. i wanted it to be bootable as well, in case my internal os drive were to fail.despite the success of others, i could not create a bootable external hard drive: i suspect that was because of my particular operating system-tiger 10.4.11.so as a last resort i decided to attempt to install two large capacity drives internally.as my internal drive buses are ide, the front with space for two drives running at a maximum of 66 mhz, the rear with space for two drives running at a maximum of 100 mhz, the first thing needed was a converter that would allow the samsung sata2 to function under ide.from amazon i purchased two sata to pata/ide hard drive interface adapters[...]these are mounted behind the drives and allow connecting them to the ide cables. i followed the advice of one reviewer who suggested placing a thin insulator between the back of the drive and the adapter just in case long-term usage might invite metal to metal contact-and therefore a shorting of the circuit. as insulation i used a heavy piece of paper adhered to the back of the drive with elmer's glue.my current configuration is one samsung, bootable os and data, at the rear carrier; one bootable samsung os and data backup at the front carrier; one bootable wd os and data backup at the front carrier. when storage requirements exceed the wd's capacity, i'll uninstall it.because of limited space behind the drive carriers and because of anomalies within the 10.4.11 system there were a number of additional issues as follows:i would have preferred mounting both samsungs in the rear carrier-faster bus and more room for the adapters.no go.for some reason the mac does not see both samsung drives if placed in the rear or, for that matter, front carriers. one must be mounted in a slot in the front carriers; the other in a slot in the rear carriers.so i ended up with a samsung at the rear carriers; a samsung and a wd at the front carriers.it's been a while since i installed the drives as i wanted to see if all continues to function well before making comment. so i don't recall if the wd at the front carrier is positioned in the forward or rear slot. but i do remember that limited space for the cables makes it imperative to install the wd and the samsung in a specific slot in order to still be able to close the mac's case.judging from the time needed to complete an automated backup, from rendering times for video, sound file conversions, and for other general usage, i would say there is no or little difference in access times of the original wds and the samsungs. further, transfer rates on the 66 mhz and the 100 mhz buses are much the same.some reviewers had noted that a firmware update issue had caused a problem: it is likely this is related to a pc installation, not the mac side.the samsung drives were installed with the factory jumper settings. i have each of the 2 tb drives set to one partition, mac os extended journaled. as i recall, there was some sort of initial problem regarding os recognition of the drives: i fiddled with the disk utility program to correct that.if you are not particularly knowledgeable about the mac, you may find this installation process daunting. but should you proceed, i hope the details i've provided will help you avoid most of the trial and error i encountered.for an investment of less than $200-the cost several months ago of the two drives and two adapters-and a fair stretch of patience i've hopefully reduced the possibility of imminent drive failure considerably, increased storage capacity from 500 gb to 3.6 tb and created three bootable disk drives.***

This knife/multi-tool (the Buck 735 X-Tract Essential) is the first Buck product I've bought in decades, and I'm very glad I did. After retiring a few years back, I somehow developed an interest in and then an enthusiasm for knives, which led me to scour knife forums on the internet to pick up tips on manufacturers, knife steels, etc. Time and again I've encountered seemingly knowledgeable people who disparage 420HC steel -- the kind Buck uses in this and many of its other knives. Still, some of the knife forum information has also mentioned that Buck might deserve an exception to their harsh judgment on 420HC steel, due to the presumably proprietary heat treating process used on Buck knives.Well, Buck specifies 420HC for this knife, so I had mixed feelings about ordering it. Still, it had exactly the three tools I wanted (the "Essentials," as they claim): a blade about the length I like, a standard/straight screwdriver, and a Phillips screwdriver tip in the size I seem to need most often. (Plus the scissors, but for me those are nonessential -- but harmless.) And, since the screwdrivers slide in and out instead of folding, they can't fold over and bite me like they've done with my old Swiss Army Tinker; that sounded pretty good, too. And I thought the blue would look cool (which it does).So I crossed my fingers and sprung for the knife. True, it wasn't much of a risk, since the price is quite reasonable, but I hate messing with returns (even though Amazon makes it simple and reasonable in my experience). I've had the tool a few weeks now, and am absolutely DELIGHTED with it. I've cut AT LEAST hardwood, softwood, plastic, rubber garden hose, anti-weed fabric for the garden, and a lot of various kinds of cardboard, and have seen no evidence of the particular disappointment I was primed for -- namely, quick loss of edge sharpness. It's holding up quite well for my purposes.As for purposes appropriate to this knife, they would not include really heavy work. The straight screwdriver tip is neither very wide nor very thick -- a clue that it's not designed for applying brute force to big screws; nor is the Phillips. Likewise, if you're looking to do some frequent and serious wood removal, this is not the knife for that; the blade may be slightly over 1/16" thick, but not more than a few hundredths of an inch if it is. But for routinely cutting cords, straps, tape, non-massive ropes, and cardboard, plus doing some occasional minor wood removal/shaving, this is a very nice (and attractive) tool.UPDATE -- JULY, 2011 -- Some months after writing the above, and after a bit of whittling on a sort of medium-hard wood, I discovered that I could no longer close the blade. It turned out that the part of the liner that locks the blade in place had worked its way all the way across the blade and slipped into the space between the far side of the blade and the knife frame. I returned the knife to Buck Knives and was allowed to exchange it for a different knife model. (Buck allowed credit at the then-current MSRP for the Essentials X-Tract, toward their internet price for the different model I requested.)I have no idea whether or not this is a problem area with the X-Tract model, or just a fluke with the one I got, so I don't know what conclusion ought to be drawn from my experience. (Rating reduced from 5 to 3, and title changed for this reason.)

Received my unit yesterday, a Saturday, when technical support is unavailable. Initial charging took several hours (using a video camera USB cable since Garmin does not provide one with the 1350). As others have noted, there is no instruction manual provided either, apparently a cost-saving strategy for Garmin, but very inconvenient for the user. Having used a Street Pilot for many years, and following the logic of spelling out the name of a city, I was immediately stymied.  Couldn't enter the second letter.  I also could not erase the letter entered.  "Back" was my only option, which sometimes required that I go back several screens.  I "played" with that issue for some time (much too much) before I discovered that you only enter the first letter of the city and hit "done" and a list appears.  Now how in the world is one to know that since there is no mention of that "feature" in the (very) tiny "Quick Start Manual"--which is virtually useless?  Strike virtually. And strike manual. I then returned to the "erase" problem.  Spent much too much time trying to figure out why nothing happened when I tapped the eraser in the upper right corner of the screen to correct a typo.  In addition, the back and forward arrows were not working properly. Checked the "Help" menu on the device and found the following entry regarding calibrating the screen: "1. Turn off your device. 2.Press and hold the power key for about 30 seconds until the calibration page appears. 3. Follow the on-screen instructions."  SORRY, that doesn't work.  The calibration page never appeared, despite (too) many attempts at bringing it up. Went to Garmin's support page on the WEB, and found the following calibration instructions:1. Make sure the Device is turned off2. Press and hold the top left corner of the touchscreen3. Power the unit on whilst keeping hold of the top left corner4. Continue holding the top left of the screen, after 30 seconds, a small  dot will appear5. Release the touchscreen and accurately touch the dots in turn as and when they appear6. Once complete a message will appear, `Calibration Complete', Touch OKThat worked. You might think that Garmin would have caught the misinformation on the device.  Or better yet, how about a basic but useful instruction manual? Before discovering how to calibrate the screen, and out of utter frustration, I was very close to calling Amazon and sending the unit back, assuming that it was defective. What is defective is Garmin's failure to provide easily accessible and accurate help information. Since I am in the complaint mode, it is also worth mentioning that getting back to the main screen (depending on where you are) can involve many taps on the screen.  An inconvenience that should be able to be corrected easily.Leaving the above aside , I am pleased with the size and weight of the 1350. I know from years of experience with my Street Pilot that the inaccuracies of the software are many, and unavoidable: suggested turns onto streets that don't exist, streets that end in fields (Arizona), streets that aren't where the unit says they are (Sioux City), and being sent the long way around because the distance (undoubtedly as the crow flies) is shorter even though the drive time is substantially shorter if one gets on a major highway(Connecticut). Miss an exit from a highway, and instead of being instructed to turn around and go back a mile or so, one (me) can be told to go miles down a parallel road--which happened to be partially unpaved in my case (Idaho)! Conclusion: don't expect miracles in terms of the directions.  Sooner or later you are going to misinformed, but that appears to go with the territory.  Don't bother calling Garmin to complain about incorrect directions.  Not only will you not get more consolation than what I have provided, you may well wait 30 or more minutes to speak to someone.In summary, I have spent too much time trying to figure out the intricacies of the 1350.  I am reserving final judgment, however, until after using the unit in my car. More to follow.Chapter 2.  First "road test."  I would give it a C- in terms of directions; an A in terms of start-up time, graphics (including lane assist), and sound. I just went to my local Trader Joe's, taking a So Cal freeway.  From the get-go, the unit wanted to take me to surface street that runs parallel to the second freeway that I normally take.  I ignored the spoken directions and proceeded to exit to that freeway, knowing that it is significantly faster and easier.  It took several hundred yards before the recalculation.  Upon leaving the freeway, the unit instructed me to turn right at the light at the end of the exit, even though the shopping center where the TJ's is located is straight ahead and across the street from the light.  I like to think that had I turned right, I would have eventually made it to the store, but I have no idea how.  After a subsequent stop at a local hardware store and heading for home, the unit wanted to take me to a main north-south street about a half-mile away even though there was a parallel one right in front of me.  I turned on the closest one, and it was several hundred yards before the recalculation.  From that point on, the directions were accurate.  In fairness, the map clearly and accurately showed both streets to which I refer in the latter example, and it was obvious that I would quickly end up on that main north-south street that takes me home.  Nevertheless. . .  It may hard to visualize what I have described, but the point should be clear: GPS technology, while impressive, is far from perfect.  I would still give the 1350 4 stars, and it is a significant improvement over my antique Street Pilot.  I should add that while putting in my favorites, I found that I could spell out the name of the streets.  Apparently my inability to do so before was related to screen calibration.LAST CHAPTER:  It is going back to Amazon today.  Over the weekend, it turned off on its own about 10 times, half while on battery and half while on car power. Called Garmin this morning and they reinstalled the software. I was just entering an address to return to the area where the NUVI had turned off, and it turned off twice in the process.  I used it last night, without it turning it off, but the accuracy of the directions, on a scale of 1-10, was a 1 (one).  It was taking me off the freeway 2 1/2 miles before the correct exit.  I ignored the instructions, and at the end of the freeway exit (which was the street where my destination was--probably the biggest N-S street in Glendale, CA) the NUVI told me to keep going straight instead of turning left and proceeding about 1 1/2 miles to my destination.  That was the most egregious of at least a dozen other examples, and those in 4 days of use. I've asked for a replacement, which Amazon is sending immediately, but as of now I am skeptical and very disappointed. Now a generous 2 star rating.

meeelectronics makes a bunch of nice phones, nearly all in-ear phones. they are know for a very good value to sound ratio. i own other sets of meeelectronics phones (m6 for work-outs, and m9). i've owned these for years with no issues and both sound way better than their price would indicate. i also own expensive over the ear cans by sennheiser, and iem's as well. due to my good experiences with meelectronics in-ear phones, i decided to try their on-ear phones, the ht-21, as an inexpensive on-ear travel/work out phone. although i've had very good luck with my other meelectronic phones, these are made of plastic and need to be handled accordingly when packing them away in a back pack.these headphones are very lightweight, made for travel or workouts (haven't tried it for the latter yet). the sound is very good especially when one considers the price. however, headphones, especially at this price range, will have noticeable compromises for their price point as well as weight and mobility.the sound sig of these phones is somewhat tipped up. if you like beats by dre, you will hate these. but then, i am not a fan of beats by dre. if you like the rather forward, detailed balance of (many) iem's, you will like these. compared directly to a more bass-centric phone, the hesh-2 by skullcandy, they appear polar opposites. the over the ear hesh envelopes you in bass. it's so pleasant at times, especially on appropriate music, you hardly notice how much the mids and upper end is rolled off. the ht-21 does a much better job of detail (transients), and voice. here the bass is somewhat rolled off, especially in comparison, but it is a faster, less muddled bass than the hesh. i've found by applying more pressure on the ear cups, effectively sealing them to my ears, i can increase the bass significantly. this phenomenon is like nearly every phone that doesn't seal off your ear. the phones do get uncomfortable when wearing for long periods. that and the degree of visceral bass response may depend upon your head size/shape to some extent.so if you want to swim in the bass beat, the hesh is a good, inexpensive choice. it is, however, bigger and costs more than the ht-21, which offers more in the way of detail, applies to a wider range of music, is more portable, and can likely be used to work out. it does fall short of more expensive phones, so buy accordingly.

This is a good device. It's cheap enough, but it's very simple to use.I swapped an internal 3.5" SATA drive for a new SSD. Before boot, I plugged the older internal drive into this and hooked it up. On boot, that drive was exactly like it had been.This thing comes with an eSATA cable, so make sure you know that before you buy one like I did.SPEED:I thought that this eSATA dock would be slower than my internal drives so I ran some very simple test with DiskBench. None of my drives are the same, so don't get caught up in the non-scientific-ness-osity of this. I copied a 130MB file from one location to another location on the same drive several times because for most of these, the 2nd+ time the file was cached and it was quicker.1TB Hitachi eSATA - avg of about 498 MB/s, (126MB/s non-cached)500GB Wester Digital SATA - avg of about 494 MB/s (458 MB/s non-cached)80GB Intel SSD SATA - avg of about 398 MB/s (484 MB/s non-cached) (this is the C drive/swap file/OS which is why the results varied between 294MB/s and 500MB/s)128GB Samsung 840 Evo SSD SATA - avg of about 518 MB/s (499 MB/s non-cached)1TB Seagate USB - avg of about 21MB/s (8.5 MB/s non-cached)So you can see that once the file I copied was cached, the copies are all as fast as the cache can make them. Before the caching the eSATA drive was about 3.8 times slower than a similar internal drive using SATA and about 4.5 times faster than the USB drive.So, this is a great choice for an external drive, especially if you already have an eSATA port. With this being hot-swappable, you can easily and quickly take the drive with you, or lock it into a fire safe, or whatever you want.

For the relatively little money paid - this is an OK receiver. My previous Sony of the similar basic level has been playing nicely the last 7 years, until it died, so I thought I'll follow-up with the brand. Well, there has been one disappointment, but big enough (for me, personally) to return it and try something different. Issue may be subjective, nevertheless... the issue is a quite flat sound, in particular the bass. The non-audiophile (i.e. reasonably priced) receivers used to have a "contour", or "bass boost" function (even the previous Sony model had it), which greatly enhanced the audibility of lower frequencies when played at low decibels. This one lacks it (and it sounds like most of nowadays sold receivers are like this), hence the sound coming out is quite flat (also for treble band), unless you go really loud. In addition, the receiver lacks a sub-woofer output, so there is no chance to improve low frequencies.Out of the other available receivers, I decided to pick (by recommendation) a little more up-scale (yet still reasonably priced) Harman Kardon HK 3390 (2 x 80W) Stereo Receiver, which has sub-woofer outputs - even though it also lacks bass boost, I am expecting it will revive the bass, even with my old Sony 10" sub.

It's just the two of us in my household so most recipes make more than enough for us two which lasts a week or two.  In freezer-tight containers, the cream stays fresh too! You can use 2%milk (I use lactose-free 2% milk) and it tastes just as good as whole milk (I've tried both).  That is what is the best about making your own:  you can add your own specific ingredients and there are no preservatives!  You know exactly what you're eating!  If ice cream wasn't so high-calorie, we'd probably be eating it all week long!  I'd highly recommend this maker!

This cable failed to connect my hard drive to my MacBook, with the computer thinking the drive was unreadable. However, the same drive consistently works fine (and at full speed) with my other cable.Either these cables are inherently marginal and will work in some situations and not others, or they have quality control issues where some of the cables are made poorly. Given the consistency of modern manufacturing techniques, and the fact that cables are quite simple devices, I'm guessing the problems with these cables (see all the reviews of people who couldn't connect devices with these) are endemic to the design. Perhaps their attempt at bold "design" was at odds with their engineering requirements, and the design folks won. There may be a reason you don't see more flat cables for high speed connections.It's possible the flat design didn't allow for sufficient shielding, or didn't allow them to use twisted pairs, resulting in the cables being prone to interference. Whatever the reason, there's a good chance these cables are simply a bad design. Even in the best case, LaCie has a good design but with severe quality control issues. Either way, I'd stay away from these.You might think that four stars is a good rating, but note that the four star average rating comes from about 80% of people giving it five stars, and 20% of people giving it one because it didn't work for them. Now, if a product fails 20% of the time, that's considered a disaster by most companies. If I told you that if you ordered this, there's a 1 in 5 chance it will be junk and you'll have to return it, would you order it? My point is that a four star review means something different when it's everybody giving it four stars versus some people giving it five and some giving it zero. Keep that in mind when deciding whether or not to order this given the "good reviews".I'm not intending to argue with the people giving this five stars; they certainly should give it five stars if it worked for them. Everybody needs to just rate this based on their subjective experience. My point is simply that 20% of people finding this product doesn't work at all is actually quite high if you think about it. I wish I'd thought of it that way before I decided to order this based on the "four star" review.

I got this mouse as a GoldBox deal and for the price I paid it is ok. Here is my assessment:- The MS Wireless Mouse 2000 is a good basic mouse. Having used aLogitech MX600 Laser Cordless USB-PS/2 Mouseprior to the MS 2000, switching took some getting used to because I liked the way the Logitech's ergonomic shape fit my hand whereas the MS 2000 is just a regular mouse.- While the product image shows a cool blue light emanating from the bottom of the mouse, in reality this is not the case. So if you - like me - are expecting a "cool factor" here, you would be mistaken. There is a blue tracking light coming from the bottom but it is not visible when the mouse is in operation.- Tracking is ok and while not the miracle Microsoft claims it to be, it does track well on all kinds of surfaces. Scrolling is a bit choppy and not too smooth but not a major issue for me.- The mouse allows for left and right button clicking, horizontal and vertical scrolling via the tilt wheel. No other special functions are available as there are no additional buttons. This is not a problem for me because I never use the extra buttons available on more expensive mice. As a matter of fact I usually disable them via software settings. But users who like and use these buttons should look for a different mouse.- What I do like about the MS mice is that they usually provide for a slot on the bottom of the mice to store the USB receiver. I have a smallMicrosoft Wireless Mobile Mouse 3000which also has such a slot and the added benefit of turning off the mouse when the USB receiver is in place. The MS 2000 has this slot too, but must be turned off separately via a switch also located on the bottom. However, it is still a great idea because it keeps the devices together when not in use. I have on occasion spent considerable time trying to find the USB receiver that goes with a particular mouse and this helps tremendously if you tend to be a bit of a scatter brain like me.I'd recommend this mouse to anyone looking for a basic mouse but if your emphasis is on enhanced ergonomics and/or functions, this is not the mouse to get.

This vacuum replaces a Hoover that I thought was okay. Comparing it to this one though, this vacuum gets a lot more up, and I really like bagless vacuums rather than replacing (or worse, trying to empty) vacuum bags all the time. The color's great (I like green), the vacuum has no trouble getting dog hair out of carpet (they haven't been this clean in a while!), it's not too loud (dog's okay with it), the dirt cup is easy to dump, and I've had no trouble with it. Haven't used many other vacuums, so there may be better choices out there, possibly for less money, but I'm totally satisfied with this Panasonic.EDIT (Nov 2012): After less than a year of occasional use, the vacuum developed a critical failure. The bearings in the rotating brush failed on me, causing the belt inside to heat up and snap. Basically, the brush would still spin, but with a great deal of friction, which causes the belt to heat up, weakening it. When it snaps, no more agitator brush. Panasonic did direct me to a local repair shop, and it's being covered under warranty, but it seems I'm not the only person on here who has had this happen. Since the warranty is only one year (other vacuums have warranties of four years or more!), I'm not sure I can wholeheartedly support purchasing this vacuum. Oh, and getting replacement belts is a pain! Panasonic decided to create a brand new belt for this new vacuum, and it was not available locally (I tried over six places that sold vacuum belts; none were even close to compatible). My local specialty vacuum repair shop couldn't even get one ordered. I do like the vacuum otherwise... it was great while it lasted.

This review is for the HB-400. I ordered this scale because of someone recommending the brand on a fitness forum. When I saw it had a cumulative 4-star review and the first few ratings looked really good (consistency and accuracy of weight were both noted), the prices was right too - so I went ahead and ordered. (Please note that I realized later that the first couple GOOD reviews listed are for the HB-500 not the HB-400 - for some reason, both of these products have the reveiws lumped together. This is confusing and deceptive for people who are trying to research before they purchase).I really like how the scale looks. It's very modern and clean looking. Standing on it I felt very stable. I also like that it has an on off button to conserve the battery power. The button is on the front similar to the wii fit balance board. Setup was quite easy - no problem there.The problems came when I actually went to weight myself. First weigh in - we'll say I was *cough* 115.6 - yes that sounds about right. So I step off and turn it off. I turn it back on and weigh in immediately again - 115.8. Hmm... that's a little odd. So I step off and turn it off - turn it on and try again - 116.2. Wow - what's going on here - I hate this scale very much all of a sudden. I give it another try... 115.0. Well - that's better... let's try this again... 116.6... ummmmmm...That's about how my weigh in went. I tried several different times throughout the day - weighing in about 5 or 6 times repeatedly and would come up with a different weight (usually within a pound or 2) each time I'd step on the scale. This is probably a pretty good ROUGH scale - if you're not trying to lose weight or keep track of your weight this scale is probably fine for you - but if you are - this won't work at all. 1 or 2 pounds of fluctuation is not acceptable for a scale used to track weight loss considering 1 or 2 pounds is what one would typically be trying to lose in a week. It'd be really hard to tell if you were successful or not.I can't speak for the body fat function, I was more concerned about it not being consistent with the weigh in - but from the other reviews, that's not too accurate either. I figure if the weight isn't consistent and the body fat estimate isn't accurate, there was no point to me keeping this scale whatsoever. I mean - I may as well stand in front of a carnie at the fair and have him guess my weight and body fat percentage and use that for my record. It'd be about as random as this scale.Sending this back and ordering a Tanita with much better reviews. Hope it works! I can live without the body fat function working but I can't live with that big of a fluctuation in weight readings. 2 stars because I think this scale would be ok for those not trying to lose weight but may just want a general idea of what their weight is, and it is an attractive design. But no higher because it's not recommended for those trying to lose weight and need to weigh in regularly.

This GPS works as well as any other Nuvi product for auto navigation.  As a matter of fact, it works great for auto navigation in my experience.  However, this unit is billed as a crossover GPS that is also suitable for marine, geocaching, hiking, and other outdoor use, and it falls well short in all these categories.Pros:- Works great for auto navigation.Cons:- The compass does not work (completely stops responding to any changes in direction) for hiking navigation under or near any cover (small trees, buildings, etc).- The trackback feature doesn't work for anything in my estimation.  It tells you to follow the track log on the screen (which you could do without an extra feature), but gives you no indication when you stray off the track.- The accuracy of your moving direction on the map screen is HIGHLY suspect.  I've changed direction by 90 degrees, and the GPS doesn't recognize the change in direction until I've walked 100-500 ft.  It keeps happily tracking along in a straight line until it catches up, and then re-draws the last 100-500 ft.  You would spend a lot of time lost if you were depending on this thing for outdoor navigation.- This unit is NOT WAAS-enabled despite documentation on Garmin's website and retailer product descriptions.- The accuracy for outdoor use is highly suspect.  Sometimes it brings you right to your waypoint, sometimes it brings you 100 ft away.- The speed does not work (completely stops responding) for hiking navigation under or near any cover (small trees, buildings, etc).- No screen lock or lanyard attachment points.  I knew about this before purchasing, but they are significant shortcomings for a crossover GPS.This unit works great for auto navigation, but you can get a much cheaper unit for auto navigation.  I would assume that many people are interested in this unit for outdoor use in addition to auto navigation, and it doesn't perform well in the outdoors.  Garmin packed it with outdoor features, but they either don't work or were falsely advertised from the beginning (WAAS).

When it has came down to MP3 Players, they really have came a long way since a decade ago with Apple's Ipod leading the way. But there aren't many companies that have made the best in strides. Creative Labs has been a mixed breed that hasn't really held its own and improved in the way we listen to music today. Most of their MP3 players in the past haven't really held up to standards. They have either slowed the computers' speed doen, or just really delivered in the way they should when music is played. But what they have shown to deliver, is half of a MP3 Player.Crative Labs Zen Style M300 MP3 Player is a mixed bag that doesn't really shine in the way that it really could. The design is a bit more like the latest Apple Ipod Nano, yet it can hold 4 GB of music playback. The design looks elequent, but the control of the music playback is a bit awkward. You are absolutely honestly better off getting another MP3 Player from either Apple with the Ipod. If you are looking for a MP3 player that has expandable memory, I would absolutely recommend Sandisk's Sansa line of music players instead. You honestly get your money's worth there than you do with what Creative Labs had brought to the table.Price: CMusic Playback: CMicro SD Playback: DOverall: C-

I did not buy this through amazon.  I bought the OXO garlic press from bed bath & beyond.So, I'm a man who cooks.  I'm kind of tough on the things I own, so I try and buy things that are durable and that I can count on.  I don't purposefully or carelessly damage things.The first garlic press I owned my wife picked up for me - was maybe 5$ from a discount store (Ross stores).  That failed due to terribly cheap construction within a few weeks.So, I figured I wanted something that would last.  I picked up the OXO brand garlic press.  I have several other products made by them, and they're generally pretty good.  This is the first OXO product that I've had a problem with.  The press itself seems pretty sturdy.  It is made of metal, and had comfy handles.  Something that is also very nice is the built-in cleaning mechanism that pushes any stuck garlic out of the holes.  Very nice feature.  Overall, the press is really pretty well designed and functional.I probably use a half a head of garlic a week.  So, to say the least the press gets a lot of use.  We love garlic.Unfortunately, this product turns out to be made of cast iron (I didn't know that until it broke).  Cast iron is strong, but brittle, and is subject to failure from metal fatigue.  After approximately 6 months of use, the "hinge" on the top failed.  This causes the press to effectively split in half (the handles are no longer held together by the hinge).  So, I'm not sure what else to say here.  It's a nice product when it works, but the metal used is cheap.  If you don't use it much at all, you'll probably be OK.  If you use it often, I would expect failure as well.  There is no getting around metal fatigue if the product is made of cast iron - use it enough, and it'll eventually break.Beware!

Kingston has quickly become my least favorite brand of flash memory.  Back when digital cameras were new, Kingston was a name I could trust for compatibility and customer service.  I have used nothing else in my digital SLR, point 'n shoot, and digital video camera.  Early in 2008 I purchased five Kingston sdhc cards.  I ran an exhaustive memory test which of course passed.  They worked fine in my Pentax K20 digital camera.  Later in 2008 I purchased another five Kingston sdhc cards of the identical type.  My memory test ran fine.  But, when I used them in my camera I was only able to shoot about 5 to 10 photos before the camera reported memory read and write errors on all 5 cards.  Switching back to the older batch of memory worked fine.I emailed Kingston for advice.  They chose not to respond.  So, I opened an RMA to return the five bad cards.  I received a prompt automated email response and I sent the last 5 sdhc cards back.  They sent me another five sdhc cards from the SAME LOT.  Surprise, they did not work either.  This time, I faxed them a letter to advise them of a bad lot of memory, gave them the lot number, and asked if they could help me with my problem.  Again, Kingston failed to respond.I would rather throw these bad memory cards into the trash and loose money rather than let Kingston sell them to another unsuspecting consumer.  Something happened at Kingston between Spring of 2008 and Fall of 2008.  My guess is they switched their manufacturing process for the worse.  Their customer service used to respond to emails but no longer.  A lifetime warranty does no good if they only swap your bad memory with more bad memory.

I frequently use my laptop out and about, but prefer to have a portable mouse for getting any serious work done. The trackpad just does not cut it for very long. I've been using a Logitech portable mouse, but wanted to compare its performance to the new BlueTrack technology. My overall impression of the mouse is that it is not as well thought out as Logitech's offerings. The mouse is a bit light in the hand and feels a bit cheap. The scroll wheel is a joke -- I much prefer having a metallic wheel with some heft to it. Additionally, the USB adapter (which, on the plus side, is very small) is difficult to remove from the body of the mouse. Another comparison to Logitech's offerings is that Logitech's mouse thoughtfully turns off the battery when you insert the adapter into the body of the mouse. Microsoft's requires you to insert the adapter and turn the unit off manually. It's a small point, but for me the grace of the design matters.The one thing that this mouse has going for it is the ability to track on some surfaces that other optical & laser mice cannot venture onto. But, quite frankly, I've never had a problem tracking with my current mouse. I don't use my laptop on glass tables and I'm perfectly happy grabbing a notepad from my backpack if there are any problems. Indeed, I typically use some kind of surface anyway to avoid gunking up the mouse.In summary, if the mouse were very cheap, I might be able to recommend it as an average mouse. But you're better off finding better alternatives in this price range. As with any device that you plan on using in your daily workflow, it's best to go to a brick-and-mortar store to try these out before buying online.

This is not a "converter" from RGB to YPbPr.  If your source device (video card, DVD player, etc) supports sending either RGB or YPbPr out the D-Sub (aka VGA port) then this cable will work once the source is set correctly.  If your source doesn't support that setting, or you aren't sure what any of this means, 99% chance this will not work for you.  Keep in mind that not a lot of devices that support sending both RGB and YPbPr out the D-Sub port.Verify your devices support YPbPr first.  Hopefully this will help someone avoid wasting money on something that won't work for them.

If you want to clean a camera sensor this is the best thing I've found but it is still not very good.  The swabs come sealed in plastic and as other reviewers have mentioned the consist of a little piece of a pec-pad on a flimsy plastic stick.Add a few drops of the Eclipse Solution to the swap and wipe the sensor.  It is as simple as that and there is little if any danger of damaging your sensor.  While these things do help clean the sensor, the pads themselves tend to shred a little bit if they touch the edge of the camera around the sensor.  While you may get the dirt off of the sensor, pieces of lint will often end up in the box where the sensor is if you try to get all the way to the edge of the sensor.  After a while the lint particles will move around in the camera box and end up in your photos.Since camera shops that clean camera sensors are few and far between you pretty much have to have these with you when traveling unless you never change lenses in an environment where there is any kind of dust.  If you do happen to be in a small town like Moab where the only camera shop in town tries to stick you for $100+ just to clean the sensor you can use these to clean it yourself.I'm sure with a little bit of practice it is possible to minimize the amount of lint that ends up in your camera.  While these things are ridiculously priced they are the best thing I've found on the market to get at least some (and sometimes all) of the dirt off of a sensor.  You could probably buy one box of these and after using each one put another piece of a pec-pad on the plastic stick instead of spending $3.00 - $4.00 on each one of these things.

Bought by G-Box Midnight MX2 Android TV device for one purpose, to view placeshifted TV content off of my Dishnetwork receivers at my home in Florida.  This was to avoid having to pay for cable (in Florida) and Dish (in Arizona) at two houses when I can only be at one home at a time.Here is my setup.  I have a VIP722k Dishnetwork HD receiver which I hooked up a Sling Adapter ($50.00 from Dishnetwork) and a my other receiver is a VIP612 in which I run a Slingbox 350 (can't use a Sling Adapter on this device).To test the viability of placeshifting using Sling on the G-Box, I installed Dish Anywhere Android App from Google Play.  I also installed Sling Player for Tablet also from Google Play (this costs $14.99 and Dish Anywhere is free).Both Apps work fine on this device.  Only issue is you need to have HIGH upload bandwidth (I have 19 mbs).  I will provide a review on the Sling devices at a later time.  There is a delay in using the user interface and when I response takes place on the screen but it is acceptable as this is a reality of network latency.Okay, so the G-Box does what I wanted it to do.  What else can I do with it?So, I buy a UKB-500-RF mini keyboard with airmouse.  Works nicely but Android is better suited for a touch pad.  I am not satisfied with this (and tried another wireless keyboard from Favi) but it is all I can find right now.  I also installed DroidMote which allows you to use your Android phone as a remote to the G-Box.  It works a bit better but still not the perfect solution.  Bear this in mind when getting the G-Box.  The remote that comes with it is not sufficient to control the applications efficiently.Okay, let's talk XBMC.  This is the open source capability installed on the G-Box that allows you to configure various applications that can stream content from the web.  It's kind of an open source Roku.  Very flexible but there are issues.  First, the navigation is different than the Android.  Bothers me as I like a more unified approach.  Also, content is vast but I still haven't found any content that really interests me.  The Amazon Video Streaming app doesn't work so bear that in mind.  As a matter of fact, you can't play Amazaon Streaming content at all on an Android device.  As I explore XBMC more, I will comment on this.The G-Box has great sound and video quality and it's dual core processor gives it plenty of capability of streaming HD 1080p content.  No issues or lag of any sort.The User Community on the Matricom forum is robust and very helpful.  If you have an issue, you can find your answer pretty quick.This device is not 100% idiot proof but it has great potential.  I like it and recommend it to any device geek.  Don't buy it if you want an out of the box solution and are not fairly technical.  I found this device to be easy to configure and use, but I have been working in technology for decades.You can run virtually any Android application that works on your phone.  For me, the G-Box does what I want it to do.  It will save me a lot of money for my particular application.  I am also finding all kinds of things it can do as well.  It works very well for streaming videos off of your media server, it can also act as a media server using Upnp.Some apps are not as robust at the G-Box can handle (the Android Netflix app from Google Play does not support HD).  You can find alternatives but I do think that the market will start to get out more powerful apps to match the more powerful hardware like the G-Box.Thank you.

Background:The Spyderco Tenacious and the SOG Flash II are popular choices and because I have both in half serrated, and they are in the same price range, I compare them both here. The flash II is more popular in stores and I think Wal-Mart even sell them.I have had and still have several Flash II's and one Spyderco Tenacious. I have carried both as EDC for extended periods in tough use, so thought I would add my experience with them. I currently carry the flash II and a SAK, but carried the Tenacious and SAK for about a year and still have it and prefer it in the woods. I have carried Benchmade's, but they are a little expensive and I fear loosing one. I fly the airlines a lot on spur of the moment notice and have given several knives including at least two Flash's to TSA having no time to go back and store/ship it or something. I gave one to some Mexicans doing drywall work in the terminal in front of TSA screening rather then give it to TSA. I try to keep a knife in my desk, boat, backpack, and a couple of cars. So more expensive knives haven't been indicated for me.I carry a folder clipped inside the pocket (clip outside), with the point down, weak hand side.Spyderco Tenacious:Pros:Solid construction. Feels better then the Flash in use (in the hand). It has Stainless Steel liners under the G10 scales. It is more conventional and probably stronger then the Flash.Good blade steel. Better then the Flash II IMO. The 8Cr13MoV sounds better when sharpening too. Ha. But, that may be due to the heaver construction of the whole knife, less dampening due to the aluminum sides under the G10, and the thinner blade near the edge (flat ground). So even though the edge is thinner, and I have put a finer angle edge on it, the Tenacious holds an edge better.Blade shape - really nice for a wide variety of tasks with a wide leaf shape. Leaves plenty of room to get your thumb against the spider hole to open the knife.Good lock up. I don't like liner locks much, but it locks solidly and secure.Size of the Blade. I like this size knife for EDC.Easy enough to open with either hand.The belt clip is more durable and versatile then the Flash. The Flash clip breaks at one of the multiple 90 bends. The Tenacious clip is lower profile, stronger, grips better in a pocket, and can be mounted up, down, left and right.Cons:Difficulty closing with one hand: I am not a big fan of liner locks, but I like them much better then spring detent locks like old school pocket knives. I pretty much cut a thumb pad off once with a Tenacious so maybe some of it is psychological. You can get your thumb caught and sliced in the blade trying to close it with one hand. Just pushing the liner lock in will will drop the blade against your thumb if you hold it in the wrong position. Not a problem with two hands using the other one to control the blade closing, but with a bolt lock on the side you can close it with one hand and never need to get your finger/thumb under where the blade goes. This doesn't happen with a assisted opening knife as the blade is always trying to open until almost closed.Heavy (this is not a big thing for me, but it is noticeably heaver then a flash due to partial aluminum sides under the G10).Made in China. But, quality and steel is very good in the case of this knife, so Made in China" is more about ethics and politics then quality in this case.SOG Flash IIPros:Assisted opening. Get it past 5 or 10 with light pressure on the thumb and it snaps open. Great one handed operation, even if injured. A little more wow, or cool, factor then the Tenacious.Light weight. Feels quite a bit lighter then the Spyderco. Perhaps even less then substantial (personal preference). The flash is all plastic actually glass-reinforced nylon (GRN). It has some kind of metal bushing between the blade and (GRN) sides.Size of the Blade. I like this size knife for EDC.Lock up is solid, as far as staying open/not closing. There is a little slop though when open in both directions. I have never tried to tighten it up. I have never worried about it closing on me in use.Safety. You can lock it so it wont open in your pocket.Easy to sharpen.Made in USACon's:Slop when open. Not bad, but not as tight as the Tenacious.Safety - I have had it come open in my pocket a couple of times in active situations. It wasn't locked when this happened. Pretty scary. I knew it was open, or partially open; in one case when I reached in my pocket and cut a fingers, and two other times when I felt the point sticking into the front of my hip. In the later two I stopped moving and then moved real slowly until I got it folded back up and under control. Front pocket, bad place for an open knife. For some reason a Benchmade Barrage assisted open has never come open in my pocket (even unlocked). Of course the Benchmade is a great knife, but at more then twice the cost. I think the flash lacks a tendency to stay closed. Better spring assisted knives seem to have more force toward closed until you pass the point where it springs toward open. It's not like the safety is a plus, so much as it is just plain needed, because of the tenancy to come open if the thumb nut is bumped in the pocket. However, the safety will come off, or turn on, in pocket. This further aggravates the above problem.Steel is softer then Tenacious and doesn't hold an edge nearly as well. Easy to ding and dull the edge. A friend of mine who knew I'd begun eating cheese again after being vegan for quite some time, (as a chef, cheese was always very important in my dishes prior and after and there is nothing I love more than a snack of gourmet cheese) bought this for me with some lovely cheeses.  I kept the cheeses but had to exchange the dome.Why?  While this is great for American marketing where one is not aware unless they talk to a cheesemonger than cheese should not be served cold, it actually inhibits the taste of the cheese for a few reasons.First, the marble does keep the cheese cold. Cheese is not even aged cold; it's aged at room temp and bringing it to room temp again will have a huge difference in flavor because the fat molecules, the primary component of cheese, are not constricted, opening up more flavor.  In fact some types of cheese in uncut wheels can be left at room temp for YEARS.  I know, the American myth...That said, there are many types of cheese and so there can be no set rule for every type. But some rules are fairly vast such as:Non-porous materials such as marble and plastic wrap suffocate cheese, bringing out an ammonia flavor (particularly in soft cheeses). They also cause cheese to mold more quickly because they trap moisture.  You will often see some gourmet cheese wrapped in a deli paper; this is the proper way and it allows the cheese to breathe.  You can also keep it in a dome with a wooden base--as that is more porous.I enjoy a snack of a few fine cheeses in the evening while I cook dinner. For this, I put my cheeses in the dome in the morning before work.  They are extraordinary when I get home.  I just bought a glass dome lid to go over a wooden block I had and that's ideal.Avoid plastic wrapped pre-cut cheeses and ask your cheesemonger wherever you buy to actually cut from the wheel and you'll also notice a big difference in flavor.  You can store in your dome in your fridge and just take out and allow to reach room temp before serving.  It's fine to be wrapped in plastic just for your trip home from the store though; and common.If you want perfect cheese with no dome, unwrap from the plastic wrap meant for travel from the deli or cheese shop and get cheese formaticum paper. It's made for ultimate freshness  If you buy a few kinds of cheese at a time, wrap in this, then just set out  awhile before you plan on serving or eating.  You won't believe the difference in taste and butteriness--like the dome.Why I personally prefer to store in a dome? Cheese kept at perfect humidity and climate is better--and this automatically creates that exact climate, which is why cheese domes are around.  Just choose one with a wooden base for proper climate.Drastic temps are not good for cheese flavor--best not to go in and out of the fridge a bunch.  You actually can leave it out and eat the next day. It's done in France everyday, afterall.And finally, if you have a type of cheese that sweats, just wipe it off with a cloth.

If I had been permitted to give ratings with fractional stars I'd probably rate this as a 2.5 star product.  I've owned one of these for 4 years but have felt the need to buy other products to provide most of my air purification needs; I now only use it in a back room on the low setting where high noise is less bothersome.  This is more an air vacuum than an air purifier in that it is very loud, even on the lowest setting.  If you are at all sensitive to noise you will not be able to sleep with one of these in the same room and even during the daytime the noise is very distracting.  I measured (using a kill-a-watt meter) the energy usage as ~70 W, 105 W, and 162 W on low, medium, and high settings, respectively, making this a real energy hog. I purchased a 50250-N, which claimed a lifetime HEPA filter, but the company has since relabeled the product as a 50250-S and now markets the HEPA filter as long life--although the actual filter seems to be unchanged.  Even if one chooses to never upgrade the HEPA filter, the carbon pre-filters are supposed to be changed every 3 months and cost about $15 each, although one can get third-party versions for less, so filter costs are still significant.  The HEPA filter is of decent quality but independent tests suggest the filter only catches 80-85% of particles in the first past due to air leaking around the filter; a good filter should score well above 95% and lots of products do.  This seems to be a strategic decision on the part of Honeywell because if a filter gets clogged (perhaps because someone took a lifetime claim literally or didn't do any cleaning) the motor would burn out if the filter had a tighter seal and the company would get lots of warranty claims. The carbon pre-filters are OK for light control of odors and VOCs but will not suffice for heavy-duty air purification.  On the plus side, the unit is easy to move around because it has an excellent handle and the cord length is reasonable.  If you are very price sensitive, get cheap electricity, don't need heavy-duty odor control, and are not concerned about noise, you might find this will meet your needs as it does move a decent amount of air. However, one can get a much better product with more features (air quality sensors, filter quality sensors, automation, etc.) that will not damage your hearing and that is only slightly more expensive. I think most people would be better served by purchasing another product.

I have lots of experience with Panasonic IP cameras, as I own several models.  Generally, they are GREAT, and this camera has some very nice features and overall is a good design.  I do agree with other reviewers about the low-light performance not being up to par with other cameras in the Panasonic line, but that is a minor problem for average use.  The price on this camera is also very good.  The setup woes encountered by some reviewers are not surprising.  It's not a simple task to enable port forwarding on a router and get everything squared away, but this camera is no worse than any other Panasonic cameras in that respect; you just have to know what you're doing (no offense; it is a learning process).All that said, this camera has a very serious design flaw.  There's a large "Privacy" button on the top to turn the camera on and off.  Unfortunately, all of the forces applied to the button get funneled down to a tiny surface-mount switch, which is edge-mounted to a circuit board.  Couple that with the fact that due to RoHS requirements, the switch is attached with lead-free solder (brittle), and you have a recipe for disaster.  If you have one of these cameras and the switch has not broken yet, consider yourself lucky, and use a very light touch when you turn the camera on and off.

In a way, I understand what Apple are trying to do with the latest nano - get back to basics.In the last couple of years, they've added features to the nano which weren't really improvements, just additions. The nano's main purpose as a take-anywhere music player was muddied by other features that didn't really fit. The screen was not really big enough to watch TV shows or movies on it. The video camera was simply not hi-res enough to be competitive or useful. As I've said in other reviews, it seemed that these features were added not because they made the nano a better product, but just because Apple could add them.With the latest nano, Apple has stripped away all those extra features, and gone back to trying to make a best-in-class take-anywhere music player. Great idea. Unfortunately, they failed in two respects - the execution of that idea, and the price.The two main design changes in this nano are the smaller screen, and the replacement of the click wheel with a touchscreen (with buttons for volume). Both of these changes make the product less successful as an on-the-go music player than previous models.Having a smaller screen makes it harder to find songs - only a few lines can be displayed at a time. On a purely aesthetic note, having the mix of icons and menus in the user interface is more cumbersome and less clean that the purely menu-based UI of previous models. Not a big deal, but Apple's appeal has traditionally been their sense of aesthetics.Removing the click wheel is a serious misstep. The click wheel made it easy to adjust the volume, scan back and forth within a track, or move between tracks in a playlist or album *without taking the player out of your pocket*. You didn't have to look at the player; just dip your hand into a pocket, quickly find the click wheel by feel, and make the adjustment. You can't do that with the new nano. While superficially cool, the touch screen makes the new nano harder to use than its predecessors.Finally, the price. Apple is charging the same price as the previous model nano, for the same amount of storage. In essence, we lose the extraneous features in order to pay for the touch screen. I would accept that trade-off if the touch screen better served the nano's core function as a portable music player. But it does not.I'm giving the new nano three stars because, despite being a step down from previous models, it's still a pretty good music player.But in paring down the nano back to its primary function, Apple also made design changes that make it perform that function less well, and then charged us for them. Far from being an improvement, the new nano is a disappointment.

I decided to purchase this camera because I wanted a camera I can take canoeing/kayaking/sailing without worrying about the expensive and delicate electronics if I should inadvertently go for a swim.  I went with this choice without GPS because I generally know where the shot was taken and can add it to the EXIF data if needed.  I went with the orange thinking the color would be easily spotted if dropped.The packaging is compact but protective.  The number of items is somewhat minimal: camera, power adapter, USB cord, battery, software and the manual.  I added a 8 GB class 10 SD card to hold what turns out to be a lot of shots (over 800 at highest resolution).  I also purchased  a charger and battery (Wasabi Power Battery (2-Pack) and Charger http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B004W82GP8/ref=oh_details_o04_s00_i02?ie=UTF8&psc;=1) because another reviewer mentioned the battery doesn't last long enough for a full day of shooting.I charged the battery using the power adapter/cord, plugged into the camera - worked fine.  After closing the battery/SD Card door and locking it, I started shooting.  The pictures are of good quality although stored only in JPEG (no DNG, no RAW, bummer). I found that I needed to have the manual next to me for the first session because the menu choices are varied (auto, manual, HDR, night, portrait, landscape, etc., etc with or without flast, red eye reduction, facial recognition etc., etc. using single point or broader focus, and exposure).  I am generally a manual or Tv or Av kinda guy with single point focus.  Anyway, I've taken about 200 shots with it so far and I'm impressed.The shots are sharp, the optical zoom works reasonably quickly, autofocus is reasonably fast.  The camera works well in low light conditions using auto ISO (another menu fuction!).  It takes nice macro pictures as well.  The menus, although occasionally obtuse, allow a wealth of shooting options which the photog in me loves.Some things to think about: the camera will sink - use a buoy wrist strap if you're concerned (sailing/kayaking - I'm concerned).
