Man, this is one powerful machine. I would never test my theory, but I'm sure this monster is powerful enough to pulverize rocks (sandstone not granite).In just a few seconds the Versa turned ice cubes into sno-ball quality shaved ice, and reduced a jar of peanuts to a smooth, creamy paste. I made delicious ice cream from a bag of frozen fruit and a bit of cream, and pesto from a wad of basil. Every food product I blended turned out perfect, and I was very pleased with the speed, power, and endurance of the Oster Versa.Things that didn't please me quite as much were the cleanup and certain design elements of the blender.✘ Cleaning the inside of the jar and the blade is a pain. It can't go in the dishwasher (Say What!), and the blade can't be removed from the jar. I mainly use my Versa to make peanut butter, and the gummy paste clings to all the nooks and crannies of the blade. You can't use a rag or a sponge because the blade snags and rips the material, so I use a test-tube bottle brush and toothpicks to get everything clean. My food processor can't produce smooth peanut butter like the Versa, but the removable blade of the food processor makes it so much easier to clean.  Note that the Versa User Manual say to not put the lid, filler cap, or jar in the dishwasher.  *** Update 2/6/2014 -- Salem1 was nice enough to provide a link to the VERSA page on the Oster website where it says: "Blend with 8-cup dishwasher safe BPA-Free Tritan plastic jar that fits under most kitchen cabinets".  So I guess the "Not dishwasher safe" statement in the manual is a misprint.  Thanks, Salem1.  I'm going to run that jar through the dishwasher ASAP.✘ The Temper is not ergonomic at all. It is fat and hard, and puts a lot of strain on your hand if you have to use it for several minutes at a time (like when making peanut butter or ice cream). The Temper would be so much nicer if it were contoured and had a rubber comfort grip.✘ Another issue with the Temper is the gap that exists between the temper and the circular opening in lid. This gap allows food particles to escape the jar. When chopping up very hard stuff I found that a lot of particles are sprayed upward toward the top of the jar. Most of the particles end up on the underside of the lid, but if you are vigorously using the Temper some of the debris manages to escape through the gap between the Temper and the circular opening in lid. I wish there was some kind of flexible rubber skirt that would create a better barrier between the temper and the opening in the lid.✘ I found the sensor that determines if the jar is set correctly on the base somewhat temperamental. It takes a few tries (and some jiggling and wiggling) to get the jar to sit correctly. If the jar is not positions just so, the safety sensor will not engage and the motor will not turn on.✘ This is probably a more personal thing, but I don't care for a dial being used to turn the machine on and off. Again, JMO, but a start/stop button used in conjunction with the dial would be so much better. Set the speed once with the dial, and then use a start/stop button to turn in on and off as needed. The inconvenience of the dial design is more noticeable if you are blending small amounts of food. If the jar isn't at least 1/3 full with food, the temper doesn't do a good job of moving the food around. For these low volume blends you need to repeatedly dial the machine off, move the food around with a long wooden spoon, and then dial the blender back on to max to continue blending. I used a recipe from the included cook books that makes a small, 2 cup batch of ice cream. During the blending I must have twisted and turned that dial on and off ten times. Each time using a long spoon to free the frozen fruit trapped under the blade. A start/stop button would have been so much easier. Set the speed once with the dial, and then use a start/stop button to turn in on and off as needed. I know I could just fill the jar up and make more ice cream (which would solve the Temper reach problem), but I have no will power and would eat it all in one sitting.✘ This thing is noisy! I thought my Oster Ice Shaver was loud, but thing is worse. I have to remember to put the dogs outside before I turn the Versa on or the poor things will howl and wail along with the blender. Music to the ears it is not!So all-in-all I love how the Oster Versa performs. It will grind up anything with ease! I just wish it was easier to clean, more ergonomic, and had an on/off button to use in conjunction with the speed dial.

My intended use for this camera:- Photographs of gardens and landscapes, mainly for before-and-after images, and for documenting technical aspects of in-progress landscape installation work. I can't complain about the price. I bought two, one to play with at home, and one for our conference room at the office.First, ignore the driver update information in the box, it (and the Netgear site) are terribly outdated. Netgear's WiDi drivers are 1.x.x and Intel is currently up to 3.5.x as I write this. Just go straight to Intel and update your drivers there. I couldn't connect to the device at all (from an Asus UX31A) with 3.0.x drivers, but after updating, I connected immediately at my office. At home, it took many tries, but I finally connected. Once you get connected, you will be prompted to do a firmware update. Do this. Once I updated the firmware, connections were much faster and easier and more reliable.The device is simple and it does work. I was disappointed by the short range -- from what I've read about other WiDi receivers, this is not necessarily a WiDi limitation.There are some other things about WiDi that bear mentioning. These are serious problems with WiDi in my opinion, but they did not play a role in my rating since they are true of all WiDi hardware. First of all, if you have an 802.11n-capable laptop and router, you'll be surprised to learn that you have to step down to 2.4GHz in order to use WiDi. It simply won't connect if your using a 5GHz connection. Second, WiDi can do 1080p, but apparently only if you run Windows in "Extended" screen mode -- your laptop screen is the "left" screen and your WiDi display is the "right" screen. Third, connecting to the device will change your screen resolution -- which also means Windows will trash your desktop icon layout. Fortunately (under Win7 anyway), the layout is restored after you disconnect, but it's still annoying.But -- it does the job for our conference room, and the annoyances were minor. For home use, it's probably a waste of money in my case. It doesn't have the range to sit in the AV closet with the rest of the gear, which also means it can't participate in my distributed-AV setup, and my living room is large enough that performance when hard-wired to the TV is still marginal depending on seating position.WiDi is a great concept, but I just don't know if it has legs...

A mostly capable media player, the MPLAY-HD's major flaw is that the chipset is NOT heatsinked or fan cooled and has reliability concerns due to overheating. Also, there are NO case vents so all of the heat remains trapped in the case. As an example with the player on (playing movie files) I have measured the 1055 chip at over 65 degrees Celsius - more than 40 degrees over the room temperature (See my uploaded photo of the circuit board showing no heatsink). I suspect Micca knows about this overheating problem based on exchanges/returns for MPLAY-HD.Reliability concerns aside, the MPLAY-HD is a compact media player that supports HDMI and playback of certain file types that the cheaperMicca MPLAYcannot playback (See my MPLAY review). The MPLAY HD has 2 USB ports and a (full size) SDcard slot for media storage.I will be comparing the MPLAY-HD to the cheaper MPLAY (note no HD) models below.THE GOOD:+ Plays x264 (H.264/MPEG AVC Part 10 encoded) video. The cheaper MPLAY cannot play x264 files and you must re-encode to MPEG4 (XVID/DIVX) for these to play.+ Plays WMV files, whereas the cheaper MPLAY cannot.+ The remote for the MPLAY-HD uses 2xAAA batteries (not included) whereas the MPLAY uses a CR2025 coin cell battery (included, but harder to find when it's time to replace). The AAAs will last much longer than the CR2025.THE BAD:- As previously mentioned there is inadequate chipset cooling - the player will probably fail in weeks/months.- Unlike the cheaper MPLAY (none-HD) model there are no buttons on the case so make sure you don't lose the remote otherwise you will be unable to operate the player.- The VOL +/- buttons are poorly located at the bottom of the remote.- Cannot play dv video (i.e. videos that use the dvsd codec for digital video). You will have to convert these to another media type.OVERALL it works and plays common files that most people will need to play. Micca has issued firmware updates to fix problems, so that's definitely a plus. However I have concerns about the potential reliability of this player due to the heat issues (might fail after warranty runs out). Micca, the case needs vent holes and a heatsink on the 1055 chip!I have also compared the MPLAY-HD to thekdLinks HD210 Full HD 1080P Multimedia Digital Signage TV Media player, please see my review on the HD210 product page.I hope you have found this helpful!

This is a very well-designed Wi-Fi router that is extremely easy to set up and to configure both on Macs and Windows.  Via the included app, it basically sets itself up automatically after you input your desired Wi-Fi network name and password. There are of course also advanced options which you may set manually if you desire to.This AirPort Extreme performs better than the prior version, even without 801.11ac devices in the network. With 802.11ac devices, it will be even faster.This contains more antennas inside the device than prior versions and also incorporates beamforming for faster wifi. The antennas sit higher and off the table top in the device which aids performance as well. When using my wifi network, things are noticeably more speedy than before.The design and foot print is also an improvement. It takes up less space on your desk or shelf since it has a smaller footprint, even though it's taller. And, I like the look of it better than prior versions as well.You can even backup wirelessly using an external hard drive plugged into this and if you use a USB hub, you can also print from any wifi computer too!A note about the product box:  be careful opening the box,  if you have it at an angle while pulling the lid off, the device will fall out and could be damaged. Also, after unboxing it, you cannot replace the base of the box because it will get stuck inside the box and be very difficult to remove after that. I recommend you put the base in sideways if you want to store the box. You will see what I mean after you get this item.Also note- this, and also the Time Capsule, has a small fan that constantly spins in it. It's not loud but noticeable if you place your ear right up to it. This is a negative over prior versions of the Airport Extreme, which were completely silent. I wonder if the fan will get any louder as time goes on, I sure hope not. It also remains to be seen if it sucks in a lot of dust over time.In summary, Apple has another winner in this latest version of the AirPort Extreme! This is a worthy upgrade from prior versions, even if you don't yet have any 802.11ac devices since it also works with 802.11a/b/g and n devices, and you will be ready for any future 802.11ac device that you may get, which is the new standard.

I can't believe these used to retail in the three digits. Such a simple little thing that made life so much easier ... and at such a great price. I got rid of cable and replaced it with a little Roku box which only outputs via composite or the HDMI cable. I was most definitely not going to use composite. I checked the TV (Sony Bravia, KDL46W4100) and, lo and behold, it had an optical digital audio OUT. I took the opportunity to consolidate all inputs (BluRay, Wii, and now Roku) and just run one audio output to the amp. CAUTION: not all TVs allow this! The previous "S" series Bravias only output the audio of the built-in ATSC tuner and not that of the other inputs. Other TVs may require changes to the output format in order for the stream to be digital, compatible with the amp (DTS, Dolby Digital, etc), etc.The device is a cinch to install as one can imagine. It has worked like a champ for a week now. The audio is crystal clear and there are no pops or hissing. I can watch movies for hours at a time or switch between TV inputs and the audio just keeps on coming.Words cannot express what a great save this was, both financially as well as in terms of headaches. In fact, it greatly simplified and enhanced an already well-functioning professional setup.

I purchased this model as an upgrade to the older model WL-330GE which is slightly bigger and doesn't support wireless-N.  I use this router primarily as a wireless hotspot - i.e. using it to connect my wireless device to another public wifi hotspot.  The point of doing this is to prevent your computer from being visible to the public WiFi network and all your devices behind this router will be protected behind a firewall and people trying to portscan your pc.While the configuration is now streamlined, more intuitive and user friendly, it has two significant drawbacks for my use:- it seems that the wireless range is substantially shorter as the older 330GE model would get a stable connection to a weak public hotspot, whereas with this router, I would experience delays while loading web pages.  I suspect this is caused by a weak signal and the connection temporarily dropping.  Note that for this comparison, I was sitting at the exact same spot connected to the same public wifi.- The older 330GE model would "remember" all the wifi networks that you've previously connected to, and would re-connect automatically to any of them when it's in range.  This newer model only remembers that last hotspot you've connected to, and whenever you switch hotspots, you automatically get redirected to the configuration page and have to manually select the hotspot to connect to, each and every time.  To make things worse, whenever you select a hotspot, the router needs to reset, which takes another 30 seconds or so, making the "bootup" process cumbersome.Unlike the old 330GE which uses a custom barrel power connection, this model uses a standard micro usb connection, and uses the same amount of power (1A/5VDC).  But given the above drawbacks, I still prefer the older 330GE model.

My wife gave me this unit for Christmas.  She's a doll and I love her very much, but she was not very versed about what to shop for or expect from a GPS unit.  I've now used the unit several hours during trips, utilizing the blue tooth connectivity with my cell phone and the included headset within my helmet.  Ive also used it in the car a lot.  They said this unit was designed by motorcyclists, but obviously the bikers TomTom consulted knew very little about the minimum expectations for features required in a decent GPS unit...especially one costing this much.I am going to break-down my review into two parts....what it has that is good...and what it lacks that makes it a non-competitive GPS unit in the US.  I've used GPS technology at work and at play for years.  Most of my background with consumer-grade GPS units is with the Garmin brand.  So it is to that brand that I will make most of my comparisons because Garmin, for the most part, has it right and does it right! (imho)I have no financial or personal relationship with Garmin, whatsoever.OK..first for the positive...it's water resistant/proof (don't really know about the proof part cause I havent had it in the pouring rain yet)...Fast processor and fast acquisition of the GPS constellation...good screen graphics and brightness...decent battery life...sensitive touch screen technology....blue tooth capable...can download your Outlook contact database....decent internal memory...heavy duty Ram mounting hardware for your bikes handle bars....USB connectivity to your computer for map downloads, etc....and if you are into directions from the unit, it has a few male and female voices from which to choose.Now for the features it should have but does not:-Should have a trip computer with trip parameters such as max speed, average moving speed, time moving, time sitting still, odometer, trip odometer, vertical and horizontal elevation, etc. None of this exists on the tomtom rider.-Should leave a track, or a bread crumb trail, as you ride along. Not available on the TTRider.  This is a real disappointment.-Should have larger fonts for speed, arrival time, etc.  Way too small to have to deal with on a motorcycle...even when set to the largest font.-Should not "snap" to the nearest road to fool you into thinking their base map is accurate...because it is not that accurate in reality.-Should come with a cig lighter plug for powering, but it does not.-Does not allow any preference setting while in motion. Despite reading negative comments in the other reviews, I decided to try the TuneTalk for myself. I thought that it couldn't be that bad. I'll tell you my personal pluses and minuses:Pluses:Set up is very easy. You'll be making recordings very quickly.The recordings are clear, but a little hissy, with or without the automatic gain control.And it's very small which is convenient.Minuses:No monitoring through your headphones while recording. I ordered a 582BioGS model after being a very happy owner of the RabbitAir BioGS421.  I wanted a unit with a higher CADR (clean air throughput) rating than the 421 for downstairs, so I paid the extra $80 or so dollars for a bigger unit. My new filter arrived today, and it works just like my 421. Which is the problem.A quick check on the Rabbitair website seems to confirm my suspicion that the 582 and 421 are identical: the dimensions are the same, the weight is the same, and all three filters are the same.  If this is supposedly a beefier unit, shouldn't it use a bigger air filter?  Shouldn't it require a mode heavy duty motor?  Most likely the only difference is that the turbine is programmed to run at a higher speed on the 582.  This leads me to a lot of questions such as, how can the 582 and 421 have the same advertised filter life if the 582 pumps more air through the same filter?  Won't the motor burn out quicker on the 582 since it is driven harder?  Unless you are running the 582 at the "turbo" setting very often and want to risk potential reliability issues a couple of years down the line, save your money and buy the 421.  I resent having paid an extra $80 for the ability to run the fan a little bit faster.

I have to think that there is tremendous quality control variability with this radio based on the wildly different reviews.I'm a radio geek and have been collecting radios for the last 40 years.  When I saw the ad for this Midland I just had to have it.  I thought it would be a perfect addition for my camping adventures.  The radio seems to be totally loaded with just about anything you would need.  It has a GRMS/FRS 2-way radio, an AM/FM radio, a weather radio, a clock with alarm and even a 3 LED flashlight.  Add to this the fact that it runs on both alkaline and a wind-up rechargeable battery!  Wow.Sadly, none of the functions work very well.  Both the AM and FM reception are very subpar.  AM reception could only receive the strongest stations and they bled over adjacent frequencies.  Many stations that I could pick up on a cheap pocket radio could not be picked up on this radio.  FM was worse, only picking up a couple of very powerful local stations.Weather band worked, but only barely.  I was able to pick up many more channels on a little Grundig/Eton wind-up.FRS/GRMS radio functions were similarly mediocre to poor.Cranking was more awkward than on other emergency radios that I have used including those by Freeplay and Grundig.On a positive note, the LED flashlight is nice and the clock/alarm is also a nice feature. You also get a lot of accessories, including an external mic, both car and AC chargers and a carrying strap.Overall, I was disappointed by this radio.  The fact that others like it suggests to me that there may be a lot of variability between radios.  However, in general, I would pass on this radio.  There are many inexpensive GRMS/FRS radios that would do a better job.  If you are looking for a good emergency broadcast band radio check out those made by Freeplay or Grundig/Eton.

The Cuisinart DCC- 1150 10 Cup Coffee Maker is a decent coffee maker overall with an equal share of pros and cons. I have owned several different coffee makers over the years and have used several Cuisinart coffee makers, but I never owned one until now. I was attracted to this particular model due to its appearance and its ability to save electricity. The unit automatically shuts off after it finishes brewing, then keeps the coffee warm in the thermal carafe as you gradually consume one cup at a time.This coffee maker brews in a similar fashion to other modern coffee makers and it does have some nice features worth mentioning. I like the water filter and the permanent filter because it means cleaner, fresher tasting water, greater convenience, and less money spent on paper filters. I also like the automatic shutoff, at least in theory, because it helps conserve electricity. The carafe is unbreakable, which is nice, and the programmable functions work well. These are all good, useful features and the unit scores points in each of these areas.Now, let's talk about the potential problems with this Cuisinart coffee maker because there are a few. The first problem I noticed when I started using this coffee maker is the difficulty in cleaning. The opening at the top of the carafe is very narrow and only the smallest hands and fingers will be able to fit inside. I have found it necessary to use a brush for cleaning purposes because there is just no way to get my hand inside. This also means, of course, that drying is a challenge. I usually turn it upside down and air- dry because other than using a hair dryer or some other air- blowing source, it is just too difficult to get inside to soak up the excess water.The next potential problem area is the one mentioned by most consumers who own this coffee maker, and that is its inability to keep coffee hot over an extended period. The manufacturer did what it could to engineer the carafe in such a way as to maintain heat, but there are still limits to its ability. The lid seals itself shut at the end of the brewing cycle and the carafe is double- walled to keep the heat inside, but it is still limited in its capabilities so you need to hurry up and finish drinking as quickly as possible or else be faced with a pot of cold coffee.One other potential drawback with this coffee maker is one you wouldn't think about at first. Because the carafe is metal and is non- see through like a glass carafe, there is always a chance you will forget about making a pot of coffee and just let the carafe sit there for days or even weeks without cleaning.  You cannot see the actual coffee and because of this, it is very easy to forget that coffee and coffee grounds are still inside the unit. I have experienced this more than once. I pulled out the carafe and basket to prepare for a fresh pot of coffee, only to notice that the carafe still contained some leftover coffee and the basket was still filled with coffee grinds, along with some mold/mildew. I never had to worry about a problem such as this with a glass carafe because I could easily see the leftover coffee.Cuisinart is known for its many fine products, but the Cuisinart DCC- 150 10 Cup Coffee Maker is not the picture of coffee- making excellence I was hoping for. I can fully understand why the reviews of this coffee maker are so mixed, because it does have some potential problems that could make its use impractical for some. I find it sufficient for my limited, fast- drinking needs but I can see how some consumers will have a problem with the lack of heat, cleaning, and other issues.

I am a fairly big Apple fan I really enjoy their phones, tablets, laptops, iPods, etc but their desktop line just isn't up to snuff. Each desktop has a major short coming. The MacPro is wildly out of date not containing modern specs and is enormous. I would love to have a box that is 50% to 75% of the current size as I don't use many of the specs it has two optical drives, two processors (which total up to twelve processor cores!) four hard drive bays, several slots I don't use, etc. Although most of Apple's portable line comes with Retina displays (the exceptions only being the iPad Mini and Macbook Air) none of the desktop line comes with Retina displays. Instead you get a massive 27" lower resolution display. I would trade that display in for a 20"-23" retina display any day.Your only other option for a stand alone computer is to go with the super underpowered Mini. A machine that comes packed with great multimedia software and with none of the power to use any of it. Along with the huge performance lag the storage limit for each hard drive tops off at 1TB and only uses the pokey 5400-rpm drives (or expensive SSDs that are very limited in capacity.)I would really like to think that the iMac is the midrange machine that offers a nice balance between the extremes of the Mini and the Pro but I am sorry to say it simply is not that machine but rather contains everything bad about both the Mini and the Pro in one machine. When the iMac was introduced Phil Schiller gushed about how thin it was but one look at the specs and you soon see were the massive trade offs are. The iMac is supposed to be the mid range machine but actually has fewer HDs then the Mini and the reasonably sized 21.5" version comes with only the painfully slow 5400 drive found in the Minis. While the Pro has more drives then I could ever know what to do with the iMac doesn't even contain an extra internal drive to do my back ups on. The last time I did a review on the iMac I was flooded with comments that were telling me that I should just plug an external drive into the iMac. Apparently there is some confusion to what an ALL IN ONE computer is. All in one means that you don't have to keep plugging in all these different devices to make it work right but that everything works all in that one computer. If it doesn't do that then failed to do the one thing it set out to do.After reading through some of the comments to my review I realized I should have brought up a couple more important points. I realize external drives are good at doing some things, I have one in fact, I just don't believe that they should be your only option for backing up. External drives are great for to keep off site in case your computer gets stolen or destroyed so that you won't loose all your data when you loose your computer.I actually stand behind Apple choice of removing the optical drive. I know that is controversial to some people but we have been using those drives on computers for over twenty years now. Technology moves on at some point you need to dump the old. There are better solutions available. For one good decision I awarded them one star. Others have asked why do I talk about computers besides the iMac in this review. It is important for me to do this since if I didn't people might think another desktop Mac might suit them better. If there is one thing you should understand about my review it is that there are no longer any good options on Apple's desktop line these days. They all have glaring problems. I am sorry to say it but it is just the truth.

Roomba Vacuuming Robots have always been convenient, innovative, and a time-saver, but in the past they lacked an optimized design.  Over the years, we have gone through several Discoveries and various other models of Roomba.  Subsystems or components in them, like the motors or brush assemblies would quickly wear out through the very heavy use that we gave them.  During the warranty periods, iRobot was always great about sending whole replacement robots to replace them, anytime there was a problem.  Then came the 500 Series.  It is completely modular and even better made than all the previous versions.  The performance is far better than any of the previous Roomba and their new over-priced competitors.The best thing about the 500 Series is that has a completely modular design.  Whether in or out of warranty, when something breaks or gets worn out, it can easily be removed from the robot and replaced.  For example, my front wheel caster assembly got so warn that the wheel wasn't staying in the assembly as well as it should.  iRobot quickly sent me a new assembly and in 5 minutes I was able to install it by removing and replacing two screws.  If this had been out of warranty the cost of the new caster on their website would have been about $5 with free shipping.Similarly, the brush assembly, including their motors can be replaced in about 5 minutes and for less than $30.  On previous designs, a burnt out motor would have required a replacement Roomba.Don't imply from my review that your Roomba is constantly going to be braking.  We run ours very hard.  We are very happy with the performance and durability of this new design.  The Roomba design has finally reached maturity.

This lotion isn't terrible; I mean, it's way cheaper than what you'd buy in the tanning salon, and way less... Fussy? I don't know, I feel like less of an idiot pulling a bottle like this out of my purse than I would the Snooki and J-Wow Ed Hardy style products my tanning salon pushes.  It also smells better than a lot of the stuff out there, sort of like an orange creamsicle, and slightly less sugary than other lotions I've tried.That said, I don't think this stuff really did that much.  First the smell, while not terrible, after tanning I still feel like I smell sort of like burnt sugar.  It's the same problem I've had with other lotions; I think it's the way my body and the tanning bed react to the chemicals, but I'm just not a huge fan of the stink. I have to go straight home and shower afterward.  As far as the function of the product, I'll admit, this is the first tan accelerator lotion I've used; the others have just been like indoor tanning protection lotions.  I'm also not a regular tanner; I only tan before vacations to get a base layer of color, so maybe one week, twice a year is as often as I'll go.But using the same bed, in the same salon, for the same amount of time, around the same time of year as I did last year (so I started the same type of pale), I burned pretty badly with this stuff on.  I'm not talking about a little pink that fades in an hour or two; that happens to me pretty much every time for a day or 2.  I mean bad enough that I'm pretty uncomfortable still the next day, and will need to skip a day of tanning so I don't fry myself.  I don't know if my skin is just not made for tanning accelerators or what, but I'll be switching back to my regular, though stinkier, lotion tomorrow when I go back. In fact, I almost feel like I'm getting less tan, although that could just be because my back and my legs, where I usually show the color best, are currently crispy pink.Maybe this is an issue of you get what you pay for, I don't know.  Maybe it's just that I, personally, have no business using tan accelerators.  I'm actually willing to bet that it's just that my skin doesn't react well to it, because it does have a lot of  positive reviews.  But unfortunately, I won't be buying it again.Editing to add: When I switched back to my old lotion, I immediately noticed I tanned darker (even though my old lotion is not an accelerator) without burning. In a world where there are a large variety of iPhone and iPod speaker docks and clock radios, I was happy to see that Philips is producing good sounding speaker docks for the Android platform. With the debut of the Philips AS111/37 Fidelio Docking Speaker for Android, Philips has made an affordable Android docking speaker/clock radio that both looks and sounds good.The Philips Android speaker dock is small and cylinder shaped, looking somewhat futuristic. It's all black, with just a snooze, volume and clock/nightlight buttons on the top. The unit itself is plastic, with fabric on top, covering the speakers. The top also has the dock for an Android phone, and the dock itself moves back and forth to fit any phone. The speaker dock also has an amber night light. Although the speaker dock is small, it produces very good sound and a balanced tone. I streamed music from both Pandora and Slacker, as well as music on my phone, I am very pleased with the sound this speaker dock produces. Highs are clear, and there's a good amount of bass present as well. The unit gets louds, and at its loudest setting, 32, it does not distort. Music plays wirelessly; the phone docks to the unit for charging purposes only. The Bluetooth connection is very effortless; the speaker dock found and connected with my phone almost immediately.So that's the good news. Now here is the bad news. Because the speaker dock has so few buttons or controls, you need an app to control the alarm clock function. Philips wants you to download its Fidelio app, but the app is pretty large, (it may be a resource hog on your phone) and buggy.The instructions, which are very bare (just a series of drawings, no real written instructions) don't really tell you much, so you have to sort of feel your way around the app to figure things out. It took me a while to find the actual alarm function on the app, which is not good if you are half asleep trying to adjust the alarm. I would suggest downloading any of the free Alarm apps available in the Android market. They are much less of a resource hog, have more features, and will not be as buggy. Waking up to music on my phone, such as Slacker, Pandora, or Sirius, is not possible, since my phone is password protected. The alarm does turn the phone on, but you have to enter a password to hear music. The alarm app will wake you to music that you have installed on the phone, or to a series of sounds (rain, waves, etc.).I have an HTC Incredible phone, which means my phone has to sit horizontal on the connector since my charging input is on the side of the phone. The phone is somewhat hard to connect to the dock, and then once connected falls off easily since it is sitting on its side. Again, if you are trying to use this in the dark, it may be very hard (and frustrating) to connect the phone to the speaker dock.Overall, I applaud Philips for putting out a great sounding speaker dock for an Android device. I use the Bluetooth to connect to the speaker, and enjoy listening to music. But I have to give this unit only three stars because of the weak Fidelio app and poor support for phones that have to sit horizontally on the connector. As a speaker dock, purely on sound, I would rate this unit a four, but the app (and a limited alarm function) brings to score down to a three.

I had high hopes for this juicer.  Based on reviews on Amazon as well as from other sites, I determined that this was a top-notch unit.  I gave it 3 stars based on the fact that it does do a good job on vegetables that I have tried in it; however, apples are a different story.  Contrary to the pictures and claims on some sites that this juicer produces clear juice with no (or very little) foam), my experience is totally different.  If you plan to juice more than 2 apples at a time, you'll need to stop the unit and clean out the auger to clear all the apple pulp.  It is like applesauce in there and will not extrude out.  You might also want to invest in some cheese cloth to further strain the pulp that is sent out with the juice.  It will clog the strainer that comes with the unit.  By using some cheesecloth on top of the strainer, you can squeeze out a little more juice.  My experience has been 4 apples will yield about 8 oz. of juice. Obviously a lot of juice is left in the pulp since it isn't forced out of the machine.  And if you don't want a lot of foam in your juice, you'll need to skim it off the top.  Without straining the juice you can end up with almost an inch of foam.  My suspicion is that any soft vegetable will have this same problem with clogging.  Tomatoes are another one with the same problem, however, when I juice vegetables I never do only tomatoes.  So there are harder vegetables that can be run thru after the tomatoes to force the tomato pulp thru the unit.  Again, a lot of the pulp will end up in your juice unless you use a strainer of some kind.  The unit does appear to be well made and I have no doubts it will last the length of the warranty (15 years).  I just wich it could handle apples and other soft food adequately.

I have had the Garmin nuvi 40LM for one month and have used it for some minor direction finding around the Des Moines, Iowa metro area.  It did a respectable job but on the two occasions I really needed help finding a new destination in that metro area it identified my destination as being on the opposite side of the road from its true location.  Now for the real fiasco:  I was traveling in the Chicago metro area and needed directions from the Ikea store in Schaumburg, IL to a location in Coralville, IA.  After inputting the Coralville address I headed toward I-90, within sight, and where I thought I should be heading.  The Garmin redirected me in the opposite direction.  My wife and I decided to trust it and followed its directions for the next hour and one half while it continually tacked away from the interstate highway system, leading us through numerous western suburbs at 35-45 mph, with many traffic lights.  We finally stopped at a Wal-Mart to ask directions to I-88, which we knew I-90 would have led us to.  Wal-Mart customer service directed us to retrace our route about two miles and to take Illinois 59 south about six miles to where it intersected with I-88.  The Garmin had actually taken us off Illinois 59 and away from I-88. After a cooling off period, I have edited this review and upgraded to three stars from one star.  I'll continue to use the Garmin but I also know now to keep a road map within reach to verify directions.

These storage chests are simply amazing! We needed one that was light weight and on casters so that we could roll it out of the way when we pull out the trundle.  This works and matches perfectly! Don't make my mistake of ignoring John Pastore complaints about how tiny these things are (I mean Parker mentions it, but no one else discloses these are sized for a child's tea party or for use by Hobbits - ha ha). I assume these get a lot of returns due to no size information in the description (which is two inches smaller than the ones I ended up with).Now, this isn't the only diminutive set, so I guess there are people who prefer what I would call small paring knives instead of something designed for cutting meat (something more sized like a fillet knife). I'm just not one of them and I wanted to remind you in case you feel the same way. As for weight, I see most people are switching from a traditional Chief's knife to a much lighter Santoku (I own Wusthof for both). In this way perhaps, all of the steak knives I looked at were similarly lighter than my 40-year old vintage Japanese Copco's these were to replace. They all also have a thinner spline. I'm personally not happy about either trend as I prefer a heftier knife and because although I hold a Chief's knife with a pinch, I push down on the spine of a steak knife (as with a butter knife) and a thin spine make doing so uncomfortable.Buyers should also be warned (as is done by many reviewers here) that the "aluminum" handles will quickly spot and discolor even if hand washed if not dried immediately and so IMHO you should only consider the black dishwasher safe resin handles.Rada is not really that famous for their knives as others have suggested (as demonstrated by making only this single version). German companies like Wusthof and Henckels and Japanese companies like Global and Shun are the ones actually well known for quality steel knives (where a single high end steak knife can run almost $100). I can only assume most reviewers have limited experience with such knives. One reviewer said he looked high and low for knives not made in China - clearly that didn't include even just checking out Amazon's top-rated knives list. Any way, I ended up with GermanWusthof Silverpoint II 4-Piece Steak Knife Set(which are just as good for making steaks as for eating them) for just a few dollars more. I have a variety of Wusthof kitchen knives and so should have started there in the first place.For me, the tiny size makes these knives not a good buy even with their discounted Amazon price. I would probably add a star (to two) if the description would just mentioned the size (7.5 inches as compared to 9.5 for my new Wusthofs).

I purchased this motherboard for an AMD FX-8150 build and was perhaps mislead by a lot of the reviews on here. I build a lot of systems but, this was my first MSI board in quite some time. I had become accustomed to the pretty (and easy to use) GUIs of similar Asus and ASRock boards, which have EFI. I was very surprised to find an old school BIOS loaded on this motherboard, even though it had shipped with the latest version.The BIOS on this board is very cumbersome to use, I've found. I had to refer a lot to the manual, which is not something I had to do with competitor's boards. The overclocking utility MSI provides is garbage, and the system would not POST if I tried messing with the "instant overclock" DIP switches that MSI brags about. I finally ended up overclocking in the BIOS, which was easy with AMD's unlocked multiplier. Admittedly, FX-8150 runs quite hot but, I should have been able to achieve a mild overclock without issues, especially since MSI brags about it.So, in a nutshell, this could have been a decent board had MSI not loaded the ancient BIOS on it. Furthermore, the quality of the board, and especially the included software, could have been improved. Long term reliability has yet to be seen but, I'm not holding my breath. Personally, I will avoid MSI for future builds. You have A LOT of better choices out there in this free market.2/25/13 UPDATE: One month later, and the board has run into serious problems. Returned to my computer powered off one day and tried turning it back on. I was greeted with sparks, a loud "POP" and electrical smoke. One of the CPU voltage regulators blew up and pieces of the IC were in the case. 1 week into the RMA now, still no word from MSI about it. For those curious, I was running a high quality 650w Corsair Enthusiast PSU and no overclock. Never had an issue with my Intel board on this PSU.4/15/13 UPDATE: After replacing the motherboard, CPU and PSU, my system worked again. Then, yesterday the EXACT SAME THING HAPPENED from my previous update. I absolutely cannot have this kind of downtime, nor keep RMAing my CPU, motherboard and power supply. Totally unacceptable. It's going to be trashed and replaced with another brand of board. Good luck to everybody trying to use this one. You'll need it.

In order to better review the Archos Vision 30c I wanted to compare it to several of the other MP3 players I have had the opportunity to test. My conclusions and the parameters of the test are included below.To accurately compare the different players I rated them on sound quality (SQ), Video Playback Quality (VP), user interface/ease of use (UI), Radio Quality (RQ), and Other Features.  I should mention that for other features I will only be reviewing the major additional features of the Touch.  All the advantages of various apps would be beyond the scope of this review.  Suffice to say that the touch acts more like a tiny tablet then an MP3 player.Jump to the bottom if all you want is the conclusions:Equipment:  The players: 8 GB Archos Vision 30c, 4GB SanDisk Sansa Fuze, 8GB SanDisk Sansa Fuze+, and 32GB iPod Touch 4G.Headphones: Skullcandy INK'd Earbuds**I know these are cheap but the SQ is good enough to allow me to distinguish differences between the players.Sound Quality:1) Fuze: 9/10The best of the bunch, great sound for an MP3 player, with clear notes and solid if not spectacular base.  With Rockbox* I would give it a 10/10.2) Touch: 8/10.Unlike previous ipods I have used I actually enjoy the quality of the 4G touch.  I could wish for more equalizer controls but I think it does a solid job, just not quite as clean as the Fuze.  Not compatible with Rockbox.3) Fuze+ 5/10For some reason the Fuze+ just doesn't seem to have the same quality as the Fuze, I don't know if they changed the chip or what, but the SQ simply isn't as good.  Moreover the Fuze+ isn't compatible with Rockbox.3) Vision: 5/10Normal equalizer setting has poor SQ with virtually no base, but the M/S equalizer does a good job of boosting sound of improving sound quality on tracks (this uses an algorithm to add and subtract the data going to different ears to provide a more surround sound feel).  I found the 3d M/S setting to be too much and to make the player overloud but the Bass setting for the MS equalizer does an excellent job of repairing the bass problem.  I like the ability to set manual EQs on the player. Not compatible with Rockbox.Video Playback:1) Touch: 8/10,The touch has a great screen, large enough to enjoy on a long trip or flight, with minimal differences in viewing quality based on angle of view.  Extremely clear and clean picture, with very little glare or reflection.  Limited handling of file types, basically only MPEG-4 is the main reason I took off points.2) Vision: 6/10For size this takes second place to the iPod.  The amount of glare and reflection on the screen however makes watching in most environments fairly difficult and watching in bright light impossible.  This however was not as big a problem inside a car and I imagine it would also not be so bad on a plane.  Since these are the two most likely places for video viewing I felt the a score of 5 was still warranted.  Diversity of file playback pushes the rating to 6.3) Fuze/Fuze+: 5/10I found video playback on the two devices to be very similar.  The screen is too small to really watch a movie or show on, but it doesn't have as much glare as on the Vision.  Both of these allow a lot of file types.  But for me the screen is just too small for serious viewing.User Interface:1) Touch: 9/10Apple is known for both industrial engineering and intuitive design, the touch is no different.  All the features you might want regularly are easily viewable with only a few swipes. The touch screen is both responsive and accurate.  There are some limitations to the operating system in terms of apps you can use and function management but they don't really detract from an excellent user experience.  Volume controls and the lock/unlock buttons are the only external buttons.  If you could press pause and play without having to take it out of your pocket this would be a 10.2) Fuze: 8/10A great tactile wheel that actually spins for song and menu selection (alla the iPod classic but the wheel spins) is super easy to use.  Moreover pressing play/pause, fast forwarding etc. can all be managed without ever removing the player from your pocket.  Menu use isn't quite as easy as with the iPod since you can't type or touch but it is still straight forward.  The actual user interface is probably a 7, no stellar user friendly design but loading Rockbox firmware I think changes the UI to an 8 due to customizability.3) Fuze+: 5/10Uses a similar UI to the fuse but the controls are different.  The Fuze+ uses an inductive touch plate similar to the LG chocolate line of phones instead of real buttons.  The plate is both oversensitive and not sensitie enough, either not responding or jumping around. Still control is manageable if difficult, and side volume buttons allow for easy volume control when the player is in a pocket.4) Vision: 1/10:The Archos Vision has the worst user interface and controls I have ever seen on any device.  There is only one external button, which controls the back function and allows you (if you hold it) to either lock or power down the player.  The touch screen does not respond at all to light touches or swipes the way the iPod does, requiring more of a push and then only responding about 40% of the time.  I found that if I used a fingernail I could get responsiveness up to about 75% but that was it.  Play/pause, SF/SB buttons are cramped in at the bottom of the screen.  If you listen to audiobooks then skipping to a point in the middle of a 30 minuet chapter requires touching on a thin line that is only visible in perfect light and at the right angle.  Doing so is nearly impossible.  FF normally by holding the skip forward button is slow and inefficient, and nearly impossible to do with a nail.  Volume controls require that you either tap on the speaker picture at either end of the volume bar or you attempt to actually touch the volume bar at a given point.  This however is as difficult as touching a point partway through a song.  Also the screen only tilts sideways in one direction.Radio Quality:1) Fuze/Fuze+: 7/10FM radio was mostly clear, and recording quality was adequate, but nothing to write home about.2) Vision:5/10 Good FM playback but recording quality of radio music is awful, the files sound like they were recorded underwater, with really muddy sound.2) Touch: 5/10Internet radio with apps when on a wif-fi network but no FM radio and no ability to record from radio.Other Features:1) Touch: 24/20Ya I know this doesn't make sense but as I said above this is only nominally an MP3 player, failure to account for that would be inappropriate.  It is the only player with internet access, e-mail, internet radio etc.  Obviously this has a ton more features than any of the other features.  An inability to add additional memory kept it from being a 25/202) Fuze 14/20It isn't that the fuzes have a ton of extra features but rather the main extra they do have, a micro SD card slot is HUGE.  Essentially this means that you can add up to 32GB (with current firmware) of storage capacity to your MP3 player, turning the 4GB player into a 36GB player.  Not too shabby.  Add to that the fact that the Fuze works with Rockbox and that's why this earns 13 points.3) Fuze+: 9/20:As I said above these points basically come from the ability to add external memory.4) Vision 30c: 1/20There really weren't any features that the vision had that the other two players did not have as well.  Additionally there wasn't anything that the vision excelled at above the rest.*****Conclusion: (consider 25-36/60 to be three stars)****1) iPod touch 4G: 53/60 (5 stars)2) SanDisk Sansa Fuze: 43/60 (4 stars) ***Best Buy***3) SanDisk Sansa Fuze+: 32/60 (3 stars)4) Archos Vision 30c: 19/60 (2 stars)If price is no issue, for sheer features, ease of use and the best video with decent sound the iPod is the best bet.For a simple mp3 player for straight music use, I would go with the Fuze, ease of use and sound quality are the most important features in an mp3 player and the Fuze has those in abundance.  Expandable memory and compatibility with Rockbox really make it the best choice.  I wouldn't choose the + over the older version.Skip the Archos at all costs.  Barring a major firmware update it is nearly unusable.*Rockbox is an open source firmware for mp3 players that supplants the stock firmware that comes on the device.  It provides significant additional customizability and control, as well as several new features.  The highlights of these features are: increased sound management controls, games, PDA type applications.  It goes a decent way towards bridging the gap between the Fuze and the touch.

After I removed this product from its package I was highly disappointed by what I saw. Amazon.com's product information for this device falsely claims "2 Pairs Of Gold Coaxial Connections For Coaxial Cable Line Protection ; 2-Line Telephone/Pay-Per-View Protection With Splitter ; Network Protection For Media Streamer Support." None of these features are present on this product. This product actually only has one pair of gold coaxial connections, not two. It does NOT have telephone line or network protection!Belkin has actually sold different models under the same "PF30" product name. I downloaded the manual for PF30 model AP20800-10 from the Belkin website, which I thought was the manual for this product. I didn't know there were different models of the PF30 other than having different colors. Amazon lists this model as AP20800FC10, but the model I received was actually numbered AP20800FC08.The AP20800-10 manual from the Belkin website showed RJ-11 connections, RJ-45 connections, and two pairs of coaxial connections, thus matching Amazon.com's description for this product. However, if you look at the diagram of the back of this product at the top of the product page, you will see that there are no RJ-11 or RJ-45 jacks, and only one pair of coaxial connectors.Amazon.com also lists the incorrect dimensions. The actual dimensions are 17" width x 8.25" depth x 2" height. Before I placed my order I could tell Amazon had the dimensions wrong from the photo.For use as a surge protector, the three important criteria to look at are clamping level, joules rating, and response time. Unfortunately the Belkin manuals and website don't give technical specs, which is a red flag. The clamping voltages (written on the PF30 itself) for this device are: Line-Neutral 330V, Line-Ground 500V, Neutral-Ground 400V. By comparison, the much cheaper APC Personal Surge Arrest Protector with Telephone has clamping voltages of L-N 330V, L-G 330V, N-G 330V. Lower clamping voltages offer better protection. ThePanamax M4300-PM 9-Outlet Home Theater Power Conditioneralso seems to have clamping voltages of L-N 330V, L-G 330V, N-G 330V based on my reading of the online user manual.

I was looking for a cable like this to declutter the cables in my car, where I currently use a 6-foot 3.5mm aux cable to connect my iPod to the aux jack in my car. That much cable was getting in the way. For that reason alone I got this Belkin MIXIT coiled cable, and while it solved my problem, it has a number of disadvantages which I list below. Here are the pros and cons:PROS:De-Clutter: The coiled cable really prevents tangling with other cables. I used this in my car, and my previous 6-foot 3.5mm aux cable got tangled up with my Garmin navi cables, passengers legs, etc. This Belkin cable corrects that problem.Looks and Sound: The bright color and coiled style look pretty cool. This of course is a purely subjective assessment. The sound is just fine, the cable carries its signal as well as other 3.5mm aux cables I own. I suppose the "Chrome-finished plugs and nickel-plated contacts" help here.CONS:Cost: For a 3.5mm Aux cable whose only unique feature is the coil, this cable is very overpriced. It should be in the $5 range. Maybe $7-8 for the color. Above $10 this cable is simply not worth it.Not Case Friendly: The jack itself is only long enough to go into your device to the point where the cap sits flush with the top of the input; there is no additional slim shank. So if you have a case on your iPhone, iPod, etc. the jack will likely not plug in all the way. This is just silly design and a rookie mistake from an experienced manufacturer like Belkin.Length: The product description says this is a 6 foot cable, but confusingly also indicates it is only 4 feet ("Coiled cable stretches to 4-Feet (1.2m)"). I imagine you could get to 6 feet if you stretched it past the point where the coils would ever recover. Even 4 feet is, *ahem*, a bit of a stretch. Practically and functionally speaking, this is a 3 foot cable.BOTTOM LINE:If you really want/need a coiled 3.5mm aux cable, this is a fine option. It does however have the drawbacks I've noted above, the biggest (as other reviewers have also noted) being the price. This cable, for what it offers, should be priced under $10. Well under.

Lately, I've been working on some of the pictures I've taken down through the years. Mostly photos of cars I see at the local car shows. I ordered it on Wednesday and it came on Thursday. Now that's fast!I ripped open the box and found the tablet, a small CD and a VERY short quick start guide. The CD contained drivers and a program called Bamboo dock; nothing else. I installed the drivers and Bamboo dock. (That's the limit of what you get from the quick start guide; plug in your tablet, install the drivers.)At this point I had a funny little box in the upper right hand corner of my screen. There were 5 small icons hanging down below a caption that says Bamboo. I clicked on one called Landmarker. A map of Europe came up. I can move a tiny picture of a paintbrush around on the map but that's it. No combination of button clicking, pressure (or swear words) produced any effect although when I used my MOUSE to move around over the map, IT managed to draw on the map. Score, Mouse 1 - Tablet 0.I then launched a game (???) called Free The Bird. I have NO idea how you're actually supposed to play the game. I guess a network engineer just isn't quite smart enough to figure it out. But, the mouse was able to make squares and circles. The tablet only managed to move the cursor around. Score, Mouse 2 - Tablet 0. I moved on to anther icon labeled Mona Lisa and got exactly the same results. Score, Mouse 3 - Tablet 0So, I went to the Wacom website and found a link called tutorials. I clicked on it and got to watch a woman take a couple of minutes to make a drawing. No explanations of what she was doing. You just got to watch. I guess I was supposed to watch REAL close and try to figure out which buttons she was pressing? So much for the tutorials. I found NO help guides for how to get started with this thing.I understand that for the most part, practice and familiarity with whatever software you end up using with the tablet will be the key to becoming proficient with the tablet. I just think it would have been nice if Wacom had made at least a MINIMAL effort to give me some sort of introduction on how to use it. Maybe write a VERY basic drawing program and give you a couple of practice lessons so you get some kind of idea of what the tablet can do.Maybe I'm just a bit naive but I expected a LOT more help getting started with a tablet from the WORLD FAMOUS Wacom. The tablet will be going into my garage sale when the weather cools down and my mouse has been feeling rather smug today. I have kids that are always in parades and other outdoor events, plus my husband and I attend a lot of open-air concerts, but I burn within minutes, so it's important for me to have shade.  I usually bring a big golf umbrella, and that keeps me from burning, but it's very cumbersome.  So I was excited to give this Versa-Brella a try.Pros:*The fabric has a silver coating on the underside to ensure total sun-blocking (see the picture I uploaded).*The umbrella can be pivoted at two joints and rotated at another, so it's super adjustable.*It's easy to carry in the included fabric bag with its carrying strap (see the picture I uploaded).*The tips of the ribs are covered by large plastic tabs, spreading out the stress (see the picture I uploaded), so you are probably less likely to have it rip there (plus it's less likely to poke someone in the eye).Cons:*The first thing I noticed was the smell.  The rubbery clamp has a strong, unpleasant chemical odor.  Plan ahead so you can let this thing air out somewhere, especially if you are sensitive to such things.  I've had my umbrella over a month, and I can still smell it (and it still leaves the smell on my hands after handling it), but it's getting better.*The carrying bag is very snug around the bulky clamp.  I wish the bag had just a bit more room so I wouldn't have this frustration point when putting the umbrella away.*If you open the clamp all the way and the screw disengages, it's a big pain getting it rethreaded.  I feared for a while that I'd ruined the clamp.*There is no wind vent, so, depending on how you have it angled, you might have problems in the wind.Other things you should know:*The dimensions of the canopy are about 36"x38".*The umbrella feels very light (good balance, perhaps), but it actually weighs in at 1 pound, 12.5 ounces.*The clamp can attach to poles with a diameter of about 1/2 inch up to about 1.75 inches.  It can attach to a flat surface of up to 1.75 inches (no minimum, as long as the surface can support the umbrella's weight).  The poles of a folding lawn chair or full-size stroller are ideal.  The thin poles of many collapsing chairs (such that you carry in a bag) will be too thin.Overall, this is a nice umbrella that seems well made.  Some reviewers have commented that it's too small, but I think the maneuverability helps compensate for that, plus it's a good compromise between coverage and portability.  If you've ever juggled an umbrella and wished you could attach it to something, this product might be the solution you've been looking for.

This film is definitely not for anyone who is especially fond of the independent, delightfully manipulative and clever boy who was the brain child of Samuel Clemens's classic.As one example, the book has great  fun with the scenes involving Aunt Polly, a simple minded soul who thinks  herself quite clever, and the genuinely shrewd Tom, who plays on catering  to Polly's illusions about her own wit. This is a far cry from beautiful,  intelligent Celeste Holm's portrayal of Polly - and the family's poverty,  clearly seen in the book, disappears, as the Sawyers occupy a beautiful  home and are close friends with wealthy Widow Douglas.Some of the plot  is distorted in ways that remove the charm of the original. Tom's taking  off to "play pirates" after Becky jilts him is changed into a  troubled kid's escape after Aunt Polly tells him how "no good"  his father was - the humour, and the engaging portrayal of adolescent  "first love" is gone. The theme of Tom's learning responsibility  is overworked, and sequences that are hilarious in the book (Sunday school,  classroom, etc) are largely left out. The enchanting Becky Thatcher is  reduced to a tomboy. And isn't much of the picnic sequence ruined when a  gathering of kids is changed to a song-and-dance outing for families? (Tom  Sawyer is quite realistic in its setting forth that kids are far more  concerned with themselves than fretting about parents - let's not turn it  into a commentary on "family values" a la 1990s political  correctness.)Johnny Whitaker's singing voice has all the appeal of  chalk squeaking on a blackboard. His rendition of "If I Were God"  (aside from its text having nothing to do with the story - Tom's only  church interests are in time to play with his pinch bug) is pure purgatory  for the listener.

I had to return it twice to finally get a unit in with the touch screen was calibrated properly. In the first two units, the bottom right of the screen won't register touches properly and I had to touch more towards the center to "touch" the bottom right.I have had the watch for about 2 weeks now. Using it daily. The watch is pretty much like a secondary screen that can be made to display all or a selected few categories of the Android notifications that you get. Quite handy when you get Facebook, SMS or other messages when you are in a meeting and the phone is in your pocket. There are a few good free and paid 3rd party plugins that make the watch even better. Search around and install them.The watch UI is not super smooth, but it's also not terribly slow. Definitely usable. I can leave the watch connected 24hr/day and it lasts for about 3 full days. Pretty impressed by that. The phone is a Nexus 4, which I think supports Bluetooth 4.0 which is supposedly more power efficient.The only two cons that bother me the most:* To go "back" from an "app", you have to do a double finger tap or a "pinch". There's no other way to go "back". So, it's impossible to use when you are holding a coffee in your hand or something similar that prevents you from using two fingers at an angle. Only one 3rd party provides a "back" button in the UI. But that's an exception, not the norm. Certainly not for the apps from Sony. I wish it came with a back button on the side. The button on the side that's there in the watch only toggles between "time" and "app screen" when the screen is on.* The watch is almost useless in daylight. You can squint real hard and make things out. But at that point, I might as well just take out the phone and check it out. But it's still quite handy enough indoors that it's worth keeping.Long story short, at this price ~$95, it's quite a useful/productive device.UPDATE **** 5/11/2013 ****My 3rd unit just died on my one day before the return period expired. So, I returned it and got my 4th unit. The 4th unit came without any calibration issues and worked well, but about a month and a half later, the battery just died abruptly. It won't hold any charge for more than 30 mins even after a day of leaving it charging. Looks like the watch can get to this state if you completely drain the battery (and cause auto shutdown) when everything is working properly. So, if you have one that's still working, I would recommend not letting it go below about 25%.This had a lot of potential, but SONY seems to have ruined any possibility of success by having terrible quality checks for the product.

Pro: great sky blue bright high end frequency response, typical JBL signature. elegant design.Con: VERY weak low end frequency response making this center channel speaker sounding weak paired up with full tower speakers. the plastic casing particularly doesn't help either.this speaker will bring out good high end details in movies that typical mass market speakers tend to miss, however, when it comes to low end punch, and explosions.... you'll definitely feel a "hole" in the spectrum. the matter becomes worse when certain dialogues are low end frequency, which makes it hard to discern. certain low end action sound effects like motor cycle engine will produce a weak "pop" sound as oppose to the true low punch thumping sound you'll get from a sound of pistol firing. all this can be improved if you have a very good receiver that can balance and calibrate your speakers to make up for the holes in the weaker spectrum. but you can put a lip stick on a pig.. it'll still be a pig. i paired up this JBL voice center speaker with two floor standing JBL Venue Stadium for front left and right, and two JBL Balcony speakers for surround, and a JBL Sub 10. i use a Pioneer VSX 1121K, which does a good job of balancing the speakers and masking the weaker low end spectrum of the JBL Voice. but at the end of the day... in certain situations you still notice the weak hole below 110hz. but consider the price i got it for...roughly hundred fifty bucks a few years ago... it's really not too bad. i do plan on upgrading in the future to a fuller center channel speaker covering fuller spectrum and wooded outter casing.

I bought this player to replace a very old DVD player, have the ability to play BlueRay discs, and to replace the ability to play videos via internet services that I had via my Roku.  I've yet to play a disc on it, but have played around with the internet connectivity, so I'll just speak to that from now.  First off, a note - it does not come with an HDMI cable, so that needs to be purchased separately.  Since you can buy one of these for $3 or $4, it's not a big deal, but I find it really annoying that in order to make the price a couple dollars cheaper Sony has decided not to include this, thus causing me an extra trip to the store or online order and wait.Regarding the online services, there are a decent amount of them, but not as many as Roku offers, especially considering Roku's library of 3rd party channels that you can load.  However, the main ones I use were there, including Amazon, Netflix, and Pandora.  The only big one that isn't available is TED. Unlike the Roku, though, Sony offers YouTube.  This seems to be offered by about every such connected BlueRay player and Smart TV, so Roku really needs to find a way to offer this again because it is a major omission.In addition, the various offerings are spread into different areas of the interface, including Videos, Music, and Network.  So there's a lot of navigating around.  The user interface is just not very intuitive, then again, the Roku isn't the best either, but Sony's is much worse.  Why these companies can't figure out that people want quick and easy access to the services they use most of the time, I don't know.  There needs to be some kind of "favorites" function that lets users quickly browse the 5-10 different "channels" or whatever you want to call them, but instead you need to go through a long list of them to find the one you're looking for.  About the only shortcut that Sony provides is a Netflix button on the remote.  This is helpful, but only for watching Netflix.Sony's website for signing up and managing content is simple, but again, could use some user interface work.  Streaming things so far worked very well through the player, better than the Roku in my initial testing.  The only issue other than the interface issues I mention above are that it can take a while to load a new "channel"  - we're talking anywhere from a few seconds to 10 or 15 seconds.  Really way too long in my opinion.

I purchased this device out of curiosity regarding the quality of Philips products. I have a lot of ownership with other MP3 players, largely with the Creative Labs Zen product line, which in many ways should be comparable to this product. In some ways, this GoGear product is superior, but it falls short in so many areas that I would seriously urge you to consider purchasing a Zen or Sansa player.The most major issue with this product is its firmware. Its about as stable as a house of cards. The more stuff you put on it, the less stable it becomes and really needs little or no help in crashing (this is with the current, fully upgraded firmware). Its really remarkable how you can't scroll through the albums without it crashing nearly ever time. There are other random things that it does that defy logic. My GoGear has inexplicably booted up in Chinese. Turn it off and turn it on and its back in English. This is stuff that shouldn't happen to products that are released.Now, provided the item actually works correctly, its interface is a little strange. Its not necessarily bad, but its definitely quite a bit different than I am used to with a Zen. One nice thing that this has over a lot of the newer touch-screens is a physical volume control. The power switch operates as a lock command, and then the player can be unlocked by pressing either the power button again or the home button on the front and sliding the little lock up the screen. It is probably worth mentioning that this locking feature is pretty much the only way you're going to get a significant amount of play-time out of your player.I will take a little aside to speak about battery life. I don't think the 22 hours listed is very realistic. My estimates (though I haven't actually run it down to zero) would put it more in the 12-15 hour range. I don't think you'd be able to watch a full movie on this, "5 hour" battery life. This rather inflated estimation, mind you, is pretty common for all manufacturers. It is, never-the-less, unrealistic what they're advertising.Returning to navigation/user-interface, the manner in which you select albums is pretty strange. There are three columns that appear and you can scroll through them all. They are alphabetized by artist, then by album within the artist, and finally by song. This will drive you insane if you want to listen to an album in order, unless the song titles happen to be in alphabetical order. The album will play, and then whatever the next album is will play. This can lead to some rather bizarre transitions when you go from Mendelssohn to Metallica. This is unlike pretty much any MP3 player I've owned where you can ask it to stop at the end of an album or repeat the album. Basically, this player wants to organize your songs into a rather random list and just keep trucking through the whole thing.One thing you will like about this product is that it has a very responsive touch screen. It may be a little too sensitive as it will pick up brushes from clothing as input, so if you're going to put it in your pocket, its best to lock it first. The color screen is vibrant and responsive and definitely on-par with other items in its category (recognizable/affordable off-brand MP3 players). I would probably enjoy this touch screen if it was on another model.Another interesting positive, this has an SD card and an HDMI out attachment. Pros1. It protects the Surface Pro pretty well.2. It is cheap.Cons1. Covers the air vent which increases temperature of laptop.2. Adds a lot of bulk.3. It is difficult to charge the laptop.4. The kickstand cannot be used all the way back.I purchased this case 1 week after purchasing my Surface Pro 2. I had purchased similar types of covers for my tablet before and I thought this one was going to do the job of protecting my laptop. If you are simply looking for protection this case does the job but it comes with a LOT of inconveniences that is simply not worth it. I am going to go over the details below.Pros (continuation)1. First let's start with the obvious. Does it protect the Surface Pro? Yes it does. It is well padded on the outside and the computer should be able to withstand most drops when it has the cover on. On the inside it has a thin layer that protects the bezels around the screen. The layer is thin and flimsy but should protect it against any scratches around that area. The case comes with a strap on the back that lets you wrap it around the laptop and you can keep it close in case you want to carry it around. It is a little more challenging to do it when you have the Type Cover on though. If you notice the picture on the product description show the device closed with the case but that is without any of the keyboard covers.2. As far as price is concerned, this is really as low as it gets. I bought the case for $15 dollars here on Amazon. It is much very affordable. It cost less than half of some of the premium cases you see here on Amazon.Cons (continuation)1. Perhaps the biggest problem I had with this case and the reason why I did not use it for more than a couple of days is the fact that it covers the air vent around the laptop. It is beyond me why they decided to do this. When you have the case on you will not feel how warm the laptop gets. However, I installed a program that measures the temperature of the CPU and the motherboard and the temperature increased significantly within a few minutes of light use. This causes the fans inside to be constantly working and consumes a lot of battery. On top of that it will probably cause long term damage to the components on the inside.2. The Surface Pro 2 by itself is very heavy and bulky. With this case on it doesn't feel like a tablet at all. The case adds about an extra pound of weight on top of the roughly 2 pounds that the laptop weights. Very uncomfortable if you are looking to use the computer anywhere else but on a table or your lap.3. As other people here have mentioned the hole that is placed around the charging port is not ideal. It is too small. You have to play around with it until it finally manages to connect. Very annoying when you have do that every single day. Not to mention it might damage the charging port on the long run.4. One of the major improvements that Microsoft Surface Pro 2 has over the original is that the kickstand has two positions. The Surface Pro 2 kickstand has a wider angle that lets you use it in your lap much more comfortably. Unfortunately, this case covers the stand and instead you have to use the lid of the case as a makeshift stand. It opens at the same angle of the original Surface Pro. This makes it very unstable to use on your lap.In conclusion I was very disappointed with this case. You get what you pay for. As far as protection goes it does its job relatively well. Unfortunately the case has a lot of design problems that hinder the user experience and could potentially damage the laptop on the long run. My biggest caution against purchasing this case is the fact that it covers the air vent.  If you are looking to travel of lot with the laptop to school or work I would recommend the Snugg protective case. You can take the laptop in and out whenever you want and use it like it was intended. Unless you are clumsy with the computer and you feel like you need an ALWAYS ON cover in case you drop it then I would recommend you skip this cover all together. Forget about how cheap it is, there are better alternatives out there.
