I've always been intrigued with the idea of cooling devices for portable PCs, although this one seems to be a kind of external (and independent) heat sink as opposed to the very simplistic stuff that was (and probably still is) available when I bought my first PowerBook MANY years ago. I tend to keep my MacBook Pro on, of all things, a plastic milk crate--I like sitting on the floor and it provides excellent circulation. However, this isn't always practical and I do worry about heat buildup on the rare occasion my Pro leaves home with me.The Belkin CoolSpot Laptop Cooler is of extremely simple design: it's a one-piece (mine's black), angled unit made of what seems to be rugged (but lightweight) plastic with grips applied to keep both the unit itself and the laptop in place. It has a built-in cable with a USB connector to power its fan. The fan is novel to me; the last time laptop coolers penetrated my consciousness (admittedly a long time ago), they didn't have fans and merely helped increase circulation. The fan is a great idea--it's non-electric and runs even if your laptop is utilizing battery power, although I imagine it would have an effect on the charge. And best of all, it does an excellent job of doing what it's supposed to do--keeping your laptop cool.Because my Pro (which cost me an arm and a leg, even as a refurb) is in a protective shell, I tend to be a bit more concerned about heat than I usually am. Not to worry with the CoolSpot--heat is quietly sucked away and dissipated with no muss or fuss. It's light enough to actually use on your lap without any discomfort and easily tucks away into a laptop bag. The CoolSpot is a very simple device, hence there's no need to belabor its very simple virtues, those being that it unobtrusively and effectively keeps your laptop cool at a fair price. Made in Taiwan which is certainly a step up from "Made in China," although one wonders why we can't make it here. VERY highly recommended.

If you have a lot of movies, photos, music and files you want to share across multiple computers, you can do a couple of things: build/buy a server, get an external hard drive you can physically move from one computer to the next, use a web-service like Dropbox, or get a network attached storage (NAS) device like the Seagate Central.  Any of these potentially work with pros and cons.  However, after this review, I'm sure you'll probably want to do either the server or portable hard drive.UNBOXING: The Seagate Central (SC) 2TB comes in a shrink-wrapped box about the size of a cereal box.  Nothing special about it.  And the interior has the packing material, the SC and an Ethernet cable.  The SC is about the size of 2 3.5" hard drives laying next to each other.REVIEW: The SC itself kind of looks like portable speaker due to it's metal grill covering the top and sides.  It has a space cutout of the back that's for the power plug, an Ethernet cable and a USB port.  Although none of the (downloaded) instructions or box instructions say whether it's a 2.0 or 3.0, the port is not "blue" so I assume it's a 2.0.I plugged it into the wall and my Airport Extreme router.  When plugging it in and turning it on for the first time, the initial set up was very simple--just follow the GUI screens and you're done.  My SC required a firmware update.  Not too difficult, but I've seen a lot of reviews say this didn't work.  Then you're required to set it up via the GUI--it offers both a Mac and a PC version of the set up process.  You are given 6 choices of what to do with your data: copy, back-up, archive, connect devices, download Seagate software, and share files.  The SC GUI has the following tabs when you're modifying the box or your content: home, users, social, services, settings.Through services tab, you can synchronize your iTunes library and any movies with DLNA.  You can also do remote access through your devices using iOS.  My iPod touch works with the Seagate app, but REALLY slowly.  The app is really basic too.  The social tab allows for connection/backup of Facebook stuff.  I don't really use Facebook, so not really much of a selling point for me.  I couldn't find an applicable app for my Visio smart tv, so that's one thing I can't use with the SC.  Oh yeah, there's no support for torrent downloads.  You can access the SC via web browser (using the user and password from the setup), but you can only transfer one file at a time (how is this useful?).Everything sounds good so far, but here're the catches.  Transfer speeds are SLOW!  Not really sure what Seagate was thinking when it released this, but on my wired and wireless-n network, I'm getting between 2MB/s and 10MB/s transfer rates, AND everything else on the network seems to slow down when transferring files.  Also, there is no modular transfer of files.  If it doesn't work the first time, then you'll have to start over.  This gets extremely frustrating when trying to transfer large files.OVERALL: So this might be an easier evaluation if you looked at pros and cons, so here goes:Pros:- Inexpensive- Simple setup- Small form factor- Compatible with Mac and PC- iTunes and Time Machine work with it- Works to back up Facebook- iOS works so far through iPod TouchCons:- SLOW transfer speeds- No torrent support- Web access limited to file by file transfer- No support for my Visio smart tv- If transfers don't work the first time, you have to start all over- Substandard instructions (manual needs to be downloaded, and isn't very thorough)- Unless you know how to use a NAS, the GUI isn't that great (too basic)- No RAID backup--if you lose your SC, everything is gone!- Sometimes the NAS doesn't show up on my PC or MacIf you don't care about transfer speed and glitch software, go ahead and get it.  It is priced for the average consumer.  Two stars for the effort, but I don't recommend the SC 2TB NAS.

Unfortunately this equivalent of the double-chime appears to be a bit flakey (like my wife in the navigator's seat), more than a few times on a trip I experienced the unit telling me to turn HERE after I'm well into the intersection. That would have been disastrous on my coast to coast road trip. This issue erases two stars. I want to keep my eyes on the road not staring at the map all the time.Another issue is much reduced street name readability of the map compared to the Lincoln nav on a similar screen size but I appreciate why this exists. The Garmin map attempts to provide a more realistic experience. So the red moving triangle on the Lincoln nav is replaced by an icon that looks like a car. The pencil thin lines on the Lincoln nav are replaced by wider "streets" that the "car" is driving along in the map and then add the 3D. The problem is that the Garmin map is much less readable for street names than my Lincoln nav. This is somewhat compensated for in the Garmin with the updated upcoming street name at the top of the screen but I prefer seeing the street names on the map above those pencil thin street lines like a scrolling list.Overall I like using the Garmin while I feel it doesn't quite stand up to my "aging" nav in the Lincoln it will do the job I need adequately because in the Taurus I'll be mostly driving through familiar territory. The feature set is great, the voice commands work great, easy to use. I found accessing the features in the nav to be pretty intuitive. The lifetime maps and traffic is a big plus.Update:I exchanged this for a 2797. The 7" screen size make a huge difference for readability.

If you are like me then you are looking for truly natural products for your body (and to put in your body, in the case of food and drink). Suave is known for being a low cost option and if they have a real natural product then you've got the ingredients for a top notch, budget natural product. But the question is: is this really a "natural" product? The answer is found in how you define "is" and "natural". (Thanks, Bill Clinton ;)There are no parabens (preservatives) in the ingredient list, which is great news as they've been linked to all kinds of nasty stuff including cancer. But there are sulfates (foaming agents), in the form of Ammonium Laureth Sulfate, which also has been linked to cancer. So is this really a natural product? Or this a marketing gimmick? (Notice that the product NAME not the product DESCRIPTION is "natural.") There are also other chemicals in the ingredient list as well.Since all these ingredients exist in the physical, or natural, world I guess you could call a shampoo or conditioner that has only physical things in it as "natural." But if you are looking for non-man-made-chemical "natural" then this product does NOT meet that definition. So it isn't really what it's saying it is.Why three stars then? Because for the price and because it is a product without most of the bad stuff, this is a good deal. All organic shampoos are crazy expensive. So products that have mostly good stuff for an affordable price is better than going with full chemical stuff. So a good step in the right direction, but not quite there.Finally, as to the product itself: it worked up a lather well (thanks cancer promoting sulfates!) and cleaned out well without residue. It smells very strongly fragrant in the shower but loses the strong scent after a few minutes. The scent doesn't smell like rain or forrest, but does have what we would consider a soapy or clean smell.

I bought and returned this unit from a different retailer.  I didn't spend a lot of time with it, but my thoughts might still be useful.The deal breakers for me were the following: This unit doesn't remember your current position in a show when switch to a different show, or when you turn the unit off.  To use this, I would literally have to write down where in a show I was before I stopped watching, and then fast forward through the show to get to the same spot.  Also, I wanted to be able to watch the shows I recorded on PC.  It turns out DVD-RAM is VERY incompatible with most drives.  None of my DVD-ROM or DVD-RW drives in any of my computers were able to read the discs, which for me was important.  (I wanted to be able to watch shows in different locations).Other negative stuff:This unit, like a VCR, doesn't record a scheduled show unless it's turned off.  That makes no sense, because the unit is capable of recording a show while it plays back.  Sony's DVD recorders, for example, don't force you to turn the unit off before it records.On that note-the image of the show being played back seems to "jump" forward-sort of like it has a bad frame rate, if a show is being recorded at the same time.  That said, the feature is at least sort of useable.I wasn't thrilled with the image quality.  I think it's possibly better than Tivo, but the colors to me looked a little washed out-not bad though.This unit, like all stand alone DVD recorders, doesn't really have that much recording time.  To get good quality you have to increase the quality setting, which drastically reduces the amount of recording time you have.  I discovered that on some days I wouldn't really have enough recording time on a DVD-RAM disc to grab all the shows I want at the quality settings I want.Also, I don't like the unit's interface.  I've used Tivo, which is of course much, much easier to use, but I even preferred the Sony VCR this was supposed to replace.  Brining up menus feels slow, the directional buttons aren't very responsive, and menus to me don't feel very intuitive.This probably sounds pretty negative, but aside from the top two points, this seems like a pretty nice unit (and Amazon's price is certainly good).  The unit allows you to set 16 shows to be recorded, and the interface for that is pretty solid.  (My old VCR only let you set it for 8 shows, which isn't enough for me).  You can also give shows you record a name-like if you record "Lost" every week, you can give it that name, so that it shows up by name in the list of shows on your DVD-RAM disc.  Entering names is a pain, but worth it for repeating shows.  The menu screen for selecting recorded shows is sort of neat-in addition to the time, station, (and optionally the name), it displays a video clip of the beginning of currently selected recording.  The response time for the menu is a little sluggish though.The unit seems solidly built, and is fairly quiet when in operation (and dead silent when you switch it off-unlike Tivo).It doesn't meet my needs, but it's worth considering!

Galco states that this holster fits the Beretta Tomcat Model 3032.  It does NOT fit the current models without modifications.  Beretta started making the slide on their Tomcats wider and heaver due to the light slide impacting the frame hard enough to cause frame cracks on some guns.  This change happened some years ago and makes the gun slide about 1/4" to 3/8" wider than the mouth of the holster, which is held in shape by an embedded wire.  The current Tomcats simply will not go into this holster.  However I found that the wire was bendable and with a couple adjustable wrenches I re-molded the wire so it fit perfectly.This is a well made and very durable pocket holster.  It should last as long as you do.This leather pocket holster is NOT molded to the firearm like a good belt holster, however there is a simply way to do this and I HIGHLY recommend you do this for easy draw.  Remember that this holster is not anchored to anything and must just fall off the gun when drawn.  This is NOT recommended by most manufacturers, but I have found no harm and great benefit.1) Oil exterior of pistol/revolver well.  Not so it is wet, just wipe with an oiled cloth or well treated gun preserving cloth.2) Wrap pistol/revolver loosely in two layers or cling wrap (saran) with the openings behind the grip.  There needs to be no openings from the muzzle to the back of the gun.  It needs to be waterproof.3) Soak leather holster briefly up to about 1/2 inch below the molded wire inside the mouth of the holster, in very warm water until it has turned dark all over below the mouth and feels more flexible.  The molded wire is likely mild steel and could rust inside the holster.  Keeping this portion of the holster dry helps avoid this.4) Hold a plastic stick pen (BIC or such) along the top of the barrel and gently force the pistol/revolver fully into the holster using your fingers to work the holster around the contours of the weapon.  BE CAREFUL NOT TO TEAR THE CLING WRAP!  The addition of the pen compensates for the shrinkage which will occur after removing the gun and makes sure that when finished the holster will fall off the gun if held muzzle down.5) Let it sit until the leather no longer looks or feels wet.  About 8 - 10 hours at room temperature.  You are now ready with a perfect fit and draw.

I had a 110 inch Carada at my old house - a great screen, great company - but when it came time to put a screen in my new house I decided to take a chance, save some bucks (hey, new houses are expensive) and try this Elite based on reviews here and over at AVSForum. I'm pretty darn pleased with the end result; using the same projector (currently an Epson 8350) this screen looks just as good as my 1.4 gain Carada did, at about a third of the price (and cheaper shipping too). If you are looking for a quality screen that will help your PJ deliver an excellent picture then this Elite does the job.I was also impressed with how this screen was packed for shipping. Somewhere in China, a young MBA sat down at the factory that makes and packs this thing and explained in great detail how spending X in up front packing costs would reduce Y in later damage claims. This advice (I assume) was taken to heart because this thing is packed like it is being sent off to war. Prodigious amounts of foam, straps, and hard plastic tubes you could ship an artillery shell in are all present. Should young Jimmy, pulling a second shift down at the docks, have one too many and confuse the left pedal of his forklift with the right, thus driving the blades directly in to the box this screen ships in, I would place better than even odds that it would survive to be hung on someone's wall. That's how well it was packed.Now for the caveats:First, having come from the Carada, I didn't realized how spoiled I was when it comes to installation - the Carada's frame is 4 pieces, machined to the nth degree so they fit together easily and perfectly, while the screen itself is secured via many easy to use snaps. If you have a screwdriver handy and any skill at turning it you'll have that screen assembled and ready to go in 10 minutes.That is not the case with the Elite. Hey, you get what you pay for, and you should only have to assemble it once, right? Just be aware that it's going to take some time, patience (supplanted with beer) and a prodigious amount of swearing to get the job done. One of the reasons this screen is so cheap (and cheap to ship, packing notwithstanding) is because the top and bottom frame pieces are shipped in two parts. In addition to having to assemble this bit (which is easy to do, but hard to master, because you have to be very careful about lining the pieces up right and screwing the bracket in the correct order) it leaves a small but noticeable seam in the top and bottom part of the screen. It's not easy to see (you won't see it sitting down) but it's there if you look. If you are the kind of person bothered by this - you know who you are - then look elsewhere.The parts are also not machined particularly well, in fact several of the screw holes in mine still had the aluminum cutouts in them, requiring a screwdriver to punch out/remove. I had a fun time getting all the corner pieces inserted correctly, and then lined up so the frame fit together at right angles. Swearing, beer, and a rubber mallet got the job done in the end.One of many things to watch out for - the "black velvet" look of the frame, which does look very good by the way, is some kind of spray-on felt deal, which attracts pet hair like you wouldn't believe. If you have pets, and you are installing this on a carpeted floor, vacuum first, and vacuum well.Finally, the screen itself is installed via some plastic tubes you stick around the edges, which are then inserted in to a groove in the frame, which are then held in place by little plastic tabs - about a million of them, if I counted right (the beer might have skewed this total). Add to this the fact that the screen needs to stretch, so by default it is smaller than the inside area of the frame at first, and you are in for a fun afternoon. All I can say is follow the directions on tab order *exactly* and it'll get done.The good news is, once I had it all up and going, it looked good, the screen itself was tensioned right - no creases, sags, or folds to be seen - and it ended up looking good on my wall, doing a solid job of reflecting the picture my PJ was blasting it with back to my eyeballs.You can get a better machined screen that looks just as good if not better, but for a far higher price. If you are looking for a budget screen this one does the job - just have a six pack handy, and maybe a buddy, for the install.

I bought the Netgear DGND3300 in April 2010.  For much of the last year, it worked decently.  I have both 802.11g and 802.11n devices so that the dual band broadcast was a welcome feature.  Combining it with an DSL modem seemed like a great way to reduce space on my desk (i.e., one device yet three separate functions).  The 'n' broadcast wasn't much faster than the 'g' primarily because my ISP (AT&T) only provides 5 Mbs in our neighborhood.  Still, it seemed like a good idea.  However, problems started to develop after about 6 months.  The combo started dropping signals and the frequency of this slowly increased.  At first, I thought it was AT&T's fault since their signal generally weakens in the evenings.  But, I realized eventually that it was the DSL part of the combo.  Over the last six weeks, it became completely erratic.  Finally, last week the DSL feed completely stopped with nothing showing but a solid red light all the time.  The rest of the router functions continued to work.  After running some tests, I realized that the ADSL feed was finished. My first thought was to call Netgear customer service.  But, after reading some of the experiences that other purchasers had with their service, I decided to just scrap the router and buy another non-Netgear ADSL/router combo.  It was close to the one year date for the parts warranty anyway and I really didn't want to waste my time arguing with the Netgear service staff in order to just get another Netgear router combo.  This is the second buggy Netgear product that I've owned and frankly it will be a long time before I buy another of theirs.  There are very few combo DSL/dual band routers on the market, which suggests to me that the technology has not yet been perfected.  It was a good idea, but...  Instead, I bought an Actiontec ADSL/'g' combo and it's been completely stable since I got it on Monday.

I purchased these speakers to use in a stereo setup in my living room, these speakers were meant to replacePolk Audio TSi100 Bookshelf Speakers. I've had the Polk speakers for a few years now and they are an absolute value for money. Very nice and full midrange with good extension into the highs. They don't have the kind of air in the high frequency range that you will experience with higher quality speakers, but the listening experience from them is very non-fatiguing. My main reason for upgrade was to get speakers with good bass extension so that I could do without my subwoofer.The SM55 speakers are pretty big and heavy, but still suitably sized for bookshelf placement or placement on speaker stands and they won't be too imposing. I actually like their design choice of a bass radiator as opposed to a port, this does make a huge difference in sound, especially mid-bass and bass. The fit and finish are good, but not excellent. I could actually see some glue remnants on the bass radiator on the top, doesn't say much about the finish. Also, with the grill off, the speaker with the mushroom head looks really odd, so from an aesthetic point of view, I wouldn't rate these speakers very highly.Coming to the sound, the biggest selling point of these speakers definitely is the bass and yes, it's unbelievably good for its size. But the fact that the bass radiator which produces most of the bass is on top of the speakers produces issues with speaker placement. You definitely need sufficient clearance around the speaker to let it perform at it's full potential. Another advantage of the bass radiator seems to be that the bass is still good at lower volumes as well, which is a big plus. However, the one aspect that bothered me most was the midrange and high frequency sound. These speakers sounded a little too bright, even when compared to my Polk speakers which I consider bright as well. The treble seemed a little too tizzy and lacked detail at times. Female voices sounded a touch hollow and not as full as I'd have expected. I listened to some Norah Jones & Sade and neither sounded right on these speakers.Eventually, after a week of listening, I decided to return these speakers as they just didn't work well for me. It's probably a matter of taste, but if you're someone that prefers warmer sounding speakers with full bodied midrange and vocals, you may find these speakers a little lacking. However, if you listen to any kind of music which requires a good amount of emphasis on bass, these speakers would be great.

I have NOTHING against the seller; my item was shipped as described and perfectly on time so 5/5 no complaints there. Thank you!Now, the G400 is basically a watered down version of the G500. While being about $10 cheaper it lacks the macro functionality of the G500 as well as the shiny buttons which was primarily why I chose to go with the G400 instead; it was more bang for my buck and in line with what I wanted. I didn't need macro capability. So 4.5/5 for value right there.Month 1: The G400 was a little heavier than my old mouse that came with my gaming computer, so that took a little getting used to but no big deal. It actually helped strengthen my wrists a bit. I noticed that response time was super fast and super accurate; although it is optical and may be a bit less precise than a laser mouse, I find laser mice actually unnecessarily precise for my liking; they tend to pick up the most subtle jitters or random things. Also many laser mice have lift-off issues which the G400 clearly did not. The G400's buttons were easy enough so that I could click very rapidly, but solid enough that they would rebound reliably. This was what I wanted in a mouse since I am primarily a first-person shooter gamer (CS:S, BF3, MW3, Black Ops, AVA, Crysis and Far Cry to name a few). Had absolutely no problems with the mouse.Month 3: Mouse acted a little weird - felt sluggish at times. Then one day all of a sudden it just disconnected for no reason. After 3 seconds of me sitting on my computer just a little confused while watching the chaos around me and moving around with WASD keys pointing in one direction because I can't look around or shoot, the G400 reconnected with an audible 2-tone beeping sound. My DPI setting had been reset so I needed to adjust my DPI again. I thought to myself "Oh this is no big deal... must be some sort of rare happenstance. Probably won't happen again. A $40 mouse can't go wrong..."Boy, was I wrong...Month 4: Mouse started acting up. Disconnects and reconnects literally EVERY SINGLE DAY for the first week, then it disconnects and reconnects LITERALLY EVERY OTHER HOUR FOR THE NEXT WEEK. I am currently in week 2 and this is disgustingly annoying. It happens with such amazing frequency that I was playing one of my games and within a span of only 3 MINUTES it had disconnected and reconnected on me 3 TIMES. My $9 mouse from Staples has never done this in its 2 year lifespan. I had never abused or tried to break the G400; it just started acting up on me like this for no reason. I researched online*brief pause and a message of warning: BEFORE BUYING A PRODUCT, KNOW NOT JUST WHAT ITS STRENGTHS ARE BUT ALSO WHAT PEOPLE ARE COMPLAINING ABOUT!*and found out that the G400 has VERY COMMON DISCONNECTING ISSUES and this isn't software related so you can't fix it. Probably due to a high lemon rate or something. I filed a warranty claim and Logitech should be responding back soon. As a serious gamer this is completely unacceptable. A $40 mouse disconnecting and reconnecting about 5 times a day only 4 months into its usage is the most absurd thing I've heard. I'll emphasize this again: my $9 mouse from STAPLES has lasted longer and STILL hasn't DC'ed on me or anything to this date.It's a good thing Logitech has great customer support. The seller was awesome too. Just buy a different product from them with fewer lemon rates; I do not recommend this product. You'll only be wasting your money. I wish they made the wiring more secure or the cords a bit thicker or something so that this issue wouldn't happen so frequently. Right now I'm using my Staples mouse in lieu of the G400 even for gaming. If it weren't for Logitech's awesome service I would have felt cheated out of my money. On the bright side, my G400 makes a pretty nice wallhanger.EDIT***: Logitech shipped me a new G400 in 3 days flat. I am very satisfied with their customer service. I'd recommend either just sticking with a sub-$20 mouse or spend even more money and get a $50 non-watered down mouse.

Optoma BG-ZD101 DLP link 3D glasses works fine with Mitsubishi WD-73838 DLP TV which has built-in DLP Link with updated software so my TV doesn't require the extra adaptor box.  That saves me money and less trouble.  Thank you Mitsubishi!!!  Just make sure you go to TV setup to choose 3D setting to "automatic", "reverse", and "DLP Link".  If you use Playstation 3 to play blu-ray movies like me, just make sure you go to Video settings and let your playstation 3 to detect your TV is capable to show 3D contents (make sure you set Mit TV 3D setting I mentioned above first) so PS3 can be set to load 3D content to the TV otherwise the PS3 doesn't know your TV has 3D capacity and will not play movies/games in 3D.The 3D image through the glasses is impressive and comparable to Imax 3D in the theatre.  I didn't notice any flickering problem at all (and I am a very detailed person).  I didn't notice any eye strain or headache or dizziness with the use of this glasses but different person may experience differently.  I also didn't notice any contrast or lighting fluctuation.  I was hesitating to get into blu-ray 3D movies or 3D games at first like other people but I am glad that I tried and I love it but I do not recommend to use these type of glasses for a prolonged period of time (e.g. more than 3 hours) and do not let your young kids to use them as there's a possible or unknown side effects to the eyes.At the beginning, I didn't change the TV 3D setting from "standard" to "reverse" and I didn't notice any 3D effects and I was disappointed and I was thinking about returning the glasses to Amazon.  But then I remember I read a review before mentioned about changing the Mitsubishi TV 3D setting to "reverse" and I gave it a try again and changed that TV setting and a 3 dimensional magic happened....wonderful 3D image in front of my eye.  I was playing the "Open Season" 3D blu-ray movie and it's amazing.  I will try the Resident Evil 3D blu-ray a little later and I can't wait as I heard very good thing about this movie's 3D effects.  I will also try to play GT5 on PS3 in 3D tomorrow.Yes, the glasses are big and bulky but I found them comfortable considering I put this Optoma glasses over my eyeglasses. I don't feel strange or uncomfortable with this glasses over my eyeglasses.Don't get the Xpand X103 glasses as they are not for DLP link 3D and they are only for use with 3D adaptor with IR transmission.UPDATE.  the 3D effects on Resident Evil: Afterlife is not as good as I expected may be because I watched "Open Season" 3D first.  "Open Season" has far better 3D effects.  May be I shouldn't compare an animated 3D movie to a filmed 3D movie.

Would you trust an 'abs' trainer if it came from someone who calls himself John Abdo? Well... the John Abdo I saw in the training videos appears to be a nice person, not over-ripped and his exercise routines are probably the only ones where you end up sweating while sitting on a chair. But, let's talk about the Ab-doer and its worth.ASSEMBLY, BUILT QUALITY (4 out of 5)Assembly wasn't over difficult. There is one bolt/nut pair that needs tightening and, I believe 5 pins. I wish the instructions were more clear and the parts were labelled but I ended up with a fully assembled Ab-doer in a little less than 30 minutes. With better instructions/labeling it should have taken half that long.The end-product is a pretty good looking little apparatus if 'orange' doesn't clash with the surrounding. The Ab-doer is well built, all parts fit and it appears to be durable.WHAT YOU GET AND WHAT YOU ARE NICKEL AND DIMED FOR (2 out of 5)The Amazon product description appears to be a little out of date. You do NOT get 4 DVDs and 3 manuals. The DVDs were consolidated into one single disc that has the intro and the 3 workouts as separate chapters and the manual booklet has everything in one place: assembly instructions, diet plan, mini cookbook, illustrations for the various motions, warranty statement and so forth in English, French and Spanish.All nice and good but the problems is what you DON'T get. For what we are paying, I don't understand why the 'extreme' exercise routine on DVD, the Power Resistance Kit (a bunch of bungees), the resistance rods (yes, 3 metal rods) and the tri-roller (a set of THREE rollers to replace the one that comes standard) need to be purchased separately at significant additional costs.The one-year warranty promises to replace defective parts unless the unit broke because unsupervised children under 18 used it or it was abused, modified or used for commercial purposes. Nothing broke so far so I can't tell how good they are at honoring it.USING THE AB-DOER, WHAT TO EXPECT (4 out of 5)This is a product that's best used in front on the TV, at least for the first couple dozen sessions. And you won't be watching the news. Each session - and it can be 'beginner', 'intermediate' or 'advanced' is fully covered by Mr. Abdo and team, from warm up, the core workout and the post-workout stretching. The workouts are quite fun and all they require is a little movement coordination. Practice makes better and, while following the team on your TV screen, you can control the intensity of your workout. Absent the optional resistance rods, you can still control the seat's swivel resistance via a dedicated knob.The one problem with the apparatus is its weight. It needs to be heavy and stable because you are going to lean back and do vigorous twists. That makes it not easy to move around and, since you may want to have it someplace in front of a TV - in most cases the living room - you may have to move it frequently. The Ab-doer is NOT easy to move.I can't say how effective these exercises are because I've only used the Ab-doer for a couple of weeks. You will probably burn more calories on a treadmill but you do get a much better abs workout with the 'doer' and you get it while sitting on a chair. Not bad.MY RATINGI am going to rate this a 3-star which means "It's okay". It's not a 5-star mainly because of the 'extras' that you learn you may need only after you buy what turns out to be the 'basic' configuration. Some buyers, and I'm one, may consider this version of the Ab-doer to be 'incomplete'. Other than that, even with the basic machine the workouts are fun for as long as you have sufficient space in front of your TV and you don't mind moving a heavy chair-like object around.I bought mine for about half the list price at a lightning deal and, for what I paid, this was a good buy.-->> Brush your teeth, it's the law! <<

I purchased the AXX200 at the CES show when it was supposed to be on a "show special" sale for $150.  Turns out the "sale" wasn't so special (same price here at Amazon).  I also have a hard time believing they'll ever get "list" price ($299) for this speaker.  Today on the Creative Web site, I see they're now trying to say the speaker is worth $375, but you can get it with the "dock worth $75" for $229 for a "launch special" (the dock is $60 here on Amazon, making your total $210).Unpacking my speaker was fun.  And it's a bit of a strange design.  But, that leaves the footprint small, and that's a good thing!  First I had to charge my speaker (there was some charge upon arrival but I wanted to get a full charge.)  Thankfully, it uses the now-standard micro USB cords that I already have many of for my phone, and other electronics (and comes with it's own charger, of course.)Bluetooth pairing with my devices was relatively straight-forward.  A handy sticker near the back reviews how to do that.  It's a good thing the sticker is in place, because, honestly, this thing is kind of a bit more difficult to use than I would hope.  Press the same button once to turn on the speaker, press it for 2 seconds to get into pairing mode, press for 5 seconds to turn off.  I mean, there's already a lot of buttons and stuff on this speaker, but they might've added a couple more. or a slider to make it easy to turn off an on, and put in pairing mode.  With my Samsung Galaxy S3 phone, I was able to get it to pair via the NFC feature okay.There are 6 "buttons" on top of the unit, along with a "slider" for volume control.  All of these buttons are just touch enabled, as is the slider.  A BRIGHT blue light on the front top shows what mode the Bluetooth stuff is in, with 3 tiny lights on the bottom showing available power left in the rechargeable battery.If you turn the unit on, even with nothing paired, it does seem to put out an awful lot of noise when held up to the ear.  Sounds almost like a fan running in there!This thing is pretty small.  Think the size of a large sunglasses case!  And a sturdy case, at that.  The front grill and back are made of a nice feeling metal.  It feels of quality.  But the size appears to also be a downfall.  As a person who listens to dance music alot, bass is important.  And this speaker produces VERY little.  Every streaming station or dance tune I played sounded distorted and harsh at louder levels.  The audio quality of a Bose SoundLink speaker, while a bit larger, FAR exceeds the sound quality of the AXX 200, and manages to give decent bass, even at high levels, and in a small package.The call recording feature seems to work fine, but it's confusing to tell whether the speaker is actually recording or not, so don't get a criminal to confess without having a backup plan.  In fact, telling what the speaker is doing is kind of the hard part all of the way around.  I've made a recording.  Now do I push "play", or the "record play" button?  What is now playing?  What mode is the speaker in?  Without the manual for regular reference, or unless using the features regularly, they're not at all intuitive.  An addition or two to the top display could've solved this.Also, "it's an MP3" player.  Yes, indeed.  NOT AVI, NOT M4A, NOT WAV.  Pretty much anything of this price range should play all of the major popular formats.  So, dragging tunes from iTunes to an microSD card will not work, unless they're MP3 (or WMA, but iTunes doesn't play those anyway.)  Don't assume they just left out the other formats in the description.  They simply don't work.The "teleconferencing" feature, otherwise known as a "speakerphone" does seem to work okay, but I have not used it in a large group to get sounds from around a room.The megaphone feature is a bit silly, but does seem to work, and some effects can make your voice sound strange.The software apps for iOS and Android seem to largely mimic the controls on the speaker itself, and while they do allow changing of the sound profile, and few other tweaks, they seem mostly unneeded.  On iOS, there is actually 3 apps, that all seem to have a crossover of features, or could have been easily rolled into one.  And really?  Do I need a "remote control" app function for a speaker with I wouldn't ever get more than 50 feet away from for it to be of use?The Creative Web site also alludes to Sound BlasterAxx Bonus Pack for PCs software, but it's not in the box (or on a simple microSD card they should have included to get you started), nor available for Mac, and further, is only a 30-day trial.  You have to download this from the Web site, where you can also get a free control panel software for your PC or Mac.  The installation of the software on a Mac actually requires a reboot.  Really?One of the features I LIKE is the ability to connect 2 BlueTooth devices at once...  So, keep your phone, and your computer connected, or iPad, or whatever.  As long as audio isn't actively playing from one, it can play from the other.  (You can't mix audio from two devices together.)At the end of the day, it's a decent speaker, and would certainly catch my eye at around $100.  At $150, I start questioning my purchase, and at $299 or $375, I think they must have gone mad.  The sound quality is sub-par to me, just because it has some highs, and a lot of mid-range, but no bass.  The noise when nothing is playing seems high, too.  The controls are not so much difficult to use, as to know WHAT you're doing.  I feel like I'll need to laminate the instruction manual to make full use of the speaker over time.  I've considered sending it back, but, alas, I've thrown the packing out, and I'm sure I'll use it for something.

After reading some reviews on Amazon on this radio as well from members on RadioReference.com, I bit the bullet and ordered one for myself for Christmas. I like the fact that this radio has a maximum power output on GMRS of 5W, not like bubble packed ones like the Motorola MR350R's I bought for my kids. I am hoping it's as good as one member said about 15mile from atop a slight elevation which we have plenty of around here in Northern New Jersey. It is also good to know that these are water resistant would make it easier to carry around during hiking or other types of outdoor rendevous. Also, having a Lithium battery is a plus which should elimiate the guessing games with the older Metal Hydride batteries. More reviews to come...-- Second Review -- *Product Design and Quality*I received the walkie talkie today from Amazon. Got here in 3 days via FREE SUPER SAVER, I can't thank Amazon enough! I opened up the box, and noticed how neat it was packed. Radio, antenna, rechargeable battery, and belt clip was neatly laid out and packed. Very good screen protector ensure that it was protected from scratches. I also removed the charger, AC transformer, and the mobile charger.I then removed the AA battery pack and installed the rechargeable one. Battery compartment has a tight seal around it, I am so far amazed at the quality. Next I attached the antenna, removed the strap, and installed the belt clip. All perfect fit, and the surface of the radio is top notch quality, heavy duty like police/military gear. When I insert the radio onto the charger, it sits nice and snug, and everthing about this unit is just awesome.I then turned on the radio, LCD display has a backlit and orange in color, real crisp, so far so good. Turned on the radio and noticed that battery shows full bar, neat. Changing the band via the BAND button. No receive so currently have it on weather for NYC. Sound coming from the speaker is like listening to FM radio, I am just blown away. I also performed a test TX with Motorola MR350R, and I like the fact that the MIC is located on the bottom of the radio. This is a good design as it forces your to raise antenna above your head for a marginally better transmit. Also, one reviewer mentioned that it's really not that stable when left stood up. Mine has no issue standing straight up on a table. Another nice feature: TX/RX meter, this is just amazing, like the one on my PRESIDENT HR2510 10m radio (with each segment lighting up as the signal strength increases), this I have to say is the nicest feature on the LCD display. This is the first time in a while that Cobra actually produced a winner as far as consumer radio goes. I wouldn't be surprised if this particular radio becomes the next benchmark for all others are judged similar to the President HR2510 currently is.Radio does say SUBMERSIBLE but would I submerse it deliberately just to prove that it can like the other reviewer? Not a chance :)I am definitely going to order a second one once the funds become available, this is a fantastic piece of electronic, I can't wait to give this baby out for a spin for quick range check. Stay tuned!--- Lazy Man's TX/RX Test ---I performed some very unscientific test today with my son with another pair of walkie talkies - the MOtorola MR350R's. He was in the house on 2nd floor next to the windows with his walkie talkie and I was in my car driving away from the house towards the big hill up towards 9W. with my Cobra MRHH425LI-VP. To my surprise, we were able to communicate to about .8 miles, much better than when we were talking on two MR350's, which sadly couldn't even do .4-.5 miles, which I actually got out of the car each time when I wanted to transmit/receive.Definitely showing some improvement with range with just one HH425; imagine if we were both on HH425? Also, I find that it is much easier to communicate with other GMRS radios if I turned off the recording feature as well as the DCS/CTCSS. I was also transmitting on high power setting on channel 15/GMRS. I am definitely considering purchasing another one, instead of getting the Midland GXT1000VP4's. Seeing is believing!--- Not Quite New ---I noticed that this radio looks new, left some clues that it may not be. Reasoning is that on the casing's crevices, I am showing some dirt and the screen, although it had the protection, there were some fine scratches on it. Not that big of a deal but this is the problem with non-blister packed equipment where you can actually remove the item and still can claim that it is new.--- Another *MUST* Update ---The rechargeable battery, even after when it's fully charged, won't last for more than few key ups on HI power mode. I found this out the hard way when I took the radio to day hiking thinking it would last me at least a day, and after a few transmission, not even holding a conversation, radio went dead. Right now I am using regular alkaline batteries but the radio takes 6 of them, it is a bad design on Cobra's part, or the rechargeable battery that comes with the radio does not have enough A/hr to handle this radio.I am acually glad that I did not buy the 2nd one because just for this issue, I would not buy this radio again.--- Final Update ---Radio's display finally gave way after it was dropped from maybe about 2 feet on my driveway. However, I had picked up 3x Baofeng UV-5R Ht's from roughly $55 each shipped from Sain Store. It has all the U.S. Amateur frequencies plus GMRS and NOAA (RX only) frequencies you can use the keypad to program and store. It's compact and more than half less than the bulky Cobra. Do yourself a favor and stay away from the Cobra and opt for Baofeng UV-5R.

It's not exactly intuitive, and if you had to change the configuration a lot, you would probably get frustrated pretty quickly.3) The swivel feature is nice--you can put the iPad in portrait or landscape orientation easily.4) The case would be really good for those who use the iPad while seated at a desk, since it raises the iPad and puts it closer to eye-level--much better ergonomically than having to hunch your back and look straight down at the iPad as it lies on the table.5) If you're looking for a case that feels warm and pleasant to the touch, this is not the one for you--it has a very cold, sterile feeling.6) When it's closed up in porfolio mode, the top piece (that covers the screen of the iPad) doesn't stay closed, it cracks a bit and flaps about. Pretty annoying, really.7) I'm just not sure how well the case would protect the iPad if you dropped it. It has cushioning, but I can see the iPad screen shattering much more easily with this case than with many others.Conclusion: #s 5-7 above are the deal-breakers for me. I'll stick with a leather-style portfolio case. Of course, if you work at a desk or on a space station, perhaps this case will fit your needs and style.

Ok, to begin, I have been looking for a non-IOS media player for quite a few months now, and I decided to go with the Z2 for a few reasons:1. I like being original. Not too many of these in the US. Ipods are everywhere. XP2. The screen resolution and type (better than Galaxy players, which were my second choice).3. The sd card expansion slot.4. Android.5. High quality sound.Ok, I got this mostly for the sound quality and for the expansion. I have over 15,000 songs, and I needed somewhere to put them all. So keep in mind I did not get it just for the Android. I bought a 64GB microSD card and formatted it; works perfectly and I have almost all of my music on it. I had to convert them all to 128bit m4a format for them to fit (which can be played with the player, but if you use the device's default encoder/ file reader, the artist tags will not be read. This can be fixed by installing Poweramp, which seems to use its own encoder, or by installing MediaFix, which "converts" your m4a files and allows the artist tags to be read).But anyways, the player itself it not bad. I mean, I have played with some other android devices, most of them running Gingerbread like the Z2, and they act about the same... I feel that the Z2 IS a little glitchy; it sometimes shuts down/ restarts for no reason (and YES, I made sure the battery did not just run out). It also goes slow or just runs out of memory for the smallest programs sometimes... but this only seemed to happen after I installed Google Play Store (all those applications running in the background)... which brings me to another point.Since the thing is Korean and not android certified, it does not come with the newest Android version nor the Google Play Store. Which is eh... but if you are decent at technology, you can easily find one of the many guides to put Google Play on the Z2. The hardest part was linking it to my Google account (which is actually hard on MOST android devices if you do not do it right on the first start up), but after trying it a couple of times, I finally got it to work and downloaded dozens of apps without much issue.But besides those few glitches and road bumps, the devices seems to work well. I wish the battery life was a LITTLE better (without wifi on, it is ok, but if wifi is even on and facebook/ google/ anything is using it in the background... :( not too great). So, the software is ok, but as others have said, an update to fix these glitches would be WONDERFUL.The hardware... I put a screen protector on before I turned it on, because I like to keep the most important part of a touchscreen device safe... yeah... so far, so good. have not dropped it yet, so i cannot tell you how durable it really is, and I am currently trying to find a decently priced/ highly rated case for it... but I have yet to find one besides the cheap/ lame looking clear jelly one online for $20. The buttons work well. The double tap for making it go to sleep is a little annoying, since I think locking the screen is unnecessary, but its something just to get used to. The charging port works well (comes with wall charger [with US power adapter], a micro usb connector [for computer] and so you have two ways to charge your device), but as stated in a previous post, they really put all the ports close, and so the cover/ stand gets in the way sometimes. Haven't used the mini HDMI yet, but shouldn't have a reason why it wouldn't work.Again, I have had the device for about a month or so, using it everyday for small games, checking FB, and, of course, listening to music. I think it is overpriced for the specs and the lack of a camera, but having about 88GB (loss of 8 or so GB due to formatting the SD card and such), is nice for someone with a lot of media (such as myself). The screen is pretty nice, and is OVERALL responsive (some apps are glitchy though, like Draw Something or any other drawing-like app). LOVE the look of the thing (boxy and black lol) and it is a lot lighter than what it looks.If you want something non-mainstream, need the room for a lot of media, and does not want to use IOS, then I would consider getting the Cowon Z2.... its not as clean and smooth as the Galaxy players and phones out there, but its a nice thing to play with and have your music on (love the volume and playback control buttons, esp while driving or multitasking). Sorry for the long review but I hope it helped you decide on whether or not to purchase this device. :)

For the price these earphones are a very good value. I am very familiar with the foam type of earplugs that go into your ear canal.  These earphones are far more comfortable than foam earplugs yet still block a lot of sound.  They won't replace the serious ear protection needed when doing very noisy work (like cutting steel with a circular saw) but will block out office conversation.The other caveat is that they are very light and should be handled with some care.  Although not fragile I do recommend always using the included case.  You can then toss them in with your "stuff" and not worry about them.When fitted with some care you do get good sound quality.  I was very pleased with the sound after some modest equalization changes on my Sony Walkman MP3 player.  If the fit is a bit off you will lose bass response but I had no trouble adjusting it.  They are very comfortable even when fitted to get good bass response (you don't have to jam them into your ears like ear plugs).If you need to block out office noise or fly frequently these earphones are an excellent value.

Let me preface this by saying I really, really wanted to like this MP3 player. I hate giving bad reviews and it's not that this MP3 player didn't work.It does work.On the bright side, the battery life is pretty good. I took it with me on a long, 4 hour drive and played it the entire way. Then without recharging it, I played it the entire way (another 4 hours) back home again. And I've played it more (again without recharging it) since. So it's pretty good.I was also able to read the screen, so that was nice.What was less nice was that for a product with a touch screen interface, you really had to touch it--hard. In fact, I found on my trip that if I wanted to skip a song (or do something else) the best way to get it to respond was to actually hold the device with my fingers on the bottom and my thumb on the screen and pinch it between my thumb and fingers. That almost always resulted in it recognizing what I wanted it to do, and doing it. Just touching it only resulted in the desired action about 50-60% of the time.I also found that it wouldn't let me build playlists on my computer that could then be downloaded to the device. This sort of bothered me because I like to group my classical music together in one list, rock&roll; in another, and so on. As you can imagine, the 4GB wasn't quite sufficient either, but it would do for someone with a less extensive music library.I wish I could have liked it better, but the performance of the touch screen made it difficult. However, the pinching technique does work, and the device is inexpensive, so I actually don't mind it so much as a backup MP3 player and one that I might take to more hostile environments like the beach where I don't want to mess up a more expensive player due to salt air/water/sand.

Dual DVI only, period. Be careful with compatibility.  Seems doubtful that any adapter will work, so I wouldn't bother trying. I made sure my GPU has a true dual-link DVI.  My AMD 7970 runs this monitor at 2560x1440 over dual link DVI, another 1920x1200 over displayport, and a third 1600x1200 over another single link DVI.No image scaler.  Your OS/GPU will have to do the image scaling if you want to run 1080p, 12x10, etc. on it.  This also means no BIOS POST screen will be displayed, so be careful if you think this will be an only monitor.  You will not be able to adjust your BIOS and you will only see an image once the operating system takes over.  This could be an issue for running something like Linux as well.  I have no issues running lower res as my graphics card takes care of scaling in games or windows, though.No OSD.  Only contrast adjustment buttons (aka "brightness," but more properly contrast where black stays black and whites get lighter or darker).  All other adjustment will have to be done through the OS or GPU driver settings.  I'm happy with the factory calibration, though, and it looks good sitting between my two Dell Ultrasharp monitors. Image quality is very good.  Nice sharp picture, great contrast and brightness.  Gamma seems pretty good without adjustment.Backlight bleeding is pretty apparent on the lower right of the screen when displaying black or a very a dark image.  It is more noticeable when the room lights are off as well.  Not horrible, but definitely oticeable and a bit annoying.  I have yet to try to fix it on my own but know there are DIY guides on Youtube and elsewhere to fix that particular problem.  If this were not an issue I'd give image quality overall a 9.5/10.  Have to lower it to about 8/10 for now.  Matte finish on display surface is good.  No glare.  No halos.VESA screw holes are NOT deep enough.  I had to add a bunch of washers (about 5-6 on each screw) as the screws bottomed out before securing the mount, but work fine otherwise.  Thread pitch and size is correct at least.  I am now using mine with a cheap Monoprice "3-way adjustable" stand.I've had mixed results overclocking it so far.  I have a Radeon 7970 3GB, used the driver patch and CRU, and just copied the 60hz settings but changed V-Sync value. With the included cable I get severe blue stippling everywhere at 120hz (completely unusable).  Even at 100hz I occasionally get small white phantom boxes around the edges of windows in the OS (they go away if I sweep a window over them), though games are flawless at 100hz. I am ordering a new 24AWG dual-link DVI cable to see if it helps. I'm not 100% blaming this monitor, though.  I'll try to follow up later with more testing.The higher refresh really helps both with V-sync on (removes a lot of stutter and lag) or with V-sync off (reduces how apparent tearing is).  A good stand-in until G-Sync is more widely available (i.e. not limited to severely overpriced crappy-looking TN panels, and also working on AMD).I have not tested super thoroughly, but I did check as best I can by eye for dead and stuck pixels against R, G, B, white, and black backgrounds and did not spot any imperfections. It's possible I missed a small flaw or two, but I'm impressed by the lack of pixel defects.I knew about most of the issue before buying, and I'm generally very happy with what I got for the price.  Extent of backlight bleeding and VESA screw holes being too shallow were not expected, nor did I forsee no BIOS POST.  These are tractable problems, and the core of what I wanted (fast gaming monitor, overclocking, good image quality) is there.

I do quite a bit of overnight laptop-travel, so I was eager to review this product and let others know what I think of it.I wouldn't recommend this for any travel longer than overnight.  You'll be able to fit tomorrow's clothing in here, but no more.  The clothing portion of the bag is about 1 inches tall.  There is a shoe pocket, but it will consume what little space there is for your clothes.  Add your toiletries and you're quickly out of space.The top-loading compartment for paperwork and your laptop is brilliant, and something that business travellers will certainly appreciate.  This is not your typical suitcase that you'll have to somehow squeeze your paperwork into.  I like how this section is apart from your clothing, allowing you to open it up at a business meeting without exposing your boxers.I have one major complaint though, and that the "check-point friendly" concept of this bag is to remove a sleve that contains your laptop.  This is stupid.  The whole point is to go through a security checkpoint with ease, but the makers of this bag want you to open the suitcase, remove the laptop sleeve, and walk through.  How is that any better than removing your laptop for security?  And the little carry handles for the sleeve get in the way of the zipper when you try to close it back up.(Other check-point suitcases feature a clamshell-type opening that is checkpoint-friendly and doesn't require taking anything out of your suitcase.)If you like pockets, zippers, and extra little compartments, then you'll really dig this suitcase.  There's plenty of room for your laptop accessories, business cards, cell charger, a pen, and whatever else.  Note that if you have any large accessories (like a USB drive or DVD player) there probably won't be a large-enough pocket unless you use one of the loose business-document sections.Another minor flaw is that the zippers provide no method to lock with a padlock.  You might get lucky with a very tiny padlock that happens to fit, but it sure wasn't designed with that in mind.The bag itself feels durable and looks sharp, though the solid-black (with a few red highlights) make it somewhat generic looking against a sea of similar black suitcases on a luggage rack.  There is no ID sleeve.The max size for laptops is 16.1 x 12.2 x 1.8, which is fine for most 17" widescreen displays.In summary, if you need something perfect for quick business trips, then you'll probably enjoy this.  If you're not carrying around 1" of paperwork, or need more than a change of clothes, you'll want to find something else.My justification for 3/5 stars was based on the implementation of "checkpoint-friendly" coupled with the suggested retail price.  For that price, you could find a nicer suitcase with laptop storage, but not the generous paperwork space.

I am a big fan of cast iron cookware, the single item I use most in my kitchen being a well-seasoned Wagner 9” cast-iron skillet. Cast iron heats well, cooks evenly and lasts forever. I have had good success with T-Fal products in the past and I was very interested in the reversible stove top grill/griddle pan and my feelings about it are very mixed. While it is quite usable and it does do what it’s designed to do, it’s far from perfect.If you look at the image of the item here on Amazon, you can see a raised area on the lower left corner of the griddle side. I was very surprised when I took my item from the box to find a nearly identical area. Either there is a flaw in the actual molding from which this item is cast or there is an impurity introduced in the process. Either way, this does not seem to affect the ability to cook, but it’s visibly noticeable.Most cast iron I have used, even well-seasoned, has had a mildly rough surface that does get more smooth over time, but this particular pan comes out of the box feeling akin to sandpaper. It is coarse and gritty all over (including on the handles). I think T-Fal cut some corners here. It would take minimal effort at the foundry to quickly grind the pan’s surface – just a little bit – so that the surface is not so rough. I may take a sander to mine and reseason when I am done.In use, it does heat mostly evenly. On my stove top I have two different-sized burners on each side so it is a little difficult to get the temperature exactly right. I usually end up with a spot close to the middle of the surface that is a little cooler, and I think this is a necessary evil with my configuration.My big test for this pan was to make pancakes. Our electric griddle is very predictable and we have gotten the process of making pancakes and other things on it down. Right out of the starting gate I was reminded that cast iron heats a lot faster and more evenly than aluminum and I ended up with a couple of pancakes that were a little more done than I anticipated (though not burnt). Once I adjusted to it, the pan allowed me to crank out pancakes faster than with the electric griddle without burning or undercooking them. This was a user issue but it bears repeating – cast iron heats differently than aluminum and switching to cast iron requires some adjustment.This is a preseasoned pan which is a good starting place, but it needs to be properly seasoned through use. Do not believe that it will be non-stick right out of the box or you will be sorely disappointed. Given time and proper care it will season to a nice non-stick usefulness.T-Fal has produced a usable reversible griddle/grill pan. It heats well and once used to it a cook can do good things with it. That said, there are a number of imperfections with it and it has a feel of being slightly unfinished. If the imperfections matter to you, there are other options available for a comparable price. If not, T-Fal’s product is acceptable. I am rounding my rating as I would give it 3.5 stars given the ability to do so. This pan is ok – neither great nor terrible.

This GPS came "free" with the purchase of four tires.  Having used it for a awhile, I now understand why this is the unit chosen for a free GPS: it has some nice features but there are some shortcuts that make this less than the top of the line.It has several positive features: the free traffic updates top the list; the sound is good; visibility is good; reliability of directions is good (although that should be a given); but the most appreciated is that it is much more patient with a detour than our Garmin.  It also has some negatives: the battery is weak (and drains when it it turned off); the power cord connection is not robust (the plug barely fits into the unit when installed in the cradle -- it is fine if the unit is out of the cradle, but that is not a safe way to drive alone); it does not cover Canada; it tends to fall back to "proceed to highlighted route" a bit too often (how is that a safe thing to do when driving?); while it has traffic updates they are usually not active (Google maps has traffic for many roads that this doesn't); it gets lost momentarily when you miss a turn (it will often tell you to take a turn you have missed for 30 to 60 seconds after passing the intersection; finally, this unit seems to have a nose for taking shortcuts through bad neighborhoods (which is one reason I am familiar with its persistence on detours).I can not say that I would have bought this unit if I had been GPS shopping, but I can see why Continental offers it free with a set of tires.  The basic description looks quite good and when you boil it down, the capabilities are not bad if you don't live near a border.  Since it is nowhere near the top of the Magellan line it should have been a reasonable price.  But issues like cradles not holding power cords in place securely make me hesitate about the Magellan brand.  There were also issues registering it -- the website would not take my serial number.  That makes me wonder if the free tire offer units are refurbished returns (and you may have higher quality results).  But I cannot say that fills me with confidence in Magellan either.

At $59.99 it's OK (certainly wouldn't pay full price for it), but it doesn't even come with a charger brick (charge through computer?  PUHLEEZE!).Take a look at the Anker Astro 3 (listed in "Also Bought").  The Anker is the same capacity (10,000mAh) and the same price but in addition to the 5V outputs, it has a 9/12V output for charging or running higher voltage items.  I got two of these Ankers for our last European trip. It has two USB 5V outputs that kept all our phones and pads and game units charged, and then the Anker also has the 9/12V output (switchable) that I used to extend the runtime of our DVD players for the long flight.  One DVD player was 9V and the other was 12V so it worked out great.  The Anker comes with a wide variety of plugs for various devices (including Apple 30-pin for all old iPhones, iPods, and iPads) and little coiled USB charging cables (or you can use your own).  It also comes with a cable and an assortment of plugs for the 9/12V output -- fit both of my players.The Anker ALSO comes with a 12V 1A (12W) wall charger that charges it up in a few hours rather than the 7-8 hours of the RAVpower charging on a 1A USB charger (5W), or 15 hours on a computer USB port (2.5W).Remember, Power = Voltage x Current, Energy (Watt-hours) is Power x Time.  10,000mAh at 3.7V is 37Wh, so the charge time is: 3h x 12W (Anker), or 7.5h x 5W (RAVPower/1A USB wall charger), or 15h x 2.5W (RAVPower/computer USB).I certainly don't work for Anker or owe them anything.  I bought the two units that I used and I'm just a satisfied customer.  I'm plugging them here because they're the same cost as this RAVPower but have so much more to offer.  That being said, the promo-code sale on the RAVPower today for $35 (see slickdeals dot net) is hard to pass up, especially if you just have 5V stuff to charge!

I bought these mainly to listen to podcasts while taking long bike rides, so as not to have my ears plugged with earbuds. For that purpose, they're OK, though not great.While you're able to hear cars better, the headset also produces some wind noise (if there's wind, or if you're riding faster than a leisurely pace.) If you turn up the sound high enough to hear well over the wind noise, you lose some of the advantage of unblocked ears. I do notice cars coming up on me more, but I would not say that there's an enormous difference between what I hear wearing the Aftershokz and what I hear through my ear-blocking LG Bluetooth headset, which I like very much.They ARE at least marginally safer, though, so I've kept them and used them on a dozen rides over the last month. For riding on city streets at low speeds, they'd be much safer than earbuds.They hang over your ears and lie against the back of your neck. This isn't very comfortable. I never stop noticing their presence while riding, especially when I turn my head.I did discover that there is another way to wear them: put them on top of your head, like headphones. My helmet fits right over them this way, and it's slightly more comfortable for me.Others have mentioned that the pressure on your cheekbones eventually becomes uncomfortable, and I confirm that. I can wear them for 30 minutes comfortably, an hour with growing discomfort. After that my face needs a break. So this isn't a perfect solution for me, since I often ride for 2-2.5 hours.I can't imagine using these to listen to music. At reasonable volumes, bass frequencies and drumbeats really hammer your cheekbones.

There is something inherently unnatural about this adapter, which lets one downsize a 1/4 inch jack to a mini jack. Why would you want to do this? I know I had my reasons, but they all led in the end to exercises in futility, and I usually ended up getting these adapters bent out of shape at the rate of one per month.Suppose, for instance, that you own audiophile headphones which you want to connect to your iPad, iPad, or iPhone. Such headphones often come with quarter-inch jacks. So you connect the phones to this adaptor and plug the adaptor into your mobile entertainment center. In principle, you have succeeded in recreating the audiophile experience in concert halls like the New York subway. In practice, all you have done is build an ungainly contraption prone to bumping and grinding on just about anything you jostle. At the least, you're going to bend the mini jack enough that it ceases to work. At worst, you're going to damage the port on your iDevice.Or suppose you are suddenly inspired to convert your iPad into a guitar synthesizer and need to interface it to your favorite Fender amp. Such amps use cables with quarter-inch jacks, so you might get this adapter to complete the circuit. Don't. Both you and the adapter will end up bent out of shape.Folks, there is a natural order to the universe. Our Higher Power intended us to plug mini jack headphones into our mobile devices, not those humongous quarter-inch thingys.  And there are devices from Griffin and others for those who want their phone to be a musical instrument. But this kind of adapter is just going to end up bumping and snagging to the point of no longer being functional, and it won't take very long. Experiments with at least five of these have shown me the futility of my ways.

In general, I like that Clear offers a third choice away from cable companies and DSL. Also, setup was easy for us and over the past year we've only needed to reset the router by power cycling it about once a month.My complaint is that this router does not support QoS (Quality of Service) or bandwidth monitoring. QoS is the system for setting device priority, and is supported on virtually all modern routers other than this one.Not having QoS means that when some device on your network decides to update itself then your streaming will break down or your VOIP phone will break down. Do you want to have to yell at your kids to stop streaming when answering the phone? Then go ahead and buy this router.Also, there's no way to monitor how much bandwidth different devices on your network are using. So if the Internet is dying, you have no idea what device is auto-updating or whatever and making that happen.If you live alone and only have 1 or 2 devices connected to this router then you should be happy with it. If you have a secondary router and are a network guru and plan to combine the devices by disabling DHCP and whatever else on this router then you should be happy. However, if you have a family in one house and are not crazy about spending hours figuring out what is killing the Internet when, then I'd look elsewhere. I wish I had.

JANUARY 2010 UPDATE:  After having used the Nokia for a week, decided on returning it because of the short battery life and then even with an updated firmware, the screen became unresponsive needing turning off and on again the device in order to use the phone features.  As much as I like Nokia, they still have a long way to go with touch screens.INITIAL REVIEW: After one year using a Nokia E-71 which I dropped and stopped working, I searched for a replacement and found this XpressMusic5800 for $219.00 OnLine.  Ordered it from the blue computer store and have been "playing with it" for only 24 hours.  Nevertheless, being a recently introduced device in the US, thought on sharing my first impression for those who are considering it.Users familiar with Nokia products will love how user friendly this phone is.  Those unfamiliar with Nokia, might have a hard time setting up the many phone's features but it's worth your time.  Once you open the box, will find a device much smaller than what you thought it would be.  The most attractive thing is how narrow it is.  Slightly shorter than an I-Phone and E-71, much narrower than both but somewhat thicker; a tad more than half inch.  Included is a wired remote control for the player, mic/headphones, the wall charger, strap, MicroSD card and a mini disk for installing the Nokia features.On the upper part of the device there is a micro USB dock, the port for the regular headset, the charging port and the on/off switch. On the right side there is a volume switch, the unlocking switch and a separate camera switch.  The left side houses an 8GB MicroSD card (included) and the SIM Card from your phone carrier.  The expected Nokia strap hooks on the lower left side of the phone.  The battery is on the back, facing downwards and to access it you need to remove the whole back cover.  The phone comes in shiny black which is a fingerprints magnet.When you turn it on it vibrates, shows the usual Nokia welcome and then allows you to program it.  I was able to configure my two main e-mails but guess you can do several more.  On my E-71 I had four different mail accounts constantly receiving messages.  The native wallpaper is black with some waves but you can easily change it to your favorite photo.  I downloaded several screens from the Apple website since the screen is somewhat similar to the I-Phone and I-Pod in shape and dimensions.On a very T-Mobile way, you can have your "four favorite people" on the main screen and once you touch their corresponding picture/icon, the phone shows a history of calls made, received, text messages and e-mails; quite innovative.  On the lower area you have an icon for phone dialing and another for your contacts.  The phone dialing keyboard works only in the vertical position but the font keyboard is accessed also while the device is horizontal.  Making a call trough the contact list is very easy the device is loaded with features.Call quality is excellent and even at its loudest setting there is no distortion.  The touch sensing screen is not as fast and accurate as the Apple devices but good enough for not needing the stylus that is housed on the rear of the phone.  As a music player it is outstanding.  Playback is trough the two micro speakers on the lower sides and sound quality as well as stereo separation are very good.  Nokia offers on this device all the goodies that make them unique such as saying the caller's name/ID, unique caller ringtones & photos and several customizable user modes. There are many features that I have not yet tried but will do during the next week or so.  My service is with ATT and works in both frequencies; EDGE & 3-G,Now, the limitations of the Nokia 5800:First; the battery life.  Nokia products have been famous for their extended batteries.  My E-71 could be used without recharging up to three days.  On the 5800, the battery drains in six hours. The stated four hours of talk time and two weeks of standby time are far from reasonable.What I did to prolong battery life was disable the vibrations when the screen gets a command, disable the 3-G (use EDGE only) and made the Bluetooth available for search for only one minute.  As of today, with regular calls, internet use, e-mails and music, after 15 hours of nonstop use, the battery still has like 40% charge.Second and quite disappointing, the installation mini disk as well as the software upgrades on the Nokia Website is not compatible with Windows 7.  After downloading all the suites, OVI, and ancillary software, many of these do not work with Win-7. Then tried these with a NetBook running Win-XP and no problem with the updates.Having stated all this, I consider that for the price paid ($219.00), the Nokia 5800 is a bargain when compared with their 51XX and 53XX series, mostly because of its music playing capabilities, awesome call features and quality.  But in my case, the battery issue might make me consider other alternate phones.  Let's see what I decide and meanwhile, I hope that this initial review helps you to decide if the Nokia 5800 is the phone for you.  In case that you are considering an I-Phone, you should wait. The new, smaller and slim I-Phone 4-G goes on sale in June 2010.

First of all, I have to stress, that I did not purchase the Lenovo K1 Ideapad tablet at Amazon. I bought it new at a cheaper price ($299 + tax) at another retailer.
