What can you say about a pan?  It's ether good or not.  This is heavier and more solid than I expected and looks good and I have no doubt will be a good pan.  I bought a cooling rack to use for dehydrating food as well as rubbing meat (small things that can fit, more on size later) etc. and that cooling rack, designed to fit half sheet pans fits perfectly.The only complaint is one that's repeated, the glue strip used to adhere the label.  It's like gooey and sticky and does NOT peal off the nice clean, smooth surface of the alum. pan and tears the label.  Why?  Beats me, it's like using a nail gun to tack a piece of paper on a tack board.  I have the pan in the freezer, hoping the glue strip will harden enough to come off easier.  And it is like a strip of narrow tape about 3" x 3/8" but is solid adhesive.As for the size, this may be the standard but here's what I found.  The description says 18x12, the label says 18x12 but I can't find a 12" measurement anywhere.  It measures 13x18 overall but 10.5" x 16.5" in the floor of the pan.  I'd really love to find a larger pan to fit ribs, brisket etc. that will go 18" to 22" easily, but I guess I'll need to pony up for a full sheet pan.It would get 5 stars, but I have to join the mob on the adhesive thing.  It's insane these days to use something like that, that doens't easily peel from metal.  If it were on the bottom it may be OK, but it's not, its in the pan.EDIT: Ok, so the freezer did nothing but make the adhesive get tougher and impossible to do anything with.  But, enough hot water running over it to heat the pan, softened it enough to almost peel some of the strip off.  What was left of course is the sticky glue and 2-3 rounds with "Goo Gone" and a paper towel cleaned it off.  It's all good now.Something else worth noting is that it has a heavy gauge wire in the rim, which others advertise and this one does not.  It's very heavy so the pan is like a tank.  However, as others have noted, that rolled edge can hold water and I'm sure the wire is not stainless or alum so it may rust.  I just washed it and tossed it in the oven under a high broiler to get it good and hot.  I did so to get the water dried out, but also to "cook off" any trapped manufacturing residue that may be in there as well.  No funky smoke or smells and the pan just laid there and got really hot.  Guess that's what they're supposed to do, unlike other pans I've had that would have started doing back flips from the buckling.  Overall, great pan, that doesn't need that strip of monkey snot to hold the label down.EDIT 10/28/11I bought another one and wanted to comment on the glue issue that fills the reviews for these Norpro pans.  This one came with a different glue.  It's not a strip of "glue like tape" it's brushed on the paper first then stuck to the pan.  Still a little chore to get off but I tried my method of putting it in the freezer and pealing it when I found it wasn't the same.  Once I got the paper off the pan I used GooGone and it came off pretty easily.  Of course my finger nails left scuff marks when trying to remove the paper but nothing that causes any issue with using it.  I'm happy with them.  Again dried it under a convection broil and accidentally left it under there too long, it was way hot!!  No bend, no buckle, no discoloration, just hot.....then it cooled.  Great pans, now that I have 2!!  I wish Amazon had their full sheet pans because I had to buy another brand.  We'll see how it compares to Norpro.

The install was pretty easy, but definitely not a slam dunk.  The install utility is very quirky.Problems:The first problem was that the Ethernet cable provided with this adapter was bad.  Luckily I had a working spare.The bigger problem is that the install utility doesn't validate the connection.  I could have typed in my dog's name or even YOUR dog's name for my network keyphrase, and it would have given me the same "success" message.  Sure it's my fault for botching the password, but the installer should have failed and given me an error.The second part of this validation problem is that you have no way of troubleshooting the adapter.  The DVR that I was connecting this to had its own quirks, so it would have been helpful to isolate the problem by testing the adapter.  The installer is browser-based, so why not have a feature that calls out to an external site?  I was hoping the firmware updater would do that, but it assumes that you've already downloaded the firmware binary and only has a Browse button to navigate to your local file system.Setting up a static IP was tricky, because the adapter has one notion of what its IP should be and the device itself has another.  I finally went with DHCP just to get an address and then reserved that address on the router for this adapter.  Then I configured the client device (a DVR, in my case) with that static address.  I've never had to go through this kind of jujitsu to get an IP address before.I have a repeater on my network, which means that I have the same SSID broadcast twice.  The whole point of the repeater though is for the device to have a choice between the strongest version of the signal to pick from.  The SSID and keyphrase are the same, so the device should freely switch between either signal, regardless of the channel.  The installer for this adapter wouldn't let me do that though.  It showed me the list of all of the broadcast SSIDs and made me pick one.  So now the adapter is married to the one channel, even if the other one is coming in stronger at the time.I know I'm whining, but I just didn't expect this adapter to require so much hand-holding during the setup.  And the defective Ethernet cable is embarrassing.

Open the "About this Mac" menu and make sure you are testing the Mac you plan to buy. Open a streaming video from a popular website like Hulu, play a movie in HD. Chances are it will skip frames or stop playing altogether. It tested Hulu on both models, the 11" and the 13" side to side, the 13" played impeccably while the 11" skipped frames till it would stop playing entirely, freezing up the whole computer. If the 11" MacBook Air can't play movies properly, then all you get is a fancy web-surfing/email reader, since the keyboard is not illuminated, I would say, you are probably better off buying an iPad for half the price.**Update**As it often happens with all all my reviews, Apple has finally admitted that there was a problem with Mac Book Air laptops and has released an update that is supposed to resolve the issue. I find it highly unlikely that a software update can fix what is clearly a hardware problem but at least there is an official admission from Apple that the freezing problem does exist even though is not as rare as they claim it is.The update is meant for the 11-inch and 13-inch Air and claims to resolve a "rare issue where MacBook Air boots or wakes to a black screen or becomes unresponsive."

I purchased this receiver in June 2010 and so have had time to digest all the options and features of this product so that I can provide a fair review.  I use this receiver primarily for home theater and its been excellent so I rate the product 5 stars.  I havent run into the video issues that have been mentioned in prior posts.  Currently, my receiver powers two Polk RTi10 floor standing speakers, a HSU subwoofer, a Polk CSi A6 center channnel speaker and two Polk bookshelf rear speakers.  Its connected to my Panasonic 50" LCD projection TV via HDMI and the main input is a Sony BDP 570 blu ray player connected via HDMI.  It took me about 6 months to really tweak the setting to my liking but thats one of the great features about this reciever is that there are numerous options to change the sound to your preference.  The first and most obvious thing to do once your ready is to run the Audyssey 2EQ Speaker Setup function and then you can tweak from there, if needed.A few things to note that I gathered from trial and error and from trolling all the AVS forums about this receiver.  When I first started playing blu ray movies I noticed the dialogue tended to be very weak and the explosions and sound effects were very loud.  All the speakers were connected properly and it wasnt the blu ray player because I tried a different brand player and got the same results.  To solve this problem, I found that setting the Onkyo Dynamic Volume option from OFF to LIGHT makes a huge difference in sound.  It will do a light compression on the sound, which some audio purist may be opposed to but it makes the dialogue so much better and louder and based on what I hear, it doesnt degrade the overall sound at all.  Just make sure you have a decent center channel speaker to handle it, otherwise you might have to decrease the center speaker setting down a couple of db's.  The other thing I noticed is that this reciever has a Late Night setting which lowers the overall volume for evening viewing if you don't want to wake your neighbors.  This setting is defaulted to Auto.  However, when playing certain movies it will trigger the Late Night feature and the volume is very muted.  This happened to me when I played Star Trek and I realized that I need to switch the Late Night setting from Auto to OFF.  This makes a big difference in sound.  The feature only applies for discs with Dolby True HD sound.  The final observation I made was that the volume level will typically be at a 50% setting for decent sound.  I initially thought this was too high because my old Technics reciever would get really loud when I had the volume turned up to 25%.  I found out later that 50% is about right and its not an issue of weakness in the reciever because this reciever is plenty powerful.As a final note, I purchased this product on Amazon and received it no problem with free shipping and no taxes so rest assured that Amazon's delivery is just as reliable for electronics as it is for books.  When I ordered this it was based on reading countless reviews here and on CNET and other audio video websites and forums.  I never went to any store to physically test out the product so it was a leap of faith on my part that I was ordering based soley on what I read and Onkyo's reputation for putting out quality audio equipment.  So far I have not been disappointed in my decision.UPDATE July 2013: I decided to recently retire this receiver and upgrade to a Marantz receiver.  In hindsight, looking back on my experience with this product I would say that it wasn't great.  I'm saying this because after hearing the sound produced from the Marantz when compared to the Onkyo I find that the Marantz produces a more balanced and warmer sound whereas the Onkyo sounds a little more harsh when the volume is turned up.  Also, for some reason whenever I start up a movie with the Onkyo it seems like the sound is a tad muted so I would go into the receiver menu options and switch the dynamic volume from Light to Off and back to Light and that would bring the sound back to normal levels.  I had to do this everytime I watched a movie and it would only work for movies encoded in DTS-MA.  Additionally, I had some HDMI issues where I would suddenly lose video and audio in the middle of a 3D movie.  I had to tinker with the connections for a few hours by trying other receiver inputs which seemed to work but I would run into instances where the video would show but the audio would cut in and out.  Eventually everything started working again and I couldn't tell if it was because of my tinkering or it just fixed itself.  So that experience left me a little uneasy.  One note - if you are watching high definition in Blu Ray with this receiver then one of the biggest adjustments you need to do is to turn off the video processing function.  The details on how to do that can be found in the other reviews here.  I can tell you it makes a huge difference in video quality especially if you are sending a 1080p 24fps video signal from the player and the tv is 1080p compatible.  The video processer really dulls down the picture but if you turn it off the picture is a lot sharper and pops from the screen.  At the end of the day I felt that the combination of all the tweaking and adjustments that you need to make to get around all the different issues encountered with this receiver did not warrant a 5 star rating product and therefore I downgraded the rating accordingly even though this is a discontinued product.

Boostcase is a great looking product with a simplistic design; too simplistic.  Basically you get a plastic case for your iPhone5 that then slides/locks on to the boost case.  You press a button and your phone is charging when you need the extra juice.  So, why then did I give it 3 stars...simple:Pros:  Great design and looks.  Stores more then ample power to get your phone from 20% to about 75-80%.Cons: The switch on the back is non-functional at best and will get pressed in your bag, pockets, etc.The idea is simple...you use their iPhone case (included) and slide it on to the boost case when you need extra juice.  Press a button on back of the boost case and voila...your phone is up and charging.  The way they would intend this to work is that you keep the phone with the slim case in your pocket and the boostcase close by in a bag, etc...so you can use it when you need power.  Great..should work.  It does....but there is one problem.  I personally want to keep the boostcase on the phone (similar to a mophie) and slide the entire thing in my pocket.  The boostcase has a tactile button on the rear of it that must be pressed to activate the extra power and charge your phone....great.  Problem is when you leave the boostcase on and throw your phone in a pocket, bag, etc...the tactile button gets pressed easily and your phone constantly charged.  While this is functional; you will soon realize that the boost case is out of power and that you no longer have any boost capacity left.  FAIL. They should have included a standard hard sliding power switch so you could turn the boost case on and off as required (learn from Mophie...).I like the case, I like the look, I dont like the tactile button design and for that alone I cannot recommend this product.  There is a picture on the product page that shows the tactile button in the back...I am sure upon looking at it you will agree with my sentiment.For me this is still a 3 star product - because it is very stylish and functional; it just needs some improvement to get to a 5 star.

When I bought my Kindle Fire, I ordered one of the origami cases. While I like it, the Fire is a community device, used by everyone in the family, including a ten-year-old and a five-year-old. They're good with it, but I thought something sturdier would be nice, especially for the younger one, to help protect the device against falls and sticky fingers.Installing the Kindle into the device is no mean feat. First you have to peel back the outer bumper, which took some digging my nails into the edges to get enough of a hold to separate the two. Then the frame has to be pulled apart in half. A small tool that looks something like a guitar pick comes along with the device, and it does make separating it easier as it slips into the crack between the frame's two halves and makes it possible to pry them apart. This is still easier said than done, though. I had to pretty much go around the frame and separate each segment one at a time.Now, given that the case is waterproof, I'm not quibbling with the necessity of having to do this. I understand it requires some doing to get a good seal in order to protect the device. However, it does make the case harder to work with and not as user friendly as some other cases.Once I got the device in, I then had to go around the entire frame and snap each individual joint together. Some were easier than others, and it did take a few minutes to get this done. Then the outer bumper had to be stretched around the frame, which was okay.The real downside occurred when I started using the Fire. The slightest gap exists between the case's window and the Fire, which means the touch screen loses a lot of its sensitivity. Trying to navigate the carousel was something of a feat, and several times an app I didn't want opened because of the loss of touch-screen sensitivity. I tried playing games and writing a Goodreads review, and it was the Goodreads review that really did me in. The game was hard to maneuver too, but while trying to use Swype to write the review, I repeatedly lost contact with the Kindle screen and ended up with a bunch of gibberish. After having the device in the case for only a matter of hours, I'm ready to pry it apart and put my Kindle back in the origami case.If you're looking for a case to safeguard your Kindle while you read in the tub or for use at the beach, I think this one would probably do the job. You don't need a lot of sensitivity to flip pages, and a case like this offers far more protection from water and sand than does a standard case. Because of this, I plan to keep the case as a backup for such situation. However, for everyday use, this case is too cumbersome.

I have a Disney Mix Max video/music player for one of my kids that we've been using for a while.  It plays WMV video and music as you'd expect.  While there have been issues with that device, I was hoping that the Philips SA32 would be at least the same.  While I have found that the user interface and controls are a bit better on the SA32, the SMV video format is terrible compared to WMV.  Both of these players support the same video resolution, but video files previously created for the Mix Max have to be converted for the SA32.  The problem with this is that video files consistently end up 2-3x the size of the original WMV file when converted for the SA32.  For example, a 1 hour and 20 minute video in WMV format was about 144MB, but in SMV format it is 543MB.  You'll find that your space is quickly consumed with video on this device if you choose to have any.  I also found the few videos I converted to be a bit jumpy and poor quality in comparison to the other player, but it's tolerable for the price.  In my case, the user of this device doesn't want to watch much video and because of that I'll keep it and only have two or three videos on it.  However, if you plan to have a video-rich media player with this, think again.  You'll get 5 hours of video in 4GB if you're lucky.Music playback seems to be fine.  Sound quality is good and navigating around the interface is easy enough.For the price it's a good device, but be prepared for the wasteful size of SMV video files.

Makes me sad!  16+ years as a degreed and certified IT guy, and this power supply is my first failure (for my home built machines).  I had this unit in my fresh build for a week and while it worked, it was fabulous.  I like the idea of the 'zero fan' until you load it up, but I wonder if that may have lent to my unit frying.  And it did fry.  I was 'pressure testing' my new build with OCCT, had a couple of hardware monitors on the desktop, keeping track of voltages, fan speeds, temps, etc. when *poof*, the box just shut off.  I looked around the room (it was night-time); still had lights in the front room and my UPS didn't indicate a power bump.  Weird.  Looked in the box and still had an MB light on, thinking 'that was strange'.  No BSD, no gradual failure, just off; like a light.Ok, let's start it up again and see what happens.  At this point, I'd already pulled my clear panel off, to feel heat sinks and check fans; hit the power button, got through the POST fine, Windows flags, flash of login screen, and *poof* once again.  This time though, I'm smelling the heat.  Took off the other panel, had the flashlight in my mouth and 'thought' I saw the barest of smoke as I pulled the panel away.  Set the panel down and feel around; no loose cables, no grounding connections on any component corners, nothing hot to the touch.  Alright, 3rd time is the charm, only now we've got lights on the PS, and I hit the button again.Almost immediately, I'm seeing smoke from the 24-pin ATX cable plug.  I didn't have a chance to hit the power switch before it shut itself down.  Disconnected it and pulled it out, but I couldn't see anything obvious and the *hot* smell was still fairly faint.  I don't have a spare PS right now, so I'll have to wait for the new one to see if I've got any damage to my components; I doubt it though.  I don't have but 55% of total PS capability in this rig.Too bad.  Oh well.  Amazon will refund and I've already purchased a new one (also a Corsair).  The new PS has a better efficiency rating anyway! ;)

I'm writing this review on my Revue connected to 55" TV, about 8 feet away from me. It feels great to be able to use my TV as a full-featured browser.When I was setting up this device I was really excited and thought it would have a lot of cool features. After I used it for 10 minutes I was disappointed... It does most of the things it's supposed to do but it has ability to do so much more. It looks like a lot of functionality is blocked on purpose to be introduced in Revue 2 and 3. Hope they are not taking Apple's route.I would be really happy with this thing if my TV wasn't already connected to the Internet. To me, there are only two benefits -- convenient keyboard with trackpad and better-organized content. Most connected TVs have almost all features of Revue sans Chrome browser. If you have one of new game consoles, most likely it has a browser as well. The strange thing is that even though Revue duplicates features of my TV and PS3 I find that I use it for all the connected tasks, instead of TV or PS3. The keyboard and UI make it much easier to access all the applications. YouTube and various Flash sites work great. This small box can handle video very well. Notwithstanding, I'll still return it and wait for Revue 2 or an alternative.Shortcomings:Cable TV content is not fully integrated (Fios). Revue downloads the listings to enable TV search but when you want to get more info on a program it simply "asks" cable box to display its screens. Same with switching channels -- Revue acts like a dumb remote control. It would be nicer if interfacing with the cable box would be seamless and all UI was from Revue.Netflix application is standard, does not allow to search for movies by directors, actors, etc. This functionality could be easily added.When searching for content Revue checks with Amazon for paid movies but does not search within Netflix. Disappointing. No reason for this feature not to be included.Even though you need to have Google account to use Revue it does not provide access to any Google applications (besides Picasa). Why can't I easily check my Gmail, Caledar or Google Docs??There are no new applications to install. Revue comes with very limited set.Podcast interface is not very intuitive, looks more like an afterthought.No chat programs. There is no reason for not including this functionality.Video camera can only be used for Logitech chat which is quite disappointing... They'll probably want to charge for service as well... Why not allow cam to be used with any application, like Skype (they would have to have Skype on Revue first, of course).Fan noise can be heard in a quiet room. A better cooling method could have been used. If the room is very quiet, the noise can get annoying.PIP does not work with Netflix -- why can't I watch Netflix movie and TV at the same time or browse web and watch Netflix. It works with TV + Chrome, though.PIP feature doesn't work very well. Going from big screen to PIP is not very smooth.Media player can see content on other computers in the house but it does not support a lot of video formats. It could probably play pictures and sound but it's useless for video streaming from PCs. My Sony TV supports almost all video formats, I'd actually expect the reverse.==========My conclusion: if your TV is not connected to the web Revue will work very well for you, especially if you plan to use browser a lot. However, you can buy PS3 (or another console) for even less $ and it would have most of the functionality of Revue just not as well organized. If you just want to watch Netflix, get a Roku.If you already have a connected TV, Revue would be useful if you want to use browser a lot. The keyboard really makes a difference.I hope next iteration of Revue will have more thought-out features and would give more control to the user.

First off, I completely understand the level of product I was purchasing.  I know this isn't a professional camera, and isn't going to produce pictures like one.  Important factors for me in buying were mpeg encoding, water resistance, HD at 60 fps.  Unfortunately, this is a camera that does one thing well, and a lot of things poorly.The one thing this camera does well is take video at 30 fps in full light situations.  That is all.As a movie camera.  It worked well on all but one setting, the 720p at 60 fps.  I would say 1 out of 4 videos I shoot at this setting have serious problems.  For about 1 out of 4 videos, playback of the videos suffer from a weird choppy accelerated mode.  It is not my computer, or tv, as I have tested them on many devices.  This acceleration also throws off the audio sync.  Audio and video for one of these videos is at least 1-5 seconds off.I paired the camera with a brand name 32 gig SD memory card.  I thought maybe the card was causing the problems.  For the about 6 hours of video I shot,, maybe 50 videos so far, I did have one error that stated it could not record due to memory card write speed.  And yes, this may be the problem.  However, I have tested the read/write of the SD card on my PC with no problems, and have never had a problem with media keeping up with the source.  Its always been the source that's the problem, in my experience.  I believe this to be true with this camera as well.The movies in the other modes was smooth and went as it should.Picture quality.  Great in bright outdoor sun.  Falls off quickly at dusk, may as well be a webcam circa 2002 at night. Generally would not use it indoors unless the lighting is very good.  As other reviewers have said, low light the camera is just not very good.As a still camera.  Terrible.  If you are shooting in anything other than bright sunlight, your picture will probably be blurry.  If its even a little dark, the picture quality will also suffer big time.  And here's the kicker that really turned me against the camera... in full sunlight, the only situation the camera takes really good pictures, about half the time, when you push the button to take the picture the camera will take 1-6 seconds to auto adjust to the light levels and focus.  Its unbelievably annoying to "take" a picture...then wait and wait not knowing when the camera is actually going to TAKE the picture.  There were a number of times I took a picture, and then just quit and put the thing away after waiting god knows how long for the camera to actually take the picture.Lastly, the waterproof quality.  I would say it worked well.  I didn't have any leaks.  However, we used this once in the ocean, salt water.  As recommended, we rinsed it immediately after getting out of the water.  However, it was too late.  The water got into the latch (as it is designed to, that part isn't waterproof).  But when the water evaporated, leaving the salt, it completely jammed up the latch mechanism that opens the door to the memory card.  I tried a number of ways to clean it and get the latch to work, the only way that worked was to literally take the door apart and clean it to get it to work.  Frustrating and annoying.Overall, if you want a cheap waterproof video camera for a vacation to a sunny place, this should work for you.  Stay away from 60 fps, if you bring it in salt water open the doors and rise out the latches immediately as well.  If you want good still pictures, bring a separate still camera with you.If it weren't for the price, I'd give this product 2 stars.

They simply do not compare to their non-running headphone counterparts. I have a pair of Bang and Olufsen A8's which I use for running, and these headphones are not even in the same league. Granted, the B&O;'s cost $165 and are not water resistant, but I didn't expect there to be such a dramatic difference. Listening to lossless audio, I expect to hear some of the "roughness" of the drums and guitar to come across. I expect to hear the musician's screw-ups to play through. These headphones gloss over the complexity of the audio and deliver a "good" sound.I have been spoiled by other non-running headphones. I will probably return these and use the B&O; A8's until they break [again], but I simply cannot accept the second-rate sound that these headphones produce.Won't someone release premiere-quality running headphones? These came very close.

I have a pocket point-and-shoot and wanted to upgrade. My wife and I use zoom on about half our shots. I saw the NEX-5 (with pancake lens) had digital zoom and realize you loose resolution when you digitally zoom. But I figured I'd get much better shots (than my point-and-shoot) when not zooming and shots about equal to my point-and-shoot when I used full digital zoom. But when I tried out the NEX-5, there is no dedicated zoom control - you have to dig down a menu to zoom - not really usable for real-time zoom decisions. Further, the video does not shoot with digital zoom, and I use zoom all the time when I shoot video. So having just a pancake lens is a real step back from my point-and-shoot. To me, this is a serious performance draw back sure to disappoint customers who didn't realize this when they "upgraded". So I returned it and have ordered the NEX-5 with the zoom lens. Now it will be too large to take with me everywhere and will need to just keeping using my point-and-shoot for various occasions where I am active.I would not have re-orderd with the "right" lens unless I liked a lot about the rest of the camera. A mode to show clearly parts of the photo in bright light AND shadow (works very nicely). There is a panorama mode (great for upcoming trip to Greece) but no paranormal mode. Great low-light performance and many other valuable features. I imagine the NEX-5 with 18-55mm zoom lens will get four stars (too bulky for five).Other nits: cheap shoulder strap is included; I bought a new one. Nothing to hold the lens cap after you remove it. I bought a lens cap leash. Initial tests went through the battery quickly - will need to use a while in real life for a firm conclusion. Even with the zoom lens on, I only get 3x (optical) zoom and the digital zoom will be effectively unavailable real time (deep in a menu), as opposed to my point and shoot that does optical zoom as far as it can (3x) then auotmatically adds digital zoom for a total 10x zoom.

In fairness, I don't have my Galaxy S3 yet (it arrives on Friday Jan 25, 2013), and I know it's bigger than the Galaxy S I currently have... but WOW!I have high hopes for the case, I've got experience with Otterbox cases for my S and for my old Blackberry Curve, so I know the products are good. My only concern is the belt clip on the holster, that's where every one of my previous holsters (non-Otter) have broken. This one seems heftier, but still has to plastic pivot points I see as a weakness. That's where they always break. If this one does the same after a couple months, I won't be happy. But, let's not get too far ahead of ourselves.One con I can see with this, if I need to pop the battery out of the phone, it will be a laborious process, and I'll have to make sure I don't get fingerprints under the screen protector or on the phone screen. I'm still not too convinced that screen protector will work for me, I may end up cutting it out. But again, I'll try not to go overboard here.I like that the phone will fit into the holster in two different directions. The release is on the side instead of on the top, so you can go flip it around it you like, as long as the screen is facing inwards.Anyway, I'll post an update once I get my phone and try it out for a week or so.Update Jan 26, 2013: Well, I'm less than impressed.I'm going to have to perform surgery on this case in order for it to work for me, even then it will be cumbersome.Some issues:- The case is NOT easy to take off. It requires a screwdriver to pop the tabs in order to release the two halves. I can't see those standing up to that for very long. Hopefully I don't have to take it apart more than once a year. Update Jan 26 again: The second time I took the case off, one of the retaining bands for the one of the tabs broke. This is not a good design. You shouldn't need tools to remove the case from your phone.- The built-in screen protector was slightly marked up out of the box. I was hoping it wouldn't be noticeable, but it is. It also creates a moire pattern or something similar when sitting against the screen of the phone. Both the inside of the protector and the phone screen are as clean as I can get them (both of these items are brand new), and the pattern is still there. I'm probably going to end up cutting the protector out and getting a standard screen protector. Update Jan 26 again: The screen protector is gone. Didn't have to cut it, it pushed out without much effort.- The rubber flaps which protect the charger and headphone ports will have to come off too. They're just annoying and don't serve any purpose to me. I'll also have to cut some of the case away near the headphone jack so I can use my Paypal credit card reader. It has to sit flush with the surface of the phone, so most cases won't work with it. Maybe I can use an extender cable instead. I'll try that before cutting bits off the case.- The rubber/silicon(?) sheath makes the buttons on the phone easy to get to, but they're hard to push. I'm comparing this to the Otter case I have on my older Galaxy S, which makes the buttons easy to locate and push. The volume controls are especially difficult to push with the Otter case in place.Some good things:- The phone is certainly well-protected It does make your slim phone significantly bulkier, but I'm not that concerned about that. Its easier to hold onto that way.- The holster seems very sturdy. Only time will tell if the belt clip (the weakest point on this style of holster) holds up in a warehouse environment.Overall, however, I expected better from Otterbox.Update April 11, 2013: Well, the holster broke, but not where I expected it to. The little tab which holds the phone in the holster broke off. Now the phone won't stay in the holster. This is definitely a manufacturer defect, since you have to apply pressure to the tab to get the phone out of the holster. That it broke in less than 3 months is very disappointing. I contacted Otter, and have followed their warranty procedure to have the holster replaced. With any luck, I'll have a new one in 7-10 days. For me that's a long time to go without a holster. I'll probably need to purchase a second one as a backup. Why can't Otter make a holster as sturdy as their cases??In other news... I haven't had to take the case off the phone again (glad the Galaxy S3 is a reliable phone, never had to remove the battery.)And I'm definitely glad I removed the built-in screen protector and applied a standard one. I had to do the same for my work-issued iPhone 4s with a Defender case as well. Dust collected rather easily under the case's screen protector. Every few days I would have to take it all apart and clean everything, even then some dust would get under as soon as I had it all together again. Very frustrating. Once I removed the built-in screen protector, screen interaction was MUCH easier. The built-in is a BAD IDEA!!!Update September 27th, 2013: As I mentioned above, I did buy a second full case (since, at the time, they didn't sell the holster alone, not sure if they do now). The belt clip on that second holster broke a few days ago. I've just submitted a warranty for that. I keep mentioning this, but it's worth mentioning. Otter, if you're reading these reviews, you need to make the holster clip less complicated. A simple spring metal clip would be sufficient, with a rotating attachment point that isn't prone to breaking.

This is my second experience with Pinzon 400-440 thread count cotton products. I own several Manfrotto and Gitzo heads and wanted to use the same QR plates on all my gear. So I was delighted when I read Manfrotto's claim that the 323 RC2 allows you to "add a quick release system to any tripod." So I ordered a 323 RC2 from Amazon and eagerly awaited its appearance on my doorstep.The best mounting solution--if possible with your head--is to remove the head's disk/platform and mount the 332 RC2 directly on the ball stem. The underside of the 323 RC2 is flat, so ball stems with a single key or boss will be too wobbly. Double boss stems should be pretty solid. I installed the 332 RC2 on aGitzo G1177M Magnesium 1 Series Ball Headwith a simple flat topped stem, so it has 100% contact with the bottom of the 323 RC2. The disk on top of the head (where you mount the camera) is easily removed (a single nut) and the 332 RC2 can be screwed onto the 3/8 inch stud sticking out of the ball stem. If you plan to use Time Machine to back up your mac, setting this hard drive up will take less than a minute. It's not precise, but you can easily see the difference between a mostly empty drive and a mostly full one with a glance.Note, though, that this is a relatively large hard drive. External drives have gotten almost comically small, but this one has some substance. It's roughly 2"x5"x7" (the footprint being 2"x5"), and made of an odd rubbery material that almost feels like a non-slip coating, as if one might need to carry this around with sweaty hands. It also does need to be plugged into the wall, unlike smaller drives which can pull power through the USB cable. It's also a little chatty, making a series of quiet but audible clicks, whirrs, and chitters while in use.--We relocated our computer and this back-up drive from a solid built-in wooden desk to a freestanding ikea desk, and suddenly it's LOUD. I moved it back to the built-in desk and it was quiet again, so it's some function of the desk material or thickness that makes it so distracting in its new location. The humming vibration is so loud that it drowns out the clicks and whirrs i noticed in the original review.

This is one of the best items I've gotten from Amazon so far. For July 4, I used the Big Boss fryer to make  grilled pork chops, burgers and hot dogs. All of them turned out juicy and delicious, and nobody missed the oil! I managed to cook the hotdogs and burgers simultaneously by putting the burgers on the bottom of the glass bowl and the hot dogs in a mesh basket on the rack. Since the hot dogs cook faster, I used the tongs to remove them when they were done and then put the burgers on the top rack for the remaining minutes of cooking time.According to the instruction booklet, the halogen heats the food from above, the convection circulates the hot air and the infared light seals in the juices. So far everything has turned out delicious and best of all, I could not detect any loss in flavor due to the lack of oil. My next project will be fried chicken using a recipe that mimics the Colonel's, so I will update this review once that's done.For a product that calls itself oil-free, however, I found it strange that they decided to include an oil sprayer, but I guess it's for a few squirts of flavor if you want it. The included recipe book says you can also use the fryer to make popcorn and desserts, such as cinnamon buns. Amazing.My main quibbles:(1) Storage. This glass bowl is HUGE and washing it is a challenge if you don't have a dishwasher (like me). Perhaps in recognition of how tough this is, the manufacturer included a "self-cleaning" function in which you can squirt some dishwashing liquid and set the device to "wash" (like a washing machine). Clever, but you still have to rinse it out. Secondly, finding a place to store this item is tough also. It takes up almost all my counter space. Since the top gets very hot, you need to find a place to put the lid down as well after you're done cooking.(2) The timer. I noticed that if you set it for less than five minutes, the timer doesn't move. The timer stopped until I turned it for a longer cooking time. Not sure if this is a defect or is true of all these machines.(3) Halogen/Infared. How safe is this method of cooking? I threw away my microwave after reading a lot of studies saying that microwaves change the chemical composition of all foods permanently. I googled halogen and infared lighting, but so far haven't seen any studies that suggest that cooking food this way is dangerous or carcinogenic. The instruction book warns you not to look directly at the light while it's cooking, however, and the light that the device emits is incredibly bright (it lit up my whole kitchen!). It looks like a safe device (for now), but I'm wondering if there are any potential health hazards to using this method.(4) Plastic holder that supports the bowl feels flimsy. The instructions warn you to put the Big Boss on a firm counter top. This is because the heavy glass bowl is supported by a flimsy plastic holder, which looks like it could melt if the glass gets too hot. The four feet of the plastic holder also does not have skid-proof padding, so be aware the Big Boss could slip and slide unless you mount it on a solid surface.(5) Doesn't cook as fast as you might think. The times given for cooking certain items isn't that much of an improvement over the conventional oven. Chicken legs take almost as much time in a regular oven as the Big Boss. In some cases a toaster oven is even faster. However, it wasn't advertised as for its speed so much as for its ability to cook with no oil, which is a big plus!Other than these concerns, I'm really enjoying the food I've cooked so far with the Big Boss, and love the fact that food could taste this good without extra added oil!

The Belkin USB 2.0 4-Port Travel Hub is a basic hub that gives you a 4 for 1 boost in USB connections.  It works as expected, and it is overall a good device with one exception.  I would expect most people to use this hub with a laptop/netbook.  However the USB connecting cable, while designed for easy storage, is at the wrong angle to connect to a laptop while the hub lies flat on the table.  You have to rotate it 90 degrees in order to line up the connector with the horizontally oriented USB port on your laptop.  With the length of the cable on the connector as short as it is this puts more torque on the cable which I expect to lead to wear and tear issues down the road.  In my opinion Belkin made the wrong decision in trading off storage design at the expense of usage design.  If you happen to be using this for a desktop that has vertical USB ports, this will be a non-issue.  Otherwise you might want to consider something that errs on the design side of usage and longevity.

BACKGROUND:  I was in the market for a small MP3 player with primary usage at the gym.  I was looking for a rechargeable unit as my previous player ate AAA batteries about every week or so.  I considered three options of which the Sansa Clip was one of them.  I eliminated the iPod Shuffle due to its cost and lack of display.  The other primary contender was the Creative Zen Stone Plus (I rejected the non-Plus model due it its lack of display).  I will reference how the Sansa Clip won out throughout the rest of the review.SET UP:  The Sansa Clip is about as simple as it gets in this area.  It requires no additional software installation.  My home system runs XP SP2 with Windows Media Player 11.  When I plugged the player in to charge, it was detected and recognized automatically.  I told windows to "Take No Action" as the default behavior when the device connects.  This allows me to maintain complete control over the syncing process.  My unit charged in about an hour.MUSIC TRANSFER:  You have the option of using simple drag and drop of MP3 files to the device as you would a USB flash drive.  However, using Windows Media Player allows you the more advanced feature of playlists.  Since I primarily use my MP3 player at the gym, I created multiple playlists for warm up, workout, and cool down.  The workout lists are about 90 minutes while the others about 20 minutes.  I really liked that I was able to create multiples of each for variety.  Right now I have three of each with about 1.5 Gb still remaining to use as I please.  Using Windows Media Player, you can sync albums, songs, or playlists as you would with any other device.  The Sansa Clip fully supports all of these options so it is a nice low effort, highly functional set up.SOUND QUALITY:  This is an area where the Sansa Clip is pretty impressive.  I previously had the Sansa M230, and I can tell a significant difference in sound quality.  I am able to hear a lot more detail in the higher ranges (such as high hat cymbals).  I am using the headphones that came with the unit, but I would image that higher quality headphones would sound even better.  The player also has a series of preset equalizer settings for different music styles as well as one that you can customize.DISPLAY:  This is a distinguisher between the Clip and the Zen Stone Plus.  The display is larger and easier to read.  The mix of blue and yellow against the black background is also pleasant.NAVIGATION:  The Clip has a normal four button dial that is common to most small MP3 players.  With the crisp, clear display it is easy to move around and select music by artist, album, song, or playlist.  The only thing that I have noticed that doesn't work quite the way I would like is that if you navigate away from the song that is playing there doesn't seem to be a way to get back to it to see the details of what's playing.  This is pretty minor, though, because I do not regularly navigate away from the song that is playing.FM RADIO:  This is about what you would expect from a unit with no external antenna.  Strong signals come in clearly, but it is not going to match what you can pick up on your car stereo.  This is a nice to have feature for me so it is plenty adequate.OPTIONS:  As I mentioned previously, my primary usage comes at the gym.  I had used the song timer to measure the time between reps while lifting weights on my M230.  However, the Clip has a power saving feature that shuts off the display after 15 seconds by default.  However, you can change this to 30, 45, 60, or 90 seconds which should cover your needs.  After adjusting mine, I wake up the display after completing a set.  When the display shuts off, it's time for the next set.USE ON THE GO:  This is the other area where the Clip separates itself from the Zen Stone Plus.  You can clip the player to your clothes or an arm strap (I use the one that came with my M230).  The Zen Stone Plus requires purchase of a separate armband accessory for an additional $15.COST:  At base price, the Zen Stone Plus and Sansa Clip are a push.  However if you factor in another $15 for an armband you have a clear winner given the other advantages.CONCLUSION:  The Sansa Clip is now the leader in 2 Gb small MP3 players.  Give it a spin and you won't be disappointed.

I am loathe to put anything on my phone -- all covers/shields are a compromise that trades the phone's native form for protection.  I went 2.5 years without anything on my Galaxy S phone using just common sense, and the only scratch I got on the screen happened at the end - the screen shattered when I dropped it on a sidewalk.  My wife, on the other hand, must keep aquarium gravel in her purse, because her Galaxy S was viciously scratched after just a couple of months.  And after I saw the first gouge on her Nexus 4 screen - I immediately ordered the Tech Armor HD Clear Screen Protector.A few quick comments:*  The Tech Armor product only covers the front screen.*  The package comes with 3 sheets.  I won't order products with only a single sheet, because inevitably, I need at least one "Practice" sheet.*  There are cut outs for the proximity sensor, front camera, and speaker.*  As noted in other reviews the Nexus 4 screen curves near the edges, and the film is cut to only cover the flat part of the screen*  It is a little short in length - the coverage is adequate, but some glass at either the top or bottom will be exposed.  I believe this is intentional and a good design because it makes positioning the the shield easier (more on that below).*  The feel of the product is a tad tacky, but I found wiping it down with eye glass lens cleaner helped a lot.*  While applying the screen protector - you can lift it up and re-position it many times without ill effect - just be sure to lift up the film with tape.  If you use your finger nail on the edge - that edge will bend and never stick well again.The curved nature of the Nexus 4 screen makes putting on any screen protector a challenge.  Any part of the screen protector that extends onto the curve of the screen will not stick.  And because the phone does not have a raised lip to use as a guide, you have to apply your screen protector using your best judgement of what is perfectly straight.  Be prepared to have to re-position the screen protector again and again and again to get it to align correctly.  This is not the fault of the screen protector manufacturer - its the nature of the Nexus 4 curved screen.  Re-positioning is easy - just use some tape to lift the screen protector off the glass.  I used duct tape - it worked great.You'll also have to lift the screen to remove the inevitable bits of dust that sneak onto the glass as you're applying the screen protector.  Again, lift the the screen protector up with a piece of tape, and remove the dust with another piece of tape.  It's actually easier than it might sound.In the end, the product works fine.  Yes, I can tell there's something on there and yes, the feel is a bit different than the native glass.  But the impact on clarity is indeed very little.  Unfortunately, I didn't have the patience to get the protector positioned exactly right on my 2 phones - you can see the edges lifting just a tad on both.  I think the product should be just be a few mm less wide to make horizontal allignment easier.  Will it last a lifetime - not if it is lifting on the edge.  But I suspect it will last half a year or so, and for the price ($7 for 3), I can live with that.

I purchased the Bose QC15 headphones primarily for use during long, intercontinental flights. They are wonderful. Plug them into your computer, smartphone, Ipod , the plane's headphone outlet or what have you, click on some music and kick back for the next 9 hours or so. These headphones really do silence out the din of the other passengers, as well as the droning of the aircraft engines and that air circulation hiss, while allowing you to be aware that your travel companion or the flight attendant is speaking to you. Thing is, you cannot clearly make out what they are saying, so if you want, you can just pretend you do not hear and go blissfully on listening to whatever. In researching these, I came across reviews that questioned the sonic fidelity, etc of these headphones. I am not a recording engineer or headphone guru, but these headphones sound perfectly fine to me. Frankly, I doubt that I could hear some of the things that the critics write about anyway. Besides which, I did not buy these headphones to sit in my  living room to listen to the 160 microphone, latest digital technology recording of a symphony orchestra or the thumping bass laden gangster rap recording of the latest MC Whoever. I bought them to provide me an envelope of relative quiet while flying on airliners, and that they do very well. My one complaint would be the fact that you cannot use the headphones as just regular headphones in the event that your batteries go dead. If the battery goes dead, then the headphones are dead. Luckily, the batteries are just generic AAA's, nothing exotic, built-in or proprietary. My solution, stick an extra set of batteries in the carrying case. Problem sort of solved.

NOTE: I would give this phone 1.5 stars if possible.A little background... I had a 2+ year old Droid 2 Global (on Verizon) before it gave up the ghost. Several email & social networks accounts setup on it ...and ~420 apps installed (which includes the Verizon unused Bloatware) ...granted, a lot of the apps not used regularly. 512 MB RAM, 8 GB of internal storage and 8 GB microSD card. Only complained of low storage after downloaded a movie or two from Google Play.Onto this quadband phone...Purpose for the phone (besides replacement) was to try alternate carriers (besides Verizon) to see if worth switching ...and also wait to see if next wave of new droid phones were worth upgrading to versus keeping this generic (Galaxy S3 clone) older / lower expense one.PROS:-Great bundle of items as listed ...plus came with 2 covers ...one with & another without a flip cover.-Can have 2 (full size) SIM cards installed ...but need to toggle what feature (Voice, Video, Data, Messaging) is used for given SIM-Works with T-Mobile (no contract / unlimited plan) ...but only 2G speeds (expected issue after some additional research) at least in New England area. Note, 3G+ for T-Mobile requires 2 frequency bands ...but the phone has only one of them.-Crisp clear screen (...barring direct sunlight).-Nice battey life for a smart phone (...over a day if minimal data or wifi is used).-Works internationally, used in Europe.--The T-Mobile SIM transitioned to roaming under "Optimus"  ...but very expensive ...did not used ...but nice to have as a backup.--Purchased pre-pay "Vodafone" SIM (w/ talk & text ...no data option) ...very good reception and call quality.-Quick load \ start up time.NEUTRAL:-Misleading packaging. Screen film states phone as quad processor ...no, it is dual. Mentions NFC, not that I could find. BUT neither of these 2 items are mentioned in the Amazon listing so they were not expected ...nor deal breakers for me.CONS:-Random shutoffs ...This may be an isolated build (quality) issue. During the 1st week, started noticing that phone was turned off when I would take it out of my (shirt and/or pant) pocket to use. Originally thought something put accidental pressure on the switch which caused it to turn off. Turns out phone is very sensitive any taps / bumps that automatically causes shutoff with no warning. This includes placing (...not dropping) phone on a table ...or even tapping the dial out button too hard ...will turn of the phone. ...NOT good if expecting call(s) ...and your phone is off. Shouldn't need to check every 10 - 15 minutes to confirm that the phone is on.-Whac-a-mole: Phone calibration is very erratic (and I did try calibrating the phone sensors several times). When making calls where dial pad is needed during the call (i.e. checking / navigating voice mail), the screen would go in and out of "screen saver mode". Felt like I was playing an unwanted game of "Whac-a-mole" where the call would eventually disconnect before I had a chance complete the dial pad navigation.-Phone storage: Amazon listing states "Internal memory: 4GB(Note: The operate system and Apps take some spaces, so only show 2GB + 502MB)". Listing is misleading. Yes, internally it showed ~1.8 GB and 450+ MB of available space. BUT, apps that require "internal" storage will ONLY use the  "500" MB portion. The 'other' 2 GB portion is an "either / or" situation in that you either use it as "external" 'phone storage' versus "external" 'microSD card storage'. Myself, I had installed a 32GB microSD card ...and defaulted to that (not the included available 1.8 GB). Based on Amazon's listed information, I knew that I would not be able to have my previous 400+ apps installed on this phone. Initially only had a little over a hundred installed. As time went on, the cache & data increased (mostly from email and social apps), so I found myself slowly removing other less frequently used apps. Now, this depends on the apps installed as some can be completely installed to the external storage. Not the case for my primary apps.I will keep the phone given the low price but will be looking to buy another phone ...and probably give this one to my son to use the WIFI connection and play his games on it.Given the shortage of app storage and mainly power downs & "screen offs", it did not fit my needs ...nor reliable enough for me.Side note, phone was fulfilled by Amazon from ProntoTec.---------------------UPDATE...By November (less than 6 months after purchase), the phone is no longer usable. Had to handle the phone 'delicately'. Any minor bounce or bump would turn off the phone ...causing me to miss calls ...or disconnect in middle of conversation. Also portion of screen lost sensitivity resulting at times not be able to easily enter the PIN to log in ...had to be very precise in specific area to touch just enough of the edge of the PIN number ...and regular navigation on screen was difficult due to usable touch area.

Although I never expected to get "professional" quality cappuccino from this little Krups machine, I was terribly disappointed that it didn't even meet my admittedly low expectations.First, as with all plastic coffee makers, there's _that_ smell and taste. I ran water through both the coffee filter and the steaming nozzle ten times and the smell was as strong as ever. I then tried four ounces of water with a splash of white vinegar, followed by five more rinses with clean water. I left the boiler cap (dome lid) off the water tank for 12 hours, which seemed to help a little, but the plastic smell came back as soon as I ran water through it again.Eventually I decided rinsing wasn't going to help, so I took the plunge and made some espresso. I started with four ounces of water and ended up with two ounces of espresso in the carafe. Instead of forcing steam down into the grounds, big billowing clouds of steam were escaping from the poorly sealed boiler cap. This wasn't a big surprise since I had noticed it during all the previous trial runs with water alone. Yes, the cap was screwed down as tightly as possible, but that didn't help. When I applied pressure, using a dish towel to hold the top down, less steam escaped from the top and more coffee dripped into the carafe. But that is a real nuisance!The frothing nozzle seems poorly designed. It's next to impossible to hold a pitcher or cup of milk under the nozzle because it's too tight against the side of the base. You need to be able to tip the cup so that you can get the nozzle to the milk, but there isn't enough room to get a good angle. So, lots of steam was hitting my hand and lots of milk was splashing out of the cup, but there was next to no actual froth.Finally, when the unit is producing steam it sometimes emits a very loud and high pitched whistle. No kidding, at first I thought it was a severe weather alert coming from somewhere. But, no...it was the espresso machine setting off a barking frenzy from the neighbor's dog.I'll give one and a half stars, rounded up to two, to the KRUPS XP100050 Steam Espresso Machine with Frothing Nozzle simply because it does make espresso, albeit not as much as it should because almost half the water/steam escapes from the top. And if I want a cappuccino, I have other frothing methods at my disposal (Aerolatte Milk Frother, Chromeor my new favorite toy theCapresso Froth TEC Automatic Milk Frother).Krups usually makes good and reliable products. I've used one of their electric coffee grinders for over a decade and it's still doing an excellent job. That makes this experience with the espresso machine both surprising and disappointing. It certainly doesn't tempt me to give up my French press.

This armor gives me a bit more confidence when I'm carrying the camera around. However, there are also several caveats that should be mentioned.THE GOOD* The armor really does feel like it would be effective in assuaging the effects of bumps, etc. Thankfully, my camera hasn't encountered a serious bump/drop to test this further.* The fit is surprisingly good. All of the buttons still work with ease. It is a little bit harder to reach the buttons on the back of the camera below the screen, but it's not a deal breaker.* The bottom plate is well designed. It comes with a tripod socket that attaches to the original socket on the camera to essentially extend it for use with the armor. It's also fairly easy to get to the battery compartment.* The LCD screen protector is hard plastic. This was a great bonus. It's very clear and seems to give a greater level of protection vs an adhesive film.THE CAVEATS* The skin adds a bit of bulk to the camera, both with weight(about 1/2 pound)and size. The skin varies in thickness from about 1-10mm and adds about 7mm to the grip. So if you have small hands, you will find it difficult to hold the camera.* It's a dust magnet.* The lens hood is sort of useless. If you have a decent lens collection, it will only work of a subset of them. This is due to the diameter of the lens (the hood will not stretch enough to fit larger lenses) and also the effectiveness of the hood itself in blocking stray light at certain focal lengths. I could have done without the lens hood if it meant a lower price.* The lens cap leash is a joke. One end attaches to the hood and the other sticks on to the cap. This is fine if you only use one lens, but pretty useless if you switch lenses.* The LCD protector uses the viewfinder area for mounting. You might have problems if you use an eyepiece extender or angle finder that mounts to the viewfinder. I haven't tested it out, but it's something to consider.* The neck strap has to be removed to install the armor. This was actually a big pain and I dread the day when I'll have to do this again to remove the armor.

The Logitech Z600 Bluetooth makes a bold statement with it's sleek and modern design, thoughtfully designed interface, and blasting bass. My interpretation of good sound quality may differ form yours.Features at a glance- Bluetooth speaker, but also can be connected through auxiliary 3.5mm jack. This also comes with a bluetooth usb dongle so you can use on your pc, mac, or laptop. Very useful.- Powered through power adapter. The power block is oddly huge. Not a problem if you're setting the speaker up stationary.- Bluetooth & power button, auxiliary connection are located on the back column of the left speaker. Hidden from view, easy to reach.- The volume control is a touch-controlled and is located on the top of the left speaker. Swipe a clockwise to increase volume, swipe counter-clockwise to decrease volume. You can tell the difference of the volume control by the rougher, matte feel.DesignThe Z600 is very stylish and sleek. The gray mesh is beautiful, long, and gives the speakers an elegant full look. They stand proudly on any desktop, table, TV, etc. The bright white back column on the speaker gives it an eye-popping contrast. The "sub-woofers" are located on the bottom of each speaker, also conveniently stating which is left or right (I don't take this for granted. Together, these speakers make a stylish statement.Sound qualityBass - the lows and bass of the speakers are very good. These speakers provide plenty of power and rumbling. They certainly have the ability to shake and rumble a small room.Overall (mids, highs)The good - perfect for watching movies, playing games, and listening to music (but don't expect top-knotch clarity and depth)Could be better - Overall sound quality can feel airy and lack depth. Most people will be happy with the full-feeling bass, but the sound quality could use some more depth. Vocals and dialogue can feel airy at times.The Z600s do a lot of things right - elegant design, good placement of buttons (with style in mind), and rocking bass. I purchased this rack a couple of months back as an inexpensive solution for transporting our bikes for charity or special riding events farther from our home than we would simply ride out to.  Having used this rack for a couple of months now, I have numerous points:- The special pin that comes with the rack for locking it into your car's hitch does work to eliminate horizontal slack on the curved, bottom portion of the rack that slides into the car's hitch.  Another review mentioned drilling the holes for this pin to work--I highly recommend NOT drilling anything!- The rest of the rack is sort of slack/loose, so due to play between the main vertical post and the curved bottom portion, as well as play between the swinging bicycle hanger arms and the vertical post, there is a great deal of rattling and noise that comes from this rack, especially if the rack is not loaded and there's no music playing.- Due to the design of the rack, both pivot points, the one between the vertical post and the hitch arm, as well as the one between the bicycle hanger arms and the vertical post, have a significant amount of friction, so the more you swing the components up and down, the more the rack actually wears.  I have worn away a good deal of paint where the hanger arms swing up and down on the sides of the vertical post, and so a lesser extent paint wear at the bottom of the vertical post where I occasionally swing the rack down for access to our SUV's cargo hatch.- There is insufficient space between the bike mounts on the hanger arm to fit more than 2 bikes if you have drop handle bars on your bikes.  There's no real way around this.  We were unable even to fit both road bikes on at the same time as a third, hybrid bike with flat bars.  Unless you have four wildly different sized and shaped bikes, don't expect to slap 4 bikes on this thing.- There are no vertical stays to prevent the bicycles from swaying.  A good example of a rack that does have these would be the Saris Bones racks--there is an additional arm that comes down from the bike hanger arms that allows vertically security of the bikes so they do not sway back and forth when accelerating or decelerating, potentially hitting the car, the vertical post of the rack and/or the other bikes on the rack.Overall, I'd say you get what you pay for with this rack.  You pay less than you would for something from Saris or Thule, but you get less quality.  I suppose I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this rack to someone else looking for an inexpensive, secure bicycle rack, but if their budget fits it, I would recommend something higher end instead.  If anything, due to the wear on the paint from normal usage, I'd say that the money saved initially on choosing this rack over others would eventually be spent on replacing the rack because it simply doesn't seem like something that would last nearly as long as the more expensive stuff.  Only time will tell how long this rack will last me (and if I remember to, I may come back in and update this review once the rach finally does fail due to rust or wear & tear).-Ed

I'm a tea junkie. Green tea, chamomile, whatever. I used to use a large microwave-safe measuring cup to heat my water. The large measuring cup meant the water lost its heat quite rapidly. Now, I tend to not like to buy devices such as this kettle. I mean, the microwave heated the water just fine, right? Honestly, this kettle is fantastic - it frees up the microwave for other family members to use, it keeps the water quite warm for a much longer period of time than my old method did, plus its nice that it shuts itself off after reaching boiling point. It also does its work fairly quickly too (5 minutes give or take a minute?).The round base is plastic, with a small cylinder sticking up from the center. Inside this cylinder is housed an electrical contact that inserts into the base of the kettle and gets things going. This design is quite nice too, because it allows one to pivot the kettle on this spindle to grab the handle from any angle which is quite handy. The cord also rolls up into the base to take up extra slack thus reducing clutter on the counter. The top of the handle has a large button that you press to pop open the top and put water in. The mechanism for that seems fairly sturdy and the lid fits snugly after countless uses. Directly across from the inside of the handle embedded in the kettle is a window that allows you to see what your water level is at inside. The instructions and this window tell you to not put water in above the very top mark. Trust me - DON'T DO THAT! I overfilled it the first time, and water leaked down from somewhere inside and came out of the bottom of the kettle which houses the heating element and wiring. I shook out as much water as I could and let it air dry for a couple of days and its no worse for the wear. Just a cautionary tale!The kettle is great because it is so simple - put water in, place on base, press the button. On Amazon's picture, the button is the little tab sticking out under the handle. I feared it would be flimsy, but it feels more substantial in use. It also turns a very attractive and bright shade of blue when the device is powered on. When you reach boiling point, it turns off and flips itself up to the 'off' position. This kettle doesn't have various buttons that allow you to program in desired temperatures. You push the button, your water boils. Overall, this is a very attractive device - I have no qualms keeping it out on my counter top. I would describe it as being almost elegant (for an electric kettle).One final point - Aroma states to never put anything in the kettle besides water (so no dumping Swiss Miss powder in when the water gets hot). I abide by this, but find it odd because the spout has a built in strainer with largish holes in it. I'm not sure what I would need to filter that is that large if I only put water in, but maybe I don't want to know.Look around locally for this item. Amazon is usually awesome with pricing but what is being asked here is crazy. Look to spend around $30.00 or so.Hope this helps!***Update 9-17-2012***I have to say that I am a bit disappointed:I have had this kettle only 4 months, and it has begun to develop a nasty rusty-looking spot on the screen of the spout. My house has hard water so that may explain some of that, but because this was stainless steel, I didn't think this would be an issue. Otherwise, it still works fine.

I never thought I'd have to troubleshoot memory as much as I did with this board. First I got disappointed with my Transformer Prime, now this.  Asus, please, get your act together.  I spent hours on this, it's a lot of money, plus the hassle of returning this.Note that 4, 8, even 16GB works fine (as long as you don't use a1 and a2...).  Asus QVL list doesn't list a single bank vendor capable of filling all slots, so THEY KNOW ABOUT THIS.  They test with 2 and 4GB banks mostly, you don't see QVL with fast 8GB banks each: you see only Corsair with 4GB modules qualified for 16GB max - WHY?  Go ahead and see for yourself on the ASUS website/manual.But why would you buy this board if that's all you really need/want?

Ordered through Amazon which indicates enclosure comes from Vantec, maker of these enclosures.First, the enclosure was not the same as advertised on VANTEC's website, despite exact same model numbers.  Enclosure I received did not have a fan on/off switch though this is shown on the website.  I must have received an old enclosure.Second, the package did not include screws to mount the hard drives to the brackets though the instructions say these are provided.  Poor quality control.Third, the fan is noisy (like a steady white noise).  This is not a small point especially in a quiet room.  Using a Sound Level Meter, I measured approximately 50 DB noise level one foot away in a quiet room.  This would be equivalent to the sound of rainfall outside or a dishwasher in the next room.  You get the point.Fourth, in my configuration with Windows XP Pro and Service Pack 3 using 2TB and 1TB Hitachi SATA preformatted hard drives, JBOD could not be used.  As described in the instructions, the enclosure has a two position switch.  One position selects JBOD and the other makes each drive appear individually as if you had two drive enclosures.  In JBOD mode drives should appear as one combined drive.  They don't.  They appear as individual drives, i.e., L:drive and O:drive.  With switch set to individual drive setting, only one drive showed up and it showed up as unformatted.Since this enclosure doesn't work as advertised for my configuration, it came with missing parts, it was noisy, and it was not the same design as advertised by the vendor, I'm am returning it.UPDATE 8 Feb 2010:  I contacted VantecUSA technical/customer support to address the issues above before sending the unit back.  They didn't care about the missing screws.  They indicated the fan on/off switch had been removed in new models because customers tended to turn off the fan resulting in overheating drives.  Another indication of poor design or poor fan implementation.  A variable speed fan or thermally controlled fan is within the price point of this type unit.  They confirmed JBOD doesn't work with a 32 bit Windows XP system using drives which exceed a total of 2TBs.  To get JBOD to work with Windows XP and larger drives, I would need a 64 bit system.  So, I'm not satisfied and I am now returning this unit.  A great concept with limited flexibility and a very poorly designed fan system.  Additionally, English is not the native language of technical/customer reps who I was in contact with.  I had to interpret their broken English.

Audio quality, well, I'm just using the stereo speakers on my flat panel 52", but I detected no digital artifacting, etc.  It claims to support DTS, but I can't test that.The overall functionality is pretty amazing, though the menu system is VERY slow.  The lag is about 4 times the lag of the BD390.  I thought this would be fine since it had more functionality, but it's an important issue to bring up.Almost everything is an LG App.  You don't pick the apps, they all show up in a separate menu.  That separate menu takes about 12 seconds to load.  Picking an app from the list then takes another 8-12 seconds to load up.  Playing network video?  That is off of the main menu, but is a separate menu that takes the same load time.The front panel is a flip out plate that covers the real front panel.  Most of the buttons, etc are obscured with the panel up.  It's spring loaded, and opens automatically when the drive tray opens.  When it's closed, it partially obscures or limits remote input.  You have to be within 45 degrees to use the remote.  If you're off to the side, it just reflects off of the cover plate.The internal drive is there, and works, but only as buffer/cache.  When I configure the SMB/CIFS server on this unit, it shows up on my network.  I can browse from this unit, from an iPad, from an XP PC, Linux 3.2, or Windows 7.  The unit shows the share, but if you try to access the share itself, the SMB/CIFS resets, and the share disappears.The unit plays some media via DNLP or CIFS, and some media it downloads the whole thing to internal storage.  If this has to pause, rewind, or reset, it drops the cached copy and re-downloads the entire file again.  Often, audio and video will desynchronize, or will change pitch (slow, muffled, underwater sounding).When downloading, the unit is very slow.  The unit has a 10/100 ethernet port, but when sync'd at 100mbit, it still transfers slower - 16 minutes for 400MBytes - closer to 3mbit.  This implies the ethernet port might actually be USB attached internally, or otherwise is low performance.After current firmware updates, the unit crashes at the home screen after initial power-up about 50% of the time.  It also MAY crash when accessing any network service.  If you play multiple episodes from NetFlix or Amazon, it may crash 30 seconds into the next episode.The warranty during the order and in the paperwork says 1 year parts, 1 year labor; however, the website claims this is an error and that it only has 1 year parts, 90 days labor.  My order was in August of 2012, but the manufacture date was August 2011.  At best, "repair" will cost me round trip shipping, plus standard labor rates, which far exceed the cost of buying a new unit.  In reality, this is a design defect that has cost them too much money, and they are encouraging people to buy new units.Lucky/Goldstar used to be THE discount brand to buy.  Features, functionality, etc were all top notch, and price was comparable to other brands.  I'm not so sure anymore.  This experience has really soured my feelings towards LG.

I've had better all-round luck with Power2000 *****I bought this extra battery for my Olympus Stylus with high hopes since a different battery from a different "No Name" brand works well in my Canon camera.  On arrival the battery looked just like the Olympus original but when I put it in the camera nothing happened.Since rechargable batteries usually arrive with enough charge to at least turn on the equipment, I wondered if the thing was DOA.  I tried charging the battery several times in the camera without success in any way.  Again I figured DOA.For some reason I eventually tried pressing the battery down lightly inside the battery compartment with my finger and turning the camera on.  ...It worked...  And it worked fine every time I tried it.When installed, the battery is a "hair" too short to touch the contacts inside the battery compartment.  The original Olympus battery has NO HINT of this problem.  I roughly compared the Olympus and Maximal batteries side by side.  If there is any difference in length it is very small but apparently enough to cause an issue.I imagine the problems with the battery having no power seen here in a few negative reviews could be from a lesser degree of the same issue, where the power connection is flawed during use or charging so one suspects the thing is no good.The work-around is to build up the end of the battery with tape or something, though such a fix could make switching batteries a real pain given the tight clearances in the battery compartment.I decided to exchange the battery and hope the replacement meets the original spec. better.  I'm encouraged by it's vast majority of 4 and 5 Star reviews.  The battery was provided by Amazon and I managed to discover the problem within Amazon's Return Window so at least the return is going smoothly, supposedly with no extra cost to me for shipping the battery back and receiving it's replacement.The replacement arrived and has the same problem.  Using several layers of scotch tape, I built up the battery end where the tiny clip holds it in the camera.  The battery seems to work fine now while still slipping in and out of the camera easily.The package has a Support number to call.  The person I spoke with didn't know of any problems like mine and recommended I return the battery to Amazon AGAIN and ...get this... TRY AN DIFFERENT BRAND.  AND though it also is marketed for other manufacturer's cameras, this replacement is SUPPOSED to be an EXACT match for the Olympus model my camera takes...It even has the same Model Code on the package (LI42B).Subsequently I was looking at replacements for a Canon NB-6L battery and saw many 1 Star ratings for MaximalPower's NB-6L battery noting that the thing was TOO BIG to fit, although otherwise that battery also has a high rating.
