Okay, first thing is the packaging. This is the most impossible, most annoying, most overpackaged product I have ever had the displeasure to open. Scissors are required but the spaces are so tight that one risks damaging the product or one's own fingers all the while trying to differentiate the wires from the twist ties. Really, this isn't a nuclear device - they're earphones that are going to be put through all kinds of wear and tear. If they need that much protection in shipping, what can one expect when they're in everyday use?The fit within the ear canal was great for me. The silicon pads form a pretty good seal and when sitting still, the earphones do a great job of canceling outside noise. I even went into the laundry room and had difficulty hearing the washing machine and dryer. These would be great earphones for a plane flight being much easier to carry than my fancy huge Bose noise-canceling earphones. There are several sizes of pads to choose from and most people should find a pair that fits.That being said, there is an issue with cable rustling noise. In other words, any time the cables are touched, the rustling sound can be heard through the earphones. Sitting still on an airplane wouldn't be a problem, but walking or running or doing any kind of moving makes clearly audible noise. I contacted customer service and was told that it's a common problem with all-in-one microphone-earphone sets -- it's called microphonics -- and that the second generation has been retooled to cut down on some of that noise. A check of my serial number confirmed that Amazon had shipped me the first generation. Customer service at V-Moda kindly offered to exchange the headset but for review purposes, I did not follow through with the exchange.I don't have an iPhone so the microphone feature is probably overkill for me. I would think that the earphones without the microphone would solve the rustling problem.Customer service was extremely fast, thorough, and understanding.The fabric-like cables have a nice feel to them, but they tend to tangle more than the typical iPod-type cables. No matter how much care is taken coiling them up after use, they still seem to get knotted when uncoiled.Also, the pause and fast-forward features are not compatible with all iPod models; i.e., not with my 80GB iPod, but they did work with my 120GB iPod. Read the information closely to make sure you have the correct model.

The Magellan RoadMate RV9145-LM is specifically designed for RVs with its huge screen, extendable windshield mount, and built in Good Sam Guide, but it needs a major speed boost.Except for it's huge screen the RoadMate looks pretty much like every other navigation system on the market.  The front is done in piano black, and the rear silver plastic.  The RoadMate is nicely assembled, the plastics are high quality, and it feels sturdy in the hand.  There is only one physical control on the RoadMate and that is the power/reset switch on top.Included with the navigation system are a computer USB cable, a cigarette lighter power cord, and a household outlet power cord.  The included windshield mount is nicely designed and extends almost a foot, making it easy to reach the navigation system when it is mounted on the far away windshield of an RV.  Still, the mount folds down nicely so you can use it in a car just as well.  The only weak point on the mount is the ball joint that holds the screen upright.  If you don't make sure it's tightly secured the navigation system will start to droop and pivot as you go over bumps. One feature I really liked about the windshield mount was that the outside edge of the suction cup is sticky, so it's easy to get the initial grip on the windshield.  After leaving the RoadMate attached to my windshield for a weekend the suction cup removed easily and left no residue behind.Choosing your destination is easy.  You can use choose to go to an address, a city center, an intersection, a point of interest, or emergency services.  Under the point of interest section is the RV centric Good Sam Guide, which contains a directory of RV parks, travel services, and things to see and do.  The rest of the points of interest choices are your standard food, fuel, shopping, etc.  The RoadMate's large screen making choosing items easy, and it speaks the letters out as you enter an address.  You are also given a few choices about the route you would like it to plan, for instance to avoid highways.In use the RoadMate is mostly a good experience.  Finding the initial satellite signal took only a minute or so, and afterwards it locked the signal quickly.  The screen is bright, crisp, and colorful and the map animation is smooth.  The voice prompts sound natural, read off the street names smoothly, and are plenty loud.  I also appreciated the chime that sounds just before your turn, as it helped me to not miss some turns when I wasn't paying attention to the voice prompts.  When encountering multilane highways a graphic of the proper exit ramp to take appears on the screen and makes choosing the correct lane easy.  The top of the screen displays the name of the next street and the direction of the turn.  The bottom left hand side shows trip information.  The current road's speed limit is shown on the left hand side of the screen, is very accurate, and can warn you when you go a certain speed over the limit.  If you miss a turn it recalculates in about 7 seconds, and if you need to take a detour you can choose to detour for a certain number of miles, which is a nice feature.The RoadMate's biggest letdown is its slow response times.  You tap the screen and wait at least a second for anything to happen.  The problem is not the touch screen itself as it chimes as soon as my finger selects something; rather it's the software running behind the screen that takes time to respond to your command.  When putting in a destination at a stop it's not a terrible issue, but when you're driving and want to alter your route, or choose a point of interest along the route, the RoadMate's slow response time means your eyes are away from the road for far too long.  Additionally, the software is a little buggy.  Twice it froze on me necessitating a reset.  Thankfully, the reset button is very conveniently placed.You can download the computer software necessary to update the maps and sync the address book on Magellan's website, and I tired the software on a PC running Windows 7 and one running Mac OS X 10.6 and it worked fine on both machines.  You need to create an account with Magellan to use the software, however.  The software is very basic, and a little slow to respond but works well enough.All in all...huge screen, great directions, but frustratingly slow.

I have been using these little phones since I discovered them many years ago. They are so lightweight and the sound is outstanding for their category. If they cost $29.99 they'd still be a deal. Not so with these little Sonys. They out-perform themselves by delivering clean sound across all frequencies.No small-diameter earphone is going to be able to reproduce bass-rattling low frequencies like a woofer or external speak does, or even a larger, standard studio style headphone. But for everyday use there is nothing to beat them, or even come close. They will promptly become your favorite digital headphones.UPDATE: As of Dec 2, 2013 the price on these is $64.99!!!! I have been buying these headphones for at least 10 yrs, have owned 4 pairs, and I paid $5.99 - $7.00!!!! The model number is still the same exact model number I bought from Amazon (that this review was based on) that I paid $7 for. That's just a rip off. If they could make a profit for so many years at $7... now to jump to $64??? I will never buy them again unless this is some kind of typo!!

ORIGINAL REVIEW:  No speed difference - on the Comcast "12Mbps" plan, my old Motorola SB5100 and the new SB6120 both showed these essentially identical (!) results from [...] over  three separate tests of each modem:  download 21.16Mbps +/- 0.01Mbps; upload 4.37Mbps +/- 0.07Mbps.  SB6120 shows bonding four channels download; one channel upload.  Comcast automatically put their newest firmware (1.0.2.4) onto the modem.Despite the failure to create faster upload or download speeds, I agree with some posters here:  web pages seem to "zing" onto the screen.  Web browsing is more satisfying.  I gotta love it - worth the money in my opinion.AMENDED REVIEW:  My Internet was working perfectly before buying and unboxing the SB6120, but I can't seem to leave well enough alone.  Newer has to be better, right?But within a couple of days after installing this modem and posting the effusive review above, I noticed that Internet was "crashing" periodically.  The modem spontaneously re-booted itself every day or two; sometimes a couple of times in a day.  I figured bad Comcast and had three separate technician visits -- including a new line to the house, new line to the modem; disconnected a TV Comcast said was injecting some noise onto the line; supervisor came and checked; 2nd line support got involved.  Comcast said their measurements showed the line was "perfect" and couldn't figure out any problem.  But the problem continued, and I was tearing my hair out.  My kids who were gaming were really upset to lose Internet in the middle of games.  Looked at the modem log; sure enough, some abstruse signals were "timing out" apparently causing the modem to reboot itself.So after a few more weeks of unreliable Internet, I wised up and remembered that change is the enemy of stability.  I substituted the prior modem (Motorola SB5100) back in.  The problems instantly went away.  It's been about three months now, and I haven't so much as had to restart the SB5100 even once in that time!  Simply rock solid Internet.  Comcast really is great when it's great.Poking around on the Internet, there's some evidence that the latest firmware for the SB6120 is the culprit.  However, since us users have no control over that (Comcast downloads and substitutes existing firmware with its preferred version), there wasn't anything to do about it.Who knows -- broadband is a very high-tech, complex technology.  Maybe the problem is my local Comcast subnet.  But I doubt it.  This is a fundamental problem with the firmware IMO.  Test better, please, Motorola and Comcast! -- How come the nation's largest cable company can't get this right?  What happens to those poor users who subscribe to speeds above 20Mbps and end up with one of these SB6120's supplied by Comcast?  I hope Comcast has the wit to sub out another brand.You'll find my SB6120 for sale on eBay this week!ADDITIONAL COMMENT:  Ended up with a second SB6120, which failed within the ?3? year warranty period.  Motorola replaced it with a spankin' SB6121, the newer model.  Wow, the SB6121 ROCKS!  What a vast improvement.  I don't think I've had to reboot the new modem at all in nearly nine months of ownership.  Rock solid, and apparently smart enough to reboot itself (judging from its internal log) every few weeks or months when the signal in interrupted.  Motorola finally got it right!  I celebrated my new reliable modem by upgrading to Comcast's Blast! service, which delivers 36/6 Mbps in "Powerboost mode" and then settles down to 24/4.  Wow -- finally Internet I can count on. We routinely run as many as three Netflix "HD" downloads simultaneously without a hiccup among them.  These days it is bonding 4 channels down and three channels up. Great modem! Get one and shut off your monthly rental fee!

I bought these to hold my side surround speakers, so I wouldn't be using them for PA DJ activity. A fairly stable speaker stand, even on carpet with light speakers, when tilted it would wobble, but not fall over. If you mount a maximum weight/capacity-sized speaker, I'd suggest adding weight to the base.I found that the knob for locking it into a fixed height must be securely tightened.  I set the height I wanted and drilled through both tubes, and then inserted a self-tapping sheet metal screw in both stands, to ensure they wouldn't slip down.The plastic dish-like panel under the speakers, even when the center holding screw is tightened, will still allow the speaker to tilt and twist, even though it's supposedly locked. (I found this to be true on the VideoSecu wall mounts, also.) Not a serious problem, since it only tilted a little when bumped.I wouldn't rely on the provided rubber strips to hold the speaker. I drove 1/2-inch wood screws through the holes in the side brackets into the speaker box.The slot it the top post easily accommodates my 14-gauge, thick insulation, speaker wire. I did not find a plug in the bottom as other reviewers had mentioned. The wire slipped down and came out the bottom, easily.Overall, it's an excellent speaker stand, if you take the added steps. I gave it three stars because of the additions I had to make to satisfy me. If the lack of ability to lock the speaker base/clamps was resolved, it would be a five-star stand.Added: 8-22-2013:I had doubts about stability, but found that bumping them (on carpet) they simply wobble and don't fall over. I have them adjusted to within an inch of the lowest height. I'm very pleased with their stability.

I purchased this set due to the convenience of the self opening lids, stainless steel exterior and size. As time passed, I too experienced the slowly dying motor. Several of my friends have the same item or a different version of the large can and have all had the same problem. I haven't looked into it myself but from what I read, the manufacturer offers a new lid for $37 plus shipping as the only recourse for an out of warranty can. This uses a motion sensor to activate the motor and has a fan type wheel that passes between another sensor to count the revolutions of the motor. This is fed back to a logic board which determines how far to move the lid based on motor revolutions. Good basic design, just has a short life motor.  As most products do, this one uses an off the shelf motor which is readily available from several different sources. The motor number is RF-500TB-18280 which can be found on Amazon for about $10 and from the manufacturer for $2.25 plus a large shipping and handling charge. I disassembled the lid and got the part number from the existing motor and ordered one. Have not received it yet but will update my review when I have it installed. It's a fairly simple arrangement, if you can solder (or splice wires together with electrical tape) you can replace it yourself. Just be sure to be careful when you open the gearbox as there are two gears that will fall out. Simple to reassemble the gears, just look closely and give it a little thought.

I was foolish enough to buy this and get all excited about my future performance gains.  I have the super high-end MacBook Pro, and the stock 750GB 7,200 rpm drive boots up in about a minute, give or take a few seconds.  I bought the 750GB Momentus XT and was expecting SSD-like boot times and app launches.  My boot up time went from 1 minute, to around 30 seconds and my apps didn't seem to launch in a noticibly snappier fassion.Even though the price of this drive has gone down $60 since I bought it 11 months ago (it was $180 then), I still wouldn't buy it again.  The measley performance gains are simply not worth the price of this drive.  You are not truly getting the best of both worlds with this one.  Let's look at the facts.  Any computer user who wants to upgrade the performance of their machine should have a reason to do so.  That means they will use their computer frequently enough to benefit from these upgrades.  However, if the only upgrade you're seeing is a slightly faster boot time, and maybe a few other files launching marginally faster, you're just not making a really smart upgrade decision.  What user spends the majority of their time booting up and watching programs launch?  None; they spend their time accessing files.  Save yourself some dough and buy a placebo, or even better, double or quadruple your RAM for roughly 1/3 the cost of this drive.  That will make things much smoother.Here are a couple other facts: first, this HD will have 750GB of storage, and only 8GB of that is flash memory.  Most operating sytems alone will use a majority of that.  I am being very fair by saying that the average OS will use about 7GB of storage space.  That leaves you with 1GB, but I'll be generous and use 2GB for the sake of the argument.  You're basically paying for a fast 748GB HD with an extra 2GB of fake SSD.  Not really smart.  2nd, because of its design, this drive will constantly be reallocating the free 2GB space based on the files you use more, but keep in mind, you really only have 1GB (maybe 2 if you're lucky) to use for this process.This brings me back to my first point: if you are a user who can really justfy this kind of performance gain, then you are going to be accessing a heck of a lot more than 1-2GB.  That's not even enough to handle the average programs that I launch at startup.  This means that the HD will be very inconsistent in its data access times because it will not know which files to store on a regular basis.  It's like having a restaurant full of hungry people, and only one server to take all their orders.  They wouldn't know which person to serve first.  Also, because this drive will be constantly reorganizing files, it might shorten its life with all the constant reads and writes.  It will be reading and writing at least 4 times more than your stock HD.My last point is this, if you want a performance boost for this amount of money, do what I did and invest in data doubler equipment.  For almost half of what I paid for this drive, I bought a 64GB Sata III SSD, an optical drive to HD caddy, and an external enclosue from which to run my optical drive.  I put my stock 750GB HD in the optical bay with the caddy, put the 64GB SSD in the main bay, and I still have full use of my optical drive (which I frankly hardly use anyway).  Let's analyze this for a moment; for way less than what I paid for this XT drive, not only did I get an additional 64GB of storage (whereas with the Momentus I didn't add a single byte), and not only did I get 64GB of usable SSD instead of 8GB fake SSD, but I got some serious performance gains.  This is why I said that the Momentus SSD speeds weren't true SSD speeds.  With the Momentus XT, my Mac booted in around 30-40 seconds (very inconsistent).  There were time that it would decide to take up to a minute, probably due to inefficient  management of the 8GB flash memory.  Now that the OS is on my SATA III SSD, my boot times are consistently at 13.8 seconds.  Now *those* are true SSD speeds, and definitely worth making an upgrade for.  Not only that, but ALL of my programs, documents, and library files are in there as well, making my machine extremely snappy.  I mean app launch in less than half a second, many times even faster.  And all this for less than the cost of this silly wannabe drive. I got it for a 6 day backpack trip with my dad and my son.  We initially were looking for a 3 person tent with 2 doors, full coverage fly and 2 vestibules.  I looked at several 3 person tents including the Mountainsmith Morrison 3 Mountainsmith Morrison 3 Tent w/Footprint: 3-Person 3-Season and found that the Morrison 3 had far more square footage than any other 3 person tent (and the others cost much more).  A little more research revealed that the Genesee offers 2 more square feet and 6 inches more height than the Morrison 3 while weighing only 4oz more and packs down slightly smaller!  At the time the Genesee actually cost about $10 less (including the additional cost of the footprint for the GeneseeMountainsmith Genesee 4 Tent Footprint).We split the tent, fly, footprint, poles and stakes into 3 pats and each carried a part.  Weight is as follows (includes stuff sacks for each group):Tent:Fly & footprint:Poles & stakes:We had rain the first 3 days of the trip ranging from a drizzle to moderately heavy lasting up to 6 hours at a time.  The Gensee kept us dry and comfortable the whole time. We had plenty of room with 2 adults and 1 teenager, and I think you could fit 4 adults but not have any room for gear.

I wanted to maximize the amount of space I have available in the room, and the fact that this particular soundbar allowed me to avoid having a sub on the floor was a huge plus.  On to the review:Pros:SIZE- it is by no means sleek, but it doesn't overtake your TV stand either.  It blends perfectly with my TV and doesn't stand out.SOUND - sound is MUCH better than I anticipated.  I was looking for a very basic upgrade in sound quality with some added bass, but this unit really kicks for a small room.  The highs are perfect and the lows are completely adequate.  I can tell you, I like a lot of bass when I'm watching a movie - it adds to the experience.  I wouldn't be willing to give this five stars if the bass wasn't sufficient.  It will not make you feel like you are in a movie theater, but it WILL give you a great movie/TV watching experience.  I would compare it to a great car stereo.  The car stereo probably isn't going to sound as good as your $1,000 home theater system, but it will still sound great.  Same thing here.SETUP - setup was an absolute breeze.  Quite literally two cables.  If you can plug in a toaster, you can set this up in 5 minutes.Subwoofer Out - This just gave me peace of mind before ordering.  If the bass isn't enough for you, you can connect an external subwoofer.PRICE - I am convinced that this is the best valued soundbar in the market.  I've searched high and low.Cons:ADVERTISING - this isn't really a con as much as it is an expectation leveler.  They really push the 7.1 aspect of this soundbar, and the feeling you get of genuine surround sound.  I would say to keep those expectations at a minimum.  You're not going to fool anyone into thinking you have true 7.1 surround sound.  Don't get me wrong, it sounds fantastic.  But don't expect a technological miracle when you have this up and running.Overall:Great product.  If you are looking for bigger, better sound in your bedroom, guest room, office, etc., this is certainly for you.  If you are concerned about the bass, I would say that you'll probably be pleasantly surprised.  Such a great value!

I wanted to like this product -- really.  After all, a $200 bread machine SHOULD be great, when most are well under a hundred. First, the idea of a horizontal loaf with two blades seems good, but in reality, the Zo loaf is the same size as my Hitachi vertical loaf. When combined with the indentations on the sides of the pan, the result is bread that you can only use at home -- not for guests or gifts.My other issues:*The motor/blades are quite loud, and the bread pan clanks and moves when mixing.*The "add" beeping feature is also loud, and makes it impossible to use overnight.*There is no crust control setting except for the basic bread (i.e., you can't change the crust to "light" in the wheat setting).*The top consistently does not brown.*The loaves are consistently lopsided.  Again, this appears due to the "dual" blade feature.  Sometimes the dough ends up on one side of the pan, and stays there during baking.*The blades do not mix the materials at the side of the pan well.  I usually have to scrape the sides while mixing.*The bread is difficult to remove.  I never had this problem with my Hitachi.*There is no indicator if you don't have the bread pan properly inserted.  So you might end up with a cooked mass of unmixed ingredients.  My Hitachi has a "bread pan" indicator if you don't get it inserted all the way.If this were a $60 bread machine, these problems might not seem so bad.  But for a top-of-the-line machine, it was very disappointing.

Out of the box, it's ready to go. It acts as a network switch (better than a hub), a broadband (high-speed network) router and a firewall. Although Linksys offers no Mac-specific support, it works with Macs, even with an AirPort hooked into it.Linksys has released several firmware upgrades, which can be easily uploaded to the BEFSR41. A TFTP program is included in the firmware update package, but it's only for PCs (no surprise there, based on my previous comment.)Mac users will need to download MacTFTP, a shareware implementation of a TFTP client. Search on versiontracker.com for the latest version.Macs and PCs can share the same internet connection.The BEFSR41 also acts as a DHCP server, so you don't need to pre-assign IP addresses to the Macs and PCs in your network.The firewall prevents others on the Internet from snooping into your network; an important consideration if you have a high-speed Internet connection that is constantly online.Changing the settings is easy and can be accomplished through a web browser on either a PC or Mac. Simply use the IP address of the router as the url. ...It will prompt you for a userid and password. Leave the userid blank and enter just the password. (If you haven't changed the password yourself, the original password can be found by reading the owner's manual.)Unless you have some very specific network requirements, the out-of-the-box configuration will work very well for most people.Make sure you write down any settings you change. When you upgrade the firmware, all settings are reset to factory defaults.The best features: extremely easy to set up and it works.

I read a review of this lens on one particular blog where the reviewer offered high praise for the lens but added that he had to send 2 copies back to Tamron before he got a good version.  I think that's what happened with me.  For this kind of money I don't want to have to test to see if I got a good copy.I just sent this lens back after having rented it for 4 days.  I used it on a Canon T3I and a 7D.  I used it indoors with and without a flash, outdoors for kids soccer and softball and then did a series of test shots with it over at a friend's house.  The colors were all great but the shots were never as crisp as they should have been.  I've used the Canon 24-70 II in the past (I know it's more expensive) and this lens just doesn't compare.  I'd rate it higher than the kit lens that came with my T3i but not much higher.For the test shots with my friend we shot pictures of a newspaper at 50mm and 70mm from about 7 feet away.  At 100% magnification the characters on the newspaper were legible but blurry.  They should have been clear.  We did the same shots with a Canon 70-200 and a Canon 50mm f1.4 at the same focal point, speed and aperture and those shots were perfectly crisp even at 200% magnification.I shot some pictures of my wife wearing a derby hat from about 8 feet away. The colors were outstanding but when I zoomed in the images were not crisp.  Her eyelashes for example were a bit blurry.  I don't think it's something someone would notice in a 5x7 print but anything larger than that, I think, would have shown the weakness of the lens.If the lens was half the price it is now I would buy it.  At its retail price though, the copy I had was not worth it.

ok so first off the clamping force on this thing out of the box is about as bad as everyone says it is. i have a pretty small head so that's saying something. it's not extremely uncomfortable except for where the bottom of the cup squeezes between your ear and jaw -- it gives a faint sensation of gagging/nausea. fortunately, this is easily and very effectively alleviated by leaving it stretched out over something slightly wider than your head (like a near-field monitor or guitar case) overnight, or by simply swapping the headband out for its (included) larger alternative. i prefer the former solution because the metal is really strong and stretched it out just enough to make it comfy but still keep a tight grip on my head. also the larger headband is huge and looks dumb.which brings me to the next common complaint: they "look stupid". yeah the cups are rectangular but they're also impressively shallow and make clever use of memory foam to conform super close to the head. they end up looking ultramodern in my opinion. definitely better-looking than most sets that protrude like 3" out. it's also worth noting they don't have that stupid annoying flashing blue light that every other bluetooth audio device insists on sticking in the most noticeable spot possible. there's a tiny led underneath the left cup that blinks during pairing, turns red during charging, and stays off otherwise.the only drawback: my ears touch the inner part of the cups. that tends to degrade the sound just a little, but it doesn't bother me.here we go, second segue: sound quality.wired, they're good. comparable to logitech ue4000.over standard bluetooth, these things suck. they sound like beats solos with slightly clearer bass.over bluetooth with the aptx codec enabled (doable on pretty much every platform except iOS), they sound VERY good. as good if not better than they do wired. i'm still kind of surprised by this.they are by no means reference quality and don't sound analytic/neutral in any sense. bass is heavy, but rather accurate and not overwhelming, and highs are about as clear as middling consumer cans get. mids are kinda distant and shaky but acceptable. soundstage and separation are actually pretty great considering how close these are to your ears. overall they sound very good.one weird thing though: low-bitrate audio files sound really bad through these. anything below 320kbps tends to crackle and distort.isolation is terrible. the cup backs are very thin/cheap plastic that block astonishingly little sound. this wouldn't be an issue if it didn't allow for such unbearable micro phonics -- literally every instance of contact with the detachable cable, headband, cups, or anything else is heard loud & clear. it's this product's worst feature and honestly a deal killer for me.are these worth ~$240? hell no. absolutely not. you'd have to be completely oblivious to the existence of every other commercially available headphone to sincerely believe they're worth that much.are they worth $100? sure. that happens to be how much i paid for them and i'm pretty satisfied. definitely not a bad investment if you need a pair of wireless casual listening headphones. if you want quality, though, you can get a lot more out of similarly priced audio technica, sennheiser, and sony sets.just don't expect anything amazing. harman/kardon and aptx codec or not, these are still bluetooth headphones.

Many times I ask a family member or a guest to do the grating while I am finishing the pasta. If you have a few small pieces of cheese prepared ahead of time, it is very easy to grate them at the last minute for use as a condiment to serve with your pasta dishes, (but never with the cream sauce pasta dishes, such as Fettucine Alfredo). Now I only use my flat or box stainless steel graters for cheese when I want to make sliced Parmesan curls as a garnish.A very durable product--highly recommended!

The Manfrotto 143S Magic Arm Flash Shoe is a plastic adapter that can be used to attach a speedlite flash to a light stand.  On top is a slot not unlike the hot shoe on a camera into which you insert a speedlite flash.  On bottom is a screw that fits into the light stand, with a knurled wheel that tightens the whole assembly to the light stand.  It all works pretty well, except that it is a little difficult to turn the knurled wheel tight enough.  I resorted to turning the entire flash and adapter to get it tight enough, only to have the flash pointing in the wrong direction.  I think it would have been better if the knurled wheel had been a little larger in diameter so that you can get a better grip on it, which would probably solve the problem.Another problem that others have noted is that newer flashes such as Canon's 580EX II have a pin in the foot of the flash that normally fits into a slot in the camera's hot shoe when the flash is locked.  The Manfrotto adapter does not have the corresponding slot, making it impossible to lock the flash into the adapter.  A work around is to drill your own hole into the adapter to avoid the flash potentially sliding out and falling to the ground.

There are numerous positive and negative features concerning the Logitech Wireless Mouse M310. Your experience with this product will depend on your needs. Here's some notes on my experience:-Ergonomically speaking, the Logitech is comfortable. I used it for several, consecutive hours and experienced no discomfort. That's a boon!-Concerning ease of cleaning, this mouse can be wiped with a cotton pad soaked in alcohol. The color will not transfer and the base will not lose its texture. Nonetheless, I have a feeling that Logitech doesn't recommend this ... so, proceed with caution. I have always used high-concentration SD alcohol (at least once a week) with my mice and experienced no problems.-As far as aesthetics, this mouse perfectly compliments my work-computer ... a red Dell Studio 17. It is a spot-on color-match. And, for my work (evaluating student writing, composing lectures, etc...), it is perfectly appropriate. However, if you require fine movements, the Logitech falls short. I tried it with my gaming computer (an Alien M15) and quickly found myself frustrated. For instance, in WoW, I persistently overshot the icons on my action-bar. (It was a sad day in arena, indeed!) The mouse jumps and skips ... but in such a minute way that one would never notice it outside of gaming or design.-I am dubious of the claim that this Logitech mouse will survive for twelve months on a single set of batteries. This is my third Logitech wireless ... the longest I have ever gone without changing the batteries is about five months. All have claimed a twelve-month life-span. Nonetheless, it warrants noting that my laptop is in-use for at least six hours a day.Bottom-line: if you are seeking a mouse for casual use (like using the internet, composing documents, or uploading photos), this will easily meet your needs. However, if you are a serious gamer, a design student (or professional), or someone who relies on precise movement, this Logitech might not be your best bet. (In fact, you'll probably be better off with a traditional, "corded" mouse ... wireless is not quite perfected yet).

I ran a series of benchmark tests comparing this switch to three others.-Compared to a four year old Netgear 10/100 switch, the Linksys was able to transfer data about 8 times faster.-Compared to a Cisco 10/100 eight port microswitch, the Linksys gigabit switch was a little more than 5 times faster.  That is quite impressive performance considering it is an $85 gigabit switch compared to the $375 Cisco 100 megabit switch.-Compared to a Cisco 24 port gigabit switch, it performed at about half the speed.  While that is not terribly impressive, it's not bad considering the $1,000+ price difference.However, what really makes this switch nearly worthless to most people is the fan.  I built a high-end custom PC recently with five case fan, one CPU fan, and one VGA fan, and the switch generated more noise!  This was absolutely, positively inexcusable.  The noise became so distracting that I decided it wasn't worth keeping anymore, so I tried an experiment.  One well-placed "whack" with a rubber hammer later, the fan stopped spinning and the blissful silence that we've all come to expect from small 8-port switches finally arrived.  It has been like that for three days now, and the switch is still working.  We'll see how long it holds up.In short, however, if this switch is going to be in your basement or closet, it's a great deal.  If it will be anywhere near you, purchase something else unless you like fan noise.

I definitely do not recommend this product and I will not purchase the full-sized version for myself. Just stick with using the Urban Decay primer on its own and you'll be much better off.

This is hands down the best portable speaker I've ever seen or used. I used to have the model of speakers prior to the Logitech S715i which I loved to take to the beach or on vacations. I've never found a need to play it near full volume.If I had to point out one flaw, it would be that it doesn't have a strong low end spectrum. But, that has to be due to the physical size. I don't think you could get better base out of a speaker so small. It is barely an issue, I just notice that my old Logitech speakers had better bass. But, they were larger and had 2 large drivers. Also, I wish it came with some sort of protective case. I travel with this in my luggage almost weekly and while it doesn't show any wear and tear, I'm always worried something will scrape the speaker cloth.On a side note, I saw a couple of reviews who mentioned they used it on the golf course. So have I. It is perfect, since it fits in a standard cup holder. Obviously, we had to turn down the volume since it is highly frowned upon at the course, but it was still great to listen to tunes while enjoying a round with the guys.

These towels are "made of" bamboo like some plastic spoons are "made of" corn. The plant material has been processed into a plastic, to produce viscose (rayon) fiber. So essentially these are much like polyester towels where the originating material is bamboo rather than petroleum.But, that's not really what matters. Are they nice towels? Well... mostly.They're very silky and substantial. They don't "feel" absorbent, but they dry me off just fine. They have a very heavy, limp drape, but at the same time they get wrinkled in the dryer easily, and the wrinkles stay. Does anyone iron towels?In general I'd like to say these feel really luxurious, but the machine my particular set was made on had some issues. There are pulled threads and hanging strands. If they were perfectly made, yes, they'd feel like something from a swanky hotel, but not flawed like this. I don't know if all towels will have the same issue, though. It still dries just fine, of course.One interesting thing to note is, if you have curly or frizzy hair, you probably know that it's a bad idea to use cotton terrycloth towels on it. Those make the frizziness worse. However, these bamboo viscose towels do not have the same problem, which is nice!Overall, recommended with some minor reservations.

Bottom line up front: if you're looking for a new BD player, you're probably not even considering this one since it's way out of date; this review is more of a rant/vent for me.We bought this BD-DVD player in 2008, when Blu-ray players were still fairly expensive, because 1) it had fairly good reviews (at the time) and 2) Best Buy was having a "Buy a BD player, get 10 movies free" deal (and the PS3 wasn't included). At first, everything was great. The picture quality was great, movies loaded quickly, and the only complaint that we had with it was the sound through the TV was too low (probably more on the TV than the player though). However, as time has passed, and firmware versions upgraded, this player has gone from being a good purchase to one of the biggest electronics regrets we've had (aside from also purchasing HD-DVD players).Where to start...where every electronic starts, with the power button. At first, from power-on to movie start was only 1-2 minutes; now, it takes AT LEAST five minutes before the disc even starts playing the intro screens (which doesn't include the time it takes to recognize whether it's a DVD or BD, which can take equally as long). Once you get past those, and finally get to the menu, moving between the menu options is slow and sluggish. Finally, when you can hit play, get ready to wait even more. By the time the movie finally starts playing, you're more frustrated than excited to watch......and then, it happens. The movie freezes on you, and you start hearing the disc spin...and spin...and spin. Hit the forward button to maybe advance past the skip, but nothing happens. Hit the eject button to see if MAYBE there's a scratch on the disc, and nothing happens. Hit the power button to turn it off, and nothing happens. Then, hopefully the plugs in an easily accessible location so you can unplug it. Once that's done, more waiting, while the system initiates and goes through what I'll call it's start-up process (which takes a fair amount of time).All that aside, this player is extremely outdated. There is no ethernet port on this player, so any BD-Live enabled movie (if you're into that) is wasted on this one. Firmware updates have to be done through a USB flash drive, as far as I know; that's how I've always done it. I've never received an update DVD from Sharp (unlike with my Toshiba HD-DVD player, which I was still getting firmware update DVD's WAY after they discontinued production), so I don't know if you can even request one.All in all, avoid this player...it will save you from lots of frustrating moments.

The Diamond VC600 One Touch Video Capture USB 2.0 installed on my Dell Desktop running Windows Vista Home Premium with a minimum of problems, which is a good thing since it comes with basically no documentation.  The unit comes with two applications a barebones recording ap and a more extensive editing and mastering piece. I used the composite video output from a Canon Z100 digital camera connected to the RCA terminals of the device. I wanted to use a video source that I knew was clear and crisp, to see how much if any "noise" the capture device added. Using the transport controls on the recording software I recorded about 3-minutes of basketball video. The resulting .AVI file was about 3-GB, which is about right for an uncompressed video file. The quality was marginal at best. There was considerable motion blur and other artifacting on the recorded video. The color temperature was way off and the frame transition was jerky. I tried the editing suit for a few minutes then gave-up. Movie maker comes with every Windows machine and is at least as powerful and MUCH easier to use. If you're buying this to archive some old VHS tapes, and aren't overly concerned with quality it will probably be alright, but I wouldn't recommend it for anything beyond that.

It is not at all unusual to experience problems with Microsoft's operating systems, and I say that based on 30 years of professional experiencce working with their products. This is a very lengthy process taking the better part of a day from start to finish.I have learned to partition my primary hard drive into two sections with the OS and applications on the C: partition and all my data files on a second separate partition. When the operating system is hosed for any reason and the computer cannot be booted then the only recourse is to boot off a booth CD/DVD and restore the operating system.That is why I bought a copy of the Windows Pro 64-bit OS disc so I could repair a computer. It amounts to having to pay Microsoft twice for their software but that is how Gates and his crew got rich in the first place - charging manufacturers for the OS even when they loaded another companies operating system onto the computers they sold.With Apple you get all the necessary utility discs to quickly recover from a problem and their OS upgrades used to cost $29 though the latest version now costs only $19. Apple computers may seem more costly but in the long run they cost less than their Microsoft counterparts if you place any value on your time and add in the cost for all the extra spyware and related types of programs one needs to buy for a Windows machine.If you have XP or Vista already installed on your machine it makes no sense to switch to Windows 7 as the performance will be only 10% better than with Visa by Microsoft's own statements and it will be only 50%  at good as with XP. For Windows 7 you need a new computer that will take at least 8GB of RAM and have the latest batch of Intel or AMD processors to compensate for the inefficiency of the Microsoft operating system. With Wintel laptops and desktops from reputable companies like HP and Lenovo selling for under $400 with Windows 7 installed there is no reason to buy this OS and install it on an old computer.

Please note this review is for the TP Link MR-3040 Portable Battery Operated Router.  Amazon lists this product several different ways which makes it quite confusing._____________________________I was a bit apprehensive about purchasing this product because of the absence of user reviews.  Apparently it just came out to the market recently.  The product features are not unique as it competes against similar products from Sapido and ZyXEL.The product presentation itself is quite impressive.  It is elegantly designed, very compact and lightweight.  There is quite a bit of "Apple-esque" about it.  Everything is white, including the cables and wall charger.  Even the packaging design is an unusual slide-out box, quite different from the typical packaging of "ordinary" devices.  If it did not have a TP Link logo on it, you would swear this device came from Cupertino.Two minor design items to note: The latch mechanism for the battery cover appears fragile and would expect it to eventually break off.  Luckily access to the battery is most likely a onetime deal so it is not that big of a concern.  The orientation of the USB jack for the 3G device would have been ideal if it was turned 180 degrees so that the indicator lights are on the same side on both the 3G device and the router.The various capabilities of this portable router can be easily Googled so I do not have to explain it here.  The important factors to me personally are both 3G AND Ethernet capability, plus portable operation with its built-in battery.After powering up, WiFi connection was established quickly with my laptop, internet connection was also established via the Ethernet source. However, I could not get internet connection when I initially connected my AT&T; Sierra Shockwave USB Aircard.  This was a bit disappointing as I expect this unit to be plug-and-play for most part.  The enclosed well written Quick Install Guide's Troubleshooting section led me to change the APN setting for my ISP as shown below.  Note that I had to do some internet research to find the appropriate settings.  Also note that only the settings shown below were changed to make my 3G device to work.Default settings as received are:APN: WAP.CINGULARUsername: WAP@CINGULAR.COMChanged to:APN: ISP.CINGULARUsername: ISP@CINGULARGPRS.COMUsing my 3G device (Shockwave Aircard), my first check on battery power operation yielded a disappointing 2.5 hours of run time (from a full charge to the solid red "low batt" LED indicator).  Note that TP Link's claim is "shared 3G network of up to 5 hours".  However, when connected via Ethernet, the battery was still going strong (solid green) even after 7 hours of operation.  I'm hoping the battery will perform better with the Aircard after a couple of charge/discharge cycles.Overall, based on my needs and expectations, aside from the weak battery performance using 3G (I doubt if I can even get close to the claimed 5 hours) and fiddling with the APN settings, this device appears to deliver on (most of) their claims in a very compact and elegant package.________________________________________________UPDATE: Aug 2012After using this device for a few weeks, I started to notice that it would not stay connected to the internet while I'm using it.  I needed to reboot the unit often and when I'm connected to our company email via VPN, at times I also needed to reboot my computer as well.  This would happen consistently every time I used it.  It appears I may have received a defective unit.The battery power also does not hold up as well as I hoped it would.  The times I noted above (2.5hours) are essentially when the unit was on standby.  When in normal 3G use, the best I could get was less than 1 hour of battery life and as short as 30 minutes from a full charge.Because of these observations, I downgraded my rating to 2 stars.  Too bad the slick/slim design was quite impressive but the performance was a bit short.

There is only so much you can say about a power adapter, as long as it supplies power there should be no problems.  However, I have a serious problem with the connector of the new style MagSafe Power Adapter.  I received the new design from Apple as a warranty replacement for my old one, so I didn't have a choice, but I suggest buying the old style if you can find one new-in-box.  Here's why:The new design still has the same great magnetic connection, but it connects to the laptop at a right angle, rather than straight out like the old design.  This is great if you only use your laptop on a desk and you want the power cord to lay neatly out of the way, directly to the rear of your computer.  However, I use my laptop while sitting on the couch, in coffee shops, and a variety of other places with power outlets in random locations.  This frequently causes the power cord at the laptop connection to be awkwardly flexed in random directions, putting undue stress on the cord where it attaches to the connector.  I can foresee this causing a break in the internal wires and possibly a bad connection in the future.Secondly, because it is at a right angle, if you want to use the USB port on the left side of the computer (pre-unibody MacBook Pro), you can only position it with the cord oriented to the rear, otherwise it will block the USB port and the microphone/line-in port.Lastly, because the new connector is very slim, it is difficult to grasp, forcing you to remove it from the laptop by pulling the cord itself, again placing undue stress on the cord.I will caveat these statements by saying I'm using the new connector style with a pre-unibody/early-2008 MacBook Pro and not a newer model that these connectors may have been primarily designed to work with.  However, judging from the photos on Apple's web site, you will have the same problems of awkward orientation and blocked ports on the current MacBook Pros as well.Bottom line, I recommend buying a MagSafe Power Adapter with the old, "straight-out" design if you can find one.  Otherwise, the new design works but takes some getting used to.

I just had to try it out immediately after getting it, so I attached it to my new Vizio TV that arrived the same day.  Get this, I tried a channel scan with the antenna sitting on the back of the couch and got over 100 channels. Oh Boy! I thought I'm cancelling the Cable tomorrow!  Unfortunately, just like Cable, there is a lot of pure junk and useless (to me) stuff streaming over the airwaves. After deleting the Spanish, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, Hebrew, Russian, Religious (in all the aforementioned languages), Infomercials, kid shows, et al., I was left with around 20 usable stations including all the major Networks.  Most had great reception with no pixelation.  Mind you I'm located 50 miles from the transmitters, and the antenna was on the back of the couch in an almost horizontal position!Next I chose a mounting location in the spare bedroom.  The cathedral ceiling is approx 11 feet high and I chose to put the antenna around 6" or so below the peak.  I cut a piece of scrap 3/4 inch thick plywood into a 3.5" x 3.5" square, drilled 4 pilot holes to match those on the antenna, drilled 2 larger counter-sunk holes, for mounting the block to the to the wall,  sprayed the block and the heads of 4 sheet metal screws with gray primer to approximately match the antenna, once dry attached the wood block to the wall using heavy duty drywall anchor screws (lite to medium duty would likely work based on the light weight of the antenna, but better safe than sorry :) ), then attached the antenna to the block of wood with the sheet metal screws into the pre-drilled pilot holes from above.  I then routed the cable through the wall for a clean install look, but I could just have easily used standard cable clips on the wall to get it to the TV.Then tested it out.  The channels that were pixelating with the antenna on the couch, no longer were, the new scan had 125 channels, but only 26 that I will watch (see above). I'm still blown away by the quality of an over the air picture in HD.  Wow, what a great picture and product!

This wasn't exactly what I was expecting. When I was younger, I had one of those, you know the ones that are a curling iron but has the different attachments that switch out, mine had two different sizes of curling irons plus a brush attachment.This John Freida has a handle and design just like a curling iron but has a brush on the end and it blows out air like a blow dryer through the bristles. The brush part itself doesn't get hot, it gets hot from the hot air coming out so you are only getting a very low watt hair dryer with a brush attachment.I'm sure for some people and certain hair types and styles, this would be beneficial. I have long, coarse, thick, hair that is hard to style and this product did add body but I only felt like it added yet another step to my beauty regime.It takes a very long time to blow dry my hair with this so it works better to partially dry it first with my regular hair dryer then finish up with this. It seems to give my roots some lift, slightly curl my ends and add body. Sounds pretty good and for some people, it would be but I still have to turn around use my flat iron to make my hair smooth and sleek because this doesn't help in those aspects and then my curling iron too. I normally blow dry, then straighten my hair then I use a curling iron to style it. I still have to do all those steps when I use this too. I partially blow dry, use the John Freida blow brush, straighten with my flat iron and then use my curling iron for styling so this has just added an additional step BUT my hair does look better when I use this. Because this does make my hair look better, I didn't want to give it less than 3 stars but I have to be honest, I almost returned this but decided that from time to time, I might use this when I had the extra time to spend on my hair.As long as you are aware of what you are getting and how it performs, you can make a decision for your hair. If you read the reviews on here that give the lower star ratings to this, I totally agree with most of them. Several years ago (before the Ove Glove existed), I bought a Super Glove at Walmart. There are several layers of heat-resistant fabric, covered on the outside with what feels like a cotton knit. This glove is covered with rice-grain-shaped, THICK "blobs" of silicone, in a lattice pattern. I loved this Super Glove so much, I went back to buy another. They were sold out.About a year, I bought two Ove Gloves. When they arrived, they looked great – lots of bright blue silicone stripes. I used The Oven Gloves for the first time tonight and they didn't work!! In fact, they were so dangerous that I had to remove them.I was holding a hot pot by its handle in my left hand, Ove Glove on. I tipped it and, with my right hand, started to scrape the contents into a casserole. Suddenly, the pot handle started slipping and rotating. I dropped the scraper and grabbed the pot with my right hand (also in an Ove Glove). I adjusted my grip with my left hand and tried to continue. The handle once again slipped and rotated in my left hand and the hot pot fell.I thought it was my fault--not tight enough grip. To be safe, I used a huge spoon to transfer the food remaining in the pot to the casserole. The pot was empty, so I put the Ove Glove on again and picked it up again with a VERY tight grip. Before the pot was raised 2 inches off the counter, it flipped in my hand.I removed the Ove Glove and put the Super Glove on my left hand. When I picked up the pot, it did NOT slide or rotate! That suggested that the Ove Gloves were not working. When I examined them closely, I noticed two things:1.  The blue strips of silicone are so THIN that you can barely feel them. Instead of silicone stripes making contact with the handle of the pot, the shiny, slippery knitted fabric makes contact, thus the slipping. The silicone stripes are so thin (not narrow, folks; THIN) I can see the knit fabric through the silicone.2.  Because all the stripes run in the same direction (instead of a criss-cross pattern), a lot of the slippery fabric makes contact with the pot.Look for a Super Glove; don't take a chance hurting yourself by using the Ove Glove.

I've worked with prosumer video cameras for many years and was looking for a small inexpensive camcorder for my personal use. I sometimes have to record training sessions where I use a wireless Lav mic on the presenter so having an external mic jack is a nice feature and is often only found on more expensive models.  It appears that with this model if you are making a long continuous recording, it won't record a file size larger than 4gb.  I recorded an hour long presentation and it created 2 files, it's not really a problem because you can easily combine them with editing software.I was also impressed with the zoom, it was very smooth and you can adjust the speed of it.  The image stabilizaton works very well.  I liked the touch screen and found it to work well and be very user friendly.  The set up and menus were easy to navigate.  The next models up from this have WiFi and a built in hard drive, but given the cost of SD cards, I felt this one was a better value if you don't need WiFi. Like many of the reviewers here, I have been a long time user of FoodSaver products, at least 20 years. I've pitched them to friends, neighbors, and relatives. I've learned the various "tricks" to successful vacuum sealing. So when I got the opportunity to try the V3835 I jumped on it. I even read all the directions before I used it, even tho I've used one for years.The idea for this device is good, but poorly executed. I sincerely think that the people who designed it have never used in a real world kitchen. I have limited counter space and can't leave it near food prep area, but move it frequently. This is where some of the design shortcomings are evident.Let's start with the shape. It is pointy and slippery so you need to use two hands to move it. A handle or hand grip molded into the back would have been a good idea.Putting the power cord recessed into the bottom is the next drawback. To use the cord you have to place it on to its curved, tippy front, dig the cord out of its tight nook and press it into the small notch on the back. The challenge when you're done with it is to get the cord back in and wrap the plug in a way it won't fall out before you get it back upright. Even Mrs. Boilermate, who is a lot more dexterous and has smaller hands, has trouble with this. A cord wrap on the back would have been more practical.The canister hose is retracted into the machine on a reel. Another good idea. It can't get lost and is always handy...if you can get it out. It is on the lower right side at counter level. The "knob" you grip to pull it out small, smooth, slippery, and too close to the counter. Again, even Mrs. B. has trouble gripping it. Just changing the grip from horizontal to vertical would be a big improvement.It has a built in bag cutter on the lower left corner at counter level. Push it once and out it pops, but it is too close to the counter to be useful for opening more than the slimmest of bags. Push it in again and it locks closed. It is best to leave it that way.The next gripe is the cover for the bag storage. It latches by a clip on either side. Again, there is no "finger hole" so you have to use two hands to open it. Once open, unrolling and cutting the bag is a snap.Vacuuming and sealing: Like many other reviewers, I had a lot of difficulty.I cut my first bag and tried to seal it. It took several tries for the end to "take" and the clamp to activate. After filling the bag, getting the open end into the slot proved, again to be a challenge. After several tries, I finally got it to vac and seal. The motor that clamps the bag is loud. The vacuum pump doesn't seem any louder than on other models.I tried two different rolls and pre-cut bags, and the result was the same...frustration. The fuller the bag, the harder it was to get the end into the slot. Mrs. B struggled with this operation, too.Did the designers actually fill a quart bag with a quart of (pre-frozen) strawberries and try to vac-seal it, as I did? I tried several times to get the end smooth enough to fit in the slot, slide one end in, and guide the rest of it in. No go. Mrs. B was able to get it after several tries, but the bag went in crooked and wrinkled. Before she could straighten it and smooth it out, the clamp came down and the bag vacuumed and sealed...crooked and wrinkled.I've gotten into the habit of double sealing my bags especially when the bag wrinkles. Unlike the old style sealer, you cannot double seal bags with this unit. It will only seal when the bag end extends into the vacuum slot, even when in "seal only" mode. In the older style, you can position the bag, close the lid and seal.The machine seals the bag about an inch from the each end of the bag. That is understandable for the end it vacs from, but a waste on the other end. An inch may not seem like much, but it adds up. Compared to the other problems, this is a minor annoyance.In the end, this machine is just not worth the hassle. There are just too many design failures. I'm going back to my four-year old V4860.

I never really got to get much use from this product.  It died before I got accustomed to using it.  Just one day, it stopped working.  USB logs show that the controller doesn't even think a device is attached.For the time being, I'll associate ADATA with flimsy products.  Or at least I will until they change their name...UPDATE:I really like the package.  I noticed that the flash chip is a SIP style, just like what is packaged with theVerbatim Store 'n' Go Micro Plus 64 GB USB 2.0 Flash Drive 97762, Black.  Since Verbatin no longer produces the Tuff-Clip, I in effect made my own out of these two drives.The day after receiving the Verbatim drive, I pried the plastic shell back to stretch the adhesive and extracted the memory chip.  The A-Data drive is a bit more difficult to dismantle.  The colored plastic shell is in two pieces that join inside the clip ring.  I carefully pried these apart and stretched the glue out until it released.  These two plastic pieces also form the axle that the USB drive rotates on, so removing the plastic pieces releases the drive assembly.The drive assembly is composed of three pieces, a plastic frame that has the flash SIP chip glued to it and a metal shroud crimped around it.  Take note of the orientation of the shroud with respect to the chip.  Carefully pry the metal just far enough so that it can be pulled off the plastic frame.  Pry the defective chip out of the frame and insert the Verbatim chip instead.  The existing adhesive should hold it in.  Straighten the metal on the shroud before re-assembling, and then slide in on from the end.The remainder of the assembly is reverse of the disassembly.  You know have a 64GB Verbatim drive in a carabiner clip package.

I pitted this AVR against a Denon AVR-2311CI.  The Denon is a older model that is replaced by the 2312.  In any case these 2 excel in different ways.  First the pioneer, the video processing is a stand out!!  With the Marvel video processing chip the HD on this was simply stellar!  It made my old TV look as if I bought a new one.  I had an Onkyo TX-SR605 before these two were brought in to test out.  The Video on that old Onkyo doesnt do my TV justice.  Not to mention I had issues with the HDMI on it several time.  Onkyo packs lots of feature but that is where it stops.  But back to the 1121, it is filled to the gills with features.  I like the iControlAVS...fun, easy but doesnt do everything.  The Apps are crude and need work.  Pandora is hard to setup and the interface is not very pleasing.  But it works and I do love internet radio.  Power is excellent and plenty of it.  The 1121 is also THX Select2 certified.  So you get all the additional sound fields and the lucas seal of approval that this AVR meets their standards for distortion and so on.  I think this is a novelty at best.  For the Denon with now THX sounded substantially better, warmer and with far more detail.  The sound processing on this unit is nearly as good as the video.  The sound processing is still very good but not excellent.  Listening to both side by side after hours of calibration the denon just flat out sounded better.  The denon is excellent with sound...period...but video pioneer takes the cake!  The remote on this is one I dont like.  Hard to read, small buttons...not very well laid out.  Connectivity is top notch it does everything...network, airplay, HDMI, Component, Opticals, Coax...you name it!  This things works well.  The network integration with airplay is very good!!  Worked with my iPad2 very well!  But is also has USB as well.In the end I gave it 4 of 5 because the sound is just not up to the level and detail that denon has.  I am keeping the denon for I cannot deny the sound quality.  It is simply amazing!  But the pioneers video processing is something incredible.  I am yet to see the picture on my TV look better...the denon was very good but the pioneer was better!  This is quite the receiver for the money pioneer did an exceptional job.  Better than the NR609 I heard as well as a number of yamahas...which would be my 3 pick for Home theater.Update 12/18/2011:  I cannot say enough how incredible the video performance is on this unit.  It is simply amazing.  I compared this to a Denon AVR-2311CI and the denon doesnt even come close!  The Denon uses a ABT video chip and the Pioneer a Marvell.  The Marvell Qdeo is really incredible but it also might be the way pioneer uses this chip!  When I tested these two receivers I had them both plugged in (Swapped in and out during testing using same cables, speakers, Blu-ray. Moto HD Cable box and TV).  Once again the sound after extensive configin and using pioneers MCACC auto config mic just couldnt get the 1121 to sound as good as the denon 2311CI.  It is solid but the denon has a more detailed sound, warmer, better imaging and depth.  The sub also performed much better on the denon...felt and heard.  I did a ton of manual adjustments and used all the MCACC Memory settings to see how good I could get it but no matter what I did to the Pioneer I couldnt get it that close to the sound on the denon.  On of the biggest things I noticed on the denon was the amount of detail and presences the rears had.  It was almost as if the 1121 rears were off...I really had to dial these up to get something solid out of them but the 1121 still couldnt do what the denon can do with the sound.So for video pioneer all day...your HD will look like it has never!  The marvell chip makes the video perform far and away beyond my expectations.  Now this can be said about the denon for audio.  I do love the pioneer and it offers soooo much!  Internet radio...not great to setup but works and the ipad app is quite nice.  The iControlAVS is good but lacks some stuff.  If you are not as critical of sound or have speakers that are not reference this is an amazing value!  It is a solid 4-4.5 star AV Receiver.

I was really excited to see this solar version of an 8000 mAh battery because it could be a wonderful accessory to charge a device when I couldn't get to an outlet.  Unfortunately, the solar component just doesn't work -- more on that later.  If I charge the battery using an outlet, however, it's a fantastic external power bank, albeit larger (because of the solar panels) than the usual.The power bank has two out ports, one 1A and the other 2A, the last one critical for charging an iPad.  The 5V input uses a standard microUSB cable for charging.  I like that it has an on/off button for conserving a charge, although I can't figure out how to tell whether it is on or off unless I have a device attached.  It has four, blue LED lights that blink when it is charging, either by wall outlet of light.As for the solar, I've had the battery on my window sill for five straight days, and it can't even charge my iPad one percent of its total.  It transfers power to my iPad, using the 2A output, for less than 15 minutes.  I thought that maybe the solar cells are used not for storage (that is, not to charge the battery itself) but for transfer while it was in the sun.  Nope.  I checked with the company to confirm that I did not receive a defective solar cell, and they told me that the solar cells were for emergency only.  Unfortunately, my experience shows that solar energy cannot be used even in an emergency.  It doesn't store the charge, and it doesn't transfer it directly.  I don't understand the purpose of including solar cells on this otherwise good power pack.The type of people who will likely consider this external battery are those who camp, hike, or want to be able to charge devices during an extended power outage.  This battery will not work in any of those conditions.  It will work, however, if it was charged at home.  Note:  I received a sample for review.-- Debbie Lee Wesselmann

I'm surprised all the reviews so far for this photo frame are mostly negative.  It's not without its problems, but it's still relatively easy to use and actually a lot of fun.  There's both a "Quick Start Guide" plus a 29 page "User Guide".  The frame is easier to use if you read the "User Guide", and consult it if you have problems.  But you also can just  push buttons on the remote, and usually get what you want.  The remote is not as sensitive as it could be.  Sometimes you have to repeatedly press buttons to get to the screen you want.  I'm not sure, however, if it's the remote itself, where you have it pointed, or the distance from the frame.  Still, there has never been a time yet when the right screen did not come up.  One very important thing to know--there are two menu screens.  When you hit the menu button, the "home" menu screen for photos, music and video management pops up.  This is the menu screen you will use the most.  But if you need the "setup menu" screen, just push the "menu" button again while the screen is on the "home" screen.  There is a "menu" button on the frame itself, along with a few other buttons, but  not all the buttons that are on the remote.Set up was easy.  You just take the frame out of the box, plug in the AC cord, and turn on the frame, with the on/off switch that is on the frame itself.  Before putting the frame down on a surface, however, make sure you EXTEND the adjustable stand.  It does extend, even though it first appear not to.  Just pull out the plastic piece on the bottom.  This keeps the frame from falling over.  You can also rotate the stand so the frame is vertical instead of horizontal.  But you also can use the remote to rotate pictures, too.How to get pictures on the frame?  E-mail is the easiest way and the most fun. (The frame only receives e-mails "within the continental USA".) There is an e-mail address on the back of the frame that you use.  (When you register your frame, you can change your e-mail address to one that you want.)  There are 60 picture downloads included with the frame, and you have 60 days to use them from the first time you get a photo e-mail, before they expire.  After that, you can buy picture packages.  There is a "Buy Photo Package" button on the "Photo Mail Inbox" screen, but I could not get the remote to click in that button.  I couldn't even get to the button.  If you can get to it, you can buy a package right there, using a virtual keyboard to type in your address and credit card info.  I went online to Pandigital to check on package prices.  It asks for your frame address before it lists prices.  My price list was:  100 Photos--$ 9.99, 400 Photos--$29.99, 700 Photos--$49.99.  According to Pandigital support, there are no expiration dates on any photo package you buy.We sent e-mails to the frame with both a PC and a Mac.  They all arrived in less than five minutes.  It's not hard to check your mail at all; there is a "Photo Mail" button right on the remote.  I guess, however, elderly people who are not use to using small remotes with arrows may have a problem.  The only solution to this would be if Pandigital had a frame that automatically sent all e-mailed photos right into the slideshow.  That would require an exclusive e-mail list, though, to keep spam from being downloaded, if there is spam for these devices.  You can block and unblock senders with this frame.  There is no "photo preview feature" with e-mailed photos, and you must download ALL photos in any e-mail you choose to open.  Hence, an e-mail with five photos counts as five e-mailed pictures, not one.  You can just delete an e-mail, too, without opening it.  Also, only successful downloads count as deductions from your photo package. Pictures must be in the JPEG format taken with a digital camera.Secure digital cards and flash drives are another way to acquire photos on the frame, as well as downloading photos directly from your computer.  A download USB cord is included.  At first, when I clicked in a picture at "My Pictures",  and clicked "send to", there was no Pandigital choice.  When I went to my Kodak  software, there was a Pandigital choice.  Then, when I went back to "My Pictures", the choice was there, too.  Pictures instantly went to the frame when using both the Kodak software and the Vista software.  You can pick and choose pictures, when you send them that way to the frame.  So, you can send a whole album or folder, and just pick what you want.  The same with memory cards.  I used an SD and that worked instantly in downloading pictures, and I could pick which ones I wanted.  I had problems with a flash drive, however.  It never would show there was a flash drive in the frame.  It turned out I had the drive in the wrong way!  I didn't even know it would go in the wrong way.  After I turned it around, I easily downloaded the pictures on it. You can easily delete pictures on the frame at any time.  And there are five folders on the frame you can use to sort your photos, and view different slide shows.  Unfortunately, you can't change the name of the folders, though.Music can also be sent to the frame, but they must be in the MP3 format.  Your iTunes library is not in that format.  Songs you buy from Amazon are in the MP3 format, and that's what I sucessfully sent to the frame using the USB cord.  (If you have Vista, go to "My Music", open the Amazon MP3 folder, click the song you want, and right click "send to" Pandigital.)  The funny thing is that not only the songs were downloaded, but so were the album covers.  Thus, when I did a slideshow after downloading the songs, there among the pictures of my nephew and his dog was Kenny Loggins!  You can even click in the album cover to play the song, instead of going to the menu and choosing the manage music button.  Deleting the album cover pictures won't delete the songs.  I guess someone could use this frame to display album covers.  They could put them all in one of the folders, so there were nothing but album covers in that folder.  You can adjust the volume of the music with the + and - buttons on the remote, but a kid might not find the volume high enough.Trying to download a video didn't work for me.  The frame only accepts JPEG videos taken with a digital camera, and that's what I thought my Kodak DX6490 took.  The video did download, but the frame said it was not a supported format, so the video would not play.  It turns out my Kodak uses .mov file format. Other features on this frame are a Wi-Fi connection with an adapter that is not included, and a clock with a stand-by and schedule modes, so you can program your slideshows.The remote has a "slideshow" button, and I had no problems with that.  I doubt an elderly person would have any problem using that button.  The slideshows are really pretty and cool looking.  The photos look great on this frame--they are very clear and the colors are very vivid.  I think this frame would be a great gift for any age group.  Even if an elderly person could not check their photo e-mail and download it, a younger person visiting them certainly could.  I think the 15" Panadigital frame might be better for elderly persons, though.  That would be the best size to get for someone who wants to display nature and wildlife pictures, too.  As I stated in the beginning, this frame is not without some problems, but it actually is a lot of fun.  As I write this, I have Kenny Loggins singing "I'm Alright" to a slideshow of my nephew doing goofy things at the beach.  But, alas, I deleted the photos of Mr. Loggins, even though he was also looking goofy on the album covers.  Maybe I should download the album covers again, and tell my nephew that's what he's going to look like when he gets older. :)
