The science of the Super CCD sounds really good.  Choosing a sensor arrangement that allows the camera to bin adjacent pixels to increase the effective size of a photosite (at half the number of pixels, of course) is a good idea for reducing both chroma and luminance noise while maintaining a decent shutter speed.  The lower noise level should permit raising the effective ISO.In fact, the Super CCD works pretty well, but not for reducing noise.  It is excellent at extending the dynamic range of the sensor (with one half of the photosites capturing bright and one half capturing dim areas).  The camera has advanced firmware that allows it to do a number of tricks such as shooting 3 pictures in rapid sequence at the same ISO, shutter speed, and aperture, and averaging out the noise.  So long as the photog can hold the camera reasonably steady, this works surprisingly well.  It also has the ability to provide an apparently small depth of field, again by taking 3 pictures of the scene and somehow identifying the subject (closest object, I think) and making one shot of the subject and two of the distance, which it then blurs together.Unfortunately this trick is less well executed.  The background just looks as if somebody had blurred it uniformly, as putting a damp sponge on watercolors.  On one shot the camera even left a hole in the blur through which one could see a fairly sharp background.  Anyway, it only works at all when the subject is quite close to the camera.Even with vibration reduction it is almost impossible to get a sharp image at a 35mm effective "250 mm" focal length using a camera this small.  Hand shake and imperfections in the autofocus combine to limit the sharp zoom range to something significantly less, say around "175mm or 200 mm" equivalent focal length, if sharpness is important to you.  The lens is also deficient on native sharpness, and when there's a bright background the chromatic aberration (purple fringing) is annoying and not removed by the firmware/software in the camera.  Given the innovative firmware used elsewhere in the camera, some CA reduction and distortion correction should have been implemented.A reasonably sophisticated user will probably find that he or she reaches for the exposure compensation button fairly frequently.  I found that the meter just didn't deliver consistent results as you changed from, say, bright sunlight to an interior.  In addition the auto white balance was consistently off, and the presets didn't help a lot.  Pictures taken on a cloudy day were uniformly too blue, whether engaging the "shade" preset or using the AWB.  In compensation, the custom WB mode is very easy to use and works better than on most compacts.The F70EXR is beautifully built, a delight in the hand, and attractively styled.  It's just not as adept at doing bread and butter photography as it should be, even at the pretty low price it's sold for at Amazon.  I am mentally comparing it to a 3 year old Canon 710is and the brand new Canon S90, and have decided that I should return the F70EXR and give the S90 a try.

A year and a half ago I changed my tires and tubes on my old mountain bike. The sporting store near me didn't have the greatest selection of tubes so I just grabbed these Slime tubes mostly due to their lower price compared to the more prestigious brands that the store carried. They install fine, just like any other tube but when I filled them I did notice that a bit of the slime would leak out of the valve when removing the pump from the valve. I wiped the slime off the valve and replaced the valve caps. I didn't really have any issue with the tubes that first year other than noticing a bit of slime residue around the valve after topping off my tires. Then come this year I noticed that my front tire was not filling properly. When I pressed on the valve there was only a small stream of air escaping. At that moment it became clear that the slime had sealed off a majority of the valve from the inside. Cleaning the outer area of the valve did nothing to increase airflow.Now I'm not gonna say the problem isn't partly with me. Sure I could have searched for warnings about these tubes sealing their own valves and made sure that I always had the valve at the 12 'o clock position in the wheel when storing my bike, but honestly I am not that diligent of a person and these are not things I feel a person should have to worry about with their tubes. Also I imagine if you did get a flat this will do nothing more than make a huge nasty green mess inside of your tire and ruin it. My old inner tubes I had for 10 years(yeah way longer than I should have had them) without any problems, these Slimes I had them for less than 2 years and have to replace them because they sealed themselves off.Do yourself a favor and just buy normal tubes and repair them with a patch when you get punctures. These Slimes are nothing but a headache and a mess and they don't even last as long as a standard tube.

Not much you can say about little round balls to shoot out of a BB rifle, except that they should be round, all the same size and have a shelf life longer than a loaf of bread. Every BB has a little divot or flat spot on it that affects its flight, making some curve away unpredictably.  Most people don't expect great accuracy from a BB.  If you want good accuracy go with a pellet.  If you live in a humid climate you need to store these like standard firearm ammunition or they'll rust and become useless. I use these in the piece of junk Crosman BB rifle I bought a few months back (see other review) just for plinking cans in the backyard and they're entertaining as they seem to have a life of their own after leaving the rifle.  This combination of Crosman rifle and BBs should be avoided.  The pellets out of the same rifle are very accurate.Don't expect the little funnel top on the bottle to be much use - you can't pour the BBs out of it in any controllable way.  The best way to load many BB rifles (especially those with a little slide-down door covering the BB compartment opening, is to fold a piece of construction paper and put the crease in the opening, then dump the BBs onto the paper and let them roll down the crease.  Do this over a pan or something or you'll be collecting BBs with your vacuum sweeper and waking the dead.

This screen protector, while smooth, has a little bit of tacky feeling.  I have tried wiping it with a microfiber cloth, but it is still not like the naked screen.  I don't know that you can create an inexpensive screen protector that can keep that smooth feeling of gorilla glass 2 with LG's coating, but if this is important to you, beware. It's not very sticky, but there is a subtle difference where you notice you finger doesn't swipe across the screen as smoothly.  I'm not deducting a star for this as this may just be the bottom line with screen protectors, but this is more of a "buyer beware" mention.There is definitely that rainbow/oil sheen effect from this screen protector.  It's not as bad as some, but its there, especially under florescent lights. There is also more of a reflection as well.Finally, the worst part as others have mentioned, it is cut too small.  I'm guessing they did it because often, when it's cut exactly the size of the screen, cases can bunch up the screen protectors because they wrap over the edges.  I don't mind much that the left and right sides are cut short (basically, the same width of the 5.2" screen), although they could have done a little wider, but the top and bottom are a little ridiculous.  I have exactly 3 mm exposed on the bottom (I measured).  The top also has a noticeable exposed edge, but the bottom is just blatant. You can adjust it so there's more on the top and less on the bottom, but either way, you will have very noticeable gaps on the top and bottom exposed so that anyone can tell you have a screen protector on.  The LG G2 is so slick looking on the front because of how clean it is, and this definitely takes away from that.For the price, I give it three stars, it is definitely not a perfect product. The picture is still very clear, but there are definitely flaws.

UPDATE-I ended up returning this unit (and looking to upgrade to ID82 with i3 CPU instead). I'm lowering the original rating as well, as I feel the PC/CPU is underpowered for use as HTPC. After all the tweaking, I still wasn't able to get 1080 playback in VLC. I successfully used Plex for 1080 playback though. But overall, everything in Win7 Ultimate (fresh install) felt way too sluggish (comparing to my 2.53 Ghz P9500- powered 4-year old laptop). I also experienced a lot of issues with the supplied remote control- it would "skip" at random and couldn't really be used (might've been a lemon). I even tested the remote on a completely different computer with the same exact results. Zotac support wasn't particularly responsive or helpful in resolving any of the issues .ORIGINAL REVIEWThis mini PC is designed and built by a Chinese company. When I unpacked it, I was pleasantly surprised as it bore no marks of the nowadays typical "made in China" stuff. Superb quality, great attention to detail in everything, including the box, instructions, mounts, everything. Even know the case is all plastic, it's of superb quality- snugly fitting, well polished (piano gloss effect). The remote, unlike many cheap-o remotes that come with gadgets these days is nice in every way. Connector ring on the WiFi antenna is made of metal- not plastic.It definitely exceeded all my expectations !Installed 320GB HD and 4GB RAM in just minutes- only two screws (didn't even require a screwdriver). Installed Win 7 Ultimate- seem to run just fine with Aero and all. BIOS has lots of settings to play with. Had to make a bootable USB flash drive to install the OS.Hit a snag with the driver installation- the main install program in the root folder on the supplied CD with drivers would only work if started from the CD itself, not from the local copy. Didn't have a USB CD drive, but got around that by installing each driver individually (they all had their own respective install programs)The Manual and the Start Guide are in Chinglish, but instructions are pretty clear.A couple of issues-1. WiFi-N only connects at 72Mbps (and my 300Mbps AP sits less than 3 feet away from the PC)2. VESA mount didn't fit my 50" Samsung plasma as the threads on my TV for the wall mount are way further apart.3.  Last, but not least- 1080 playback using the latest version of VLC (H.264, mkv) stutters, even with the GPU accelerated decoding turned on. Tweaking VLC (skip the loop filter for H.264) didn't help. While playing 1080 content without GPU on, CPU utilization hits 90%+ (the resulting picture is really bad). With the GPU on, CPU is only 20-30%, but the picture is still jerky.Content up to 720 (even 800) plays just fine- watched a whole movie (about 800 vertical) without a snag.Emailed Zotac support about both wifi and 1080 issues- no response yet. Will update.Some online reviewers seem to have no issues with 1080 playback on this box. It may be a matter of OS (Win vs. Linux) and/or Player (VLC vs XBMC etc). I'm going to play with Plex and XBMC next.For now, to those who are considering buying- ID82 has a much more powerful Intel i3 CPU, which should be a "guaranteed" bet for 1080 playback. Probably more power consumption and heat too. And an extra 100 bucks...

As others have noted, while this keyboard/case is physically compatible with the new iPad (3), its magnet fails to turn the iPad on and off when the case is opened and closed. Many cases have this problem, which is due to a change in Apple's design: the iPad 3 requires that the magnet have a certain polarity, while the iPad 2 did not. Thus any case made for the iPad 2 (including, by the way, Apple's own Smart Covers!) has a 50-50 chance of working properly with the iPad 3.However, there's an easy fix in this case (pun intended):1. Slide the Bluetooth keyboard out of the ZAGGfolio case.2. Inside the case, where the spacebar end of the keyboard rested, there is a thin (1/4") plastic strip. Insert a knife blade into the gap at the top of this strip and gently pry. The strip will come out fairly easily, leaving behind a few blobs of glue.3. Update: June 5th 2014I wanted to take a moment to thank the Tech Armor support team. Although this product wasn't suitable for me, they did refund this.----Couple of notes first:Had this one and iPhone 5 bought for me via my wish list, so although purchased via Amazon it will likely not show as verified purchase.This review is for the Privacy screen version, NOT the transparent one (Amazon appears to be coalescing the reviews) installed on a white iPad mini retina.To summarize:+ Easy to install when closely following directions+ Would likely protect screen from scratches+ At ~40 degree angle the screen is barely readable (good privacy), though not as total as 3M filters.+ Easy to remove. The videos on the tech armor website are clear and concise and within 15 minutes I had both this one, and the iPhone 5 privacy screen installed with no bubbles, no fingerprints, and aligned as well as possible. Looked a bit off as the dark filer contrasted with the white iPad surround, though acceptable.After installation, the initial image quality appeared significantly degraded. It's now 4 days since installing this and I just had to remove it. Nikon Coolpix S210 8.0MP Digital Camera with 3x Optical Zoom (Graphite Black)I have only gotten a few pages into the manual and can only operate a few settings. Yet virtually every shot has come out good. 8"x10" prints from a color ink jet paper printer look great unless you really look close; just faint lines from the printer. Now THAT is a good camera and it would fit in a cigarette pack if you wished.I've used large, medium and 35mm formats and did my own developing and printing for a few decades. Grain? Very simple: film speed. 100 was ideal, 200 a touch of grain, 400 noticeable and so on. The higher the film speed, the more grain you get. Nothing is free, there is always a trade off. The more difficult you make it for a digital camera, the more problems with the photo.The best thing I ever did was take a photography class. Minimal cost, 4 or 5 evening classes, and I understood the trade offs between film speed, aperture and lens speed. I imagine digital has similar factors; if I was 100 miles closer to a city I would already be signed up.Don't expect miracles, but if you understand the basic principles you'll be able to handle tough conditions and get good pictures.

The build is quite impressive, what with the stylish triangular metal alloy housings, and the thick braided cable. The housings are sturdily built and are actually rather heavy, probably the heaviest of any IEM I've tried. I didn't have much of an issue with them in terms of weight but wearing them cable up was certainly preferable to wearing them straight down in terms of comfort.In addition, iPhone and smartphone users should be pleased to note that the Vortex includes a 1 button remote and microphone for taking calls. This is a superfluous feature to me but I'd imagine it'd worth noting.Speaking of comfort, the silicone tips were a bit too shallow in my ears and I ended up replacing them with Sony HybridsIn terms of sound quality, I must say I'm impressed for the price I paid. The low end has more presence and impact than I was expecting, which, at least in terms of sheer volume can run with just about every heavy-hitter I have in my collection. It extends in a linear fashion to the lowest sub-bass regions and remains powerful and rumbles nicely at 30Hz or so. The Moshi loses out in terms of bass texture to the harder edged Atrio M5 and Miles Davis Tributes but seeing as the Moshi is less than half the price of either those two, I'd say its low end performance is quite impressive.The midrange is slightly recessed compared to the lows and can sound a bit smeared at times and lacks transparency, especially when compared to something like the RE0 or the ADDIEM. The Vortex isn't a bad performer in terms of its midrange but its thick sound likely won't appeal to everyone. Moving up to the high end, the Vortex is somewhat laid back, much like the midrange, though its lower treble edges close to the sibilance line but never quite gets there. On the whole, the Vortex portrays treble detail decently but lovers of sparkle and airiness in the upper frequencies should look elsewhere.On the whole, the Moshi Vortex has a thick and dark sound signature. It can sound a bit strained when confronted with busier tracks and doesn't have the same clarity as some of its competition but bassheads should be quite pleased with these, with their fairly tight, if a tad slow, low end with fantastic extension and a lack of a distracting midbass hump.But here's the rub. While these retail for $80, I managed to get them for $20. At the latter price, I think these are a great deal and are well above most similarly priced IEMs. At the full retail price, I'm not so sure. For the bass lover, there aren't many IEMs that can compete with these, even at $80 and the sound quality is good, but not as good as my sub $100 benchmarks.But, if you're a basshead looking for an iPhone compatible headset, this is a pretty good choice under $100.

I live in a very dry region and am already the happy owner of a Vick's brand vaporizer.  I thought that having a second available for guests might be nice, so I decided to give this one a chance.  Unfortunately this machine is far too noisy and messy for me to use.I knew right away there were going to be issues because there were conflicting instructions in the manual.  At one point you are told to add any medications directly to the tank, but in another place it says to not add any medications to the tank.  I wasn't planning on using any medication, so I decided I didn't need to worry about that.  So I looked for the fill line.  And I looked, and I looked, and I looked.  There was a big line around the middle and it took me forever to find that it was marked "max fill" since there was no contrast to the letters.  I filled it to the line, placed it in the desired spot, and plugged it in (no on/off switch, just plug/unplug) and waited to see if I needed salt.In just a few minutes, hot steam was pouring out of the vaporizer, so I will give it credit that it can absolutely produce massive steam fairly quickly.  But it comes at a price.  Within moments of the steam starting, the machine started to sputter hot water.  I know that it was not overly full as I had been very careful to make sure I only filled it to the line.  I unplugged it, waited a bit for it to cool down, then took it and poured off some of the water.  Even with it well below the fill line, the little machine wanted to sputter hot water, but at least it was less.  So I put down a little towel and sat down to read.But I couldn't read because the sound was far too distracting.  I felt like I was in some sort of B-movie science lab with all the bubbling, the occasional whistles, not to mention the gurgles and gulps coming out of the machine.  I excused myself to another room so I could let it run for a bit and see if it worked itself out.  I returned a little over three hours later to find the machine no longer producing steam and the water mostly gone.  No where near as long as it was expected to produce.It was difficult to clean.  No drain means you have to try to shake any remaining water out of the top and that is nearly impossible.  I ended up shaking out as much as I could and using a towel to mop out the rest.  I did try to give it a second chance, but the noise and the mess were just too much, so I shut it down after just a few minutes.I cannot recommend the purchase of this item.  I have serious concerns about the safety of the product, especially if used around children.

To say I am impressed is really understating my experience with this SSD! Installed neatly in my Dell inspiron 13z-5323, perfect height at 7mm.I did not clock boot times or perform any other speed test, however the increase in boot goes beyond noticeable. From power on to the login screen went from 30 seconds to doggone warp speed; the boot options F2 and F12 only show up for a blip the process is so fast!The longest part of my boot was after logon taking upwards of 2-3 minutes and take mere seconds anymore.That said I did spend a considerable amount of time to setup since I wanted the original DataSafe restore partition intact.First, i tried the utility from western digital to clone the disk; it is actually an acronis true image software and did not clone correctly leaving a slightly larger recovery partition. Highly multi-threaded applications are really all that shine on the Bulldozer chips.Overclocking is a joke, with the 125W TDP. I could not achieve anything above 3.8Ghz at full load, on the stock heatsink. The stock heatsink is decent however, with copper heatpipes. If I had to do this over again, I would probably pay more for the Core i5 and get A LOT more performance with it.

Its pretty much been well reviewed here. Just to reiterate some points and clarify a few others. First off, this player DOES play DVD-R disks, I know, I have done so! Plays just fine if you know how to properly burn a disk, DVD-R can play ;-)Fair WARNING you may think you have enough room in your entertainment center, think again. I thought I had enough room with my behemoth of an entertainment center. But you are not aware of an additional extention on the rear panel that sticks out alot (this houses the actual disk player). Do yourself a favor and double check the measurments. I nearly was forced to either remove the cabinet doors or chop out the back panel of the entertainment panel (so hate doing that) or even return the unit. I got very lucky and it just barely fits.OK, other than those points, the player function itself resides with being just a giant DVD/CD storage unit. Depending upon how you look at it, it is either a very simple player or a very complicated player. Noting is intuitive about this player! It is relatively quiet. It is slow. It is annoying to get hanged up with those FBI warning screens, the player does, as mentioned before, upon power on autoplay the first disk, nothing you can do to stop it, and your forced to watch the FBI warning unless you proactively remember to do as stated to try and avoid this happening (at the end of a movie hit stop once so next time you can power on and just go to any of the menu sytems).God help me if I have to move it. I am not going to even try to with out first removing the disks inside as recommended. Just looking at it I believe others comments about the likelyhood of things getting jammed. But that means having to fully remove all the disks and then you guessed it, having to reinput ALL the data if disks are not keep in there specific order.This is by no means a solution. I purchased from Amazon for $279 with free ground shipping (not to mention additional $30 off, net price of $249 how can I pass that up). It was here in record breaking time 2 days! If it was not for the price, I do not think I would have taken this challenge. Overall, I am OK with it. It does "clean" up my living space. Thats basicly all that it has going for it which is its main selling point.EDIT-I just scanned reviews for the previous model 985V, and an alarming situation has been brought to my attention, it seems that there is a possibility for disk damage! You can read all about it on the other product page. This in all suggests inorder to safeguard and ironicly better the disk info and autoplay bug/glitch, that you copy your disks first, in addition strip the FBI warning out, and preinput all the disk info. And then the system will operate much more smoothly. Caution in regards to the possible disk scratching issue, check your disks weekly, randomly, while still within the return period!EDIT-DISCOVERED A WORK AROUND TO KILL THE FBI WARNING SCREENS IT APPEARS THAT IF YOU USE THE FAST FOWARD, CHAPTER SKIP BUTTONS I.E. "NEXT", YOU GET TO JUMP PAST THE WAIT AND THEN CAN QUICKLY EXIT OUT. THIS WORKS ON MAJORITY OF WARNING SCREENS, THERE WAS A VERY FEW THAT IT DID NOT WORK FOR. Someone mentioned about CNET review saying use of the FOLDER button is also a work around but I have found that that does not work. After a week, getting a little more comfortable, but am still very weary about the disk scratching issues, still doing random checks before return period expires.

I've had many canalphones/earbuds over the years.  From $20 cheapos to $250 higher end.  Money doesn't always dictate quality, mind you, as one of my favorite earbuds for many years was an $85 pair by Shure.  At any rate, Acoutstic Research HP1000's gets a 3 star rating for me because the build quality and lack of comfort is like a 2-3, while the sound quality is like a 4-5.  Obviously both categories are important, so I'll break things down a bit more specifically:PROS (mostly sound)- Solid bass.  As with all inner-ear phones, you have to have a tight seal to appreciate the bass- Crisp highs- Good atmospheric range (spacial sound stage is quite good)- Comes with a nice zipper case for portable storage - essential for these types of headphonesCONS- Very short cable length- Cable feels flimsy, though I haven't had them a long time to withstand a time test- No right-angle plugin jack (so important with portables these days)- I can feel them in my ears... the best inner-ear phones feel like there is nothing there.  I know everyone's ears are a different size/shape, but typically the middle-size earcups fit me perfectly.  These feel like I have to push them in deeper for better sound, resulting in some discomfort.I do feel bad not giving these a 4-star rating, because indeed the sound quality is crucial with headphones, and these do deliver good sound, but I'm not happy with the feel, and chord length is extremely important to me... this is about 3.5 feet long from plug to buds, and that's just insane.

இ Fuzzy Wuzzy's Summary:ѾѾѾѾѾ Highly recommended with warm fuzzies!փ Positives:փ Affordably priced.փ The articulating jointed arm and legs can prop up everything from an iPhone to a large 12" tablet.փ When folded up, the light 3.0-ounce 7.1-inch long stand is compact, with rounded corners, making it easy to carry in a purse, pocket, laptop bag.փ Although light in weight, the plastic construction and build quality feel solid.փ The iPad or tablet can be left inside its sleeve or case when used on this stand.փ This stand can be left on a table to display an iPad/tablet as a digital picture frame.ჯ Negatives:ჯ Not really a "negative", but this stand can only be used on a flat surface, and cannot be placed directly on top of your lap.This adaptable travel stand can be configured to prop up everything from an iPhone or other smart phone, iPod Touch, Kindle, on up to a large 12" tablet.  When its two legs and one jointed arm are folded up, its light 3.0-ounce size is just 7.1" long, 1.2" high, and 1.0" wide, making it easy to carry inside a purse, pocket, or laptop bag.  The tips of the arm and two legs are curved, with rounded edges, with no sharp corners that can jab or get caught on something if you carry it in your purse or pocket.  The two legs each independently swivel out and click-lock into place around a toothed cogwheel hinge at two different angles, 15 degrees or 30 degrees, to accommodate various widths of Kindles, e-readers, and tablets placed onto its two V-shaped grooves.  The two leg grooves have a non-skid soft rubbery paddding stuck onto it to both protect the edge of your Kindle or tablet from scratches while it sits on the legs and to also hold it in place.  The same non-skid surface is glued to the underside of the two legs to keep the stand from sliding across a surface, and the upper arm section is also coated with this non-skid pad to help hold your electronic device in place.  The single articulating arm employs two hinged joints that can click-lock into a variety of angles.  By adjusting the two hinges of the arm separately, a multitude of viewing angles can be configured.  This stand is designed to be placed on a relatively flat surface such as a desk, table, airline seat tray, lap desk, pillow top, or mattress top, but it may be too difficult to balance directly on top of your lap.With its versatility, you can even use this stand to prop up a cell/smart/iPhone phone or iPod Touch, either by using the stand with both legs closed together, or by swinging just one leg out to its 15-degree angled position.  In this configuration, your phone must be in vertical/portrait orientation.When used as an iPad stand with the iPad positioned in vertical/portrait orientation, you can adjust the viewing angle from a 90-degree upright position to almost totally laying flat.  The stand is slightly less adaptable if you view the iPad in horizontal/landscape orientation, with the viewing angle being adjustable from a 90-degree upright position to about 30 degrees.  If you like to frequently type using the iPad's virtual keyboard, this stand is sturdy and stable enough to support your typing motions if it is placed on a flat surface.  However, while typing on the iPad in horizontal/landscape orientation, the 30-degree angle may pivot your wrists too high up for comfortable extended durations of typing.  If the middle hinge in the arm had been designed so that it could pivot backward more, then the bottom arm section could have been pressed flat to the leg sections and the top arm section could have then positioned a landscape-mode iPad to a flatter 10-degree or 20-degree angle for a more comfortable typing angle.  But this is just a minor quibble with this design.Along with propping up my Kindle or iPad for reading, another great use for this stand is to hold my iPad when using it as a digital picture frame.  You put the iPad into "Picture Frame" mode from the lock screen.  When the lock screen appears, do not slide to unlock.  Instead, tap on the icon that is to the right of the "Slide to Unlock" bar.  That is it; the iPad will start up a slideshow of your photos and images held in your photo library.  You may want to take a look at some of the basic settings for this feature as well.  To do so, tap the "Settings" icon.  You will see that "Picture Frame" has its own section, just below "Brightness & Wallpaper".  Tap there and you will have access to these settings: 'Transition': Choose from "Dissolve" or "Origami" for the transition effect between photos.  'Show Each Photo For': Set how long each photo stays on the screen for (from 2 to 20 seconds).  'Zoom in on Faces': Toggle on or off.  'Shuffle': Toggle on or off.  'All Photos or Albums': Choose whether you want to display all photos or select just certain albums to display in photo frame mode.  So when you are not using your iPad for work, reading, or browsing, you can place your iPad on this stand and run a "Picture Frame" slideshow to display your favorite photos.  You can place the iPad on this stand either with or without a sleeve or case wrapped around the iPad.If you use this stand as a docking station to park your iPad in vertical/portrait orientation, there is not enough clearance for the charging cable to plug into the iPad from underneath.  But this is easily remedied by turning the iPad upside down in "inverted portrait" orientation so that the Dock Connector charging port is on top while you continue to read the iPad in vertical orientation.௫ Fuzzy Wuzzy's Conclusion:This is a great, affordable, simple, and creatively adaptable stand that can serve as a stand to hold a variety of personal electronics like Kindles and tablets.  Another low-tech portable stand that I have previously used to prop up my Kindles and iPads at various viewing angles is theTwo Wire Display Stand; Set of 2 6A - Black.  While this Fold-Up Travel Stand weighs a light 3 ounces, the wire display stand is even more compact and weighs only 1.5 ounces.  But this Fold-Up Travel Stand can hold a device as small as a cell/smart phone, whereas the mentioned wire stand cannot hold a device that small.At the time of this review's writing, there are two other identical models of this folding stand currently being listed and sold on Amazon:Arkon Portable Fold-Up Stand for Apple iPad, Galaxy Tab, BlackBerry Play Book, and Amazon's own AmazonBasics-brandedAmazonBasics Portable Fold-Up Travel Stand for the new iPad, iPad 2, Samsung Galaxy Tab 10.1 and 7.0, Kindle Fire, Kindle Touch (Black).  Since this is a patented design from a manufacturer in Taiwan, I suspect that these are all the exact same stand from the same Taiwanese manufacturer being sold by different vendors.  HOWEVER, note that two of the other Amazon listings for this stand that I mentioned may be shipped from Hong Kong by a merchant called "Get N' Go" or shipped from the U.K. by a merchant called "Navitech".  Some other third-party merchants listed as alternative vendors are based in the U.S.  But by purchasing Amazon's own AmazonBasics-branded version of this portable travel stand that Amazon lists as "Ships from and sold by Amazon.com in certified Frustration-Free Packaging", you can receive your delivery quicker instead of inadvertently ordering from another merchant who may be actually shipping the product from another country.  As with purchasing any product from an Amazon third-party merchant, you should verify the location from where the product is being shipped and not just assume that everything is shipped from the U.S.

I have purchased and reviewed many headsets.  I was looking for a stereo blue tooth headset that could handle multiple devices and provide good sound.  Over the years I have purchased and used many Plantronics headsets, some which I still use today.Reading other reviews I was excited at this headset, light, easy to use and good sound.  When I received the headset I was impressed at the build and design, the cable did seem a little short and got caught on my clothing at times.  I struggled for a long time to find a fit where I could be confident that the earbuds would stay in my ear canal, on a walk or run.  It is important to ensure a snug fit in order to achieve the bass that the product claims.  My best success was with the smallest earbuds and using the loops lodged in the outer ear piece.  I still experienced times when they fell out and am now looking for aftermarket buds that will provide a better fit.When fitting into the ear, the sound is good, I do not experience the connectivity interference I have seen with other blue tooth headsets when phone in pocket.  The mic is good when not windy.  Volume range is acceptable and controls are easy to use, though I wish lower down the cord as can be tricky to access.Pairing the headset is easy as with other headsets, hold down the power on button (middle button) until it flashes blue/red.  I was disappointed, however, with the way it handles multiple devices, which the headset claims.  I was hoping like other Plantronics headsets that I could switch between by pressing a button and it would connect to two devices at a time.  In order to switch between devices you have to turn off blue tooth on one device and turn the blue tooth on for the device you want to use.  The other option is to go into the settings for blue tooth on the device to use and select the headset.  I carry two phones and this was a big requirement for me, this made my headset a wasted purchase.I would recommend other headsets or stick with a conventional wired headset.

I want a camera bag that I can carry either my Canon 5D MKII and my workhorse lens, the Canon EOS 70-200mm f/2.8L along with a couple of primes and a flash, or my new love, my Olympus OMD E-M5 with the multiple lenses I use.  This bag is overkill for my micro 4/3 kit, but I can almost put both setups in it if I wanted to cart everything around.  I think that Thule sees this as a bag to take hiking, biking, skiing etc. — but for any of those I would want something I could get to my camera quickly without laying it down on the ground – this is not the bag for that.The bags outer material is specially-treated nylon. I tried spraying it with water and the water beaded well on the surface and didn’t get through. The pack also comes with a rain cover that you can flip up over the entire bag for extra protection. All of the zippers are supposed to be waterproof and the zipper pulls are large blue plastic ovals that would be easy to grab even with gloves.The interior is made of medium-density ” thick brushed-cloth coated foam. It kind of feels cheap for some reason, but that may be just me. This isn’t a hard-case and won’t protect your gear if you crash. It does have sufficient rigidity to act as travel luggage.The back panel of the pack is made from a single, rigid piece of plastic with three soft foam pads to cushion your back and provide some ventilation . . . this is also the cover of the camera storage compartment (more on that later). There are hip-belt pads that can be tucked away under the bottom foam pad. The shoulder straps are wide but I had a hard time getting them comfortable when I had multiple layers on. Minus one star for fit and interior finish.I did notice that the pack’s contents tend to bounce around a bit. There’s no way to strap the camera in place once it’s in the compartment, the body with a smaller lens is going to move around a lot when you’re skiing or biking. The camera compartment can be divided into three sections. The adjustment is limited since the side compartment dividers are only a certain width (one side measures 3.5”, the other is 4.0”).  It really didn’t work well for the M4/3 gear as it is all too small and just doesn’t get enough padding.  The main camera compartment does hold a medium to large camera with an attached lens well, even the 5D with battery grip attached fit in.My biggest issue with the bag is using the main storage area for storing other lenses or the flash unit. Since there is no way to secure these accessories, it’s possible they could fall out if you were to leave the bag open.  If you take your camera out and want to move around you could dump all of your gear out accidently.The Perspektiv uses a back access cover for the camera compartment so you have to take it off your back completely to open the bag. Supposedly you can access your camera or change lenses without setting the bag down.  For the life of me I couldn’t figure out how to do that without taking a chance on dumping everything. I assume the water-resistant fabric would allow you to set it down almost anywhere to get to your gear. Minus one star for the access.The computer pocket is well padded and fit my 13” laptop easily.Bottom LineI think the Thule Perspektiv would be good for hikers.  I don't think it would work for biking and skiing. When I tried it on my bike, my Canon camera definitely bounced around even with the big lens on and all the items in the top compartment would also rattle. I could see it as your protective carry-on bag when traveling, with a full DLSR kit it would be tight.  It is exactly the right size for the airlines overhead bins.  It definitely is not usable for Micro 4/3 equipment as you can’t adjust it tight enough to hold the camera or lenses.

I will consider Transcend along with SanDisk in the future, and unless there is a clear technical advantage, will go with Transcend's lower price.

I bought this case based on the other Amazon recommendations, however after using it for a couple of weeks I'm not very thrilled with the design. The build quality is decent enough - it's a faux leather case with a soft felt interior. It hold the Nexus 10 in place pretty well, has a strap for putting your palm into to hold it one handed, has all the proper cutouts for the various ports.However I think the design is fundamentally flawed. When I first got the case, I kept thinking that I must have the Nexus in upside down or something, but I do not as the ports line up perfectly when I use it as intended.First of all, there are solid corner "clips" that hold the corners of the device to the case. To use the case as multi-angle like you see in the pictures, you have to pull pretty hard on the bottom corners of the Nexus to unclip the bottom two corners from the case. It's pretty hard to do as those clips are designed to keep the Nexus pretty securely fastened to the case.You're practically bending the clips just to free the Nexus in order to get the device in kickstand mode, which weakens them over time. Thus, every time you put your device in kickstand mode, you're loosening the case's hold on your Nexus. Your device eventually doesn't stay in the case because the securing clips have been bent out of shape. Plus you're putting alot of mechanical stress on the plastic corners of your Nexus due to the constant pulling and pushing back into those clips.Then, when you close the case, unless you fiddle and snap those bottom corners back into it's clips, you have a "bulging" case because half of it isn't clipped in.The hand strap is positioned the wrong way as well. If you slide your palm into the hand strap, you are naturally holding the device in Portrait mode, whereas the Nexus is primarily designed to be held in Landscape mode.Finally, when you have the case folded over itself in most common, non-kickstand use, the back facing camera is covered by the case itself. So if you wanted to take a picture using your tablet, you have to let case cover flop around while you hold up the device.Again the quality of the case is fine, and for $15 the price is right, however it's just that it could have been better designed.

As one of my recent Vine orders I had the opportunity to review the TP-LINK Model TL-WA850RE 300Mbps Universal WIFI Range Extender.To begin with, because of the configuration of the cable setup when our home was built in 2004 - i.e. the access to cable outside, and it's entry point into our home; we only had one option for our wireless access point - on one side of the house on the ground floor. At times we have signal strength issues on the other side of the house, in the basement, and in upstairs bedrooms.As for the set up instruction for the  TP-Link  Universal Range Extender. You're given 2 options to get the device configured and connected to the network.  I started with Method 1 which involves plugging in the device, pushing the WPS button on the front of the unit, and allowing the device to automatically detect and connect to the wireless network.  Our device was unable to connect to our network using this method.  Method 2 uses a web browser and gives you the option to connect the device to your computer with a wireless connection or an Ethernet cable.  I elected to try the wireless method using my laptop.  After powering on the device, you open a browser window on the laptop, type in the URL provided and follow the on-screen instructions to complete the set-up. As part of the set-up I chose to retain the existing wireless network name so that devices set up to automatically connect to the network would not need to be changed.  I was able to successfully set up the device using this method.  I performed the set-up in the same room as the wireless access point, then moved the range extender to a central location on the main floor close to the area which is most central, and both equidistant to the upstairs and the basement.The first thing I did was verify that devices were still able to successfully connect to the network.  My husband and I use laptops, our kids have Kindle Fires, and we also have an Xbox that uses the wireless network.  All devices successfully connected to the network.  Next I checked signal strength on the laptops. The said they had a good signal - two kids in the basement, and one in the farthest upstairs bedroom.  My signal went from 4 bars to 5 bars on the main level and from 3 to 4 bars upstairs.The other laptop - a newer Asus Windows 7/ Windows 8 - which hadn't had issues up until we connected the range extender, started to have connection issues. Things seemed to be going well for everyone else  though. However,  over the course of the rest of the day we began to have issues with web browsing using the laptops.  Web pages wouldn't load, we had to stop and refresh on multiple occasions to view web content, we'd get error pages which wouldn't reload, and at one point  I had to shut down my computer.  As the number of occurrences increased, so did our frustration level.  Eventually, we unplugged the range extender and the issues stopped.  There were no issues that we noticed with Fires or the Xbox.Upon retrying the device, in a new location, we experienced similar problems on our laptops - connection issues, web pages wouldn't load, and  web page error messages. The Kindle Fires operated well no matter their location, but they always do. The Xbox is located on the main level and had no issues either, but it has never had issues either.*One thing I will say in defense of this product is that we recently switched to AT&T; and I did a Speed Test because our RoKu kept reloading (and this is no joke) every minute! I was SO frustrated I wanted to see what the upload/download speeds were. They were abysmal! The upload and download speeds were BOTH less than 1 (ONE) Mbps!!! That HAS to have an effect on the TP-Link  Universal WIFI Range Extender! (and it's maddening because we're paying for a minimum of 15Mbps!)*  When I reviewed the other TP-Link products we were with Time Warner, and had no such problems - they worked really well! However, at the time our download speed was 15 Mbps. Our upload speed was tragic - for our son anyway as he's a YouTube(r). Less than 1Mbps!Anyway, based on the fact that I think there are outside influences at play here, and initially upon setup we did experience a good outcome, I would say this product does indeed hold promise. If your internet connection is slow as molasses, take care of that before installing this product to see what it can really do. We plan to get with AT&T; to resolve the issues (hopefully) and try the extender again.I do have to give it a 3 overall because of our experience - after all we simply could not use it. Despite the extenuating circumstances. I do apologize! I hate it when people review something that seems to have nothing to do with the product. I will try to revise after we see what can be done by AT&T.;Ease of setup:  4Signal strength boost:  4Web browsing performance:  2Tablets and Xbox performance: 4Laptop performance: first laptop 3 / second laptop 1Overall:  3  *with extenuating circumstances*

I turned it off and went home, and when I turned it on again, the spots were ebbing into little black lines.By the next day, two large lines were across the LCD. I could even see them when the camera was off. I took it back and exchanged it for another one.That night, we went out for dinner and I took the camera with me. Within taking about 10 pictures, the same thing happened-a long, thin black line appeared across the LCD.I fell in love with this camera and seriously considered keeping it despite the flaw, but then came to my senses when I realized that no brand new device should be doing that. I didn't exchange it again after I read customer reviews on the camera, and found that apparently this black line problem is a recurring one with this model.So basically, if you want to take the gamble and see if you're one of the lucky ones with no LCD problems, this is a great camera. This is actually a cool little amp. I bought this for a home made docking station I am building for my mp3 player. It is very small and light weight. It's louder than I expected having only 4 watts output per channel, but I don't think it would be quite loud enough to run in your car or truck. I experimented with several speakers and got the best results with larger home stereo speakers. The few car speakers (4 ohm) I tried sounded a bit flat. I think this amp prefers 8-16ohms for best sound quality. The best sound I got was using my pair of Bose 701s (vintage 1977 models!) wired in series with a pair of Polk Audio bookshelf speakers. Sweet.This amp does get hot. After running it at about 3/4 volume for 20-25 minutes it got quite warm, enough that I got concerned and turned it down. If I planned to use it often at loud volumes I might consider adding a small cooling fan.Sound quality is pretty good also. I had both the bass and treble cranked but wished the bass would turn just a little more. Very clean sounding with excellent highs and decent enough bass.This amp runs fine using a 2 amp wall transformer (wall wart). It also runs fine using a pair of 6v lantern batteries.All in all I like this amp and would recommend it providing you don't need a lot of volume.

After plugging it into my laptop and changing the default IP, then connecting it to my router/modem, I finally got it to work with WPA-Personal security. Since hidden SSID's does not seem to work to well on Vista Home or at all for that matter. I use MAC filtering along with WPA. (Two Vista Home laptops and one BB Bold all have problems connecting to my wireless network when the SSID is not being broadcast.)Took about an hour to set it up, but for some reason Cisco/Linksys wants you to use their startup cd and disable all security. Default IP and access codes on the first page would be more helpful.I paired the bridge to a Linksys WRT600N Dual band wireless router, I also had to move the wireless router to get a signal. No wooden walls in my house.Best connection speed is 13.5mbps on the 5Ghz side of the router, and around 6mbps on the 2.4Ghz side. on the plus side I have 5 bars on the laptop in every room in the house and the blue LED's match my AV equipment. I also connected the Blackberry Bold to the wireless network.Why I got this: I needed network connections in my living room and did not want to run cables along the walls or cut channels. The bridge is connected to a small 100MB hub. Samsung Blue Ray DVD and Sat Receiver are connected to the hub which goes to the bridge which makes a wireless connections back to the WRT600.It works for me, since I got it setup I've had to pull the power cord out once to reconnect to the WRT600.It does the job I need it to do. Setup issues could be avoided by listing the default IP and access codes up front. I guess I wasted 30 minutes using the CD and the quick configure feature, I did not read all the instructions. The setup instructions/wizard are for people who have wide open wireless networks.Look for the default IP and username/password first. Setup a static IP to match, then configure the bridge to match your network. 15 minutes to 20 minutes and you should be good to go.

Last year, I reviewed Miu's Silicone Cupcake Baking Cups and rated those as a five star product.  I stand by that review, but feel that Wilton's Silicone Baking Cups are equally as good.  As previously stated, I bake fat-free breakfast muffins on a regular basis; they stick to paper cupcake papers so that one loses half a muffin to the paper.  My daughter wanted to start using silicone baking cups for her breakfast muffins, but we were unable to find Miu again.I found the Wilton baking cups to be thicker and even more sturdy than Miu; they are not nearly as flexible.  There is little chance of the baking cups spreading from the weight of cupcake or muffin batter.  This is particularly helpful if one must sit the cups on a cookie sheet to bake or if one is not using a deep silicone pan to hold the cups and batter for baking.  The fill line is particularly nice when baking cupcakes as it allows one to put an equal amount of batter in each cup so that baking time does not vary within a batch of cupcakes/muffins.There are several ways to address the other reviewers' issues with these silicone baking cups.  I freeze my breakfast muffins and have found that if I allow my muffins to sit out for about 5 minutes and then carefully peel off the silicone baking cup, there is little to no baked good sticking to the cup.  If some does stick, I simply fill the cup with water and allow it to sit for awhile before hand washing the cup.  The second way is to put the muffin cups into your baking pan and then spray all of the cups with non-stick spray.  Be sure to do this over your sink to avoid the mess of overspray.  Then bake as directed by your recipe, allow the muffins to cool for 5 minutes and then turn out of the pan.  The muffin cups will come off easily without damaging the baked goods.As for accidentally throwing out these silicone cups, I remove them just before serving cupcakes or muffins to guests.  If you freeze the baked goods and remove the cups before serving, you will need to allow enough time for the product to thaw and come to room temperature.  Since there are little to no crumbs sticking to the cup, the treat is not damaged by doing this and my silicone baking cups are safe from being accidentally discarded.We were able to find Wilton Baking Cups at the big home store where they sold for $7.99 for 12; by using a $5 off $15 purchase coupon, and stacking the 10% off coupon on one item, my daughter was able to reduce her total cost for two sets to around $10.

MARCH 29, 2013:  Changed 5 star to 3 star. I've had this pan 6 months. It has never been in a dishwasher and never cleaned with anything but mild detergent and a sponge.  I've never used metal utensils in the pan...only non-stick silicon pieces. Wanted to have this one for a long time so treated it with kid cloves.  I just found a tiny little blister on the bottom on the fryer where the non stick coating has separated from the surface of the pan.  It's very small but it's there which means it will start chipping some time soon.  As soon as it does, it's in the garbage.  I'm really disappointed because I do love to use it.  Now to the original review..............I purchased this skillet a month or so ago.  Used it almost every day and, so far, must say I'm very pleased.  I'm going to take very good care of this one.  I've had non stick before and aways became disappointed in it's longevity.  I'd like to get at least a few years out of a pan before sending it to the trash. Finally gave up on non stick and went with cast iron and stainless steel.  That was fine for years.  Now I need lighter weight cookware and less work.This skillet is a nice weight, seems to be well comstructed, and feels sturdy.  It heats evening.  I find medium to medium low is best for all types of cooking in this pan.  I seared two very thick pork loin chops tonight in this pan.  I seasoned the chops, added some olive oil to the skillet and seared each side for 5 mins at a time.  I think I turned each chop 3 or 4 times until I hit my internal temp of 145 degrees.  The chops seared beautifully on each side without any signs of burning at all.  The color was perfect. Sliced it up and topped with a Balsamic Reduction Glaze.  Perfect.  Eggs are a pleasure to cook.  Beside scrambled eggs I like to put a pat of margarine in the pan...Heat until it just starts to sizzle...Break eggs into the skillet...Let the bottoms of the eggs cook for a minute or so until they turn white and then add a few tablespoons of water and put the lid on.  The tops of the eggs steam so they're not raw...as runny or as firm as you want depending on how long you leave the lid on.  My kids called them dip eggs.  They come out like perfect "fried eggs" without the grease.I'm still not happy about cooking in non stick cookwave but I'm getting too old to worry that much about it.  I'm looking for ways to continue cooking from scratch and making it easier.  Non stick fits that bill for many foods I cook.  I have a cast iron pan but it's work and heavy.  I'm looking for less work.  I'll still pull out the Wagner though from time to time just for tradition or to cook something that can only be properly cooked in cast iron.  Can't give it up completely.

Its a good idea --- a long piece of nylon strapping material with a half moon clip on either end for mounting. To hold the hats, are plastic tabs - no clips - clasps - buttons - or snaps just these plastic tabs that have been stitched onto the nylon strap, facing upwards. The premiss of this is to secure BOTH ends taught enough to just make the plastic tabs stick out slightly - and pop a cap onto that tab. Amazon is currently offering a nice discount and will likely do so again in the future.)With MSNTV, you cannot download any software of your choosing. Seems like every year I add another device that either requires a wall plug or a USB charger.  So, like many others, I wind up looking for ways to add additional outlets to my work areas.  Since I have the older style round outlets that have a center screw for mounting the wall plate (something this adapter requires in order to secure it in place) I decided to order this unit and give it a try.  Here is what I liked:1.  The unit, once mounted, is very secure and you do not need to worry when unplugging a cable that you might pull the unit out of the wall.  (NOTE: this unit is secured to the wall via a small screw that attaches to the same hole in your outlet that you attach the cover plate to.  As such, this will NOT work on a square outlet as there is no center hole to attach it to.)2.  The unit lets you know if you have a valid ground (led indicator) and also lets you know if the circuit surge protector is functional (another led indicator).3.  There are two USB charge (not data) ports that have a combined rating of 10 Watts.4.  The six outlets are spaced such that you can actually use all of them.What I did not like so much:1.  The design of this unit uses only one plug on a wall plate for actual power and uses just the ground port of the second outlet to stabilize the unit in the outlet.  This means that if you were hoping to use this on an outlet where one plug is switched and the other is live all of the time that you not be able to use one of the functions (depends on which outlet is switched).  All 6 plugs will either be switched or will all be powered on constantly.  Keep in mind that if this is switched, it also means that your USB power ports will also be on the same switch!!2.  While there are two USB ports, for some purposes only one will be usable!  This will all depend upon the device you are trying to charge.  If your device requires 1 amp or less, then you can plug in two such devices without issues.  However, if your device requires a 2 amp charge, you will only be able to plug one device into the USB ports since that limits out its capability.  A perfect example of this would be charging an iPad.Something to think about:If you will are thinking of using a Powerline type of data connector on this unit, think again. Most Powerline adapters will warn you NOT to connect their unit to a surge protector as it can interfere with data rates.  Does that mean that it will not work?  Not necessarily, but it will down grade the data link rate in most cases.This is an excellent product as long as you remember the limitations that I mentioned above.  For me, it works well in the applications that I am using it on.

Sony, we love and hate them.  They come out with slick design and lots of features ahead of competition, then decides to lock themselves into some priorietary technology that doesn't play well with the masses.  In an ideal world, I would have a reader that looks sexy and does all the formats plus HTML with all different encodings.  To me, that's the most important format of them all because the wealthiest source of information comes from HTML pages.  This unit doesn't do HTML directly but it claims it can do PDF, so I settled for that.However, after getting over the initial excitement of reading default books and converting some online content, I found it extremely inconvenient to use.  Yes there are some free programs that do all sorts of format conversions, but none had worked out well so far.  I read a lot of Chinese text, and to convert a HTML-based Chinese text into either PDF or ePub or BBeB is extremely slow to load and read.  It renders the text ok, however to zoom in it will take minutes and to flip a page will take a good 30 seconds.  I tried several techniques and none worked out well enough to make me believe this is a mature product.Even contents in English are slow if it has photos.  I downloaded some free-distribution documents that are professionally distributed, and still it's unacceptable.  If it takes me 20 seconds to read through a page, I don't want to spend 30 seconds to turn a page.  It really boils down to the basics.  A specialized product like this needs to do what it is supposed to do very well, otherwise with netbooks nowadays for $200-$300 I don't see a need for a dedicated reader at all.p.s. I do have to acknowledge that perhaps Sony's strategy is to funnel people to buy their online content, and maybe their content is optimized to be used for this viewer.  But then we all suffered through the BetaMax and MiniDisc and MemoryStick and blah blah blah.  Even a product as successful as iPod supports generic MP3s and it remains the most popular music format, so I hope for the day Sony sees the same light.

There's lots of reviews here about the Pro's and Con's of this keyboard and mouse combo so I will address just 2 things that I think are worth mentioning.1. Other reviews(rated most helpful) have mentioned that this keyboard is SPILLPROOF: (and I quote a Vine reviewer)"The keyboard itself is black, with a clear transparent plastic frame overlaid on top with a slight bit of overhang. It's a nice clean design, and reminds me of some of the "floating glass" frames of certain Sony Bravia TV models. The transparent plastic also has a functional purpose, in addition to being aesthetically pleasing- it makes the keyboard spill resistant.""Logitech added a nice aesthetic design touch by bordering the keyboard with thin clear plastic" (by another Vine reviewer)My comment: The transparent plastic is part of the PACKAGING to protect the keyboard until it is purchased. You are supposed to remove it! Just like you peel that plastic off the face of a brand new iPod or cell phone screen. Of course, I guess you could leave it on if you like the nice shiny look.But, there is NO mention in either Amazon's description of this product or at the Logitech website of this keyboard being spillproof. It just isn't. The only way to make it spillproof would be to buy a skin designed to fit over the entire keyboard.2. TheLogitech Wireless Mouse M310 (Silver)which comes with this keyboard lacks a MANDATORY feature that ANY new mouse should have in this day and age. Another reviewer called it "BARBARIC" that the mouse does not come with "Back" and "Forward" thumb buttons for web browsing.My comment: If you walk into any electronics store you will see walls of mice without the thumb buttons and I wonder to myself when I see them "Who would buy these?". Can it be because many people have never had a mouse with them and are being duped into thinking they are complicated or worse yet "gaming" mice? If you spend any amount of time browsing the web, it's a feature you can't live without once you've had it. The "Back" thumb button takes you back to the page you were on before and the "Forward" button takes you forward again to where you started from. Simple as pie and Oh so useful! I think some people are afraid of these 2 extra buttons on a mouse. They're afraid they might accidently press them and something terrible will happen. One reviewer thought touching them might cause the mouse to "implode" in his hand. Please people, do not be afraid! Why do you think they are selling so many new mice in all those pretty new colors like theLogitech Wireless Mouse M305 (Blue Swirl)or theLogitech Wireless Mouse M305 (Pink Balance)or theLogitech Wireless Mouse M310 (Big Top Stripe). They're charging you for OLD technology with the gimick that they are "designer". Do yourself a favor and at least get yourself aLogitech M510 Wireless Mouseor something similar and make your life easier.COMMENT: If you have tried a mouse with back and forward thumb buttons and just hated it, please don't rate my review as "unhelpful". I'm just trying to make some people aware of something they may be missing out on. My 91 year old mother likes the M305 mouse because it is simple. At her age and with her "late in life" introduction to computers, I can't expect her to appreciate or assimilate an understanding of extra buttons that she has to think too much about as her use of the computer is limited largely to e-mail.On the other hand Logitech's use of the unifying receiving  that works with multiple accessory devices on this combo is nothing short of BRILLIANT. It in itself is a huge reason to buy and own multiple Logitech mice, keyboards. You can connect up to 6 devices that use it on a single computer. Of course it won't work with older Logitech mice and keyboards that used the somewhat larger USB receiver. Too bad they couldn't have made it backwards compatible.UPDATE 3/13/12: This is actually a pretty unusual package deal. The M310 silver mouse that comes with this combo uses the newer unifying receiver, but if you buy an M310 mouse separately it uses the old "nano receiver". The unifying USB receivers all have an orange star on them; the older ones say "nano receiver" on them; that's how to tell them apart.

Initial review: 15-July-2011My wife asked if we should get a Dyson. $500 for a vacuum? No way... I started looking...Amazon sent me a notice offering theHoover MultiCyclonic Canister - SH40060for $144. I bought it; my wife was pissed because we didn't have a discussion first. End of background statement.I put it together without needing the instruction booklet. GOOD SHOW, Hoover!The entire vacuum structure is plastic. So is my wife's high-precision $2000 Bernina sewing machine. Not a confidence builder, but not a problem, either. It makes the business end light and easy to move around.I pulled out the cord and plugged it in. The cord is almost 1/2 the length of the cord on our Royal upright. BAD SHOW, Hoover. This is a substantial, but far from fatal, annoyance - I can vacuum my entire 1300-sq-ft ground floor with the Royal plugged into one outlet. I have to move the cord 4 times to do the same floor with the Hoover.The first thing I noticed when I turned on the MultiCyclonic: it is quiet (compared to the Royal). TV and normal-voice conversations are possible with the thing running. WELL DONE.Venturing across hardwood floors, I found the machine works just wonderfully. It picks up hair from our beagle with no problem, and demonstrates it's prowess with a ball of fur whirling around in the transparent canister. VERY NICE.Here is the bad news: the soft, flexy hose does not have rotating couplings to keep the hose un-wound. When I tried to double back to a corner I had missed, the hose kinked and collapsed under high torque or bending loads, and it did so at both the canister end and at the handle end. The cyclone depends on high-velocity flow, which ends abruptly when the hose collapses.BAD BAD JOB, HOOVER. THE HOSE IS THE WEAKEST POINT OF AN OTHERWISE VERY GOOD DESIGN. WHY CHEAP IT OUT WITH A 10-CENT PIECE OF HOSE? In the quantities these things are manufactured, a chunk of reinforced hose with rotating couplings would add at most $2 to the purchase price. Big deal. I worry about whether these kinks will set into the hose as permanent creases, causing me to wonder whether the typical manufacturer's scam for a replacement part will cost me $50 or more. The hose on our Royal upright has some issues, but when we pull on it, IT NEVER EVER kinks, no matter what direction we move relative to the machine.Despite the impressive hardwood floor performance, I CANNOT RECOMMEND THIS VACUUM CLEANER BECAUSE THE HOSE IS JUNK. I'm willing to test a better hose; Hoover can contact me through Amazon.Coming up: completing the evaluation by vacuuming the stairs and (gasp) testing on carpeted bedroom floors.Final review: 19-Jul-2011I tried the thing on medium-pile carpet. Didn't work all that well.A couple reviews state that the power head (for carpets) seizes up. Apparently plastic housings don't work all that well when bearings begin to heat under mechanical load (duh). Out of curiosity, I went to Hoover's web page. A replacement hose can only be had as a complete hose/head assembly. HOOVER WANTS $121 FOR IT? FOR A $5 HOSE? ON A $140 VACUUM? Come ON, people!As of this date, Hoover is in the process of selling itself to any investor interested. Producing junks product like this is going to make it a tough sale.On the basis of poor design and very uneven performance, I am returning this vacuum.OVERALL GRADE: FAIL (and I've never before written a review quite this harsh)

When this device is working properly, it's a really handy little widget.  The trick is keeping it working!  Like many similar devices, the temperature probe will eventually fail. Also, the temp alarms and beeper can drive you crazy if you're slow cooking or smoking a piece of meat.  When the target shifts up and down a degree (as often happens in smoking), the alarms go off over and over, and there's no way to custom set this function.One more word on the probe: the insulation is NOT very rugged.  The best cabled probes I've used were encased in a braided insulation that really held up well when (inevitably) pinched between two metal surfaces.  The plastic (silicone?) insulation on this probe will melt off the first time it brushes against anything hot, and the wiring can't survive being pinched, which makes it a problem for leaving in an oven, smoker, or closed grill.I own several thermometers, and while this one was exciting and fun to play with when first purchased, it has quickly been pushed to the back of the drawer.  Hell, I've had such mixed results with this style thermometer in general that I've gone back to sticking an old-school bi-metal analog probe into larger cuts of meat, just because I know they'll work without being fussy.

With a few changes, the Bloggie 3D could have been a great video camera. But its high price tag and lack of accessories earn it only 3 stars.On the positive side, the camera does seem to take pretty decent 3D videos. As advertised, its twin camera lenses enable you to take both still shots and full-motion video in 3D. (It's also possible to take traditional 2D photos and videos). The camera can even snap still shots while simultaneously recording a video.Videos can be played back on a 3D TV, through the YouTube 3D Channel, or right on your Bloggie screen without glasses (though this requires you to look at the little screen from a certain distance and angle, and tires the eyes quickly).As the name "Bloggie" suggests, this camera is all about social networking. It's a breeze to make your video, plug it into your computer, trim the length, and then with the click of a button you can upload it to sites like Facebook or YouTube.Nevertheless, this camera has some real shortcomings. It has no optical zoom and takes very poor still shots. Even in good outdoor lighting, I was disappointed. It does not have a flash, though it does come with a mediocre LED light. You will definitely want to buy a separate digital camera if you plan to take a lot of still shots.The design of the back of the camera also makes it difficult to hold with one hand. When taking a video, my thumb keeps wanting to bump into the directional key, which causes the lens to zoom in or out. Another big drawback is that the Bloggie does not have RCA jacks to plug into a traditional TV, nor does it have an AC Adapter (you have to charge it using the USB cable, which means you'd better have your computer with you if you plan to do very much recording).If you want to dabble into 3D movie-making, then the Bloggie might be right for you. It's not a bad camera, but at a retail price of $250, I expected more from Sony than this.

This is for the Anker 2nd Gen Astro Pro2 20000mAh battery pack.There are a few different products in the reviews for this product so you have to read carefully.This is designed very well, beautiful finish and easy to operate.This can achieve 80%+ efficiency when you are charging a device that charges at 5v 1000ma. Better efficiency can be achieved when you are charging devices that draw 2000ma. However, if you are charging a device that only charges at 500ma, the battery pack does not last nearly as long due to several factors.  It's effective charge potential can be as low as 2,500ma if you are running a 50ma LED light for example. (50 hour run time).  The reason for this is common in the marketplace for these style batteries due to the 3.7v to 5v/12v circuits. It is rated at 3.7v @ 20,000 mAh or 74 watt hours. You can subtract 1 watt (270 ma) per hour the unit is on and it will be completely depleted if on for 74 hours with load. (Auto-shutoff prevents this). My LG phone draws about 30ma and peaks to 75ma every 15-20 seconds so the unit does not turn off after the phone is done charging.  If my phone has 98% battery and put it on charge with this battery when I go to bed, it will use 7-10% of the battery in 8 hours.  If I left the phone unplugged, it would still be on 98% in the morning. I bought this one for the flexibility of using 12v for charging the unit and misc items I have like a 12v rechargeable lantern. The Charging circuit uses about 270ma + (charge mA * (Output Voltage / 3.7). I.E. If you are charging a 500ma device, it draws 945ma (675ma + 270ma) off the battery.  When charging 500ma devices, You will get about 20 hours of charging before battery is dead. This example is far below the 80% efficiency it claims. Including the power conversion factor, it is 69% efficient using the example above.As the market and technology goes, this unit is par with others on the market. All of the multi-volt units draw about a watt due to the circuitry required.  Cost wise, this unit is worth the money.  I gave it 3 stars because of the deceptive marketing Anker and many companies use.  I would much rather have all the information above disclosed and not have to discover it myself.  Just like UPS companies, Buyer beware because the numbers are designed to look much better than they are. If the output power is 5v and 12v, capacity should be disclosed for each voltage. This is rated by the 3.7 battery.  While you might get close to the same wattage - 1w/hour charging, you won't get anywhere near 20,000mAh.  Again, the entire industry does it this way.  Some are starting to disclose this information.  I wish they all did.mAh output for each voltage:5v = 14,800 mAh - (200ma * hours used)12v = 6,166 mAh - (83ma * hours used)Power used for conversion from 3.7v to 5v is minimal.  The unit itself does get warm when charging so if you charge via a 12v solar panel, it is best to keep it out of the sun.

I purchased the original iPad 64GB with Wifi back in October of last year.  If I had know that an updated model was going to become available so soon, I would have waited for the iPad 2. So, do you really need the iPad 2?  Frankly, there are three major differences between the original iPad and the iPad 2.  First, the iPad 2 is noticeably lighter and sleeker.  It is more comfortable to hold for longer periods of time, especially if you like to read e-newspaers or ebooks. Secondly, the iPad 2's processor is a lot speedier.  Page turns are quick, boot time is fast, and surfing the internet is a breeze. Last of all, the iPad 2 has a camera. This, however, is its weakest feature. Do not expect the same results you would get from a digital camera or digital webcam. (I could have lived with a model that has no camera.) The other differences are minor (e.g., the automatic turn on/turn off feature). For me, the iPad 2 is a better product for what I needed (reading and surfing the net).  Before you get rid of your original iPad, I would check it out at a retail store along side your original.

Let me start by saying that I like and own several Gerber products and buying from Amazon was a cinch as usual. Now that being said, I am not very impressed with this particular product but I shall digress for the moment for a little history.  I bought the original version of Gerber's light weight synthetic handle camp axe years ago when it first came to market.  I still own that axe and it is still awesome.  It holds an edge exceptionally well when properly used for bushcraft projects and light fire wood processing as was intended.  The sheath that covers the blade is very well made and keeps both me and the axe protected when not in use.  Very important since I keep the axe strapped to the ouside of my pack where one trip and fall could prove disasterous with a lesser sheath.  The handle is hollow and didn't come with a saw.  I supplemented this with a Gerber folding saw in it's own sheath that rides in my pack.  The hollow handle would make a convenient place for a survival kit if one were so inclined.  Though the handle is thin and made of a light weight synthetic material, it is very durable and incredibly strong.  The axe head itself is the most impressive part.  It was made by Fiskars of Finland who have been in the blade making business since the 1650's.  Not only is it razor sharp but it stays that way with light honning as is done with my knives.  This can only be due to the supperior manufacturing process involved in a hammer forged peice of steel also evident in the lack of seams or casting marks anywhere on the head.NOW FOR THE REVIW of Gerbers Gator Combo Axe II.  I was looking to get a second camping axe for my wife to use and thought the saw in the handle of the combo model was a pretty good idea.  Turns out that the rather well made saw is one of the only things I actually like about this product.  Since I bought this on line and not in person I didn't get to handle this product first or I would not have bought this.  The handle is a little thiner than the original and has a gimmicky section of traction adding rubber like material that is glued on and will eventually fall off.  The sheath looks exactly like the one on my original and is extremely well made.  Now if only the new axe head were the same as that found on the original I could have given this thing 5 stars as the saw in the handle would have made up for the gimmicky ruber stuff.  But that is the reason that this thing gets 2 stars.  The head is horrible and no longer wears the Fiskars brand.  Cast marks are clearly visible and I am pretty sure it was completely made in China.  Now I know that China has been making blades for a long time too, like thousands of years.  Good for China.  But not so good for Gerber because they obviously went to China to save money at the cost of quality.  The only good things about this product are that it has a very well made little saw in the handle and if my wife beats the axe head into the ground while splitting wood I wont fret since it's already junk and it keeps her away from my good axe.So, if you want the original quality of the Gerber Camp Axe as it used to be, you have to buy a Fiskars 14 inch X7.  If you want the saw, you simply buy a good folding saw and keep it with the axe.
