Purchased this wireless extender hoping to extend the wireless signal from my Fios router which is located in the basement (where many of the devices that require a hardwired connection are).  We live in a ranch, and the signal from the Fios router only reaches about 3/4 of the way down the length of the house.  I was hoping this wireless extender would do the trick in extended the signal to those hard-to-reach areas in our master bedroom and some of the other bedrooms, where we get 0-1 bars most of the time with the Fios router.Unfortunately, it didn't live up to the promise.  Setup was extremely simple, I used method 2 and synced the device with my router quickly enough.  I placed the device about halfway down the length of our ranch, and the device was able to extend the wireless range giving us as much as 2 bars in our master bedroom, when before we would get zero.  It is indeed a plug and play device and did extend the range of our wireless considerably.However, as others have mentioned, devices such as smartphones and tablets will not stay connected to the TP-LINK consistently.  During my testing just walking around the house, my wireless connection on my Galaxy Nexus would drop and reconnect frequently.  Even though I could get a few bars in the master bedroom, the connection was so inconsistent with frequent drops that it was impossible to do anything with it.I even tried standing directly next to the device, and my phone still dropped connection about once every 30 seconds.In addition, connection speeds for desktops connected to this device were extremely slow.  Our Fios connection is 50 mb, but with the TP-LINK I was getting about 8-10 mb.  That is a huge dropoff.Pretty disappointing. I'm not sure if this is a case of "you get what you pay for", as this thing is fairly cheap.  However I don't think I'll try my luck with another wireless extender.  I'll go the powerline route (I have one in the house now).Can't recommend this item.

I have quite a few cameras, Fuji Finepix 3800 (digital cam), Olympus E500 DSLR (w/multiple lenses), Casio Exilim EX-Z500 & Fuji Finepix A400 (pocket digital cams), and this Kodak Z5010.  All have their specific purposes during my picture taking.  I played around with this camera since October.  As compared to my other cameras:LIKES:-Easy to use.-Decent zoom.-Uses regular batteries.  I take a lot of pictures and can easily wear out the first set of batteries.  I always bring along another set of either recharged or alkalines just in case.-Bulky.  I like the feeling of an camera that I can get a firm grip on and not hold daintily, like the pocket cam.DISLIKES:-Viewfinder.  Just my preference, but I like to look through it, I don't like looking at the screen, especially on a sunny day.  It's nearly impossible to see in bright sun.-Delay when taking multiple pictures.  I can normally take two or three consecutive shots, albeit with a delay, but the delay on this one bothers me, a lot.  Almost like it's struggling to save my previous picture.  I've tried different classes of memory cards and the result is always the same.-If you turn the camera on without taking the lens off, you get an annoying error message that the cap was left on.  Even if you try and pop that cap off right away after you've turned it on, the message still shows, even though you can see that the camera also sees something on the screen.  Too much of a delay IMO to resolve itself.-LCD has low resolution.  Not a dealbreaker, but an annoyance.-Share button is useless to me.  So is on-camera editing; I use Fuji Finepix & HP & Irfanview software for my editing preferences.-Untrue: "Intelligent capture control--automatically adjusts camera exposure, focus, and ISO for clear pictures in any environment, even in low light".Horrible results (blurry, fuzzy) in low light situations.  This has become a given with most digital cameras, in all the camera's I've tried.-Another difference from any other camera is that when I plug it into the computer, it tries to download the photos using whatever is installed on the camera.  If I want to use my Fuji Finepix software, I have to copies the photos, put them into a temporary folder, and only then can I import and save my photos using the Fuji software.  Any other camera is easily identified and files accessible in Windows Explorer; this camera is not.  Major annoyance.  I purchased an SD card reader thumb drive which makes transferring photos 100% easier. Zentral AV Remote Control arrives in a tiny box and the actual Zentral Receiver is even smaller, which is good for those of us who don't like large gadgets filling up the entertainment center. The receiver uses Bluetooth commands from the Blackberry and translates them into infrared or IR commands to control the devices.There are 3 ways to set this thing up - using the IR emitter wire, using the receiver's built in IR emitter or a combo of both methods. In order to use the built in emitter, the manual states that devices have to face the Zentral Receiver or be directly above it. The wires are good if you have an entertainment center that conceals your devices.The manual does warn that the placement of the receiver is very important if you want to use the built in emitter. However, my receiver was smack dab in FRONT of the TV and cable box, and I could not get it to work. After some hassle, I connected up the receiver with the included IR emitter wire. I don't have hidden shelves and all my devices are out in the open, so I would not be happy with this arrangement long term. The receiver pairs up with the Blackberry fairly easily, and downloading the Blackberry app was simple as well.What I found to be a real pain was setting up the AV Remote account and then setting up the Blackberry app with all the devices. Definitely have to follow the manual VERY CLOSELY here.All in all, I got the Zentral Receiver set up (with much pain) and got my Blackberry to work as a remote, but I must ask, WHAT IS THE POINT? Do people really need to use their Blackberry to control their TV and other devices? I know I don't. I need my Blackberry for other functions much more, and I'm pretty happy with using the regular remotes - turning the Blackberry into one is not worth the effort.

If you read Amazon's description, you'd think that this is a sort of organic or green non-stick cookware.  But I think it's inadvertantly misleading because as I understand it, the description for this cookware covers a number of different products in BergHoff's "EarthChef" line, some of which have non-stick coatings.  In fact, you can see the non-stick coating in the photos, but these appear to me to be regular stainless cookware and not non-stick cookware.I sent an e-mail to BergHoff over a week ago to ask where these pans are made and I also asked what the thickness of the stainless was.  To date I have not received a reply. Not good.So what's the quality of the pans like?  Frankly, I think it's just so-so.  Most of my pans are All-Clad, Calphalon or Meyer.  Generally, I think these pans are much lower quality.  Obviously, you'd expect them to be inferior to All-Clad and the like, but even if you can get it out of your head that I even mentioned All-Clad, I think these are just ok pans and pots.  Not great, not bad.The material used seems thin.  Also, I experienced more discoloration than what I was used to after only my first use.  There was also a clear sticker over the copper disc on the bottom and I didn't see this.  So it melted all over my burner and then baked on, making for a messy clean up.This cookware is "copper clad" and while it took longer to heat than I might have expected, it did retain heat well.  Not sure what make this cookware so Earthy, as they seem like regular old stainless pots and pans to me.The cookware arrived packaged well and I did not notice any warping, as did another reviewer.As of this writing, this set is a somewhere under $200 with free shipping.  So that strikes me as being a reasonable deal for someone looking for a cookware set.  So I suppose that I would generally recommend it, but you get what you pay for.  It's a decent set, but not a great one, in my view.  I'm disappointed that BergHoff doesn't promptly respond to their e-mails too.  Hopefully, my experience was the exception and not the rule.

I purchased two of these cards for use in a HD camcorder. I used Checkflash to run an exhaustive speed test on the card. I also used my built-in SD reader on my desktop and a brand new SDXC reader just to make sure that the reader was not the limitation. The speeds on both were virtually identical. The write speed is 11.28MB/s which is almost double the requirement for recording full HD video. It is above Class 10 but just barely. The read speed is 19.19MB/s. The write speed is definitely NOT 30MB/s, it is barely above the 10MB/s minimum required for a Class 10 rating. Perhaps the read speed is faster with a burst test but the sustained test was only 19MB/s.The card meets the requirements of Class 10 but I am not impressed with the 30MB/s claim. I have other Class 6 cards that are as fast in both read and write.

I left my Nikon D90 home on vacation this year and wasn't disappointed.The TG-2 Camera takes very nice pictures, even got some videos of Dolphins jumping in the surf.Are the pictures as nice as the D90? no.But here's the best part: not dealing with the hassle of wrapping the much bigger camera in  plastic bag, lugging it to the surf, sneaking it out to get a few shots and putting it back in the bag. Then keeping an eye on it to make sure it isn't in the surf.The TG2?I hung it right on the beach chair. Leaving me only having to worry about raising my cigar when a big wave came in.TIPS:- Olympus Tripod nice for taking team shots with timer- floating strap saved the camera when my daughter dropped in ocean- The zoom lens is odd but works - requires a menu setting change to use, so a pain but increases utility of camera- BATTERIES! very important - three days into vacation camera freaked out, thought it was water inside, turned out to be the el cheapo non OEM battery. When I put the Olympus battery back in no issue. I'd be leery about non-Olympus batteries and given the battery life with everything running (GPS altimeter etc.) is better than a day, not sure you'd need a second battery.- GASKETS! - the gasketing is decent (reference: I'm a mechanical engineer) - multiple ridges are effective at keeping water out IF YOU CHECK THE AREA FOR FOREIGN MATERIAL EVERY TIME YOU OPEN AND CLOSE. Even a hair caught in there would be enough to wick water in under the right circumstance.So for the over 40 crowd, get out your reading glasses and make sure there isn't any sand hair or anything else on the gasket or surface it seals against.BOTTOM LINE: Good at what it does and widely acclaimed as one of if not the best "waterproof" camera out there.

Okay so I only drink the rare hot latte, otherwise I'm all about iced coffee with milk or iced lattes -- luckily I live in a warm climate so my preference is seasonable nearly year round.  At home this means a few options -- pre-made drinks full of sweetners that I am not a fan of- cold brewing coffee myself, preferable but messy cleanup- buying packaged cold brew- instant coffee drink mixes, these tend to be full of sugar or other sweetners too- brew coffee and stick it in the fridgeThis is basically the brew coffee route.  It brews coffee same as a regular coffee maker does.  Pour in water.  Add a coffee filter with coffee.  Brew into a pitcher full of ice.  It is basically using less water and taking into account all of the ice it's brewing onto.  It does take quite a lot of ice.  I have a pretty standard ice maker in my freezer and had to use most of the ice to make two quarts (it brews one or two).The quality is fine but it will take some tweaking to get right - it obviously depends on the coffee you use.  You can adjust the brew strength.  You'll want to play with just how much coffee and ice to use, I followed their suggested on strong brew and it turned out rather weak / looked like ice tea color wise.  It's easy to use and clean.  In my opinion if you're truly an iced coffee junkie, cold brewed is nicest but that is a lot messier clean up wise.  If you want to brew traditionally and only drink iced, this is an ideal way to go as it brews fast, plots out how much water vs ice to give you chilled coffee right away leaving room for milk, syrups, sweetners right in a pitcher you can put in the fridge.  If you rotate between hot and cold coffees this machine might be a waste - just use your regular maker.

Summary:* A toy, but a usable one.* If you want a waterproof camcorder, there aren't too many choices.  And this happens to be a decent one at that.  If you're on the CHEAP side and/or want to go into deeper waters, look at the other "toy" camera from GoPro.  I also have that, by the way.  GoPro takes (slightly) better photos than this, but this takes much better videos.  Note GoPro has no LCD screen, so you're shooting almost blind.* Get a tripod, or at least a monopod, especially if you're going to zoom in a lot.* I'm not unhappy with it.The good:* Waterproof!* Excellent battery life (almost enough to fill 16GB card with 720p video).* I guess the face chaser thingy kind of works.* Umm, it's... small?  Oh oh, it turns on relatively quickly.  It's no DSLR, but it's not bad.The not-so-good:* No image stabilization.  You say it's got the "digital" image stabilization?  Whatever!  It's useless.  Hope you have steady hands or at least a monopod.* Horrible still pictures.  Its ISO50 pictures look worse than (Canon) 40D's ISO3200 pictures.  ISO1600 with this?  Is that a photo or some kind of an artistic painting?* Not so great image quality.  But then, who's expecting great HD image from a 1/6" 1280x888 (guessed) bayer-patterned sensor?  I'd actually prefer better quality 854x480 over 1280x720.  Of course, I can always scale it down after I take the video, but that takes up more room in the card.  I'd also have liked it to take 720x480 (native standard definition NTSC resolution) instead of 640x480.* Low light performance is, well, not very good.  Again, we're talking about a tiny 1/6" sensor.  The high-sensitivity mode helps a little since what it's doing is slowing the shutter down and basically giving you 15 frames per second video (or rather 30 frames where every other frame is repeated).* 30x zoom is nice, but I'd rather have wider lens.  28mm equivalent would be really nice, but that's probably asking for too much.  At minimum, 35mm equivalent would've been nice.  43mm equivalent is too, umm, normal.Other:* No comments on the software compatibility.  I mostly just use open-source stuff to play them.  Check out avidemux ([...]) for simple editing job.

Upon opening this Sound Bar audio system I was surprised to see how massive the main triple speaker is; it was about the entire length of my 50" plasma TV but it's black, sleek and thus looks the part so I plopped it in front of the television and began to set it all up. It was then I notice a rattle inside the receiver - a loud, clunky rattle that indicated that Houston has a problem!Ordinarily I would have boxed it all back up and returned it but the darn package is so big and cumbersome I felt it would be easier just to crack it open and see what was going on, plus this would give me a chance to check out the insides of the receiver itself. After removing four screws I was able to pull out the main PCB from the back of the receiver unit about 4 inches and peer inside the particle board box. It was then I saw the problem - two 2" blocks of wood with braid nails and glue just floating around inside there, so I reached in and pulled both of them out. It appeared that these two blocks were corner supports for the structure of the receiver box and had simply come off either during shipping or when sitting in a hot warehouse. Clearly whatever glue Sharp had used hadn't stood the test of time, but it didn't look like there was any damage nor did it seem to affect the integrity of the box itself so I screwed it all back and hooked everything up.The system comes with color-coded speaker wire ends making the install easy as pie and within minutes I had my cable box and blu ray hooked up and some nice sound was pouring out of the bar. I tweaked the bass and enabled the X bass and was very happy with the sound produced from both the speaker and the sub. It was also very cool that the TV and Sharp system were communicating to each other on a level I haven't seen before and when you adjust the volume of the sound bar the TV's own onscreen volume display matched the volume levels of the receiver. I've never seen that before and thought it was an excellent addition, especially given how small the little back lit display is on the receiver.Now I also have a 7.1 surround on another TV so I have something to compare with and I think it's obvious that a three speaker system at this price doesn't hold up to a dedicated set of surrounds. Having said that, what comes out of this set up is vastly superior to the built-in speakers of my (new) TV so I'd say audio-wise it sits somewhere in between on-board TV speakers and a dedicated 5.1/7.1 surround receiver.Some people don't want to run speakers and extensive wiring around behind them especially if the TV is in the bedroom and I understand that and so this system might be a perfect compromise to your set up and at the price point it's an excellent buy. Just give it a little shake before setting it up!(Oh and don't bother rummaging through the extensive packaging looking for the batteries for the remote; none are included. Shame on you Sharp)

I bought the Nikon Coolpix L10 as my first digital compact P&S; camera. I read quite a few reviews and settled on this camera. I had it for a couple of weeks, until mine had a 'lens error' that basically made the camera inoperable (it was stuck open). It might've been due to batteries running low, but I tried another set (which I now think was also low). But it would've been nice if the camera gave a hint that there wasn't enough battery charge left to extend or retract the lens instead of a generic 'lens error' msg. The LCD turned on enough to display the error msg, and then shuts off after about 7 seconds.I took close to 150 pictures with the original AA batteries that came with it. I returned the camera and decided to upgrade to a more advanced Kodak Z712 IS (7 MP 12x optical zoom & image stabilization) because I wanted to do more than just vacation snapshots once in a while. The picture quality from the L10 was very good, a bit of barrel distortion was noticed in the wide angle and shooting tall skyscrapers (noticed by the curve along the side of the frame where the buildings are supposed to be straight).Another gripe I had with the camera was how slow the auto-focus was. It would basically go through the whole range of focus every time I pressed the shutter half-way and then some. Also because it lacks a AF assit lamp, it failed to focus in dim lighting. This became more annoying the more I used it.The camera tended to keep the ISO low in the auto mode. Which meant to get enough exposure, the shutter speed had to slow down, which meant in most hand-held shots, one has to have very steady hands or the result will be blurred images. Now that I think about it, I probably would've preferred more aggressive ISO bumping because in low light situations, I'd rather get a clearer, noisy high ISO picture, instead of a low noise but blurred picture. Eventually a lot of my pictures came out blurry, including outdoor overcast days with 3x optical zoom. Basically anytime there's zoom & less than ideal lighting, I would have to have rock steady hands to get non-blurry pictures.Overall it's a good camera if you can overlook the issues I mentioned.

I know that reading headphone reviews is one of the most confusing things.  How can people love and hate the same headphones??? I will never understand.  I love music and primarily listen to hard rock, rock, pop, dance, 80s, 90s, some 70s, smooth jazz, metal, etc. (yeah I know...).  Headphones have amazing sound, there is no doubt about this.  I had trouble finding the right size tips even though there are MANY included. Also, the headphones are somewhat heavy and tend to come out of the ear due to the weight at times.  I solved this by using third party tips, which worked well for me before.  Overall, great headphones for the price.  Recommended.

Headphone cable:  Sonically, I think it is very good.  However, I also believe that wiring typically only makes slight differences in sound.  The cable looks very nice, like a long braided silver necklace covered in a thin, translucent insulation.  However, microphonics are horrible.  Any time you move and the wire hits something hard (or rubs against itself), you will hear it click.  I may have to replace the cable for that reason alone!  So, I give the wire a "nice idea, but fail" rating.  I wrapped the wire where it V's left and right (and for a few winches before that) in Teflon, which helped very slightly.Headphone case:  It's a nice, big box with ample padding.  However, I don't think the exterior is very sturdy, and it is too big for carrying on public commuter services.  There is no handle to make it easy to carry either.  I don't think I will store my headphones inside the box; I'd prefer to hang them on a headphone stand.  The box makes a wonderful item to protect the phones when double boxed, and protected by Styrofoam during shipment.  Other than that, there is little use for this box.  I would have preferred that the big purchase price had included a hard, interior padded case with a handle, which was meant for commuters (perhaps like the HiFiMAN traveler's case).  In summary, I give the box 5/5 stars for shipment protection and a "useless" rating for anything else.Earpads:  Most people agree with me that the velour pads are superior for music listening (and perhaps comfort) than the pleather.  Therefore, the velour pads should have been installed at the factory instead of the pleather.  It is nice that both kinds of pads were sent.  People can make jerg pads from them if they want.  Personally, I would have preferred some fluffier, angled velour pads.  The velour pads look like they are worth less than $10, but they do the job.  Still, this is another area where the manufacturer (and aftermarket people) could improve the product.  In summary, I give the company a "fair" rating on what they did with the pads.Comfort:  These aren't the most comfortable headphones.  They aren't terribly uncomfortable either.  Mediocre comfort is all you get.  They are heavy, unbalanced (sometimes slips on my head), headband can't be adjusted low enough, ear pads are round and don't cover my big ears well, and the clamp force is a bit much for real comfort due to the geometry of the headphones (i.e. where they press on my face makes it more of an issue).  Sennheiser does a spectacular job making comfortable headphones.  HiFiMAN should definitely take notice of how they do it.  Again, HiFiMAN only rates a "fair" here.Music:  Outstanding!!!  This is easily the best headphones musically that I have ever heard (older Stax, AKG K-701, HE-400, Etymotic ER-4P, Shure, and others)!  I love the music because no frequency range is accentuated, but everything is done well.  They have the great bass of the HE-400, but also get the midrange beautiful as well.  In the area of mids and low treble, they are clearly superior to the HE-400 in my opinion, and I need the female vocals to be perfect for vocal jazz from Diana Krall and others.  The highs are good, without being stressful.  The timing of the sounds and decay seem right too.  Ambience (staging/image) is good too.  These headphones may very well be the pinnacle of musical quality in terms of value.  I expect that you can find headphones that are marginally better, but only at a big increase in price.  HiFiMAN gets a "spectacular" rating here on the most important aspect of headphones, the music.  Go HiFiMAN!Associated equipment: Headroom Maxed Out Home Headroom amp, Musical Fidelity VDAC II with outboard power supply, J-Rivers Media Center 18, computer serving flac files from many different musical genres including some high resolution (24 bit/96 KHz) files.  (An amp more suited to these headphones is on order, but the Headroom seemed to do an acceptable job.)

I bought this to replace an older model of the same pad, which lasted about six years. The older one was the non-plush top model, but the same brand. The power supply on the older pad failed under warranty and the company promptly sent me a new power supply. After six years the connecter on the pad got very hot and stopped working. The connector on the new model has been relocated and should be somewhat less vulnerable.The thermostat is silent, lights up, and seems to regulate the pad reasonably well. While I like the low voltage concept for its safety and very thin wires, the rather large power supply emits a very high pitched whine, even when off. The whine pulsates slightly when in the on position. The sound is amplified if it sits on a hard surface. We have two of these pads and they both make the same sound. I have good hearing and sleep in a very quiet room, so I find this somewhat irritating - my wife can barely hear the sound.The plush surface makes the thin heating wires virtually undetectable, unlike the stiff wires in the full voltage pads. The plush feels similar to a fleece jacket, and it is quite warm under the sheets even with the pad off. It may be too warm for some people in milder weather. I like the plush better than our previous smooth top because it keeps the sheets from sliding around.The pad heats up fairly quickly and can get quite warm on the higher settings. It produces a very soothing heat and quickly compensates for the chill in a bedroom too far from the wood stove. This would be a five star item if not for the noisy power supply and rather high price.

The good is that it's a well built camera that takes sharp pictures and has a great feature set for its size.  I considered the Sony RX100 and this camera, the  newest pocket cameras with larger image sensors.  I chose the s100 since:-RX100 didn't really have a long term track record as it was only recently released.-Smaller size and weight of the S100, excellent image quality given its size.-Much lower cost of the S100-Lens error due to heat/humidity had been fixed in later production batches according to a recall bulletin by Canon; the camera's serial number began with 46 and was not a part of the recall-Other than the above lens error issue the camera had a good reliability record from several forumsThe bad is that I got the lens error where the lens gets stuck in the out position and fails to retract after extending and retracting while on vacation in Japan.  I'd taken a few pictures here and there, put it back in my camera bag or pocket, repeat several times for an hour or two.  After a dozen tries, the lens finally retracted but then failed to extend.Luckily, there was a Canon service center less than 20 minutes away from my hotel by foot and subway.  Long story short, since I didn't have my warranty card or proof of purchase with me on my trip other than from my Amazon account which I offered to bring up given Wifi access, they "offered" to repair it for just under 11,000 yen.  After pointing out that I'd  be returning home to the United States before the repair completion date, they responded that I could either come back and pick it up or I could arrange to have it delivered to me (what I understand is a polite way of saying owner pays delivery cost).  So let me get this straight, a camera designed and built in Japan that I bought less than a month ago fails in Japan under normal use and I would have to pay to get it repaired?  I would have purchased a new camera at a local electronics store, except that all the labels/menus were in Japanese and the only one I could figure out how to use at the store was a Canon S100.After a few days of occasionally turning the camera on and off, the camera suddenly started working again for whatever reason and the lens extended.  Unfortunately that particular time was while sitting in a stairwell while holding it wrong and the camera slipped from my hands and tumbled down a flight of concrete and steel stairs with the lens extended.  Other than scratches and dents on the body and the lens barrel, the camera took great quality shots and worked as good as new the rest of the trip.Summing up the bad experiences with the camera:-Lens error apparently not fixed-Bad service experience overseas-Should have bought an extra battery for the trip, video and GPS seem to suck up a considerable amount of battery life-HDR mode useless without a tripodI knew the technical limitations of this camera and also that batches with the lens error fix did not have an extended track record and went with this camera anyways.  I took a bet on this camera and lost (at least a few days).  In any case this camera is now working fine as far as I can tell.12/18/2013 update:Took it on a 2 week vacation, hit a lens error once when zooming and the camera shut down (retracted the lens though).  I hadn't hit a lens error again until this occurrence.  Started it up again and all was well, no further issues.  Still not sure if I can rely on this camera though...

Edit 2: the Mount came in a separate package...a week later. The seller actually quoted an estimate delivery of up to 40 days. I guess China post is all a gamble, but it should've been in one package to begin with. Not only are they saving by reducing the quality of the flashlight, but also shipping two packages. The only saving grace is the mount seems to be decent and you can actually break off the top and insert it back in to take your flashlight on and off. I wasn't expecting quick turnaround, but I have ordered many many items that shipped from China and by far this is the slowest one. If you don't mind some compromised quality and up to a month long wait for something to arrive in separate packages, go ahead and pick the cheapest option. However, I would suggest paying a couple dollars more for a fulfilled by Amazon seller or one that ships from within the US. The quality is likely to not be compromised either.Edit:I bought another one for a second bike. I could not find the original seller so picked whichever was cheapest. The prices in general from every seller have all gone down. The package came with NO MOUNT and the headlight was very different from the original one, which I still have. It's literally half the weight, feels far far cheaper, the focus mechanism is very loose, and the lens is cheap and very dirty. The light it gives off is also dingy, and weaker than the original. It's a complete knockoff of the original. Either that, or the original has been discontinued for the newer, far far crappier and cheaper model.Unless you want to play russian roulette with the dozens of chinese sellers, don't bother with this product anymore. I don't even know if the old one exists anymore, but the version I received is not worth the price or wait time, and didn't even come with a mount. Go to your nearest physical store that sells flashlights and buy a decent flashlight instead. Unscrew one of your reflectors and duct tape the light to it and stick it on your handlebars. It's not elegant, but its better than what I have now, and the light output will definitely be better.Original:For $8 you get a really nice and well built little flash light that you can mount on your bike. The build quality is high with no scuffing or blemishes, made of hard metal. The button on the back is big and very clicky and durable. You can cycle between bright, dim, and annoying blinker modes by pushing the bottom several times. I usually have it set to dim as I don't need it that bright and can save battery. You can also twist the top to focus the light more or spread it out. It goes from a funny little square shape to a large round circle that can bathe an entire street. The mount is simple to understand and all you do is screw it to loosen or tighten it. When you insert the flash light in the mount, it takes a bit of force to push it in all the way, but it keeps everything tight and secure. I keep the mount a slight bit loose so that I can easily rotate it up and down around my handlebar to shine a light on either closer or farther distances. The mount also comes with custom fitted and durable rubber spacers to increase your handlebar's girth if its too thin for the mount. You can easily unscrew and pull out the light to use as a mini flashlight on the go. It's basically a mini flashlight anyway. A really bright one.I had previously gotten a $15 combo front light and tail light from Walmart. The front light was no better than a plug-in LED night light, and made of super cheap breakable plastic and a frustrating mount that required several cheap electrical tape looking inserts instead of rubber spacers. The NowAdvisor light is 10-100x brighter and much bigger/farther/wider and far more durable and versatile.

This product cannot be stabilized as a platform for a netbook even if you are mechanically minded and able to make modifications to a device to get it to work. It would be easier to prop your netbook up on the passenger seat so the screen is visible. It would be no less distant from your driving line of sight. Issues: after bolting the gooseneck to a seat bolt as instructed and bending it so it contacts the seat for added stability, it's obvious this will be insufficient to truly stabilize the attached plate intended to support your netbook once the vehicle is in motion. The fix would be additional bracing; perhaps strapping. The hand-turn screw intended to lock the rotation of the shaft to the netbook attachment-plate is not strong enough, turned by hand, to permanently do its job. Your netbook will either rotate immediately or eventually. Fixing this would require glue strong enough to prevent rotation. I setup the 4 cams and used my tv as the monitor, had it up and running in about 30 min.  Mounting the cams and getting the view I wanted and installing the cords to where they were hidden took me 2-3 hrs.  Daylight images are pretty good quality. The cams are not waterproof and as other said over 20 ft details get fuzzy.  I have cam 1 overlooking the driveway set under the eaves above garage, cam 2 in mudroom overlooking main entrance and garage (cam1), cam 3 inside looking at back sliding glass door, cam 4 inside living room looking at main entrance. I installed the outdoor wire through a 25 ft long 3/4" diameter plastic conduit to prevent someone cutting it (use a lubed up electician's fish wire tool helps).-1/2 star for during the night mode the LEDs cause too much reflection to have the cam setup to record vid through a window even with an antiglare shield.  I recommend when you get the cam angle you like, use a bit of lock tight on the clamp screw (the temporary kind, not the permanent) I can see the clamp getting loose during natural cold and heat cycles.The settings I use are best quality recording and only on Alarm mode (movement). The motion detector is fine during the day, a bit buggy during the night mode (-1/2 star). car lights shining will activate the recording, moths and bugs also are attracted to the IR light during night mode even with the sensitivity turned down.  During the night mode also there is about a 1-2 second delay from detection to start of recording... the suggested setting is 24/7 record on low quality unless Alarm or movement mode activates a higher quality record setting, but this will eat up a lot of HD space and you end up with a lot of nothing video.I use about 1% of HD space a day on Alarm only record mode on Best quality so it will possibly record up to 100 days before rewriting, which is pretty darn good.-1 star is converting the vid (H.264 format) you want to web friendly or any computer viewable (AVI format) requires a few steps and you end up with a pretty large file (the option to convert to MP4 or other format can be done with a secondary converter, will give you a smaller file with decent quality). You can use USB thumb drive or an alternative you can have another external HD and dump your vid there, then use a PC and the provided AVI converter.  You can only convert the one cam vid at a time, so if you have 20 some events on different cam views it will take a while to convert.  Practice this step a few times just in case you need to do it for an incident where you have to submit video as evidence to police.The remote control is very cheaply made and if you have a fat thumb like me it was a bit cumbersome to use... I only use the remote because it has the easiest to find PB button (playback) compared to going through the menus manually.  I mainly use the provided mouse to navigate otherwise.If you want better night vid, there are other better quality waterproof outdoor cams available (any brand with a Sony CCD is good or Panasonic).

However, it does address some of the 730's sluggish autofocus mechanism issues for fewer blurred images.That notwithstanding, the 700 was my favorite digital camera for a long time, that is, until the 720 came along. Then along came the 730, which maintained the 3+ megapixel resolution of the 720, while reinserting the 10X (true optical) zoom (the 720 has an 8X). Think of the 740 as a refreshing of the line while Olympus was waiting for the truly improved 750 to hit the streets.In point of fact, zooming on any of the 700 series at 8X or at 10X without a tripod or image stabilization (not present on either the 700 thru the 740) is extremely challenging. Anyway, this camera is beautifully made and ergonomically engineered. The aspherical all glass lens system is excellent and the resulting 3 megapixel images are crystal clear at 8" x 10" and quite acceptable at 11" x 14". The zoom of course remains the trump card on the 740, and the smoothness (just the right damping) with which it reaches its 10x limit is awesome. Another nice feature is its ability to take QuickTime movies, which really adds to its versatility. However, these have no sound, a drawback the 750 will address.The 740 (a feature that began with the 730) is the second Olympus to utilize the new xD memory card format, the "xD-Picture Card". This is a new type of ultra-compact memory media developed jointly by Fuji and Olympus. The main features of the xD-Picture Card are its ultra-compact size (20.0 x 25.0 x 1.7mm), its lower power consumption (the xD Picture-Card users will benefit from the convenience and savings of longer battery life on a single charge) and its faster read/write speeds. Of course, a new card means a new card-reader will be needed, but these are inexpensive and aren't immediately needed, as the camera can be linked by the included USB cable to your PC without too much fuss. Overall, I think the 740 is a camera I'd take a pass on. If money is an issue, go with the 730 or even an earlier model (I still love my 700); if features are what you long for, pop for the 750.

First and foremost, this bridge works fine.  I have this in my entertainment center providing a wireless bridge for my bluray player, xbox, and vonage.  I've noticed no degredation in my speeds since reluctantly cutting the gigabit switch and cable I had running to my router (my wife didn't like a big white cable in the middle of the living room despite my qualms about speed).My biggest gripe with this device is they advertise "High speed connection (up to 300 Mbps) for fast transfer rates".  However, you will never ever see anything close to these speeds on your downstream device.  The fastest you will ever see is 100 Mbps.  And why is that?  No, it has nothing to do with theoretical vs. actual wireless N speeds.  Nope, nothing to do with contention on the 2.5GHz band.  The reason, gentle reader, is because Cisco put a 10/100 switch in the back of this box.  Thats right!  Despite a blazing fast, fancy schmancy wireless N connection, a downstream device is hamstrung by the slow wired port in this bridge.  WTF cisco?  Why not put a Gig-E switch in the back?!  This seems like an advertising slap in the face, and if the device hadn't been free (gift certificates) I would have bought something like this:TRENDnet 450Mbps Dual Band Wireless N HD Media Bridge TEW-680MBYes, I understand if I am streaming everything over the internet, I'm never going to see anywhere near 100Mbps let alone 300Mbps to see the bottleneck rear its ugly head.  But its the principle of thing.  I think I'm gonna put my cable back when my wife goes to bed.UPDATE 1.3.13As several readers have (correctly) pointed out, it would be possible to saturate the 300Mbps theoretical bandwidth with 3 (or more) downstream devices each pulling at the switch limited 100Mbps. I overlooked this use case when reading the description almost two years ago.Based off of other comments, and my own personal use of this device, one of the more likely deployment scenarios for this device is to connect a home theater. In this situation, a user would be far more likely to only need to feed one node at a time (streaming video, transferring media to a HTPC or game console, etc) and would likely hit the 100MBps limitation long before saturating 300Mbps radio link with multiple devices all pulling at 100Mbps.  If not blatently wrong, I still say the advertising is misleading and that costs you two stars.

I received my Plantronics Backbeats yesterday, which is excellent timing given mySony MDR-AS40EX Active Style Headphonesare hanging on by a thread (literally).  I should start by saying that I am hardly an audiophile, but I do demand great performance from my headphones.  Also, I put my headphones through a lot of grief so they need to be resilient.When I first plugged them in, I sampled a few pop songs on my iPhone 3G (MP3 format; quality over 256 Kbps).  Right out of the box, the bass was deep and "punchy."  The middle and high ends were weak, by comparison, but after several hours of "burn in" I expect the mix to even out a bit.  I am actually pleasantly surprised with the audio quality.  These definitely sound as good as my trusty Sony's (or maybe even better!)As for the construction of the physical headphones, at a glance they look identical to the official Apple "iTunes headphones."  But upon closer inspection, they actually look cheap and clunky. The stereo plug-in is straight (not a 90' elbow style) so it should fit the vast majority of all iPhone and iPad cases. However, For MP3 players and gym use, note that the stereo plug is reinforced with a ~ 1cm length plastic sheath which may cause the cord to stick out awkwardly off your hip/arm band.  The earbuds themselves tend to protrude conspicuously out of my ears.  This is more than likely due to the rather long silicon cone earpiece.  Either way they look a little larger in my ears than I would like.  On a similar note, the in-line microphone and pause button also has a cheap appearance compared to the official iTunes headphones.  Finally, the headphones themselves feel a little heavy in my ears.  This causes them to start falling out/annoying me while I'm running laps at the gym.Overall, for regular every day use (i.e. - around the house, walking around town, sitting on an airplane) they are very nice choice.  They are not "noise cancelling" however, they do an excellent job drowning out both ambient and loud sounds in your environment.  They definitely give you an immersive sound experience with outstanding bass and crisp highs/middle tones--a huge step up in performance from the official iTunes headphones.The major downsides: a little heavy and "clunky" in appearance.  They do protrude a bit far out of your ears making it difficult to work out in these or listen to music while lying in bed. Also, if you prefer to wear more "professional" or discrete looking headphones, these are definitely not for you.I would give these a B+ rating.  For the gym, I'm staying faithful to my Sony's but these are definitely a worthy alternative to my iTunes headphones.  I would most likely use these for travel situations.

This is a very small and lightweight laptop. It fits in my backpack, so it's easy to travel with. The battery is not removable, and lasts around the advertised time of 3-4 hours. I was able to make it last around 5 hours by turning Wi-Fi off, power-saving settings on, and decreasing the brightness of the screen. It starts up pretty fast and wakes almost instantly from sleep mode, which is convenient when working on projects.It runs Windows 8 and is equipped with a touchscreen to better take advantage of it. I use the touchscreen mainly for browsing the internet, but I've found the track-pad easier with the majority of programs I use. (Most of them are not developed or optimized for Windows 8.) The touchscreen works well with the applications that were designed to work with it, especially Google chrome and Internet Explorer. It's usually responsive, unless Windows 8 has something running in the background (it seems to like to run maintenance, or updates, when I'm trying to work, I usually just cancel, or kill the process).The track-pad works well, and software is included to allow you to use gestures to control different functions. Swiping from the corners allows you to switch from different Windows 8 applications, check the status of the computer, and access the start menu and options. You can also tap with two fingers to right click, as well as touch, hold, and drag with 2 fingers to scroll. I have found this to be really convenient and useful. My only small gripe is that it can sometimes take a while for this functionality to be activated on the track pad because it has to start up every time you use the laptop.This laptop doesn't have a CD-Rom drive, but I rarely use one anyway so it's not critical for me. It has 3 USB ports, 2 look like regular 2.0 ports, but there's a blue USB 3.0 port on the left side. It also has an audio jack, SD memory card reader, a Kensington security slot, a LAN port, and a VGA and HDMI port. It also comes with a camera, 0.9 megapixel, and microphone. They are ok, suitable for video conferencing programs like Skype, though I haven't used them much at all yet.It has enough power for web browsing and projects, but I wouldn't recommend it for any mid to high-end gaming, or graphically intensive video or photo editing programs. I have tested games like Minecraft, and Rollercoaster Tycoon 3, and they ran surprisingly well. However, I use it for basic college work, and it suits the job perfectly.I haven't found any big problems or flaws with this laptop so far, and it has been very convenient and useful alternative to my desktop computer.

I'm a bit disappointed that this device doesn't come with Audacity 2 support out of the box. It's not like Audacity is an unknown app, or not widely used. The ShuttleXpress requires the user to create their own usage map, and that's time consuming. Without knowing the device as well as I will in, say, a month of use, I'm just taking stabs at what will and won't work with it.Having said that, it works nicely once it's set up, and it comes with dozens of other programs that are already part of the driver package, Adobe Photoshop being one. My use, however, was to combine this device with my recordings on Audacity that I do for Librivox DOT org. I wanted it to emulate a jog wheel that is part of a dedicated video or audio editor so that I can advance or back up to a specific point and then mark it. The Xpress is limited to the keyboard shortcuts that are available in Audacity, as it is with any other program. If something can't be done via the keyboard, then you won't be able to do it via the ShuttleXpress either. Therefore, if you're looking to provide the functionality of a dedicated editing system, the ShuttleXpress is not going to work. In addition, this is not meant to supplant a mouse or trackpad, it's designed to work in conjunction with it. That gets back to the statement that the ShuttleXpress will only work with existing keyboard shortcuts. Anything else you'll need to do manually.I do think that once I get accustomed to using it, and have it programmed, that it will be a big help in my recording and editing chores. Unfortunately, as stated above, the lack of Audacity 2 support out of the box is very disappointing. I simply can't be the only person using this device for this purpose. Unfortunately, both the Audacity and Contour forums aren't of much help in finding a driver map that can be imported or adopted, so if that's your software, be aware that you'll have to create it on your own. Ditto for any other software that isn't supported out of the box by Contour.Lastly, for Mac users, if you're upgrading to Mountain Lion, you'll need to download an updated driver from the Contour website. Save yourself some aggravation of having to uninstall the one that comes with the device (a suggested requirement by the manufacturer for the updated driver), and download it first, then proceed with your software installation.All in all, a pretty capable device that would, in my case, have had much more utility with an existing Audacity map.

Hopefully, at some point, Apple will incorporate a much better battery and wireless charging into the iPhone, but until they do, the Duracell Powermat PowerSnap Kit will have to suffice, as it is currently your best option for an iPhone case with a snap-on battery pack. The case itself is quite insubstantial and seems very flimsy, but again, if you want a case with backup battery capability and/or wireless charging, this is still your best bet.The kit consists of two pieces, which are a snap-on case and a removable snap-on battery . The snap-on case is a thin and light plastic frame that adds the wireless charging capability. The snap-on battery pack attaches to the case for on-the-go power.The battery slides and snaps into place on the back of the case, holding itself in place with one tab at the top and two and the bottom. With the battery attached to the case, the case feels far sturdier, but also a lot bulkier. On the back of the battery are four LED indicators and a power button to control the flow of juice from the battery to the iPhone. Also on the battery is a spring-loaded door that covers a micro USB port for charging both the battery and iPhone when connected.You can charge the iPhone and the snap-on battery together or separately. To charge you simply place the battery and/or the case-clad iPhone on a Duracell Powermat (sold separately). Once the battery or iPhone is placed on the Powermat correctly, a chime confirms charging.I found that my iPhone alone gives me about 8 hours of talk time, and this kit adds approximately 5 hours to that, for a total of about 13 hours. If you can get by on your iPhone's included battery power/talk time, I do not recommend this kit due to the fact that there are MUCH better regular cases available. But if you do need the added talk time, I DO recommend this case as currently there isn't a better option, and the wireless charging is pretty darn cool.

I bought this to replace the battery in my MacBook Pro Late 2011. I thought it was the battery doing it. After a little research I found it's a bug in how OS X handles new ACPI profiles. Since the new battery changed the ACPI profile, the laptop couldn't handle it. Use this information at your own risk or get a knowledgeable friend to do it.

This headset has a lot of pluses, but connection issues have reduced it to 4 stars.Pluses:I have connected it to a number of devices including my two Apple iPads, a Microsoft Surface, Nexus 7, Galaxy Note 8.0, and my Dell 2720 all-in-one. It has connected to all of them without any problems. The problem that I have with the headphones is that you can connect this device to only one unit at a time. This wouldn't be a problem, except that you have to disconnect from each device before you can connect to another. This won't be a problem if you plan to connect to only once device. The other problem that I had was that the software you can download from Logitech for connection works fine on my desktop, but it doesn't work on the Surface Pro. It doesn't make the software available for use on the Surface Pro. Other than these complaints, the headset is really very good.Pros:- The sound quality is excellent depending on the input. For ITunes, the sound at maximum is just at a comfortable level, but it can't be cranked up. For internet and other applications, the sound level can be cranked up to a level that would be uncomfortable for most. If the input provides stereo, this can definitely be heard with this headset. The separation is very good. At least for my hearing, which is pretty good, the quality of bass, midtones, etc. are very good.- Bluetooth connection in my house is about 20 feet, but I have a lot of walls. This is fine for me because I don't plan to travel a lot when I use them.- Can be use with Bluetooth or connected to USB. This is a plus because they can be used while they are charging. The charging cable is a standard mini USB that is commonly used for cell phones and other devices. This is convenient because you don't need to carry multiple cables.- Controls on headset are convenient for accepting cell phone calls and for adjusting volume. There are raised notches that make them ease to feel without taking off the headphones to see the controls.Cons:- The headphones need to be connected each time you use it on a different device, and in some cases the stored configuration of the headphones have to be deleted and refound for each use. Previously used devices must be disconnected be for a different device can be used.-Signal distance is not a good as advertised.All in all, I would recommend these headphones. They are very comfortable, and can be worn for a period of time without discomfort. The controls are easy to locate, and convenient. They can be used with Bluetooth or USB. The sound quality is very good and stereo separation is excellent. The Bluetooth dongle can be stored in the headset if it is not needed. I plan to use this headset primarily for my desktop computer. So connectivity with other devices is not a major issue for me. When I turn them on, they are immediately connected. I think they are so much more convenient than a wire headset.Update: 9/9/13I have since bought the Bluedio R Bluetooth headset to compare to this one. The Logitech H800 is fine for normal computer or phone use, but it's not the greatest for listening to music. and even videos containing voice have a raspy sound to them. I have reduce the stars from 4 to 3 because of the poor sound quality for listening to music or even video audio. The Logitech H800 is much easier to turn off and on using a simple toggle switch, whereas the Bluedio requires holding the MF button for a period of seconds to shut it of. For me, this is not really a big deal. The Bluedio headset has much better and fuller sound, and also has the option of using a microSD card to listen to music. The biggest downside of the Bluedio vs. the Logitech H800 is that the H800 can be used when it is charging by USB. The Bluedio cannot be used when it is charging. This means that you have to make sure that it is charged before you plan to use it. A full charge takes 3 hours. For me, this is really an inconvenience. Headsets of this kind always seem to lose the charge when you want to use them. So, although I prefer the Bluedio headset for the sound quality, I may keep the Logitech H800 as a backup in case I need a headset and the Bluedio charge runs out. I also have one of the expensive Bose headsets that I never use for just this reason. Every time I wanted to use it, it needed to be charged. If the Bluedio headset could be use while charging, this would be almost my ultimate headset.

For a number of years I have had a love-hate relationship with shampoo and cream rinse - mostly hate.  I've become so allergic to something that is in most of these products that until recently I haven't been able to use cream rinse in a decade or so and had stopped shampooing my hair in favor of baking soda and cider vinegar.  Anything else made my head itch so badly that I've been known to scratch it bloody and every time I "shampooed" I would have to vacuum the floor because of the resulting blizzard. Meanwhile, my hair was so dry that I could have gone a month without shampooing it. Talk about a mess!Then awhile back I was offered some Clear Anti-dandruff shampoo and cream rinse and that has changed my life. The itching is gone, the flaking is gone, my hair is not dry as a bone and recently I've been able to switch between the Clear and an all-natural shampoo with good results.  Sadly it never dawned on me that the "Naturals" inSuave Naturals Rainforest Fresh Shampoo, 22.5 OunceandSuave Naturals Rainforest Fresh Conditioner, 22.5 Ouncedoes not mean that it is, in fact, an all-natural shampoo or even a mostly natural one.  As the bright green color indicates (that is not the color of the bottle!), among other ingredients, these products contain artificial colors.At any rate, I did try both theSuave Naturals Rainforest Fresh Shampoo, 22.5 Ounceand theSuave Naturals Rainforest Fresh Conditioner, 22.5 Ounce.  While I didn't particularly like the smell, it was not overpowering.  Very little shampoo or cream rinse was required for a great head of suds - a spot the size of a dime was more than adequate even for my very long, still thick hair.  These are large family sized bottles, but they are relatively easy to grip even with wet hands.The products left my hair nice and shiny, though it was nowhere near as easy to comb out as the Clear leaves it, and even my baby-fine hair is not terribly fly-away. Sadly, before my hair was even dry my head began to itch - and Itch - and ITCH.  At first I considered trying the products separately to see if I could determine which was the problem, but sensibility won the day over scientific inquiry.Grandma's $0.02 - While thisSuave Naturals Rainforest Fresh Conditioner, 22.5 Ouncemay work well if you do not have the chemical sensitivity problems that I have, this is definitely not for me.  I'll stick to the products that I know don't bother me.

The Munitio Nines are well-built earphones, but their muddy sound doesn't remotely live up to their price.The Nines are designed to look like bullets and are marketed in weird, macho poor taste ("tactical" earphones? seriously?), but the gamer marketing may be deceptive: the build quality is first-rate.  Both the surprisingly heavy machined metal earphones and their sturdy, fabric-covered cords feel great in the hand.  The packaging and presentation are nice if bare-bones, including a military-chic fabric case, extra tips, and earhooks (which I found the earphones actually fit better without).  Everything but the sound, that is, fits the price point well.But the sound is a deal-breaker.  The Nines feature an insanely overboosted bass -- which sounds okay by itself, if only for hip-hop and dance music; anything else, at first blush, sounds like a car stereo with the bass turned up to 11 (and the treble also mildly boosted to try to compensate, leaving the midrange way too low).  In this way they reminded me of theAtrio MG7s, another dynamic-driver headphone with a deliberately heavy bass sound, designed for the "Beats" demographic.  But it's not just the bass-heaviness that makes the sound so poor: the Nines' worst quality is their muddy, undefined midrange response.  Between the overboosted bass and the Nines' overall muddy/sloppy response, entire instruments disappear into the mid-tone valley -- a rock guitar vanishes behind the bass line, or a jazz band somehow loses any trace of its piano, or the drummer's cymbals, falling imperceptibly behind the upright bass and the brass section.  I compared the Nines directly against several Ultimate Ears models -- my old favoriteSuperFi 5 Prosand the new top-lineUE 900s-- and the difference in definition, clarity, and beauty was simply night and day.  The Ultimate Ears made my music sound new again; the Nines made me wonder why I ever enjoyed listening to it before.While the Nines are not terrible earphones, especially considering the build quality, they're still very bad compared to their competition at this high a price.  Far superior sound is offered, albeit in a less gimmicky and lighter-weight package, by Ultimate Ears,Klipsch, and many other competitors.  I'd recommend listening carefully to these before even considering buying them.

If you have heard of Tenqa, raise your hands.  That's what I thought.  After some Google searches, I found that they are most likely based in Arizona and sell their 3 Bluetooth products almost exclusively through Amazon.com.  Not a bad retailer to partner with.  When I got the chance to try the SP-109 Bluetooth Stereo Speaker, I thought it would be fun to see how my first Bluetooth speaker would do.  And how'd they do?PROS:- It works- Sounds much better than expected- Attractive and compact design- Auxiliary line-inCONS:- Distortion at high volume- No battery-operated option- Port locations less than ideal- No instructions on connecting to a Windows or Mac machineThe unboxing was rather uneventful as there was only the speaker, a 3.5mm audio cable,  AC adapter, and brief paper manual.  It took me longer to unbox it than to pair it with my Motorola Droid smart phone.  After turning the SP-109 on, you notice the blue light in the lower right corner blinking, which means it is waiting to be paired.  I set my Droid to search for devices and it was quickly found and paired.SOUND QUALITY & PERFORMANCEI had very low expectations but was rather impressed with the sound.  The highs were quite good and mids ok.  Bass was poor, but acceptable for light duty and small rooms.  There was noticeable distortion at high volumes.  The Bluetooth connection was quite solid and I was able to walk quite a distance away from the speaker and maintain a static-free connection.  The stubby antenna probably helped quite a bit.DESIGNI found the aesthetics be quite pleasing but Tenqa's decision to place all the control ports on the right side of the speaker is puzzling.  The power switch, volume dial, AC power and auxiliary in ports are all on the right side.  This made an otherwise attractive wireless speaker look messy with exposed cables.  If you look at the 5th photo with the woman on her laptop with the SP-109 beside her, it is cropped to hide the AC power cable.  Why couldn't they have put the AC power and line-in connections in the rear, like most other portable speakers?  I also found the power switch and volume dial to be unergonomic and flimsy.  I would have preferred the volume dial to be located on top of the speaker for easier access and the power switch to be an actual button.COMPUTER PAIRINGI spent a total of about an hour trying to get it to work with my laptop and Windows 7 64-bit.  I even updated my driver to a non-approved Bluetooth driver just to try and get it to pair with the SP-109.  I finally got it to connect after rebooting my computer and trying over.  I selected Add New Device then paired it with the code, "0000".  I then had to select the SP-109, which shows up as a headset and "Control it" which brought up an option for me to connect to it.  You know you're connected when the blue light stops flashing.  Still, I got no sound when I played an MP3.  What I had to do was go into Windows Sound Options and change the default speaker to be the SP-109.  Cue angels singing; I got sound!  The bummer is that when you disconnect, you have to reconnect again manually.  No autopairing.MISCTenqa also sells aportable Bluetooth speakerthat can be battery-powered.  The SP-109 is not that big and could have benefited immensely from being powered by batteries too.  This would have allowed me to place it on ANY bookshelf or location but as is, my wireless speaker is tethered to an electrical outlet.SUMMARYFor the listed MSRP, the Tenqa SP-109 speaker is a rather expensive option.  However, since the actual selling price is significantly lower than MSRP, the Tenqa SP-109 is a reasonably good choice for those who don't mind plugging it into a wall in order to get better sound than the really small Bluetooth speakers.  If not for the odd port placements and lack of battery operation, I would have given the SP-109 at least 4 stars.

The Zagg invisible shield is probably the toughest screen film available for ipod touches and iphones, and other devices with large LCD displays.  It is difficult if not impossible to puncture.  But there are other reasons why I recommend you look elsewhere.My wife and I each have a second generation ipod touch with Crystal Film (a competing product from a company called Power Support - Amazon sells it and Apple stores sell or used to sell it).  I bought a new third generation ipod touch and bought a Zagg invisible shield from Best Buy and paid extra for installation.  In my review, I compare the Zagg shield to the Crystal Film and to having nothing at all on the ipod touch display.The biggest problem with the Zagg film, for me, is clarity.  The Crystal Film literally disappears - the only way you can tell it's on is that the edges of the film are visible (but don't really stand out because they line up with the edges of the ipod touch display very well).  The Zagg film, on the other hand, is easily visible, whether the device is on or off.  More importantly, the Zagg film degrades the quality of still images and video, while the Crystal Film does not.  The difference is not HUGE.  With the Zagg film, you will still enjoy showing off your photos to your friends, and watching you-tube or downloaded videos.  But there IS a difference, and to me, once you see what video looks like with Crystal Film (or with nothing at all), the slight loss of clarity from the Zagg film is just not acceptable.  After all, a big part of why we spend so much for an ipod touch is because of its beautiful display.The second problem I have with Zagg is more subjective.  To me, the film feels gummy, slightly sticky.  When it comes to how your finger feels sliding across the screen, I think the Crystal Film is best, followed by a naked ipod touch display, followed by the Zagg shield in last place.  But this is subjective and some people like the thicker, gummier feel of the Zagg film.The last problem I had with Zagg, which apparently some of you have not had, concerns the installation.  I paid for professional installation at Best Buy, and the lady who installed it assured me that she had installed Zagg film for many dozens of customers and would do a good job on my device.  10 minutes later, my new ipod touch had a zagg shield with bubbles and a slight crease.  She said this is normal and would resolve in 24-48 hours.  Fine.  After one week, some bubbles had gone but there were still flaws in the installation that were simply not going away.I took my two ipod touches to Best Buy so they could see the difference; they agreed that the Zagg was inferior and kindly refunded my money, including the money I paid for the installation.  I then ordered Crystal Film and installed it on my new touch and have been much happier.As I said, the Zagg is the most puncture-resistant film.  I'm not even sure a bullet would pierce it.  However, if you put it on your ipod touch and shot a bullet at the screen, you'd surely destroy the display, even if the Zagg wasn't punctured.  My point is that puncture-resistant is not the protection you want, since the screen could be broken without puncturing the film.  What you want is protection from scratches and light dings, and you will get that from almost any film.  I'd go further and say that puncture resistance is not only unnecessary but undesirable, because making a film puncture-resistant requires making it thicker, which starts to impede the clarity of the film.I see there are many reviews here from happy Zagg customers.  Maybe Zagg would work better for you than it worked for me.  But I think you're probably better off with Crystal Film, which you can find here on Amazon.Powersupport TU301LL/A Crystal Film for iPod Touch 2G

There was a little girl who had a little curlRight in the middle of her forehead;When she was good, she was very, very good,And when she was bad she was horrid.Rating is based the average of 4 when when it works, and 0 when it doesn't, with another star deducted for warranty service.WHEN IT WORKS, this is the best mouse I've ever used, but it is far from perfect.What I like:It's cordless, it has 5 buttons, it has a laser, a nano receiver, and it has hyper-scrolling, the best innovation in mousing in a long time.What I don't like:It's best for small hands, which mine aren't. The Setpoint software is dodgy and often crashes (but doesn't crash the system). The forward/back buttons could be better placed; they require awkward finger contortions use. Buttons are backwards: depress the scroll wheel to alternate between ratcheting and free-wheeling scrolling; there's a programmable button in back of the wheel that takes the place of the usual scroll wheel middle click function. The scroll wheel should have retained the middle click function, the the other button used for turning the hyper-scrolling on and off.WHEN IT DOESN'T WORKAfter 2 years of use, the hyper-scrolling wasn't as free wheeling as it was when it was new, but I could live with that. What I couldn't live with is that a single left click started double clicking. After Googling, I found that this is a common issue, and usually starts happening before 2 years.  What's galling is that Logitech appears to have only a non-toll-free phone number for warranty service, with most people reporting extensive wait times. I finally did find a way to request warranty service online, and they sent me an email saying I should hear within 48 hours. It's been more than a week now, and I've heard nothing.I bought a second mouse, and out of the box all of the buttons worked properly, but the scroll wheel didn't. After hyper-scrolling, stopping the wheel stopped the scrolling, but after taking my finger off the wheel, it would jump an additional few lines, and sometimes as much as a half-page. This too, is a known problem. It went back to Amazon.My (long-discontinued) Microsoft Intellimouse Optical is still great ergonomically; make it wireless, give it a laser and hyper-scrolling, and it would be close to my idea of the ideal mouse.What I consider deal-breakers (scrolling up or down a few extra lines and double clicking) others take as "normal" (at least eventually) and give the Anywhere MX 4 stars! This is NOT normal and is unacceptable even in a $10 mouse.When the Anywhere MX is good it's very, very good, but when it's bad it's horrid, as is warranty service.=====UPDATE Feb. 3, 2013Logitech did send me a new mouse. In the last of their 4 emails, they requested info I attached to the first email.The new mouse is OK, but not as good as my original mouse when it was new. Sometimes the left button doesn't seem to register, and I have to click a second time. The scroll wheel is acceptable, but does not seem as precise as my original. Setpoint 6.51 software was always crashing on my XP machine; I went back to v 6.32 and problem solved.Most reviews from new users are going to be 4 or 5 stars because they haven't used it for very long. Scrolling up or down a few extra lines and double clicking are inevitable, and usually don't show up from 6 months to 2 years. At least that's within the warranty period. Those that just give up and buy a new mouse shouldn't: That can cost you $20+ a year for a mouse. Use the warranty service.Wouldn't it be nice if Logitec could fix their software, fix their quality control, and could fix these 2 known problems?All things considered, I change my rating to 3 stars.

I expected great results from the Wahl Healthy Infusions Pro Straightener. The blue-glow of the LCD screen said, "high-tech" ... which I associated with "superior product." Unfortunately, I found the straightener awkward and ineffective.I have medium thickness, long (mid-back) hair. Since it is wavy, I either play-up the waves or straighten them (depending on my mood). I usually use theT3 Tourmaline Straightenerbecause it is highly recommended by stylists for its protective properties. And though a serious investment, it was worth every cent. I picked up this Wahl straightener for travel purposes and gave it a test run before packing it away in my luggage. The results were, unfortunately, disappointing.The product itself was a little cumbersome ... with the comb attachment adding extra thickness and heft. Worse still, the comb attachment pulled my hair (though I had thoroughly brushed it before I even began). When I finished straightening, hair was stuck in the comb area and in the seams of the straightener ... hair that had been pulled out. Since I aspire to a pin-straight look (which is why I straighten rarely), I took my time with the Wahl ... but it simply could not manage the job. The unwieldiness of the instrument made it difficult to get close to the roots. Overall, most of my hair was "kind of straight" except for the root area which was still a little unkempt.The conditioning strip is an odd add-on. It gave my hair more weight than I care for. Moreover, I question how for how long these strips will be available ... a year? Then what? Even still, I wish that the ingredients were more environmentally-friendly/healthy for hair.Finally, the Wahl does not come with a protective bag/travel bag (unlike similar brands) ... so take that into consideration when purchasing (you may want to put a protective bag in your cart).The Wahl straightener did not fulfill my personal needs. Maybe I'm just spoiled by my T3, but my vote is that since you are already paying a hefty price for this product why not invest a little more and get the T3 or a similar high-end, healthy-hair straightener.

The Nike+ concept represents a great idea for walkers and runners and others who exercise to musical rhythms and want the cool features of Nike+, but what a shame the product and/or its companion software is a bit failure prone! I'm on my 3rd sensor and hoping this one performs much better than the first two.The first sensor was dead on arrival, the second died after two walks, and the third did not work until I power-cycled my iPod Touch (4th gen). There are two functional units to the Nike+ system: The sensor/transmitter and the receiver/processing software. It occurred to me that maybe the problem might be in the receiver/processing side. So when my iPod did not pick up the sensor/transmitter signal today, I power-cycled the iPod and the sensor was picked up promptly after I took a few steps!  I was beginning to think the Nike+ sensors might be missing some QC at the factory across the Pacific, but now I am convinced the problem might just as well be in the receiver/processing software side! Not sure yet but working on isolating the problem so I know whether to take back #3.Design wise the device has issues like these:-- no positive feedback so you don't know what's going on,-- no indicator function in the iPod side of Nike+ to let you know if the sensor has fallen off your shoe - no alarm or indication in the first 100 feet or so anyway,-- no way to recharge or replace the battery,-- no indication whether the sensor is in awake mode or sleep mode, etc.But again, the concept is strong if only Nike can improve the design and make it work much longer!

This wasn't a huge problem, but it did require that I purchase a wireless extender for another area of the house. It was something that needed to be done anyway, as my family's use of wireless devices has expanded, and the router needed to be in the same area where those devices are most often used. I used the extender cord on the Chromecast because my TV has the HDMI ports in an awkward place. I also use the AC adapter for power.
