So I got this RT N-53 router becuase 1) I like ASUS products, generally and 2) I wanted to be able to share WIFI with my neighbors, securely.  I paid a premium price for what has so far been a frustrating product.So far, I have been disapointed because the major selling point of this router is the ability to create separate "GUEST" SSIDs on the 2.4 Ghz band.  This is true,  but the problem is that those guest SSIDS are only separate from other 2.4 ghz band SSIDs, NOT from the 5ghz band.  Asus offers no phone technical support, as far as I can tell, and their online support forum registration process did not work for me. (also, their support forum search feature does not work, so there is no easy way to see if someone else has solved this problem) In my opinion, poor access to technical support is a major flaw, one that will impact future purchases.Here is my setup, using the latest (as of feb 2012) 1.1.1.40 firmwareI have set up 3 wireless Networks on my RTN53:A  2.4 Ghz SSID:  "HOME 2.4" networkA  5 Ghz  SSID:  "HOME 5" networkA guest 2.4Ghz SSID: "GUEST" networkAll are set up with wpa auto encryption, and the "GUEST" ssid  is set to have internet but not LAN access.  All devices can access the internet without problems."GUEST" connected devices are prevented from accessing devices on "HOME 2.4".  This is as it should be. The Problem is that "GUEST" devices are able to access all devices on the "HOME 5" network.  They can ping, can see my shares, and can download music from devices on the "HOME 5" 5ghz network, even though they are supposed to just have *internet* access.Obviously this is a major security hole. Now I have to choose between using an INSECURE, but fast 5ghz connection, or a slower but less vulnerable 2.4 connection.To summarize: when the major selling point of the device is secure VLANs on multiple SSIDs,  it is absurd that this problem exists.

If you understand archery at all, you know the arrow has to flex around the bow's riser to shoot straight.  If an arrow is too stiff for the amount of energy the string puts into the nock-end, it will fly off with the arrow yawed at an angle away from side of the bow from which it was shot.  If it's too flexible, the bow string's force will warp the arrow around the riser too much and the arrow will fly away yawed toward the side of the bow from which it was shot.The arrows stiffness must match the bow's force.  The bow's force is determined by the limbs, and how far the string is being drawn.  Youth bows usually have less force in the limbs, and the draw lengths from youth archers are usually short too, which means relatively little force is put into the nock end of the arrow.  Therefore the arrow should be relatively flexible to shoot well.An arrow's stiffness is determined by it's "spine" characteristics, it's length, and any weight in the point, the inertia of which helps to flex the arrow shaft upon release.  These arrows at 24" are short -- and the shorter the stiffer.  You'd have to shoot a really powerful bow to flex these short shafts enough.  Yet a lot of buyers will think to get the short arrows for the smallest archer's and their bows.  The arrows also have very light weight sheet metal points.  They should have heavier metal points to help flex the shaft for bows of low draw weight and archers with short draw lengths.These fiberglass arrows are no where near as flexible as 1/4" or 5/16" cedar arrows of the same length.  Get those instead.  If you do by these fiberglass ones, at least get the more flexible 30" version and do a bareshaft test.  You can cut them down based on your test results using heavier points.

This speed loader works just fine.  Many of the low ratings are people who have grip interference.  If your grip sticks out where the cylinder is when open, any speed loader is going to catch on it, that's just how it is.  You either need to trim/change your grips, or accept speed loaders won't be ideal for you.This worked fine with my SP101, though the grip does prevent it from seating fully.  But just turn the knob and the rounds will all drop in fine.It also works, or at least can be used, with my LCR.  It will not fit all the way in, but you can nose the rounds in, turn the knob, and they drop in fine.  You do have to be careful not to push them too far or it will bind.  It isn't ideal, but HKS does not state or claim that this speed loader will work with the LCR.  And if you look at an LCR and an SP101, the cylinders are not the same size.  So it's not that surprising that it binds on an LCR.I initially had a bit of trouble with one of the slots.  The "catch" wouldn't swing out to lock when a round was in place.  I pushed the cartridge lip into the loader a bit, while pushing the knob in at the same time, and it locked over it.  I haven't had any subsequent issue loading it.  And you don't fill a speed loader in a critical situation, you empty it.  So I'm not too concerned.  But that's why it is only 4 stars.

After an exhaustive search to determine what burr grinder I should buy for my new espresso machine I settled on the Capresso 560. While reviews on every site were mixed, I decided that given the price and the number of positive reviews it was a safe bet -- I was WRONG! The product is much worse than I anticipated, and left me wondering how sooo many people could give this product a 5 or even a 4 or 3 rating. My experience left me in wonderment regarding the amount of ground beans left in the machine.  Numerous people complain about the "static" problem, but honestly this is only part of the problem.Before I go further, let me state for the record that the only reason I wanted to buy a burr grinder was that I want daily properly fresh ground espresso beans. The key word here is: FRESH. For anyone who is a coffee connoisseur, you know that the minute that air comes in contact with a ground bean the flavor begins to change - the longer the amount of time the less "fresh" the taste. Ergo, when one uses a grinder the vast majority of the ground beans needs to end up in the container or doser, and then should be used shortly thereafter. This is where the Capresso has problems; after grinding there is so much left in the body of the grinder that it ends up taking me 15 - 20 minutes to clean it out (this versus the less than 2 minutes to grind the beans).  I have several friends who have higher quality grinders that I have used (one of my favorites is the Rancilio Rocky, but at $325 I bought the Capresso to save money).  In hindsight and based on personal experience, the Rancillio is the better bargain.My only recommendation regarding the Capresso is buy it if you want or do not mind the following:1. An inexpensive grinder that does a good job grinding and operates fairly quietly2. Having the majority of your daily ground beans be stale given that most of what ends up in the container is from the previous grind (the ONLY way to avoid this is to spend 10 times as much time cleaning the grinder after every use as is spent actually grinding the beans)!My conclusion: spend a lot more money to buy a top quality product (such as the Rancilio grinder) or spend a lot more time cleaning your grinder than you do grinding your beans, making your drink, and drinking your beverage.

I couldn't mount this unit in my car. I don't have a small dash vehicle, I'm driving a G8GT so I have plenty of room on my dash and below. The problem wasn't finding a place that didn't block my visibility, the problem was that whenever I hit a pothole the Magellan 1700 fell down. I tried both of the mounting brackets provided, but the unit is simply too heavy for the support systems provided. I handed it to my passenger and they directed me. Driving alone, that would make the RoadMate 1700 useless. With a passenger, I found that it oriented itself quickly and responded fairly well to changes in my trip. It did take about six miles before the unit accepted the first freeway it directed me to was blocked and allowed me to take another. I can't say if it has a feature to skip part of a route or recalculate because I couldn't view the screen while driving and the short battery life didn't permit me to learn all the features out of the vehicle. Choosing 'shortest route' was a problem. I tested the unit on some longer drives I know very well between Orlando and Miami. In Broward, heading to Broward Blvd on the turnpike, the unit wanted me to exit the freeway at MLK/Coconut Creek Parkway and travel on local streets. This route would have added at least half an hour of city travel and taken me through several neighborhoods I'd rather not break down in. Instead, I stayed on the freeway and the unit adjusted within one exit to the route I normally take. However, all the routes it directed me toward in the other counties matched the routes I would normally take. The lack of Mac support is a problem as well.On the positive side, the interface is very intuitive. The AAA tour information was useful and helped me find the gas station brand I wanted easily. It was accurate in all the cities I traveled in. The feature that removes letters you won't need for an address made typing things in quicker and less likely to be prone to spelling error. My passenger had no trouble at all directing me from the lane change options on the screen and the computerized voice is pleasant enough, not jarring like some units. I am going to take this on an upcoming trip from San Jose to Benecia, as I will have someone with me to read the directions and I will appreciate having information from the unit as a backup. The inability to mount this securely renders the unit unusable for me but if you routinely travel with a 'copilot' and  can leave it plugged into the charger this unit could be very useful. The screen is clear and responsive to touch, the letters are very easy to read. (Be sure you will be using it with a Windows PC for updates!)UPDATE: After taking this on a few more local street trips, I have to reduce down to two stars. On one trip the system under 'fastest route' tried to redirect me from a highway heading toward my destination to a toll road heading away from it. Later, it insisted I needed to u-turn on a the same road my destination was on, go to a different road, take a series of turns and rejoin the road I was ALREADY ON a half mile down the way. I didn't u-turn and it was quite some time before the unit recalculated to accept that I was not leaving the road I was on (known to me to be the quickest route and where the place was). My next destination programmed led to me unplugging the unit. It was not helpful in the Port St Lucie area at all. I will still try it in California, where I don't know as many of the routes well, but I'm taking maps as a back up.UPDATE: Used the unit between Benecia and San Jose - for highway driving it was great. Clear, easy to follow, grabbed signal quickly. Still required my passenger to hold it, however. In the city, (specifically San Francisco) it was just about useless. Four times it completely froze up on me, telling me to exit the bridge long after I was deep in the financial district or not realizing I had left Golden Gate Park and was over at Cliff House. I had to reboot it twice in one hour as it become unresponsive. Outside of the city, it was back to working well.UPDATE: After almost one year of very light use (perhaps a dozen) I'm tossing this unit out. I kept it in a protective case in my glove box with nothing touching it. The touch screen has become very finicky, the sound no longer works, and the unit likes to randomly reset itself from 2D to 3D. Useless. Taking it from 2 stars to 1 because I realized every time I try to use this unit I get annoyed by it.

I'm glad because now I can tell people the ups and the downs (no pun intended), and how to minimize the downs. First and foremost the Push Up Pump is intended to help people who can't do any push ups at all, and secondly for people who would like to get multiple sets in.  I fall into the latter category. The three different hand positions will determine the amount of push ups you will be able to do because of the different muscle groups involved. I find the inner handles to be the most difficult. The item comes partially unassembled, but it is relatively easy to set up. What initially threw me off is that the product is somewhat smaller than it appears to be on television.  I bought mine directly from their website, an experience that was very strange. I placed the order and at first got no confirmation. Five weeks later I received an e-mail confirming my order was on the way. Two weeks after that the item finally arrived. What I hated was the fact it came with no concealment as to what the product is. There it was on my doorstep sitting there till I went out to check my mail, as if it was shouting to the neighbors "HEY LOOK! CHUBBY BOY IS GOING TO TRY TO GET IN SHAPE WITH A CRAZY GADGET! I'm sure the FedEx people were snickering through the whole process. All that aside let's get back to the safe and proper usage of the pump. Finding the perfect area for your chest for maximum comfort will take a little trial and error, but once you've done that your push ups will become very comfortable. The more comfortable you are the more reps you will be able to do. I recommend placing a non skid rubber mat under the pump. When setting yourself up to the machine crawl your knees up close to the pump grab the selected handles then extend your legs behind you. Always crawl your knees up to the Push Up Pump before grabbing the handles. You must also crawl up to the pump when you are finished before standing up. Failing to do so will result in the pump falling forward and you hitting your face on the floor. The claims that the Push Up Pump is a full body workout is true, but it works the lower half of your body to a lesser degree than the upper body. You only begin to feel your legs being worked when you learn to do a lot of reps. For me it was about 30 reps before my legs began to feel engaged. I also suggest not attaching the resistance cords to the unit at first for a few days just so you can get a feel for the use. What annoys me a little though is the way the cords that are not being used get a little snagged when pushing yourself upward. The one final thing I want to say is that you must also learn to do unassisted push ups. Only unassisted push ups will force your muscles to firm up, strengthen and potentially grow, but the Push Up Pump will help many people achieve that. The Push Up Pump AND unassisted push ups is the goal to strive for.

Some information to start with; 4K resolution is 4096 x 2160, Ultra HD or Consumer 4K resolution is 3840 x 2160 (8.3 megapixels).If you look at all of the TV brands and what type of 4K they are, most if not all say Ultra HD or something similar, which is only 3840 x 2160, not 4096 x 2160.Eventually all of the manufacturers will have true 4K. But at this time 4K is just Ultra HD and they are using a native 3840 x 2160 LCD screen, which is the reason for the high cost, as it is much harder to make these LCD screens. They are still doing some upscaling as some of them say they have 24 million sub-pixels (See native mega pixels above).Sharp is using a 1920x1080 (2.1 megapixels) LCD screen, which is the reason for the lower cost. Through hardware and software, they are upscaling it to 16 million sub-pixels. So basically this TV can do 3840 x 2160 with 16 million sub-pixels instead of 24 million sub-pixels.For the cost difference, I can live with the difference in sub-pixels. The TV looks great, even though I am still tweaking the settings here and there. But I like to do that sort of thing. DVD TV shows look very good, much better than on a normal 1080p TV. The TV show Home Improvement, which has horrible DVDs, looks good now. Some scenes look almost HD in quality.1080p content looks even better than it already does of course. You will have to work at getting the settings for you and the location you have the TV in to make it look the best.Remember that if you set the settings during the daytime with all the curtains open with lots of light and expect it to look good when you are watching the TV in the dark, you have just made a mistake. Calibrate the TV during the time you would normally be watching the TV and don't expect it to be perfect at any other time. No TV can be perfect at all ambient light settings. It's all in what you can tolerate. It will always look very good in my opinion, but at times it will look amazing.I went to several Brick & Mortar stores and looked at the Ultra HD TVs vs 1080p TVs vs this TV. I could tell the difference, between each one easily enough. This TV is several steps above the 1080p TVs, and several steps below the Ultra HD TVs, but not so far as to warrant the cost difference between the Ultra HD and this TV. It is easily worth the difference between the cost of a 1080p TV and this TV, in my opinion.I calibrated my TV using the AVSHD 709 DVD, I used the the AVCHD download since I only have a DVD Bruner, the HDMV is for those with a Blu-ray burner and a Blu-ray disc to burn too. I ordered the THX glasses from THX.com for doing color correction as well. Before starting I set the TV to the factory defaults and then choose the Movie setting, but that is just me. Yes, this is a lot to do and it doesn't have to be done if you like any of the factory set modes. Just enjoy the TV.Again, I think everything I have said is correct, feel free to correct me on any part of it.A side note, if you get a used version of this TV and the plastic bezel is scratched, just use a good plastic polish to fix it. Be careful of the screen of course. Only do it on the shiny black bezel parts.

I have about 6 of these made of the original Corning pyroceramic and we use them all the time to reheat foods. However, these as shown are not the "real thing."The original "French White" Corningware was made of Corning's famous pyroceramic glass, which could be used on the gas stove, put directly in the freezer, put under the broiler right from the freezer, and oh yes, also used in a microwave. And it was very unlikely to shatter if dropped. If you pounded on it with a hammer and nail you might have gotten it to break.When World Kitchens bought the license from Corning, they decided to halt production of a line of cookware that would take anything and last forever, and dupe customers, especially brides, into thinking the stoneware "French White" was the same thing as the wonderful French White pyroceramic cookware previously available to their mothers and sisters.The pattern is very attractive and can be used with any decor, and they  do offer many sizes, but this stuff is not, repeat, really not, what people mean when they say "Corningware."Le Creuset can do most of the above mentioned, but it being metal you cannot use it in the microwave. Stoneware cannot go on top of the stove, and repeated trips from the freezer to the oven or microwave, which you are likely to do with these little dishes, will eventually cause it to craze and crack. And stoneware will also chip, and break if dropped, etc. Pyrex glassware cannot go on the gas stove although you can take it from the freezer to the oven, and also microwave it.The only product which could do anything was pyroceramic, and World Kitchens has chosen to remove it from the market because it is "too good."They have recently brought back a few of the old square shapes, with the Cornflower, or plain white, calling it "vintage," but the French White shape is not making an appearance yet. If you want it, email them and ask for it!Meanwhile, don't buy this stuff. Get Le Creuset for cooking and roasting (yes it is expensive but it lasts forever and cooks beautifully), and reheat things in Pyrex in the microwave.

8/25/2012 Update:  I'm going from 5 to 4 stars on this watch due to epic failure of preposterously stupid proportions.  During a triathlon, after the first mile of the run, WHEN I NEEDED IT MOST, it pops up a screen that says "Lap Database Full".  Instead of doing something intelligent, like deleting the oldest database entry and resuming operation, it just continues to beep and flash the message every few seconds -- for the remainder of the race.  I couldn't see my time or pace because the message never went away, it just flashed and beeped.  Apparently the engineers at Garmin all flunked their Digital Systems course and never learned what a FIFO is.  If you guys want to save some face, you better find someone in marketing to blame this on, because even a second-year summer intern is smarter than this.  The watch was completely unresponsive, the buttons and bezel did nothing.  Annoyed does not begin to describe how I felt, I wanted to rip it off my wrist and throw it in the lake.It turns out you have to manually delete the history from the device, because that's how I like to waste my time, doing something extremely simple that any intelligently designed device would do all by itself.  When I see mistakes like this it makes me wonder what other poor design issues await me in the future.  The watch does give you a warning that the lap database is almost full, when you complete a lap while exercising.  However, if you are biking at the time, as I often am, you will not hear the extra beep. It would be considerably more helpful if it would give the "lap database almost full" message when you set the watch into training mode, before you start your workout, instead of after the first mile (or lap) or your workout.  Actually I've thought of a dozen ways they could have designed this better with very little effort.You might wonder why I did not go to 1 star, and I probably would have it I hadn't waited to write this update.Also, after having used the watch more, the menu system can drive me batty at times and it can be extra frustrating if you are moving and trying to navigate.  My best advice is set is up and leave it alone while you run/bike/whatever.  You also need to make sure anything you wear doesn't touch the bezel.  For me, gloves are a problem (biking in the summer, XC-skiing in the winter).A number of reviewers mentioned this watch doesn't work for heavy sweaters.  I consider myself in that category, especially given our abnormally hot and humid summer, and I have not experienced the issues they have.The watch is highly configurable.  There are three configurable training views.  While I initially was using the mile pace for a speed indication while riding my bike, I found I could set up a new training view with MPH instead.  I also bought the cadence sensor for my bike, which is helpful for training and working on maintaining a higher cadence.  I set up the third training view for doing interval workouts.  You can also configure workouts in the watch and pick select them when you want to work out.------------I've had my Garmin 405 for about 3 weeks now and am generally very pleased with it.  I was on the fence about buying the 405 for about 6 months before I pulled the trigger.  The negative reviews were a small factor, the main reason was the lack of water resistance.  I run triathlons and not being able to wear the watch for the swim is a significant detriment for me.  I finally decided I could use it just for training and pulled the trigger.I originally bought the 405 for running.  I have a "computer" (abuse of the term) on my bike and wanted that functionality for my sneakers.  However, I've found it pretty useful on the bike as well.  While the bike computer gives distance, time, and average speed, the average speed is accumulative over the entire ride.  The 405 gives "lap" updates every mile so I can track my status on individual segments of the ride.  I leave the display on heart rate so I can keep tabs on my level of effort along the way and the 405 beeps every mile and briefly displays the time for that mile.  This may not sound as useful as the average speed, but it's perfect for me because previously I would often do the math in my head to convert mph to min/mile to give my brain something to do while riding, so I have a fair list of the times/mph memorized.If you are one who tends to run in the dark (early morning or evening), the light works well.  The screen is a little harder to read with the back light vs daylight, but that's typical of all watches/HRMs I've used.  This one is easier to read than both my Timex Ironman watch and Polar F6 HRM.If you like a little competition in your workouts but don't have an actual running mate, you can use the virtual running partner.  It keeps track of where you are relative to a predefined pace and has a funny little graphic showing your relative positions and time difference.  Cute feature but it is one more touch of the bezel for me flipping between heart rate and the pace/distance screen.  Maybe you can turn it off.The bezel is fairly easy to use, but does occasionally cause me fits.  You can lock and unlock the bezel by pressing and holding the two buttons on the side, which is nice.  I did try to use the watch in my last triathlon by strapping it to my bike, but I couldn't get it to start.  It would only cycle between the current time/date and the battery status, and locking and unlocking the bezel didn't change that.  So that was frustrating.  But again, I bought it knowing it wasn't ideal for tri's.  The issue could have been because I was wearing my Polar F6 also, I haven't tested them together and will have do that.  A race was the wrong place to experiment, but I didn't putz with it long either.So having your pace and distance during a run or bike is very cool, but the real coolness comes when you get home.  Connecting the ANT USB dongle (follow the directions for installing the drivers first) to your PC and letting it sync the data to the Garmin Connect website gives a complete visualization of your workout data.  This was a very well thought-out interface which I find very useful.  You get a map of the route from the GPS, charts with HR, speed, and altitude (if you have that enabled) and can actually "play" the workout which has little indicators progressing on the map and charts so you can see where your speed and HR varied (and altitude) relative to the route on the map.  There are also other "tabs" with tables of data which you can view and/or copy-paste to another program like MS Excel or OpenOffice Calc (free) if you feel the need to further manipulate your workout data.The battery life is not great.  I might get a week out of charge if I don't work out too much.  I recently went for a 4 hour bike ride with 65% battery at the start and it died before I got home.  The rechargable battery is a nice (and needed) feature and it doesn't seem to take too long to put a full charge on it.  Will have to start doing that before the longer rides.Finding satelites at the start of your workout can be a pain.  I get impatient, part of generation-ADD.  I may have to start putting the thing in training mode and leaving it on the driveway while I get my bike ready or stretch for running.  I once left on a bike ride shortly after turning it on and starting the timer and it missed over 1/2 mile of the ride.I still haven't cracked the manual on this thing, so I suspect there's more features and settings I have yet to discover.  Below is a list of my pros and cons as I see them today.  I will try to remember to update this after I get more familiar with the 405.Pros:-Readable display-Pace and distance seem fairly accurate.-Awesome workout data analysis on Garmin Connect website (free)-Good backlightCons:-Not water resistant for swimming-Battery life-Bezel takes some getting use to-Not the fastest finding satelites

Over the years my wife and I accumulated a mismatched pile of ice cube trays.  When we bought a "new" house with a late-model fridge, we ditched the trays in favor of the fridge's automatic ice maker.  It turns out that the ice maker took up a third of the freezer and had other issues.  The ice maker had to go.  So we found ourselves back in the tray market.  After some study on Amazon, we bought a pair of the Orka Ice Cube Trays.  Our findings:1. First and biggest finding: you will likely not be able to pop the cubes free using only the flexible silicone bottom membranes on the cube sections. You either must run the tray under warm water or simply do the old flex-the-tray routine you always did with plastic ice trays.  The silicone push panels make it easier but they usually won't do the job on their own.  I'm a 6 foot man with reasonable hand strength.  My 5 foot wife doesn't even try.  She hands the tray to me.2. The top cover is a useful feature.  It keeps you from popping the cubes and other bits of ice around the room when you're freeing the cubes from the tray.  You loosen the cubes, flip the works over, and you get an open tray full of easily grabbed ice cubes.3. The forms on the tray cover allow secure stacking of Orka trays.  In our crowded freezer this is a good thing.Conclusions: these are not bad ice trays and they have some nice features.  We'll use them.  Would we do it over again for $9.95 a copy?  Probably not, but I don't yet know of any that are better.

I have both the G7 and the G9. The 2 extra megapixels are unnoticeable. The reason I purchased this camera for my recent vacation was the ability to use RAW mode which works so well on my Nikon D200 (for which this is my backup camera). After using it for a month, it has near zero advantages over the highly functional G7.While it can capture a good image, the only way to convert the raw image to a jpg is to use their wimpy, me-too image editor, one at a time. Their batch convert gives the error message: "Unable to export movies, sound files or raw images". Additionally, I see another error message about "Information added by [various programs] will not be included in the exported images" which indicates to me that any titles, captions or key words you enter will be destroyed.I tried both the CD sold with the camera as well as the most recent upgrades of both the zoom browser and the eos utility on both my laptop as well as my desktop, each a standard XP machine with the latest patches. The errors follow the software, not the machine.The functionality of their software is abysmal. For instance, when browsing you can't use the left and right arrow buttons like most other, modern image viewers support; you must use their next button. The performance in rendering the image is roughly 20 times slower than Photoshop or Bibble when rendering a raw image. You see tiny, 1/2 inch chunks appear on the screen in a very tedious rendering process making me wonder whether they are using decade old, recycled, 16 bit code to save money for canon.After taking over 1200 images on vacation, mostly in raw mode, I have no way to extract them from the canon proprietary ".CR2" format other than spending days doing each one by hand with an extremely slow, klunky, proprietary program. At roughly a minute each, it would take 20 hours of hand editing to convert each by hand. Picasa shows the images, but the colors are horribly mangled. I can only select a few of the very best images to process by hand and wait for Bibble to support the G9 raw format in batch mode.canon technical support claims to provide "no hassles, no run-around, total satisfaction" while on hold. The support person person told me that I was free to use any third party conversion software but could not suggest one. She offered no diagnostic support whatsoever nor any comment on the error messages. Am I dealing with burger flippers turned technical supporters ;-o ?Canon, please get out of the software business in which you have negligible competence, stick to making camera hardware and hire a qualified third party like Bibble Labs to write functional image processing software for you.My recommendation is to avoid the G9 until the raw mode conversion works in batch mode with user input annotations.Update: after a half hour wait on technical support hold, it has just been confirmed that the export function is broken for raw (".CR2") files and that individual hand processing, one at a time, is required to export raw files to .jpg or .tif.Claiming to support both raw and .jpg images is one thing. Omitting a clear and conspicuous disclaimer warning that raw file batch processing is broken in their software would seem to be a gross oversight if not an unconscionable withholding of critical information from potential buyers.Very unhappy with the camera package. :-(

Dear Amazon Shopper,After attempting to purchase Viridian's C5L on two occasions, I had just about given up on purchasing anything more from Viridian (see my review of the C5L).  However, upon noticing that Viridian had released a second-gen version of it's X5L laser/light combo, I decided to give the company another shot.The X5L does not have the fatal cross-threading issues pervasive in its lighter C5L model.  It appears to be quite ruggedly contstructed and both the green laser and weapon light are very robust.  I currently have the X5L mounted on an FN 5.7x28mm (an extremely light handgun), to which it adds a good amount of weight.  The weight is by no means overbearing and is actually welcome as it feels like it helps keep groupings more consistent.  The light is a good weight for the features it provides.That having been said, there are three issues with this light, two of which have been mentioned by other reviewers.1. This light will by no means be a stealthy addition to your firearm.  The entire length of the laser is starkly visible in dark environments (environments in which its use is presumably contemplated, due to the addition of the light), so I recommend that you have a good sense of where your target is before flipping on the laser.  On the upsdie, if you are in a home-defense scenario and you know your opponent is unarmed, this laser could be quite intimidating.2. The point of aim DOES appear to shift as one other reviewer mentioned, though not to the extent said other reviewer experienced.  I keep my five-seven in a hard case with standard foam inserts.  I imagine that the pressure constantly exerted on the weapon light could be responsible for the shift in its point of aim, which I have found to be one to two inches at the range at which I have it zeroed (15 yards).  Note that this is far less than the 8+ inches experienced by the other reviewer.  It's possible that if you make foam cutouts in a pelican case, this issue can be averted entirely, though it seems that when properly mounted a laser this expensive ought not to shift at all, regardless of the foam your case employs.3. The last issue I have with this light is that it is manufactured by Viridian, which means you get Viridian QC and support.  My X5L arrived with NO RAILS WHATSOEVER.  Viridian basically shipped me a fancy laser-pointer with a built-in light that could be mounted to exactly nothing.  I called Viridian customer service but was unable to reach a rep.  Viridian did, however, respond to an e-mail I wrote within a couple of days and told me that my rails would be shipped immediately.  After not too long, I got the package from Viridian, but it contained only ONE set of rails.  I had said that I intended to mount the X5L on a 5.7 and the rails were the right ones for that purpose, but I paid for a product that should have afforded me options as to what weapon I wanted to mount it on.  Rather than go through the hassle of contacting Viridian again, I mounted the light and wrote off the other rails sets as a cost of doing business with Viridian.Bottom line - If you're in the market for a green laser this is as right as Viridian has managed to get a product, provided you can deal with a couple of minor foibles and Viridian customer service.

After a normal system shutdown & cold boot, I have an issue with the version F12 BIOS reporting "The system has experienced boot failures because of overclocking or changes of voltages" and reducing the memory speed.  This is becoming a bit annoying, so I am lowering my rating.  Note that I am NOT overclocking, which is what makes this so aggravating.  This issue seems to be resolved by the UEFI BIOS version U1, mentioned below.Except for the cold boot issue, motherboard is working fine so far with an Ivy Bridge Core i7-3770 processorIntel Core i7 3770 Processor 3.4 GHz 4 Core LGA 1155 - BX80637I73770that is **not** overclocked and withCorsair Vengeance 8 GB ( 2 x 4 GB ) DDR3 1600 MHz (PC3 12800) 240-Pin DDR3 Memory Kit for Intel Core i3, i5, i7 and AMD Platforms SDRAM CMZ8GX3M2A1600C9.This model motherboard currently ships with non-EFI BIOS (version F12) and UEFI BIOS (version U1) is available for download from GIGAbyte's website.  The UEFI BIOS version has fewer configuration settings available, and also renumbers all PCI device positions versus the non-EFI version so all Windows device drivers will need to be reinstalled after upgrading.  Once you upgrade to the UEFI version, there seems to be no way to downgrade to the non-EFI version.  The UEFI BIOS version U1 may default to VT-d enabled which caused linux OS crashes and device driver failures; I had to disable VT-d to get the system to work.I like the embedded Firewire support (I use it for ripping video from a camcorder), the embedded serial port (NOTE it does not come with a DB9 cable or bracket), and optical Digital Audio output.  This motherboard has plenty of USB connectors on the inside, but not enough on the back IMO (only 6) due to the video connectors for the Intel embedded video.  That said, I'm glad to have 4 different types of embedded video connectors on the rear panel, and I can always add front-panel USB connectors or use a USB hub for additional USB ports.I would have preferred the 6 sideways SATA connectors to be facing upwards instead of to the side (which makes the connectors difficult to attach & remove), but I guess the purpose is so the SATA cables don't interfere with any long PCIe option cards that one might install, and I shouldn't have to attach & remove the connectors very often anyway.  The 7th SATA connector is facing upwards.

This four port USB wall charger works, but its bulk and low output when using all four ports just doesn't compare to another four-port outlet that I own. Although this wall charger is designed for travel, you have to manually attach the prongs or leave them attached, which in either case doesn't make for a compact package. I'd much rather have the prongs fold into the body. And if I'm going to have four ports, I'd like to be able to charge four devices at full speed. Other wall chargers that I own have at least one 2.1 amp port for charging an iPad, and this remains constant, no matter how many other devices are attached. Not so with the Etronic Quad Port.I tested this with four devices -- iPad, iPhone, iPod, and Kindle -- all of which had 50% or less battery charge remaining. To mimic what I would do in a hotel room, I plugged them in using the Etronic Quad port before going to bed and unplugged them first thing in the morning. All four had full charges by morning. The sticking point, however, was the iPad, which displayed "not charging" after a few minutes of being plugged in. Still, it continued to charge. This also happens when I plug the IPad into certain USB hub ports because there isn't enough power running through them. It charges, but at a very slow rate. Using the Etronics with the iPad and other devices at the same time was the equivalent of using a low-powered USB port on my computer.This wall charger is okay if you won't include a tablet in your four devices or if you'll always use it overnight. In fact, it's quite convenient to be able to charge four devices from one power source. Note: I received a sample for review-- Debbie Lee Wesselmann

These drives are good for backup and long term storage. I have a number of them in place for that purpose. They are not appropriate for primary computer hard drive or for use in a NAS device. While the drive is active it automatically parks it's heads every 8 seconds by default. In a NAS the drives are accessed frequently. Over a year's time the drive will park itself over 300K times. At that point experts say the drive is in jeopardy but many have drives still working that have even twice that many. You are better off with a Black or Blue labeled WD drive for primary hard drive.

I got it installed: A novice would have sent it back. (At least one already did :O)Here are some tips for you other persistent Geeks: The on board video card MUST be disabled before the new card is physically installed. Otherwise you will have no video at all when the computer starts. And it matters not which card you have your monitor hooked to. They will both be dead. I disabled the on board Dell card with the computer running and plugged the new card in hot. (Make sure you are grounded.) If you try to install the drivers from the included driver CD, you get a "Acess Denied" message. I installed the Windows 7 64 bit drivers I downloaded from EVGA's website. Hooked the monitor cable up to the new card and restarted the computer. Although there is a marked improvement in the desktop - especially text, my "Windows Experience Index" dropped from 4.1 to 3.5. The card is the guilty party as was the previous one. Everything else is 5 to 7's. Don't know why. All settings are spot on. This was installed to replace a dying on board NVIDIA 3200 video card for my everyday desktop. Works fine for that purpose. Gaming or video editing I would look elsewhere.

If you want it to stay hot, rinse it out with hot tap water then let it stand full of hot tap water until you are ready to fill it with coffee or whatever. Then dump out the tap water and fill it with your drink or soup etc. It will stay hot as claimed. That is our experience with them.The same applies to cold. Fill it with cold water and put it in the fridge awhile. How we do it in summer is to clean it and fill with cold water the night before and put in the fridge, then the next morning dump our the water and fill with whatever you want to keep cold. If it's water... then fill it with your filtered water and put it in the fridge then use the next day.If you refuse to preheat or precool it will till keep your food hot or cold but probably not for as long. The laws of physics are what they are. :-)I recommend these completely. Have not found better by anyone else.

After going through numerous auxiliary-jack cables I decided to start shopping around for a permanent replacement and more elegant solution for listening to music in my vehicle. The Miccus Mini-jack RX seemed perfect for the job. My phone supports A2DP and my vehicle has the requisite aux-jack.The Miccus is the second such device I've ordered. The other device I ordered and then returned - the WCI Quality Bluetooth Audio Streaming Receiver was also plagued with battery issues and was returned.The Miccus would be a perfect little device if not for the battery life and the charging option included from the manufacturer. Simply put I didn't get anywhere near the advertised 7-hour battery life on playback. In fact after noticing the short battery life I made it a point to keep track of exactly how much playback I got on a full charge and I came in at around 2hrs 40min. I mainly used the Miccus on my drive to and from work - about a 20-minute one-way commute. I was always sure to power off the device after reaching my destination.The other issue with this device is that the manufacturer only included a USB charging solution that requires using a computer to charge the device. This is a poor, slow and inefficient way to charge the device. Sure this can be remedied by purchasing a USB car charger or other charging device but adds additional costs.Beyond that I actually really enjoyed using the product. The interface is simple - hold the power button down until the unit flashes a blue LED and you're ready to start streaming music from your device. Pairing is a simple affair for anyone who's ever paired a BT device before. Audio quality was fantastic and I didn't notice much interference or dropped signals at all. Still, the short battery life ruins the product for me.

Egad!  What a nightmare.  I'm tech savvy but I fought with this for most of a day before I got it working.  I originally intended to use this as a wireless repeater, but I never got that working right despite all the extra setting requirements outlined in other reviews here that the manufacturer does not mention, even in their latest guide.  When I set the ZyXEL's SSID and security settings to the same as my D-Link DIR-825 main router, all hell broke loose, even though it showed it was finally associated properly, etc.  Most of my wireless devices dropped off the network and no longer could get IP addresses assigned even after I disabled the ZyXEL and performed repeated main router and device reboots.  Eventually I did a main router reset to defaults, reinstalled my settings and recovered the network.  That was fun.  I gave up any hope of getting the range extender mode to work.  So, I thought it would be nice to eliminate a couple of Linksys bridges I was using even though they were working well with my Samsung Blu-ray and TV.  The Linksys bridges are "g" protocol and do take some time to join the network when the TV and Blu-Ray are powered on.  The main problem I had with getting the ZyXEL to work in bridge mode, despite all the good direction here, is that the network tests inside the TV and Blu-ray failed, saying they could not connect to the gateway.  I fiddled with IP/gateway/DNS settings for hours before I discovered that the bridge mode was in fact working after all.  I'm not sure why the test failure occurred when the Linksys bridges passed.  Along the way I did change the IP address of the ZyXEL in its LAN settings to a fixed IP just above the DHCP range of my main router and set the gateway to the IP of main router.  I don't know if that matters at all, but I saw that mentioned in another review.  All I know is that it is working as a bridge and is noticeably faster to connect and transfer media than the Linksys "g" bridges it replaced.  So, all's well that ends well, but I probably should take off more than 2 stars for the extreme aggravation.  Merry Christmas.

I bought an old bike and wanted to replace all the hardware. I'm not a bike mechanic, but how hard could it be? So I bought one of these derailleurs. The derailleur itself is great. However, apparently Shimano expects that you already know how to install the product, because it included no instructions. That's right! It wasn't a mistake either, because I ordered a Shimano rear derailleur and shifters which were the same way. The documentation that was included states "this information is for adjusting the Shimano parts that came on your bicycle."In other words, Shimano expects you to have these parts installed by a professional, or they expect you to just know how to install them based on your past training as a bike shop repair guy. No doubt if I called Shimano asking how to install it, they would tell me to take it to a bike shop, or buy a book on bicycle repair. Apparently they feel no obligation to help by producing a small piece of paper with a couple of diagrams on it for the hundreds of thousands of units they will sell.Ultimately the installation was not rocket science. I got it done, but with very little thanks to Shimano. Installation is not easy enough that instructions are not required, but not hard enough that they have any excuse for not including them. Additionally, the small paper that details adjustments had printing at about microfiche-size, and was almost unintelligible. Again, this is not rocket science. I would appreciate it if Shimano invested a few dollars in improving this aspect of the product.So I'd give this part 5-stars for engineering, design, and build quality. One star for attempting to make the product easy to install. Results in a three-star rating.

I currently own Sony Cyber-shot DSC-HX200V which I LOVE and take on all of my travels. But the price difference between my Sony and this Fujifilm is about $150 which makes the Fujifilm more affordable for people looking for an all in one camera.Pros:*Very easy to navigate on screen- able to change how you take pictures and speeds*Gives you almost all the functions of SLR in one complete camera without having to worry about changing lenses.*Has very quick focus and super fast shutter speeds. I shot some pics of the boys playing basketball and this camera is great at capturing them mid-air or at other times when they are running back and forth. A common problem with Non-DSLR cameras is that they can't capture objects moving fast enough or they do but them come in really blurry. With my Sony, I am able to capture people in mid-air but when they are running back and forth it can become a challenge to get a clear picture. I say with my Sony 1 in 4 will be perfectly clear but with this Fujifilm 3 in 4 come in clear.*Super zoom function with clear focus- My Sony can only do 30x zoom while this Fujifilm can do 50x!*Easy to grab photos from camera to import into your computerCons:*For a non-DSLR this camera is a bit heavy and bulky. When I compare the weight and size with my Sony this camera is both bigger and heavier. For a person looking for a camera without having to change lenses the weight and size shouldn't be an issue. But for others who are looking for a slimmer non-DSLR camera that they can throw into a backpack and not worry about extra weight, this camera is not the right one for you.*Doesn't have high quality low light/night shot ability. My main factor in purchasing my Sony was how frustrating my old point and shoot would take museum pics and night shots. Even though this Fujifilm says it works well for low light/night shots I am personally not impressed by it. If one of your main buying reasons for this camera is low light shots (such as museums,concerts, and late night parties)I have to tell you to look somewhere else. The pictures still come in very dark and blurry if your object is in motion. Now if I where to take the same pics with my Sony... as my hubby says "Hey look your camera just made these night pics into day pics!"Overall for the price and what this camera can do I think it's a great value(unless you wanted a camera for low light and night shots) and has everything all in one camera. The zoom function is amazing and even though my Sony can go up to 30x.. with 50x the zoom I can just imagine all the shots I could have taken of Our Lady Liberty while I was on the Staten Island Ferry. And trust me my Sony got some AMAZING shots of her! So instead of buying a true DSLR that can cost you over $1,000 and you will have to carry multiple lenses, I suggest paying 1/4 the cost and investing in this Fujifilm. If you love this camera abilities and just wished it could provide good quality low light and night shots, I have to suggest Sony Cyber-shot DSC-HX200V.

I bought this to backup very large avi files that I create during video capturing and editing.  The only thing worse than having to capture and store all this video would be to have to do it again!Anyway, I've got a Dell XPS 420 running Vista Home Premium, and with that eSATA port that I paid for and was determined to use, so after almost tearing out my already thinning hair I decided to go for this one.  One bonus is that the styling matches my new Dell perfectly.  They look like they belong together.So, I plug it all in and my computer immediately recognizes it, just like the start-up guide says.  But this thing comes formatted in FAT format, so the main selling point -- backing up those huge video files -- cannot happen until the drive is reformatted as an NTSC drive.  This is easy enough to do with Vista; it just took an extra couple hours or so up front.So, now I've got it reformatted and I copied a folder with about 160 gigs of avi files and it took a bit over a half an hour.  It seemed to do about 60Mb a second (I never thought that I was ever going to get 1.5 Gig a second).  That's reality, and it's still by far the fastest external hard drive I've got.The one bummer is that my Vista machine will not recognize it when I click on "Safely Remove Hardware".  So, I can't dismount it and switch it off.  I'll have to power it up or down when the computer is off, and that's an inconvenience.  Perhaps that's due to the eSATA connection.Finally, this thing runs hot.  I've got it mounted vertically to maximize surface exposure and it really heated up while formatting and copying those files.  I've ordered a mini desk fan that I'm going to run to circulate air between my computers and external hard drives.So, as far a longevity goes, that remains to be seen, but if this thing dies before a year is up I'll be updating this review for sure.Oh yeah, the bid blue bar light (blue when it's ready, red when it's not) is not cool.  It's annoying.  How many bright lights do I need in my face in my peripheral vision when I'me using my computer?  A little "dot light" would have done the same thing.  I'll probably end up covering most of it with electrical tape.Postscript:  I just purchased a second external hard drive.  It turns out that one need not buy an "all in one" unit like this, but you can also get "package deals" where you get a hard drive enclosure with the eSATA plug, and then you can choose your own hard drive for the enclosure.  I've got an eSATA enclosure with a Seagate Barracuda drive with a three year warranty inside it.  That's cool!After all, with this unit, you don't know what exatly you got for a hard drive in there.  So, go for the hard drive you know, and find an eSATA enabled enclosure for it.
